UK food supply chain affected by cyber-attack which hit supermarkets and food suppliers across Europe on Monday. UK's cyber chief says it's still "too early to say" who was behind the hacks

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6n8.title: Apple unsure when it will get more foldable iPhones ahead of Christmas
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6n8.text:
Apple has said it does not know when it will get more of its new foldable iPhones back in stock as the company heads towards the key Christmas trading period.

The iPhone Duo sold out just over a week after its launch, despite being Apple's most expensive smartphone at a cost of nearly $2,000.

The company warned of "constraints" in sourcing key components and admitted it was "really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance".

Meanwhile, Apple's new chief executive John Ternus said the firm was seeing an "unprecedented" price rise in memory costs, including chips, as the artificial intelligence (AI) industry continues to invest billions of dollars in building data centres.

Ternus launched the Duo after he took over from previous boss Tim Cook in September.

It is the smartphone's first major design change in almost 20 years but some buyers have reported problems with the Duo's screen.

Last week, the company said it would replace any handsets that were affected by an issue that caused a "small number" to crack along the inside fold.

As it released its latest financial figures on Monday, Apple's executives did not mention any problems with the iPhone Duo.

Ternus said he was "thrilled" by the early reaction to the foldable phone. Chief operating officer Sabih Khan said the company was working hard to get the Duo "into the hands of our customers as quickly as possible".

Apple's results for the three months to 26 September did not include sales of the Duo, which was released at the end of October.

Nevertheless, Apple said it had sold more iPhones globally over the last year than ever before.

iPhone revenue for the quarter rose 17% to $57bn (£42bn).

Sales of Mac computers also grew over the three months by 27% to a record $10.7bn.

Overall, Apple's sales between July and September rose from $102bn to $114bn. Pre-tax profit also increased, from $32.8bn to $36.1bn.

However, sales for both the iPad and Apple's wearable products, including its headphones and watch, fell by 10% and 7%, respectively.

Khan said that most Apple devices were still experiencing supply constraints driven in part by difficulty in getting enough microprocessors with advanced nodes.

Those components are essentially computer chip technology that allow Apple devices to operate more quickly, most of which it has manufactured through TSMC, which is based in Taiwan.

Khan said the problem was expected to continue into next year, particularly impacting iPads and Macs.

The situation has been made worse by what the company has repeatedly insisted is "unexpected demand" for its products.

Ternus noted, too, that Apple is still seeing "unprecedented" cost increases for memory, or the ability of devices to store data like apps, photos and text messages.

Much memory storage runs through data centres, which have experienced a boom in demand for space as AI chatbots and platforms - including those developed by the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic - have become popular.

Storage prices have gone up for tech companies like Apple.

Earlier this year, Cook referred to a sudden increase in data centre costs as a "thousand year flood".

Apple has lifted prices on nearly all of its hardware products by around 20%.

Sunil Krishnan from Aviva Investors told the BBC's Today programme that Apple posted "a reasonably solid set of results" with a "pretty good performance" from its iPhone business.

While there were concerns over the company's guidance on profit margins and the cost of memory chips, Krishnan added that in the broader context, "margins well north of 45% for a very well-established company, I think, are pretty impressive".

However, Apple's share price fell by 1.8% in after-hours trading.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6re.title: North Korea denies being behind record $6.3bn Binance hack
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6re.text:
North Korea has denied claims that it was behind the record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance, calling the allegations "absurd rhetoric".

Kim Yo Jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said on Tuesday that the accusations are another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage Pyongyang's public image.

The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Secret Service and cyber analysts have said North Korea orchestrated the hack, which has been described as the largest in history.

This is the latest hack to be linked to North Korea, which has been accused of relying on cyber-crime to help finance its sanctioned economy.

Blockchain analysts and the FBI have said the attack was led by state-backed hacking group TraderTraitor.

The FBI has called on industry partners to help block transactions involving cryptocurrency accounts linked to the group.

"The US has made a trite provocation of linking it with the Democratic People's Republic of Korea again," Kim Yo-jong, the director of North Korea's General Affairs Department, said in a statement.

"It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads the international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds," she said.

But Pyongyang has been blamed for a number of major cyber attacks in recent years - accusations that it has denied.

The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.

Pyongyang has systematically built its cyber operations, recruiting promising students from universities and sending them to hacker units overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, research groups like the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies think tank have said.

The country has consistently denied such claims.

Kim Yo Jong said "it is the consistent policy stand of the DPRK government to resolutely oppose all sorts of malicious acts in cyberspace".

Binance did not respond to the BBC's queries about North Korea's alleged involvement in the hack.

Since the incident, the crypto giant has largely focused its public statements on the technical nature of the breach and its response to protect users.

The company's spokesperson said that a net $4.72bn has been withdrawn from the exchange since transactions resumed on Sunday.

The net outflow represents a "relatively limited portion" of Binance's total assets, which stand at approximately $157bn, the spokesperson told the BBC on Tuesday.

That figure reflects the impact of the hack, subsequent withdrawals and market price changes.

"Withdrawal levels are stabilising to what we would consider normal and expected on-chain activity," she added.

The company said last week that initial checks indicated that an engineer's laptop had been compromised, enabling an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals.

Trading in major cryptocurrencies on Binance has since resumed after the exchange worked with issuers to freeze assets impacted by the hack.

The company has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack and that it has so far covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/weather/articles/c.title: One of the year's most prolific meteor showers to light up the night sky this weekend
https://www.bbc.co.uk/weather/articles/c.text:
The Leonid meteor shower is set to dazzle sky gazers across the UK throughout November.

The celestial spectacle takes place from now until 30 November with the peak taking place on the night of 17 November.

There could be the chance to spot up to 10-15 meteors per hour.

The shower is made up of dust particles from the Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which leaves a trail of debris as it follows its path around the Sun.

These particles enter the Earth's atmosphere at up to 44 miles (71km) per second - meaning these streaks of light are the fastest meteors in the sky.

Experts advise finding a safe, dark location away from sources of light pollution such as street lights.

The meteors will be visible with the naked eye, with no binoculars or telescope required.

However, giving your eyes some time to adapt to the dark - perhaps 20 or 30 minutes - will give you the best chance of spotting them.

A wide open space is the best place to be, giving a full view of the night sky.

Meteors could be visible anywhere but the Leonids' radiant - the point from which they seem to appear - will, as the name suggests, be around the head of the constellation Leo, meaning this is the best part of the sky to focus your gaze.

As with all celestial spectacles, clear skies will be a must.

This weekend's forecast will not necessarily be great news for those hoping to catch the start of the shower.

While the weather will often be dry, large amounts of cloud are expected to fill the sky in many areas with the chance of a few spots of rain or drizzle.

At the moment the best opportunities for clear skies appear to be in southern and western areas of England and Wales on Friday and Saturday nights, with more cloud in northern England, Northern Ireland and Scotland.

By Sunday night it is likely that more parts of the UK will be clear.

However, fog could be an additional issue, forming in any areas where skies remain clear for any length of time, obscuring the view.

Overnight temperatures will drop into single figures with the chance of a touch of frost in a few locations so if you are looking at the night sky for any length of time you will want to wrap up warmly.

You can always check the hour-by-hour cloud, fog and temperature forecast for your area by checking BBC Weather online or the app.

And if you miss them this weekend then take heart that viewing conditions look particularly good around their peak in the middle of November. This is because the Moon will be below the horizon around midnight, meaning its reflected light will be less likely to spoil the view.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy4d.title: How climate change worsens heatwaves, droughts, wildfires and floods
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy4d.text:
Many extreme weather events are becoming more common and more intense around the world, fuelled by human activities such as the burning of fossil fuels.

Here are four ways that rising temperatures are affecting weather extremes.

Even a small increase in average temperatures makes a big difference to heat extremes.

As the range of daily temperatures shifts to warmer levels, hotter days become more likely and more intense.

Scientists use computer models to simulate how individual extreme weather events unfold in two scenarios:

That way, they can estimate how much a particular heatwave, storm or drought was affected by climate change.

The UK experienced its hottest summer on record in 2026, which the Met Office said was made 130 times more likely by climate change.

Five widespread heatwaves affected the country, resulting in 40 days of temperatures above 30C (86F).

Head of Climate Attribution at the Met Office, Dr Mark McCarthy, described summer 2026 as "remarkable" and warned that extreme heat events would only become more common as the world warms.

Climate change has also intensified multiple heatwaves across the world this year, according to scientists at the World Weather Attribution group (WWA).

Examples include Australia's worst heatwave in six years in January, the 45C that India experienced in April and Europe's deadly June temperatures.

Heatwaves can happen as a result of heat domes, which are created when an area of high pressure stays over the same area for days or weeks, trapping hot air underneath.

Higher temperatures in the Arctic - which has warmed nearly four times faster than the global average - may be affecting the fast band of winds high in the atmosphere known as the jet stream.

One theory suggests that this is making heat domes more likely, although this is not clear cut.

For every 1C rise in air temperature, the atmosphere can hold about 7% more moisture.

With more moisture available, rainfall can become heavier.

UK winters were 13% wetter in the decade from 2016 to 2025 than between 1961 and 1990, the Met Office says.

However, the large annual variation in rainfall makes it difficult to draw conclusions from a single decade, its scientists warn.

Globally, heavy rainfall events have become more frequent and intense over most land regions due to human activity, according to the UN's climate body, the IPCC.

For example, in October 2025, Hurricane Melissa became one of the strongest hurricanes to ever hit the Caribbean.

WWA researchers found that climate change increased extreme rainfall associated with the storm by 16%.

Linking climate change with specific droughts can be difficult because there are lots of different factors that affect the availability of water.

Natural weather systems like El Niño can play a key role, as was the case with drought in southern Africa in early 2024.

But climate change is shifting global rainfall patterns. While some of the world is getting wetter, other parts are becoming drier, which can make them more prone to drought.

And heatwaves fuelled by climate change can worsen dry conditions when they do occur by increasing evaporation from the soil.

This makes the air above warm up more quickly, leading to more intense heat.

During periods of hot weather, increased demand for water, especially from farmers, puts even more stress on the water supply.

Climate-driven heatwaves worsened drought conditions throughout Europe this summer, according to the EU's Joint Research Centre.

Four of Europe's key rivers - the Loire, Po, Rhine and Danube - reached record low levels.

Drought was declared in all of Wales and two-thirds of England, with the highest category - "severe drought" - being used for the first time in parts of southern England.

Elsewhere, the WWA found that climate change intensified a severe drought in Jamaica and Puerto Rico from May 2026.

Global warming made extreme dry conditions 40% more likely in Jamaica and 30% more likely in Puerto Rico, the WWA said.

Fires happen naturally in many parts of the world.

It is difficult to know if climate change has caused or worsened a specific wildfire because other factors are also relevant, such as changes to the way land is used.

But climate change is making the weather conditions needed for wildfires to spread more likely, the IPCC says.

Extreme, long-lasting heat draws more moisture out of soils and vegetation.

These tinder-dry conditions provide fuel for fires, which can spread at incredible speeds, particularly if winds are strong.

In January 2026, fires in Chile and Argentina resulted in 55,000 evacuations. The area burned was around 36% larger due to climate change, according to a global report on wildfires.

More than 5,000 wildfires burned across Canada this summer, resulting in some of the worst air quality levels in the world being recorded in nearby cities.

Climate change made the conditions which enabled the fires to spread twice as likely, according to the WWA.

Many fires are started deliberately or accidentally by humans. But rising temperatures may also increase the likelihood of lightning in some forests, which can in turn trigger more fires.

The combined effects of shifting land use and climate change mean extreme wildfires are projected to become more frequent and intense globally, according to the UN Environment Programme (UNEP).

The number of the most extreme fires may rise by up to 50% by 2100, UNEP suggests.

2026 was the UK's second worst year for wildfires after 2022, according to provisional data from the housing department.

In Stourbridge, two fires destroyed 19 homes on the hottest day of the year.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9w1.title: A really simple guide to climate change
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9w1.text:
Human activities are causing world temperatures to rise, posing serious threats to people and nature.

Things are likely to worsen in the coming decades, but scientists argue urgent action can still limit the worst effects of climate change.

Climate change is the long-term shift in the Earth's average temperatures and weather conditions.

The world has been rapidly warming for around a century, causing weather patterns to change.

Since the 1980s, each decade has been warmer than the previous one, the Met Office says.

2024 was Earth's hottest year on record, with climate change mainly responsible for the high temperatures.

It was also the first calendar year to surpass 1.5C of warming compared to "pre-industrial" levels of the late 1800s, according to the Copernicus climate service.

Temperatures remained high in 2025, despite a slight cooling from a natural weather pattern called La Niña.

The opposite El Niño pattern, combined with climate change, makes it likely that 2026 will also rank among the hottest years ever recorded.

The climate has changed naturally throughout the Earth's history.

But natural causes cannot explain the particularly rapid warming seen over the last century, according to the UN's climate body, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).

This has been without doubt caused by human activities, especially the widespread use of fossil fuels - coal, oil and gas - in homes, factories and transport systems.

When fossil fuels burn, they release greenhouse gases - mostly carbon dioxide (CO2). This CO2 acts like a blanket, trapping extra energy in the atmosphere near the Earth's surface. This causes the planet to heat up.

Since the start of the Industrial Revolution - when humans began burning large amounts of fossil fuels - the level of CO2 in the atmosphere has risen by more than 50%.

The CO2 released from burning fossil fuels has a distinctive chemical fingerprint. This matches the type of CO2 increasingly found in the atmosphere.

Climate change has already had a huge effect, including:

These changes are already having serious consequences for people and economies around the world.

Flash floods in Nepal killed more than 1,400 people in August 2026. Nepal's Finance Minister, Swarnim Wagle, said it could cost up to a tenth of the economy to rebuild.

Climate change increased the chances of the glacier collapse which triggered the flood, World Weather Attribution group scientists said.

The more the world warms, the worse the impacts of climate change become.

Nearly 200 countries pledged to try to limit global warming to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels in the 2015 Paris agreement.

That target is generally understood to mean an average annual increase of 1.5C over 20 years rather than a one-off rise in a single year.

Long-term warming of 1.5C would bring serious consequences for many populations.

But an increase of 2C or more would bring even greater impacts, the IPCC says.

The call to restrict temperature rise to 1.5C was partly designed to avoid crossing so-called "tipping points".

It is not clear exactly where they sit, but once these thresholds are passed, changes could accelerate and become irreversible.

These could include the collapse of the Greenland Ice Sheet, warm Atlantic Ocean currents or further loss of the Amazon rainforest.

About 3.3 to 3.6 billion people are highly vulnerable to climate change, the IPCC says.

People living in poorer countries are expected to suffer most as they have fewer resources to adapt.

This has led to questions about fairness, because these places have typically only been responsible for a small percentage of greenhouse gas emissions.

However, knock-on impacts could be felt over wide areas. For example, crop failures linked to extreme weather could raise food prices globally.

Reaching net zero CO2 emissions is essential to limit global warming, the IPCC says.

This means reducing emissions as much as possible and actively removing any remaining emissions from the atmosphere.

Most countries have, or are considering, net zero targets.

There has been encouraging progress in some areas, such as renewable energy and electric vehicles.

But humanity's CO2 emissions are still at record highs, causing long-term warming to reach 1.4C in 2025.

The latest UN Emissions Gap Report said the 1.5C limit was likely to be breached in the coming years.

A return to 1.5C by 2100 was possible, but it would require "urgent and stringent cuts to greenhouse emissions", the report added.

Otherwise, global warming could reach nearly 3C by the end of the century, the UN said.

World leaders meet every year to discuss their climate commitments.

In 2025, the COP30 climate conference ended without any new agreements on fossil fuels or deforestation in the final deal.

Countries had previously agreed on the need to "transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems" at the COP28 talks in 2023.

At COP29 in 2024, richer countries committed to giving developing nations at least $300bn (£223bn) a year by 2035 to help them tackle climate change. But this is far less than poorer countries say they need.

Governments are gathering in Turkey for the next round of talks, COP31, in November 2026.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c93d.title: What is the Paris Agreement and why does 1.5C matter?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c93d.text:
In Paris in 2015, almost 200 countries signed a landmark agreement designed to limit global warming to 1.5C and avoid its worst impacts.

But despite some progress in areas like renewable energy, the world has continued to warm at a rapid pace.

A recent UN report said the target was likely to be breached in the next few years and that "urgent and stringent" action would be needed to return the world to 1.5C.

The Paris Agreement is at the heart of the international commitment to tackle rising global temperatures.

It came into force on 4 November 2016 and saw almost all the nations of the world agree to cut the greenhouse gas emissions which cause global warming.

However, the United States - the world's second biggest greenhouse gas emitter - withdrew from the deal in January 2026 under President Donald Trump.

The US also withdrew during Trump's first presidency, but it rejoined in 2021 under his successor President Joe Biden.

The only other UN member states outside the Paris agreement are Iran, Libya and Yemen.

The Paris Agreement lists a series of commitments:

The 1.5C target is generally accepted to refer to a 20-year average rather than a single year.

So, while 2024 was more than 1.5C warmer than pre-industrial times, it did not mean the Paris Agreement threshold has been breached

Every 0.1C of warming brings with it greater risks for the planet, such as longer heatwaves, more intense storms and wildfires, according to climate scientists.

But a very large body of scientific evidence shows that warming of 2C or more would bring far greater impacts, on top of those felt at 1.5C, UN scientists say.

Some changes could become irreversible if so-called "tipping points" are crossed.

It is not clear exactly where these sit, but once these thresholds are passed, changes could accelerate and become irreversible.

These could include the collapse of the Greenland Ice Sheet, warm Atlantic Ocean currents or further loss of the Amazon rainforest.

The Paris deal restated a 2009 commitment that richer countries should provide $100bn (£73bn) annually by 2020 to help developing nations deal with the effects of climate change and build greener economies.

Although only $83.3bn was raised in 2020, data from the OECD shows the goal was reached in each of the three years after 2022.

Almost two-thirds of the money in recent years has gone towards efforts to limit global warming, while around a quarter has been used to help nations adapt to climate change.

In 2023, countries agreed for the first time that a fund should be established exclusively for loss and damage. This is money to help countries recover from the impacts of climate change.

Nepal became the first country approved to receive money from the fund after a flash flood in August 2026 killed more than 1,400 people.

At COP29 in 2024, richer nations committed to providing $300bn (£219bn) a year to developing nations by 2035. Developing countries - which had hoped for more - criticised the "paltry sum".

World leaders meet every year to discuss their climate commitments at international summits known as COPs (Conference of the Parties).

All COPs since 2015 have tracked how countries are building on what they promised in Paris.

At COP28 in 2023, countries agreed for the first time to "contribute" to "transitioning away from fossil fuels", although they were not forced to take any specific action.

Countries also agreed to treble the global capacity of renewables - such as wind and solar - by 2030.

But the final deal at COP30 in 2025 failed to directly mention fossil fuels. Instead, the host of the conference, Brazil, published a voluntary roadmap for moving away from fossil fuels, which will be discussed at COP31.

That COP is taking place from 9 to 20 November 2026 in Antalya, Turkey and is co-hosted by Australia.

A "coalition of the willing" composed of 57 countries has also organised its own conferences separate from the COP process to discuss phasing out fossil fuels.

The first meeting was held in Santa Marta, Colombia in April 2026, and another conference is scheduled for July 2027 in Tuvalu.

The long-term 1.5C global warming target has not yet been breached.

But the latest UN Emissions Gap Report said the limit was likely to be exceeded in the next few years after "decades of insufficient climate action".

In the "lowest possible" scenario, warming would still reach 1.7 to 1.8C by the mid-century, the report said.

A return to 1.5C by 2100 is possible, but it will require "urgent and stringent cuts to greenhouse emissions", the UN added.

Specifically, emissions would need to be cut by 18% between 2025 and 2030.

The report found that the pledges governments have made so far would only cover half of these cuts.

Without further action, global warming could reach nearly 3C by the end of the century, the research said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx23.title: What is net zero and is the UK on track to achieve it?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx23.text:
Achieving "net zero" is the world's key strategy to fight climate change, which is already having serious consequences for people and nature around the globe.

But the political consensus around the UK's net zero policies has collapsed, with the Conservative and Reform parties now branding them too difficult and expensive.

Net zero means balancing the amount of planet-warming "greenhouse" gases produced by human activities with the amount being actively removed from the atmosphere.

Effectively this means no longer adding to the total amount of these gases in the atmosphere to limit climate change.

Greenhouse gases include carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane. Their levels in the atmosphere are increasing rapidly due to human activities, including burning fossil fuels, chopping down forests and farming.

In practice, reducing these emissions means switching from coal, oil and gas to cleaner energy sources like wind and solar power.

It also involves adopting green technologies like electric vehicles and heat pumps to replace petrol or diesel cars and gas boilers.

But not all emissions can be eliminated.

So remaining emissions must be matched by things like planting trees, restoring peatlands or using machines to remove CO2 from the air.

But there are limits to these "carbon removal" techniques in scale and cost. That is why most of the focus is on drastically reducing emissions in the first place.

The world is warming because of humanity's greenhouse gas emissions, which increase global temperatures by trapping extra energy in the atmosphere near the Earth's surface.

This is bringing more heatwaves and extreme weather as well as melting ice sheets and raising sea levels.

In 2026, the UK experienced its hottest summer on record, which the Met Office said was made 130 times more likely by climate change.

Aiming to avoid the worst of these impacts, nearly 200 countries signed the landmark 2015 Paris Agreement. A target was set to reach net zero globally in the second half of the century.

Around 140 countries have their own net zero targets, covering roughly three-quarters of global emissions and 80% of the world's population.

It's widely accepted that richer nations will need to get to net zero before poorer ones, which often have fewer resources to switch to cleaner technologies and have contributed less to climate change historically.

The UK's greenhouse gas emissions have fallen sharply: in 2025 they were 54% lower than in 1990, according to provisional data.

This figure only includes emissions generated within the UK and not from products manufactured abroad and imported.

Successive UK governments have pledged to reach net zero by 2050 and the target was written into law in 2019.

To help achieve this, the current Labour government has committed to:

These policies began to be implemented under Sir Keir Starmer's government and have continued to be pursued by Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

However, recent decisions have led some environmentalists to question whether the government can still meet its targets:

In June, the government's independent adviser, the Climate Change Committee (CCC), warned that the UK was "not moving fast enough" towards net zero.

However, the Chancellor, John Healey, said in his autumn budget speech that the government remained "unshakably committed" to the goal.

When former Conservative Prime Minister Theresa May signed the UK's 2050 net zero target into law in 2019, it passed through parliament with the support of all major parties.

But that political consensus has since fragmented. The term "net zero" is often used by critics to attack environmental targets, which they claim are being put ahead of economic goals.

Labour Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he is "determined" to meet the 2050 deadline, a policy also backed by the Liberal Democrats.

Meanwhile, the Green Party wants net zero "as soon as possible, and more than a decade ahead of 2050".

These parties argue that it's in the UK's economic interest to move away from fossil fuels, which can be volatile in price. Supplies can also be interrupted by international events like the US-Israel war on Iran.

But the Conservatives and Reform UK want to scrap the UK's net zero target, calling the current plans costly and unachievable.

They argue that, in isolation, the UK's efforts make little difference to climate change, not least because UK emissions are much smaller than those of countries like China and the US.

The SNP has targeted net zero by 2045 for Scotland, while Plaid Cymru has introduced a 2040 deadline in Wales.

There is no single path to net zero, which means there is no fixed price.

But the Climate Change Committee says the policy will require tens of billions of pounds a year by the end of the 2020s, most of which it expects to come from the private sector rather than government spending.

By the early 2040s, the CCC calculates that the savings from moving away from fossil fuels to cleaner, more efficient technologies should outweigh the costs.

Multiple studies have found that, globally, the economic cost of tackling climate change is much smaller than letting warming continue unchecked, which would result in widespread and increasing climate hazards.

However, as with any transition, the costs and benefits can be unequally felt. For example, while there is huge potential for new clean energy jobs, those employed in the oil and gas industry are likely to be negatively affected.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/weather/articles/c.title: Could the earliest weakening of the polar vortex on record bring UK snow?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/weather/articles/c.text:
What is the polar vortex?

High above the Arctic, powerful winds usually circle the North Pole each winter, helping trap some of the coldest air on Earth.

But this circulation, known as the polar vortex, has weakened and shifted position in recent days.

While such disruptions can occur during winter, scientists say an event this early in November is unprecedented in modern observations.

Similar disruptions in past years have sometimes been followed by colder weather affecting parts of Europe and North America.

However, as this is happening so early in the season, there are few historical examples to compare with and it could throw current winter forecasts into even more uncertainty.

The polar vortex develops every autumn as temperatures fall in the Arctic.

Strong westerly winds form in the stratosphere, roughly 10 to 30 miles (15-50km) above Earth's surface, locking the coldest air near the pole.

Atmospheric disturbances can cause the air high up to start warming which then makes the vortex winds weaken. This sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) can eventually lead to the strong westerlies reversing into easterly winds.

In the following days and weeks these changes can alter the position of the jet stream, increasing the chance of a blocked weather pattern where it can become drier with a colder northerly or easterly wind bringing Arctic air in.

It can also boost the possibility of snow, especially in eastern UK.

Read more on how the the polar vortex can impact UK weather

Most SSW events tend to occur from mid-winter but we are currently witnessing a dramatic weakening of the strong winds with some forecasts even showing a reversal of the polar vortex winds by mid-November.

Due to this weakening, the vortex has stretched and briefly split into two smaller circulations around the Arctic.

Sudden stratospheric warming can lead to a weakening of the polar vortex, resulting it in becoming disrupted, even split, high above the Arctic region

If the winds continue to weaken and end up reversing as forecast, this will be known as a major SSW event.

Jeff Knight, lead climate scientist from the Met Office, told the BBC: "It would appear to be the earliest on record looking back over the 75 years we've been observing…with most experts agreeing this is a very unusual event."

The current earliest major SSW event occurred on 28 November in 1969 and 2025.

Reasons for why we're seeing such an early event is not clear. It could be just part of the variability of our weather patterns.

But we also know in a "normal" El Niño year, this can typically bring a weakening of the polar vortex towards the end of winter.

While the warmer waters of the Pacific in an El Niño directly disrupt the weather around tropical areas, pulses of energy in the atmosphere, known as planetary waves, can cause disturbances even at polar regions.

These waves can push the polar vortex out of position and break the circulation up.

With the current record El Niño taking us into uncharted territory in terms of disruption to worldwide weather patterns, Knight suggested it could have "helped load the dice for this SSW event. However, because this is so rare, there's not enough evidence".

A link between a strong El Niño and early onset of a SSW event is unclear and will need further research.

Long-range forecasts issued by the Met Office show that the UK was more likely to see a stormy start to winter, followed by a colder spell to end winter. This is consistent with expectations from an El Niño pattern.

However, this unusually early SSW event was not widely expected.

Professor Andrew Charlton-Perez, meteorologist at the University of Reading, said: "The typical response to a SSW is for colder and drier conditions over Europe and the UK."

"Because we haven't seen a SSW event quite like this before, it is harder to anticipate a cold spell at the moment."

One reason is the timing.

The Arctic is not yet as cold as it becomes later in winter, with the polar vortex itself having only recently developed.

Any influence it may have on weather patterns could be weaker than during a mid-winter disruption.

And because the air isn't at mid-winter temperatures yet it means cold and snowy weather for the UK is far from guaranteed.

While snow is not likely in the coming weeks, a possible continuation of drier than average conditions will be concerning for replenishment of our reservoirs

Long-term forecasts are based on large-scale climate signals and how they have affected weather patterns in previous years.

Much of the forecast for this autumn and winter has been focused around the influence of the exceptionally strong El Niño, pointing to a stormier start to winter, with the potential to be followed by colder and drier conditions from January.

But this unusually early disruption of the polar vortex and SSW presents meteorologists with a situation for which there are few modern comparisons.

For Charlton-Perez, the "concerning thing would be if this event ends up bringing the typical drier weather pattern and lack of rain" associated with a sudden stratospheric warming over the coming months.

With most of England and Wales still in drought, we need to rely on a wetter winter to fill up extremely low reservoirs.

For now, experts stress that it is too early to know whether recent changes in the polar vortex will change the winter outlook.

Remembering the Beast from the East

Stormy autumn, cold winter - how might El Niño affect the UK weather?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/weather/articles/c.summary: The Beast from the East Stormy autumn, cold winter, could affect the UK weather. Strong westerly winds form in the stratosphere, locking the coldest air near the pole. Sudden stratospheric warming can lead to a weakening of the polar vortex.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm78.title: Delhi's toxic winter air is back - is the Indian capital prepared for pollution?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm78.text:
There are two cardboard boxes in Meenu Rana's living room in Delhi. One is filled with Diwali decorations and twinkling lights. The other holds air purifiers.

"The mornings have already started feeling stuffy. It will get worse in the coming days, so it's better to be prepared," says the 43-year-old teacher.

She is not alone. Every year, as winter and the festive season approach, residents of India's capital begin preparing for something far less celebratory: months of breathing polluted air.

Delhi and its satellite cities record some of the world's highest pollution levels through the year. But as winter sets in, the air often becomes unbearable.

Falling temperatures and slower winds trap pollutants close to the ground instead of allowing them to disperse. Smoke from crop residue burning in neighbouring states adds to emissions from vehicles and factories, as well as construction dust. Firecrackers used during festivals often worsen air quality.

The result is noxious air and a familiar question: why does pollution return year after year, and why hasn't more been done to tackle it?

This year, however, the Delhi government announced its Winter Action Plan months before the worst of the smog arrived. The plan is in place from 1 November to 28 February, covering the months when pollution usually spikes.

Experts have called this a step in the right direction, noting that in previous years measures were often rolled out only after the air quality got too bad to ignore. However, they say this by itself won't be enough, calling for more holistic, long-lasting measures.

Just days after the plan came into effect, the city is slipping back into a depressingly familiar pattern.

This week, a grey haze hangs over Delhi, along with a distinct smoky smell that residents unwillingly recognise. People complain of irritation in their eyes and difficulty breathing, and coughs and sneezes are heard everywhere.

For those who can afford them, air purifiers have become a household necessity. Outdoors, people wear masks or cover their faces with cloth, trying to protect themselves from the worst of the pollution.

Tackling pollution was among the promises made by the governing Bharatiya Janata Party during its election campaign last year. Its winter action plan is now a major test of that pledge.

The plan restricts the entry of older, more polluting vehicles registered outside Delhi and denies fuel to vehicles without a certificate which shows they meet emission standards. Demolitions and outdoor construction work that generate dust have been temporarily banned.

Private vehicle use is being discouraged - the government has asked offices to allow half of their employees to work from home, introduced staggered office timings for its staff and doubled parking charges. It says it will also strengthen pollution monitoring and enforcement and promote public transport and electric vehicles.

These measures are separate from the Graded Response Action Plan (Grap), which is overseen by the federal Commission for Air Quality Management.

Grap introduces restrictions in stages, with stricter measures kicking in as pollution levels rise. This week, its second stage is in force, restricting the use of diesel generators and burning of coal and firewood.

Experts say on paper, these actions collectively provide a roadmap for responding to rising pollution levels but their success ultimately depends on enforcement.

"There are a lot of positive changes as far as planning is concerned, but when it comes to execution, we probably still stand at the same level," says Parthaa Bosu, strategic adviser at the Environmental Defense Fund, a non-profit group focused on delivering climate solutions.

Others argue that the problem goes much deeper.

"If we want to reduce pollution, we need to set targets for every sector - including power generation, industry and transport - not just vehicle entry, construction and stubble burning," says Manoj Kumar, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.

"We know how much each sector and each state contributes to pollution. We can set targets to reduce emissions from each of them over the next five years."

Bosu points out that an issue which does not get enough attention is secondary pollutants - when gases in the air react with sunlight, water vapour and other substances to form harmful particles that contribute to pollution.

"Pollution is not just caused by biomass burning or vehicles," he says. "Dust being stirred up from the ground, coal and fly ash, materials burned at brick kilns and the large-scale burning of urban waste are also contributing to the problem. And much of this is still not being stopped."

Delhi's pollution problem is also affected by what happens outside the city. Pollutants travel into Delhi from neighbouring states and other parts of northern India, worsening the situation, Bosu explains.

This means that measures taken by Delhi can achieve only so much. Tackling the problem requires neighbouring states and the wider northern region to work together, he adds.

In the meantime, pollution is harming people's health every day.

During winter, government monitoring stations in Delhi frequently record Air Quality Index (AQI) readings above 300, classified as "very poor".

On particularly bad days, readings can reach 500, the highest point on India's scale. That does not mean pollution cannot rise further, only that domestic trackers do not record it. International trackers such as Swiss-based IQAir have recorded readings close to 1,000 on some days.

The World Health Organization recommends average PM2.5 levels over 24 hours should not exceed 15 micrograms per cubic metre. In Delhi, levels are often at more than 25 times that limit during pollution season.

Dr Manoj Goel, pulmonology unit head at Fortis Memorial Research Institute near Delhi, says these tiny particles "can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream, triggering inflammation and affecting multiple organs".

Even short-term exposure can cause throat irritation, coughing, wheezing and breathlessness. It can also worsen existing heart and lung conditions.

A 2025 report by the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago estimated that air pollution could reduce life expectancy in Delhi by up to 8.2 years.

For residents, the challenge is not just limited to breathing. The restrictions also disrupt everyday life.

Delhi is closely connected to its satellite towns, Noida and Gurugram, with thousands of people travelling between them every day for work. Long queues form at the city's borders as vehicles are stopped and checked, leaving commuters stuck in traffic for hours.

While the new rules offer some hope, frustration is growing.

Protests, political arguments and court interventions have become part of the annual cycle. But despite public pressure and government measures, the pollution returns every winter.

Rana keeps her windows closed and curtains drawn, and has added more indoor plants.

The arrival of another winter fills her family with dread, but unlike many others, they are not planning to move out of Delhi.

"I would have left the city long ago had there been an option, but my son has his school, my husband and I have our jobs as well, which makes it practically impossible," she says.

"What option do we have? It is unfair but we will have to live with it."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm78.summary: Delhi and its satellite cities record some of the world's highest pollution levels through the year. Delhi and other cities record high levels of pollution as winter sets in.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx1l.title: Investigation into 'major fish kill' after pollution incident
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx1l.text:
A investigation is underway after "a major fish kill" in a County Down river, the Department for Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (Daera) has confirmed.

The pollution caused the death of brown and migratory sea trout in the Gransha, Ballystockart and Inler (also known as Enler) Rivers.

Glenn McKibbin, the secretary of Inler Angling Club, said about 1,000 fish were killed in the incident and it "could not have happened in a worse location on the river or at a worse time".

The Northern Ireland Environment Agency (NIEA) and Daera Inland Fisheries are working to "identify the source of the pollution and to finalise the numbers of fish killed".

The Department said the incident was reported by a member of the public on Tuesday at 09:30 GMT.

McKibbin said that "current and future fish stocks obliterated for years to come".

He added that resident and non-resident migratory fish, which only return at this of year to spawn, have been impacted.

"Knock-on effects for other wildlife such as resident kingfishers, herons & otters unavoidable.

"For our members and volunteers who work tirelessly in a bid to improve the river this is soul-destroying, particularly as the river was still in recovery from major pollution incidents / fish kills in 2013 and 2015," McKibbin said.

"Waterways up and down the country continue to be treated like sewers.

"The paltry fines that usually follow incidents of this nature are not a deterrent and the current 'system' is broken."

Many migratory fish, such as trout and salmon, swim up smaller tributaries to lay their eggs in cleaner, gravel-bottomed, or cooler waters away from larger predators in the main river.

A tributary is a smaller river that flows into a larger mainstem river where many migratory fish, such as trout and salmon, swim up to lay their eggs away from larger predators in the main river.

Inler Angling Club Chairperson David Pyper said: "For those who dedicate so much time and effort to caring for the river, witnessing the sheer loss of fish in circumstances such as these is particularly disappointing.

"The club hopes that the forthcoming investigations will establish the cause of this latest incident and help ensure appropriate steps are taken to protect the river and its wildlife."

The club has encouraged local representatives and authorities to continue to prioritise rivers and direct resources towards improving water quality and preventing further incidents.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx1l.summary: The pollution caused the death of brown and migratory sea trout in the Gransha, Ballystockart and Inler Rivers. Inler Angling Club secretary Glenn McKibbin said about 1,000 fish were killed in the incident. The Department for Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs confirmed the incident on Tuesday.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw33.title: Typhoons batter East Asia as El Niño makes Pacific 'burn with fever'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw33.text:
Wild weather is a way of life for people living along the coast in the Philippines, Taiwan, China and Japan. But the last few months have been extraordinary.

A wave of intense and, at times, unpredictable storms exacerbated by the El Niño weather pattern has killed dozens, shuttered major airports and wiped out crops and infrastructure across a swathe of East Asia.

In October, nearly all of Taiwan shut down as a monster storm big enough to engulf the island of 23 million roared towards its north-eastern coast. Equivalent to a category five hurricane, Typhoon Champi's 295km/h (193mph) winds had the power to flatten homes and whip up destructive waves.

Thankfully it did not make landfall in Taiwan, skirting past the island while dousing it in rain. But it had far-reaching impacts: hundreds of flights were cancelled in Hong Kong, Taiwan and Japan. In the Philippines' Batanes archipelago, seaside highways shut as huge waves crashed onto the shore, and in southern Japan's Okinawa islands, power was cut to 15,000 homes.

El Niño is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon in which warm waters pooling in the eastern Pacific and altered wind patterns drive extreme weather events around the world.

It happens around every two to seven years, lasting for around a year. This year's El Niño, which the UK Met Office has forecast to be the "strongest in living memory", is likely to last until February or March.

In June, Japan watched two storms - Typhoon Mekkhala and Severe Tropical Storm Higos - race towards its eastern coast simultaneously, forcing one million people to evacuate. In July, Tropical Storm Narra grazed China's southern coast along Guangxi, submerging villages and displacing tens of thousands.

August brought Super Typhoon Dolphin, which churned across the Pacific for 16 days - before slamming into eastern China, triggering heavy floods and dozens of casualties.

Later that month Typhoon Saudel made landfall in three south-eastern Chinese cities over one week, shutting transport networks and forcing thousands to evacuate.

The Pacific Ocean, heated to record levels by El Niño, is now brimming with typhoon energy, according to the Accumulated Cyclone Energy (ACE) metric which measures the total intensity of a season's storms. This year, the ACE reading for South East and East Asia is forecast to be nearly double the 30-year average.

El Niño also affects wind patterns and in this case, that means typhoons are tending to form further east than usual. They are also becoming stronger as they remain over warm waters for longer.

The Pacific can be likened to someone "burning with fever", says Ana Liza Solis, head of climatology at the Philippines' national weather bureau. "It can go into convulsions soon," she said at a press briefing in Manila in September.

Forecasts suggest the worst may not be over. Last month, sea surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific - the area monitored by the Japan Meteorological Agency for its El Niño predictions - soared to 4C above normal, the highest since records began in 1949. The previous record - 3.6C - was set in December 1997.

China's climate agency has warned of sea surface temperatures continuing to rise over the next three months because of the El Niño.

Despite typhoon season usually peaking around September to October, this is likely to raise concerns across a region that has already been battered by back-to-back storms.

In August, Typhoon Chan-Hom baffled storm watchers in Japan by crossing the country from east to west, as opposed to the usual south-to-north trajectory. Japan's well-resourced and prepared authorities were able to evacuate people swiftly, but this would be far more challenging in some neighbouring countries.

To get a better picture of how rising temperatures could amplify the risks, Manila-based climatologist Rafaela Jane Delfino and colleagues simulated the effects of warmer conditions on the Philippines' most recent monster storms, including 2013's Super Typhoon Haiyan (Yolanda) which killed more than 6,000 people.

They arrived at what she describes as "very, very scary findings": higher temperatures increased total accumulated rainfall by 26%. It's a devastating prospect in a country where flooding from monsoon rains and some 20 tropical storms per year has emerged as one of the main disaster risks.

In recent years, floods have paralysed entire cities for days, and tired of the annual ordeal, Filipinos have taken to the streets to protest against corruption which they say is gnawing away at millions of dollars from flood-control projects.

Delfino, in an article on the University of the Philippines website, insists leaders and officials must gain a better understanding of climate hazards if communities are to be better prepared.

Countries are bracing for the immediate impact. Japan has urged citizens to stockpile food and essentials for the typhoon season, and to secure outdoor furniture that could become deadly projectiles when typhoon winds hit. China has asked local officials to identify vulnerable areas and is upgrading its warning and monitoring systems.

The Philippines and its South East Asian neighbours are preparing for disruptions to food production, especially rice, and have increased support for famers, including the provision of fertilisers.

But what happens in the long term is less clear. The window for governments to act on El Niño is "closing", the United Nations Development Programme in Asia and the Pacific said recently.

"How severely a community experiences an El Niño is decided years in advance, by where roads and settlements are built, how water is managed, who is covered by social protection and whether public budgets have room to absorb a shock.

"Every El Niño tests the resilience we have built; this one should also drive us to build more," it added.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c699.title: Delhi air quality worsens ahead of Diwali as firework restrictions enter force
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c699.text:
Delhi is once again battling worsening air pollution as the onset of winter brings a familiar deterioration in air quality to India's capital.

The city's air quality index (AQI) - which measures PM2.5, fine particulate matter that can clog lungs - has crossed 300, entering the "very poor" category and raising health concerns for millions of residents.

Breathing such polluted air over prolonged periods can cause respiratory problems and worsen existing illnesses, with children and older people particularly vulnerable.

Authorities have responded by invoking Stage II of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP), introducing measures to curb dust, vehicle emissions and other sources of pollution.

GRAP is a set of emergency measures that become progressively stricter as pollution levels rise. The latest restrictions include more intensive road cleaning, higher parking charges to discourage private vehicle use and increased public transport services. Delhi Metro has introduced 20 additional weekday train trips, while authorities have been directed to stagger government office timings to ease traffic congestion.

Officials said the measures were introduced after forecasts suggested air quality would remain very poor over the coming days.

Delhi and neighbouring parts of northern India grapple with hazardous air every winter, particularly around Diwali, one of India's biggest festivals, which is just days away.

The festival is celebrated with lights, lamps and fireworks, which often worsen the city's already poor air quality by releasing fine particles and harmful gases into the atmosphere.

The annual pollution crisis is driven by a combination of factors, including vehicle exhaust, industrial emissions, falling temperatures, low wind speeds and the burning of crop stubble in neighbouring states.

The sharp rise in pollution follows an unusually clean October, when Delhi recorded its lowest average AQI for the month in eight years.

Experts have attributed the sudden deterioration to falling temperatures, slow winds and an increase in crop-residue burning in the neighbouring states of Punjab and Haryana.

A recent storm had brought rain and stronger winds, helping clear the air. But as the weather settled, northwesterly winds returned, carrying smoke from burning fields towards the capital.

India's pollution watchdog classifies AQI readings between 301 and 400 as "very poor", while anything above 400 is considered "severe". On Wednesday morning, Delhi's AQI stood at 377.

The index takes into account eight major pollutants, including PM2.5 - tiny particles about 30 times smaller than the width of a human hair that can penetrate deep into the lungs.

With Diwali just days away, there are concerns that fireworks could push pollution levels even higher.

Last year, Delhi woke up to a toxic haze the morning after the festival, despite a court directive to use less-polluting firecrackers.

Authorities have imposed restrictions on firecrackers over the years, including outright bans on their manufacture, sale and use, but enforcing them has proved difficult.

On Monday, India's Supreme Court allowed the manufacture, sale and use of certified green firecrackers in Delhi and neighbouring areas for a limited period.

It said the crackers could be set off only between 06:00 and 07:00 local time (00:30-01:30 GMT) and between 20:00 and 22:00 (14:30-16:30 GMT) on 7 and 8 November, during the Diwali weekend.

The court also banned fireworks within 300m of hospitals, care homes, schools and other designated silence zones.

Green firecrackers use modified chemical formulations designed to produce fewer emissions than conventional fireworks. They must carry QR codes that allow buyers and authorities to verify details of their manufacturer and certification.

But ensuring that only approved firecrackers are sold remains a major challenge.

In its latest order, the Supreme Court acknowledged that conventional firecrackers had continued to be sold as green alternatives, even when a complete ban was in place.

It has directed police to patrol designated sales areas, carry out random QR-code checks and seize illegal firecrackers.

During particularly severe pollution episodes, Delhi authorities have also introduced measures such as hybrid schooling, work-from-home arrangements and restrictions on certain vehicles.

The problem is not confined to the capital. Mumbai, India's financial hub, has also recorded elevated pollution levels over the past month, despite benefiting from coastal winds that typically help disperse pollutants.

On 24 October, Mumbai's AQI had reached 322, placing it in the "very poor" category. The spike was attributed to a combination of low wind speeds, construction dust, garbage burning, firecracker emissions and pollutants carried from neighbouring regions.

The city's air quality has improved in recent days - and it recorded an AQI of 89, classified as "satisfactory", on Wednesday. Neighbouring Navi Mumbai recorded a "moderate" AQI of 118.

The improvement follows nearly two weeks of smoggy conditions, with residents sharing photos and videos of the haze on social media.

Follow BBC News India on Instagram, YouTube, Twitter and Facebook.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c699.summary: Delhi's air quality index has crossed 300, entering the "very poor" category. The city's air pollution index has been hit by a sharp rise in pollution. The sharp rise follows an unusually clean October, when Delhi recorded its lowest average AQI for the month in eight years.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr62.title: Prince William says UK faces terrifying risk of more wildfires due to climate change
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr62.text:
There is a "terrifying prospect" of more UK wildfires in future due to climate change and preparation will be "crucial", the Prince of Wales has said.

Visiting Treherbert in Rhondda Cynon Taf, which was threatened by a huge mountain fire in August, Prince William praised a "gargantuan" effort to save homes, land and lives.

"We need to start taking wildfires as seriously as the continent has done," he said, raising issues such as a lack of firefighting aircraft.

He also suggested the community's response to the incident was an example for others to follow, after locals rallied around to support those fighting the flames.

The hillside, just metres away from the community centre where Prince William met fire crews, military personnel and local volunteers is burnt black.

"You looked up [and] the mountain was alight - it was like lava," explained Kath Edwards, managing director of charity Valleys Kids, which runs the building.

"I genuinely thought we were going to lose the centre - but more importantly people were going to lose their homes.

"You never think this is going to come literally to your door and that's what it was - it was just crazy."

South Wales Fire and Rescue Service (SWFRS) declared a major incident as it was forced to respond to 14 wildfires at the same time in August, including the one above Treherbert.

Support was drafted in from 22 other UK fire services while soldiers were deployed to dig fire breaks and help supply 2.1 million litres of water to douse the flames, including 200 members of the Queen's Own Gurkha Logistic Regiment.

Aled Bound, who is crew manager at Maesteg fire station and a retained - on-call - firefighter at Treorchy told Prince William it was "the hardest wildfire season" he and his colleagues had ever dealt with.

Months of record-breaking heat and dry conditions sparked a wave of wildfires across the UK through spring and summer.

He described it was "mentally and physically draining".

"I've never had to take so much water up a mountain to put on a fire and still come back the next day because that fire has relit, because it's so deep-seated," Bound said.

With climate change, he warned it "could well be a sign of what's to come".

Figures from the National Fire Chiefs Council show a new all-time high for recorded significant wildfires - 1,350 across England and Wales, up by more than 300 on 2025 and more than 1,000 on 2024.

Prince William told firefighters that 2026 was the first summer "where I've felt generally worried about the scale of the wildfires in the country".

He added: "We might go again next season... it's quite a terrifying prospect if we're not... on the ball."

He asked about availability of firefighting aircraft, noting that "the need for aerial assets has been hoisted quite high up in government" as an area "we're lacking".

The prince served a three-year tour flying Sea King helicopters with the Search and Rescue team at RAF Valley on Anglesey between 2010 and 2013, qualifying as a captain.

He recalled flying water bowsers in the Falklands "putting out range fires... and once the Sea King went, we don't have the assets any more".

"I think it's front and centre of many people's minds now, how do we recreate that."

Conversation turned to the kit available to fire crews working in unbearable heat, proactive land management practices and whether social media firms could do more to discourage people from setting fires.

Recently, the UK government announced that the RAF's Chinook helicopters and A400M aircraft would be equipped to fight fires in future.

A separate Welsh government wildfire summit also led to promises of action to improve preparedness.

"It feels like this is something we're going to have to live with as a country or as a world now every summer," Prince William said.

"It's fair to say that we've learnt a lot from this season... and there's lots that we'll be putting into place, particularly following the wildfire summits," said Adam Openshaw, deputy chief fire officer for SWFRS.

He described the response of people in Treherbert as "the best demonstration of the community coming together to support the wildfire response".

He said it really helped as fire crews worked "tirelessly" in "challenging circumstances".

Edwards explained that volunteers kept the community centre open 24 hours a day from the Saturday evening of the fire until the following Thursday "to provide whatever service we could".

Due to the unprecedented nature of the fire, the centre became a control hub for the firefighting operation, a place to rest and regroup and a focal point for people wanting to show their support.

Businesses donated food - "40 pizzas arrived within the first 20 minutes" - and there were regular visits from an ice cream van.

Prince William asked whether volunteers should be used more in future and was told the community's efforts, hand in hand with military support, enabled the fire service to focus on bringing the incident under control.

"From something really quite horrific, the valleys did what the valleys do very, very well - we pulled together to make a difference," Edwards said.

Communities in the south Wales valleys were already experiencing the effects of climate change, she warned.

"We've had floods, fires... we've got [coal] tips that move as well.

"I think the message I was keen to get across is... we are motivated as a community to ask how do we solve this?

"How can we work together as a community and voluntary sector to support agencies [like the fire service]?"
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr62.summary: Prince William visited Treherbert in Rhondda Cynon Taf, which was threatened by a huge mountain fire in August. He praised the community's response to the incident as an example for others to follow.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw98.title: New Forest wildfire restoration work begins
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw98.text:
Restoration work has begun at the site of a devastating wildfire in a national park.

More than 1 sq km (247 acres) of the New Forest was destroyed after a fire spread from a blazing van on 9 August.

The fire caused damage to rare heathland and an ancient woodland, as well as burning through a surface layer of peat in some of the boggy areas, reducing their ability to store carbon.

Forestry England said it had begun a long-term project to help nature return to the affected area, with specialist teams starting work to protect the most vulnerable areas ahead of winter and helping to reseed areas of heather.

The agency, which is responsible for managing publicly-owned forests in England, said the blaze spread across the heathland, removing all the plants on the surface before travelling underground to destroy layers of roots and seed banks.

At its height, the fire closed the A31 - a major tourist and commuter route between Hampshire and Dorset - for nearly two weeks.

It came during an exceptionally busy summer for Hampshire and Isle of Wight firefighters, and is estimated to have cost the fire service £600,000.

Forestry England's Dave Morris said: "The scene immediately after the fire had gone through this part of the forest is something I will never forget."

Morris added: "Large areas were reduced to piles of charcoal, burnt soils and torched trees. At that time, it was difficult to imagine it would ever fully return to a place where nature could thrive.

"Undeterred, our specialist staff immediately got to work to see how we could help the area recover."

Heather full of seed was harvested from nearby parts of the forest and has been spread across the worst-affected parts of the fire site to form a "protective mat" and encourage new plants to grow.

Forestry England used the same technique after part of the New Forest was destroyed by a previous wildfire in 1989.

"Almost 40 years later, this area is now thriving and has been fully restored," it said.

Teams are also looking at ways to protect the vulnerable roots of ancient beech and oak trees damaged in this summer's fire.

The boggy areas of the fire site sustained the least damage, acting as a barrier to help slow the blaze from moving more widely across forest, and have recovered the quickest.

"The fire has reminded us that nature is remarkably resilient and in the boggy parts of the fire area we can already see plants and wildlife returning," said Morris.

"It will take many decades for the area burnt by the fire to recover completely but, with the right help at the right time, we can give it the helping hand it needs."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw98.summary: More than 1 sq km (247 acres) of the New Forest was destroyed after a fire spread from a blazing van. The fire caused damage to rare heathland and an ancient woodland. Forestry England said it had begun a long-term project to help nature return to the affected area.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmx2.title: 'Extra special' tamarin twins born at zoo
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmx2.text:
One of the UK's smallest accredited zoos is celebrating after "extra special" pied tamarin twins were born at the site.

Shaldon Wildlife Trust, in Devon, said the critically endangered twins were born on 29 September to mum Bobby and dad Pedra. Its director, Zak Showell, said it was a "challenge" to breed the species.

The trust said the animals were among the most endangered primates in South America. Bosses said the infants were "thriving" and had started to hitch rides on their parents' backs as they explored their habitat.

Showell said: "For a zoo of our size to achieve this and to be one of just two European zoos to manage it this year is an unbelievable proud moment for our small team."

"It has been an incredible year for births here at Shaldon, but these twins are extra special," he said.

"Pied tamarins are exceptionally delicate animals, and breeding them successfully is a challenge."

The trust said the primates required "stress-free environments and specialist care".

It said zoo keepers intentionally kept the news of the arrivals under wraps for a few weeks to give the "delicate family complete peace and quiet".

The species is listed as critically endangered on the International Union of Conservation and Nature's (IUCN) Red List.

The zoo said, in the wild, they were restricted to "a shrinking pocket of rainforest" around Manaus, Brazil.
