https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmrl.title: US rockets firm eyes up mothballed Highland spaceport
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmrl.text:
A rockets manufacturer says the mothballed Sutherland Spaceport could become its first launch site outside the US.

Colorado-based Leap has agreed to work with Highlands and Islands Enterprise (HIE), which owns the area of peatland near Tongue, to develop the plans.

Little work has been done at the site after Moray-headquartered rockets firm Orbex put construction on hold in 2024. The company later collapsed and its assets were sold off.

Leap said the spaceport could potentially be used for launching small satellites for customers in the UK and mainland Europe.

Leap is designing rockets that could be mass produced in factories.

Chief executive Chris Beckman said: "We're not just building a rocket. We're building a global logistics network, and a network needs launch sites wherever customers require them.

"Sutherland is an ideal starting point for a network that begins in Europe, and HIE shares our ambition to make recurring spaceflight from Scotland real."

HIE and Economy Secretary Stephen Flynn have welcomed the agreement.

The site is on Melness Crofters Estate, an area of small-scale farms on the A' Mhoine Peninsula in Sutherland in the north-west Highlands.

Chairwoman Dorothy Pritchard said the estate was delighted to welcome Leap as a potential launch operator.

She said: "We believe their presence here will be an important step towards establishing a thriving and sustainable spaceport that can bring long-term benefits to Sutherland and the UK's growing space industry.

"Alongside other UK launch sites, both developed and emerging, an operational Sutherland Spaceport will become an integral part of a resilient and diverse UK launch ecosystem, securing the UK position within the global space economy, something we welcome and support.

"Melness Crofters Estate looks forward to seeing the spaceport become a driver of economic opportunity."

Last month, the UK and German governments said they planned to use another Scottish spaceport - SaxaVord in Shetland - as part of increased co-operation between the two countries.

The agreement followed a meeting between Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Berlin last week.

In a joint statement, the two governments said they would deepen strategic co-operation on civil, commercial, security and defence interests in space.

SaxaVord in Unst is the UK's first fully-licensed spaceport and has regulatory approval for up to 30 rocket launches a year.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmrl.summary: Colorado-based Leap has agreed to work with Highlands and Islands Enterprise. Little work has been done at the site after Moray-headquartered rockets firm Orbex put construction on hold in 2024.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjg4.title: Do the Shetland Isles need Cold War-style military protection?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjg4.text:
Calls are being made for the defence of the Shetland Isles to be strengthened after increased sightings of Russian trawlers off the coast of Scotland.

Recent analysis by the Daily Telegraph also revealed that there have been more than 500 incidents where Russian boats have been stationed above undersea cables linking Britain with Europe and the US.

These cables carry the majority of telecoms data abroad.

The growing importance of undersea infrastructure prompted a parliamentary report last year to warn of security vulnerabilities in areas including transport and supply chains, financial services and payment systems.

There are also concerns that the £30m SaxaVord Spaceport in Shetland could be a Russian target.

But do the Shetland Isles really need better protection by the military?

In recent years there have been a number of incidents in the Baltic Sea where underwater cables have been damaged or completely cut.

In December last year, Finnish police detained a vessel sailing from Russia, which was suspected of damaging an undersea telecoms cable running from Helsinki to Estonia, across the Gulf of Finland.

In 2022, Shetland was cut off from the mainland after a nearby subsea cable was damaged.

And last year there were two cable breaks in Shetland, which disrupted internet services and, in one case, took weeks to repair.

There has been no suggestion that there was any Russian involvement in the Shetland incidents but they demonstrate how fragile the cables are and show the devastating effect on the islanders when they are damaged.

In July, Royal Navy warships and helicopters spent 21 days monitoring Russian activity in UK waters and the North Atlantic - this was a 25% increase on previous time spent monitoring.

The recent Telegraph revelation of more than 500 incidents where Russian boats have been stationed above undersea cables has also caused concern.

Jon Sandison, a high school history teacher and Shetland tour guide, said there were real concerns that Shetland could be attacked after Germany invaded Norway in 1940, during World War Two.

"Shetland could have been a stepping stone towards Orkney and mainland Scotland," he said.

There were many army, naval and RAF personnel stationed across the isles and coastal defences were built to defend Lerwick and the rest of the archipelago.

The SaxaVord Spaceport sits on a former RAF base and RAF Skaw played an important role in efforts to detect enemy aircraft from 1941.

RAF Saxa Vord was later involved in Nato's radar network to monitor Soviet activity during the Cold War.

The radar station closed in 2006 but it was revived in 2018 for Arctic surveillance as an automated remote radar head.

Sandison said that while military presence reduced in the second half of the 20th Century, Shetland's geographical position would never change.

"Where we are in the UK is always going to be a pivotal geographical location in relation to the North Sea, the Arctic Circle and wider scope of Britain," he said.

He added that coastal infrastructure was built very quickly during the Second World War.

"Air raid shelters, anti-aircraft defences - it's remarkable how much was built in a short space of time," he added.

"Not much of the infrastructure remains. It's part of our history, and part of our past."

First Minister John Swinney has accused the UK government of leaving "Scotland's vast coastline dangerously exposed".

He pointed to waters off Shetland as an area of significant Russian activity.

"I don't think we've got nearly the presence in those areas that we require today," he told BBC Scotland News.

Liberal Democrat MP Alistair Carmichael, whose constituency covers Shetland, has urged the UK government to step up efforts to protect critical infrastructure.

He told the BBC's Radio Scotland Breakfast programme: "This is something we do need to be taking seriously.

"We're not expecting an imminent problem here but this is a time where the government is already telling us that we should all be keeping baked beans and a wind-up torch in a cupboard."

Carmichael added that if the world had changed so much, some of the decisions made by the UK government to remove military presence from the northern isles may now need to be looked at again.

He said that over the last 20 years, there had been just one local full-time soldier running a reserved unit in Shetland but they were now managed from the Scottish mainland.

Carmichael said there should be restoration of a full-time presence to support the unit and more reserves should be recruited in the northern isles as numbers were low.

But he added: "If the signal that the government is sending the community is that we don't even think its important enough to send one full-time solider to run these units then you can't expect the community themselves to be particularly enthusiastic about it."

SaxaVord in Unst is the UK's first fully-licensed spaceport with several companies interested in using the site to launch small satellites into orbit.

In September, the UK government announced investment of £30m in the project, as part of a new £7.8bn space strategy.

Alistair Carmichael said the spaceport would draw more attention to Shetland as a significant asset.

The German and UK governments plan to use SaxaVord to deepen their co-operation on space.

In October, Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Chancellor Friedrich Merz met in Berlin and announced plans to work more closely on economic growth, defence and technology.

SaxaVord Spaceport was identified as a focus for immediate work on European launches.

Two German companies are currently in a race to be the first to test a rocket in Shetland.

Chief executive Scott Hammond said: "The space strategy is absolutely critical.

"We're at the heart of the UK government's plans for assured access to space.

"That's also for our economic and Nato partners."

He added that the UK government had joined as one of its majority investors, with a member on the board, but stressed that SaxaVord Spaceport was still a private commercial company.

A Ministry of Defence spokesperson said: "We are clear-eyed about the threat Russia poses.

"Through the UK-led Joint Expeditionary Force, we are leading allied activity across the High North, strengthening Nato's northern flank and increasing our ability to respond rapidly to emerging threats.

"This government is also investing in the capabilities needed to meet those threats, with £1.5bn backing Atlantic Bastion to deliver a next-generation Hybrid Navy and a further £330m to strengthen the protection of critical undersea infrastructure."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjg4.summary: More than 500 incidents where Russian boats have been stationed above undersea cables. There are also concerns that the £30m SaxaVord Spaceport in Shetland could be a Russian target.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5pv.title: Scientists detect signals at the smallest scale ever explored
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5pv.text:
Scientists have picked up signals from the smallest scale of nature ever explored – 100 billion times smaller than an atom.

A world so small that some physicists have nicknamed it the zeptoverse.

The research, led by scientists based in Cambridge, was obtained from an experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC).

This vast machine at the European Laboratory for Particle Physics (Cern) on the Swiss-French border smashes atoms together to break them apart and discover what is inside them.

The result is important because it could help researchers develop a new, more complete theory of how the Universe works.

Dark matter makes up a large part of our cosmos, and yet researchers have struggled to detect it.

Scientists know it is there because its gravitational force influences normal matter, but in all other respects it has remained completely invisible.

So in this experiment, particles were smashed together at high energy and scientists studied the material that was thrown out - the shrapnel of collisions.

One of these is a sub-atomic particle - smaller than an atom - called a beauty quark.

The particle is unstable and exists for just one and a half trillionths of a second before breaking down into other forms - decaying.

Despite its short lifetime, researchers managed to detect it interacting with other tiny particles at a scale of a billion-trillionth of a metre.

Some theories suggest that at these scales particles are more sensitive to dark matter and it could influence how the quarks interact and break down. So, detecting activity in this tiny world could help scientists detect dark matter.

"We're knocking on the door of this zeptoverse," Dr Harry Cliff, of Cambridge University who led the analysis of the data, told BBC News.

He said this sub-atomic dance provided researchers with a ringside seat to the behaviour of possible new particles.

"And what we want to do now is go in and explore and find what new particles are waiting there. And to do that, what we need is more data," Cliff added.

The 28 countries involved in the project have agreed a £150m upgrade to this detector at the Large Hadron Collider (LHCb), which would increase the frequency of these decays tenfold.

"With that we can probe inside the zeptoverse and see what's waiting," Cliff said.

But last year the UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) agency, the government body in charge of research funding, announced that it was withdrawing its share of the money for the planned upgrade.

It later announced cuts to several other particle physics and astronomy projects this Summer, including Jodrell Bank's iconic Lovell telescope.

Although this research was led by scientists based in Cambridge, because of the cuts, Prof Tim Gershon, who leads the LHCb international collaboration, told BBC News that the UK's full involvement in the research would be in doubt.

"The UK is at risk of not being involved and making really major discoveries," he told BBC News.

"But I think the biggest long-term impact comes from the fact that the UK won't get the benefits from training young people who really are our greatest product."

Among those early-career researchers is Dr Mary Richardson-Slipper, who is part of the team that made the zeptoverse discovery. She is reconsidering her future in light of the physics cuts.

"I love being here in the UK, but I am looking at jobs abroad because that seems to be where there are more opportunities at the moment," said Richardson-Slipper.

She added that "lots" of her fellow researchers working in fundamental physics had already moved.

The cuts are being made despite an overall record increase in the science budget.

Prof Brian Cox, TV presenter and particle researcher at the University of Manchester, who is not part of the research team, described the result as "important".

But he condemned the recent decision to cut UK funding for the Cern project.

"It would be extraordinary to walk away from UK scientific leadership at this moment, damaging the future research programme and seriously damaging our hard-won international reputation," Cox said.

The UKRI told BBC News that it remained a fully engaged member of Cern as its second largest funder at around £175m per year.

A UKRI spokesperson said: "We sought independent advice and have taken forward an exciting portfolio of new infrastructure investments, which include projects in clean energy, medical imaging and cultural heritage.

"However, as usual, there were more exciting applications for funding than we were able to support."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqx2.title: 'Rok' solid recognition for Slovenian space scientist
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqx2.text:
As a child growing up in Slovenia in 1999, Dr Rok Nežič couldn't have known that an asteroid that was discovered in New Mexico that year would be named after him almost three decades later.

The Orchard County may be best known for its apples, but for Nežič the real attraction was astronomy.

He first arrived at Armagh Observatory and Planetarium (AOP) in 2015 to complete his doctorate in space and climate physics, and has remained there ever since.

More than a decade on, he is one of two AOP employees to have recently been chosen to have a celestial body named after them.

Nežič, who works at the planetarium as a tours and outreach officer, said he thought it was "so cool" when he learned that asteroids can be named after people.

Speaking to BBC News NI, Nežič said he wished he "could get there some day" and, now that he has, he described it as "a dream come true".

"I'm not sure how to believe it myself,” he admitted.

He explains that an asteroid is "a smallish rock in space" compared to planets, and that his one is named (20560) Nežič.

"That's its official name, so the number there tells you basically the order of discovery."

It is currently "sitting safely out in the asteroid belt and just going around the Sun, just like we are", he explained.

The naming process for small bodies in the solar system is governed by the International Astronomical Union. Asteroids can be named by their discoverers once their orbits are sufficiently known.

Nežič's asteroid is 10.9km across, while that belonging to his colleague Shane Kelly is 15.6km.

"They're both actually quite large as far as these asteroids that are named after people tend to be, because most of the really large ones were discovered first," Nežič said.

"So they were named a long time ago, and now we're finding smaller and smaller ones."

Nežič's asteroid was discovered by "one of the big missions", he said.

"This is an Earth-based mission in this case, which is looking for lots of asteroids, essentially, because the more we know about them, the more we know where they're going, the more we know which ones are not hitting us, including mine and Shane's."

To be considered for an asteroid namesake, someone must nominate you, and in Nežič's case, two people put his name forward.

He doesn't know who chose him for the honour - but his PhD supervisor, and a former astronomer from the observatory nominated him.

Nežič focused on comets with polarised light for his studies and years later is "still" talking about space.

The planetarium and observatory is "punching well above our weight", he said.

"Even though we're a small institution, people who work here can just focus on the research so much that we have really top researchers in the field."

The planetarium's neighbouring observatory has monitored the weather for more than than 230 years.

Shane Kelly, who is the principal meteorological observer at Armagh Observatory, was nominated by the emeritus director.

Since 1999, his role involves opening what is known as the Stevenson screen which holds sensitive thermometers, before noting down his readings for the day into the handwritten ledger.

His hand has entered far more lines of data than any of his 17 predecessors and his asteroid is called (7050) Shanekelly.

Kelly has been "doing this for 27 years", the institute's director said.

"He's probably observed the weather more than anyone else in the world, I suspect," Prof Michael Burton said.

"So this is in recognition of Shane's contribution to the observatory and to the measuring of the weather."

Kelly's asteroid was discovered in Chile in 1982.

Burton said it's "fantastic" that the two members of the team have been awarded in this way.

"There are now 29 asteroids which have some connection with the observatory and planetarium here in Armagh."

The AOP now plans on recognising their achievements with a new LED dome, which will show the asteroids and their orbits.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqm2.title: Wales scraps controversial Uganda tree-planting scheme
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqm2.text:
The Welsh government will end funding for a tree-planting scheme in Uganda that was branded "woke" by opposition politicians.

Wales has given more than £4m to climate change charity Size of Wales since 2015, to work with Indigenous communities to plant trees in the African nation.

Ministers said budgetary pressures meant "difficult decisions" had to be made and the charity would lose its grant for the scheme at the end of March 2027.

Size of Wales has called on the government to reconsider.

Right-wing parties in the Senedd welcomed the decision, whilst left-wing politicians criticised it, with the Welsh Liberal Democrats accusing the Plaid Cymru-run government of "out-Reforming Reform".

Size of Wales works with Indigenous and local people worldwide to grow trees and protect at least two million hectares of tropical forests - an area the size of Wales.

The scheme, funded by previous Labour-run Welsh governments, has seen more than 25 million planted around Mbale in the Mount Elgon region of eastern Uganda.

Previous criticism by opponents of using taxpayers' money for the scheme led to Labour ministers last year pointing out that it amounted to about £270,000 a year - equivalent to 0.001% of the government's total annual budget in 2025.

A document published in August 2025 by the previous government stated Wales was "helping some of the very poorest people in the world adapt to climate change and improve their livelihoods" and protected local people in the Mount Elgon region from deadly landslides.

Plaid took over the Welsh government in May, with the decision to end the tree-planting scheme coming as it prepares to publish its draft budget for 2026-27 later this month.

A Welsh government spokesperson said it was developing "a new international strategy for Wales" and was "working to ensure that future investment demonstrates impact and value for money and delivers clear benefits for Wales as well as our international partners".

"We do not intend to renew grant funding for the Size of Wales Mbale tree-planting programme beyond its current end date of 31 March 2027," they said.

"That is not a judgement on the quality of the work. The programme has planted millions of trees and built important links between Wales and Uganda, and we look forward to continuing our dialogue with Size of Wales."

The spokesperson said that recognising the success of a programme "is not the same as committing to fund the same delivery model indefinitely", and the government had to "make difficult choices about where limited resources can have the greatest impact".

They added: "We will never retreat from Wales being an outward-looking and globally responsible nation."

Responding to the decision, chairman of Size of Wales Tim Birch said: "At a time of deepening climate crisis, we need to strengthen, not retreat from, our commitment to global responsibility.

"As we prepare for COP31, Wales must continue to show global leadership.

"Taking action to protect tropical forests is in Wales' own national interests and working with international partners to restore ecosystems and build climate resilience is more important than ever.

"We urge the Welsh government to reconsider this decision and continue supporting the long-term partnerships that are so vital to our shared future."

The tree-planting scheme has long been criticised by Reform UK and Welsh Conservative politicians in the Senedd.

Reform UK's leader in Wales, Helen Jenner, welcomed the announcement and said her party had been calling "for an end to this ridiculous woke spending for years now".

"We have changed the conversation in Cardiff Bay and demanded that Welsh taxpayers' money be spent in Wales and not sent abroad for things like Ugandan trees," she said.

"Now, thanks to us, Welsh households will not be funding those trees."

The leader of the Welsh Conservatives in the Senedd Darren Millar said the decision was "long overdue but it is better late than never".

"It's outrageous that the Welsh government has been spending so much taxpayers' money on planting trees in Africa while our schools and hospitals have not been getting the cash they need," he said.

"It has no responsibility for foreign affairs or international development, so every pound spent on these things is a pound that is being taken away from our NHS, our education system and helping the Welsh economy.

"The Welsh government should put the people of Wales first, not vanity projects overseas."

But the leader of the Welsh Liberal Democrats Jane Dodds described it as a "short-sighted" decision.

"Tackling climate change and protecting nature isn't a luxury," she said.

"Size of Wales has planted millions of trees, built real links between Wales and Uganda, and helped communities protect forests that matter to all of us.

"Plaid are out-Reforming Reform by cutting international funding for work ministers admit has been a success.

"Wales' global responsibility shouldn't be the first thing to go."

Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates said: "In opposition, Plaid Cymru repeatedly championed international programmes.

"Yet again, it seems that what Plaid say is very different to what they actually do."

The Welsh government also provides a grant of £280,000 a year to the charity to deliver an education programme in Welsh schools, which runs until the end of March 2027, with a proposal for the future of the programme to be submitted and considered by the country's rural resilience and sustainability minister.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqm2.summary: Wales has given £4m to climate change charity Size of Wales since 2015. Ministers say budgetary pressures meant "difficult decisions" had to be made. Scheme has seen 25 million trees planted in the Mount Elgon region of eastern Uganda.

It's the time of year when nations come together to try and agree on a plan to futureproof the planet. But in the lead up to the Conference of the Parties 31, another meeting takes place – a smaller gathering, but one some would argue is just as important.

COP17, the 17th meeting of the Convention on Biological Diversity, brings nations together to assess progress towards the global commitment to protect at least 30% of the world's land and seas by 2030. Yet, with less than three years left to meet this ambitious target, the world appears to be falling short.

Brian O'Donnell, Director of Campaign for Nature, reflects on the successes so far, the challenges that remain, and what more needs to be done to meet the global 30% protection target.

Mirium O'Duill uncovers the story of the overlooked scientist who first discovered carbon dioxide's heat trapping properties.

And mathematician Kit Yates joins Tom to share the latest science news you may have missed this week.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/c914d4.title: How to move 1,300 plants for Kew's Palm House mega makeover
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/c914d4.text:
The world-famous Palm House at the Royal Botanic Gardens Kew in London is about to undergo a massive makeover.

The £66m restoration is taking place because the hot and humid conditions inside the Victorian glasshouse have taken their toll on the ironwork and glass.

The work will begin in autumn 2027, and the Palm House will be closed for up to four years.

But before it can start, the glasshouse has to be completely emptied of the 1,300 tropical plants and trees it has inside.

BBC science correspondent, Pallab Ghosh, takes us into the zeptoverse and explains how it could change our ideas of how the universe works.

The BBC's Ricky Boleto looks how previous SpaceX test flights went.

Some parts of the globe had a chance to see the rare event when the Sun, Earth and Moon line up in the night sky.

The powerful natural climate phenomenon, that is developing over the Pacific Ocean, is likely to be the strongest in living memory, the Met Office has warned.

The new record surpasses the previous official hydrogen combustion title set in 2004 by more than double the speed.

Organisers say 23 runners from seven countries took part in races at the Arctic's geographic North Pole.

The Soyuz spacecraft will carry Nasa astronaut Anil Menon and cosmonauts Pyotr Dubrov and Anna Kikina to the ISS for an eight-month mission.

Sophia Herod has some tips for helping animals that might visit your garden or neighbourhood.

See how the powerful storm is expected to move across east Asia on Saturday.

This occurrence of aurora australis, or Southern Lights, was captured by Nasa astronaut Jessica Meir.

A volunteer diver has described shaking as he filmed his encounter with an endangered Great White shark between Tunisia and Sicily.

Science correspondent Pallab Ghosh explains why the explosion is a setback for space exploration.

A Blue Origin New Glenn rocket exploded on a launch pad at Cape Canaveral in Florida on Thursday night.

In a video message from Buckingham Palace, wildlife helps the King deliver a birthday card for Sir David Attenborough.

The forest where the Sumatran orangutans live has been split by a road.

Newly released video shows the moment the hatch of Artemis II's Orion capsule is unlocked to a joyful reunion with the four astronauts.

France's Eiffel Tower and Barcelona's Sagrada Família Basilica were among the famous global landmarks that went dark for an hour on Saturday night.

The 98m tall Space Launch System (SLS) and Orion spacecraft made a four mile journey from their assembly building to Pad 39B at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cdep.title: First dinosaur bone from Antarctica found in a drawer
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cdep.text:
An unassuming-looking fossil that spent 40 years lying forgotten in a drawer has turned out to be the first dinosaur bone ever found in Antarctica.

The specimen was unearthed in 1985, but the team that discovered it was not sure what it was - so it was stored away in the geology collection of the British Antarctic Survey (BAS) in Cambridge.

Now the fossil has been studied by palaeontologists who have confirmed that it is a tail bone from a type of dinosaur called a Titanosaur - this group contained the largest dinosaurs to ever walk the Earth.

The discovery helps to reveal more about how these beasts lived in a part of the world where the fossil record is sparse.

Dr Mark Evans, the collections manager at BAS, recently spotted the fossil amongst thousands of specimens brought back from expeditions to Antarctica over the decades.

"It's only when you start thinking 'what's in this drawer', that sometimes you come across something and you think, 'Ah, this looks interesting'," he said.

The specimen was originally collected on James Ross Island and its discovery was recorded in a field notebook kept by geologist Dr Mike Thomson.

Alongside a tiny, neat sketch of the fossil dated 9 December 1985 he has written "vertebra of large reptile", noting it was about 10cm wide.

Evans says the team that found it probably thought the fossil belonged to a marine reptile.

But as soon as he saw it, Evans realised the vertebra looked very dinosaur-like. And the date of its discovery meant it would have been the first dinosaur fossil found on the continent.

He called in Prof Paul Barrett from the Natural History Museum (NHM) to confirm his discovery.

"Although it's not too much to look at, it actually has a really distinctive shape," Barrett told us, holding the fossil in his hands.

He pointed to a hollow on one end of the fossil and then turned it over to reveal a rounded bump at the other. The vertebrae line up to create a series of ball-and-socket joints running from head to tail.

"As soon as I saw it, I knew what we were dealing with… it was a dead cert we were dealing with a Titanosaur," he said. "This is a combination of features that's completely unique to these types of dinosaurs."

More than 100 species of Titanosaur have now been identified around the world.

All are four-legged plant eaters, with very long necks that helped them reach up into trees and long counter-balancing tails. The very biggest Titanosaurs were more than 115ft (35m) long and weighed about 60 tonnes.

From the size of this tail bone, the scientists estimate the Antarctic Titanosaur was about 23ft (7m) in length.

"Maybe it was a juvenile dinosaur, or maybe it was a genuinely small one - one that was actually bucking the trend for the rest of the group as a smaller adult," explained Barrett.

This dinosaur would have lived 82 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous Period when Antarctica was very different from how it is today. It would have been covered in lush forest, providing ample food for the plant-eating beast.

The long-forgotten fossil now holds an important place in the history of exploration in Antarctica. Other dinosaur fossils have been found in this remote part of the world in the years after 1985 - but not very many.

Antarctica is a challenging place for palaeontologists to work and the ice conceals the prehistoric record in the rock beneath.

"It shows that an area that we now think is really uninhabitable was once actually very habitable and had this huge cast of characters living on it," explained Barrett.

"It's helping us to work out how they fitted into these broader ecosystems at the very bottom of the world about 80 million years ago."

A paper on the discovery has been published in the journal Acta Palaeontologica Polonica.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cdep.summary: The fossil was discovered in 1985 but was stored away in a drawer in Cambridge. It was discovered by a team of palaeontologists who were not sure what it was. The fossil is a tail bone from a type of dinosaur called a Titanosaur. This group contained the largest dinosaurs to ever walk the Earth.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy5d.title: How the UK's extreme heat is shifting the conversation about air-con
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy5d.text:
Mandy Bourne lives with her 80-year-old mum in a top-floor social housing flat in the West Midlands. Both struggle with health conditions exacerbated by the recent heatwaves.

For Mandy, temperature shifts can trigger flare-ups of her chronic lung condition. "I've got COPD and sometimes I can't breathe," she explains.

Across the UK, solid brick homes like theirs quietly absorb heat the way they have for decades. Charged-up walls radiate warmth back into rooms that never get the chance to cool.

Mandy says she is constantly reaching for her inhaler as her flat overheats. "It's red hot in the flat. The sun is just beaming in."

That retained warmth can push night-time temperatures in urban centres up to 7C higher than the surrounding countryside. This is the urban heat island effect and it is at its most dangerous in the early hours when bodies need cooler air and cannot find it. Modelling of a previous West Midlands heatwave by researchers from the University of Birmingham reached the bleak conclusion that the heat island impact alone accounted for roughly half the 130 heat-related deaths.

Jo Shields, head of sustainability for Mandy's housing association Walsall Housing Group, known as whg - which owns 23,000 homes across Walsall and the Midlands - hears the same complaint time and again. "The heat gain stays within the concrete or the brick," she says, "so the night-time cooling becomes harder".

Last summer, as the region baked, the residents of Ellum Pointe - a whg scheme for the over-55s - began telling their landlords they simply could not cool their flats. The response was improvised.

"We took the community room, closed all the windows and doors, and we put a mobile air-conditioning unit in there," Shields says. "And basically, we created an internal cool room." She likens it to the warm spaces opened during the pandemic for people who couldn't afford to heat their homes.

Shields' job has previously focused on decarbonising - reducing the emissions from the housing stock - but she now has to balance those pressures with the need to adapt homes to rising heat. Across the country, landlords are facing similar choices.

As Britain enters a new kind of summer, with homes built to trap warmth and heatwaves intensifying, two questions loom: should we embrace air conditioning despite its costs and consequences, and how much should we spend on adapting homes versus cutting carbon?

For 40 years, wealthy countries have focused heavily on cutting the carbon emissions that cause climate change, known as mitigation. Adaptation such as designing housing so it is more resilient to hotter temperatures and installing air conditioning has not always had the same focus.

Reducing emissions was seen as morally right because richer nations produced most of the gases that have warmed the planet. And with that focus came a funding imbalance.

In 2023, $1.8tn was given to mitigation, while adaptation did not secure even 5% of that – it scraped $65bn globally.

Spending too much on adaption was seen by many as giving up on the fight against climate change. But this mainstream view has now been challenged.

In a memo published last year, Bill Gates - a man who has poured billions into clean technology - argued that the climate movement's "doomsday" fixation on temperature targets had diverted money from the things that most improve lives in a warming world.

Climate change is serious, he wrote, but "will not lead to humanity's demise". Governments, he added, should be investing in cooling for the countries that need it.

The publication sparked backlash from climate scientists who accused Gates of making arguments based on "false dichotomies" - pitting mitigation and adaptation against each other.

Some, including US President Donald Trump, saw it as sign that the billionaire was "finally" supporting the belief that climate change was a hoax.

Gates insisted he was not arguing against cutting emissions, but rather for spending money where it saves the most suffering.

The row that followed exposed the real fault line that's coming to the surface this summer: not whether to cut carbon or adapt to the heat – but how much to spend on each.

There's another reason that muddies the waters and helps explain why cutting carbon became the prime focus – it was investable. Heat pumps and EVs can be sold. Spending on shade, ventilation and cooler hospitals and homes all produce little in the way of bankable returns - even if it reduces costs of climate change long term.

Baroness Brown - also known as the engineer Julia King, who chairs the adaptation committee of the government's Climate Change Committee - argues this imbalance is written into UK law.

Under the Climate Change Act, the mitigation half of her committee recommends legally binding carbon budgets that ministers must deliver and are marked on every year.

Adaptation has no such teeth: the government writes its own risk assessment and its own plans.

"Essentially, the government writes an essay, and our job is to say, is it doing the things it said would do in its essay. It's not actually to say, are these things any good."

Her committee has spent, she says, "almost 20 years pulling our hair out" - but this year has been different. With exquisite timing it produced a report just as the first heatwave was striking Britain in May - urging lawmakers to set hard adaptation targets.

"We've actually looked at the difference that providing some sort of support with cooling for the 30% of most vulnerable homes, and cooling in our hospitals, [with] preventive care visits. The modelling we've done suggests that that would reduce 40% of the increase in heat-related deaths that are predicted for 2050."

"We're saying these are the actions that can make a big difference."

One of the most controversial ideas in the report is on air conditioning. Right now, only 5% or so of English homes have a cooling unit. The Committee recommends fitting these devices in hospitals and care homes within 10 years, and schools in 25 years.

This goes against years of government advice that passive cooling was the preferred method - using shade, ventilation and other design features to bring down temperatures, not mechanical means.

Prof Mat Santamouris from the University of New South Wales, is the world's most-cited researcher on urban overheating.

Machines, he argues, should be the last line of defence: reflective roofing alone, in one of his studies, dragged indoor temperatures from around 43C towards 30C, while a ceiling fan gives comfort for a fraction of the cost.

Putting up unshaded glass towers in cities, he says, is "crazy". "We cannot air-condition our way out of climate change."

Santamouris is scathing about who is driving the air con demand - the industry, he says, is "extremely powerful" – adding that passive cooling adds its own economic growth, as money is spent on plumbers and builders.

Against him stand those who think Britain's hostility to cooling has curdled into a type of masochism.

David Lawrence, of the Centre for British Progress think tank, puts it plainly: we don't tell people to insulate their homes in winter and then skip the radiators. So why insist shade and shutters are enough in summer?

He points out that air conditioning is standard now in offices, hotels and shops, "but we don't expect it for schools and hospitals - which is kind of odd, because those are places where millions of people are every day", and where heat measurably dents concentration, learning and health.

This dispute over the pros and cons of the technology is becoming political.

Some London councils, following a planning "cooling hierarchy", say low-energy ways of keeping homes cool should be prioritised over air conditioning and in a small number of cases have ordered property owners to remove them; the Conservative front bench calls it "dark ages" miserabilism; other MPs and political commentators demand an "air-con revolution".

Since April, in England and Wales the Boiler Upgrade Scheme has offered £2,500 towards a reversible air-air heat pump: a machine that warms a home in winter and cools it in summer. It is, in all but name, Britain's first air-conditioning subsidy - but it is badged as a heat pump, and only worth a third of the £7,500 for a heating-only model.

Such has been the silence around this grant, that in its first month only around 45 households claimed it. By comparison, the numbers claiming a heating-only model ran into the thousands.

In Scotland homeowners can also get a £7,500 grant for a heat pump via its Home Energy scheme - but for air-air versions that could offer cooling there is no funding at all. And in Northern Ireland there is no universal heat pump grant offered for households.

Under the terms of the England and Wales scheme, some people cannot apply at all. It is closed to social housing and new builds - which many argue shuts out the very people most exposed.

Take Woolwich, in south-east London, where a resident called Keisha says her top-floor flat reaches 43C in a heatwave.

She calls the building "inhumane"; she and around twenty neighbours in Canada Court and Clifton Lodge are taking their landlord, the housing association PA Housing, to court over homes they say are unfit to live in.

Even the landlord half-concedes the ground: its chief executive accepts that a growing number of residents face "uncomfortably warm temperatures … due to the changing climate", in homes "designed to keep heat in rather than keep them cool".

Keisha is exactly the tenant the state's new cooling grant might have been written for. But as a social tenant, she is barred from it.

Baroness Brown's committee finds the most deprived neighbourhoods are more than seven times as likely to be badly exposed to heat.

The government had a long-running scheme for supporting upgrades to social housing - ECO - but it will close after this year over reports of "cowboy" installations. The replacement scheme, if it continues under the new government, will not start until next year.

There is a cruel physics beneath the financial unfairness.

Air conditioning doesn't destroy heat, it moves it - out of the flat and into the street, where, Santamouris says, it warms the air your neighbours breathe and drives up the demand for still more cooling, by about a third in his studies of Sydney.

The machines keeping the financially comfortable cool make everyone else's nights worse; and as wealthier households cool their rooms, the rest fall further behind. A thermal divide, opening street by street.

And it lands on the electricity grid at the worst possible moment.

The electricity demand for cooling peaks on still, hot evenings - just as the wind drops and solar fades, leaving gas to supply the extra energy. In so doing, further greenhouse gas emissions are generated, adding bit by bit to the climate change effect – the very one driving the temperatures and the demand for air conditioning.

And the same heat that drives the demand also weakens the supply: gas turbines lose output as the air warms, and in June several UK plants had to be turned down.

But such is the scale of the heat that people are voting with their wallets - demand for portable air con units is through the roof, regardless of grants and the environment.

The evidence from experts is that we should not go down this road.

Santamouris and Baroness Brown reach for the same answer: passive cooling first, machines where genuinely needed, clean power behind them, and the lesson that France learned painfully in the deadly heatwave of 2003 - the vulnerable protected rather than left to improvise.

Cooling every home by machine would strain the grid and warm the streets, hampering the effort to slow the warming that drives the demand.

In Tokyo, Santamouris says, so many air conditioners now pump their waste heat into the air that the exhaust alone generates heat that's measured at close to a thousand watts of warming on every square metre - as much energy as falls from the sky at midday. "It's another sun," he adds with emphasis, "another sun."

"It's not the same in London. But if we continue in the same way, in some years we will have the same results."

The heat of this year and last, and the prospects of it being repeated, is a future Jo Shields is upset by.

"It's our survival," she says. Most days, she tries to bury the thought of it - "because otherwise it terrifies me."

Meanwhile, Mandy says she is grateful that the new community room with its air conditioning is providing some immediate respite for her and her mum.

"We sit there all day with it on, it helps so much I want one in my flat."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq2e.title: Tempted by snacks before bed? Here's why - and what you can do about it
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq2e.text:
You've eaten dinner, you're comfortably full, and yet half an hour later you're raiding the kitchen cupboards. Sound familiar?

Research suggests about a third of people are snacking every night after their evening meal - for those aged 18-24, four in five are unable to resist.

Dietitian Dr Kristine Beaulieu says this spells trouble. She points to evidence showing that the more people eat within two hours of going to bed, the "greater the odds" of weight gain and obesity.

So, why are evening cravings so common? And what can you do to keep them in check?

Despite the fact we spend longer going without food when we are sleeping, research suggests our appetite naturally peaks in the evening, almost regardless of how much we have eaten earlier in the day.

Prof James Betts, who researches how the body handles food and energy at the University of Bath, says a big factor is that our "hunger hormone" ghrelin is generally higher later in the day.

"While it tends to be suppressed by meals, that really only happens after the first meal of the day, not after lunch or dinner."

But what you eat also matters. Meals rich in protein, fibre and volume tend to keep us satisfied for longer.

Betts says not having a nutritious or satiating evening meal can lead to a "crash" later, which sees people snack.

For others, the fear of waking up hungry during the night is also a motivating factor, while habit plays a role too.

"If snacking often happens in the same setting, the surrounding cues can start to trigger cravings," says Prof Suzanne Higgs, an expert in appetite at the University of Birmingham.

"For example, if someone usually snacks while watching TV, simply turning the TV on may make them feel like eating."

It's not just feelings of hunger that increase later in the day. Research suggests our appetite for calorie-dense foods also becomes stronger, driven by the brain's reward system rather than a genuine need for energy.

"Our liking and wanting for high-fat foods are greater later in the day compared to low-fat foods," says Beaulieu, who splits her time between the University of Leeds and University of Moncton in Canada.

"That hedonic drive can override signals of fullness, making us want to snack or eat a dessert even though we're full."

Even after a substantial evening meal, foods rich in sugar, fat or salt can continue to activate reward pathways in the brain, helping explain why many people find themselves reaching for something more.

So when you find yourself standing in front of the biscuit tin at 9pm, it may not be a lack of willpower. Your biology is stacked against you.

The evidence is mixed. But certainly eating a large meal late affects digestion and the body's normal preparation for sleep.

What about snacking? Here the research becomes less clear.

There is some evidence that foods high in refined carbohydrates and added sugars, from white bread and white rice to biscuits and cakes, may be linked to poorer sleep.

Researchers think this could be because such foods cause bigger swings in blood sugar levels and may alter some of the hormonal signals involved in regulating sleep and appetite.

However, teasing out cause and effect is difficult. People with poor sleep may be more likely to snack on sugary foods.

"Sleep deprivation is known to not only increase appetite, but also a desire for energy-dense foods," says Prof Jonathan Johnston, a sleep and body clock expert at the University of Surrey.

It means it is very difficult to draw firm conclusions on whether snacking in late evening disrupts sleep, says Betts.

"The evidence is far from clear and perhaps may reflect that some people respond differently to others to different foods before bed."

First, work out what's driving the snacking.

"Eating while distracted, for instance watching TV, can lead people to consume more because they pay less attention to how much they've eaten," says Higgs.

But there's no need to ban evening snacks completely, says Beaulieu.

"It's OK to eat those craved foods once in a while in moderation."

The trick, she says, is to make the healthy choice the default.

"If those craved foods aren't in the cupboard on a regular basis and a healthy option is, it means you are more likely to choose the healthier option."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq2e.summary: Research suggests a third of people are snacking every night after their evening meal. Four in five people are unable to resist snacking after their meal. The more people eat within two hours of going to bed, the "greater the odds" of weight gain and obesity.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqj3.title: UK doctor infected with Ebola being treated at London hospital
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqj3.text:
A British doctor who tested positive for Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo has been flown back to the UK.

The man, who has not been identified, landed at RAF Northolt before being transported to a specialist infectious diseases unit at the Royal Free Hospital in north London.

It is the first confirmed case of a UK national contracting Ebola during the most recent outbreak of the rare but deadly virus in DR Congo, which has so far led to more than 5,000 deaths.

Dr Renu Bindra, deputy director of the All Hazards Public Health Response team at the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), said there are "well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this" and the risk to the public remains low.

The infected doctor was brought to the UK on a medical evacuation flight as part of a joint effort by the UK and DR Congo governments and their international health partners, the Department of Health (DoH) said.

A convoy of emergency vehicles were on hand to complete the transfer following the man's arrival at the RAF base.

Three large police vans travelled at either end of the convoy, while two ambulances and another support car were involved.

Traffic was stopped and police exited the vans to keep the public away as the convoy arrived at the Royal Free Hospital.

The man is now being treated in a "highly specialised" isolation unit at the hospital, the DoH said.

The Royal Free Hospital successfully treated three health workers who had been evacuated after the Ebola outbreak in West Africa in 2014 and 2015.

There have only been four confirmed cases of the virus in the UK - one, in 1976, resulting from a laboratory incident, and three involving health workers who were responding to an outbreak in West Africa between 2014 and 2015.

None of these cases have resulted in a death.

There have been more than 10,000 confirmed cases since the recent outbreak in DR Congo started in May, which has grown to become the second most deadly recorded spate of infections, behind the outbreak in West Africa in the 2010s.

The current outbreak in DR Congo has a fatality rate of 48.6% reported at the end of last month.

Ebola can result in serious illness and death. Early symptoms include vomiting and diarrhoea but it can progress to organ failure and internal bleeding.

The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.

The ongoing outbreak centred on DR Congo is fuelled by the Bundibugyo variant of the virus.

There is no approved vaccine but the World Health Organization said experts have recommended adding two new candidate drugs to an ongoing clinical trial.

The vaccines, one developed by the University of Oxford and the Serum Institute of India, and another by the firm Moderna, will join the trial once they are approved by Congolese health authorities.

It will be the first time jabs specifically designed to protect against the Bundibugyo virus are tested during an outbreak.

Since the outbreak, Ebola cases have also been confirmed in Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmdx.title: Cocaine overtakes heroin as leading cause of drug deaths in England and Wales
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmdx.text:
The number of deaths from cocaine use in England and Wales has nearly quadrupled in a decade, overtaking those attributed to heroin for the first time.

Cocaine was linked to more than one in five drug poisoning deaths registered in 2025, more than any other single substance, with charities blaming its increased purity and availability.

Meanwhile a record 115 ketamine-linked deaths were registered, almost twice as many as in 2024, according to Office for National Statistics data.

The overall rate of drug deaths fell for the first time since 2012. But experts pointed out regional inequality was growing, with the rate of such deaths more than twice as high in the North East as in London.

There were 5,519 drug poisoning deaths registered in 2025 in England and Wales, the equivalent of 92.4 deaths per million people.

Of these, cocaine was mentioned in 1,233 cases - slightly fewer than the previous year but higher than the 1,210 deaths linked to heroin or morphine, which also marked a fall from the previous year's level.

However, deaths linked to opiate and opioid drugs combined were still higher. The ONS also said there was a lag between deaths occurring and being registered.

The fatality rate fell from 93.9 deaths per million people a year earlier, representing the first annual decline since 2012.

In September, National Records of Scotland said drug deaths there had risen by 11% in 2025 on the year before, marking the worst mortality rate in Europe,

In May the Northern Ireland Statistics and Research Agency said drug-related deaths rose by 7.1% between 2021-23 and 2022-24.

Dr James Morgan, who specialises in addiction and mental health at London Metropolitan University, said while there had been a slight decrease in deaths "the numbers remain objectively high", with total drug fatalities in England and Wales roughly doubling since 2012.

"What we are seeing is increasing polarisation and growing inequalities, where the poorest regions are falling behind, and more affluent regions doing better," he said.

The steepest increases were found in formerly industrial areas with high levels of poverty and unemployment dating back to the 1980s, including the North East, Wales, Yorkshire and the Humber, the North West and the East Midlands.

Morgan pointed out that cocaine death figures included not only those who snorted the drug but also users who injected it or smoke crack cocaine in combination with opioids or counterfeit pharmaceutical drugs.

"The small decline in deaths related to cocaine should not be over-interpreted. Most important is that deaths relating to cocaine remain roughly quadruple what they were in 2015 and are now more frequent than deaths relating to heroin or morphine," he said.

Meanwhile, ketamine was referenced in 115 deaths last year - almost double the year before and up from just seven fatalities 10 years earlier.

Morgan said this was down to lower prices and use of the drug becoming normalised. He said there were increasing reports of young people becoming dependent on ketamine and suffering acute health difficulties such as bladder damage.

Mike Trace, CEO of the addiction charity Forward Trust, said drug poisoning deaths remained high because of factors including the proliferation of very strong synthetic opioid drugs called nitazenes.

"We know that increasingly potent drugs like nitazenes are making their way on to the market. We know that established drugs like cocaine are growing in purity which means they come with much higher risks to users," he said.

Nitazenes can be many times more potent than heroin and have been linked to hundreds of UK deaths.

Tom Powell and Nyk Irvin's brother Anthony Irvin died from drug poisoning in Ramsgate in September 2025 at the age of 52.

His siblings believe his death was caused by a supply of drugs being contaminated with synthetic opioids, but say delays in blood testing mean they will never know for sure.

"Today's figures are shocking," Powell said. "We are fighting to wake people up to the scale of the problem."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm9q.title: 'Multi-cancer' blood tests coming to some GP surgeries soon
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm9q.text:
New blood tests designed to check for multiple cancers in one go will be offered to NHS patients in some 200 GP surgeries in England as part of a trial.

The aim is to detect hard-to-diagnose abdominal cancers, including liver, ovarian and pancreatic cancer, much sooner. These cancers are often found only after they have spread.

The tests look for proteins or fragments of DNA in the blood that may signal cancer. Results could help doctors decide which patients with vague symptoms need further investigations.

More than 20,000 patients aged 45 and over with symptoms such as pain or persistent bloating will be eligible to take part.

The government-funded trial, led by the University of Birmingham, will assess whether the tests are accurate enough for wider NHS use.

The idea of a blood test that can identify multiple cancers is not new.

A separate NHS trial of a test called Galleri recently failed to meet its main goal of reducing diagnoses of late-stage cancers, although researchers are still assessing its potential benefits.

Prof Peter Johnson, NHS England's national clinical director for cancer, said detecting abdomen cancer early was "notoriously difficult" because symptoms can easily be mistaken for other less serious conditions.

Earlier diagnosis gives patients a much better chance of successful treatment and survival.

Around 71,000 people in England are diagnosed each year with pancreatic, stomach, liver, ovarian or bowel cancer, and nearly 35,000 die from these diseases.

The new STRIDE-RCT trial is about detecting bowel, small bowel, stomach, oesophageal, pancreatic, liver, bile duct and gallbladder, ovarian, endometrial, kidney, bladder and prostate cancer.

Patients will provide one or two tubes of blood, taken at their GP practice, alongside routine tests.

Scientists will then analyse the samples for signs of cancer and, if present, may be able to pinpoint where in the body the tumour is located.

A positive result does not automatically mean there is cancer, and a negative result is not a guaranteed all-clear.

Health secretary Yvette Cooper said she hoped simple blood tests such as these would help identify patients needing urgent investigation much sooner.

Michelle Mitchell from Cancer Research UK said: "GPs have long needed better tools to help them navigate that uncertainty by identifying which patients require further testing and this trial in England is an important step towards addressing that need."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm9q.summary: New blood tests designed to check for multiple cancers in one go will be offered to NHS patients in some 200 GP surgeries in England. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw1m.title: Parents' concerns to trigger urgent checks in A&E
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw1m.text:
A new early warning system is being introduced in hospital emergency departments in England to help busy NHS staff identify sick children who are dangerously deteriorating.

A high overall score means a child needs more urgent attention. Concerns from staff, parents, carers or the child themselves will trigger an immediate escalation of care.

It comes after Health Secretary Yvette Cooper promised to stop "corridor care" for sick children because of long waits for hospital beds.

The new National Paediatric Early Warning System (PEWS) asks staff to check, log and grade vital signs, such as blood pressure, heart rate and oxygen levels.

The initiative is designed to save lives ahead of winter, when pressure on the NHS is at its highest.

On the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Cooper recently talked about the case of two-year-old Finlay Roberts, who died in 2024 after spending hours in a hospital corridor before being discharged.

Cooper apologised to Finlay's parents on behalf of the NHS, saying: "No child should be treated in a corridor. No patient should be treated in a corridor."

Whittington Health NHS Trust, where Finlay waited for treatment, extended its condolences to the family and said it continued to experience periods of exceptional demand across emergency care and, at times, some patients may receive care in temporary clinical areas, including corridors.

A coroner raised concerns about a lack of basic observations done by busy staff.

A similar "early warning" system to identify acutely ill adults, including those with sepsis, is already in use in emergency and general NHS hospital wards.

More than 90 hospitals across England have been using the alert system in children's wards, with different age-appropriate assessments available for babies through to teenagers.

The NHS has already said it will expand Martha's Rule to all hospital emergency departments in England. The rule gives patients, families and carers the right to request a rapid review if they are worried that a patient's condition is getting worse and their concerns are not being responded to.

The initiative is named after Martha Mills, who died aged 13 in 2021 after developing blood poisoning, or sepsis, in hospital following a bike accident.

A coroner ruled that her family's concerns about her worsening condition were not listened to and she would probably have survived had she been moved to intensive care earlier.

Martha's parents Merope and Paul came up with the idea of the rule in a bid to change the culture that contributed to her death.

A&E units will have a dedicated phone number that can be called to trigger an urgent review of a patient's care.

Duncan Burton, chief nursing officer for England, said the new early warning system for children in emergency departments was an "important next step in improving care for children and young people across England for this winter - and beyond".

He added: "In fast-paced emergency departments, staff need to spot quickly when a child's condition is deteriorating.

"This standardised approach will help them recognise the warning signs, communicate concerns, and make timely decisions when every moment matters."

The early warning system for children, PEWS, is a collaboration between NHS England and the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health and the Royal College of Nursing.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw1m.summary: New early warning system is being introduced in hospital emergency departments in England. It is designed to help staff identify sick children who are dangerously deteriorating. Health Secretary Yvette Cooper has promised to stop "corridor care" for sick children.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw5y.title: Biggest fibre boost could be scraps in your bin, experts say
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw5y.text:
Eating fruit and vegetable scraps such as peels and stalks could provide a health boost that most of us are missing, say UK researchers.

They say scraps are an overlooked source of dietary fibre and are encouraging people to try "root-to-tip" eating, including watermelon rind, pineapple core and butternut squash seeds.

Most adults do not get enough fibre. Official figures show only 4% meet the recommended 30g a day, despite its well-known benefits for gut health.

Fibre aids digestion, helps you feel fuller for longer and is linked to a lower risk of heart disease and bowel cancer.

As a rule of thumb, the skins of fruit and veg pack more fibre than the insides.

Eating a kiwi with the skin on provides 50% more fibre than having a peeled one, for example.

For their study, the scientists at King's College London analysed 12 raw or uncooked fresh foods - beetroot, bell pepper, broccoli, butternut squash, cauliflower, celeriac, curly kale, fennel, kiwi fruit, leek, pineapple and watermelon.

They found many discarded parts contained more fibre than the sections people typically eat.

Fibre is essential for your gut to work properly and helps prevent constipation.

Project lead Dr Rachel Gibson said the findings suggested people are throwing away a significant amount of fibre.

"This isn't just a nutritional loss, it's also a financial one - you're effectively throwing away a substantial portion of what you've paid for."

King's College London has been experimenting in its canteen, offering staff and students root-to-tip meals, such as banana skin curry.

At home, people might want to try leaving skins on kiwi fruit, using broccoli stalks in stir-fries or adding bell pepper seeds to dishes, the researchers suggest.

While cooking can change the fibre content, it doesn't usually destroy it all.

Steaming, microwaving or quick sautéing tends to preserve nutrients best.

Gibson said: "This isn't about perfection and this isn't about forcing people to eat unpalatable food – it's about recognising the nutritional value in components we've been conditioned to discard."

She acknowledges some may be hesitant to try it.

Some diners raised concerns during the canteen trial.

Over the nine-week period, "root-to-tip" dishes made up a third of total daily hot menu sales at the university.

Those choosing the new dishes were less likely to finish their meals than diners eating from the conventional menu.

Kirsten Jackson, a dietitian with the British Dietetic Association who specialises in irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), says the food hacks are useful as long as produce is washed thoroughly.

She suggests blending pineapple cores into smoothies, but says the tough skins are not something she would recommend.

Some stalks may need to be cooked or finely chopped to make them more palatable, she adds.

"Just because a broccoli stalk doesn't fit into tonight's meal doesn't mean it needs to go in the bin. Chop it up, freeze it and add it to a soup or stir-fry another day," she said.

She advises increasing fibre intake gradually to avoid bloating, noting that people who have IBS may find it harder to tolerate.

And there are some things to avoid entirely, said the British Nutrition Foundation.

Green potatoes and rhubarb leaves contain toxic compounds, while tough stalks and seeds may not be suitable for young children.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw5y.summary: UK researchers say scraps are an overlooked source of dietary fibre. They say they are encouraging people to try root-to-tip eating, including watermelon rind, pineapple core and butternut squash seeds. Most adults do not get enough fibre, according to official figures.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm78.title: I didn't know I was lacking in vitamin D until I collapsed at work
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm78.text:
Twenty-three-year-old Saskia Reeves-Priestley was at work when she suddenly collapsed.

"I just felt really dizzy, really nauseous, was having heart palpitations and was really hot," she says.

Saskia, a special educational needs teacher, was a keen goalkeeper who played football four times a week and felt fit and healthy. While her symptoms are not directly linked to vitamin D deficiency - she realised something was wrong.

Blood tests later showed her level was so low - it was "next to nothing".

In the UK, low vitamin D rates are increasing in some age groups - particularly in girls and young women.

According to data from the National Diet and Nutrition Survey, last year nearly a quarter of 11- to 18-year-olds were classed as deficient.

Vitamin D can come from our diet, in foods such as oily fish and meat, or supplements.

But most is made by our body when UV light in sunlight hits the skin. Lower levels of sunlight - depending on where in the world you live or the time of year - decrease the body's ability to produce it.

Covering parts of the body and wearing sunscreen also has an impact - despite their protective advantages.

Those with darker skin need exposure to stronger light to produce the same amount of vitamin D as lighter skin.

Doctors don't routinely offer blood tests to check for vitamin D deficiency, but will offer a supplement if a patient is concerned they might be high risk.

Vitamin D deficiency is linked to the bone disease rickets in babies and infants. In adults it causes a similar weakening of the bone called osteomalacia.

"They call it the silent disease," says Dr Suma Uday, a paediatric endocrinologist who wants to raise awareness of the problem.

She warns that vitamin D deficiency in young people and adults is difficult to spot and can be missed or misdiagnosed. Symptoms include fatigue and joint and bone pain.

Uday says: "It's basically silently eating away at the bones, leaving them softened and prone to breaks."

Amaka was in the middle of making dinner at her university house in Liverpool when she started shaking.

"I couldn't really see in front of me," she says. Her housemate took her to A&E - later she too would be diagnosed as vitamin D deficient.

Other than feeling tired, she says she had no symptoms: "I'm a 21-year-old student. I've got work and uni - I'm always feeling tired."

She remembers her mother suffering from low vitamin D but says she did not realise it could happen to her.

After taking supplements, Amaka feels a lot better, but she is anxious in case it happens again. "It was scary and I don't want to experience that again."

Uday joins other clinicians and academics who have formed a group - ACT NOW Vitamin D - calling for the threshold at which you are classified as deficient to be raised.

She says that would "catch" more people with low vitamin D and give a more accurate picture of how widespread the issue is. It would also mean they can treat the deficiency earlier, she says.

Uday warns of "a lifelong deficit" in women - in adolescence, then pregnancy, and then the newborn is affected.

"If you don't correct it from the very beginning," she says, "this is going to affect multiple generations."

"It's shocking," says Prof Martin Hewison, from the University of Birmingham.

He tells me that despite being 100 years on from the discovery of vitamin D "rickets hasn't gone away".

"If we have rickets in the community, there are going to be many more people who are vitamin D deficient."

He says the government should look into wider fortification of food in which vitamins are added to foods during production. Countries like Canada and Sweden have mandatory policies.

In the UK, some foods such as breakfast cereals and spreads are already fortified with vitamin D, but it is voluntary.

During the winter months, people start to lose their vitamin D levels.

"We might have to accept that for certain groups vitamin D supplementation is a matter of course," says Hewison.

Saskia is now taking vitamin D supplements regularly - and is back in goal.
