https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm78.summary: Low vitamin D rates are increasing in some age groups - particularly in girls and young women. Vitamin D deficiency is linked to the bone disease rickets in babies and infants. In adults it causes a similar weakening of the bone called osteomalacia.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq14.title: Hundreds of GP practices lose online services after collapse of tech firm
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq14.text:
Patients in many parts of the country have been left unable to access their GP surgery online after a tech firm went into administration.

Silicon Practice ran digital services, including websites, online booking and consultations, for around 500 practices in England – just under 10% of the total.

Practices across the country, including in London, Gloucestershire and Norfolk, have reported problems. Services in Wales are also affected.

GP leaders said the problem would cause huge disruption, given the scale of online booking that now takes places.

Patients in areas that are affected are being advised they will have to make appointments via the phone. The NHS app is working.

Since last year, all practices in England have had to offer online appointment booking. Currently, more than 40% of appointments are made that way.

An NHS England spokesperson said while "the majority" of GP practice websites were running as normal, some using Silicon Practice will be affected.

"If your GP practice website is unavailable and you need help, you should contact your practice by phone or in person as usual."

Affected practices have been contacted by NHS England with advice on how to maintain business continuity and minimise the impact on patient care.

Silicon Practice ran the digital tool FootFall, which it advertised as reducing patient phone calls to practices by 30%, by working to "free your reception team from routine admin and manage demand more efficiently. Proven in 1,000+ GP practices across the UK".

Prof Victoria Tzortziou Brown, president of the Royal College of GPs, said: "GP practice websites are an increasingly important way for patients to access care, book appointments and find information about the services available to them.

"When websites are not working, it can be hugely disruptive for patients and place additional pressures on already stretched practice teams.

"It is vital that any disruption to practice websites is addressed promptly to ensure patients are able to access care."

She said affected practices must receive prompt, practical support from NHS England and local NHS organisations to restore their websites, minimise disruption and ensure patients know how to contact their practice and access the care they need in the meantime.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq14.summary: Silicon Practice ran digital services for around 500 practices in England. The NHS app is working and the majority of practices are running as normal. GP leaders said the problem would cause huge disruption, given the scale of online booking.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c804.title: There's finally a treatment for my five-year-old's dementia - but it'll cost me £3m
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c804.text:
The mum of a five-year-old boy with a rare form of dementia has to pay almost £3m for his life saving treatment.

Tate McDaid, from Swansea, was diagnosed with Sanfilippo Syndrome - a form of dementia that just over 100 UK children have - when he was four.

In September, the first gene therapy to treat the condition in children was approved in the US.

His mum Tammy said she spent "months praying" for its approval but discovered the treatment is to set cost £2.95 million per child, with it unclear how families outside the US can fund this.

Health officials from Wales are currently talking to those in the US to see what potential access pathways there are for Tate.

"I was excited when the treatment initially got approved but then reality hit hard the next day," Tammy said.

This was when she read the US price for the one-time treatment had been set at $3.95 million.

Tammy contacted Ultragenyx, who developed the treatment, in the hope of understanding how families outside the US, who do not have health insurance there, will cover the costs.

"We understand what they are charging for American citizens, but they've got health insurance," she added.

"What is it for us in the UK?

"Not even just the UK, but everyone else in the world looking for this treatment."

Explaining how the US approved drug, FAYUVI, would work for families outside the US, Ultragenyx said: "There is not a single estimate we can provide for the total cost of care for an international patient, as those costs would depend on the patient's individual medical needs and the treating institution."

The Society for Mucopolysaccharide Diseases, a charity which helps children living with Sanfilippo Syndrome, said about 140 children in the UK have the condition.

There is currently no cure for Sanfilippo Syndrome Type A, also called Mucopolysaccharidosis type III (MPS III), but the new drug could delay its onset, and allow Tate to remain active for longer.

The condition, described as "childhood Alzheimer's" or "childhood dementia" due to its neurodegenerative nature, causes the gradual loss of abilities, such as walking and eating.

It can progress more rapidly after the age of five, which is why Tammy said "it's really a battle of time" for her to raise enough money to get her son the treatment that is not available yet in the UK.

She said: "If a millionaire turned around tomorrow and gave us the money, we'd go to the US straight away."

With Tate turning six this month, Tammy doesn't believe time is on their side.

"Tate is already shown signs of cognitive decline," she added.

"The older he gets the less the treatment will work and the more ability he will lose in the process.

"I feel like we are at a turning point and I'm petrified."

Describing him as "the happiest little man" who is "blissfully unaware" of his problems, Tammy explained how important Tate's mobility is to him.

"He doesn't speak, he's never spoken. But his mobility is everything to him and that is why I'm fighting for it," she said.

Tammy began raising money before the new drug was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration and now has more than £160,000.

But this covers only about 5% of the total estimated cost of the treatment.

"Unfortunately, we're in a world where we need millions, not hundreds of thousands," she added.

"I'm just really hoping by some miracle the pharmaceutical company eventually come back to us and say they can do it for a little bit cheaper, but it's still going to be in the millions."

Ultragenyx said: "We are pursuing a global regulatory strategy, and FDA approval is an important first step in our long-term goal of bringing this treatment option to families around the world.

"We also understand the urgency families affected by Sanfilippo syndrome Type A face in identifying treatment options and why some may consider travelling to the US to access gene therapy.

"We recommend families work with their child's healthcare provider to understand what potential access pathways may exist before assuming this is their only option."

Staff from the Noah's Ark Children's Hospital in Cardiff are currently discussing this with officials in the US on the family's behalf.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c804.summary: Tate McDaid, from Swansea, was diagnosed with Sanfilippo Syndrome when he was four. The condition causes the gradual loss of abilities, such as walking and eating. His mum Tammy spent "months praying" for its approval but discovered the treatment is to set £2.95 million per child.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c20e.title: 'You feel that you're not alone' - the young people finding community in grief
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c20e.text:
Luke Alfano was 21 when his dad, who just two weeks earlier had been diagnosed with cancer, died.

At the time, Luke did not know what to do or where to turn.

Five years later, he founded Too Young to Grieve, a community offering young people a casual space to "have a moan, have a laugh, talk about your grief and just know that people understand you".

The group is based in more than 20 locations, including London, Manchester, the US and Australia - and now, Belfast.

Losing someone you love is never easy. But for Luke, the shock of his dad dying so suddenly, and so early in Luke's life, was especially difficult.

"I lost my dad when I was 21. I didn't feel like there was much out there for young adults experiencing loss," Luke told BBC News NI.

"That initial first year or two, I didn't really know what was going on.

"I didn't know what this thing called grief was, I just ignored it."

It was not until Luke, then 25, lost his grandmother that he realised he had "not really processed" his dad's death.

"That experience was a trigger to think back to what happened with my dad and think I don't want to experience that again, so let me try and understand it a bit more," he said.

Luke founded Too Young to Grieve, which offers young people who have experienced grief the opportunity to meet in person, with activities ranging from walks and hikes, to pottery painting and football tournaments.

"When you're 18 to 35, you're grieving someone that most people are going to turn to for a lot of the most important decisions in your life," he said.

"You just want to talk about your person, or just have a space to talk about how you're feeling."

When Chris Guiller's dad died at the age of 57, just five months after being diagnosed with cancer, it came as a shock to the whole family.

Chris was just 26 at the time.

"You think you have your parents until later on in life, so when it comes at such a young age, it's difficult," he told BBC News NI.

As a young person, he felt isolated by his grief.

"I didn't have people around me that understood what I was going through," he said.

Almost two years later, Chris now runs the Belfast branch of Too Young to Grieve - an experience he describes as "fantastic".

"You know you're not going through it by yourself. What you're feeling is normal," he added.

In 2025, two days before Christmas, Katherine Macauley's fiancee Peter died following an accident at work.

"I still can't believe that it's real," the 32-year-old said.

Though she believes her grief will "never end", her hope is to find "ways to cope" with it.

And one such way has been Too Young to Grieve.

"Too Young to Grieve is a really lovely way of bringing people together that are in similar situations," she said.

"You feel that you're actually not alone and that other people can have some shared experience with you, and that you can learn from that and you can comfort each other through that.

"It's a really, really wonderful community and group of people."

Luke Alfano said he would like to see resources around grief and coping with bereavement better signposted in schools and universities.

Last year, the Department for Education published statutory guidance that said lessons on loss, grieving and bereavement should take place in primary and secondary schools from September 2026.

However, no such guidance exists in Northern Ireland.

A spokesperson for the Department of Education said "schools have pastoral care policies and structures" so that children know who they can contact if they require support regarding bereavement.

"In terms of curriculum, the Council for the Curriculum, Examinations and Assessment has provided a range of resources which address grief, loss, and bereavement both at primary and post-primary level," they said.

"I lost her when I was 14."

In 2017, William Gregg's mother died. At the time, he did not know "how to handle it".

"It tore me apart for a little while, I sort of lost my way," he said.

"It can be quite catastrophic and emotionally damaging."

William said Too Young to Grieve had been "very helpful".

"It's good to know that there people out there who have gone through something similar and are able to talk about it.

"Whenever I was young, I didn't really have anybody to talk to."

He added that the community has been especially beneficial for his mental health, as the group gives him a space to "express yourself freely".

Chris Guiller agrees.

He said that socialising was especially important for people who were grieving, as they often will not leave the house.

He explained that Too Young to Grieve helped people "build friendships so you have a community around you that you can fall back on".

Chris said the group was "really needed" in Northern Ireland, a region academics have previously said spends less on mental health services per head than other regions, despite having "more complex cases".

"The mental health side of things over here is a bit further behind than other parts of the UK and Ireland," he said.

"You need something like this here because there are a lot of people suffering out there that think they're alone. And they're not.

"I know my dad would be extremely proud."

Luke said the group has helped him grieve.

"Having the opportunity to share things about my dad has given me a great perspective on grief, and it's helped me on my own healing journey as well," he said.

So what does Luke think his dad would make of the group built in his legacy?

"My dad wanted me to be a professional footballer. Unfortunately I wasn't quite good enough.

"But in terms of the community we've built, it could fill a lot of professional stadiums."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c20e.summary: Too Young to Grieve offers young people a space to talk about their grief. Luke Alfano, now 25, founded the group after his dad died two weeks earlier. He says he felt isolated by his grief as a young person.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx4g.title: Under-16s could be banned from buying energy drinks in Wales
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx4g.text:
Young people and experts say they support the Welsh government's plan to ban children under-16 from buying high-caffeine energy drinks.

The Welsh government said that evidence suggests a link between "consumption of high-caffeine energy drinks and negative health outcomes", and was considering a ban on under-16s buying them.

BBC Wales spoke to young people in Cardiff who said they supported the proposed ban, with one 17-year-old saying it was "really easy to start relying on them".

The British Soft Drinks Association said the proposed ban was "unnecessary and not supported by robust evidence of overconsumption or harm".

The news follows the ban in England where drinks like Red Bull, Monster, Relentless and Prime will be illegal to sell to under-16s from April, aimed at reducing obesity levels, disrupted sleep and anxiety.

Any drink containing more than 150mg of caffeine per litre will be illegal to sell to children and younger teenagers in shops, restaurants, cafes, vending machines and online.

Lower-caffeine soft drinks, such Diet Coke, as well as tea and coffee are not affected.

Excessive caffeine consumption has been linked to headaches and sleep problems, and experts say young people can be more sensitive to caffeine as they have smaller bodies and their brains are still developing.

Some popular drinks brands contain more caffeine than two cups of coffee or four cans of cola.

Vee, 17, from Cardiff, said she was happy about the proposed ban, while Sunny, 16, urged people to "just have a coffee" instead of an energy drink.

Too much caffeine can cause a rapid heart rate, abnormal heart rhythms and seizures, and although rare, there have been some deaths linked to excess caffeine.

The sugary versions of the drinks can also contribute to obesity and damaged teeth, according to the Association of UK Dieticians.

Currently any drink, other than tea or coffee, with over 150mg requires a label warning of its high-caffeine content that says it is not recommended for children or pregnant or breast-feeding women.

For most adults, up to 400mg of caffeine a day, or about four cups of instant coffee or five cups of tea, is safe.

Aisling Pigott, a nutritionist and registered dietician in Cardiff, said she was pleased to hear of the proposed ban but that it was probably "10 years too late".

She said Wales had "disproportionate concerns around diet and lifestyle" and while this would not be a "magic bullet", it was a "step in the right direction".

Pigott described caffeine as "a bit like going into your overdraft - you might immediately have a little bit more money or cash, but that does need to be repaid in some format".

She said someone may have a little more concentration, but that was "followed by a crash".

"Because I'm a dietitian, my concern around excessive consumption of these drinks also sits with what what are they not consuming when they're drinking?

"I see and hear a lot of children and young people drinking these drinks instead of food, so using the sugar and caffeine as an easier access to give energy than really nutritious, healthy, balanced diet."

In a written statement, Public and Preventative Health Minister Nerys Evans said the latest evidence suggested a link between consumption of high-caffeine energy drinks and negative health outcomes in children.

"This includes increased frequency of headaches, irritation, tiredness and stomach aches, reduced sleep duration and quality and increased risk of stress, anxiety and depression," she said.

"The previous Welsh government consulted and gathered evidence on proposals to restrict the sale of high-caffeine energy drinks to children under 16, with broad support for action."

Evans added: "Having considered the evidence and responses to that earlier consultation, the current Welsh government intends to take forward proposals to prohibit the sale of high-caffeine energy drinks to children under 16, subject to the outcome of this consultation.

"These are drinks, other than tea or coffee, that contain over 150mg of caffeine per litre."

The Welsh government said the consultation would seek views on the proposed "enforcement framework", including "online age-verification arrangements, assessing compliance activity, sanctions, implementation timescales and monitoring arrangements".

British Soft Drinks Association said its members had not marketed or promoted the sale of energy drinks to under-16s since 2010.

"All high-caffeine beverages carry a 'not recommended for children' label. The available evidence shows that the vast majority of caffeine consumed by children and adolescents comes from sources other than energy drinks."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx4g.summary: Welsh government considering ban on under-16s buying high-caffeine energy drinks. Ban follows ban in England where drinks like Red Bull, Monster, Relentless and Prime will be illegal to sell to under- 16s. British Soft Drinks Association says proposed ban is "unnecessary and not supported by robust evidence of overconsumption

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crn8.title: Health minister instructs trusts to pause cuts to Phone First service
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crn8.text:
Northern Ireland's health minister has instructed trusts which have not yet stood down their Phone First service to "pause any planned cessation" of the scheme.

The telephone triage system has already been scrapped by the Belfast Trust; it was to end within weeks in the Northern Trust and is under review in the Western Trust.

Phone First is aimed at reducing unnecessary visits to hospital emergency departments (EDs) by providing advice to patients on appropriate care options.

In a statement to BBC News NI, the Department of Health (DoH) said health trusts that have not yet stood the service down will be "liaising with their external providers for an extension".

The Northern Trust's line was due to close on 27 November, but its interim chief executive, Suzanne Pullins said on Thursday that they have been told to "pause the formal withdrawal to allow for reassessment".

Pullins announced the development as she appeared before Stormont's Health Committee to answer questions about the trust's savings plans.

Last month, committee members had expressed concern that Phone First was being cut just as hospital EDs prepared to deal with increased winter pressures.

Pullins acknowledged those concerns on Thursday, saying the decision to stand it down was in "no way a reflection of the service" which was "very valued".

But she explained that there were "no easy choices" given the scale of the financial savings the trust had been asked to find.

Phone First costs £500,000 to run and the trust has been asked to make £53.8m in savings for this year.

The DoH statement said that the Belfast Trust had redeployed its Phone First staff "to urgent care services to secure access to Urgent and Emergency Care".

It added that all trusts are focused on supporting EDs "to ensure optimal patient flow and access to the right care in the right place at the right time and from the right clinician to meet the patient needs".

Phone First was initially introduced during the pandemic in late 2020 to reduce the risk of Covid-19 spreading among patients in crowded hospital waiting rooms.

Under the system, patients call a dedicate line before travelling to hospital to check if they really need to go to an ED or if they could be treated elsewhere

Operating in a similar manner the NHS's non-emergency 111 medical helpline in England, Scotland and Wales, it was designed to be used in urgent but not life-threatening cases - the public is still advised to always call 999 immediately if someone's life is at risk.

It was trialled in Causeway Hospital before being gradually rolled out across all five hospital trust areas.

However, it was run by five separate teams who each had different hours and different contact numbers.

Before it closed its line at the end of September, the Belfast Trust estimated that move would save it approximately £500,000.

At last month's health committee meeting, senior staff from the Belfast Trust were questioned about their decision to cut the line as winter approached.

"It's frustrating, it's not something that we wanted to do... but we felt that it was the least worst option," said Claire Corry, Director of Finance at the Belfast Trust.

Her boss, Chief Executive Jennifer Welsh, explained the projected £800m shortfall in Northern Ireland's health budget meant all trusts had been instructed to find savings that "could be delivered without causing harm to service users".

Welsh explained Phone First was scrapped in Belfast in order to prioritise other services that "we think would generate more benefit for patients and staff".

She told Northern Ireland Assembly members at the 22 October meeting that there "wasn't a huge uptake in the service" and that it "wasn't having a huge impact".

However, Northern Ireland-wide statistics show a rising trend in usage over the past six years.

The Belfast Telegraph reported that calls reached their highest ever level in the same month that Belfast Trust closed its line.

There were 18,263 calls in September, 12,098 (66%) of which resulted in patients being referred on to EDs.

It was suggested to last month's committee that because two thirds of callers end up in EDs anyway, Phone First was less effective than some other services at reducing pressures.

But committee chair Philip McGuigan, of Sinn Féin, pointed out that Phone First may have helped to keep more than 6,000 callers out of ED in September alone.

During that meeting, McGuigan secured the support of the committee to write to the DoH to ask about the future of Phone First.

Before the minister announced the pause, BBC News NI had contacted all five trusts this week to ask about the future of their telephone triage services.

The Belfast Trust said its decision to stop its Phone First was taken "in the context of the very significant financial challenge" it and the wider health service was facing.

It added "other care options are still available" and pointed patients to its Choose the Right Care webpage in cases of urgent but non-life-threatening illness or injury.

The Western Trust said its Phone First service was being "assessed against current spend and affordability" as part of its savings plan.

"No decision has been made at this time and the service continues to operate as normal," its spokesperson added.

The South Eastern Trust said its Phone First service at both the Lagan Valley and Downe hospitals "will remain unchanged".

It added that Phone First is "not required" at the Ulster Hospital because its Urgent Care Centre directs patients "to the most appropriate service when they arrive".

A spokesman for the Southern Trust told BBC News NI it has no plans to withdraw Phone First.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crn8.summary: Northern Ireland's health minister has instructed trusts to "pause any planned cessation" of Phone First service. Northern Ireland-wide statistics show a rising trend in usage over the past six years. Ulster Hospital says Urgent Care Centre directs patients to the most appropriate service.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c65y.title: The NHS is relying more on charities - and that might be creating problems for patients
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c65y.text:
The distress of the man on the other end of the video call was clear to dementia specialist nurse Louise Burns. He was struggling to get his elderly mum, who had the condition, out of hospital - she needed support to move into her home.

Burns was able to put him at ease. She is part of a team running virtual clinics that support more than 100 patients and family members a week: "No matter what stage they are at, we try to help," she says. She explained the discharge process and where to go for help. The man's mother was soon back where she wanted to be.

Traditionally, a service like this would have been run by the National Health Service – but the clinic, which was set up during Covid and continued because of strong demand, is entirely funded by the charity Dementia UK.

The charity's chief nursing officer Paul Edwards says it is "trying to fill the gaps" within stretched NHS services. Burns adds: "The NHS and social care are under such huge pressure and dementia cases are rising - it's not always easy to get the support you need."

Dementia UK is just one of many charities working in the health sphere. From children's care to mental health and cancer services, charities are playing an increasingly important role in caring for patients.

Some - largely in England - have formal NHS contracts, while others work side-by-side with the health service across the UK, trying to provide additional support to patients in a way the NHS cannot.

A desire from governments of different parties from the 1990s onwards to develop a market of providers – NHS, private and voluntary sector – has meant the charity sector is now big business in health.

It's estimated that cancer charities alone raise more than £1bn a year, and the NHS in England spends nearly £2bn a year buying services from the not-for-profit and voluntary sector.

But there are concerns about the scale of charities' involvement in delivering frontline services - including from within the voluntary sector itself. Those directly providing services say they are having to subsidise squeezed NHS budgets.

And despite the good intentions of the charitable sector, some critics say its work with the NHS means more money ends up in wealthier communities. Defenders of charities' involvement, however, say much-needed funding should be welcomed.

So is the growing role of charities a symptom of a health service at breaking point - or a positive way of involving the public in their health care? And what are the risks?

There's nothing new about UK health charities taking on a major role in delivering services. Prior to 1948, British healthcare was provided through a patchwork of local charities, voluntary organisations, local authorities and private arrangements. Many hospitals depended on charitable donations, subscriptions and fundraising events to survive.

The creation of the NHS transformed this model. Most hospitals were brought into public ownership and funded through taxation. NHS founder Aneurin Bevan believed healthcare should not depend on charity, and restrictions were placed on NHS hospital charities actively raising money. But they did not disappear completely - they could still receive gifts and donations.

A major shift came with the Health Services Act 1980, which encouraged a more active fundraising culture. From then on, NHS charities expanded significantly and became increasingly professionalised. By the 1990s and beyond, they were raising substantial sums for equipment, buildings, research, and the likes of play areas in children's wards and well-equipped staff rooms.

Today, distinct from charities devoted to particular diseases or conditions, there are now more than 220 NHS charities attached to hospitals or community services, which raise £620m a year.

Ellie Orton, chief executive of NHS Charities Together, which represents them, says that while this sum may sound high, it represents only around 0.3% of the health budget.

She says the very purpose of the charities is to provide support, equipment and services that are additional to what the NHS provides. Recent schemes involve things like CPR training for members of the public, defibrillators being placed in community venues and green spaces in hospitals.

But it is a fine line. Scanners, blood transfusion equipment and emergency department co-ordinators have also been funded by charities. Some would say say core NHS functions like these are exactly what we pay our taxes for.

Orton defends this. "It's just the way it is now. We shouldn't get too ideological about this. It's not helpful to think the state can do everything. Yes we pay taxes but that has to cover lots – and it's finite. If our fund-raising means a parent of an ill child can stay close to their child while they are in hospital in a room funded by a charity, why not?"

And she says her discussions with the government suggest that there is increasing interest in what charities can raise and also what larger philanthropic donations by individuals or organisations can achieve.

In recent years, huge one-off sums have been raised. During the pandemic, the NHS Charities Together Covid appeal resulted in a £10m donation by the trading firm XTX Markets, while the Rausing family - best known for founding the food packaging giant Tetra Pak – gave £5m.

Rugby league legend Sir Kevin Sinfield's fundraising in support of his friend Rob Burrow helped bring in £6.8m for a specialist motor neurone disease centre at Leeds Teaching Hospitals.

"Of course, we are not talking about going back to a pre-1948 situation, but there is real interest in what such philanthropy can do," says Orton.

But there are inequalities. The NHS charity sector is dominated by some of the big London hospitals and specialist cancer and children's centres. The Royal Marsden and Great Ormond Street charities between them are responsible for nearly a sixth of the investment made by NHS charities.

"This does concern us," admits Orton. "It's not always a level playing field, but the answer to that is to help the NHS charities that don't raise as much to raise more."

The legislation change in the 1980s, coupled with the market reforms of the 1990s, also helped pave the way for specialist disease-specific charities such as Macmillan, Marie Curie and Dementia UK to get involved in the delivery of NHS services.

For example, over the past three decades, Dementia UK has developed a well-established network of specialist dementia nurses known as Admiral Nurses, who work in a range of hospital and community settings. The model is based on the charity co-funding posts with the NHS for up to two years with the expectation that the NHS will then take on the funding.

But with demand increasing, Edwards says it is becoming a "struggle" to get the funding needed from the NHS or from donations. "We are being asked to fund them for longer or find more than half the cost," he says. "Services are really being cut back."

And it is not just in dementia care that charities are noticing a squeeze. The charity WellChild has helped establish a network of 54 specialist nurses who work with very sick children. It funds these posts for the first three years, before responsibility for funding is expected to transfer to the NHS.

But disappointingly for the charity, for the first time this year a nurse post was not kept on, says Amy Mitchell, WellChild's director of programmes. What's more, WellChild's nurses are only meant to carry a caseloads of 15, but the average is currently 40. "Services are being dismantled - and our nurses are propping things up," Mitchell adds.

Others in the voluntary sector agree. Charities are increasingly being asked to do more with less, says Mark Yates, chief operating officer of Rethink Mental Illness, "and there is too often an expectation that we will absorb shortfalls ourselves to keep essential services running".

Parkinson's UK told the BBC its funding has helped the NHS pay for around 70% of the specialist nurses working in the field - and its chief executive officer Caroline Rassell says it's unfair on people affected by the disease.

"Charities having to fund these posts is effectively an additional 'tax' on people with Parkinson's as they are our main donors," says Rassell. "Nursing care should be the cornerstone of what the NHS offers."

Polling by the National Council for Voluntary Organisations shows 71% of health charities say the value of their contracts are not enough to meet the demand for the services they provide with many using their own donations to keep them going.

The survey dates back to 2023, but the NCVO says there is nothing to suggest the situation has eased.

NCVO chief influencing officer Leigh Brimicombe says it's quite clear charities are having to "subsidise" the NHS and wider public services and the government needs to address it by offering contracts that "cover the full cost of delivery".

"Otherwise, we run the risk of services being reduced or cut completely, at a time that communities in need are relying on them most."

For its part, the NHS is adamant that charities remain a valuable partner. NHS England points out that while the value of contracts to the voluntary sector in terms of proportion of the budget has dropped, it has still risen in cash terms.

In a statement, NHS England told the BBC the current 10-year plan looks to build on the "potential" of these partnerships and given the sector a "stronger voice" in health and care.

It's a complex relationship, believes Helen Gilburt, of the King's Fund think tank. Charities bring "real benefits" through their expertise and close ties to communities, she says, and there is "an element of subsidising" as the NHS seeks savings. But the situation has also "created inequalities" in the funding and support available for different diseases, she believes.

For instance, some areas, like cancer, have an established charitable sector "which is able to attract large amounts of funding", she says. These charities have been able to advocate for their patients, work with the NHS to enhance specialist services, and use their funds to develop services of their own.

Then, she says, there are charities in some sectors - "Parkinson's and dementia are good examples" – which are investing their own funds to develop specialist roles. "But they would argue this does not go far enough to meet the needs of people they serve.

"Then there are other areas, like sickle cell disease for example, where the charity sector is small and has even less funding."

Inequalities exist within sectors, too, say experts. Take hospices, for instance. "The fact remains that some communities will be able to give more than others, leading to inequalities in hospice provision," says Toby Porter, chief executive officer of Hospice UK.

And as a result, says Sarah Scobie, deputy director of research at the Nuffield Trust think tank, "more people from deprived areas die in the place where most people say they don't want to die – in hospital".

Not all of these differences can be explained by fundraising capacity. Health literacy – people's ability to navigate services and advocate for themselves – can also affect access to support, she says.

But her concern is clear – the scale of charity involvement in the NHS can widen inequalities.

As Orton points out, the UK is not returning to the pre-NHS era, when healthcare depended on charitable giving. Yet charities are no longer operating on the margins of the system, either.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm0r.title: Why a US-funded vaccine trial on babies was cancelled in Guinea-Bissau
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm0r.text:
A proposed trial of a hepatitis B vaccine on newborn babies in Guinea-Bissau has been cancelled following accusations that the trial was "unethical" and "neocolonial".

The trial was funded by the US, under Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, who has a long record of expressing scepticism about vaccines.

Police have seized a batch of vaccines from the research centre at the heart of the controversy.

The proposed trial drew international criticism because it planned to withhold a vaccine recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) from half of the participating newborns.

Some public health experts argued that the proposed trial raised broader questions about whether vulnerable populations in African countries were being asked to take risks that researchers would not accept in wealthier countries.

The BBC has asked the US department of health and human services for comment.

Here is what you need to know.

The study was planned at the Bandim Health Project, a research centre that has operated in Guinea-Bissau since 1978.

It was designed to involve 14,000 newborns, with half receiving a hepatitis B vaccine shortly after birth and the other half not being given the shot.

Bandim said the trial aimed to investigate whether the hepatitis B vaccine given at birth has broader health effects beyond preventing infection.

Previous studies in The Gambia and Guinea-Bissau have raised questions about a possible link to increased mortality.

Researchers argued that because Guinea-Bissau does not currently offer routine hepatitis B vaccinations at birth, despite WHO recommendations, they have a unique opportunity to study its effects before such vaccines are introduced in 2028.

But critics questioned the ethics of withholding the vaccine from some babies, particularly in one of the world's poorest countries, where the infection is widespread.

The Trump administration funded the proposed study, with the CDC awarding the University of Southern Denmark (SDU) $1.6m (£1.2m) in December 2025.

Walter Kazadi Mulombo, the WHO representative in Guinea-Bissau, told the BBC they became concerned after receiving questions about the study and finding no publicly available protocol.

He said the main ethical concern was that the trial would withhold an intervention already proven to protect newborns against hepatitis B.

"The vaccine has been used for more than 30 years in more than 115 countries," he said. "A study that will withhold that intervention from other newborns is unethical."

He warned that babies could be exposed to the virus during childbirth if their mothers were infected, as well as later in life.

Nearly a fifth of the population of Guinea-Bissau are infected with hepatitis B, a viral infection that affects the liver.

Those infected during infancy are particularly likely to develop chronic infections, which kill up to 25% of people, mostly through liver failure or liver cancer, according to data published in 2020.

The WHO is working with the government to bring forward the birth-dose vaccine.

"The country had been expected to add it to its routine immunisation schedule in 2028, but officials are considering introducing it in the first quarter of next year," Mulombo said.

Guinea-Bissau currently vaccinates children against hepatitis B at six weeks, which means it is less effective.

Guinea-Bissau's government prohibited hepatitis B vaccine trials involving children in January. At the time, it requested a team of experts from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) to help evaluate the study.

Health Minister Quinhin Nantote said in October that the suspension remained in force and had not been overturned by the Council of Ministers after reports emerged claiming that the trial would be taking place after all.

"We were surprised to learn from media reports that the study might proceed," Nantote said. "We are outraged because even I, as the minister responsible for this sector, was not informed."

The dispute intensified after the SDU said a revised study protocol had received ethical approval "from the relevant authorities in Guinea-Bissau", which Nantote denied.

Dr Gavin Yamey, a professor of global health and public policy at Duke University in the US, criticised the proposal.

"The proposed trial reeks of neocolonialism," he told the BBC, questioning why the research was not being conducted in Denmark.

His criticism centred on the decision to withhold a recommended vaccine from some newborns in a country where hepatitis B is widespread.

SDU dean Jakob Grauslund said the trial had never started, no babies had been enrolled and no vaccinations administered as part of the research.

The SDU said it had received a separate, positive assessment from the university's own research ethics committee.

Grauslund said the university had sought an additional independent assessment, although Danish law did not require one.

He added that the relevant Danish statutory research ethics bodies were unable to undertake the review.

Following the approval from the SDU's ethics committee, Grauslund decided that the project could proceed.

He, however, stressed that this did not replace the separate authorisation required from Guinea-Bissau's authorities.

On 19 October, Guinea-Bissau's Judicial Police searched the Bandim Health Project's facilities in the capital, Bissau, and seized a batch of hepatitis B vaccines.

Police said the batch was intended for vaccinating children but did not disclose how many doses had been seized or the specific grounds for the investigation.

They stressed that the seizure did not, in itself, mean the vaccines were defective or unsafe.

The police have not explicitly said whether their investigation relates to the proposed trial, the importation of the vaccines or other circumstances surrounding the batch.

Grauslund said he could not comment on the seizure of the vaccines.

The proposed trial was funded by the US government at a time of significant changes to vaccine policy under President Donald Trump and Health Secretary Kennedy.

Under Kennedy's leadership, a US vaccine panel attempted to end a longstanding recommendation that all newborns receive a hepatitis B vaccine at birth, but a federal judge later blocked this, along with other changes to vaccine policy made by the Trump administration.

Critics have questioned whether the research could help support that policy shift, although the study's stated aim was to investigate potential effects of the vaccine beyond preventing infection.

Kennedy has praised the Danish researchers as "the deities of vaccine research", and cited earlier findings from their work in support of concerns about vaccine safety. A subsequent study by some of the same researchers, however, found no evidence of the previously reported effect.

There is no evidence that the proposed trial was designed to justify a change in US policy.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8r4.title: Period products 'essential not optional'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8r4.text:
Sanitary towels and tampons are "basic health and hygiene products" which are "essential and not optional", the public health director has said.

Matt Tyrer's department is spearheading the rolling out of a scheme which will see women and girls on the Isle of Man access free period products.

The Period Products (free provision) Act bill was introduced by MHK Joney Faragher as a private members bill in 2024. It has now been given Royal Assent but it will not come into force until October 2027.

Tyrer said making the products available would also ensure women or girls will not have to miss school, work or everyday activities.

Making them available to households on low incomes, he said, ensured women, girls and those who menstruate, can access them.

"We want to ensure people who need them have access to them as these are basic health and hygiene products that are essential and not optional," said Tyrer.

The scheme follows similar programmes in Scotland and Northern Ireland.

One of the co-founders of the Manx Menstrual Movement, Rhian Evans described Royal Assent as "a long time coming".

In 2023, Evans and Nicki Gaskell created the movement after speaking about period poverty and the basic right to have access products.

They then set up donation stations across the island as well as a pick and mix station at Douglas City Library.

They praised MHK Joney Faraghar, who they approached in 2024, saying she had done "a lot of work behind the scenes for this".

Evans said the pick and mix station started as an interim solution but they hoped it would continue.

"It is so important, it is also bittersweet because it also highlights that there is period poverty here and we wholeheartedly believe that your financial background does not matter, anyone who menstruates, should have this access," she said.

Becky Rolwey, head of public health communities, said the organisation would now engage with people to understand the needs going forward.

"We really want to ensure that people aren't embarrassed to access it, be it a father or brother or even a male friend and that they can get it easily," she said.

Rolwey said over the next year public health needed to determine the best and most sustainable products it could make available.

"Some people say a pad only costs X amount and is really cheap, but we know that those are not sufficient for everybody's needs," she said.

While exact locations on where the products could be found are not yet available, Tyrer said local authorities, schools, libraries, the Isle of Man Foodbank and other charities could potentially be used.

He added: "Fundamentally we want anybody who needs period products to be able to access them in a place that is convenient and appropriate."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cv62.title: 'The veil of shame around postnatal depression needs to go'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cv62.text:
"Women, since the beginning of time, have birthed and looked after children and I just couldn't be bothered. I thought I was lazy."

Those are the words of Laura, 45, from Cheltenham, in Gloucestershire, who weeks after undergoing an emergency Caesarean section struggled so much with postnatal depression that she needed psychiatric care.

The NHS says postnatal depression, also known as postpartum depression, is a "common" mental health condition that can happen after having a baby.

"Postnatal depression can happen to anyone and this is why the veil of shame needs to come down, through education or through listening to people," said Laura.

Symptoms can include feeling fearful, anxious or irritable, alongside difficulty concentrating and sleeping.

It can also be accompanied by suicidal thoughts and struggling to bond with your baby.

An NHS spokesperson advised seeking support from your GP, health visitor or midwife if these symptoms persist, in addition to charities such as Mind and PANDAS.

According to the NHS, the condition affects more than one in 10 new mothers.

Laura said her birthing experience with her son Arthur in June 2018 was "traumatic but incredibly quick" after he became "very stressed" in the final stages.

About two months after his arrival, Laura said simple household chores triggered negative thoughts which eventually spiralled into suicidal thoughts.

"I used to think anything I did wasn't good enough," Laura said. "I thought, 'I'm a fraud, they all think I've got something wrong with me'."

Laura and Arthur were admitted to the mother and baby unit at the Barberry - a national centre for mental health in Birmingham.

There, Laura received 10 weeks of specialist inpatient care which she said had made all the difference.

For Jade, 33, from Sherbourne in Dorset, it was a peri-mental health team and an admission to a mother and baby unit in Bournemouth that helped her to get better.

She experienced postpartum psychosis about two weeks after she gave birth to her daughter in December 2020.

According to the NHS, the condition affects about one in 1,000 new mothers and can include symptoms such as hallucinations, mania, confusion and depression.

The NHS said it should be treated as a medical emergency.

Jade said she had spent almost three days in labour before she was induced and she finally delivered her daughter with the help of forceps.

"I didn't realise at the time but, after going through therapy, I realise it was quite a traumatic delivery," she said.

"I experienced tearfulness right away and I think that was trying to process it as I'd wanted a water birth, so it was very different to what I'd envisioned."

Jade sought counselling for her symptoms but was told the NHS was stretched. She was asked if she could seek private help instead.

In March 2021, she was prescribed anti-depressants but she suffered her first psychotic episode two weeks later.

"I was in a completely different reality," she said. "I felt at a loss and things were getting progressively worse.

"I was getting intrusive thoughts which I was too scared to say out loud."

Although she experienced depression following her return home and a relapse of psychosis in January 2024, Jade said the consistent support from her community mental health team and her care co-ordinator had been a "complete lifeline".

Jade said she wanted to share her experience so people knew what the signs of postpartum psychosis were.

"If a mum is acting out of character... and the unusual behaviour isn't right, it's really important that's flagged and is seen as a medical emergency," she said.

After her diagnosis, Laura began to volunteer with the perinatal mental health team "as a way to give back" to the NHS, which she said had carried her through "the lowest time of her life".

She also wrote the book Something to Live For about her experience to raise awareness of postnatal depression.

She said she had received "the most heart-warming messages" from fellow mothers and praise from fathers who credited the book with helping them to understand what their partners may have been going through after birth.

Correction 6 November 2026: A previous version of this story said about one in 1,000 new mothers experience post-natal depression. This statistic related to post-natal psychosis. More than one in 10 people experience post-natal depression, according to the NHS.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqe9.title: Midwives concerned over possible baby unit closures
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqe9.text:
The Royal College of Midwives (RCM) said it was concerned by reports that two maternity units could close.

Norfolk has maternity units at hospitals in Norwich, Gorleston and King's Lynn, with the latter two also serving Cambridgeshire and Suffolk.

The trade union posted on Facebook that local maternity services should be invested in rather than cut.

The Norfolk and Waveney University Hospitals Group (NWUHG) has set out its "Case for Change" on how services could be delivered in future, but stressed that no decisions had been made and no consultation had begun. NHS leaders said any move to concentrate services at one or two sites would be based on providing safer care for women and babies.

The BBC also understands the health secretary is talking to the chief executive of NHS England regarding what has been happening in Norfolk.

The RCM warned that closing units serving rural and isolated communities could mean women travelling "unacceptable distances" while in labour.

If maternity services were removed, the Norfolk and Waveney University Hospitals Group (NWUHG) said that neonatal units and children's inpatient wards would also close because the services were inter-dependent.

Options include keeping services as they are, or closing consultant-led maternity units at the James Paget Hospital in Gorleston, the Queen Elizabeth Hospital in King's Lynn, or both.

As well as women in Norfolk, the plans could affect women in Lowestoft and north Suffolk who give birth in Gorleston and those in Wisbech and north-east Cambridgeshire who travel to King's Lynn.

The RCM argued the proposals risked worsening existing inequalities in maternity outcomes and said the answer was investment and more staffing, rather than allowing services to "shrink".

It also said closures could result in midwives being redeployed further from home.

The Facebook post said: "Women and babies deserve safe, local care, and closing units is not the answer."

A Department of Health and Social Care (DOHSC) spokesperson said:

"While decisions about individual NHS maternity services are made locally by NHS trusts, any changes to services must be based on clear evidence that they will deliver better outcomes for women and babies."

It added that: "We expect that any further development of this work will involve patients and the public and carefully consider issues such as access, travel times and the needs of local communities."

The department said any future plans would need to take account of National Maternity Standards and the upcoming Maternity and Neonatal Action Plan.

NWUHG said 60 clinicians had helped develop the review.

The Case for Change argues that falling birth rates, workforce shortages and increasing numbers of women requiring more complex care are making it harder to sustain specialist services at every site.

Lesley Dwyer, NWUHG chief executive and a former midwife, previously told the BBC the review was one of the most significant pieces of work undertaken by the organisation and was aimed at making services sustainable in the long term.

"The scenarios examined so far are a starting point for further assessment, not formal proposals," she said.

"No preferred approach has been identified and no decision has been made to close or relocate these services.

"Patient safety must remain at the centre of this work. We also need to understand what different approaches could mean for choice, travel, access and the experiences of women, babies, children and families."

The work comes after NHS bosses said that smaller maternity units across the country may have to close.

The Case for Change will now be submitted to NHS England before further research and any public consultation takes place.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c98r.title: 'It took years to get pain-relieving surgery - I hope a robot means others won't have to wait'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c98r.text:
Like thousands of women in Northern Ireland, Colleen Crothers waited decades for medical help to treat chronic endometriosis - and, now thanks to an all-island first, she's hoping her long road will be a thing of the past.

"Robotic surgery came too late for me," she said. "I hope other women won't have to wait as long."

She is talking about a new breakthrough for female patients in Northern Ireland - the da Vinci gynae robot at Belfast City Hospital.

Operated by humans, the robot's wrists can twist and turn in tight pelvic spaces and it is said to be more precise at complex surgery than a human hand because it is steadier.

Belfast's da Vinci robot is the first of its kind on the island of Ireland and one of only a few across the UK.

It has the potential to massively reduce complex gynaecological surgical waiting lists in Northern Ireland, which affect thousands of women's physical and mental health and their ability to have children.

With an average wait of about seven years for complex surgery, which involves several specialities, delayed treatment means some women require a hysterectomy, like Colleen at 41.

She has lived with chronic endometriosis all of her adult life, having first begun to experience chronic period pain aged 14.

But it took another 22 years before she was referred to gynaecology and a scan confirmed she had both adenomyosis and endometriosis.

"I missed out so much of family life due to daily pain - pain that went on for years," she said.

"I can't have children - I have had to have a hysterectomy and I'm in early menopause.

"To be told you can't have children is hard to swallow," she said.

An urgent case, Colleen missed out on a da Vinci operation by just weeks earlier this year.

She knows the robot's arrival could mean a much better outcome for girls and women coming behind her.

"This type of technology is fantastic and it's amazing that it is now here.

"If anything like that can help another woman, I'm happy she won't have to suffer like I have."

And while her surgery was conventional rather than by a robot, finally getting the treatment she needed has been a relief.

"The outcome was good - my tummy feels lighter, and compared to before I am more or less pain free."

da Vinci became part of the Belfast City Hospital's gynaecology team in May.

It cost £2.4m and was funded through charitable donations for gynaecological services within the trust.

To date it has performed 130 surgeries - 105 of them being on women with complex endometriosis - and four consultants have been trained to use the robot.

It means that complex gynaecology cases are being treated as a priority and are not being bumped when other surgical cases, including cancer cases, come in.

BBC News NI was given access to see the da Vinci in action - and, like a real-life sci-fi creation, it has multiple towering robotic arms that hover over the patient.

While humans are also in the theatre, it gives the surgeon a digital boost with incisions more precise and less invasive.

Dr Hans Nagar, a consultant gynaecological surgeon and oncologist, is one of the surgeons trained to operate da Vinci. He said women with complex endometriosis had previously been ill-served in Northern Ireland.

"They require complex surgery involving different specialists and now da Vinci lets us do that," he said.

"It will take some time to bed in but I believe it will make a big difference and there will be other robots going elsewhere in Northern Ireland.

"That encourages young staff to either stay or to return after a time in Canada, Australia, the UK and the Republic of Ireland," Nagar added.

On Monday, endometriosis services across Northern Ireland are to get a financial boost when the health minister is expected to announce an investment of £1.95m to improve services.

That includes a £700,000 investment in two regional endometriosis centres located within the Belfast City and Altnagelvin Area hospitals, which will help develop specialist services for women with complex endometriosis problems.

Each health trust will also receive £250,000 as part of a phased investment for those women with less complex symptoms.

Ahead of the announcement, Health Minister Robbie Butler said the investment marked an "important milestone in efforts to improve women's health services" in Northern Ireland.

"By strengthening specialist and local services, reducing variation and expanding access to modern treatment options, it will help ensure more women receive the care they need, when they need it," he said.

Although Colleen has had her operation, she continues to need specialist care for endometriosis.

The symptoms she lived with for years included heavy bleeding, severe cramping, pelvic pain and tissue growing and getting trapped in the wrong places.

A night in the emergency department - where she was screaming with pain - brought things to a head and her consultant advised surgery as soon as possible.

In June, she had surgery, which included a hysterectomy and a full bowel shave to try to remove endometriosis tissue which attached her womb to her bowel.

She said the pain felt like she was being stabbed in the stomach - pain that has now been relieved thanks to surgery.

Endometriosis is a condition where tissue similar to the lining of the womb grows in other parts of the body, most commonly around the ovaries, fallopian tubes, and pelvis.

The problem with endometriosis tissue is that it behaves exactly like the womb lining but it is trapped in the wrong place.

Lauren Best, a theatre nurse, said the arrival of da Vinci and a dedicated endometriosis centre was what women in Northern Ireland needed.

"I know how important it is for women to get back on their feet as quickly as possible and I am seeing that happen as da Vinci means less scarring and quicker recovery time - that's good for patients," she said.

Nagar said he hoped all those who gave donations that led to the purchase of da Vinci could see the money had gone to good use.

"I want to say thank you to everyone who donated to all the patients, their families, including those who have lost a loved one - their donations are helping others, and we all very grateful," he said.

Four months on from surgery, Colleen is also grateful.

She is back to work, walking her dog and said she is finally getting her buzz back.

While she is having to deal with early menopause and knowing she will never be a mum, the fact she is pain free is, at present, enough.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c98r.summary: Northern Ireland has a dedicated endometriosis centre in Northern Ireland. The hospital is now offering a new centre to help women in Northern Irish.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck3r.title: 'I could barely stand up straight with menopause after cancer'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck3r.text:
A woman who went into medically induced menopause immediately after breast cancer treatment has described the experience as "horrible".

Rachel Bowman from Hove was 46 when she began treatment for breast cancer four years ago, but the medication put her into complex menopause, when symptoms happen abruptly and often more severely due to medical interventions.

"I could barely move. I could barely stand up straight. It was terrible," said Bowman.

A new pilot clinic to help breast cancer patients manage complex menopause after treatment has now opened in Brighton.

Dr Renske McFarlane who leads the project at the Royal Sussex County Hospital, said that for many women, living with the effects of treatment can continue for years.

"I felt we needed to do more to support women with that aftercare," she said.

Complex menopause happens abruptly due to medical interventions like cancer treatments, making symptoms such as hot flushes, joint pain and low mood much more severe and harder to treat.

Bowman said for her, complex menopause happened overnight.

"Your body has no time to adapt and it is like night and day.

"I had an ovarian suppressant injection one day - the next day I was dealing with 20 to 30 hot flushes a day.

"The onslaught of them was unbelievable and I was so not prepared for how I would feel and how horrific it would be," she explained.

Natural menopause is a gradual, natural, biological transition where hormone levels slowly decline over several years.

Treatments such as chemotherapy, ovarian suppression and endocrine therapies can trigger an early extreme complex menopause or cause menopause-like symptoms, including hot flushes, sleep problems, joint pain, fatigue, low mood and changes to sexual health.

To better support patients, University Hospitals Sussex (UHSussex) has launched the pilot clinic within its breast service.

A specialty doctor in breast surgery, Dr McFarlane said the pilot clinic was working to improve support for patients experiencing symptoms of complex menopause.

"Nationally, we're very good at screening, diagnosing cancers, operating and providing initial treatment," she explained.

"But for many women, living with the effects of treatment can continue for years.

"I was having more and more conversations with patients about how they were feeling, the impact on their confidence at work, their relationships and family life."

Patients can be referred to the pilot clinic by their surgeon, breast care nurse, oncology team or GP and there are plans to develop the service across Sussex.

Bowman now works with the charity Menopause and Cancer to personally try and improve support for women who have had a similar experience.

"Actually being able to speak to a clinician one-on-one and have a conversation about my personal circumstances really, really helped and really made a massive difference."

The medication put her into complex menopause when symptoms happen abruptly and often more severely due to medical interventions. A new pilot clinic to help breast cancer patients manage complex menopsause after treatment has now opened in Brighton.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck98.title: New charity uses outdoors to improve mental health
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck98.text:
A new charity hopes to use activities ranging from cold-water swimming and archery to hill walking and breathwork to improve men's mental health and reduce isolation.

Connect Outdoors is being officially launched alongside an International Men's Day event at the Venture Centre in Maughold, where organisers expect about 80 people to take part in a range of outdoor activities.

The charity said it wanted to gather research on what kind of support men are most likely to engage with, arguing that services have often been designed without asking men first.

Chief executive Kate Bergquist said it had grown out of years of work in social care, public services and outdoor wellbeing programmes.

She said: "We have this abundance of landscape on the island that is never used enough for health.

"This should be embedded into everyone's health and wellbeing routine every week."

Activities on offer include high ropes, bushcraft, mindfulness, breathwork, yoga, archery, ice baths and guided walks, alongside informal spaces designed to encourage men to connect with one another.

The charity is built around what is known as "green and blue health", which encourages people to use natural environments such as forests, beaches and the sea to improve their health.

Bergquist said a key focus would be addressing men's mental health through activities that encourage conversation without making mental health the main selling point.

As part of Sunday's event, attendees will be invited to complete surveys that organisers hope will help identify which activities and approaches are most effective at engaging men.

Among those supporting the event is Gary Thomas, who runs Walking for Wellness and takes people on Manx hill walks where they can talk through any challenges.

The former serviceman and mountain leader said many people found it easier to open up outdoors than in a traditional counselling setting.

"It gives them that opportunity to feel secure and have that ability to open up in an environment that's not oppressive," he said.

"Nature's not clinical, nature's natural."

Thomas said group activities could also help tackle loneliness by creating new social connections.

"We've had people turn up and find their own circle of friends and common interests," he said.

"Then they go off afterwards and explore things together, which is brilliant."

Also involved in the event is Douglas barber Joshua Moore, who completed suicide prevention training through the Lions Barber Collective.

Moore runs Renegade: Cuts and Clobber, and said barber shops often became places where men felt comfortable discussing difficult issues.

"The barber chair is a very special place," he said.

"You can leave feeling a little bit better about yourself, whether that's having a nice haircut, but also just having the opportunity for somebody to listen to you."

Moore said he had seen first-hand the impact mental health struggles could have on families and communities, and wanted to support initiatives aimed at encouraging conversation and early intervention.

The International Men's Day event aimed to introduce men to new activities and point participants to support available to improve both their physical and mental wellbeing.

Organisers expect about 80 people to take part in a range of outdoor activities. Activities include high ropes, bushcraft, mindfulness, breathwork, yoga, archery, ice baths and guided walks.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmd7.title: 'I was heading for a breakdown, then books saved my life'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmd7.text:
International bestselling author Kit de Waal has told the BBC how a chance conversation changed her life after she left home at 16, struggled with drugs and found herself on the brink of a serious mental breakdown.

The Birmingham-born writer said she was "a couple of months away from a very serious breakdown" before a solicitor's reading recommendation changed the course of her life.

Speaking to BBC Upload, she said: "I found the world of reading, the world of imagination.

"I can honestly say it saved my life."

Born in Birmingham to an Irish mother and a Caribbean father, de Waal grew up in Moseley at a time when mixed-race families were rare.

"My father came over from the Caribbean in 1956 and my mother is an Irish immigrant," she said.

The family lived on the edge of a predominantly middle-class area, but de Waal said her childhood was marked by poverty.

"We were very, very poor. I was brought up in poverty, there's no other way about it."

She said those experiences later became central to her writing.

"What I learnt from it was difference, what it's like to be an outsider, what it's like to be poor, hungry, lost, not fit in, the damage that poverty does, the damage that racism does to children."

Yet she also remembers acts of kindness.

After her family moved into a largely white neighbourhood, one neighbour invited the children into their home to see their pet tortoise.

"I learnt from that the power of kindness and the profound effect it has when other people aren't being kind."

When she was six, her mother became a Jehovah's Witness.

De Waal left home at 16 after deciding she no longer wanted to follow the faith.

The years that followed were difficult.

"I was wild," she said. "I took a lot of drugs, drank a lot, did everything you can imagine."

The deaths of friends from heroin overdoses forced her to confront where her life was heading.

By the age of 21, she said her mental health had deteriorated badly.

"I was really very, very unwell.

"I would say a couple of months away from a very serious breakdown."

After returning home and finding work with the Crown Prosecution Service, an off-hand comment from a solicitor would prove life-changing.

Seeing her yawn during a meeting, he suggested reading to help with her insomnia.

At the time, de Waal said she disliked books and had never developed a reading habit.

The solicitor gave her a list of 10 novels, including War and Peace and Madame Bovary.

"I've never cured the insomnia," she said.

"But I have found a world."

Reading became a lifelong passion and eventually inspired her to start writing herself.

Despite believing she could write a novel in a matter of months, de Waal said it took more than a decade of rejection and learning the craft before she was published.

Her breakthrough came with My Name Is Leon, the story of a young boy in the care system growing up in 1980s Birmingham.

The novel became an international bestseller and was later adapted by the BBC after Sir Lenny Henry, who narrated the audiobook, became determined to bring the story to the screen.

It is now studied in schools.

Yet de Waal said the most important lesson from her success was a simple one.

"If there's a lesson, it's write the thing you really care about."

Now one of Britain's best-known authors, she remains a passionate advocate for reading in all its forms, including audiobooks.

Despite an international career, she still credits reading with changing the direction of her life.

"I found the world of reading," she said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmd7.summary: Kit de Waal says she was "a couple of months away from a very serious breakdown" after a solicitor's reading recommendation changed her life. The author was born in Birmingham to an Irish mother and a Caribbean father. She says she learned from kindness and the power of kindness when other people aren't being kind.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw23.title: 'Quiet quitting' could be hitting the economy - here's why
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw23.text:
The so-called "quiet quitting" trend where workers do the basic requirements of a job but refuse to do anything more might be hitting the economy, analysis has found.

Over the last decade, Britons have become less engaged with the jobs they do and are less willing to put in extra effort, according to a Resolution Foundation report.

The thinktank said this could partly help explain the slump in productivity since the pandemic.

"This is self-evidently bad for workers, but it also doesn't bode well for productivity and labour supply, both of which are vital for lifting living standards in the years ahead," said Hannah Slaughter, principal economist at the Resolution Foundation.

Quiet quitting was popularised on social media shortly after the pandemic.

Frustrated by high demands, low pay, and a squeeze in living standards, many online posts said workers should only do what their bosses asked and nothing more.

So you still show up for work, but no more helping out with additional tasks or checking emails outside work hours, instead focusing on work-life balance and "acting your wage".

Yet, far from being just a talking point on TikTok, the Resolution Foundation said the findings in its report were "consistent" with the idea of quiet quitting.

The percentage of those surveyed willing to go the extra mile to help their employer has sunk from 69% in 2015 to 55% in 2025, according to their survey of 4,656 adults.

Meanwhile, those who were not even "fairly" satisfied with their roles has sunk to one-in-four, the lowest level on record.

In addition, workers are less likely than 10 years ago to say they have an interesting job, with 63% of those surveyed saying so, down from 74%.

"Workers today are indeed a little less committed to their employers, and a little less intrinsically drawn to work in general, than workers were a decade ago," the report added.

This shift over the last decade "may have contributed to weak productivity growth", which has slowed since the financial crisis and weakened again after the pandemic, the Resolution Foundation found.

Workers were also more focused on pay than in the past, which it said was "perhaps unsurprising... given the flatlining living standards of the past decade".

Sir John Curtice, politics professor and co-editor of the report, said the analysis does not mean that young people have "become more 'work-shy', nor have workers in general become more reluctant to change jobs".

"But if workers are to be fully engaged in their work, it has seemingly become more important for employers to provide jobs that are both financially rewarding and have flexible work hours," he added.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw23.summary: Britons less engaged with jobs and less willing to put in extra effort, says Resolution Foundation report. Study says this could partly explain slump in productivity since pandemic. Survey of 4,656 adults found workers less likely to go extra mile to help their employer.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c24y.title: Doctors vote to take strike action in row over pay
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c24y.text:
Doctors on the Isle of Man have voted in support of taking strike action in a row over "pay erosion".

The British Medical Association (BMA) said 104 of its 168 eligible members took part in the ballot, with 95% voting in favour.

The union said inflation had seen doctors take a "real terms pay cut of 29%" since 2008.

Manx Care said it remained "hopeful" its new pay offer - made on 18 June - would be accepted. A ballot on the proposed improved deal is due to conclude next week. No date has been set for industrial action.

The strike ballot result coincides with the departure of Manx Care chief executive Teresa Cope, who has been at the helm since its creation in 2021.

Cope's resignation was followed by the announcement that the healthcare provider's chair Wendy Reid would also be stepping down this summer.

Doctors on the island called off a planned walkout in January 2025 after a deal was reached covering two financial years from 2023-24.

That saw the awarding of an 8% pay uplift for the first year, along with another 6% rise from April 2024 and a further 2% from February last year.

The BMA said, despite those rises, doctors' real-terms pay was still significantly below what it was in 2008.

Chair of the Isle of Man Medical Society Dr Prakash Thiagarajan said the latest vote was "a clear message that the current situation cannot continue".

Pay erosion had left doctors "feeling undervalued and increasingly concerned about the future of the profession on the island", he added.

BMA deputy chair of council Dr Emma Runswick said, in voting for strike action, doctors were "standing up for fair pay, recognition of their expertise, and the long-term sustainability of medical staffing on the island".
