https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgl.title: Policing needs reform to cope with modern criminals, Met Police chief warns
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgl.text:
The police system in England and Wales cannot cope against sophisticated modern criminals without urgent reform, the head of the Metropolitan Police has said.

In a speech on Friday, Sir Mark Rowley argued the system was "heading for failure" without change.

He is proposing eight to 10 regional police forces, supported by hundreds of local policing commands and a new national force, in what would be the biggest overhaul of policing since the 1960s.

The changes would replace the 43-force structure with three tiers: local teams dealing with neighbourhood issues, regional forces sharing specialist resources and a National Police Service tackling the most serious crimes.

In January it seemed that the many senior police officers were in favour of creating a National Police Service, and that organising into much larger regional forces had won the argument.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood produced a white paper that aligned with their ideas and asked the former Metropolitan Police Commissioner Lord Hogan-Howe to look at what the force boundaries might be.

But everything changed in July when Andy Burnham became prime minister. So far, Burnham has not spoken publicly about the plans, and the police chiefs are nervous that they may not have his backing. That may be why they have come out so strongly today, warning of the potentially apocalyptic effect of doing nothing.

As well as pushing hard for large regional forces, they are also making an argument about money which is familiar from the defence funding argument.

Sir Mark also pointed out that police funding in England and Wales has fallen from 0.9% of GDP to 0.7%. Implicit in that is that while the slice of the cake being allocated to defending the country is growing, the slice being allocated to defending people's communities and their homes is getting smaller.

In his speech, Sir Mark said organised crime groups, fraud networks, cyber-criminals and those involved in online child abuse increasingly operate across regional and international borders, while police forces remain organised around local areas.

"The victim remains local but increasingly the threat does not," he said citing the example of children who are "groomed by predators on another continent".

He argued that the current system is struggling to keep pace with these threats, saying: "We have 43 overstretched forces trying to do too much, with too little."

Merging forces would reduce duplication and could free up thousands of roles to be redirected towards front line policing, he believes.

Speaking on BBC Breakfast prior to his speech, Sir Mark said crime had changed a lot over the years but the police was largely organised how it was 60 years ago.

"Obviously the world's moved on a long way in that time."

His proposals follow a consultation launched by Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood in January. This included plans for a National Police Service to tackle the most complex crimes and a possible merger of the 43 forces into fewer, larger forces.

However some rural police and crime commissioners have described the plans as "political manoeuvring" by larger forces to "load the dice in their favour".

Dorset Police and Crime Commissioner David Sidwick reiterated his strong opposition to proposals to merge the forces.

"My concern is simple. If funding is diverted away from frontline services in Dorset to establish new national structures, local communities could end up receiving less rather than more."

In addition, Kent's Conservative police and crime commissioner Matthew Scott said: "[Sir Mark believes] policing should suffer a decade of disruption, that local policing services should be cut back and made more remote, and that this can all be done without ever asking the public what they want from their local police force."

The Association of Police and Crime Commissioners (APCC) has also questioned whether merging forces is the best way to improve policing.

It said: "The case for modernisation and a National Police Service is clear. The case for reducing 43 forces to nine regional 'mega-forces' is not."

Outgoing Cheshire Chief Constable Mark Roberts also said a future policing model needs to be built in a way that retains the places that already work well so that they do not "get subsumed" and end up "scrabbling to try and get resource from some of the metropolitan areas"

"Bigger isn't always better - we see some high performing big forces, we see some poorer performing big forces.

"The aim is to raise everyone at least to the minimum standard of the best," Roberts said after Rowley's speech.

Asked on Breakfast what would happen if the reforms were not put in place, Sir Mark said: "the risk is failure".

"Failure means solving fewer crimes, less local presence, when you get exceptional incidents like a certain outbreak of disorder like we saw in Hampshire."

In September police clashed with anti-migrant protesters in Portsmouth when 120 migrants arrived in a single dinghy.

"Standing still looks like a degradation of policing day by day, struggling even more as criminals outpace policing because we're not organised to meet it," Sir Mark added.

A Home Office spokesperson defended the plans, saying: "Our current model of policing has not changed since the 1960s and is no longer fit for purpose."

Sir Mark has also highlighted the financial pressures facing policing, saying that spending on policing had fallen from about 0.9% of GDP to 0.7% since 2010, which he said was as "a big hit".

"We do need investment as well, but if you threw loads of money at the current system it's still not going to fix the fundamental problem, it's not designed to meet today's challenges," he told the BBC.

"Throwing money at the current system isn't going to work."

Sir Mark said in his speech that years of underinvestment has left forces relying on ageing technology, and officers are increasingly diverted from neighbourhood policing to deal with other demands, including mental health and social care.

He also pointed to falling police performance, saying positive outcomes nationally are now less than half the level they were 12 years ago, while public confidence has fallen by 9%.

Additional reporting by Olivia Ireland

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c699.title: Thatcher's Right to Buy created a generation of homeowners - did it also fuel the housing crisis?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c699.text:
Growing up in a council flat in the 1980s and 1990s, my mum would often point out homes that tenants had bought from the council. You could usually tell just from looking. A plain wooden door had been replaced with something fancier. New windows had appeared. Sometimes there was a porch or pillars outside the front door.

Those houses were bought under the Right to Buy scheme - arguably the most consequential housing policy of my lifetime. It was introduced in 1980, three years before I was born, when Margaret Thatcher's government gave council tenants in England the legal right to purchase their homes at a discounted price.

Supporters welcomed the chance for working-class families to own their own home and build wealth. Critics argue it hollowed out the country's stock of social housing and contributed to today's housing crisis.

Some of my neighbours "made a killing" from the policy, in the words of my mum. One bought an almost identical flat to ours in 1989 for £21,200, after receiving a discount of £18,800. Eight years later it sold for £54,500. Five years after that it changed hands again for £143,000. (Notably, the person who made the most money from that flat wasn't the original council tenant - it was the people who bought it afterwards.)

But Andy Burnham doesn't like the policy. The Right to Buy scheme has seen various changes since its introduction in the 1980s, and Labour has weakened it significantly since coming to power in 2024. Then, in September, the prime minister told Labour's conference: "We will reform Right to Buy. Not taking the right away from anyone in an existing home, but removing it from new homes." This would help to keep council houses in public ownership "for generations to come", Burnham told delegates.

He has previously compared trying to solve the housing crisis while continuing to sell social homes to "trying to fill a bath with the plug out".

More than 40 years after its introduction, Right to Buy remains a debate about political values as much as housing policy, balancing the home ownership ideal against the desire to preserve social housing for future generations.

Since 1980, more than two million homes have been sold through the scheme in England.

In fact, about 40% of England's council housing stock has been sold through Right to Buy. Most of those sales took place in the early years, says Prof Rebecca Tunstall, a housing academic at the University of York and London School of Economics. At the time, Labour was vehemently opposed to Thatcher's plans. Yet many of its own voters went on to benefit from them.

Labour now argues that not enough of those two million homes were replaced. Sir Keir Starmer's government restricted the scheme, including by heavily reducing the maximum discount that councils were allowed to give tenants.

And now Burnham is removing the right to buy entirely from any new-build social home. The measures are included in a bill currently making its way through Parliament. The government says that before Labour's various restrictions on the scheme, England was projected to see a net loss of 26,000 council homes over the next decade. Now there will be a net gain of 18,000 homes over the same period, it calculates.

This opens up a political divide: some opposition parties, like the Conservatives and Reform UK, say they would keep or even extend the scheme.

For those who became homeowners, Right to Buy turned a dream into reality.

Barbara Stevens, now 80, bought her two-bedroom council flat in Kentish Town, north London, through Right to Buy for around £35,000. Now mortgage-free, she estimates it could be worth between £600,000 and £700,000.

"I've always wanted to own my own property," she says.

Her friend Trevor Abrahmsohn believes her story demonstrates the success of the scheme. "If you want to condemn the poor to poverty, make them lifetime renters," he says.

Those arguments were central to Thatcher's vision of a "property-owning democracy".

Few people are more closely associated with Right to Buy than Lord Heseltine, who was the cabinet minister responsible for housing when it was introduced. When he and Thatcher launched the scheme in 1980, council tenants were offered substantial discounts to purchase their homes.

A relative of mine whose parents bought their council home in Croydon told me it was the only time "anyone would ever give you a hundred grand for free".

Even Housing Secretary Angela Rayner - part of the government that's restricting Right to Buy - bought and later sold her own council home for a profit.

In 1980, Lord Heseltine described the scheme as the biggest transfer of capital wealth from the state to ordinary people. "It certainly was," he says now, almost half a century on.

I ask him if, looking back, he would have designed the policy differently. "No," he answers.

He thinks Right to Buy gave its beneficiaries an important asset. "People who bought their own homes made a great deal of capital gain," he says.

But to its detractors, Right to Buy is responsible for many of Britain's housing woes.

Prof Tunstall says the policy is partly responsible for making social housing scarcer, which meant more people competed for homes in the private rented sector, pushing up rents.

Lord Heseltine says it was originally assumed that councils would use sale proceeds to support new housing. He acknowledges that did not happen after he left government.

That failure to replace sold homes sits at the heart of the modern criticism of Right to Buy.

For Molly Harris from the New Economics Foundation, it is "private landlords [who] are the real winners".

Her think tank's research found that 41% of homes sold through Right to Buy are now privately rented out. "Homes that were built with public money, and with the aim of providing an affordable and secure path to home ownership, have since been turned into assets," Harris says.

She says the shortage of social housing means more people need help with housing costs in the private rented sector, where rents are higher. So taxpayers are effectively paying twice: once to give a discount on the initial home; and then again, via housing benefit, when that home is rented out to someone who can't afford the payments. A former council home rented privately could now be valued at double, triple or quadruple what it cost when it was under local authority control.

I put that criticism to Lord Heseltine, asking him whether the scheme has failed because some ex-council homes are now effectively being rented back to the state, at higher costs.

He dismisses it as "rubbish", adding: "The scheme was wildly successful in spreading ownership across the country."

According to Harris's research, the government spent more than £58bn between 2021 and 2025 "subsidising private landlords" through the benefit system.

Newham Council says almost half of the 9,000 council homes sold under Right to Buy in Newham were later "flipped" into private rentals. The borough now has the biggest council house waiting list in the country. Last year, The Big Issue reported that Newham Council made a loss of more than £20m of taxpayers' money buying back homes it had sold just a few years earlier. The council said it was a quick way to provide new housing, and was a cheaper option than some alternatives.

And some council tenants say they are not interested in buying their homes. Ruth Crabb has lived in her flat in Havering since 1997. "I wouldn't buy my flat because I didn't want it to go out of circulation, as social housing is for those who come after me," she says. But, she adds: "I don't judge anyone who bought their property with Right to Buy."

Supporters of Right to Buy also argue that you can't appreciate the true value of the scheme by looking at numbers on a spreadsheet.

The benefits of the policy extended for generations, they say, helping the children and grandchildren of those who bought homes.

Research co-authored by Matteo Sandi, an economics professor at the University of Milan, looked at children growing up in areas where Right to Buy uptake was highest. He found better educational and economic outcomes, including higher GCSE attainment, greater chances of attending university, and increased earnings in adulthood.

"What we find is that there is, in fact, a lasting benefit from growing up in an owned property," he says.

He believes it's because ownership encouraged families to invest more heavily in their homes and neighbourhoods.

One of my relatives backs this up. He tells me his parents were able to move elsewhere in the country, enjoy a better standard of living and finally afford things that had previously been out of reach. He believes Right to Buy transformed their lives.

But Prof Tunstall argues home ownership is not the only route to a stable family life. "The critical things for safety and for children's development and for happy families are security and affordability," she says - and children can also get that from social renting, she thinks.

Looking back, that resonates.

When I was a child and my mum rented from the council, she knew what she would be charged every month. She knew we wouldn't suddenly be forced to move. My siblings and I knew we wouldn't have to change schools. At that point, in the 1980s, one third of houses in England were council-owned. When my mum became pregnant with me, it was safe to assume that a home would soon become available - and within about a year, one did. She moved out of my nan's and into her new council flat.

The children I now meet through my work often do not have that certainty. Today, the average wait for a family-sized home in London is 27 years. Some children are moved repeatedly between hotels and hostels. Councils across England now spend £8m every day housing families in temporary accommodation.

Sandi is careful not to present his findings as an unconditional endorsement of Right to Buy.

"My take is the Right to Buy scheme was a good policy with a big limitation," he says. "More social housing should have been built."

But curbing Right to Buy could take a long time to bear fruit, says Prof Tunstall. Scotland abolished its Right to Buy programme in 2016 and Wales followed in 2019 - but Prof Tunstall says it "hasn't made a huge difference" yet in those nations, because the changes are too recent. (Northern Ireland continues to operate a scheme similar to Right to Buy.)

And deeper challenges will remain; Right to Buy is not the only culprit of Britain's social housing shortage, she says. Supply has also been reduced by council estate-clearance programmes, she says, which saw thousands of homes demolished from the 1990s. Like Lord Heseltine, she also blames decades of under-building: had governments continued to build at their 1980s rates, she argues, the sale of council homes might not have resulted in an overall loss of social housing.

The housing landscape has also changed dramatically since 1980. Many councils transferred responsibility over council housing to housing associations, meaning they have lost the skills and expertise to build their own stock.

More than 25 years later, I return to the street where I grew up. It looks much the same, although a few new front doors suggest more homes have been sold. My mum never took advantage of Right to Buy; she continues to rent a council flat on a small estate in south London.

I ask her if she regrets that. She says she simply wouldn't have been able to afford it.

I tell her that the flat she could have bought for around £20,000 would now be worth somewhere between £350,000 and £400,000.

"You're kidding?," she replies.

No-one in the 1980s could have known what would happen to house prices or the cost of living.

But whatever people think about Right to Buy, there is broad agreement on one point: the problem was not necessarily selling the homes. It was failing to replace them.

Additional reporting: Jade Thompson, Larissa Tairo.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c60m.title: More Mandelson papers set to be published before Christmas
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c60m.text:
The government is preparing to publish more documents about the appointment of Lord Mandelson as US ambassador.

Batches of papers were published in March and June - but others were withheld because they were part of a Metropolitan Police investigation.

The Cabinet Office has now said a number of extra documents will be published, likely before Christmas. Some will still be withheld at the request of the Met.

Cat Little, permanent secretary at the Cabinet Office, said that some of the documents could "now be published without prejudicing their investigation".

The Met Police had launched an investigation over allegations that, while he was serving as a government minister, Lord Mandelson had passed on market-sensitive government information to the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Writing to the chair of Parliament's Intelligence and Security Committee, Little said: "The Cabinet Office is now beginning the process to prepare these documents so that they may be laid before the House in response to the humble address motion as soon as possible."

She said the documents would be reviewed and in some instances may need to be redacted "for the purposes of avoiding prejudice to national security or international relations".

The process is expected to be completed before Parliament rises for the Christmas recess on 17 December.

Lord Mandelson was arrested on 23 February on suspicion of misconduct in public office.

He has repeatedly let it be known that he believes he has not acted criminally, did not act for personal gain and is cooperating with the police.

"Our investigation into alleged misconduct in public office is ongoing," the Met Police said in a statement.

The lifelong Labour politician became the British ambassador to the US in February 2025, but was sacked in September after Downing Street said new information about the extent of his relationship with Epstein had emerged.

After his sacking, the government - then led by Sir Keir Starmer - was heavily criticised for giving Lord Mandelson the job and in February MPs voted to force the government to publish papers relating to his appointment.

Mike Wood, shadow Cabinet Office minister, said: "We still haven't got to the bottom of the Mandelson scandal.

"Labour did their utmost to hold this information back and it was only released because of the Conservatives humble address."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmqj.title: Putin not invited to G20 summit in Manchester, says Burnham
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmqj.text:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said Vladimir Putin is not invited to the G20 summit in Manchester.

Asked whether the Russian president would be invited to the annual meeting, which the UK is hosting in November 2027, Burnham said "no" because of sanctions against the Kremlin.

The UK has a longstanding policy not to have direct, bilateral engagement with Russian ministers since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.

But US president Donald Trump has sparked controversy by inviting Putin to this year's G20, which he will host in Miami in December. The Kremlin has not yet said whether Putin will attend.

Russia is a member of the G20 - a group of 19 nations, the European Union and African Union - while Ukraine is not, but the ongoing war in Ukraine has loomed large over recent summits.

Putin has not attended any major global summit since he launched his invasion and ongoing war in Ukraine.

Asked about inviting him to the G20 in Manchester in 2027, Burnham told The Economist he "will not be coming because of an outstanding sanction" on senior Russian figures.

He said the meeting would provide "a real opportunity" to work with Chinese president Xi Jinping on safety regulations for artificial intelligence (AI).

Pressed on whether the UK could bring the US and China around the same table to agree on global AI supervision, Burnham said: "As I sit here today, that feels challenging, but we've got to hold out the need to find global agreements on AI.

"If we don't, the risks of recent times will magnify, they will significantly intensify.

"So you've got to go into it with that aim."

His decision not to include Putin in next year's gathering in Manchester comes after European diplomats refused to stand for an official photo with Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov at the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting in October.

The so-called "family photo" would usually include representatives from all nations in attendance, but this year it was cancelled.

The US decision to invite Lavrov in the first place - which itself came after further public rows between Trump and Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky - also attracted criticism.

Discussing Ukraine, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband later told Lavrov at the summit: "Let me say this directly to the Russian foreign minister: We all know who the aggressor in this war is."

The UK last hosted the G20 summit in 2009. Next year's two-day event will take place in the Manchester Central Convention Centre in Manchester city centre and host thousands of diplomats and delegates, as well as world leaders.

The government has said it will use its G20 presidency in 2027 to "reinforce global economic stability" and "benefit people in every part of the UK".

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqz0.title: Farage says he is worried Trump will step up Iran war after midterm 'disaster'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqz0.text:
Nigel Farage has said he fears Donald Trump will "aggressively" continue his war with Iran after his "disaster" in the US midterm elections.

The Reform UK leader said the US president was still a friend, but accused him of having "broke a promise" to the American electorate by launching the war.

The war in Iran, which the US began in February 2026, weighed heavily in the midterm election results earlier this week in which the Democrats swept Trump's Republicans out of power in Congress.

Farage, who had initially urged people to support the war, said that following the election results he worried Trump would respond with more strikes on Iran.

Asked how he thinks President Trump will respond, Farage told broadcasters on Thursday: "I suppose I worry that the president will continue aggressively attacking Iran.

"That worries me because that would have even more serious implications for the price of oil, for inflation, for the whole western world".

He acknowledged he had initially supported the war but stressed he "never supported endless war".

Asked if the war was a mistake, he said: "There's no question about it."

The US president had "always kept his promises," added Farage, but "in this case, he said no more foreign wars and here we are in month eight of a war with no sign of ending."

"That and the resulting fuel prices are what in the end has done the damage."

Trump said on Tuesday that the poor results for Republican congressional candidates were partly due to the war and the related surge in oil prices.

But he insisted he did not regret launching a joint attack with Israel on Iran.

In recent weeks, Trump has warned the US and Israel could return to all-out war after the midterms if a deal to end the conflict cannot be reached with Iran.

There have been various warnings, including from politicians in the UK, that Trump may now step up his attacks on Iran but Farage's criticism was more vocal than many have been.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said earlier this week he hoped the midterm results meant there was an "opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that's the cost of living".

Farage said he had not spoken to Trump since the midterms but described it as a "complete wipeout" and "an absolute shellacking" for the Republicans.

"Trump has had an amazing career - he has beaten the pollsters, he has gone way beyond expectations," he added.

"This was his last big election and they all say, that all political careers end in failure."

His comments came at an event to announce Reform's first defence spokesperson, after the party was criticised for not having one.

Angus MacIntyre said he had stood down from a 40-year military career, including as a Wing Commander in the Royal Air Force (RAF), to take on the role.

MacIntyre pledged in a speech to end prosecutions of serving military personnel and veterans within the first 100 days of a Reform government.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and Tory leader Kemi Badenoch had criticised Reform for lacking a defence spokesperson despite having dedicated posts for immigration, the economy and education.

Farage said MacIntyre would form part of "a team we will build to represent us" on the issues of defence, security and cybersecurity.

Farage says he worries that the US president will continue to attack Iran. He says he has not spoken to Trump since the midterms but described it as a "complete wipeout" for the Republicans.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6y4.title: Algorithm allocates Highland 'significant increase' in asylum-seeking children
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6y4.text:
Highland Council says a Home Office algorithm has allocated it with a "significant increase" in unaccompanied asylum-seeking children to look after.

The local authority said it had received national recognition for its work with the young people, many of them fleeing war or persecution.

But it said the rise in numbers would be challenging due to a lack of housing in its area, adding that the algorithm did not take into account the local situation.

The Home Office said councils had a statutory duty to support children arriving in the UK without a parent or guardian, and it was committed to working closely with authorities to help them meet their obligations.

Unaccompanied asylum-seeking children (UASC) are those under the age of 18 who arrive in the UK to apply for international protection on their own, without the support of an adult.

Many of them are fleeing their homeland because of political or religious persecution, war or famine.

There are 380 UASCs being looked after in Scotland, according to Scottish government figures for 31 July 2025.

Highland Council is currently responsible for 72.

The council said it was contacted by local authorities body Cosla in July about a revised Home Office rota allocation formula.

In a report, officials said this had presented it with "significant challenges" and five times its previous number of UASCs.

Previously, Highland Council took into its care system one child per cycle, but this has now gone up to five.

There can be a period of two weeks to a number of months between cycle, depending on how many children arrive in the UK.

Highland Council officials added: "The Home Office algorithm by itself is not an adequate tool without some understanding of local conditions.

"For example, the fact that Highland has significant housing challenges, both in terms of housing availability and cost, coupled with a lack of available workforce, means Highland is not an attractive option for asylum support providers."

The local authority has previously said its area needs an extra 24,000 houses over the next 10 years. New homes are needed to address a long-standing shortage of affordable homes.

The officials also said the Home Office had not so far placed any adult asylum seekers in the Highlands.

"This lack of adult asylum seekers in Highland has had the effect of increasing the number of UASC in 2026," they said.

In June, the UK government scrapped plans to house up to 300 male asylum seekers at Cameron Barracks in Inverness.

Eligible UASCs, like other young people in foster, kinship or residential care can remain under local authority care up to the age of 21.

Some care leavers are eligible for support up to their 26th birthday.

Highland Council receives core funding of £143 per child, per day for under 18s. For over 18s it is £270 per week.

The Home Office said it was a priority to ensure vulnerable children received the care and support they needed.

A spokesperson said: ''Local authorities have a statutory duty to support unaccompanied asylum-seeking children and care leavers, and we are committed to working closely with them to help them meet these obligations.

"Through the National Transfer Scheme, we work with local authorities across the UK to ensure responsibility for supporting unaccompanied children is shared fairly."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6y4.summary: Highland Council says it has received national recognition for its work with the young people. But it says the rise in numbers would be challenging due to a lack of housing in its area. There are 380 UASCs being looked after in Scotland, according to Scottish government figures.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crq5.title: Swinney criticises UK move to ban new North Sea drilling
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crq5.text:
First Minister John Swinney says he does not support the UK government's plans to ban any new exploration for oil and gas in the North Sea.

The SNP leader told MSPs fossil fuels would be required "for some years to come".

He argued there was a "rational" case for further exploration if the project's carbon emissions was lower than using imported fuel.

The Scottish government, in its 2023 energy strategy, set out a presumption against new oil and gas drilling.

If passed by MPs, the UK government's Energy Independence Bill would remove the North Sea Transition Authority's ability to grant fresh oil and gas licences, in line with a Labour manifesto pledge not to grant permission for new fields.

It does not affect the decision on whether to allow drilling at Rosebank off Shetland - the UK's largest known untapped field - which was approved in 2022 before being subject to legal challenges.

Swinney has repeatedly refused to be drawn on whether he explicitly supports drilling at Rosebank.

Asked about the bill at First Minister's Questions, Swinney said: "The government has set out our view that because we are going to be using oil and gas for years to come there is a rational basis for considering oil and gas developments within our own jurisdiction if they offer lower carbon emissions than imported oil and gas."

He told parliament the UK government's bill includes several measures his government supports, adding: "But we do not support the provisions of that bill in relation to the position on the granting of new licences."

Swinney said this was because "any particular applications need to be considered in relation to their impact on our carbon reduction target and given the fact we are going to be using oil and gas for some years to come".

Decisions on new oil and gas licences are made by the UK government.

However, under Nicola Sturgeon's leadership, the Scottish government proposed a presumption against new oil and gas developments.

The Swinney administration appears to have shifted away from that position, especially since the outbreak of war in the Middle East.

Scottish ministers nevertheless continue to stress any oil and gas developments should be compatible with the government's ambitions to cut carbon emissions over time.

Scottish Greens co-leader Gillian Mackay described Swinney's comments as a "shocking U-turn".

She said: "It is a huge departure from only a few years ago when the Scottish government was committed to a presumption against oil and gas.

"When even the UK government is taking a stronger position, it shows how far the SNP has drifted. It is a shameful retreat and a slap in the face for future generations."

Reform UK Scotland leader Malcolm Offord said: "I welcome this breaking news from the first minister as it overrules the SNP's long-standing presumption against new oil and gas exploration."

Although the UK bill would prevent the granting of new licences, it would allow existing oil and gas fields to provide additional production from within its existing boundaries, or in nearby areas.

The UK government said the move could produce about 60 million barrels of oil and support hundreds of jobs.

It vowed to sustain "growth and investment across North Sea communities as the energy sector transitions".

The wide-ranging bill would also formally scrap gas standing charges and introduce reforms designed to speed up grid connections.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said the bill would help to "build a clean energy future which people feel in their pockets, households and communities, ensuring support reaches those who need it most".

The SNP will seek to remove the ban on new oil and gas drilling from the bill. If this does not happen they will oppose the legislation despite supporting other measures contained within it.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crq5.summary: First Minister John Swinney says he does not support UK government's plans to ban new oil and gas drilling. He said there was a "rational" case for further exploration if the project's carbon emissions were lower than using imported fuel. Scottish government set out presumption against new oil & gas drilling in 2023 energy strategy.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6kg.title: Reform councillor's post branded racist by Labour
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6kg.text:
A Reform UK councillor has been labelled a "racist" and accused of posting "xenophobic conspiracy theories" by a Labour councillor, after questioning whether migrants and their children should be allowed to stand for elected office.

Essex county councillor Carl Johnson posted a picture of Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood next to London Mayor Sadiq Khan, and wrote "we have been deliberately infiltrated".

Labour county councillor Lee Scordis called on Reform to "expel him immediately".

Johnson and his party have both since defended his right to free speech.

"Open debate and free speech should not be shut down simply because others disagree with a particular viewpoint," said Johnson, speaking to the Local Democracy Reporting Service (LDRS).

Johnson shared the image of the two prominent Labour politicians on Wednesday.

In his accompanying message, he wrote: "We have allowed people who arrived as asylum seekers to settle and then have second generations, gain positions of political power, and then push to change our laws to better reflect their own religion and culture.

"That is unacceptable. No foreigner should ever be allowed to stand for political office in this country."

The Facebook post has since been removed from the page of councillor Carl Johnson and the BBC contacted him for a response.

Both the home secretary and London mayor were born in the UK and are the second generation of migrant families.

Scordis said the Reform councillor had suggested that politicians like Winston Churchill and Rishi Sunak, who had at least one parent born abroad, "could not be elected in any role, let alone prime minister".

A Reform spokesperson said: "[The party] is committed to net-negative migration and will prioritise the needs of the British people.

"Councillor Johnson is entitled to his own personal views."

The Braintree Conservatives said they "strongly oppose these remarks, and the obsession of some Reform politicians openly challenging the identity of Britons born in this country".

Meanwhile, Essex County Council said it was "aware of the social media post by councillor Carl Johnson" but would not comment on whether a complaint had been received.

Johnson told the LDRS: "My concern is that individuals who hold positions of political influence in the UK should always act in the interests of this country and its people.

"There have been well-publicised cases where questions have been raised about political figures advocating positions that appear to place the interests of other countries, cultures or ideologies above those of the United Kingdom."

The home secretary's parents immigrated from Kashmir, and Khan's from Pakistan.

Earlier this year, Mahmood told the BBC that friends and family had recently experienced racist slurs "when they had gone 20 years without hearing those words said to them".

"I think we're living in a more divisive, more polarised world. I think social media has a lot to do with sending hateful, divisive stuff through the algorithms," she said, speaking in January.

Johnson did not refer to them directly in his post, but the image he shared of them included the caption: "One changing our capital city, the other bringing in Islam in the thousands."

The Facebook post, before it was removed, had received 14,000 interactions and more than 3,000 comments.

He is the county councillor for Three Fields and Great Notley, which includes MDP Wethersfield, where hundreds of asylum seekers are accommodated.

The Reform leader of Essex County Council Peter Harris has also been approached for comment.

Johnson questioned whether migrants and their children should be allowed to stand for office. Labour councillor Lee Scordis called on Reform to "expel him immediately" Johnson and his party have both defended his right to free speech.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqly.title: More asbestos found in Parliament, as MPs urged to get on with revamp
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqly.text:
More asbestos has been discovered in Parliament, the BBC has learnt, as MPs come under pressure to sign off on a major revamp of the crumbling home of UK democracy.

Known asbestos items in the Palace of Westminster and wider parliamentary estate, such as insulation, roofing, floor tiles and ropes, now number more than 1,650 - an increase of 500 since 2021.

It comes as the government considers holding a vote on refurbishing Parliament, which could cost up to £40bn and take 61 years, after years of indecision and delay.

The Commons public accounts committee this week warned it was "crunch time" for Parliament's restoration, with every additional year of delay costing taxpayers £420m.

More asbestos items were found during surveys in preparation for the long-awaited refurbishment project, parliamentary authorities said.

Asbestos has been identified as one of the main reasons for the refurbishment, given the dangers to human health when its fibres are airborne. While asbestos is largely fireproof, surrounding fire and heat can release fibres over long distances.

In the past five years, 700 items of asbestos have been removed from Parliament but the total has still risen, a Freedom of Information request by the BBC found.

Under Health and Safety Executive guidelines, most of it is classed as low risk in concealed areas, meaning it is less likely to be disturbed, but almost 200 items are classed as medium risk meaning they may require remedial works.

A spokesperson for UK Parliament said its "absolute priority is the safety of the those who work on and visit the parliamentary estate" with improved asbestos monitoring, new awareness training, and plans to further remove it.

Kris Gledhill, the son of former Labour MP Alice Mahon who died in 2022 of malignant mesothelioma - a type of cancer linked to asbestos exposure - told the BBC "asbestos should never be considered low risk".

"A precautionary approach should be adopted: this includes assessing the fact that in addition to the risks from buildings deteriorating over time, there are also risks of damage from extreme weather events, floods and fire, and from disturbances caused during renovation and maintenance work," he said.

"Alice was well aware of the risks relating to asbestos and mesothelioma," he added.

"She was able to identify two workplaces where she might well have been exposed, one of which was the Palace of Westminster."

The Commons authorities told the BBC "an asbestos-free building cannot be achieved in practice" because that would require demolition or extensive damage to the fabric of the building.

Dr Hannah Moody, chief executive of charity Mesothelioma UK which campaigns on asbestos-related diseases, said she backs introducing a national asbestos register and the phased removal of asbestos from public buildings.

"Although asbestos was banned in 1999, it remains present in many public buildings across the UK and continues to cause serious illness and work-related deaths, including from the aggressive cancer, mesothelioma," she said.

Workers should be given health and safety advice to manage the risks, she added.

The findings come as the Commons Public Accounts Committee on Wednesday published the results of its inquiry into Parliament's restoration and renewal (R&R) programme, which is exploring options to revamp the site.

Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, the Conservative MP who chairs the committee, told the BBC that if a small fire broke out in the building "the whole lot would go up" - with 24-hour fire patrols in place.

"Consider the impact of global rolling news footage of Notre Dame-like flames licking out of the building's roof, resulting in the destruction of our heritage, or worse, injuries or loss of life," he added.

He said this was a "real and rising... grave risk" and criticised "a political allergy to gripping the nettle" of refurbishing Parliament after years of delay.

The committee said there was enough information for MPs and peers to vote on a way forward before the end of this year.

The BBC understands government whips have discussed holding a debate and vote by then, but no date has been scheduled.

This vote would decide whether to proceed with up to £3bn of initial works and narrow down four current options, ahead of a final decision by 2030.

One proposed option would see MPs and peers move out of the site for up to 24 years from 2032, costing up to £15.6bn.

Another involves moving only the House of Lords out of the building, costing £39bn and taking 61 years.

Among the "critical" setbacks the committee identified were an overcomplex decision-making process and delays in acquiring a temporary home for the Lords in the nearby Queen Elizabeth II conference centre, which is owned by the government.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqly.summary: More asbestos items found in Palace of Westminster and wider parliamentary estate. More than 1,650 items found during surveys in preparation for long-awaited refurbishment project. Government considers holding a vote on refurbishing Parliament, which could cost up to £40bn and take 61 years.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crp3.title: Could this be the last Bonfire Night for noisy fireworks?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crp3.text:
Bangers, rockets and screamers have long been part of Bonfire Night - but the traditional celebrations might sound a little different next year.

The government is currently considering reducing the noise limit for fireworks by 50% for those bought in shops for private use, after pressure from campaigners concerned about the impact on nervous animals and people with Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD).

Professionally organised displays would continue to have no maximum limit provided the noise level is not harmful to human health.

About 20 million people enjoy fireworks at home every year, according to industry figures.

Andy Hubble, of the British Fireworks Association (BFA), said displays had already been getting quieter and a balance must be struck to prevent a black market in noisy fireworks springing up.

The end of October sees the start of several celebrations traditionally marked by fireworks and bonfires, including Halloween on 31 October, Guy Fawkes Night on 5 November, and Diwali, which is on 8 November this year.

The government has said an outright ban on the public buying fireworks would not be proportionate.

But Business Minister Kate Dearden said her department was considering "reforms to fireworks legislation, focused on their key harms associated with their misuse - their noise, and contribution to antisocial behaviour – whilst still allowing individuals to enjoy fireworks safely and responsibly for the important community and cultural celebrations they play a part of."

It is already illegal to sell fireworks to under 18s, or to set fireworks off after 23:00, with exemptions for special occasions including Bonfire Night, Diwali, New Year's Eve and Chinese New Year.

But campaigners have raised concerns about the impact of loud bangs on nervous pets.

Dog owner Katherine Alderson, from Clacton-on-Sea, told BBC Breakfast: "It's a nightmare every single year.

"This year I've actually barricaded my bedroom window with numerous layers of insulation to try and keep out the noise of fireworks."

Asked whether reducing the bangs would take the fun out of fireworks, she said she believed displays "should be about the lights and colours" and suggested "a complete ban" on the sale of fireworks to the general public could be the solution.

But other campaigners say a ban is not needed, including Alan Friggieri, from the charity Combat Stress, which supports veterans with PTSD.

Giving evidence to MPs on the Commons' Business Committee, Friggieri said calls to their helpline jump at this time of year because loud bangs can trigger PTSD symptoms.

"Nothing quite sounds like an AK47 other than fireworks going off - it's that crackle," one veteran who had been shot multiple times had told him.

Friggieri said veterans need to be able to plan around key dates, but he said he was not calling for a ban, because his organisation understands the cultural importance of firework displays.

Calling for better enforcement of existing rules by police to stop antisocial behaviour, BFA vice chairman Hubble warned a ban in Ireland had seen a flourishing black market in firework sales.

"There is a real risk here that if we make fireworks quieter that there is still a demand then we could create an illegal market where fireworks are coming in through internet sales and white van sales," he told BBC Breakfast.

"At the moment we have a really well-regulated market where we have enforcers that know the products and can test them but as soon as these products go undercover then we lose that.

"We could actually create a louder and noisier environment because those are the sorts of fireworks that we're seeing coming in through illegal sales on the internet."

Asked whether it was true that displays were getting noisier, Hubble said: "No, no, it's a lot quieter than it used to be - we used to have bangers and air bombs and and screamer rockets that used to be on sale and they were withdrawn from sale."

The government is considering reducing the maximum noise limit from the current 120dB, equivalent toa thunderclap, to 110dB, which is equivalent to a car horn.

Hubble said a BFA assessment of firework sales shows a 50% noise reduction to 110 dB would impact up to 60% of firework sales to the general public.

Lowering levels to 90DB, equivalent to a lawnmower, as some campaigners want, would affect about 95% of fireworks.

"That's effectively a ban on consumer fireworks, not a modest reduction in noise," he said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqdr.title: UK commits to 'time-bound' talks on slavery apology
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqdr.text:
The UK has signed up to "structured, time-bound, inclusive and good-faith" talks that address the "historical harms" of the transatlantic slave trade, Commonwealth leaders in Antigua have said.

The formal conclusions marking the end of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, known as the communique, is the joint text setting out what has been agreed.

The 18 page document includes a paragraph in which the leaders "welcome the agreement of the Government of the United Kingdom to engage in a structured, time-bound, inclusive and good-faith dialogue with affected parties addressing the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans and its historical harms".

It comes after Prime Minister Andy Burnham opened the door to a formal apology on behalf of the UK for its role in the slave trade, while ruling out the prospect of reparations.

Officials said the timeframe for the talks would be agreed at a later date, though the Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has suggested they are likely to conclude in around a year.

Asked whether the government might reach the point of a formal apology by the time it hosts the G20 leaders' summit in Manchester next November, Miliband told BBC Newscast: "Broadly speaking, yes."

The rationale among British diplomats in committing to the wording in the communique is to try to offer reassurance that there is a sense of urgency to deal with the issue, even if a date for doing so is not yet confirmed.

This will be determined, sources said, in the "structured dialogue" the UK is promising with countries that have long demanded that the pain and lasting legacies of the slave trade are, as they see it, properly addressed.

Burnham said his "new approach with the Commonwealth" had been "well received" at the summit.

He said it had "been the most successful meeting of the Commonwealth in recent times," adding that "the King's words have resonated powerfully here and we're really pleased with how it's gone".

King Charles III, speaking in his role as Head of the Commonwealth, told the meeting: "The transatlantic trade in enslaved persons still casts a shadow over these islands and other Members of our Commonwealth.

"As I have said before, that shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow."

The UK has signed up to "structured, time-bound, inclusive and good-faith" talks. The talks will be held at a later date, though the Foreign Secretary has suggested they are likely to conclude in around a year.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmwy.title: 'Not my job to set a budget,' says secretary of state
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmwy.text:
The Northern Ireland secretary has said that it is not his "job" to set a budget and that it is the responsibility of the Northern Ireland Executive.

This comes after no resolution was reached in negotiations between executive parties and Sir Chris Bryant.

He is understood to have presented a set of conditions, including revenue raising, to be attached to any potential deal on a Stormont budget.

Sir Chris said: "They really have to take me seriously when I say there is no more money."

Seven months into this financial year the Northern Ireland Executive has still not agreed a budget.

Speaking after a series of one-to-one meetings, the First Minister Michelle O'Neill said there was still "no white smoke".

Democratic Unionist Party leader (DUP) Gavin Robinson said he felt there was a level of optimism that was "not matched by the reality inside" the room during talks.

Speaking on BBC Newsline, Sir Chris said it is the "legal responsibility and duty" of the executive to set a budget.

He described talks ending without agreement as "a bit frustrating" but added that he's still "hopeful".

He said: "I just wanted to get a move on" and added: "Whatever the total envelope is you have to live within it".

Sir Chris also said he would only set a budget for Northern Ireland if the executive parties asked him to.

"They should be able to put together their budget but they have to decide what their priorities are."

After talks with the secretary of state, the first minister said that while there may be things dividing the executive, her party would persist in trying to get a budget deal done that allows public sector pay awards to be made for this year.

O'Neill also said she was getting "impatient" with the government and that she would take no lectures from it about managing finances.

The DUP leader said: "As it stands today, the secretary of state is not moving, the practical, honest reality of that is that without additional resource, there will not be a balanced budget".

Robinson added that "there will be no legal ability to do what it is we think the executive needs to do, and what we want it to do" without a budget.

Stormont ministers argue the UK's devolution funding formula no longer delivers enough for them to balance their books.

The government had offered them an additional £525m this year, but they said it still left significant gaps in managing their spending pressures, particularly delivery of pay awards for public sector workers.

It is not clear what the shape of a final budget agreement could look like, with some parties insisting there is still scope to "reprofile" some of the financial package.

Bryant's conditions are believed to include the executive committing to £200m in additional revenue raising in 2027/28 and 2028/29.

He has also asked that they should improve "discipline" around promises and delivery of pay parity to public sector workers in Northern Ireland.

Ulster Unionist leader Jon Burrows said he did not want to sound "defeatist" and would continue to engage with the government.

But he said there was a real prospect that it would be resolved in time to avert the potential of strike action by health care workers waiting on pay uplifts for this year.

Speaking before talks with the secretary of state, Alliance's Agriculture Minister Andrew Muir said it is now "make your mind up time" for the executive.

"This needs to be resolved not in weeks or months, but days. We need to come to a final conclusion and give certainty to people who deserve proper pay but also in terms of investment in public services we need to get this done," he added.

Speaking on BBC NI's The View programme, Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) leader Claire Hanna said a budget is "an agreement to take responsibility and an agreement to prioritise".

Her party, which is the official opposition in the legislative assembly, is "very clear about the severe constraints," she said, but added: "the fact is by not having a budget in month eight of this financial year, everybody who's trying to operate in that budget is running at 95%".

Talks between the government and the executive parties have been taking place for several months now, but earlier this week O'Dowd warned that a "crunch point" is approaching.

On Tuesday, the executive met again, with O'Dowd saying afterwards that he planned to present a series of options to his ministerial colleagues in the days ahead about a way forward.

He did not divulge what those may be, but the government has already said no to a request from the executive to allow a larger chunk of the money in the three-year offer to be spent this year, referred to as "front-loading".

Without an agreed budget, departments face operating on emergency spending restricted to 95% of the prior year, with warnings that funds could run out by January.

The secretary of state has also warned that a cost-of-living £100 payment cannot be made to households in Northern Ireland until an executive budget is agreed.

That came after the government announced its first budget under Andy Burnham last week, with Northern Ireland getting an additional £270m for public services as a result, of which £131m can be used this year.

Sir Chris has said that he is exploring contingency measures to allow him to pass a budget bill at Westminster, in the event that a deal cannot be reached to do so at Stormont.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmwy.summary: Northern Ireland Secretary of State says it is not his job to set a budget. Sir Chris Bryant has presented a set of conditions to be attached to any potential deal on a Stormont budget. First Minister Michelle O'Neill says there is still "no white smoke" in talks with the executive.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6kg.title: Time to focus on cost of living, says PM after US election results
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6kg.text:
Andy Burnham has said the results of the US midterm elections meant there was an "opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that's the cost of living".

Speaking to broadcasters from the Commonwealth leaders summit, the prime minister promised to push for a resolution to the conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine in the wake of the US elections that saw Donald Trump's Republicans suffer heavy losses.

He said he couldn't ease cost of living pressures until the US's conflict in Iran had been resolved.

Responding to the midterm results, the US president acknowledged that rising fuel prices - caused by the Iran war - had played a part in his party's defeats.

Speaking to Fox News, President Trump said: "People agree with what I'm doing on Iran but they really probably weren't willing to do the short term consequences of paying more for gasoline - I understand that."

Giving his reaction to the results, Burnham said the voters in the US have said they want to "see the world coming together and focusing on the things that matter to people".

Asked whether he thought the results might make the US president more unpredictable, Burnham said: "President Trump has accepted the results, and I feel the world has an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that's the cost of living.

"That has been the issue that I have put front and centre in my first three months in Downing Street, and we've made moves.

"But I can't get people's cost of living pressures down until the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, the conflict in Ukraine started by Russia.

"These are the things we have to focus on now, and I hope the world has a moment to do that.

"And certainly, in my calls with leaders, that is what I will be asking everybody to do."

The subject of the US midterm elections was raised at Prime Minister's Questions, which, in Burnham's absence, was taken by Cabinet Office Minister Louise Haigh.

The Liberal Democrat's deputy leader Daisy Cooper said American voters had rejected Trump's "warmongering and the economic chaos that it has caused".

She expressed concern that the US president was planning further strikes on Iran and urged the government to "stand together with our reliable allies and send a clear message to Trump and Netanyahu: there must be no more strikes."

Haigh replied: "The US are one of our most important allies and our priority absolutely is de-escalation."

She said the Iran war had been "catastrophic for the cost of living crisis" and said the Conservatives and Reform should "consider very carefully their judgment in calling for us to jump so readily into it".

Asked about suggestions there could be an attack on Iran in the coming week, Trump told the Financial Times on Tuesday: "The US was "locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no need for it".

Indirect talks between the two sides have been stalled for months and some analysts close to the Iran regime have suggested prolonging the negotiations, in the hope that the rising cost of fuel would damage Trump electorally.

Although the US Congress, now controlled by the Democrats, can restrict funding, Trump will still have significant authority over foreign policy.

Burnham is preparing a 10-year plan for government, and will be hoping that his strategy isn't blown off course by the actions of an unpredictable US president in his last two years in the White House.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6kg.summary: Andy Burnham says the US midterm results mean there is an "opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all" The US president acknowledged that rising fuel prices had played a part in his party's defeats. He said he couldn't ease cost of living pressures until the US's conflict in Iran had been resolved

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c64g.title: Children spending too long on maths app TT Rockstars, MP warns
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c64g.text:
Concerns have been raised with the government about the amount of time primary school children are spending on a game designed to make learning times tables fun.

TT Rockstars, which allows children to compete with their classmates for virtual coins and rock-star themed characters and outfits, is widely used by schools for maths homework.

Labour MP Emily Darlington said the app and others like it could be harming children's development because it rewards them for "length of time rather than quality of time spent online".

Bruno Reddy, founder of the firm behind TT Rockstars, said he shared concerns about screen time and was working with schools to bring in curfews and time limits.

He said the company discourages long sessions, adding: "Every game in TTRS is deliberately short, and our characters remind children to take regular breaks.

"The rule of thumb we give schools is: three minutes, four or five times a week. In September, a typical child played on three days, for about six minutes each time."

He said that from 24 November "every school will have a curfew and a daily time limit switched on, and leaderboards switched off as default".

Darlington told BBC News that while education technology, or EdTech, can have a place in the classroom "when gamification is used, children spend hours online to 'earn' the latest outfit".

"Parents are concerned that this causes conflict on time spent on devices and the pressure to perform against classmates," she added, and this could deter them from taking part in real life, rather than screen-based, activities.

The Milton Keynes Central MP raised concerns about TT Rockstars on Tuesday at the Commons Science Committee, which is investigating the impact of screen time and digital devices on children's brain development.

The company behind TT Rockstars, Maths Circle, says that the app and a similar programme for addition and subtraction, Numbots, is used in 17,000 schools and over 100,000 households.

Reddy, a former maths teacher, said TT Rockstars had been designed to "boost learning in the classroom: recognising progress, celebrating achievement and making learning enjoyable".

He added: "We've deliberately steered away from features designed to keep children playing, such as streaks, random rewards, chat messages, loot boxes or notifications.

"There's no advertising and schools pay the same subscription however much their students play, so we have no commercial reason to want children on screen for longer."

The government is in the process of drawing up guidelines for schools and parents on the amount of time five to 16-year-olds should spend on screens.

At the committee, early years education minister Paul Waugh said: "Gamification isn't the way to learn.

"That's the propaganda they [EdTech companies] will give you but it is all about driving their screen time and their screen use. So it's profit driven."

He said there were "ways of making learning fun" that did not involve "competition with yourself or with someone else" and EdTech should be about supporting teachers and not replacing them.

It comes amid growing calls for the use of EdTech in the classroom to be limited.

Charlotte Ashton, co-founder of Generation Focus, which campaigns for smartphone-free schools, said: "Increasingly parents and teachers are saying no to Ed Tech because for the vast majority of digital 'learning tools' there's very little evidence they actually improve learning and growing evidence they can be harmful."

She added: "Not all tech is bad, but until we are confident that new digital tools improve children's learning without doing harm or imposing unintended consequences we are supporting schools to stick to proven teaching methods."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c64g.summary: TT Rockstars allows children to compete with classmates for virtual coins and rock-star themed characters. It is widely used by schools for maths homework and is widely popular with pupils. Labour MP Emily Darlington says it could be harming children's development.

The BBC's political correspondent Joe Pike outlines the highs and lows of Sir Keir Starmer's premiership.

Sir Keir Starmer resigned as PM and leader of the Labour party in a statement outside No. 10 on Monday

Sir Keir Starmer resigns as leader of the Labour Party, in a statement outside 10 Downing Street.

Andy Burnham delivers his victory speech after Makerfiled by-election.

Labour's Andy Burnham wins the Makerfield by-election, paving the way for him to challenge Keir Starmer as Labour Party leader.

The former Mayor of Greater Manchester won the Makerfield by-election - paving the way to challenge Starmer.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmr4.title: Palestine Action ban undermined confidence in anti-terror laws, Supreme Court told
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmr4.text:
The banning of Palestine Action has led to a "crisis in confidence" in the UK's anti-terrorism laws and triggered unprecedented civil disobedience from law-abiding protesters, the Supreme Court has been told.

Opening a major legal challenge to the group's proscription last year, lawyers for co-founder Huda Ammori said that no other protest organisation had been treated the same way.

They told the five justices that the UK's highest court had never before had to consider whether banning a group under terrorism legislation was compatible with freedom of speech and protest.

Twenty-seven protesters were arrested outside the Supreme Court on Wednesday as the hearing took place, the Metropolitan Police said.

Lawyers for Ammori told the court that thousands of elderly people, many veterans of other radical causes, had been arrested for holding up signs supportive of the group since its proscription.

Home Office figures seen by the BBC indicate that there have been more than 4,000 arrests so far at protests in which people have held up signs supportive of the group.

In practice, many demonstrators have been arrested more than once, with 1,200 charges authorised by prosecutors to date. Those trials are in limbo until the outcome of this case.

Henry Blaxland KC told the court that "far from depriving Palestine Action of the oxygen of publicity" and "far from discrediting its brand", proscription of the group has had the opposite effect.

"All it's done is to pour fuel on to a fire of one of the most publicly-contested issues of our time," he said.

"It was disproportionate to do that and in my submission completely unnecessary."

During often tense exchanges with the judges, Ammori's team accepted that Palestine Action could not be described as an ordinary and peaceful protest group.

They said that its members had carried out "direct action" protests by occupying or vandalising firms linked to Israel's military - with only three of 385 incidents assessed by the Home Secretary as constituting an offence under the Terrorism Act.

The UK's definition of terrorism includes incidents of serious damage to property for a cause - and at least two break-ins at defence firms have been described in criminal courts as having caused millions in damage.

Raza Husain KC, for Ammori, said that the judges had to put aside allegations of criminality - for which the state had many powers - and consider whether the Home Secretary's decision to label the group as terrorists had been disproportionate.

"Palestine Action was proscribed on the basis of less than one per cent of its actions over five years assessed as falling within the outer limits of a definition of terrorism," he said.

"The Home Secretary's own experts confirmed the vast majority of its direct action would not constitute an act of terrorism on the basis that any damage to property is typically more minor. Common tactics include graffiti, petty vandalism, occupation, and lock-ons."

One Palestine Action member has been convicted and jailed of fracturing a police officer's back with a sledgehammer - but the court was told that the group had never advocated such violence.

The Supreme Court has received arguments from free speech campaigners, arguing the ban interferes with the right to protest.

But another submission from a coalition of Jewish groups argued that Palestine Action was a "sinister" organisation intent on attacking its community interests.

"The Court of Appeal [following earlier hearings] rightly concluded that PA is a violent organisation concerned in terrorism with a wide range of targets," said Adam Wagner KC in written submissions for the Jewish communal groups.

He continued: "Its activities are often undertaken covertly with no suggestion of restraint or proportionality, and that at the point it was proscribed it had an escalating trajectory of seriousness and an expanding focus."

Wagner said Palestine Action's "crosshairs" had moved from targeting Elbit, a defence firm with an Israeli parent company, to "figures or institutions deemed by PA to be 'Zionist'".

"Because most British Jews and Jewish institutions have a connection with Israel, a campaign against institutions PA's activists consider to be 'complicit' with Israel is, in practice, a campaign that threatens the mainstream Jewish community," he said.

However, Jewish Bloc, a group that campaigns in solidarity with Palestinians, told has also written to the court to say that claims that PA targeted their community were a "fundamental misrepresentation of the underlying evidence".

Rachel Scott KC, for the organisation, told the justices: "Neither the Jewish Leadership Council (JLC) nor the Community Security Trust (CST) have any democratic mandate. Claims that either organisation can be viewed as the voice of British Jews must therefore be viewed with very significant caution.

"The framing of PA as an organisation which threatened and intimidated 'the Jewish Community' is demonstrably false and a deliberate elision. The evidence instead shows that it targeted entities, organisations and institutions with an established link to Israel's illegal activities against the Palestinian people."

The case continues on Thursday with a judgment expected at a later date.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmr4.summary: Palestine Action has been banned from UK anti-terrorism laws since last year. Lawyers for Huda Ammori say no other protest group has been treated the same way. They say the ban has led to a "crisis in confidence" in the UK's anti-terror laws.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6ly.title: Power deal between Labour and Greens in Sheffield
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6ly.text:
The leader of Labour on Sheffield City Council has said a deal would be announced in coming days about continuing a power-sharing deal with the Green Party.

It came after a bitter row over Zionism, which saw Labour nationally telling 11 councils, including Sheffield, to break power deals with the Greens.

Until this afternoon's council meeting, it had been expected that Labour would move to run matters in the city on its own, by ditching power-sharing with the Greens.

Speaking to a delayed full council meeting, Labour leader Fran Belbin said talks had been going on, and a joint statement would be made "in coming days" to show they could continue the current administration.

A protest was held outside the town hall ahead of the meeting, chiefly by pro- Palestine supporters.

Inside, the full council meeting was delayed for an hour as talks between Labour and the Greens continued.

Once underway, Belbin apologised to councillors for the delay and went on to explain that the two parties would "work more constructively together going forward".

She went on to indicate that a joint statement would soon mean that the current arrangement with the Greens would not change.

The power deal between Labour and the Greens in Sheffield came about following May's local elections, in which no party was left in overall control.

Commenting on the announcement by Belbin, councillor Martin Smith, leader of the Liberal Democrat Group, said: "This is an extraordinary U-turn and a shameful abandonment of principle by Labour.

"Just days ago, Labour were telling us that trust with the Greens was completely broken and that they could no longer work together. Now they've decided to carry on as if nothing happened."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm8e.title: Miliband says slavery apology will not bring cost for UK taxpayers
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm8e.text:
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has insisted the government's willingness to consider formally apologising for the UK's role in the transatlantic slave trade will not lead to higher costs for the British taxpayer.

The prime minister has said the UK will not pay reparations to affected countries, but declined to say whether his new approach could involve additional taxpayer money.

Speaking on the BBC's Newscast podcast, Miliband said previous British governments had a "sweep it under the carpet" attitude to the pain and consequences of slavery, citing what he described as former Prime Minister Sir Tony Blair's "sorry not sorry" remarks on the issue nearly two decades ago.

In 2007, Sir Tony said the UK's involvement in the slave trade was a matter of "deep sorrow and regret".

"Tony Blair did sort of do a kind of sorry not sorry situation. He kind of expressed sorrow, and then said sorry, and then it was walked back by number 10," Miliband said.

Miliband said the former prime minister's approach was still referred to and came up in a recent conversation between Andy Burnham and the Prime Minister of Barbados Mia Mottley.

In addition, Miliband claimed, he and Burnham inherited a more recent mess, which is how the last Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) played out in Samoa two years ago.

Miliband said: "On the second day as my time as foreign secretary, I was told, 'look, one of your tasks is CHOGM 2024, which happened in Samoa, didn't go well.' To use sort of diplomatic speak, it ended up in a sort of punch up, a sort of verbal punch up about this whole issue."

He added: "This has really been hanging around as an issue for the Commonwealth for sort of 20 years, really. But it's grown and grown."

Given that, Miliband said, "we thought it was right to confront this issue and not to just try and sort of pretend that it didn't exist".

Burnham now says the government is open to formally apologising for slavery.

Ministers are beginning what they call a "structured dialogue" with affected countries, with the expectation that the apology may come at around the time the prime minister hosts the G20 Summit of world leaders in Manchester in November 2027.

"Is it weak to do this? I think it's the opposite of weak. I think fragile weak countries can't face up to their past. I'm really proud of Britain, but being proud of your country is also being willing to face up to things you didn't do, right?" Miliband said.

He said he had asked to be provided with a historical digest of the UK's involvement in the slave trade.

"Over three million people shipped, really with the British state's complicity, over a long period of time, couple of centuries actually, hundreds of thousands of them didn't make it and died," the foreign secretary said.

"Those who did make it had appalling conditions. Reading about the conditions on the ships and what happened to them when they arrived in the Caribbean and the Americas is really pretty harrowing."

Now he and the prime minister begin a process likely to formally apologise for this -and, they hope, create space for the Commonwealth to turn its attention to other things.
