https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck4g.title: Potty training scheme to roll out to 20 more areas
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck4g.text:
The number of children who were toilet-trained before starting school this year has increased significantly in a city where parents were given potty training guides with their first school offers.

York was the subject of the city-wide pilot, which also put on workshops for parents and offered special training for early years staff.

Twenty local authorities across England are now signed up to launch similar schemes to tackle the number of pupils starting school without being fully toilet-trained.

The government said the pilot's results were "encouraging", and confirmed they were committed to 75% of pupils reaching a good level of development at the end of their first year in school by 2028.

Since April this year, parents across York have been targeted via GP surgeries, pharmacies, family hubs, schools, nurseries and libraries with information and offers of support on how to potty-train their child ahead of starting school.

Potty training guides were sent out to all families across York who had a child starting reception in September - with the aim that all children could use the toilet independently by the time they started school, except those with medical issues or special educational needs.

The results from all 55 mainstream primary schools across the city, shared exclusively with BBC News, suggested there had been a 43% drop since last year in the number of children who were not fully toilet-trained when they started school.

Across York last September, 148 out of 1,364 reception pupils (11%) were recorded as not being toilet-trained when they started school. This year, that fell to 85 reception pupils out of 1,374 (6%).

Parents Natalie and Lucy, who both have daughters starting reception next year, have welcomed the extra support on offer.

Lucy said she had noticed the drop-in sessions on potty training in her local children's centre and thought it was a "really good idea".

"I think it's really important that children are more prepared for that aspect of starting school," she said.

Natalie said getting her daughter Freya potty-trained in time for school has been a priority, but feels there is a lot of pressure on parents to do so.

"I think going to school is hard enough for children," she said.

"But for me it was really important that she's confident enough to use toilets, to be independent, to be able to go without relying on the help of teachers perhaps in an environment where they've already got lots of children to look after."

Natalie said the popularity of disposable nappies might be a reason why parents often wait longer to potty train.

"When I was little, we still had the terry towelling nappies and they had to be washed and hung on the line. So I think with disposable nappies it's easier," she said.

Around one in four children started school in England and Wales last year not fully toilet-trained, and teachers said they have been spending over an hour a day changing nappies, according to the latest research from the children's charity Kindred Squared.

Felicity Gillespie, chief executive of Kindred Squared, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that children not being potty trained when starting school was "a real concern for teachers".

"They tell us that they're losing, on average across the country, a day a week of teaching time to dealing with potty-training issues."

Gillespie is keen to spread the message that "it's best for children to be coming out of nappies" when they are between 18 and 30 months old.

"When the teacher's leaving the class to change someone's nappy, the rest of the class is having their learning broken up. So everybody loses out,” she added.

Jo Mould, who teaches reception at Robert Wilkinson Primary Academy in York, said she has noticed an improvement in pupils being ready for school this year.

"We've spent more time teaching in these last three weeks than we have in previous years," she said.

"The children have come in so ready to learn, because they're more settled and regulated socially and emotionally. We've had a really, really positive start to the school year."

York councillor Bob Webb said the impact of the scheme had been "so positive" for both schools and families.

But he acknowledged a potential "gap in support" for parents between seeing health visitors with their toddler, and the child later arriving at school.

He said the key to the scheme's success was collaboration across health visitors, schools and other community settings, but that there was "always more that could be done at an earlier age".

Twenty local authorities across England have now committed to adopt York's model, developed by Kindred Squared, and use it to encourage earlier potty-training in their areas.

Just over two-thirds of children in England (68.3%) leave reception class with a good level of development - a key measure of school readiness which includes things like communication skills, as well as physical, social and emotional development - according to the latest government stats.

That means they were assessed by teachers on being able to complete tasks like going to the toilet and paying attention in class.

The government has said it is still committed to increasing that proportion to 75% by 2028.

Early Education Minister Paul Waugh said it was "encouraging to see this pilot helping more children develop the confidence and independence they need before starting school", stressing the importance of parents taking early steps towards toilet training.

In York, Mould said she hopes next year's parents will take on potty-training even earlier.

"Ideally we'd be at the point where [children] don't need that support when they get here, because they've already been trained by the time they get to us."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck4g.summary: York pilot put on workshops for parents and offered special training for early years staff. Twenty local authorities across England are now signed up to launch similar schemes.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmn0.title: Badenoch unveils plan to end £100,000 childcare 'cliff edge' ahead of Tory conference
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmn0.text:
Kemi Badenoch has said a Conservative government would scrap the "cliff edge" that means parents in England lose out on childcare support when they earn more than £100,000 a year.

Speaking to the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg, the Conservative Party leader said: "What we want to see is that people who work harder don't get punished for doing so."

The earnings limit means only families where no parent earns more than this threshold are eligible for 30 hours of government-funded childcare or tax-free childcare.

The announcement comes as Conservative members gather for the party's annual conference in Birmingham.

Badenoch, who arrived in the city on Saturday, has vowed the party was new and different from the one that lost the 2024 general election.

The Conservatives - who have been polling behind Labour and Reform UK over the past year - are expected to use the four-day event to lay out more of their policy agenda ahead of the next general election.

Ahead of the conference, the Conservatives produced a 100-page essay setting out their principles including a "central" belief that business, rather than governments, create growth.

It argues that governments should create the conditions for growth, particularly through the tax system.

In her interview with the BBC, Badenoch pitched herself as a "classic old-school Conservative" adding: "I believe in common sense - people working hard and being rewarded for that effort."

She insisted the Tories would keep the state pension triple lock, which Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to change if Labour wins the next election.

She said the policy, under which state pensions rise each year by the highest of inflation, average wages, or 2.5%, was "the right policy for pensioners".

She added: "What we don't want to see is people going after the elderly, chasing after vulnerable and disabled people, and then the extremely large cohort of people who can work, who are not working, are left alone."

The Conservatives have long called on the government to cut the growing welfare budget including by implementing tighter restrictions on claimants.

The party said its childcare announcement would be a "first step" in broader efforts to address issues in the tax system which damage incentives to work or invest.

This will be a theme of shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith's conference speech on Monday.

Since September 2025, working parents in England have been entitled to 30 hours of free childcare for children aged between nine months and four years old.

However, to qualify both parents must earn less than £100,000 a year, although all three and four-year-olds are eligible for 15 hours of free childcare, regardless of parental income.

The same £100,000 eligibility threshold also applies to the government's tax-free childcare scheme, and has remained unchanged since it was originally set under the Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government.

For every £8 paid into an online childcare account, the government adds £2, up to £2,000 per child per year, which parents can then use to pay for childcare.

The Tories said that if they return to power, they would remove the £100,000 threshold entirely for tax-free childcare and government-funded childcare hours.

The threshold has been criticised by economists, who point out it can leave parents worse off overall even after a pay rise of tens of thousands of pounds.

In her interview with Kuenssberg, Badenoch said: "What we want to see is more people in work and not taking the wrong decisions or the wrong choices, and it doesn't matter whether they're earning £10,000 or £100,000 - what matters is that people are out there working".

Asked if this could result in someone who earns £1m a year getting free childcare under a Conservative government, the Tory leader responded: "It doesn't matter what you earn - we don't want you to be punished for working hard. What we're trying to do is grow our economy."

The Tories argue the threshold may mean some people may delay having children until their incomes change, or decide not to start a family at all, describing scrapping it as "both pro-family and pro-growth".

By providing an increased incentive to work, the Tories said the move would also boost economic growth.

They added that it would tackle the "unfairness" that the threshold is calculated on an individual earner's income rather then for the whole household.

The party said the policy would be funded by cutting the number of public servants working in "executive non-departmental public bodies" - organisations which have a role in the processes of national government but operate at arm's length from ministers, such as Arts Council England and the Environment Agency.

It said this would save £1.6bn by 2029-30, covering the estimated £700m cost of removing the childcare "cliff edge".

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq07.title: Woman deceived ex-partner that she had given birth to his babies, judge rules
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq07.text:
A woman convinced her former partner she had given birth to two children who most likely did not exist in what a High Court judge described as an "extraordinary" and "elaborate campaign of deceit".

The man, who has not been named but was referred to as John in the judgement, applied to the Family Court after he was told the woman had sold their two children for a combined £500.

The case heard that the man received messages and photos of the children and paid the woman around £30,000 over the course of two years.

But in a hearing in February, the woman, who was referred to as Jane, told the judge she had lied about the pregnancies for revenge, claiming the man had abused her.

The court heard the man believed he was the children's' father because in late 2022 his partner told him she was pregnant, sent pictures of an ultrasound image and had become "visibly pregnant" as time went on.

In May 2023, shortly before the first baby was due, the woman called the police alleging she had been assaulted by the man.

He was arrested and subsequently held on remand for several months, Mrs Justice Judd said in her ruling which was published on Friday.

Following this, the woman sent a message to his stepfather saying the baby had been born as well as sharing baby photos.

At one stage she is said to have sent voice notes to her former partner's mother in the middle of the night with the sound of a baby crying in the background.

Later, she told the man she was pregnant again and the baby was due in August 2024.

However, before the due date, the couple split up and did not reconcile.

The woman would go on to tell the man's mother the baby had been born.

The woman admitted to the court she had told him she was pregnant when they were together, and afterwards, but conceded she had told a series of elaborate lies and that there were, in fact, no children.

She argued she was menopausal at the time and could not have been pregnant and bank statements show she attended a tanning shop on the day she said she had given birth, Mrs Justice Judd said.

In her judgement, the judge concluded that the "factors that weigh against the children genuinely existing were very strong, stronger than the factors pointing the other way".

She said the man was the victim of a "sustained and elaborate campaign of deceit" which also impacted his mother and closest friend.

"Added to this, the behaviour was cruel, leading a man and his mother to believe they had children and grandchildren respectively.", the Judge said.

The judge added she was unable to conclude the woman's motive for her behaviour but said financial fraud was a "possibility" and that the "complex mental health problems" she suffered from may have also played a part.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr2k.title: Employers should teach primary-age children about work, says Milburn
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr2k.text:
Children should be introduced to the world of work at the start of primary school, says the author of a major report into youth activity in the UK.

Former minister Alan Milburn says children as young as four should be learning about different careers, with work experience placements made mandatory for 14- to 16-year-olds.

However, teaching unions warn of the "significant pressure" already facing primary schools and say practical considerations must ensure all schools have access to the support.

The latest data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) suggests 981,000 people aged 16 to 24 in the UK were not in education, employment or training (known as Neet), between April and June 2026.

Milburn told the BBC "in primary school, it's really about opening their eyes and giving them a sense about what is possible".

Despite a push towards apprenticeships and work experience in Years 10 and 11, for many the journey towards becoming Neet starts well before their 16th birthday.

As a result, Milburn says children should be introduced to the world of work much earlier in their school journey, with dedicated space in the curriculum to "broaden horizons".

He told the BBC this could be achieved by employers giving talks in primary schools and offering taster sessions to children.

"It'd be good if employers came into schools and said, 'Look, this is what's going on, these are things that are possible.'"

Milburn says that for Key Stage 4 pupils - aged between 14 and 16 - experience must be given in a real workplace with employer feedback.

"Work experience needs to be mandatory. It makes a big difference," he told the BBC.

Milburn also emphasised the difficulty some young people face when trying to find work experience placements.

"There are about four in ten people aged 14-16 who aren't getting any work experience at all," he said. "In other schools, students are told to go off and find their own work experience and that often relies on the network of Mum and Dad."

These recommendations are due to be published in the final instalment of his government-commissioned report into the issue, which is expected to be published in the autumn.

Education is devolved in the UK, so while Milburn's review looks at the picture in all four nations, his recommendations regarding education are specific to England.

Currently in England, careers guidance must be offered to students aged 11-18 and work experience is not statutory.

The government has said its vision is to "guarantee two weeks' worth of work experience for every young person" in England.

In both Scotland and Wales, career-based learning is already a requirement in schools for students as young as three.

Emma, from Kirklees, has grandchildren in Years 1, 2 and 4 and thinks primary school is too young to be introducing careers talks.

"In primary school, there is too much trying to get little kids to grow up too quickly," she says.

"Just let them be little kids. I know they have to learn and the world's changing, but still, give them a chance to be kids."

But Zoe, another parent, disagrees.

"I think it's a good idea," she says. "It's something that everyone has to do, so if you learn early, it's something they don't have to learn later on."

Teaching unions have responded positively to the idea of introducing career-based learning into schools at a younger age, but have warned about the burden this could place on primary schools in particular.

Paul Whiteman, general secretary of school leaders' union National Association of Head Teachers (NAHT), warns of the "significant pressure" already facing primary schools.

"Whenever new mandatory requirements are proposed, it is important to be clear about what might have to give way to make room for them," he says.

Whiteman also highlights the value of existing programmes such as "Primary Futures", which bring in volunteers from different professions into schools to "challenge stereotypes and raise aspirations".

"The earlier young people can begin to make connections between what they learn in school and the possibilities that lie ahead, the better," Whiteman says.

Pepe Di'Iasio, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders (ASCL), says having someone come into the classroom can really "enlighten [children's] motivation... and give them that sense of passion for all the opportunities beyond the classroom". Although he acknowledges that finding opportunities in rural areas could be more challenging.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr2k.summary: Alan Milburn says children as young as four should be introduced to work experience. He says children should be taught about different careers at the start of school journey. But teaching unions warn of the "significant pressure" already facing primary schools.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm98.title: WhatsApp introduces optional parental controls for teenagers
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm98.text:
WhatsApp is introducing new parental controls for teenagers, as tech companies continue to come under pressure to provide more age-appropriate experiences for children.

The social messaging app's new tools will give parents a range of options, such as being told when their child joins or leaves a group. It will also let them decide on privacy settings for their account.

In a blog post, WhatsApp, clarified parents would not be given the power to see the messages their teen is sending and receiving, which along with calls would stay private and protected by end-to-end encryption.

And it said the controls were optional, which social media analyst Matt Navarra called an "obvious weakness".

He said the move was "fairly convenient" for Meta, which owns WhatsApp, because it reduced the company's reliance on age verification by putting some responsibility on parents and teenagers.

"Meta is trying to show regulators we have a child safety system, we have parental controls and we're rolling it out across our platforms," he said.

"I think the big unanswered question is whether enough families will actually use it."

The minimum age to use WhatsApp is 13 in the UK, although it is higher in some countries.

According to the firm, parents will be able to adjust or switch off the controls at any time.

The settings will be "straightforward to set up" using a Pin set by a parent, which teens will need if they want to switch off the controls.

Some of the new privacy tools include selecting who can see a child's profile photo and who can add them to groups.

Parents can also choose how their teenager uses Channels, which allows organisations and public figures to send out content.

And they will have the option of choosing between the default 13+ setting for Meta AI, the app's optional built-in AI assistant, or a stricter "Limited Content" option.

"All of these controls are being designed to support open conversations about how to use WhatsApp between parents and teens, while keeping everyone's personal messages private," the company said.

The changes come as pressure mounts on tech companies from governments and regulators to change the way they operate in order to better protect children using their platforms.

In June, the government announced it plans to ban under-16s from social media platforms, with the restrictions expected to come into force in March 2027.

It said "highly effective age assurance" measures would be used to check the age of those using social media.

WhatsApp is currently excluded from the ban because the government considers it a messaging service.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm9d.title: Parents warned to be on alert after school data breach
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm9d.text:
Parents have been told to be alert for unexpected emails or phone calls after a Northern Ireland school app used by almost 50,000 people was affected by a data breach.

The Equipple app is used by many schools to schedule and book meetings between parents and teachers.

There have been concerns that the breach may have allowed access to parent contact details and some pupil information.

In a statement to BBC News NI a spokesperson for Equipple said they were taking the matter "extremely seriously" and that there is "no evidence of any ongoing unauthorised access to the platform".

"Equipple recently identified unauthorised access to part of its cloud-hosted environment and immediately activated its incident response procedures," they said.

"We secured the affected systems and, with the support of independent cybersecurity specialists, have implemented additional safeguards."

Equipple had informed schools immediately of the breach and said that an investigation, supported by specialists, was continuing.

Some schools who use the app have contacted parents to inform them of the incident.

One email to parents seen by BBC News NI said that the data breach had "resulted in unauthorised access to personal information held within the service for a very short period of time".

The email said that that the "intrusion was immediately identified."

"The incident may have allowed access to parent/carer contact details: telephone number: home address and email address. Pupil information: name, date of birth and registration group," it said.

Parents were also advised by the school, as a precaution, "to remain alert to any unexpected emails, telephone calls or other communications which refer to you, your child or their school."

The email also said the incident had been referred to the Education Authority (EA) information governance team.

In a statement a spokesperson for the EA said it is "providing guidance on the schools' data protection obligations and appropriate next steps".

"Schools are writing directly to parents and carers with relevant information and advice and are reviewing whether any additional security measures are required."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvrl.title: School failed to deal with racist bullying, father claims
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvrl.text:
A family whose son says he suffered racist bullying have accused the school and council of failing to deal with the abuse.

The son, who the BBC is not naming, says racial slurs have been aimed at him daily at Ysgol Dyffryn Conwy in Llanrwst.

The school say they do not tolerate any racism or bullying and that it is a safe environment for all pupils.

Conwy council say the school is suitable for the boy and arrangements have been made to continue his education.

The boy said he has received racist abuse at school "every day".

"Teachers have heard it. I know they have because there's no chance you don't hear it.

"But they choose to ignore it. They don't deal with it, they act like it's OK," he said.

Newyddion S4C has seen racist online messages the family say were sent to the son by other pupils.

They have not been shared with the school, the family say, in case he becomes a greater target.

North Wales Police say they have dealt with reports of racist online messages and an alleged racial assault against the boy.

"I can't go out because if someone sees me, I'll be attacked," said the boy. "I've got to be careful where I go, so I just stay indoors."

The boy's father said: "There's only one victim. If he goes, the school can pretend there's no problem. They can sweep it under the carpet.

"I understand schools are under pressure and classrooms are busy, but you cannot let racist language become normal. It's shocked me to the core."

After a complaint from the father, the school governors' complaints panel rejected each matter, but noted areas to be "strengthened".

The governors said they followed their complaints policy thoroughly and accurately.

The school later told the family they cannot control the behaviour of pupils in every location and that investigations into allegations had to be fair and balanced.

They offered to increase monitoring, change the academic timetable, provide a safe haven and change staff intervention processes.

The school's anti-bullying policy was updated, the family were told, with more staff training and a new anti-racism action plan to change culture.

But the father says the family have lost faith in the school and called the council response "atrocious".

"They've done their best to isolate, shut down any conversation and just brick-wall everything and everyone," he said.

"We've felt completely alone battling them to hear what a vulnerable child is going through and they've had deaf ears to it all.

"What's going to take time to get over is the council's inaction and unwillingness to even have conversations, more than the actual harm the kids have done."

The family say the council offered to meet only after journalists approached them about the allegations.

The council have now agreed to make different arrangements for the boy, but the family remain unhappy because the school and council insist the school is safe for him.

The family were supported by Ethnic Minorities and Youth Support Team Wales (EYST) who say racism is common in schools.

"Sadly, schools don't record a lot of incidents and children don't report it either, so there's things to tackle," said EYST's Selima Bahadur.

"We've seen a rise in racism online, social media. It's common and these are the trends we're seeing in schools, children saying these things openly to each other."

A statement from the school and its governors said: "Ysgol Dyffryn Conwy does not tolerate any racism, bullying or discriminatory behaviour.

"Whenever concerns are raised they're considered seriously and dealt with in line with school policies, statutory duties and safeguarding responsibilities.

"The school works closely with pupils, families and local authority to ensure support is available and that concerns are considered thoroughly and with care.

"We are confident Ysgol Dyffryn Conwy is a safe and supportive learning environment for every pupil."

The school said it was committed to equality, inclusivity and respect and would keep working to deal with concerns and help every pupil's wellbeing.

Conwy council said it was sorry the family were not satisfied with how their concerns were handled.

"Conwy County Borough Council does not tolerate any racist behaviour" they said.

The council accepts the situation has been difficult for the boy and say it has worked to provide support.

"For these reasons we do not accept we ignored the concerns raised by the family.

"We maintain that the school is suitable for the boy.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c35y.title: Former permanent secretary alleges he was 'bullied' by education minister, says MLA
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c35y.text:
A former permanent secretary at the Department of Education (DE) alleged he was "bullied" by the education minister, a Sinn Féin assembly member (MLA) has said.

The vice-chair of Stormont's education committee, Pat Sheehan, made the claim during a committee hearing on Wednesday.

"Everyone knows the accusation was from the permanent secretary at the time, Mark Browne, who alleged that the minister had bullied him or pressurised him into trying to promote another official within the department," Sheehan said.

In a statement to the assembly in March 2026, Paul Givan had clarified that allegations of "bullying" had been made against him by an unnamed civil servant.

Givan said that a confidential Civil Service Human Resources (HR) review had been carried out into "the conduct and performance of a civil servant".

But he said that he understood that the review had "rejected" their assertions of bullying.

An investigation was held into the circumstances in which the former DE permanent secretary Mark Browne was replaced in November 2024.

A permanent secretary is the most senior non-political official in a government department, effectively the department's chief executive.

But the outcome of that investigation has not been made public.

On Wednesday MLAs on the education committee questioned the Head of the Civil Service, Jayne Brady.

Brady said that she was the "line-manager" for permanent secretaries in government departments.

Sheehan asked Brady when she "first became aware of allegations that the Education Minister had bullied the permanent secretary within the department?"

In reply, Brady said that it was not appropriate for her to discuss personal or personnel issues in open committee session.

"Why the secrecy?" Sheehan said.

"It's an issue that goes to the heart of governance and transparency within the education department."

Brady said that there were "protections for confidential processes," including in employment law.

"Confidentiality is fair enough when we're dealing with personnel issues," Sheehan responded.

"This wasn't a personnel issue, this is about governance."

"This is about how a minister was treating the senior civil servant within his department."

Givan has previously told his officials not to attend the education committee due to what he called "unacceptable behaviour" by Sheehan.

The action has meant that DE officials have not given evidence to the committee or provided written briefings to it.

The committee chair, Alliance MLA Nick Mathison, has called the minister's move "unprecedented and unacceptable".

Sheehan, who is the committee's vice-chair had previously rejected "any suggestion that I bullied or harassed officials in any way".

The minister's direction to his officials came after a committee hearing on 23 September, where there were terse exchanges between Sheehan and a senior DE official, Suzanne Kingon.

Sheehan had asked Kingon a number of questions, including about her social media activity.

At one point Kingon said she was prepared to withdraw from the hearing during questions by Sheehan.

At the committee meeting on Wednesday, Mathison said that the committee was considering using rare legal powers to compel DE witnesses to appear at meetings.

Section 44 of the Northern Ireland Act 1998 allows a committee to call people to attend its meetings or to produce documents that are in their possession or under their control.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwly.title: Scottish colleges need £2.5bn  investment boost by 2037, report warns
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwly.text:
Colleges in Scotland will need £2.5bn to meet required investment in their infrastructure over the next decade, according to a new report.

The Scottish Funding Council (SFC) estimated £1.3bn was needed to maintain the college estate to a good standard, while an additional £1.2bn would be required to fund improvements.

The College Infrastructure Investment Plan (College IIP) said the "condition, configuration and expense" of some further and higher education buildings meant they were "no longer fit for purpose".

Colleges Scotland chief executive, Gavin Donoghue, said the report laid bare the "scale of the challenge" facing the sector.

The SFC is the body which allocates public funding to higher education.

This report covers all of Scotland's 24 colleges - which are spread across 99 campuses and 270 buildings - and spans a 10-year period between 2027/28 and 2036/37.

It said about £200m of the required funding would need to be used to tackle a maintenance backlog.

But the SFC warned only dealing with the most urgent investment needs would result in further deterioration of college infrastructure.

Donoghue said investment needed in 2027/28 alone was estimated at £262m.

He said a flat cash settlement from the Scottish government's budget on 3 December would "barely allow some institutions to address their most urgent issues".

Donoghue added: "Colleges need modern, sustainable and digitally enabled learning environments if they are to continue supporting learners, employers and Scotland's ambitions for productivity, net zero and inclusive growth.

"Investing in colleges would be a key part of ensuring colleges have a firm future as civic anchors as the public sector reforms and changes in the coming years."

Scottish colleges are publicly funded, have no borrowing options and are highly dependent on grants from the SFC.

That is in contrast to universities, which benefit from research income, international student fees and private donations.

A previous SFC report warned "insolvency remains an imminent risk" at some of the country's colleges.

Only three are currently forecast to break even.

The combination of an extensive backlog of maintenance, Raac issues and problems with cladding are central to the issues with infrastructure.

However, many buildings also require to be modernised and that pressure combines to create the £2.5bn figure in the report.

Paul Devoy, interim chief executive of the SFC, said: "This report underlines the need for change if we are to realise our ambitions within the funding available.

"It will now provide the foundation for our work with colleges to consider realistic, affordable and sustainable options for future reform that will deliver high-quality learning environments for future generations."

Tertiary Education Minister Alyn Smith said the Scottish government was aware a "significant transformation" was required across the college sector to guarantee its long-term future.

He said the government was working with Colleges Scotland and the SFC to create the "college sector of the future" which would aim to shape colleges for the next generation.

Smith added: "Scotland's colleges play a vital role in our economy and wider society, and this report is a useful piece of work on the extent to which their collective estate will need significantly more funding over the next ten years unless things change.

"We are well aware that significant transformation is required across the sector to guarantee its long-term future, which is why we provided a 10% uplift in core college funding to £764m in this year's budget."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cxnv.title: 'One heck of a rollercoaster' - foster carers urged to come forward
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cxnv.text:
For almost 24 years, Beverley Craig and her husband have had 14 "wee ones" – or foster children – through their doors.

And despite the "emotional rollercoaster" of nurturing a child destined to leave sooner rather than later, she would not change a thing.

"There isn't one that has come through our door that my husband and I weren't able to love very much and take them like our own," she said. "It's just been a joy."

But with record numbers of children in care, more foster carers – like Beverley - are needed.

It is not a new problem. In recent years, Northern Ireland has not had enough carers to cope with demand.

But it appears it is becoming more acute, with the Fostering Network, a charity that supports foster carers and children, saying the number of children in need of care has been going up at a time when the number of carers is going down.

"We are not really keeping up with the level of recruitment that we need to see to ensure that every child who becomes looked after has the right opportunity to be placed with a fostering family," the charity's chief executive Sarah Thomas said.

For Beverley being a foster carer with children's charity Barnardo's is challenging but rewarding.

"Well, I suppose you are giving up your whole life, it's 24/7 so you do need to think about it very carefully," she said.

"But when you do it, it is amazing you'll not regret it."

If foster carers have room in their homes and "the capacity to love other people's children like your own" the rest "comes naturally", according to Beverley.

"The children come through your door and it is amazing - you are on one heck of a rollercoaster."

Colin Jamieson is also a foster carer with Barnardo's and said it was hard to pinpoint why more people do not come forward.

"I suppose sometimes there is a bit of bad press around," he said. "But we've got to remember we are talking about young, vulnerable children who just need someone there to support them."

He said there were a lot of people "quite capable of doing that".

"Those are the people we need to come forward, just to support these children and to give them what they need and that real start," he added.

Hilary Armstrong, operations manager at the charity, has suggested a number of reasons why people are not coming forward to foster.

"The cost of living is always a big factor for families and we know things have got very expensive," she said.

Armstrong explained there were financial supports available.

Another obstacle to fostering is societal change in families, she said.

"So it's things like young adult children that are remaining at home for longer," she said.

"Or perhaps they are going off for a period of time after school, but they are coming back home again to save for deposits for maybe having their own house in the future," she said.

"I think 10 or 15 years ago there was less of that around."

Health Minister Robbie Butler has first-hand experience of providing foster care and said he would like to encourage people to come forward to foster.

"My wife and I provided foster care for maybe around 17 years," he said.

"We had two kids of our own, both of us were working full time while we fostered children.

"I get a little bit embarrassed sometimes by people saying 'oh you were really good', but what we provided was short term respite and emergency."

Butler said his family were able to provide "a safe, loving, stable environment for children, for a short period of time".

"As health minister what I want to do is drive that awareness to help foster families," he added.

As of the end of March, 4,287 children and young people were in care in Northern Ireland, according to the Department of Health (DoH).

This was the highest number recorded since the introduction of the Children (Northern Ireland) Order 1995.

The DoH said even though there had been an increase in health trust-recruited foster carers, there were still significant pressures in providing a placement for every child who needs one.

In England, the number of children in care increased by 17% from 2015 to 2025, while in Wales the increase across the same period was 26%, according to official statistics.

In Scotland there has been a decrease of 23% in the same time period.

The DoH said within the wider children's social care services reform programme, a draft strategy for fostering recruitment and retention had been developed.

Work is under way to start to implement the plan, although this is challenging within the current financial situation - with the department previously stating it is facing a projected deficit of between £800m-£1bn this financial year.

The department added it was committed to ensuring fostering was an attractive and valued option, with recent developments including uplifts in care allowance and the progression of a new regulatory framework.

If you are interested in becoming a foster carer, contact your local fostering service.

This can either be the social services department in your local health trust, Health and Social Care (HSC) NI Adoption and Foster Care, or an independent fostering agency.

They will explain what is involved and will help you decide whether fostering is right for you and your family.

Further information and advice is also available on the BBC Bitesize website.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cxnv.summary: Northern Ireland has not had enough carers to cope with demand for foster carers. Fostering Network says number of children in need of care has been going up. Health Minister Robbie Butler wants to encourage people to come forward to foster.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cxvg.title: How Kenyans got caught in $130m US ghost student scam
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cxvg.text:
In May 2024, Francis Mogambi arrived in the United States after winning the Diversity Visa lottery, a programme that gives people from around the world a chance to become permanent residents.

Just over two years later, the Kenyan national found himself at the centre of a US investigation into an alleged nationwide scheme to defraud the federal student aid system.

On 19 October 2026, a grand jury in Nebraska indicted Mogambi on five counts of theft of government money and five counts of aggravated identity theft.

Prosecutors allege that, between November 2025 and May 2026, he worked with associates in Kenya to steal the identities of US citizens and use them to fraudulently enroll fictitious students in American colleges.

Once the fake students were enrolled, Mogambi allegedly diverted their financial aid payments to himself, keeping 30% and sending the remainder to his associates in Kenya.

The intended loss in his case was $20,000 (£15,000), according to prosecutors.

Court documents say Mogambi received $2,000 a week and attempted to recruit another person into the scheme. He allegedly told the individual he needed a business that would allow him to cash larger cheques without paying taxes.

Mogambi was arrested shortly after the indictment was returned and is being held in custody pending trial. He has not yet commented on the allegations against him.

His case forms part of a wider US investigation, dubbed Operation Ghostbusters, into the alleged use of stolen identities to enrol fictitious students at colleges and claim federal financial aid that resulted in a loss of $130m in taxpayers funds.

US authorities say the investigation has so far resulted in five indictments that involved Kenyan nationals, while a further 40 investigations remain open. Hundreds of people have been affected after fraudsters allegedly stole their personally identifiable information (PII) and used it to access federal student aid.

The stolen personal information was sometimes sold online for between $4 and $8, with fraudsters targeting low-income Americans who had never had the opportunity to attend college.

At a news conference on 29 October announcing the first charges in the investigation, Assistant Attorney General Colin M McDonald, who heads the Justice Department's National Fraud Enforcement Division, vowed to pursue those involved.

"If you steal taxpayers' dollars, if you exploit a programme meant to help students, we are resolved to find you and prosecute you," he said.

The Justice Department says those behind the fraud use what is described as "super intelligence" to place fake students in classrooms and complete coursework, creating the impression that they are attending college and allowing financial aid payments to continue.

"The goal is to keep the ghost student in school as long as possible. Semester after semester after semester stealing money from the taxpayers," McDonald said.

But the consequences extend beyond the financial losses suffered by the US government.

People whose identities are stolen can find themselves facing unexpected student loan debts, even if they have never enrolled in college.

"His identity was stolen, his credit is now at risk, and his name is on the bill," McDonald said, describing the impact on one victim.

He also said that nearly a third of community college applicants in California in 2024 had been identified as fraudulent.

The scale of the suspected fraud is significant.

Investigators identified 830,840 potentially fraudulent Federal Student Aid identification numbers associated with nearly $130m in September and October 2026. They recommended that the Department of Education disable them.

The figure represents financial aid associated with potentially fraudulent accounts, not confirmed losses.

"In a flash, the money vanishes, often overseas in places like Kenya," McDonald said.

The investigation has also exposed alleged financial links between the US and Kenya.

In September, US officials travelled to Kenya to work with local law enforcement on extraditions, prosecutions and the recovery of money allegedly stolen from American taxpayers.

With the help of Kenyan investigators, US authorities seized more than $750,000 from a cryptocurrency account belonging to a Kenyan national connected to the wider scheme. The Justice Department described it as the first international seizure of its kind in Kenya.

The seizure was not connected to Mogambi's individual case.

In a separate case in Virginia, prosecutors allege that a Kenyan national received more than 700 fraudulent student-aid refunds totalling approximately $1.44m. At least $1.3m was subsequently transferred through thousands of transactions to accounts in the US and Kenya.

Meanwhile, in New Jersey, three people have been charged with allegedly acting as money mules in a scheme to obtain more than $1m in federal student aid.

Prosecutors say they received the funds through US bank accounts, kept a portion for themselves and transferred the remainder to alleged co-conspirators in Kenya linked to a purported safari company.

If convicted, Mogambi faces a mandatory prison term of at least 10 years, according to the Justice Department.

Authorities say those convicted will also face appropriate orders for forfeiture of assets and restitution to victims, in addition to any prison sentences.

U.S. employers hired at a vigorous pace in October, adding 165,000 jobs. The unemployment rate fell to 4.1 percent.

Note: Data is seasonally adjusted. The average is calculated as a three-month moving average.

Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics.

By Keith Collins and Jacqueline Gu

Hiring was unexpectedly strong in October, when employers added workers at a vigorous pace.

Employers added 165,000 jobs last month, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday, and the unemployment rate dropped to 4.1 percent. Job gains for August and September were revised upward by a total of 84,000 positions. Average hourly earnings rose 3.1 percent compared with the same time last year.

The report reaffirmed the general picture of the labor market as healthy. Employers have broadly continued to hire despite President Trump’s volatile tariff policy, the war in Iran that has cranked up energy price and uncertainty over artificial intelligence. Businesses have held onto their workers, keeping layoffs at historically low levels. And employees have been reluctant to leave their jobs.

Short-term strength, long-term stability: Employers have been adding workers at a slow but steady pace for months. The unemployment rate has stayed low, hovering in a narrow range for the last two years. The robust October report underscored the labor market’s resilience but did not change this overall picture.

Trouble spots: Though the labor market has remained solid, people who are looking for work, including recent college graduates, have found limited opportunities. And even those who do have jobs have been losing leverage, as wage growth has slowed and inflation has continued to erode their spending power. Those factors could help explain why so many Americans are feeling dour about the economy.

A.I. jitters: One big question hanging over the labor market is the impact of artificial intelligence. So far, the technology does not appear to be leading to widespread job losses. But there are some indications that the rise of the technology is depressing hiring, particularly for entry-level positions in sectors including financial services and information.

Green shoots? There have been some tentative signs that the labor market may be on the verge of perking up. The Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey this week showed that the quits rate rose in September, a sign that workers may be feeling more confident in their ability to get new jobs.

Is artificial intelligence taking our jobs?

It’s arguably the single biggest question facing the labor market right now, all the more so after Tuesday’s midterm elections showed widespread public animosity toward A.I. and data centers, in particular.

The evidence, though, is far from clear.

White-collar industries like accounting, legal services and finance mostly added jobs in October, but their growth has been decidedly weak over the past few years. The information sector — a broad category that includes much of tech but also media companies — has been cutting jobs steadily since late 2022. Microsoft last week announced that it was offering buyouts to tens of thousands of employees, making it the latest tech giant to cut jobs.

Economists are cautious about attributing that softness to A.I., however. Other forces, such as high interest rates and shifting demand patterns following the pandemic, could also be playing a role. And despite announcements like Microsoft’s, layoffs remain low, even in white-collar sectors.

Similarly, some economists have highlighted relatively high rates of unemployment among younger workers, especially young college graduates, as evidence that A.I. is displacing entry-level jobs. But that, too, could be the result of other factors, including the generally low rate of hiring and turnover, which is particularly hard on people trying to break into the job market.

To the extent there is a consensus among economists, it looks something like this: A.I. hasn’t had a striking effect on employment, but it may be starting to show up in some corners of the labor market.

Even if A.I. is taking a toll on hiring, it isn’t quite clear what that means. Are companies using A.I. to replace workers? Or merely pressing “pause” on hiring while they figure out where these new tools will be most useful? Or are they spending so much on tokens and A.I. infrastructure that they are looking to cut costs elsewhere? Those explanations could all look similar in the moment, but have very different implications over the longer run.

The impact of A.I. is showing up clearly in one place, however: blue-collar jobs. The data center build out is helping to prop up employment in the construction sector, even as high interest rates have led to a sharp pullback in home building. Demand for chips and other A.I. equipment is also creating jobs in manufacturing, offsetting losses elsewhere in the sector.

The future of that boom now looks uncertain following this week’s election results, however. The plunge in share prices for tech companies on Thursday — partly reversed on Friday — reflected investors’ concern that public backlash to data centers could lead to a slowdown in construction, which could have broader economic implications given the extent to which A.I. has been driving growth.

Note: Data is seasonally adjusted. Charts represent cumulative percent change since January 1, 2022.

Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics.

By Keith Collins and Jacqueline Gu

Following the jobs data today, we also got a preliminary report on U.S. consumer sentiment showing Americans are feeling better about the economy than they did the month before. The survey, conducted by the University of Michigan, showed consumer sentiment ticked up 6 percent month over month, but is still down 10 percent since February, when the United States and Israel launched strikes against Iran. Sentiment is also flat year over year, according to the release.

Markets opened higher on Friday, with the S&P 500 up 0.7 percent and the tech-heavy Nasdaq up 1.7 percent. Those gains are a reversal from tech-driven turmoil that plagued stocks yesterday, which was its worst day in two years.

Mr. Hassett also addressed the A.I. market sell-off from a day ago. “The market dropped a lot yesterday, I think in part because data centers have been a big, big part of the financial market story, and there’s a lot of uncertainty about what the political change is going to mean for data centers going forward, and for the companies that have these very intricate relationships with each other,” he told CNBC.

But the main focus of Mr. Hassett’s interview was the tumult in financial markets around artificial intelligence and data centers, after Tuesday’s election swept into office a group of lawmakers who may more tightly regulate the industry. Voters also approved a series of new ballot measures putting a halt to data center development in their communities.

Mr. Hassett said they “respect the localities that decide that’s what they want to do, but America is a big place,” noting that data centers under development now may not be affected by those ballot initiatives. He said there was “plenty of room” elsewhere for those computing facilities.

Kevin Hassett, the director of the White House National Economic Council, said the hiring numbers for October reflected “runaway job growth.” Appearing on CNBC, he also pointed to other data points this week, including low claims for unemployment, as a sign that the economy overall remains strong.

One of the hallmarks of this labor market has been that most people are working, but if you need a job, it is hard to find one. The October data drives that point home. The unemployment rate fell to 4.1 percent, but the average duration of unemployment — how long the average jobseeker has been out of work — rose to 27 weeks, the highest level since the end of 2021. Nearly 2 million Americans have been out of work for more than six months, the standard definition of “long-term unemployment.”

The unemployment rate for Black workers fell four tenths of a point to 6.6 percent, partly reversing a big jump in September. The monthly figures are noisy, and economists cautioned against taking the earlier increase at face value. But even after the October decline, the Black unemployment rate has been creeping higher, and is far above the 3.7 percent rate for white workers. And as my colleague Talmon Joseph Smith reported last month, this labor market has been particularly hard on Black professionals, and especially college-educated Black women.

The unemployment rate has been at or below 4.5 percent every month since September, 2021 — a record streak that surpasses the period of low unemployment in the late 1960s. (Whether the current streak is 60 or 61 months depends on how you count last October, when the Bureau of Labor Statistics didn’t release a jobs report because of the federal government shutdown.) But while unemployment is low, this hasn’t felt like a strong labor market to many workers, in part because hiring has also been slow and wage growth has been relatively weak, especially compared to inflation.

Note: Data is seasonally adjusted. The Bureau of Labor Statistics did not release an unemployment figure for October 2025.

Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics.

By Keith Collins and Jacqueline Gu

Manufacturers added 19,000 jobs in October, the fifth straight month of gains. But the sector, which President Trump has long made a centerpiece of his economic agenda, has still lost jobs since the end of 2024.

Stocks haven’t reacted much to today’s jobs numbers, with futures on the S&P 500 up 0.1 percent. Treasury yields are up slightly.

The monthly jobs numbers are volatile and subject to revision, so economists caution against reading too much into any one report. But between the strong October numbers and the upward adjustments to prior months, this report makes the recent trend in job growth look meaningfully better. Employers have added an average of 137,000 jobs per month over the past three months. Before this morning’s numbers, the three-month average stood at just 51,000 jobs.

Those numbers have slightly pushed up expectations for rate increases next year, which had been falling as markets sold off in recent weeks. Investors are betting on the Fed next raising rates in January, with another quarter point rate increase to come after that as well.

White-collar sectors mostly added jobs last month. Professional and business services — a broad category that includes accountants, travel agents and many other office jobs — added 70,000 jobs. The financial sector added 7,000, while employment in the information sector fell slightly. Weakness in those sectors in recent months has contributed to concerns that artificial intelligence is eroding white-collar jobs. But the October data suggests some strength.

Note: Data is seasonally adjusted. Charts represent cumulative percent change since January 1, 2022.

Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics.

By Keith Collins and Jacqueline Gu

This jobs report will affirm the Fed’s view that the labor market is on solid footing and that officials can afford to keep their attention trained on taming inflation, which has accelerated this year. That is likely to translate to additional interest rate increases unless there is a substantial sell-off across financial markets that is extreme enough to begin to weigh on growth.

Today’s jobs data reinforces a point that even some Republicans had made before the party’s election rout: There were bright spots in the economy, including stable hiring, but none were enough to change the minds of voters hammered by persistent inflation.

Despite the pickup in monthly jobs growth and a slight decline in the unemployment rate, wage growth has stayed relatively subdued. Average hourly earnings picked up a bit in October, rising 0.4 percent for the month or 3.1 percent compared to the same time last year.

Note: Data is not seasonally adjusted. Inflation data is the year-over-year change in the Consumer Price Index. Wages are year-over-year changes in average hourly earnings. October 2025 is missing from the inflation data because of the government shutdown.

Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics.

By Keith Collins and Jacqueline Gu

Totals for August and September were both revised up, by a combined 84,000 jobs.

Stocks were slightly higher ahead of the numbers with futures on the S&P 500, which allow investors to bet on the market before exchanges open for trading, up 0.3 percent.

The numbers are out! U.S. employers added 165,000 jobs in October and the unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1 percent.

One aspect of the labor market that has fortified the Fed’s gradual approach to raising rates is the fact that wage growth has stayed subdued. That suggests the labor market is not contributing to inflationary pressures. Any indication that this dynamic is changing could alter the Fed’s pace of tightening.

Slowing economic growth coming from the expanding artificial intelligence industry is likely to take the pressure off inflation. This would give the central bank more ability to focus on the labor market, prompting investors to dial down expectations for how quickly the Fed will raise interest rates.

It didn’t get much attention because of the election news, but the Bureau of Labor Statistics on Tuesday released data showing an increase in both job openings and hiring in September. Layoffs, which have been consistently low, fell further, while more workers voluntarily quit their jobs, a sign of confidence. None of the numbers suggested that the labor market has broken definitively out of the “low-hire, low-fire” stasis that it has been in for the past couple years. But the report did provide some encouraging hints that activity could be starting to pick up.
