https://www.npr.org/2026/11/01/nx-s1-602.title: Do you know signs of a stroke? BE FAST are the words to remember
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/01/nx-s1-602.author: Diane Webber
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/01/nx-s1-602.text:
Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., speaks to reporters in March 2026, in Washington. Murphy suffered a stroke on Saturday and is expected to recover.

Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., suffered a stroke on Saturday. His prognosis is excellent, according to his office. His case illustrates the importance of knowing the warning signs of a stroke.

For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.

The American Stroke Association says following the six letters in the acronym BE FAST — can help save stroke victims and prevent permanent brain damage.

Murphy, 53, had the "A" for "arm weakness" — he felt numbness in his arm while he was at his son's hockey game, according to a statement from his staff. And they said he acted quickly to get care — that's the "T" for "time."

Being seen by medical professionals as soon as possible — be fast! — gives people the best shot at survival and full recovery.

Here are all six of the stroke-spotting signs in the BE FAST acronym, according to the American Stroke Association:

Dizziness, trouble walking or a sudden loss of balance are all signs that a stroke may be occurring.

Is the person having trouble with their vision? Blurred vision, double vision or loss of sight in one eye are important symptoms.

Ask the person to smile. Is their smile uneven? Numbness or drooping on one side of the face is a symptom.

Numbness in one arm, as Murphy had, is a symptom. Weakness is too. Ask the person to raise both arms. Does one arm drift down?

Trouble talking is another common symptom. Can the person repeat a simple sentence? Is their speech slurred or hard to understand?

If you or someone you are with is experiencing any of these symptoms, call 911 as soon as you can. Getting care quickly is very important for survival and to minimize long-term effects.

A stroke happens when blood flow to or within the brain is interrupted. It can happen when an artery is blocked or when a blood vessel in the brain bursts. Brain tissue that is deprived of oxygen can be permanently damaged, resulting in long-term disability or death.

Other important symptoms of a stroke are a severe headache, confusion and numbness on one side of the body.

Stroke is the #4 leading cause of death in the U.S., killing more than 162,000 people in 2023, according to the American Heart Association.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-602.author: Henry Larson
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-602.text:
A North Carolina musician was fascinating by the sound of singing sand dunes. He asked researchers from all over the world for help turning them into an instrument.

The balance of power is shifting in Washington, and thousands of miles away on a certain looming sand dune in the Mojave Desert, a lucky hiker can hear something shifting, too. To the ear, it sounds like singing.

ALEX DAVIS: You would need to have a very deep voice because the dunes resonate at frequencies that are somewhere in the 70 hertz to 100-and-something hertz, so it would be like this. (Vocalizing).

(SOUNDBITE OF DUNES VIBRATING)

DAVIS: My name is Alex Davis. I am a composer and sound artist living in Black Mountain, North Carolina.

SCHMITZ: Davis was drawn to these haunting recordings, taken from sand dunes all over the world, by tales from the ancient explorer Marco Polo.

DAVIS: Marco Polo himself chronicled this. He either heard these sounds himself or he heard of others. A thousand years ago, these were, like, ghosts and spirits singing.

SCHMITZ: But those ghosts were actually vibrations caused by footsteps and motions on the surface.

DAVIS: When the dune is large enough and there's an avalanche, which can be either natural or caused by researchers sliding down the dunes on their butts, that sand causes a vibration similar to a cello being bowed.

(SOUNDBITE OF CELLO PLAYING)

SCHMITZ: Davis decided he wanted to build an instrument that would let people manipulate these sounds into their own melodies. So he sent out emails to all sorts of researchers asking for their dune tapes.

DAVIS: In Colorado, California, Chile, China and in the Middle East - the way that they modulate and the way that they almost sound like a voice, like a deep voice, is both beautiful and haunting.

SCHMITZ: Turns out sand makes more noises than just hums.

DAVIS: Sand also talks and screeches and sounds like birds, all different crazy sounds.

SCHMITZ: He wants to add those to his instrument, too.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/05/nx-s1-602.title: Discursive Verses: Is 'Spend Dat' the best financial indicator of America's grift economy?
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/05/nx-s1-602.author: Rodney Carmichael
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/05/nx-s1-602.text:
LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA - JUNE 27: Yung Miami performs onstage during BETX Main Stage presented by Hyundai during the 2026 BET Experience Fan Fest at The Beehive on June 27, 2026 in Los Angeles, California.

After spending three hours counting the pores on Elizabeth Holmes' and Nathan Fielder's faces, I couldn't help but think how perfect Yung Miami's "Spend Dat" would've played over the closing credits. Whatever you feel about the veracity of the protagonist in the blockbuster doc You Can See Everything, there is no doubt about her innate ability to cop and blow money fast. She's probably about as familiar with Diddy's favorite City Girl as she is with Abbott & Costello. But a scammer of such ill repute deserves an apropos theme song. Hell, maybe we all do.

When people complain about hip-hop no longer being political, what they're really talking about is commercial rap's long-fizzled countercultural agenda. The politics of consumption and corruption however have never enjoyed a louder ringing endorsement. Like a billionaire hogging the bully pulpit. To that end, no song in 2026 comes closer to mimicking the feeling of being the violated and the violator. On its face, "Spend Dat" is a get-money flex dedicated to all the "scammers" and "booster b*****s." But behind that seductive veneer is the sadomasochistic loop of late-stage capitalism's long, punishing con. An inflation indicator like no other, it's easily our most American anthem of the year. And we're all transfixed, nodding along in unblinking commitment to the charade.

The video for "Spend Dat" feels like a throwback to the early 2000s, when making it rain in strip clubs was still obligatory signposting for selling the dream. It almost feels trite now that prediction markets allow us to place digital bets on democracy and buy-now, pay-later loans keep expanding on our freedom to fall deeper in debt. At least a good lap dance came with a tangible return on investment. Now we're all just being teased to death.

When India.Arie echoed the public denouncement of "Spend Dat" — which included a call for Black folk to boycott the Billboard-charting song of the summer — another film, I Love Boosters, had just hit streaming. Unlike the aforementioned documentary on the blonde-haired, blue-eyed, white-collar scammer Holmes, rapper-turned-director Boots Riley's fictional narrative centered on the supposed scourge of the hood. In it, Keke Palmer plays an illegit booster, selling high-end fenced clothing out of the abandoned fast-food chicken joint she's squatting in while harboring her own fashionable aspirations. It takes an international worker-led intervention — and a sci-fi bopgun full of Marxist intentions — for her to realize the minor disruption she and her shoplifting girlfriends are causing is but a necessary cog in the ever-churning, exploitative wheel of global capitalism.

What Riley wants us all to understand, as an avowed communist who switched his weapon of choice from fronting Bay Area rap group The Coup to writing screenplays, is that we the people are hardly the problem. Even when sufferers turn into self-styled hustlers out of desperation instead of pooling their collective power. Like WEB DuBois before him, Riley calls his art propaganda. And he's equally adamant about calling art on the other end of the spectrum of propaganda, too. "When The Coup first came out they would call us a political rap group. And we'd be like, 'No,' " he said on a recent episode of Novara Media's podcast Downstream. "Don't call us that unless you're calling everybody that. Because what it then made it seem like was as if everything else was just what it is." Rather, art magnifying the status quo is not some benign representation of a fixed reality but an uncritical regurgitation of everything indoctrinated by the moneyed elite.

When the controversy surrounding "Spend Dat" reached a fever pitch earlier this summer, it came with the usual diatribe. The song was criticized for being culturally degrading. Even India.Arie caught a bunch of flak for stating the obvious when she said, "Everything you listen to see or eat is going to influence you." I don't blame anybody Black for getting in their feelings over the seemingly negative portrayals or stereotypical depiction centered in rap. But the buck doesn't stop there. It never has. "We are bound by all sorts of customs that have come down as second-hand soul clothes of white patrons," as DuBois so eloquently stated 100 years ago this month in his essay Criteria of Negro Art. "We are ashamed of sex and we lower our eyes when people will talk of it," he says, concluding with this thought: "Our worst side has been so shamelessly emphasized that we are denying we have or ever had a worst side."

The same week "Spend Dat" went platinum, Yung Miami appeared on "The Breakfast Club" to promote the release of her solo debut, Watch Dis. When asked about the criticism the song received, she defended it as inspirational music "that builds you up to want to be somebody." Rap may have started at the bottom. But at some point the script flipped. The systems hip-hop was oriented to rebel against became the metric for its success. The victors, in this case, were found striving for the same spoils. Having finally achieved the market share and visibility we'd been denied for decades, we became centrists: a marginalized culture subsumed by the mainstream. Commercial rap made itself a useful tool of the establishment, and the perfect racially coded scapegoat.

If the American Dream really is a pyramid scheme, as commonly critiqued, all hail the original scammers who bricked up the foundation. Even with their fuzzy slave-owner math (discounting Blacks as three-fifths human) and gender restrictions on equal rights (ratified while rocking powdered wigs), the nation's so-called founders created a system even the lowest caste could be constrained and cajoled into aspiring to.

It reminds me of the funniest meme I encountered online last week: a comic strip calling cap on the promise of Black capitalism. It pictures two brothers chopping it up, with one plainly stating, "You can't buy your way out of a system that was built on selling you." Totally undeterred, the other replies back, "Well, I'm gonna try!" before invoking the Black power era's "by any means necessary" rhetoric. In the next panel, Malcolm X expresses frustration over his words being misused to validate participation in the futile American experiment.

We've been hoodwinked, indeed. Bamboozled. Led astray. Run amok and flat-out deceived like a mug.

The grift is so complete that it's almost impossible to distinguish the mark from the actual con artist. Whether it's a convicted felon hiding fraudulence behind white tears, or a ride-or-die who bossed up with the boosters and got it off the muscle. In a year when prediction markets and predatory installment loans sucked us all dry, inflation skyrocketed and tech billionaires quickened the apocalypse, an ode to America's undying hustle and flow might be the closing credits theme we all deserve.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/05/g-s1-1489.title: Fat Joe: Tiny Desk Concert
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/05/g-s1-1489.author: Bobby Carter
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/05/g-s1-1489.text:
Credit: Photo: Elizabeth Gillis/NPR

When Fat Joe walked into NPR headquarters, he intended to shake the table (or desk, in this case). He wanted to "touch the third rail," meaning it would be anything but your typical Tiny Desk concert, and the audience would be treated to a new level of spontaneity. The way this show is treacherous and unpredictable, yet lands on incredibly solid footing, directly reflects how Joey Crack's career has survived and thrived for over 30 years.

In the five years since his Tiny Desk (home) concert, Joe Cartagena has continued to reinvent himself, leaning into his polarizing takes and storytelling as an internet personality, writing a book and, more recently, co-hosting the popular Joe and Jada podcast with another Tiny Desk alum, Jadakiss. Fat Joe's music has remained the driving force, with consistent album output and hit records.

For his Tiny Desk, the Bronx emcee flexes the benefits of loyalty and longevity, inviting a laundry list of guest appearances from Remy Ma, Stove God Cooks, Stevie Mackey, Dre (from the production duo Cool & Dre) and Jadakiss, in support of career-spanning set list and songs from his latest album, Organized Rhyme.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/05/g-s1-1520.title: Bob Dylan comes knockin' on pope's door as Leo welcomes legend to Vatican
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/05/g-s1-1520.author: The Associated Press
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/05/g-s1-1520.text:
Pope Leo XIV, left, and the singer and Nobel prize winner Bob Dylan, right, pose for a photo during a meeting in the Vatican on Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026.

VATICAN CITY — Bob Dylan came knockin' on Pope Leo XIV' s door Wednesday, as the American singer-songwriter and poet visited with the American pope at the Vatican during a break between concert dates in Italy.

The Vatican said the encounter was brief, with Leo giving Dylan a rosary and Dylan presenting the pope with a copy of his autobiography, "Chronicles: Volume One."

Leo had quoted from an unpublished protest song Dylan penned in 1963, "Go Away You Bomb," in his 2026 book "Disarmed and Disarming: Peace Is a Gift."

Leo was warning against the race to rearm and the recourse to nuclear weapons and quoted the lyric, addressed to a hypothetical atomic bomb: "I hate you cause yer man-made and man-owned, an' man-handled."

Two Vatican officials accompanied Dylan: the Rev. Antonio Spadaro, a Vatican culture ministry official who also accompanied Patti Smith to a July audience with Leo; and Andrea Monda, the editor of the Vatican newspaper, L'Osservatore Romano.

Pope Leo XIV, right, and the singer and Nobel prize winner Bob Dylan, left, talk during a meeting in the Vatican on Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026.

Spadaro said Dylan had wanted to speak with Leo, and the two met in private for a few minutes. In an essay in L'Osservatore Romano, he recalled that the former Robert Prevost, who was born in Chicago in 1955, grew up familiar with Dylan's music.

He also noted that Dylan was very familiar with St. Augustine of Hippo, the inspiration of Leo's spirituality and Augustinian religious order, penning "I Dreamed I Saw St. Augustine" for the 1967 album John Wesley Harding.

Pope Leo XIV, right, and the singer and Nobel prize winner Bob Dylan, left, shake hands during a meeting in the Vatican on Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026.

Dylan, who won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 2016, wore a black hoodie and a loose tie. Vatican photos of the encounter showed him with the hood over his head.

It wasn't Dylan's first papal encounter: He played for Pope John Paul II, and thousands of other people, in 1997 during a concert capping a religious congress in Bologna, Italy.

Dylan, who changed his name from Robert Zimmerman, was born to a Jewish family in Minnesota. He famously became a born-again Christian in 1979 and alienated some of his longtime fans with songs like "Gotta Serve Somebody" and "Saved."

In more recent years, Dylan has been more circumspect about his religious beliefs. In a 2022 interview with the Wall Street Journal, Dylan said that he was a "religious person" who reads the scriptures, meditates and prays.

Dylan met with Leo in between concert dates in Italy. He played in Milan on Monday and is playing Rome on Thursday. In his most recent concert before the meeting with the pope, Dylan sang his 1997 song "Tryin' to Get to Heaven" that contains the lyric, "I've been all around the world, boys/Now I'm trying to get to heaven before they close the door."

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/04/nx-s1-574.title: Herbert Blomstedt, conductor of great orchestras for seven decades, dies at 99
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/04/nx-s1-574.author: Tom Huizenga
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/04/nx-s1-574.text:
Herbert Blomstedt conducts the Gewandhaus Orchestra of Leipzig in April 2026, at the age of 98.

Herbert Blomstedt, an American-born, Swedish conductor whose remarkably long career saw him leading many of the world's major orchestras, including the San Francisco Symphony for 10 years, died on Wednesday at his home in Gothenburg, Sweden. He was 99.

His death was announced in a statement released by his management company, KünstlerSekretariat am Gasteig.

In a profession routinely flush with elderly practitioners, Blomstedt, year after year, retained his title as the world's oldest active conductor. He worked into his late 90s, conducting concerts this year, at the age of 98, with the Detroit Symphony and the Gewandhaus Orchestra of Leipzig, Germany.

"Retirement is not a question of age," Blomstedt told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation. "It should be flexible. I just love the music so much that I just can't give up." And he didn't.

Blomstedt suffered falls in 2022 and 2023, and an ear infection in 2025, forcing him to cancel performances in Europe and the U.S., but he was undaunted. He resumed adding dates to his schedule, leading the world's top orchestras. In recent years, he conducted while seated at a piano bench. He had plans to conduct a series of concerts with the San Francisco Symphony in May of this year and again in January 2027, both of which were canceled when health concerns got in the way.

"The music-making of elderly conductors can sometimes be either lofty or slow, sometimes both," Martin Kettle wrote in The Guardian in 2022. "Neither quality applies to Blomstedt … his conducting in old age radiates both flow and glow. Blomstedt does not force or underline the music, he releases it. But the attentiveness to pulse, phrasing and dynamics are unflagging."

Blomstedt brought clear-eyed structural integrity and a strict devotion to the composer's score to wide swaths of orchestral music — and eras — from J.S. Bach to Elliott Carter. But late in his career, he distilled his repertoire down to a few favorite Scandinavian composers and a handful of Germanic staples by Bruckner, Brahms, Schubert, Haydn, Mahler and his beloved Beethoven.

He recorded all nine Beethoven symphonies twice, once with the Staatskapelle Dresden, which he led from 1975 to 1985, and later with the Gewandhaus Orchestra of Leipzig, where he was chief conductor from 1998 to 2005.

"Both cycles remain beacons of good taste, with a distinctive spiritual power shining through," David Allen wrote in The New York Times in 2022. "That's particularly true of the Fifth [symphony], which may be less brutally violent than under other conductors but has a merciful empathy to its relative restraint." Asked by Allen why Beethoven remains such an obsession, Blomstedt pointed to the humanity in the composer's music.

"It can represent the suffering of everyone," Blomstedt answered. "Not only his, but mine. The suffering of today in Ukraine, for instance. That helps it outlive the personal situation of the composer, or the personal situation of the interpreter. It's something that we go through, as humans."

Herbert Thorson Blomstedt was born on July 11, 1927, in Springfield, Mass. to Swedish parents, both Seventh-day Adventist missionaries who returned home when Blomstedt was two, settling in Gothenburg.

In his youth, Blomstedt learned piano, violin and organ, then fell in love with symphonic music. He memorized the names of orchestra players and when the revered German conductor Wilhelm Furtwängler performed in Gothenburg, the shy young Blomstedt asked the maestro for an autograph.

In 1945, Blomstedt entered the Swedish Royal College of Music where he began to study conducting. His education continued with a broad range of influential figures, including stints with John Cage at Darmstadt, Igor Markevitch in Salzburg, Jean Morel at Juilliard and Leonard Bernstein at Tanglewood in 1953, the year in which Blomstedt won the Koussevitzky conducting prize. His formal conducting debut came in 1954 with the Stockholm Philharmonic, moving directly to his first professional post with the Swedish Norrköping Symphony Orchestra.

Blomstedt had close relationships with dozens of orchestras around the world, including the San Francisco Symphony, of which he was music director from 1985 to 1995.

"Blomstedt inherited an orchestra that was skilled and committed but lacking in discipline," says Joshua Kosman, former classical music critic for the San Francisco Chronicle. "Under his guidance, everything became sharper, cleaner, more crisply focused. It was also during his time as music director that the San Francisco Symphony began to tour internationally and record. These two developments were related. Blomstedt made the Symphony, as it were, ready for prime time."

In 2003, Blomstedt returned to lead the Symphony. Kosman said in a review at the time that it only took a few measures of music to realize how much the former music director was missed, especially in a performance of Schumann's Fourth Symphony.

"Looking spry and attentive, Blomstedt led a wonderfully vital performance," he wrote. "And the orchestra — clearly delighted to see its former music director — responded with some of its finest, most spirited playing."

While Blomstedt could elicit ecstatic performances from his orchestras, his own demeanor on the podium was calm and economical with no hint of spotlight-craving showmanship. At times, perhaps too much control led to the occasional indifferent performance. Another return visit to the Symphony in 2013 left Kosman cold. "The program began with the Prelude and "Liebestod" from Wagner's Tristan und Isolde, done with plenty of orchestral richness –- the strings sounded especially robust –- but not much fervor or freedom," he wrote. "Blomstedt is too rational and cautious an interpreter, I think, to make much of this music's luxuriant eroticism."

Blomstedt believed that music could be what he called "an enormous ethical force in society." Speaking with broadcaster Bruce Duffie in 1988, the conductor tried to explain its power. "I'm not so naïve that I think everybody who leaves the concert hall after a Bruckner symphony is saying, 'I won't do so many bad things tomorrow,' but something in that direction," he said. "To experience the order and beauty of great music brings the listener in contact with something greater than himself, something that is meant to be perfect and positive, and this is one of the greatest blessings of great music."

What Blomstedt sensed as something greater than himself was spiritual. A devout Seventh-day Adventist who eschewed alcohol, coffee, tobacco and meat, Blomstedt, early on, refused to rehearse on Saturdays, when he observed the sabbath. It cost him some jobs, he admitted. And yet he conducted concerts on those days, rationalizing that all the real work had been done in rehearsal and performing great music was a spiritual communication to the glory of God.

"I'm a seeker," Blomstedt told journalist Paul Bodine in 2004. "I find God in many places, in nature and scores, in people. I think the ultimate aim of every artist is not to project himself, but there is something in the music that he thinks is important, and when understood by listeners will bring them close to an answer to these eternal questions: Where we come from, why we are here, and where we are going?"

Blomstedt was married to Waltraud Blomstedt, also a Seventh-day Adventist, who held a degree in musicology. She died in 2003 at age 74 in Lucerne, Switzerland, where the couple had lived for years. Blomstedt moved back to Sweden, near Örebro, where three of his four daughters reside.

Earlier this year, the Danish Radio Symphony Orchestra announced plans for Blomstedt to conduct concerts during the three months leading up to his 100th birthday next July.

Always thinking about music and looking ahead, Blomstedt mused, in an interview with Die Welt in the fall of 2025, when he was 98, on what he might conduct for his centennial concerts. Mendelssohn, perhaps, he said. That same year, he told CBS News Sunday Morning, "Without work, I don't live. If I just twiddle my thumbs, that is not living." He said he wanted to be remembered as modest, but truthful and genuine.

"I'm not tired," he said firmly. "Because every time I stand in front of the orchestra, it's like a flame starts to sparkle again. The moment I hear the sound of the orchestra it transforms me."

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/02/g-s1-1489.title: Jungle: Tiny Desk Concert
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/02/g-s1-1489.author: Robin Hilton
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/02/g-s1-1489.text:
Credit: Photo: Lexy Beale/NPR

It's hard for any band to make the old sound completely new, but Jungle has spent much of the past decade transforming vintage soul and R&B into something almost alien. The grooves are deep and warmly familiar, with wistful reflections on love and longing. But even in the brightest moments, there's often a thread of mystery and melancholy that leaves you questioning whether everything is as it seems.

Fronted by the trio of Tom McFarland, Josh Lloyd-Watson and Lydia Kitto, Jungle is known for fluid live sets, with songs that spill into each other. True to form, at the Tiny Desk, they perform more than a half-dozen tracks that run together in a single, continuous groove. "We're gonna keep the music rolling," Lloyd-Watson tells the NPR crowd as the band melts seamlessly from 2018's "Beat 54 (All Good Now)" into "Dominoes" from the 2023 album Volcano.

The members are all smiles here, even as they sing about faded dreams ("Casio"), dead-end infatuations ("Someday, Somewhere") and the struggle to hold on when everything falls apart ("The Wave"). The most animated and infectious moment arrives about halfway through the set, as the group showcases its stunning six-part harmonies on the 2025 single "Keep Me Satisfied," before closing with a moody, slow-burning take on 2023's breakout song, "Back on 74."

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/01/nx-s1-600.title: The National Symphony Orchestra is at a crossroads. Can it survive?
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/01/nx-s1-600.author: Tom Huizenga
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/01/nx-s1-600.text:
Music Director Gianandrea Noseda leads the National Symphony Orchestra in its season-opening concert in September at the Music Center at Strathmore in North Bethesda, Md.

When the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington, D.C. closed its doors on Sept. 15, it left an important American orchestra all but homeless.

The closure followed months of sinking ticket sales, boycotts and a legal battle in federal court over the addition of President Trump's name to the Kennedy Center's façade. Trump took control of the center in early 2025, after firing members of the organization's board of trustees and Kennedy Center president Deborah Rutter.

The 95-year-old National Symphony Orchestra has been performing in the Kennedy Center since it opened in 1971. Now, the musicians and their charismatic music director Gianandrea Noseda are musical nomads while the future of the arts complex, with its proposed renovations, remains uncertain. The new reality came as a shock to Noseda, the Italian conductor who has led the NSO for nine years.

"It was absolutely unexpected," Noseda admits. "The news of the closing of the Kennedy Center came like a cold shower. And my first reaction was, 'What will we do now if we don't have our home?'"

The NSO scrambled to find six alternative concert venues around the greater Washington, D.C. region, all the while hoping that at least part of its budget would remain intact while the string of Kennedy Center controversies continues to play out. It's a recipe ripe for disaster.

"The Kennedy Center is such a mess," says Anne Midgette, former classical music critic for The Washington Post. "I was very concerned that there might not be an NSO season. I was concerned there might not be an NSO — because the NSO is so bound up with the Kennedy Center."

National Symphony Orchestra music director Gianandrea Noseda checks out Strathmore Hall in North Bethesda, Md., before the orchestra's opening night gala. The hall is one of six alternative venues the NSO will be performing in while the Kennedy Center is closed.

Most symphony orchestras announce their upcoming seasons in early spring. But because the NSO had to wait for budget approval from the Kennedy Center Board of Trustees, the new season was revealed in mid-August. That was a short six weeks before the NSO's opening concert, which took place only 11 days after the Kennedy Center locked its doors.

On Sept. 26, Noseda and the musicians traveled to the Music Center at Strathmore, a hall in Bethesda, Md., north of Washington, where they opened their season with a mix of new music by Carlos Simon, surrounded with classics by Tchaikovsky and Respighi.

"Opening night was this wonderful but very bittersweet evening, where it was so great to see them together, but so amazing that this major orchestra in a major city has to be performing [outside] of its hall," Midgette says.

It's a significant blow to the finances and the morale of the orchestra that critics are saying has never sounded better.

"It's a huge setback in economic terms," Midgette says. "It's a much reduced season. On the other hand, it's a triumph that they were able to pull off a season at all under these circumstances. I think it will be really interesting in terms of their identity. Everybody has to question: 'What does this mean to us? How much do we want it?'"

It means a great deal to Rick Barber, the associate principal double bassist, who joined the NSO in 1995. Like Noseda, he didn't see the Kennedy Center closure coming.

"We were stunned at first, honestly," Barber says. "And the months after that, there was definitely a lot of uncertainty — I would say, anxiety." He doesn't believe the orchestra will fold. If anything, Barber is even more focused on the music.

"I'm like any other normal person when I'm going about my non-musical life — anxiety happens," he confesses. "I see the political divisions in our nation. But when I'm playing music, I don't think about those at all."

Perhaps the one person who gives Barber the most hope is Noseda — always the optimist. "The idea [is] to see the glass half full and not half empty. Let's try to reach out to new audiences in different places. So that was my way to approach the situation."

Noseda's most important approach to the situation was not to leave it. After Rutter was fired, Noseda might have looked for an exit. Instead, he extended his contract with the orchestra until 2031. "I thought that would have been a little bit too easy," Noseda says. "And may I use the word 'coward' — to leave that situation. When you are a music director, you are a leader, of course. But you have to serve the orchestra, the music and the community."

As rollicking music by Respighi capped off the opening night concert, a packed house in Bethesda roared with approval for Noseda and the NSO. You'd be tempted to think everything's going to be just fine. But is it?

"This is the $64,000 question," Midgette replies. "How many people really do care? How many people are vitally interested and invested in the orchestra? And I will say that this season, in all these different halls, is going to be a real acid test."

But the NSO is just one high-profile example of an even larger story. How much do Americans – right now – care about symphony orchestras? All around the country, symphonies are struggling financially and some, most recently the Phoenix Symphony, are shutting down. Part of the problem comes down to basic affordability.

"The simple realities of buying a ticket and getting yourself to hear something, if you don't have the gas and the groceries are expensive, is more challenging," Midgette notes. "We live in a really challenging time for the arts right now."

The NSO is, arguably, fighting for its life. This season it will play about half as many concerts as usual. Will audiences show up? And can the orchestra woo back the donors it lost? In August, The Washington Post reported that ticket revenue is expected to be down by about half and donations down by a quarter, in part due to massive cuts in the Kennedy Center's development department. Add to that the orchestra is without most of its former staff, including former executive director Jean Davidson, who left her position in March, citing the turmoil at the Kennedy Center as the prime reason for her departure.

"I think it's so hard to predict how it's all going to play out," Midgette says. "If the orchestra sticks together, yes, it will be one for the history books."

The upbeat Noseda finds strength in the power of what the orchestra produces. "I suspected that we had to go through challenging times, but I strongly believe in the value of the art, and the music can really still bring people together."

It's unclear how long Noseda and his NSO players will be out of the Kennedy Center and on the road. It could be a long journey, but one that may make them stronger.

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/31/nx-s1-602.title: Pianist and podcaster on the timeless joy of jazz music
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/31/nx-s1-602.author: Michael Levitt
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/31/nx-s1-602.text:
NPR's Sacha Pfeiffer speaks with Jazz pianist Joe Alterman about his podcast The Upside of Jazz from NPR member stations WABE in Atlanta.

SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:

When Joe Alterman was a baby, there was no question about what he was going to end up doing, at least according to his father.

JOE ALTERMAN: My dad said, right when I was born, he saw how long my fingers were. And he just said, this guy's going to be a piano player.

(SOUNDBITE OF JOE ALTERMAN'S "THE UPSIDE OF DOWN")

PFEIFFER: Turns out dad was right. Alterman grew up in Atlanta, studied jazz piano at NYU and has gone on to have a successful career playing and composing around the world. He's performed at the Lincoln Center, the Kennedy Center. He's released multiple albums, and he now hosts a podcast from NPR member station WABE called The Upside of Jazz. When I spoke with Alterman earlier this week, he explained how he started playing in the first place.

ALTERMAN: I don't know why, but when I was around 3 or 4, I asked my parents for piano lessons. And I wanted to quit, but my parents wouldn't let me. So from 3 or 4 till 11 or 12, I was taking classical piano and always getting in trouble for what they call changing notes.

PFEIFFER: Improvising with their sheet music?

ALTERMAN: Exactly (laughter). Yeah. I'd hear a little variation on a melody and want to try it out, but that wasn't encouraged at the time. And, thankfully, I found Bluegrass music, specifically a song by Doc Watson, the guitarist. It's called "Freight Train Boogie," and all I wanted to do was learn how to play that on the guitar.

(SOUNDBITE OF SONG, "FREIGHT TRAIN BOOGIE")

DOC WATSON: (Singing) Now, Casey Jones, he was a mighty man, and now he's resting in the promised land. The only kind of music he could understand was a big eight-wheeler under his command. He made a freight train boogie.

ALTERMAN: So I got guitar lessons on the condition that I kept at my piano ones. And my guitar teacher - he made me realize that boogie-woogie music, or boogie music, was written for the piano, and I had already been taking piano. So that was kind of what got me, you know, back into the piano. But at the same time, I loved this bluegrass music, and my dad was getting me all these records of jazz musicians. And a lot of the records included songs that I was used to hearing in a Bluegrass context. But hearing the way in which the jazz musicians played these melodies or interpreted the melodies kind of blew my mind. So it wasn't really the solos that drew me at first. It was the tasty ways they interpreted the melodies. So that's really how I got to the genre.

PFEIFFER: (Laughter) Tell me about some of the jazz music your dad introduced you to that most grabbed you and made you think, I really like this.

ALTERMAN: Well, so my dad - he introduced me to the music of Ramsey Lewis, which blew my mind.

(SOUNDBITE OF RAMSEY LEWIS' "WADE IN THE WATER")

ALTERMAN: Coincidentally, my dad introduced me to Ramsey's music, and I got to introduce my dad to Ramsey. I was very...

PFEIFFER: 'Cause you brought him on your podcast.

ALTERMAN: No, actually, Ramsey - sadly, he passed away before I got to do the podcast.

ALTERMAN: But he was one of my piano mentors, and I was his opening act for years. So it was a treat. My dad introduced me to so much music I loved, and I got to introduce my dad to many of those same musicians.

(SOUNDBITE OF RAMSEY LEWIS' "WADE IN THE WATER")

PFEIFFER: Jazz is a type of music that I think really divides people. Some people love it. Some people find it very alienating and kind of dissonant. How do you have conversations on your podcast that will appeal to a broad audience when there are such wide feelings about jazz?

ALTERMAN: First of all, I agree with a lot of the people that are alienated with the music.

PFEIFFER: Oh, really?

ALTERMAN: Not everyone. But, I mean, I feel like there's so much music out there. There's so much jazz. And I think there's, you know, an amazing 1%. And I talked to Pat Metheny on my program about this. And he said, yeah, 1% of it is the greatest music ever, and 99% I can't relate to. I don't like.

PFEIFFER: (Laughter).

ALTERMAN: I don't think it's jazz necessarily that people are drawn to. I think it's specific personalities in the music. So, for example, like, I love Oscar Peterson, but I don't love every piano player that plays jazz, if that makes sense.

(SOUNDBITE OF OSCAR PETERSON'S "YOU ARE MY SUNSHINE")

ALTERMAN: I think jazz, the genre, has a way of bringing out personalities, and it's certain personalities within the music that I'm most attracted to.

PFEIFFER: One of the huge legendary jazz musicians you spoke with on your podcast, and, in fact, I think, within months of his death, was Sonny Rollins. On your website, you called him the Saxophone Colossus himself.

(SOUNDBITE OF SONNY ROLLINS' "ST. THOMAS")

ALTERMAN: I mean, in my world, that's like the equivalent of talking to, like, Shakespeare or Bach or, you know, one of the great originators of this music. I couldn't believe, you know, we were alive at the same time. One of the things that brought me closer to this music was when I was a kid, I suffered from a very severe obsessive-compulsive disorder, and my days were kind of spent dealing with these obsessions and compulsions while being at school and trying to act like everything was normal around my friends. And finally, when I made it to bed and didn't have any more compulsions to do before I fall asleep, I put on Sonny's music.

(SOUNDBITE OF SONNY ROLLINS' "ST. THOMAS")

ALTERMAN: I felt like it understood my feelings in a weird way, what I was going through, but it also gave me hope. It made me feel like things will get better. And, you know, I wrote him a note. I just said, you know, how helpful his music had been - this was 20 years ago. And he wrote back. Dear Joe, your comments were appreciated. We all have to use adversity as an opportunity to find a way. So keep a strong mind throughout this short existence. Your examples give us all hope as all of us here in this life have to struggle.

PFEIFFER: A letter from Sonny Rollins himself to you.

ALTERMAN: Yeah. And that became, like, the greatest advice. I mean, I still have it in my pocket. So getting to talk to him 20 years later, I basically - I think the first thing I asked him was some people say jazz is a deep journey of self-exploration. You know, other people have told me it's man's contribution to nature. So I asked him what it is to him. He said it's God talking to him and him talking back to God.

(SOUNDBITE OF SONNY ROLLINS' "ST. THOMAS")

PFEIFFER: One of your episodes takes a very serious turn, and it's about the role that jazz played in Nazi Germany. Where do those two things connect? I would think many people think they don't connect.

ALTERMAN: My interest in this kind of began a few years ago. I visited Auschwitz, and I was given a tour. And the tour guide pointed to this spot in the grass, and he said, this is where the orchestra played. And we were sitting right across from that sign that says, work makes you free. He said, the music here was just as deceptive as that sign. It was actually loud carnival music. And when the transport trains arrived, you know, it kind of made them think maybe - like the work makes you free - maybe things will be OK here.

PFEIFFER: That music greeted Jews as they were arriving at Auschwitz? That's what they were hearing?

ALTERMAN: Yeah. Also, at the same time, it's loud and it drowns out the screams of the families being separated. I had never heard of music being weaponized. The more I researched, I just kept finding amazing hypocrisy. You know, the Nazis - they condemned jazz, yet so many of them loved jazz and listened to it privately.

I mean, one of my greatest heroes in life - I discovered a character named Louis Bannet. He was known as the Dutch Louis Armstrong before the war. The guy is taken to Auschwitz. He goes to audition for the orchestra, and he picks out a trumpet. And for some reason, decides to play "St. Louis Blues" by W. C. Handy for the audition.

(SOUNDBITE OF W. C. HANDY'S "ST. LOUIS BLUES")

ALTERMAN: He credited, you know, music for helping get him through. You know, at one point, he was put in charge of the Romani orchestra, and this woman in the orchestra said, how can you play for these people that want to kill us? And he says I don't play for them. I play for me.

So, you know, so many of the people in these camps - they either - the music either helped them get through or was just it was very hard to play at times. 'Cause, also, the prisoners, the fellow prisoners would look at these musicians playing this music that was torturing them and see the musicians almost as collaborators. So it's a very wild world. And that's - yes - I did an episode on that, and it led into, you know, the treatment of jazz in the Soviet Union and beyond. There's so many of these stories.

PFEIFFER: That is Joe Alterman. He's the host of the WABE podcast, The Upside of Jazz. Joe, thank you.

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/31/nx-s1-599.title: Plans for a data center threaten scenic wilderness and dark skies in West Virginia
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/31/nx-s1-599.author: Scott Neuman
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/31/nx-s1-599.text:
White Grass Ski Touring Center in Canaan Valley , W.Va., is celebrated for its unusually curvy and hilly cross-country skiing terrain.

DAVIS, W.Va. — Stretching nearly a million acres through the rugged mountains of eastern West Virginia, the Monongahela National Forest links some of the state's best known natural attractions. The vast area ranges from the ski slopes of Canaan Valley to the dark skies of Blackwater Falls and Spruce Knob and includes the small towns of Davis and Thomas that serve as gateways for visitors to the region.

For the past seven months, Kaleb Skelton, his wife, Ella, their 2-year-old son, Ryder, and dog Mabel have lived in a camper in this corner of West Virginia's "almost heaven." Kaleb is finishing a seasonal stint as a campground manager on a lake near Spruce Knob, the state's highest point.

On clear nights atop the isolated peak, they get to experience a river of stars in one of the very few pockets of darkness remaining in the Eastern United States. The area has become a draw for amateur astronomers.

Spruce Knob Lake Campground hosts Kaleb and Ella Skelton, at their site at Spruce Knob on Saturday, Oct. 10 2026 in Spruce Knob, W.Va. The couple from Texas have been at the site since April and said they have never seen darker skies than atop Spruce Knob.

During summer's new moons, Kaleb says, one in four campsites he oversees is occupied by someone with a telescope. He thought his family's cabin in eastern Texas offered "the craziest" dark skies he'd ever seen, "but coming out here definitely rivals it."

Those inky-black nights — and the natural beauty they shelter — are now under threat from what many residents see as a modern-day version of extractive industries like logging and mining that once defined the region. In a place where tourism, outdoor recreation and community are deeply intertwined, a gigantic power plant and data center campus in nearby Tucker County would bring large-scale development into the heart of it all.

A stark image of the town of Davis from 1885, during the heyday of logging, is a reminder of that transformation. The photo shows a handful of squat buildings amid a broad clearing littered with forest remains.

They used to call it "Stump Town," says Kim Williams, president of the Snow Sports Museum of West Virginia in Canaan Valley. At the turn of the century, massive first-growth trees dominated the landscape.

Then, logging companies "came in and clear-cut the whole valley and everything around it," he says.

By the early 20th century, entire mountainsides of red spruce and eastern hemlock had been stripped bare. Then came the coal companies, which left the nearby Blackwater River acidic and dangerous to drink.

Today, the scars still show. The big trees won't return for generations, but a century of natural regrowth, conservation and deliberate restoration means the land is on its way to healing.

While few expect that the latest tech boom presages anything like the environmental destruction of the past, many see the proposed new Ridgeline data center as a big step backward, undoing the progress the local community has made to recover.

A roughly 785-megawatt generating plant is slated to be the first part of "a large-scale data and energy infrastructure project designed to support artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and enterprise systems," according to Purcellville, Va.-based Fundamental Data LLC, the company behind Ridgeline.

The photo "The Birth of a city, Davis, W. Va. in 1885" by William Henry Jackson shows a handful of squat buildings amid a broad clearing littered with forest remains.

The complex would rely primarily on natural gas, with diesel as a backup fuel source. Power generated on-site, rather than purchased from the regional grid, could ease some concerns about the project's effects on electricity rates. It does not, however, resolve concerns over air and water pollution.

Located on a reclaimed coal-mining site, plans are for an initial 291 acres that could eventually expand to 10,000 acres — 15 square miles — and include parts of neighboring Grant County, according to local news reports.

Speaking to NPR, Casey Chapman, listed in court documents as Fundamental Data's "responsible individual," declined to speculate on the facility's ultimate size, saying only that "if fully developed … it would be thousands of acres."

Light pollution is a common complaint from residents living near data centers. Chapman says the company will use "well-designed" lighting to help minimize the effects of sky glow, in an effort not to jeopardize nearby Blackwater Falls State Park's pursuit of an official dark-sky certification.

An analysis by the Northern Virginia Astronomy Club, which hosts an annual star party in the region, found that Ridgeline's initial footprint could increase sky glow near Blackwater by 528%, transforming its nighttime rural sky to one comparable to a suburban area. (The same analysis found only a minimal impact on Spruce Knob.)

But safety and security — not light pollution — take precedence, Chapman says. The facility will be "an industrial plant that runs around the clock," he notes. "Crews need proper lighting to operate and maintain equipment safely."

Chip Chase is among the skeptics. He runs White Grass Ski Touring Center, a popular cross-country ski area that he helped found 45 years ago. He is a fixture in the local community that he describes as "Vermont, with Southern hospitality."

"If you're an outdoor person, this place is paradise," he says. "People come here to get away from data centers. People want dark skies here. People want to have a peaceful, quiet recreational area."

Chip Chase, co-founder of White Grass Ski Touring Center, at the cross-country ski resort in Canaan Valley, W.Va., on Oct. 11.

Economic development, however, is a top priority for the state of West Virginia. It ranks among the poorest in the country and has the unique distinction of having lost population since 1950.

John Deskins, director of the West Virginia University Bureau of Business and Economic Research, says data centers could be a boon. "As long as we're making sure that we follow all the proper procedures around noise pollution, water pollution, [and] other elements of environmental pollution ... I think they're a good opportunity," he says.

It is those proper procedures that worry people in Tucker United, a grassroots group opposing the data center plans. As in so many other places across the country, they are battling what they see as a lack of transparency.

The first anyone in the community heard about the Ridgeline project was March 2025, when an obscure notice appeared in a local newspaper announcing the request for an air-quality permit for a proposed power plant, says Davis Mayor Alan Tomson. A resident called him to ask if he knew anything about it. "I told her that I did not," Tomson says. He then called the mayor of neighboring Thomas. "He also had not heard anything about it."

Mayor Alan Tomson on William Avenue in Davis, W.Va., on Oct. 11.

From there, Tomson says, things moved quickly. A month later, the Republican super-majority in both houses of the state legislature passed a highly unusual bill exempting certified microgrid districts and high-impact data centers from county or municipal zoning or any local restrictions related to horticultural, noise, viewshed, lighting, development or land use.

Opponents quickly gathered 1,000 signatures on a petition urging Republican Gov. Patrick Morrisey to veto the bill. They were unsuccessful. Signing the legislation, the governor noted the state's need to "continue to focus on economic development and utilizing our many natural resources," adding that "companies will now be able to quickly build, expand, and increase job creation right here in West Virginia."

"They completely got rid of any … sort of regulation or guardrails for these data center developments," says Tucker United spokesperson Nikki Forrester. "They want to sell us out, … extract our resources and leave us with the mess."

Pedestrians walk past data center protest signs on Front Street in Thomas, W.Va.

The West Virginia Department of Environmental Protection approved Fundamental Data's air-quality permit without, according to Tucker United and other activist groups, conducting a comprehensive assessment of the facility's potential public-health impacts on the surrounding valley. When asked by NPR about Tucker United's concerns, the West Virginia Department of Environmental Protection responded that it "does not comment on active litigation" and declined an interview request.

Opponents of the project subsequently commissioned their own analysis finding that the Ridgeline plant could cause between $19 million and $35 million a year in health-related damages and premature deaths.

Tucker United, the West Virginia Highlands Conservancy and the Sierra Club challenged the air-permit decision in court. Their appeal was dismissed in August on jurisdictional grounds. The groups say they will go to the state's Supreme Court.

Chapman says Tucker United's air-quality study assumes Ridgeline will emit the maximum amount of pollution allowed by its air permit for an entire year, when in fact the permit sets an upper limit and "we're going to operate within those limits," he says.

There are other environmental concerns. Forrester notes that Canaan Valley's bowl shape and temperature inversions can trap air pollutants near the ground. As for water, she says, "storing 30 million gallons of diesel right on a creek that feeds into our water supplies is really dangerous and puts not just our community, but every community downstream at risk."

Nikki Forrester, director of communications with anti-data center group Tucker United, in Davis, W.Va., on Oct. 12.

Fundamental Data's Chapman says the storage would be safe and that all of the tanks would not need to be filled at any given time.

In addition to the potential environmental and health hazards, many residents find it particularly galling that West Virginia House Speaker Roger Hanshaw, a Charleston-based attorney with the law firm Bowles Rice, is listed as lead attorney for Fundamental Data in the permit dispute.

"Here's a guy who's writing laws [and] sponsoring legislation while under contract for one of the people that he's working for," complains Gary Berti, a retired homeowner in Davis. "To me, that's a conflict of interest."

In an email to NPR, Hanshaw stated: "I am not now, nor have I ever been, employed by Fundamental Data. I am a partner in a law firm. It is public record that the law firm of Bowles Rice is currently counsel for Fundamental Data in a litigation matter pending in West Virginia."

Fundamental Data believes building the Ridgeline facility would bring thousands of temporary jobs and about 500 permanent ones in IT, electrical and cooling systems, engineering and security.

While no two data center campuses are alike, a Brookings Institution study found that on average, data centers produce around 100 to 200 permanent jobs.

Berti agrees that West Virginia needs jobs, but "there are places that need it more than others," he says, and is skeptical that data centers would bring many permanent workers to the area.

And if artificial intelligence ends up being more hype than substance, he says, it could be a repeat of history.

"A lot of times they leave us behind," he says, referring to the coal and logging industries. "When I moved here 40 years ago, it was two rundown towns," he says, referring to Davis and Thomas. "Look at them now. They're doing well."

Davis, W.Va., has a population of roughly 600 people and attracts tourists from across the country.

Given that history of exploitation, Tomson, the mayor of Davis, says he thinks the data center developer thought it could run roughshod over residents. But they got more than they bargained for, he says.

"This is a very educated community," Tomson says. "Many of the people here that have retired had very high-level scientific and technological careers elsewhere, and they bring that knowledge and expertise to bear on this situation."

Despite the organized opposition, some residents have voiced support. Tucker County Sheriff Jake Kopec thinks much of the criticism amounts to fear-mongering. The landfill for Davis and Thomas blocks the view of the Ridgeline facility from those towns, he says. "I really believe that you would drive past it and not even know it's there."

Kopec acknowledges that the dark skies will be less dark. But he says the county has more immediate needs that the Ridgeline facility would help remedy, including better-paying jobs and tax revenue to fund essential public services. "We have no cops on after midnight in this county, but we serve a million-plus visitors a year," he notes.

Davis and Thomas — both with populations of roughly 600 people — are not only a base of operations for skiing, hiking, mountain biking and white water rafting, but they've also developed a lively arts and music scene.

"This area was just about written off," according to Tomson. "And what ended up happening was music and artists discovered the city of Thomas, and there was a beginning of a resurrection of the area."

On a Sunday night in October well before the start of the ski season, there's a poetry reading at Creature in Thomas and a few doors down at the Purple Fiddle, a standing-room only performance by Driftwood, an Americana/folk rock band from Binghamton, N.Y.

Most of the hundred or so people in the bar are tourists like Adam Brooke, from Charlottesville, Va. He has been visiting the area for the past decade, taking in the mountains and the color of the fall leaves.

"We're mostly hikers," he says. "We just like getting out there on some of the lesser known trails and just enjoying nature for a bit."

Despite the obstacles, opponents of the Ridgeline facility remain optimistic. They're buoyed by the growing national opposition to data centers.

In their own state, Gov. Morrisey — a strong advocate for data centers in the past — appears to be pumping the brakes somewhat, with a recently proposed 20-year plan for "responsible" data center development. It's not much, Tucker United's Forrester says, but it's something.

She also points to the region's past grassroots successes. "Tucker County does have a long history of fighting bad development proposals … but we've been successful in every single one of them."

A motorist drives past a "No Power Plant Data Center" sign in Canaan Valley, W.Va. (Chris Jackson/For NPR)

Forrester and others point to two major environmental fights in the 1970s: a proposed hydroelectric project that would have flooded Canaan Valley and part of Dolly Sods — a protected wilderness area now popular with hikers and skiers. A second, at Otter Creek, saw the West Virginia Highlands Conservancy successfully challenge plans for coal exploration and road construction in the Monongahela National Forest. Both were halted.

Those victories are tempered by the region's darker past, too, she acknowledges.

"They're playing by the same playbook they've always played here," Forrester says. "People don't want to relive that history again, and they will fight every step of the way to make sure that doesn't happen."

A proposed new data center in nearby Tucker County would bring large-scale development into the heart of it all. The state's governor has approved a permit for the facility.

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/31/nx-s1-602.title: After last year's storm, this remote Alaska town is still picking up the pieces
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/31/nx-s1-602.author: Samantha Watson
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/31/nx-s1-602.text:
Construction crews work on houses and other building throughout Kipnuk after ex-typhoon Halong hit Alaska's coast in October of 2025.

Last fall, the remnants of Typhoon Halong tore through numerous small Alaska Native villages off the road system in Western Alaska. The storm destroyed infrastructure, floated homes off their foundations, and displaced over a thousand people. A year later, hundreds remain displaced as the slow work of repair in a remote part of the state continues. And in one of the hardest hit communities – the small town of Kipnuk – people still aren't sure when they'll be moving back.

The village of under 200 homes is situated on the wide open tundra and only consistently accessible by plane.

A year ago, 90% of the residences here were damaged by the remnants of Typhoon Halong, according to the State of Alaska's Emergency Operations Center. Dozens were swept off their foundations, some with families still inside. The community is now largely scattered across Alaska – some outside the region their ancestors have lived in for thousands of years.

Kipnuk 10 months after ex-typhoon Halong hit Alaska's coast in October of 2025.

Throughout the past year, crews have been working on repairs.

On a clear day in August, Eddie Chuckwuk's construction crew attempted what sounded like magic: raising a building back onto its foundations using air compressors.

Chuckwuk is one of several dozen people who have been working long days to rebuild the place where he grew up.

"We're working as fast as possible as we can to get the people back in town," Chuckwuk says. "That's what I just want to see – for everybody to come back and enjoy where they grew up instead of being placed in a different place … where they're not used to. It's pretty hard."

Workers helping clear debris from the tundra around Kipnuk and construction crews working on houses 10 months after ex-typhoon Halong hit Alaska's coast in October of 2025.

This work is critical to getting Kipnuk's homes in shape to live in again, but the town is far from being fully restored.

According to the state, most people in Kipnuk didn't have home or flood insurance. They estimate that funds from the Federal Emergency Management Agency will make most of the homes livable by Thanksgiving – meaning replacing wet insulation and repairing windows, doors and roofs. But the funds won't be enough to return some severely damaged homes to how they were before the storm. The state is currently appealing for additional funding to build replacement housing.

There's also no estimate on when the school will reopen.

Leona Paul, who has been working as a cook to feed the construction teams, says even if the houses are habitable, some people were too traumatized by the storm to return.

"I think it's too overwhelming for them," she says, "especially the older people."

And climate change is making towns like Kipnuk more vulnerable to future storms. Most people in town want to rebuild the village somewhere safer but the funding they have received so far from FEMA can only go towards restoring what was damaged. Kipnuk hasn't yet found the money to move.

In August, damage from the October 2025 storm was still visible in Kipnuk.

Right now residents may not have a better option other than moving back. Many say living in bigger towns, or cities like Anchorage, has been tough. People aren't speaking as much Yugtun – the native language. They're farther from loved ones. Their kids, who are used to playing all over town, have to watch out for cars.

Leona Paul, who spent part of the summer in Kipnuk, says she likes being there. "You're free to do anything you want," she says. "In a city you just can't do whatever you want."

Being displaced from the village has also meant separation from the Alaska Native cultural practices of hunting and gathering traditional food on the land.

Some residents, like Burt Paul's family, traveled home for the summer to practice subsistence and be together.

Upriver from Kipnuk on a lush tundra bluff, his family filled buckets with sweet, orange salmonberries, or naunraqs as they are called in coastal Yugtun. He says after last fall's destruction – he didn't know when he'd see these native plants growing again.

"It beats my mind that I see food growing, grass growing, fish coming in," he says.

Burt Paul's family traveled home for the summer to practice subsistence and be together. On August 12, 2026, they went berry-picking upriver from Kipnuk.

Paul's family evacuated after the storm, but he stayed behind in Kipnuk, acting as a community leader through the aftermath. Usually, his family goes camping and berry picking for days. This summer, their trips were shorter – confined to when everyone was in town.

Short as those trips may have been, he says they were important: "We have to keep things going some way, somehow, no matter what situation we go through," he says.

He's not sure when his family – or his village – will all be back together again.

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/31/nx-s1-601.title: Oyster stocks have plunged in the Chesapeake. This resident wants to bring them back
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/31/nx-s1-601.author: Ari Daniel
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/31/nx-s1-601.text:
John Consoli marvels at oysters. "I think I'm more enthusiastic about something that's like a rock than anybody else could possibly be," he says.

John Consoli stands on the edge of his pier, which juts out from the southern tip of Maryland's Kent Island and into the Chesapeake Bay. He leans over and hoists a mesh the size and shape of a pillowcase out of the water.

It's packed with oysters. He manages to get it onto the pier. "These are brand new oysters from this year," he says. "When I got them, they weighed nothing. And this is just three months of growth. The net is chock full, I can hardly pull it up."

Once he catches his breath, Consoli marvels at these molluscs. "I think I'm more enthusiastic about something that's like a rock than anybody else could possibly be," he says with a big grin. "I really can't think of many more creatures that do the good that oysters do."

Oysters underpin the Chesapeake's coastal and estuarine ecosystem. Each adult filters up to 50 gallons of water a day. Cleaner water leads to a healthier bay and more sea grass. "That helps crabs and other organisms," says Consoli.

Plus, oyster shells are a habitat unto themselves. "Because of all the nooks and crannies," he explains, "a lot of small fish and crabs live and eat amongst them and hide, so it creates a biodiverse environment. I even found a seahorse, which was incredible. I've never seen a seahorse in my life!"

Oyster reefs used to abound in the Chesapeake, but overharvesting decimated their ranks — by over 99% by 2011, according to one estimate. This monumental shift in the bay contributed to poorer water quality and less habitat for other species.

Oyster farming in the Chesapeake has expanded in recent years, despite environmental and disease challenges, says Ryan Carnegie, a biologist at the Virginia Institute of Marine Science. He adds that wild oysters have also made a partial comeback, helped by better management and investments in restoration. But, says Elizabeth North, a fisheries oceanographer at the University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science, "there is still a lot of room to grow."

Consoli's goal, therefore, is to be a caretaker of sorts, stocking the bay with ever more oysters and looking after their wellbeing. He floats them just below the surface where he says the nutrients are concentrated to help them grow quickly. And although his oysters aren't intended for eating, a cleaner bay does mean better habitat for those that are harvested commercially.

Consoli came to oyster conservation in a roundabout way: He's a professional photographer at the University of Maryland and he was doing a shoot involving the campus's oyster research — namely, efforts to understand and support oyster reefs.

"Seeing great minds coming together to solve problems showed to me that there's a real need here," he says.

Miao Yu is one of the great minds who inspired Consoli that day. She's a mechanical engineer at the University of Maryland who has observed that despite the recent, modest gains in oyster abundance, farmers continue to face two daunting tasks — both of which are stymied by the bay's murky waters.

The first is knowing where to plant the babies. A young oyster needs to settle upon a hard substrate. But finding that ideal spot is much easier said than done. "Sometimes it's dropped into [the] mud," she explains — where the young oyster suffocates and dies.

The second task involves figuring out where and when to harvest the adult oysters. "It's the biggest challenge," she says. "We cannot see like a couple feet down there."

This means that the recovery of oysters, often via dredging, tends to be inefficient, and even damaging: It can harm the seabed or pull up oysters that aren't yet ready for harvest.

The fishermen, she says, "don't have a whole picture of what's going on. So our goal is to transform that guesswork into precision."

Yu is trying to do that with the help of robots. She and her team frequently work inside the Neutral Buoyancy Research Facility on campus, which houses a giant cylindrical tank.

Mechanical engineer Miao Yu is using robots and AI to inform oyster farmers about when and where to plant and harvest.

On a recent fall morning, one of Yu's PhD students, Michael Xu, uses a joystick to steer a raft-like robot called Oysterbot. Oysterbot, which the team built in-house, consists of a collection of electronics and cables atop a couple of pontoons. A sonar is mounted below.

"We're able to do a large-range scan to get a general view of what's going on down there," says Xu.

The team can also deploy a smaller off-the-shelf robot known as the BlueROV to examine something underwater more closely through a live video feed. Together, the two robots paint a portrait of the seabed.

The lab then uses AI to stitch the visuals together and analyze them "to determine if the oysters are present, how many of them are alive or dead, and how big they are," says Xu.

They're still refining the algorithms, but Yu says the eventual goal is "to turn that sonar image map into an oyster information map." In other words, she wants to provide farmers with actionable intelligence to know when and where to plant and harvest their oysters.

Beyond the Chesapeake, her team has conducted field work along the shoreline of Washington state and the Gulf coast. Yu is hoping that within a decade, the technology could be modified and scaled to coastlines nationwide, "so that we can help the oysters for the entire United States."

This interest in aiding oysters elsewhere appeals to Consoli as well. Ever since he got hooked, he can't help but spread the good word to a growing number of neighbors with access to the bay.

"Every time I meet a new person, I ask them, 'Hey, do you like oysters?" he says. "And even if they say no, I say, 'Well, somebody in your family likes oysters. Have to be! You have a brother, uncle, a brother-in-law.'" Once he establishes such a connection, he says to them, "Hey, can you grow them? It's not that hard."

And most of the time, Consoli finds that people are quite receptive. That includes a couple of octogenarian neighbors of his on Kent Island.

"I really am impressed that the oysters clean the bay," says Earl Collins.

On one occasion, Ann Ziegler, who lives a couple doors down from Consoli, says she pulled her oysters out of the water with her family to eat them raw. "And then, at Thanksgiving, since no one had died, we ate them again," she says.

Consoli has also met new neighbors through this work, like John Patrick. "It's just amazing the amount of marine life that I've seen around the pier since I've had these oysters in the water," he says. "I had croaker, crabs and eels in here this morning."

Even Consoli's dental hygienist has gotten involved.

Perhaps most ambitiously, Consoli worked with a local restaurant called Libbey's Coastal Kitchen in August to place a million baby oysters around their dock pilings.

"We had eight people in wetsuits and life jackets," he says. "There were jellyfish everywhere. It was probably the most difficult installation we could ever do."

Restaurant operator Andrew Westlin says he was instantly attracted to the idea.

"This was a no-brainer for us, honestly," he says. "We felt that this was a cool way for us to give back and just be part of the community." Soon, there will be a sign next to the pier explaining the oyster project to any restaurant customers and passersby.

Consoli's wife, Kathy, says all this oyster work is "the most hardworking hobby there is. I call him now the Pied Piper of oysters because I think he's up to 80 people possibly."

She's right. Consoli calls it his Peer to Pier Network.

"We're really just trying to make sure that we can restore as much as we can to the bay," he says, "whether that's with robots or other techniques… It teaches me just how something that seems so insignificant can make a difference."

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/29/nx-s1-601.title: Even birds get jet lagged, study shows
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/29/nx-s1-601.author: Geoff Brumfiel
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/29/nx-s1-601.text:
Manx shearwaters race back to their nests after spending weeks hunting at sea. New research suggests they get jet lagged on their journey home.

New research shows that humans are not the only species to get jet lag: Some birds appear to experience it too.

A study published in the journal Science found that a type of seabird known as the Manx shearwater appears to become slightly disoriented during long flights across the Atlantic Ocean. That disorientation, the authors say, is due to the bird's internal clock falling out of sync with the sun's position in the sky.

Manx shearwaters are a common bird in the British Isles. They look a little like seagulls, but "they're actually very closely related to an albatross," said Patrick Lewin, a behavioral ecologist at the University of Oxford.

Shearwaters mate for life, and when they breed, a couple lays just one egg.

Then they take turns incubating it: "One partner will sit on the egg nonstop while the other one goes out to sea," Lewin said.

For up to two weeks the hunting partners scour the North Atlantic for fish and squid, often travelling hundreds of miles from their nests.

Once these birds' bellies are full "they absolutely bomb it back to their colony," Lewin said. Often they make the long journey home in just a day or so.

Which raised an interesting question: Do Manx shearwaters feel jet lag (or perhaps more aptly, flap lag)?

To see if these little birds really did feel the effects of flying through time zones like humans do, Lewin used a remarkable tool – for 20 years, his colleagues had been tagging birds with GPS trackers and collecting data on their flights out to the Atlantic and back.

He figured he could see the jet lag in their flights. That's because the Manx shearwaters are believed to use the sun to navigate.

"To use the sun as a compass you have to know what time of day it is," Lewin said.

In the morning, the sun is in the east, at midday it's slightly to the south (if you're in the northern hemisphere) and then in the evening it's in the west. If the shearwaters had the wrong time of day, they would fly the wrong way.

That's exactly what Lewin and his colleagues saw. As the birds rushed back to their partners and eggs, they veered ever-so-slightly off course. It wasn't much: A seven-degree error, the maximum deviation observed, only took a bird out of its way by about three miles on a 600-mile journey. "It's a really small addition," he said.

"This paper is so cool," said Alice Boyle, a biologist at the Centre for Animals on the Move at Western University in Ontario, Canada who was not part of the study.

Boyle said pretty much every creature on the planet, from corals to chipmunks, has to navigate its environment, yet it's rare to see a study showing navigation decisions in action. That's what makes this type of GPS work so valuable.

"It's using these wild birds that travel to completely remote places and we're able to learn so much about how they do that," she said.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Kenyan doomsday sect leader jailed for 200 years for murder of 190 children
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Carlos Mureithi in Nairobi and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Paul Mackenzie convicted over deaths of children and one adult after followers were ordered to starve themselves and their families

The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history.

The sentence, comprising 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, came two weeks after the court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa found the cult leader guilty of the crimes.

Prosecutors said Paul Mackenzie and his Good News International church ran ​a Christian doomsday sect whose members were ordered to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.

His accomplices threatened and beat victims to ensure they followed his orders. The emaciated bodies were found scattered in shallow graves and dumped in latrines. Some had been buried alive.

Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest near the coast in south-eastern Kenya.

In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered. Many were severely decomposed and only 26 could be identified.

Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve, but the court rejected that argument.

The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in the forest more than three years ago.

It raised questions about how Mackenzie was able to continue operating despite being on the radar of the authorities since 2017, when police searched his premises.

In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated ‌to the Shakahola forest, police said.

The case has also led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.

Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, describing such institutions as satanic.

Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names such as Jerusalem and Judea.

The plight of his followers began ​to emerge in March 2023, when a man told ​police his brother and wife had starved their children ​to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.

Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives said he brought forward the date ​on which he told his followers the ‌world would end. Police rearrested him and ​started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.

Last month’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into more than 200 other deaths are continuing.

Justice Diana Kavedza-Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.

Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths, including those of terrorism, which he has denied.

Prosecutors said that while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.

Reuters contributed reporting
