https://www.theguardian.com/science/ng-i.title: Thunderstruck: what does the future hold for lightning?
https://www.theguardian.com/science/ng-i.author: James Bradley
https://www.theguardian.com/science/ng-i.text:
Humans have always been awed by the power and beauty of lightning. How does the experience and understanding of it change in a warming world?

In a rock shelter in Kakadu national park in the north of Australia is an image of a being the Bininj people call Namarrkon. His flesh bleached away to reveal the bones beneath, he wears stone axes on his head, elbows and knees, and wields a great band of lightning that runs from his ankles up, over his head.

Namarrkon’s journey from the Arafura Sea to the Arnhem Land escarpment helped shape the landscape, according to the dreamtime stories of the Bininj. And in the great storms that arc and rumble across the landscape during the buildup and the wet season, it is Namarrkon who splits the clouds with his stone axes to create the thunder and lightning and release the life-giving rain.

Around the world there are an average of 60 lightning flashes a second, some extending more than 800km. Each flash can release up to seven gigajoules of energy, the equivalent of 1.67 tonnes of TNT, fleetingly heating the air around it to about 30,000C, five times hotter than the surface of the Sun. This constant discharge of energy plays a vital role in regulating Earth’s electrical field and the ionosphere. It helps drive the nitrogen cycle by cracking open nitrogen molecules in the atmosphere and making them available to plants, aiding in the production of ozone, and helping break down greenhouse gases such as methane. And it underpins the cycles of fire that shape the ecologies of forests, savannahs and grasslands across the planet. Lightning, as the story of Namarrkon captures, is an integral part of life on our planet.

Yet as the planet heats up, not just lightning’s role in these systems but lightning itself may be changing. And the consequences of this could be severe. In July more than 48,000 lightning strikes ignited massive wildfires in Canada and the north-west United States, destroying homes and casting a pall of smoke over cities across North America. During last summer’s British heatwave, nearly 30,000 lightning strikes hit south-east England in a single day.

Already, globally around a quarter of a million people are struck by lightning every year, resulting in about 24,000 deaths. In Australia alone lightning kills five to 10 people a year and injures about 100.

The awesome power of lightning is written deep into human cultures around the world. Frequently it expresses a kind of duality, conjuring beauty as well as terror: from the earliest-known poet, the priestess Enheduanna, describing her goddess as having a “glance like striking lightning” to gods whose domain includes both storms and agriculture in ancient Mesopotamian, Maya and Aztec cultures.

Often those who wield the lightning are protectors of humankind: in the Rig-Veda of ancient India, Indra slays the evil serpent Vritra with a thunderbolt and releases the rains and the rivers, while the Norse thunder god Thor was a guardian of humans. And many Native American cultures across the Pacific north-west, Great Lakes and Great Plains incorporate a powerful being known as the Thunderbird, who safeguards humankind.

Although writers and philosophers have sought a physical explanation for lightning for more than 2,000 years, it was not until the 18th century that the American polymath Benjamin Franklin proved the connection between the discharge of static electricity and lightning. Franklin theorised electricity was an invisible fluid that could be passed from object to object or held in substances such as water vapour.

Scientists no longer speak of invisible fluids. Instead, lightning is understood to be created when warm, moisture-laden air rises into the cold upper reaches of storm clouds. As the temperature falls, the water vapour condenses and forms tiny ice crystals. These collide with particles of soft ice called graupel, passing electrons from the ice crystals to the graupel. Now positively charged, the smaller, lighter ice crystals begin to rise into the upper reaches of the cloud, while the heavier, negatively charged graupel sink. As they move away from each other the resulting electrical field grows more intense, until finally the difference between the two neutralises in a sudden discharge of energy. It’s this discharge we see as lightning.

However, the question of precisely what triggers the discharge is still not yet fully understood. This is partly because the electrical fields generated by this process are only about a tenth as strong as they need to be to generate a spark. Recent research suggests it is cosmic rays that provide the spark, although other studies point to the runaway buildup of “streamers” of ionised air.

More than 80% of these discharges take place over land, and although the distribution of lightning changes with the seasons, it is concentrated in central Africa, parts of South America and the Himalayas. The most lightning-prone place in the world is in Venezuela, in an area known as Catatumbo, or “House of the Thunder” in the language of the Bari people, where warm, water-laden air blowing in over Lake Maracaibo collides with the high ridges of the Andes and can generate thunderstorms on 140 to 160 nights a year. By contrast lightning is extremely rare in polar regions.

But while the bulk of lightning occurs over land, particularly storm-prone areas of the ocean can achieve far higher densities of flashes: in one 1998 storm in the Indian Ocean lightning flashed eight times a second, so often that to the human eye it would seem the sky was permanently illuminated. And, in a testament to the power of human activity to shape the weather, storms over the ocean are also enhanced over shipping lanes. Aerosol particles emitted in the exhaust of ships appear to be changing the process of cloud formation.

As the climate crisis heats the atmosphere it seems reasonable to assume that thunderstorm activity will increase. A warmer atmosphere holds more water vapour and the additional heat provides more energy to drive deep convection within thunderclouds. Yet the reality is more complicated than this suggests.

A recent review of lightning studies now under peer review finds that projections ranged from an 11% decrease to a 44% increase in lightning per degree of global warming, with a mean increase across all projections of 7.5% per degree. Despite considerable uncertainty about how tropical regions will be affected, it also finds broad agreement lightning will increase in high latitudes.

Andrew Dowdy is associate professor in climate science in the School of Geography, Earth and Atmospheric Sciences at the University of Melbourne, and one of Australia’s leading experts on lightning. He says that while “it’s clear that in a warmer world, some of the conditions that are conducive to thunderstorms and lightning can be enhanced”, there are still “large uncertainties” when it comes to understanding how lightning will be affected by climate change.

Some of these uncertainties relate to the difficulty of modelling the fine-scale processes that cause lightning, others to the relative paucity of high-quality, long-term data relating to lightning; until the launch of satellites capable of measuring lightning from space in the 1990s it was necessary to rely on ground-based observations and regional radar. Nonetheless, by combining records relating to cyclones and fronts with thunderstorm data, Dowdy and his colleagues have been able to track the frequency of such events as far back as 1979. This has revealed an increase in such events along the eastern coasts of continents alongside a poleward shift in cyclone activity in the southern hemisphere.

Separate research by Dowdy has found that while thunderstorm activity has increased in eastern and south-easternAustralia, other areas, especially in the tropical north, have experienced a decline.

But lightning can strike without a storm.

Just last week, a report released by the Emergency Leaders for Climate Change in Australia warned that the number of fires started by dry lightning – lightning that strikes the ground without accompanying rain – was increasing. The advocacy group noted that forests in Australia’s south-east recorded 50% more dry lightning strikes in 2000–2016 than in the previous two decades, helping create a “step change in fire conditions”.

“Lightning is the natural ignition source of fires,” says Dowdy, who also notes that “lightning fires tend to burn larger areas on average compared to fires that are ignited by humans. And that’s because lightning can occur in remote places that are hard for response crews to get to, but they can also occur in large clusters.”

The connection between any increase in dry lightning and fire is not straightforward, however. In Tasmania the number of fires sparked by dry lightning events has increased significantly since the 1990s. The fires that devastated Tasmania’s remote north-west in 2025 were sparked by a massive lightning storm that saw more than 1,200 lightning strikes reach the ground in less than 24 hours. Yet while it was lightning that started the fires, the landscape was already primed to burn by a combination of unusually dry conditions, strong winds and high temperatures, a convergence of factors that is rapidly intensifying as the planet heats up.

“It’s clear that in a warmer world you get more dangerous conditions for fire weather in many places,” Dowdy says.

Similar mechanisms are at work elsewhere in the world, perhaps most visibly in the United States, where dry lightning is combining with increasingly dangerous fire conditions to create megablazes such as the August Complex blaze, which burned more than 4,000 square kilometres in northern California in 2020.

More intense fires are driving an increase in another form of lightning, however.

When fires grow ferocious enough they can begin to create their own weather, as the heat and moisture they release can combine into giant thunderheads known as pyrocumulonimbus (pyroCb). Turbocharged by the intense heat of the fires, these terrifying formations reach far higher than ordinary storm clouds, often boiling up into the stratosphere, creating a massive vortex which sucks the moisture released by the fire up into the upper reaches of the atmosphere at speeds that can exceed 200 km/h. There, in the swirling darkness of these monstrous structures, this moisture freezes, collides and creates lightning.

Until recently, pyroCb storms were relatively unusual, but in the past decade they have become increasingly frequent, not just in Australia but in the United States, Canada and Russia, and most recently Europe, where one was reported during the fires that devastated France in July and August of this year.

Jason Evans is a professor at the Climate Change Research Centre at the University of New South Wales. He says there has been a “massive increase” in the number of pyroCB events in Australia. In the black summer fires of 2019-2020, he notes, there were almost as many recorded as in the 40 years prior combined.

PyroCb are not just a symptom of our planet’s increasingly deranged fire cycle, they also create feedback loops, spreading and intensifying the fire, as lightning strikes and embers borne by the strong winds they generate start new fires. This process can extend across very wide areas: during Australia’s black Saturday fires in 2009 pyrogenic lightning from a 15-kilometre high pyroCb ignited new fires 100 kms ahead of the fire front.

Evans says that once a pyroCb “kicks off”, it’s “not containable. We can’t control it really at all. All we can do is get out of the way. They’re even too dangerous for the firefighting aircraft to try and get close enough to get their water on to.”

The spectacle of pyroCbs is just one more example of the way human activity is transforming the planet. Whereas we once were at the mercy of the lightning, now we are helping create it. What this will mean for us and our world remains unclear. For as the stories of the Bininj and others remind us, lightning has always embodied an uneasy duality. Simultaneously beautiful and terrible, feared as well as exalted, it can be both life giver and destroyer.

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: Want to have a better chat? Scientists say the secret is ‘pink noise’
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Ian Sample Science editor
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
The most enjoyable conversations strike a balance between exploring a topic and pulling in fresh ideas, study finds

As an early stab at rules for conversation, Cicero did a fine job: watch your tone, never look bored, never lose your temper and never ramble on, particularly about yourself, he advised.

Now scientists have followed in the great orator’s footsteps and discovered a telltale signature of an enjoyable chinwag. The secret of a mutually satisfying exchange is a healthy dose of pink noise, they say.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The colour of noise tends to animate physicists more than linguists, but researchers at Dartmouth College in New Hampshire in the US found the concept provided fresh insights into what makes a good conversation.

Kathryn O’Nell, the first author on the study, said: “In physics, people talk about pink noise as existing on the edge of chaos, where you can stay at a stable point, but you’re not stuck there for ever.

“It’s particularly cool for conversation, because you can stay somewhere long enough to really get to know each other, to understand the topic, but you’re not stuck there while it gets stale.”

The researchers analysed more than 1,000 conversations between strangers, who answered questions on the chats afterwards. People enjoyed conversations more, wanted to continue chatting, and felt a stronger sense of connection when the tête-à-têtes exhibited more pink noise, they found.

To see whether the effect applied beyond strangers, the researchers ran a similar analysis on conversations between friends about their formative experiences. Again, more pink noise meant more enjoyment.

The effect had real-world consequences, too. When the scientists turned to speed-dating conversations, they found that more pink noise predicted which pairs met up for a second date. Details have been published in Science Advances.

Nailing down what makes a great chat is notoriously tricky, the researchers said. In a bold opening statement to their paper, the authors write: “Good conversation is like pornography – it is difficult to define, but we know it when we see it.”

Colloquially, people talk about being in sync, but the metaphor misses something, said Dr Emily Finn, a neuroscientist and senior author on the paper. “In sync can be incredibly dull,” she said. People can be in sync when they repeat each other’s words and circle a single subject. They might well be immensely bored.

In the study, the scientists took conversations and fed each side into an AI called MPNet. The program scored every turn of the chat on 768 different criteria, covering aspects such as meaning, tone and context. This allowed the scientists to quantify how conversations ebbed and flowed over time.

Conversations exhibit white noise when people fail to follow what has just been said: the chat might jump all over the place, or be dominated by a person who seems oblivious to the other person’s responses. Other conversations can have red noise, which arises when people mirror each other’s language and fall into a conversational rut.

Pink noise lies somewhere in between: a conversational Goldilocks zone that balances stability and flexibility. People will synchronise as they explore a topic, then drift apart as they pull in fresh ideas before converging again to explore those.

The pinkiness of a conversation depends on the people involved, but O’Nell said she suspected the skill could be learned and developed. As part of the study, the team analysed podcasts fronted by two hosts and found that the pinkiness of their conversations increased over the first 50 episodes.

Prof Elizabeth Stokoe, a conversation analyst at the London School of Economics, praised the researchers for moving beyond the idea that “more similarity is better”. But asking whether a conversation is enjoyable risks missing the point, she added.

“There’s a lovely study of a phone call in which a father and his daughter, a young woman with learning disabilities living in residential care, take a long time to say goodbye, and the ending is painful and poignant,” she said. “Reducing conversations to whether they are ‘enjoyable’ can feel bloodless, since many of the conversations that matter most in our lives are like this.”
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.summary: Scientists at Dartmouth College in New Hampshire in the US analysed more than 1,000 conversations between strangers. They found people enjoyed conversations more, wanted to continue chatting, and felt a stronger sense of connection when the tête-à-têtes exhibited more pink noise.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: Origin of Stonehenge’s altar remains enigma as north-east Scotland theory ruled out
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Steven Morris
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Geologists say they are getting closer to solving mystery as tests suggest stone may have come from elsewhere in Scotland, northern England or even Ireland

They spent countless hours on weather-battered Scottish hills, a hardy band of geologists searching for the origin of one of Stonehenge’s most intriguing features.

But the prehistoric monument tends to yield its secrets reluctantly, and a new scientific report reveals that the origin of Stonehenge’s altar stone remains elusive – and the wind-whipped geologists may very well have been looking in the wrong spot anyway.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

One described the altar stone’s beginnings as an “enigma”, another a geological detective story with no neat ending so far.

It all felt different in 2024 when specialists from universities in London, Wales and Australia examined grains of sandstone from the altar and hypothesised it came from north-east Scotland, more than 400 miles from Stonehenge.

A member of the team described the find as “jaw-dropping” and it led to speculation about how the six-tonne stone had been transported – by sledge or ship? – and about the long-distance relationships that neolithic people must have had.

More experts were brought in, from Canada, Italy, Sweden and Scotland, and work was done on the precise composition of the slab, including non-invasive examinations of the stone in situ, and examinations of eight fragments held in museums.

Armed with this profile, members of the team headed to north-east Scotland to try to make an exact match with outcrops there, thus pinpointing the altar stone’s origins.

Nick Pearce, an emeritus professor of geochemistry in the department of geography and earth sciences at Aberystwyth University, described the hunt for the origin of the altar stone as a search for a needle in a haystack.

“The problem is, it’s a very big area, thousands of square kilometres. The only way to do it is to get out there and find the samples,” he said.

“You have to plan carefully. One of my colleagues was there recently and he got caught in the storms, which isn’t ideal field weather for geology. We’ve taken about 70 samples, brought them back to laboratories and tested them.”

The testing has suggested it is unlikely the altar stone came from north-east Scotland.

Pearce said he wasn’t disappointed that they had not solved the mystery yet. “We’re getting closer. In a geological detective story such as this, ruling out potential source areas is just as important as identifying new ones. Every location eliminated narrows the search and brings us closer to discovering where the altar stone originated. I’m not disappointed. It’s part of the process.”

Sign up to First Edition

Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters

after newsletter promotion

Duncan Pirrie, an emeritus professor at the University of South Wales, who led the study, concluded it was “very unlikely” the altar stone had originated from north-east Scotland. He said the stone also definitely did not come from southern Britain. It may have come from somewhere else in Scotland, northern England or perhaps even Ireland.

Pirrie said the stone’s origins remained an enigma, but added: “This is the most comprehensive geological investigation of the altar stone ever undertaken. By combining a wide range of analytical techniques, we have built the clearest picture yet of the stone’s composition and tested the leading theories about its origins.

“So far, none of the locations examined have the same set of characteristics as the altar stone, but the search is not over.”

Mike Pitts, a renowned Stonehenge expert who was not involved in the study, said detecting the origin of the altar stone was an exciting prospect. “Doing so would greatly help fit the altar stone into the world of the people who moved it. We’d get to see the landscape through their eyes. To know exactly where the journey began.”

The study, Searching for the origin of the Stonehenge altar stone, is published in the Journal of the Geological Society

But the prehistoric monument tends to yield its secrets reluctantly, and a new report reveals that the origin remains elusive.

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: Swapping from dairy to plant-based milk, cheese and yoghurt ‘could lead to micronutrient deficiencies’
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Ian Sample Science editor
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
Young people and women most at risk, study finds, as researchers call for vegan products to be fortified with iodine in particular

Switching from dairy products to plant-based alternatives could lead to deficiencies in vital micronutrients, especially among young people and women, a study has found.

Even moving partly to vegan alternatives to milk, cheese and yoghurt could lead to falls in iodine, calcium, riboflavin and vitamin B12 if the substitutes, often based on soya, almonds or oats, are not fortified, scientists said.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The greatest concerns surround iodine, a trace element used by the thyroid gland to produce hormones that regulate metabolism and support healthy growth and brain development. More than half of UK teenage girls already have inadequate iodine intake, the researchers said.

Replacing a fifth to a third of dairy intake with plant-based alternatives would lead to prevalence of iodine deficiency rising from 54% to 65% of adolescent girls and from 32% to 42% of women aged 19 to 49 years old, according to modelling based on typical market levels of fortification.

“There are known health effects of iodine deficiency and that’s why we want to raise awareness of this,” said Dr Sarah Bath, an associate professor in public health nutrition at the University of Surrey. “The population groups that seem to be at risk and have the lowest intakes were the young women and women of childbearing age, and that’s the key life stage where iodine is particularly important.”

Plant-based alternatives to milk, cheese and yoghurt have grown in popularity, though there are signs some consumers are shifting back.

In the UK, children get about half, and adults about a third, of their total iodine intake from dairy products, but there is no formal requirement for vegan alternatives to be fortified with micronutrients.

The researchers looked at the impact of replacing dairy with plant-based alternatives on the UK market, including 146 non-dairy milks, 76 yoghurts and 67 cheeses. While 61% had added calcium and 46% added vitamin B12, only 19% were fortified with riboflavin and 12% with iodine.

At these levels, the scientists’ modelling showed that swapping a third of dairy intake for vegan alternatives led to a 9% to 21% drop in iodine intake, with calcium, riboflavin and vitamin B12 also falling. Switching to 100% non-dairy alternatives led to inadequate levels of iodine reaching 80% in teenage girls and 72% in teenage boys.

Requiring all non-dairy alternatives to be fortified with iodine would prevent average declines, the study found. Adding iodised salt to bread helped reduce the proportion of teenage girls with inadequate iodine intake in the modelled scenarios. The study is published in the Lancet Planetary Health.

Some companies already fortify their dairy substitutes. Niamh Brannelly, the head of nutrition and science communications for Danone in the UK, said its core range of Alpro products was fortified for calcium, iodine and vitamins B2 and B12.

Caroline Orfila Jenkins, a vice-president for science and technology at Oatly, said all its unflavoured, non-organic oat drinks were fortified with nutrients including iodine, calcium, riboflavin and vitamins B12 and D. “This research underlines the importance of appropriate fortification as diets become more plant-based,” she said.

Nichola Ludlam-Raine, a registered dietitian and spokesperson for the British Dietetic Association, said the work raised an important population-level concern but did not mean that everyone who switched would become nutrient-deficient because overall diet mattered too.

“For anyone choosing plant-based milk, I’d recommend checking the label and choosing one fortified with iodine, such as Alpro,” she said. “Organic drinks aren’t fortified with added nutrients, so they’re unlikely to provide iodine. White fish such as cod or haddock, as well as eggs and yoghurt and kefir for those who consume them, can also contribute iodine. I wouldn’t recommend relying on seaweed or kelp supplements as an iodine source, as the iodine content can vary widely and may be excessive.”

More than half of UK teenage girls already have inadequate iodine intake, study finds. Replacing a fifth to a third of dairy intake with plant- based alternatives would lead to prevalence of iodine deficiency rising from 54% to 65% of adolescent girls

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: US prosecutors drop criminal charges against scientist detained over frog embryos
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Marina Dunbar and agency
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Kseniia Petrova was detained for four months after arrest with research samples, and feared deportation to Russia

Federal prosecutors have dropped all criminal charges against a Russian scientist who spent four months in immigration detention after flying into Boston with frog embryos intended for cancer research at Harvard Medical School.

Kseniia Petrova, 31, was arrested in March 2025 after returning from a vacation in France, where she had visited a laboratory specializing in cutting extremely thin sections of frog embryos. During her visit, she obtained a package of samples for her research back in the US.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Customs officials questioned Petrova about the samples when she arrived at Logan international airport. She was later charged with smuggling, concealing facts and making false statements to government officials.

Petrova’s case was one of the many shocking, high-profile, immigration-related arrests, especially involving academics, in the early months after Donald Trump returned to the White House promising a crackdown on immigration.

Petrova had fled Russia after being arrested for protesting against the invasion of Ukraine, and colleagues at Harvard University called her research talents “spectacular”.

On Wednesday, the US district judge Leo Sorokin granted prosecutors’ request to dismiss all charges against Petrova without holding a hearing.

The case began unraveling when a federal judge determined that a customs officer had improperly canceled Petrova’s visa. Petrova had feared that she would be deported to Russia, where she could face imprisonment. In May of last year, a judge ordered her release.

Her attorneys had challenged the criminal prosecution, arguing that the charges were vindictive and had been filed only after it appeared Petrova would prevail in her immigration case. They maintained that criminal prosecutions involving conduct like hers were uncommon.

On Tuesday night, the US attorney Leah Foley submitted a motion seeking to dismiss the case “based on developments in this case and an assessment of the office’s priorities and resources”.

“At this stage, the resource costs of continuing this prosecution outweigh the public interest in its resolution,” she wrote, adding that the “defendant’s claims of vindictive and selective prosecution are meritless”.

Following the dismissal, Petrova’s attorney Daniel Marx criticized the decision to pursue criminal charges against the scientist.

“The DOJ never should have brought this highly unusual ‘smuggling’ prosecution against Kseniia Petrova, a talented scientist at Harvard,” Marx said in a statement. “Ms Petrova only sought to advance medical research into aging that could benefit everyone, and her handling of scientific samples – inert, non-living, non-toxic, frog embryos – never posed any danger to anyone.”

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) had continued to defend Petrova’s arrest, maintaining that she had lied to federal officers about the frog embryos.

Petrova is among numerous noncitizen academics who have been arrested or threatened with deportation by the Trump administration.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Kseniia Petrova, 31, was arrested in March 2025 after returning from a vacation in France. She was arrested with frog embryos intended for cancer research at Harvard Medical School. She had fled Russia after being arrested for protesting against the invasion of Ukraine.

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: Nasa telescope launched in 2004 to plunge back to Earth after failed rescue mission
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Edward Helmore
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory is expected to re-enter Earth’s atmosphere Wednesday, burning up in the process

Nasa’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, which has spent two decades studying the most powerful explosions in the cosmos, is expected to re-enter the Earth’s atmosphere on Wednesday, burning up in the process.

The satellite, which was designed to operate with its three telescopes for just two years, is no longer able to steer or observe, and its re-entry is uncontrolled.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The US Space Force predicts the 3,200lb spacecraft will hit the atmosphere at about 3.30am ET on 4 November. Nasa says most of the spacecraft will burn up, but some components are expected to survive.

“Re-entry locations of any surviving components can vary from hemisphere to hemisphere and depend on when it re-enters,” the agency said in a blogpost, adding that surviving fragments are limited between 20.6 degrees south latitude and 20.6 degrees north latitude.

The agency added: “The risk of harm coming to anyone on Earth is unlikely – approximately 1 in 2,100. NASA and Space Force will continue to monitor the re-entry and update predictions.”

The observatory was launched in 2004 to explore the universe’s most powerful explosions, called cosmic gamma-ray bursts, and quickly return its observations of location and strength to Earth.

Over the course of its operational life, the observatory detected and tracked more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) that are considered the most powerful explosions the universe has seen since the big bang.

Nasa says these bursts of energy occur approximately once per day and are brief, but intense, flashes of gamma radiation and come from all different directions, and can last from a few milliseconds to a few hundred seconds.

But scientists do not know what causes them – theorizing that they may be the birth of a black hole in a massive stellar explosion or produced by the collision of two neutron stars, or some other phenomenon.

Swift was launched as part of Nasa’s medium explorer, or Midex, program. In July, it observed a wandering mega black hole shredding star, which occurs when a star passes fatally close to a supermassive black hole.

“Crumbs of the splintering star heat up as they swirl around the black hole, creating a glow astronomers can see from far across the cosmos, and the black hole launches a relativistic jet into space,” said the agency.

The black hole, described as an “orphan”, lit up as it devoured the star on the outskirts of a galaxy, in what scientists call a “tidal disruption event”. Nearly every galaxy has a supermassive black hole at its center, and a tidal disruption occurs about once every 100,000 years.

The star-shedding event occurred 2,600 light-years from the center of the host galaxy, but the Swift team observed one more than 30,000 light-years away.

Sign up to Headlines US

Get the most important US headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning

after newsletter promotion

“We were looking for these star-shredding events as a way to find otherwise invisible supermassive black holes wandering away from the galactic cores where they usually reside,” said Robert Stein, a research fellow at the University of Maryland, College Park, and Nasa’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, at the time.

A paper describing the results published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, said: “The tidal disruption event outshone its entire host galaxy in ultraviolet wavelengths, temporarily radiating with the light of about 10 billion suns.”

Still unknown is how the black hole came to drift so far. Stein said it could have started off in a small galaxy that merged with the big one, but the key question was how common are wandering black holes.

Nasa attempted to push Swift into a higher orbit last year using a private space contractor but the mission did not succeed after they failed to rendezvous. Last month, Swift was estimated to be orbiting 171 miles above the Earth and it was commanded to end operations to prepare for re-entry.

Nasa said Swift has “broadened our understanding of a wide variety of cosmic objects and events, from active galaxies powered by supermassive black holes and stars undergoing X-ray flares, to supernova explosions and comets and asteroids in our own solar system”.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: Historians say King Verica persuaded Rome to invade Britain. But could Verica actually have been a queen?
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Nicola Davis Science correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Controversial theory that Verica, who incited Emperor Claudius’s AD43 landing, was a woman could put a new spin on British history if true

It was a moment that changed the course of British history: in AD43, Roman troops under the emperor Claudius landed in Kent. Now, an archaeologist has claimed the British ruler who persuaded Claudius to invade was not a king but a queen.

The controversial conclusion, made by Dr Miles Russell, the director of archaeological fieldwork at Bournemouth University, could throw new light on Britain’s history.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

“It’s critical because … without Verica there probably would be no Roman invasion,” he said. “Also, it changes the politics, it changes the dynamics of iron age Britain.”

Verica was a Romanised Briton who ruled the Atrebates tribe who controlled parts of what is now southern Hampshire and West Sussex. After the death of another powerful tribal leader, Cunobelinus, and the rise of Cunobelinus’s son Caratacus, Verica was exiled and fled to Claudius in Rome.

Russell says among the evidence for a rethink of Verica’s sex is that Latin names that end in the letter “a” often belong to women.

What’s more, Verica used the term “Rex” on coins – a word Russell says was used to refer to firm allies on the edge of the Roman empire in the late first century BC and early to mid first century AD. Unlike the words “Regina”(queen) and “Regis” (king), “Rex” did not imply a particular sex, Russell says.

Russell also noted that coins minted under Verica appeared to show a naked woman on horseback, whereas those minted under rulers including Cunobelinus and Caratacus show overtly male naked characters on a horse. “I think the imagery is overtly feminine because that’s basically saying that’s who Verica is,” Russell said.

And while abbreviated Latin inscriptions on the coins have been taken to mean “son of …”, Russell says they could also mean “daughter of”.

Russell’s claims will appear in a new book, Caratacus: Great King of Britain. Work by Russell and colleagues has previously revealed that women were extremely important within iron age society.

The idea that Verica was a woman chimes with criticisms made of Claudius by the Roman writer Cassius Dio, who claimed the emperor was influenced by slaves and women, Russell added.

Prof Roger Tomlin, a British archaeologist specialising in the translation of Latin text and epigraphy based at the University of Oxford, said there were Latin men’s names ending in “a”, but the existence of the masculine form “Vericus” was the best argument that “Verica” was feminine.

However, Tomlin said Cassius Dio assumed the ruler was a man, referring to him as “Bericus” – something Russell argues could be down to a garbling of names, with Dio writing more than 200 years after the events. His work was a result of translating and transcribing by multiple generations.

Tomlin also said there was little evidence the term Rex had been used for both male and female rulers. “Of course the Romans recognised client-queens as well as client-kings, but Russell must prove, by finding other examples, that they referred to them both as Rex,” he said.

He added that the depiction of what appears to be a bare-breasted warrior on the reverse of the coin did not prove Verica was a woman. “It reminds me of the argument that Queen Victoria was really a man, because the reverse of her gold coinage depicts her as a male horseman killing a dragon,” Tomlin said.

Dr Daphne Nash Briggs, a British iron age archaeologist and coin expert, also voiced scepticism, noting that some coins bearing Verica’s name depicted a clearly male form on horseback, while others appeared to show a portrait of Verica in male priestly dress, and some showed Verica’s head and neck – with an Adam’s apple.

Russell argues the latter depicts the emperor, and it is not clear that the figure in priestly dress is male or that it was Verica.

Russell is aware his arguments may cause controversy. “If it does create debate and argument, I think that’s for the better,” he said. “The one-sided story’s been there for so long. We need that to change. We need to have this discussion.”

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: Why pharma firms are going to Earth’s orbit in search of new cancer drugs
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Linda Geddes
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
A space capsule 300 miles above us is growing the tiny crystals of a potential cancer drug in microgravity

R
oughly 300 miles above our heads, three washing machine-sized capsules are orbiting the Earth. Inside one of them, tiny crystals of a potential cancer drug are being grown in the weightlessness of space. The others are testing heat protection materials and navigation systems for when the capsules plunge back through Earth’s atmosphere at hypersonic speeds. Together, they represent a small but significant step towards what some hope will become a lucrative new industry: manufacturing drugs and other materials in space.

The spacecraft belong to California-based Varda Space Industries. On 1 October, it launched two onboard the same rocket, followed by the third on 20 October. With a record three spacecraft now simultaneously in orbit for the first time, the company is edging closer to its ambition of operating a fleet of orbiting pharmaceutical factories.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

“We’re the first company in human history to launch multiple commercial re-entry vehicles simultaneously, and as the frequency of launches increases, the once ‘crazy future’ of manufacturing products in space is becoming more and more certain,” said Will Bruey, Varda’s chief executive.

There are several reasons for wanting to manufacture certain materials in space, one of the most important being microgravity. On Earth, gravity causes particles suspended in liquids to settle, while differences in density create currents. Both can interfere with the growth of crystals. “If you are able to remove those effects, you can make crystals grow in a much more ordered sort of way,” said Dr Meganne Christian, mission manager for in-space manufacturing at the UK-based Satellite Applications Catapult.

For pharmaceutical companies, this could open up new ways of formulating medicines, as the size, shape and arrangement of drug crystals can affect how easily drugs dissolve, how stable they are and how they can be administered. In some cases, this could enable drugs that currently require intravenous infusions to be reformulated into more convenient injections.

Other materials, such as the semiconductors used in everything from smartphones to electric vehicles, could also benefit from being manufactured in space, where microgravity and the absence of air could help produce purer crystals with fewer defects.

“Personally, I would really love to try and make graphene in microgravity,” said Christian. “Theoretically, it is this incredible material, but in practice you get a whole lot of defects in the crystals. It’s a similar story for semiconductors. If you can reduce the number of defects, you can get a much higher-performing material.”

Scientists have been experimenting with manufacturing in microgravity for decades, particularly aboard the International Space Station (ISS). But the ISS has predominantly served as a “test kitchen” for scientific ideas and is scheduled to be retired around 2030. “It wasn’t necessarily designed with manufacturing in mind,” said Dr Ryan Reeves, deputy chief scientist for the ISS National Laboratory.

Several companies are developing commercial space stations to replace the ISS, while others are designing specialist laboratories and equipment for conducting experiments aboard them. Among them is the UK-based BioOrbit, which recently sent a microwave-sized laboratory to the ISS as a step towards the production of self-injected cancer drugs.

However, for large-scale manufacturing and certain industrial processes, “you need to get humans out of the picture, because we’re dirty, we cause vibrations, and we require a whole higher level of safety,” said Christian.

This is where Varda’s autonomous factories come in. Known as free-flyers, they hitch a ride into orbit aboard SpaceX rockets, carrying miniature laboratories in which materials can be processed without astronauts. Once the experiments are complete, a capsule separates from the spacecraft, plunges through the atmosphere and parachutes safely back to an uninhabited region of Earth.

Varda is among the furthest advanced in demonstrating this approach, having already returned several capsules from orbit. It plans to launch another seven missions in 2027, and a further 10 in 2028.

The ability to conduct experiments frequently is particularly important for drug development. “If scientists have to wait 10 years between experiments or even a year, that really doesn’t fit into the speed of modern drug development,” said Michael Reilly, Varda’s chief strategy officer.

While Varda’s manufacturing ambitions are focused on pharmaceuticals, other companies are developing similar systems to produce different materials. For example, Cardiff-based Space Forge is exploring a hybrid approach, in which semiconductor crystals grown aboard spacecraft could be returned to Earth and used as templates for growing larger quantities, much like a sourdough starter.

Its first spacecraft, ForgeStar-1, recently demonstrated some of the processes needed to manufacture these semiconductor “seed wafers”, although it has yet to produce a finished material and return it to Earth. Andrew Bacon, the company’s co-founder and chief technology officer, said they hope to demonstrate the entire manufacturing and return process before 2030.

For Bacon, recent developments, including Varda’s launches, suggest that space manufacturing is approaching a turning point. “Since we started in 2018, nobody was talking about it. Now a lot of companies [are] talking about it,” he said. “People are starting to take this market very seriously. It does feel like we’re at the start of a new Industrial Revolution.”

Falling launch costs and increasingly frequent commercial rocket flights have helped to fuel this optimism. But significant challenges remain, including demonstrating that the benefits of manufacturing in orbit justify the expense. “It’s not going to be commercially viable for every application,” said Christian. “We have to identify those high-value use cases where it makes sense to do the work in microgravity.”

Regulators will also need to adapt to accommodate space-manufactured products. Later this year, the UK’s Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) is expected to publish a plan clarifying how existing medicines regulations will apply to drugs manufactured in orbit.

But for now, one of the biggest challenges is demonstrating that space manufacturing can deliver consistently reliable results. “To get something to a commercially viable point, it needs to be done again and again and again,” said Christian. “That’s what these capsules need to do. They need to demonstrate this repeat performance.”

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: Fossilised red blood cells found in 115m-year-old dinosaur’s bone, say scientists
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Ian Sample Science editor
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
Chemical tests on Aratasaurus bone identify presence of heme, the organic compound that allows haemoglobin in blood to carry oxygen around body

It could be the opening of a Jurassic Park rip-off: scientists examining ancient dinosaur bones find what appear to be fossilised red blood cells, and traces of the molecule that gives the beast’s blood its distinctive crimson hue.

But that is what researchers are claiming to have discovered after analysing the hind leg bones of a small, meat-eating dinosaur called an Aratasaurus that lived and died in what is now north-eastern Brazil 115m years ago.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Electron microscope images of the dinosaur bones revealed small, round structures that resemble red blood cells in fine channels where blood vessels once ran, while chemical tests identified the presence of heme, the organic compound that allows haemoglobin in blood to carry oxygen around the body.

Such claims are controversial because biological tissues and molecules can break down fast, leaving little or no trace in ancient fossils. But if confirmed, it would open up entirely new avenues for scientists, allowing them to investigate dinosaur blood, metabolism and even their activity levels.

“We are seeing a mineral and molecular echo of the dinosaur’s original biology,” said Prof Kliti Grice at Curtin University in Western Australia who led the research team. “Fossilised red blood cells with distinct chemistry related to heme have never been found in situ in any fossil, let alone a dinosaur. This is a world first.”

The fossilised remnants of the Aratasaurus were discovered in a mine in 2008 and have since been held in the National Museum of Brazil, where researchers continue to study them. While analysing the dinosaur’s hind leg bones, Grice spotted the structures that resembled red blood cells.

The scientists’ suspicions that they were looking at red blood cells were bolstered when chemical tests came back positive for heme and its breakdown products. Tests also found traces of the amino acid building blocks for collagen, a key protein in connective and other tissues.

If the structures really are fossilised red blood cells, as the researchers contend, it raises the question of how they were preserved. According to Grice, a manganese compound called hausmannite, which formed in and around the blood cells, may have lent a helping hand by stabilising them prior to fossilisation. The same process might have helped preserve the amino acids, she added. The study appears in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

The work is already stoking debate. Prof Mary Schweitzer at North Carolina State University in the US, who has discovered remnants of blood vessels and soft tissues in dinosaur fossils, is not convinced Grice and her colleagues have found red blood cells. One reason for her doubt is that the dinosaur’s red blood cells should have a “nuclear bulge” making them appear dome-like on both sides. The structures Grice found are concave, suggesting they might be something else.

Schweitzer was more persuaded by the discovery of heme and collagen amino acids in the bone and said there was so much more to learn from exceptionally well-preserved fossils. Schweitzer added: “The conventional wisdom in palaeontology that all endogenous organics would disappear in a million years or less is being routinely challenged, and will continue to be as technological approaches to palaeontological specimens are more routinely applied.”

Another question the research raises is what other biological material might lurk in fossils collections around the world. On this, Grice urges extreme caution, adding that her work does not imply that large biological molecules such as proteins or DNA live on in ancient fossils. “Any extraordinary claim needs extraordinary analytical evidence,” she said. “The aim isn’t to find Jurassic Park DNA, it’s to determine how much genuine molecular information deep time can preserve.”

“The really exciting implication is that extraordinary molecular information may already be sitting in museum collections around the world, waiting for us to ask new questions of old fossils,” she added.
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.summary: Chemical tests on Aratasaurus bone identify presence of heme, the organic compound that allows haemoglobin in blood to carry oxygen around the body. If the structures really are fossilised red blood cells, it raises the question of how they were preserved.

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: Cryosphere faces permanent damage when world overshoots 1.5C, scientists warn
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Ajit Niranjan
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
UN-backed report finds even temporary rises above Paris agreement target could cause harm to glaciers and polar ice sheets

Earth’s icy regions face such dangerous melting that global heating should be brought back below 1C after an inevitable period of overshooting global temperature targets, a UN report has found.

Permanent and widespread losses of snow and ice expose a “persistent myth” that overshooting the 1.5C target of the Paris climate agreement – to 2C or 3C – could be manageable or even preferable to urgent cuts to emissions, the report found.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The planet has heated by 1.3C since pre-industrial times and failures to curb greenhouse gas emissions and protect nature have led scientists to conclude that some level of overshoot is inevitable as they fight to keep end-of-century warming to 1.5C.

But extreme effects on the cryosphere – Earth’s water in a solid state, including all its ice and snow – mean temperatures must rise above that threshold for as short a period as possible, the scientists urged. Added to this, enough planet-heating carbon should be removed from the atmosphere to bring long-term warming down much further, ideally below 1C by 2150.

The high overshoot expected under current policies – with peak temperatures of about 3C – would thaw nearly all near-surface permafrost, make “severe and possibly abrupt” disruption to ocean circulation likely, and lead to widespread acidification, the report found. The latest scientific research suggests sea ice recovers more slowly than previously thought.

The report, written by 80 scientists brought together by the International Cryosphere Climate Initiative (ICCI) and the UN Environment Programme (UNEP), found much of the damage would be permanent even if global temperatures were brought back down to 1.5C, such as glacier melt raising sea levels and threatening water security.

James Kirkham, a glaciologist at ICCI and the lead author of the report, said the cryosphere is “one of the most sensitive components of the climate system”, and the consequences of its loss affect the whole planet.

“This year, we’ve already seen one of the largest and most deadly ice rock avalanches ever recorded, on the Nepal-China border – it killed thousands of people and left damage equivalent to 10% of Nepal’s GDP in a single event,” said Kirkham. “Switzerland has lost 20% of its glacier ice in the last five years, and thousands of glaciers worldwide are expected to become extinct in the coming decade, every single year.”

The report, which comes as world leaders and diplomats converge on Turkey for the 31st annual Cop climate conference, documented rapid and accelerating melting of the cryosphere and polar oceans, with damages that range from the loss of the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets, driving sea level rises that threaten hundreds of millions of people, to thawing permafrost, which releases more planet-heating gas.

Glaciers, which are still responding to historical warming, would only preserve about 70% of their current volume over a timescale of centuries if long-term heating were brought back down to 0.8C, the report found.

Meanwhile, the ice sheets covering Greenland and Antarctica, which are melting about six times faster today than in the 1990s, would continue to lose ice even in scenarios where overshoot is brief and temperature rise returns to 1.5C, the report found. The scientists said a safe, long-term temperature limit for polar ice sheets lies much closer to 1.0C of global heating, and possibly even lower.

“Snow and ice respond rapidly to every fraction of a degree of warming,” said Kirkham. “But most of these systems will take centuries or millennia to recover after overshoot, especially if tipping points are crossed that cause changes to become essentially irreversible.”

Last month, a UNEP report found the world must cut emissions by 18% by 2030 and by 45% by 2035 to have a good chance of keeping temperatures from rising 1.7C above preindustrial levels. It found there were “no good outcomes” of remaining above 1.5C.

The cryosphere report found that current policies, which will result in 2.8C of global heating, would reduce the mass of glacier ice to below 10% in the Rockies, Alps, Iceland and Scandinavia. If warming was limited to 1.5C, about 20-35% of the mass would remain.

In the Hindu Kush Himalayas, where glaciers are a source of water for nearly a quarter of humanity, current policies will leave just 41% of the ice mass. If warming was limited to 1.5C, 83% would remain.

Bill Hare, a climate scientist and the CEO of Climate Analytics, a policy institute, who was not involved in the report, said: “Ice sheets melting six times faster than 30 years ago, sea ice and mountain glaciers disappearing at record speed, sea levels inexorably rising, the life-giving polar oceans acidifying: all irreversible now on human timescales, all laden with worldwide consequences, and all taking climate impacts past limits of adaptability.”

He added: “Every government minister and every fossil fuel executive who’s ever succeeded in watering down climate action can look at this report and see how their actions have fundamentally damaged the world we live in.”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Very good boys? The dark, dystopian rise of robot dogs | Arwa Mahwadi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Pups that carry your shopping are one thing – but what about the mechanical canines being bought up in the US by ICE? Or the mutant mutts due to be developed by a startup called Warhound?

H
ave you ever wanted to hang out with a dog with no fur, no face and a chip in its shoulder? If so, I suggest you head to San Francisco, where a startup called Dimensional has been paying people $20 (£15) an hour to walk four-legged robot dogs. This isn’t because the dogs need the exercise – it is because the company needs the training data. As reported in the New York Times, the goal is to develop “operating systems that can integrate with AI agents so the machines can act more independently”.

What exactly will these machines do when they can act more independently? The founder of Dimensional insists they will help people. They might carry groceries home, for example, which is certainly something my tiny chihuahua-mix is incapable of.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

While it is nice to think that robo dogs are all going to be very good boys, there is a darker side to the industry. A couple of months ago it was reported that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) planned to spend up to $2m (£1.5m) on robot dogs made by the company Boston Dynamics. ICE has said the dogs won’t be used for anything nefarious but, considering everything the agency has been up to lately, this isn’t particularly reassuring.

Look, you might say, while this is all very dystopian, these things aren’t really dogs. They’re just canine-shaped robots. At least we’re not seeing the rise of real dogs with AI-powered armour. Alas, that’s just around the corner. Last month a startup called Warhound launched with the aim of creating genetically modified dogs equipped with “advanced cybernetic augments, software and battlefield situational awareness”. What does that mean in plain English? Details about Warhound are sparse, but I’m pretty sure it likely means mutant dogs that kill people.

I base that assumption, by the way, on the people behind Warhound. One is bioscience entrepreneur Ben Lamm, who made headlines for trying to bring the dodo back from extinction. The other is Palmer Luckey, a mullet-loving, seemingly-war-obsessed billionaire who founded weapons company Anduril. “Societies have always needed a warrior class that is enthused and excited about enacting violence on others in pursuit of good aims,” Luckey said in 2024. “You need people like me who are sick in that way and who don’t lose any sleep making tools of violence in order to preserve freedom.” I’m not sure about that, Mr Luckey. I for one would sleep a lot better if we left dogs alone and put billionaires on a tight leash.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The next global pandemic could be brewing on a mink farm in Utah – and little is being done to stop it | George Monbiot
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: George Monbiot
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Mink farms are the perfect petri dishes for deadly flu strains to emerge. Yet officials appear to be protecting business interests over human lives

C
ould this be ground zero? Could it be the spot where the next pandemic begins? It’s certainly a candidate, not least because the chain of events that could trigger a plague far worse than Covid-19 looks like the opening sequence of a disaster movie. A really bad disaster movie, in which the levels of carelessness and turpitude defy belief.

A report by the investigative news service ProPublica reveals that bird flu has been raging in a mink farm in Utah since August, and it appears next to nothing has been done by public officials. In 2023, I warned in the Guardian that mink farms could scarcely be better designed to generate lethal plagues. This is for three reasons: mink are fed on the offcuts of chickens, cows and other farm animals, in which new viral variants often develop; mink readily host both avian and human flu viruses, which can then exchange genetic material, turning a bird disease into a human one; and mink possess extremely high “zoonotic potential” – the ability to infect animals of other species, including human beings.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

I pointed out that bird flus that jump into the human population can be extremely dangerous: of those known to have contracted the H5N1 variant since 1997, 48% have died. The first death in the US from avian flu this year has just been announced: the victim caught it from an infected dairy herd. While it is devastating to wild bird populations and some mammals, fortunately its transmissibility between humans is so far extremely low. If the perfect mixing vessel of a mink farm were to generate a variant that was both highly lethal and more transmissible, you would do well to get on with writing your will. Both for this reason and because of the pointless cruelty of the fur business, I called for a global treaty to ban mink farming.

I didn’t expect governments to leap into action, however compelling the case might have been. But nor did I expect them to act as if their aim were to assist a deadly virus. This is how officials in the US appear to have behaved.

ProPublica discovered that, instead of trying to contain the virus by shutting down the farm and slaughtering the mink, Utah departments have sought to contain the story. Public health officials have failed to test workers on the farm for symptoms, or track their contacts, despite the fact that they’re in touch with the infected mink every day, and are often bitten or scratched. Why? Because of complaints from the state agriculture department that “farmers were annoyed” by testing.

Utah’s state veterinarian, Amanda Price, said that the outbreak was “devastating”. But she wasn’t talking about public health. She was talking about the effect on the farmer. “This is his life’s work that he’s seeing be destroyed. I really hope that you understand the humanity behind this situation.” Yes, we do: 8 billion people could be at risk if something isn’t done. Culling the mink could kill the farmer’s business, and he should be compensated for it. Not culling could kill much more than that. Could there be a clearer case of giving the impression of putting special interests above the general interest?

She also remarked: “There’s just not a lot of options out there other than kind of sitting and waiting and seeing what happens … If we started seeing people actively dying from this, obviously that would change how we respond to this.” By which time it would be too late.

The primary effort appears to have been to protect the farm’s interests. The state has not declared an emergency because, officials reason, that might “alert animal rights groups”. It might also alert public health groups, or anyone who cares about human life. Now we’re into flu season. The longer it goes on, the greater the chances that a highly transmissible variant will develop in the mink farm.

These people make the scientists in the first episode of Pluribus look like responsible citizens. The officials here are not following the signals sent by extraterrestrials. Instead, they appear to be following the signals sent by commercial interests. If there’s one thing we’ve learned from the influence of the tobacco and sugar industries, it’s that corporate lobbyists should have nothing to do with public health decisions. Yet they are embedded in every form of decision-making. This, regardless of the issue that strikes the killer blow, could be our downfall.

While mink farms are especially dangerous, all forms of livestock farming present a high risk of generating and propagating pandemics. Indeed, it’s the combination of mink farming with chicken, pig and dairy farming that creates such a high potential for disaster. The edible livestock industries can be seen as disease amplifiers, creating the conditions in which a low-pathogenic strain can easily mutate into a more pathogenic variety. Feed the animals’ innards to mink, to mix this virus with human flu, and off we go.

Here, too, the level of neglect seems psychopathic. The US “health” secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, has argued that chicken farmers “should consider maybe the possibility of letting [bird flu] run through the flock so that we can identify the birds, and preserve the birds, that are immune to it”. The US agriculture secretary voiced support for the idea. Not only would this be phenomenally dangerous; it would also be fruitless, as genetic variation has been reduced to an absolute minimum, to produce almost identical chickens. It’s similar to the “let the virus rip” attitudes of the Donald Trump and Boris Johnson governments during the first wave of Covid-19. Kennedy has also claimed that the H5N1 variant “doesn’t appear to hurt wild birds – they have some kind of immunity”. This is completely false.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Though we are more alert than we once were to the machinations of the tobacco, sugar, alcohol, junk food, gambling and fossil fuel industries, most people remain unaware of the levels of threat posed by the livestock industry. It’s not only among the greatest causes of greenhouse gas emissions, habitat destruction, wildlife depletion and extinction, and river and marine pollution. But it is also the greatest risk factor in the development of new pandemics, both directly and through its transformation of ecosystems into farmland. It might also now be the leading cause of the spread of antimicrobial resistance. All from the folks who brought you meat, eggs and milk.

We’ve often been warned that the things we should fear most are those we’re not thinking about. It’s time we started thinking about this.

George Monbiot is a Guardian columnist
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.summary: A report by ProPublica reveals that bird flu has been raging in a mink farm in Utah since August. It appears next to nothing has been done by public officials. The primary effort appears to have been to protect the farm’s interests.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: As cancer treatments become more effective, we must ask: what is life like for the people who receive them? | Ranjana Srivastava
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Ranjana Srivastava
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Many treatments are now extending lives but the measure of progress should not end with a scan or a survival curve

T
wo decades ago, a dear friend called me in a trembling voice. Was there hope for his young nephew, whose cancer had spread to the brain? Sadly, “no”, I said. But today, for such patients, there are options that were unimaginable back then.

Recently, researchers at the European Society For Medical Oncology presented the latest chapter results from a randomised controlled trial of a bespoke cancer vaccine for patients with high-risk melanoma. The trial involved 1,137 patients whose melanoma had been surgically removed but remained at high recurrence risk. They received either pembrolizumab, an established immunotherapy, or pembrolizumab combined with an experimental mRNA vaccine, designed to help the immune system recognise and attack targets unique to the patient’s tumour.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

At two years, 82.2% of those who received the combination were alive without their cancer returning, compared with 70% of those given pembrolizumab alone – a difference of about 12 percentage points. The combination also reduced the relative risk of distant metastasis or death by 38%.

These results raise the prospect that personalised vaccines could become an important addition to cancer treatment. Whether they will deliver similar benefits in other cancers remains to be established.

Overall survival data are not yet mature, so we don’t know whether the combination helps people live longer. Fever, injection-site pain and fatigue were common with the vaccine combination. Rates of severe treatment-related adverse events were similar between the groups; quality-of-life data is not yet available.

The standing ovation for the researchers was deserved, as was praise for the pharmaceutical companies that backed an idea that was once a pipe dream. Yet as cancer treatments become more effective, another question gains importance: what is life like for the people who receive them?

Treatment can delay a cancer’s return but can impose a considerable burden. Side-effects, fatigue, impaired mobility, psychological trauma, financial strain and the disruption of family and career all shape the experience.

In my work, I am often sobered by the juxtaposition of scans showing no cancer with a patient who cannot sleep, work or enjoy what others take for granted.

Recently, a retired academic approaching 90 told me: “My dear, the best thing you could do for me is get me safely home.” For this patient, their priority was clear; pursuing intervention would have caused a serious decline in their quality of life.

That does not mean some people should automatically be offered less treatment, or that the value of treatment depends on age alone. But it does mean oncologists must understand what each person hopes treatment will achieve, and explain what they may have to endure to get there.

My experience with elderly patients has made me more conscious of my other patients who are mid-career, raising children or caring for relatives.

The parent whose persistent nausea makes school drop-offs impossible.

The hairdresser who can’t work due to neuropathy.

The executive dismayed by cognitive fog.

A treatment that offers a cure or extra months of survival may be worthwhile to one person, even with significant toxicity. Others may place greater value on earning an income, caring for a child or living independently. These are not competing definitions of success: they are individual priorities that good medicine should respect.

Yet quality of life is often reported less rigorously than response, recurrence and survival. Less than a third of trials report quality-of-life measures in the primary publication, which most professionals read, and just half publish them at all.

Patient-centred care demands that information about quality of life should appear alongside the main findings, not years later in a separate publication, or not at all. When patients ask, “Doctor, how will this treatment affect my life?”, the information gap can become an indirect permission for oncologists to skim over the granular details.

A recent paper in The Lancet Oncology urges better reporting of health-related quality of life in trials of adjuvant treatments (treatments given after surgery to reduce the risk of recurrence). The researchers argue that average scores conceal important differences between patients: trials should instead report how many people experience a clinically meaningful deterioration, how long it lasts, and whether and when they recover.

Collecting quality-of-life data is not simple but, when data is missing, we should know why. Questionnaires are burdensome for sick patients and doctors have a different notion of quality of life from their patients. Of course, for a patient facing a life-threatening diagnosis, a chance at cure may reasonably outweigh significant toxicity concerns, but imperfect measurement is a reason to improve the status quo, not to look away.

From where I sit, I see immense gratitude for modern therapies but not inconsiderable decisional regret: “If only I had known.” We should empower patients to ask and be ready to tell them not only how likely a treatment is to work but also what it may cost them in daily life. Far too often, they find out later that treatment can bring months, years or even a lifetime of adverse effects.

None of this downplays scientific progress. Many treatments are now extending lives and personalised medicine may bring further gains. But the measure of progress should not end with a scan or a survival curve. Researchers must collect quality of life outcomes diligently, clinicians should discuss them openly and health systems should treat them as central, not optional, to care.

While writing this column, my thoughts returned to the young man and his family, whose happiness for today’s melanoma patients is tinged with regret for their own loss. Today’s advance stands on the shoulders of the patients who generously volunteered to a take part in a study not knowing if they would themselves benefit. They deserve our gratitude.

Our ambition should be not only to keep people alive but to protect the lives they want to live, and to recognise that the true cost of treatment is measured in more than money.

Ranjana Srivastava is an Australian oncologist, award-winning author and Fulbright scholar. Her latest book is Every Word Matters: Writing to Engage the Public

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: From gold rush to cosmic questions: a South Dakota mine and the search for the secrets of the universe
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Ian Sample Science editor
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
A mile beneath the Black Hills, scientists are building giant detectors to analyse neutrino particles – and possibly find the answer to existence

F
or more than a century, the mining town of Lead, in the Black Hills of South Dakota, attracted workers with a taste for gold. Now, a flagship experiment being built in the old mine is drawing scientists in search of more intriguing riches: answers to the deepest mysteries of the universe.

Construction of the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (Dune) in the former Homestake mine is due to start on Monday. Engineers will begin assembling four giant detectors inside caverns blasted from rock a mile underground.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Once switched on, the detectors will quietly spark and flicker as ghostly particles called neutrinos hurtle through them. Some will arrive from the sun and distant supernovae, others in an intense beam sent through 800 miles (1,300km) of rock from a government laboratory near Chicago, Illinois.

Observing the neutrinos could uncover entirely new science and shed light on cosmic spectacles, such as the death of stars and the birth of black holes. Scientists are particularly hopeful of solving one of the most enduring puzzles in nature: why everything around us is made from matter and not its “evil twin”, antimatter. In other words, why we, and why anything, is here at all.

“It’s a super exciting time to be working on this,” said Dr Kate Shaw, an experimental particle physicist on Dune from the University of Sussex. “Neutrinos do not make sense yet and they could open a door to new physics.”

Neutrinos are the most abundant matter particles in the universe, outnumbered only by photons, the massless particles of light that illuminate the universe. They are produced in natural nuclear reactions, such as those that power the sun, in radioactive decay and in particle accelerators.

Even by physicists’ standards, neutrinos are oddballs. The chargeless particles barely interact with other matter: about a trillion pass unnoticed through your body each second. Neutrinos come in three varieties, all with minuscule but different masses. Weirdly, they change from one variety to another, a process called oscillation, as they travel. “It’s a very strange behaviour,” said Shaw. “It’s like me throwing you an apple and it turns into a banana.”

Lead has a history with these peculiar particles. In the 1960s, the physicist Ray Davis followed miners down the shaft and built a detector from a 100,000-gallon tank filled with dry-cleaning fluid. Shielded so deep beneath the ground, the detector became the first to record neutrinos from the sun as they struck chlorine atoms in the fluid and turned them into argon.

The mine closed in 2001 and transitioned, thanks to visionary forethought, into a dedicated subterranean laboratory, the Sanford Underground Research Facility (Surf). It is already home to the Lux-Zeplin (LZ) experiment which last month reported the first potential detection of dark matter.

“We’ve gone from mining the Earth to helping scientists explore the universe,” said Robin Lucero, Lead’s city administrator, whose family has lived locally for generations. “We’re incredibly proud and lucky that Dune is happening here, and Surf, which has other experiments like LZ. Having world-class science brings new opportunities, new people and new possibilities for our local businesses and especially our young people.”

Unlike Davis’s apparatus, the Dune experiment is enormous. Made from more than 4,000 tonnes of steel, the detectors will stand up to five-storeys high and hold a combined 70,000 tonnes of liquid argon that must be chilled to -200C. Assembling the detectors should take nearly three years. Filling them with liquid argon, another year.

“This is a heavy duty engineering operation,” and a partnership with the skilled local workforce, said Prof David Newbold, of the UK’s Science and Technology Facilities Council and a Dune spokesperson. “It’s like building a ship underground.” The UK is the largest international partner in the US-led experiment and is making core detector components, critical computing to reconstruct events in the detectors, and the graphite target needed to generate neutrinos at Femilab, a particle physics facility in Illinois.

Once operational, Dune will study an intense beam of neutrinos sent from Fermilab through 800 miles of the Earth’s crust and mantle. Most neutrinos will shoot straight through, but every so often one will strike an argon atom, creating a flicker of light and a pulse of electric charge. Analysing these will reveal intimate details about the mysterious particles.

One big question surrounds the masses of different neutrinos. Which is lightest and which heaviest? The answer could reveal fundamental new forces of nature. And in an attempt to answer the matter v antimatter question, Dune will look for subtle differences between neutrinos and their antimatter twins, antineutrinos.

Beyond the beams of particles sent from Fermilab, Dune will also study neutrinos arriving from space, carrying with them fresh information on stellar explosions and the formation of black holes.

Earlier this month, the Nobel prize for physics honoured the Belgian researcher Francis Halzen, who used a cubic kilometre of Antarctica to detect high-energy neutrinos from deep space. But detection is far from the end of the story. “This really is going to be a golden era,” Newbold said. “There’s a lot more of that to come.”
