Not signed in before? Create an account

Begum, 40, is preparing to lower the potatoes into a khraw, a traditional underground storage pit lined with straw and sealed against the cold. For generations, khraws have kept potatoes, turnips and cabbages through Himalayan winters, when heavy snowfall cuts villages off from the Kashmir valley and temperatures fall below -20C (-4F) – cold enough to crack pipes and freeze diesel.

But the practice is slowly dying out. As roads have improved and young people have left for work and education, fewer families maintain the pits. Their decline threatens not only a traditional way of storing food but also the local potato varieties themselves and the knowledge of which ones store well, resist rot and produce reliable harvests.

“When I was young, almost every family had three or four pits,” Begum says. “Now, down in the main valley, they have abandoned the practice altogether. Only a handful of families still use them. The rest buy from the market or subsidised ones from the government.”

Begum learned from her mother how to tell potatoes that store well from those that rot or sprout too quickly. She is passing this on to her daughter, but is unsure whether the skill will survive into another generation.

Gurez is a high-altitude Himalayan valley perched near the Line of Control, the heavily militarised boundary separating Indian- and Pakistani-administered Kashmir. About 80 miles (125km) from Srinagar, the valley remains cut off each winter when snow closes Razdan pass, its main road link, which sits at roughly 3,600 metres.

It is home to the Dard-Shin people, an Indigenous community who speak Shina and have a culture that is distinct from Kashmiri, with community links across the border in Gilgit-Baltistan, administered by Pakistan.

Potatoes account for about 45% of Gurez’s cultivated area, according to a 2019 study by the Indian Council of Agricultural Research’s National Bureau of Plant Genetic Resources (ICAR-NBPGR), a government body that studies and conserves India’s crop diversity. Yet the genetic diversity of the valley’s potatoes has not been systematically documented.

Dr Sheikh M Sultan, a senior scientist based at ICAR-NBPGR’s Srinagar station, surveyed the valley and later struggled to find some of the varieties he had once encountered. “When I first visited, I saw many varieties,” he says. “Later, I could hardly locate even one sample of some. The loss of genetic diversity is tremendous.”

Sultan says migration, improved roads and changing lifestyles have contributed to the decline. As traditional farming disappears, so does knowledge about selecting, cultivating and preserving local varieties.

“When people stop producing their own seeds and start relying entirely on commercial varieties, the loss can be irreparable,” he says.

He warns that research institutions often prioritise introduced varieties over indigenous crops whose characteristics remain poorly understood. “Our indigenous varieties may possess valuable characteristics, including tolerance to cold and resistance to certain pests and diseases,” he says.

“These are resources we should be studying and improving, rather than neglecting.”

Climate breakdown is adding to the pressures on farmers across the Himalayas. People in Gurez report drier springs, reduced snowfall and water shortages, which they say have affected potato production.

Abdul Jabbar Mapnoo, 70, a farmer in Chorwan, remembers winters when deep snow covered the valley. “Every house used to have two or three khraw, each holding about five quintals – 500kg – of potatoes,” he says. “The springs are drying up, and there is less snow in winter. Potato production has fallen. I remember winters when six feet of snow would cover the valley in January or February.”

As farming becomes more difficult and markets easier to access, households have less incentive to grow their own potatoes. Varieties adapted to local conditions over generations could disappear from cultivation before researchers establish what makes them distinctive.

Dr Parveen Kumar, a scientist at the Sher-e-Kashmir University of Agricultural Sciences and Technology of Kashmir, says locally adapted varieties should not be overlooked. “Climate change is a reality, and farmers need to be aware of adaptation strategies,” he says.

Pressure on farmland poses another risk. In Gurez, where cultivable land is scarce, the Kishanganga hydroelectric project has affected land in the valley through acquisition and submergence. Among the areas affected is Badwan, a village known for its potatoes.

One potential route for preserving the varieties could be through using geographical indications – a designation granted by the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization, and is similar to the French appellation d’origine contrôlée. It can be used on goods that have a specific origin and possess qualities or a reputation linked to this – which can help increase the market value and give them greater recognition. This, and the globally important agricultural heritage systems programme have helped areas such as the saffron-growing landscape of Pampore in Kashmir.

However, recognition alone will not preserve the varieties. They must be identified and documented before they disappear from cultivation, along with farmers’ knowledge of how to select, store and replant them.

In Chorwan, Begum unloads the last sack of potatoes into the pit and covers it, ready for another winter. Some will feed her family; the rest will be replanted in spring. Knowing which potatoes to eat and which to save as seed relies on knowledge passed down through generations.

If these varieties are not documented while they are still being cultivated, Kashmir may lose a living agricultural treasure trove before scientists can fully understand what it contains.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: ‘Bunch of baloney’: calls grow for Cop summit reforms as countries on track to fail nature targets
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Patrick Greenfield
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Cop17, focused on protecting nature and restoring ecosystems, concludes on Saturday with critics saying system allows ‘one idiot’ to stall progress

Calls are growing for major reforms to UN biodiversity summits as countries fail to deliver on their promises to halt the destruction of the natural world, with governments likely on track to continue their record of never having met a target in the 34-year history of the convention.

Two weeks of negotiations at biodiversity Cop17 in Yerevan, Armenia, concluded on Saturday morning with countries vowing to redouble their efforts to meet this decade’s targets, which include commitments to protect 30% of the planet for nature, restore nearly a third of Earth’s degraded ecosystems and reform $500bn (£410bn) of environmentally damaging subsidies.

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Agreed just four years ago by nearly every government on the planet, they aim to transform humanity’s relationship with nature. Despite progress in some areas, governments are way off track on meeting almost all of the targets. The UK is set to meet just three of the 23.

After talks that ran overnight from Friday into Saturday morning, countries signed off several measures, including a commitment to ramp up action on meeting existing targets and reaffirming a goal to increase biodiversity finance to $30bn a year by the end of the decade.

During the conference, environment ministers, activists and officials appealed for significant changes to the way the summits function to ensure governments follow through with meaningful action on the drivers of biodiversity loss.

Panama’s environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, a veteran conservationist, said the Cop process had been “designed to fail”, arguing that decisions should be taken by a majority as the consensus-based process allows “one idiot” to prevent agreement.

“A lot of what’s going on out here at the Cop is just a bunch of baloney and beautiful speeches and BS,” he told AFP earlier this week. “We cannot have – we cannot expect – a consensus between every nation on Earth on every topic. That’s ridiculous. Cops have been designed to fail, and they are not disappointing.”

He also argued that the UN should host a single environmental Cop each year to tackle the climate, biodiversity, plastics and other issues in one go.

“This just makes my blood boil, because while we fiddle, Rome burns,” he said.

The negotiations in the Armenian capital have seen Argentina, Saudi Arabia and Russia water down language on environmental ambition in the final agreement, while wealthier governments were divided on who would contribute more financial resources.

European nations would like to see additions to the list of donor states, as China and several of the Gulf states are still classified as developing countries in the UN process despite decades of rapid economic development. The final agreement in Yerevan left this issue open.

Key decisions on a fund to mobilise resources from firms that make money from digital forms of biodiversity, such as pharmaceutical companies, were postponed to the next summit in Ecuador in two years’ time. It had been hoped that the fund would generate £1bn a year for nature conservation, with a significant share going to Indigenous communities, but it has so far raised just over $10,000.

The calls for changes to the biodiversity Cop process echo an intervention by leading policy experts during climate Cop29 in Azerbaijan in 2024 who said the summit was “no longer fit for purpose” and needed to shift to focus on implementation.

Ruth Davis, the UK’s nature envoy, said she recognised that the meetings could be “extremely frustratiing”, but a huge amount of implementation was happening around the world.

“We’ve got to make the system actually deliver outcomes for people, otherwise they’ll lose confidence in it,” she said. “In the end, this is a process that is owned by governments who are parties to it. But I know we are going to find friends and allies in making the process work for the citizens of countries for whom this is really important, not least because they are the ones facing the impacts.”

Efforts to reform the UN’s sprawling environmental agenda are already under way. Inger Andersen, the executive director of the UN environment programme, said that the current systems were driving change, but they were moving too slowly.

“Right now, the environmental agenda is very cluttered. There are lots of meetings, important as each one is. Let’s begin with the easy stuff, like programmatic overlap between conventions, which has an energy-sapping effect,” said Andersen. “We identified the illegal wildlife trade back in the 70s as a problem, then we identified migratory species, then broader biodiversity, then wetlands.

“Each of these conventions came along at the right time, but we now have a plethora of them. Maybe we should think about that.”

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Twice as many plants and animals sold in wildlife trade as previously thought, says report
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Rebecca Ratcliffe
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
More than 100,000 species are traded globally, whether illegally smuggled, sold as ornaments or in fisheries, timber and fashion industries, study finds

The number of plant and animal species in use or sold in the wildlife trade is more than twice as high as previously thought, researchers have discovered.

A study, published in Science Advances, warns that there are huge gaps in global assessments of how wildlife is traded, and that past estimates have failed to keep up with changes such as the boom in the online exotic pet trade, where sellers offering to post spider eggs across the world or sneak reptiles on to planes are just a click away.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

“The dimensions of trade have changed. Without monitoring it in a representative way, we cannot manage it,” said Alice Hughes, a professor at the University of Melbourne and lead author of the study. “At the moment, we are completely underestimating what modern trade looks like – for the pet trade and for the ornamental trade, we are not capturing it. And it poses a major risk to species.”

The study comes as the US-based nonprofit, the Center for Biological Diversity, filed a petition asking the US Fish and Wildlife Service to list the Javan slit-faced bat under the Endangered Species Act, warning that consumers are buying the bat for decor, placing it at risk of extinction. Taxidermy bats are sought after, particularly by US consumers, who are looking for gothic or spooky decorations for Halloween or Christmas gifts, the centre said.

The wildlife trade study identified 107,356 species that are either in use or traded globally – far higher than a previous estimate of about 50,000, which was made by the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES).

The study draws on more comprehensive datasets, as well as newer research papers that have tracked species sold online for decoration. It shows flaws in our understanding of what species are at risk; for example, the number of butterfly species found to be traded is greater than the IPBES’ entire estimate for all traded terrestrial invertebrates.

Molly Brown, programme officer for wildlife use and trade at the International Union for Conservation of Nature and a co-author of the paper, said the findings were a reality check. “The number of species that we are talking about is still an underestimate, and that’s really clear in the paper, because we cannot access and we do not have the type of monitoring data that we really need,” she said.

Discussions about the wildlife trade often focus on criminal activities, such as illegal smuggling of ivory or pangolin scales. However, the wildlife trade encompasses sectors such as fisheries and the timber trade as well as fashion and the sale of species as ornaments. This includes activities that may be sustainable, as well as trade that is driving species to extinction.

Even assessing the value of the legal trade compared with the illegal trade is challenging. The under-regulation of wildlife trade has created loopholes that allow species, including sought-after exotic pets, to be “laundered into legality”, researchers said.

Four years ago, nearly 200 countries agreed to ensure that trade of wild species was “sustainable, safe and legal”, as part of a landmark set of targets aimed at ending the destruction of nature. Efforts to meet these targets are hampered by a lack of data about what is being sold and where it originated.

The main data point for measuring progress on a globally agreed wildlife trade target refers only to fish stocks, which would account for at most 3% of all traded species, said Hughes.

Experts say there needs to be more systematic data collection and sharing. Globally, fisheries are monitored by the UN Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, while the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (Cites) monitors and regulates international trade in about 40,000 species to protect them from over exploitation.

However, researchers said that this excludes large numbers of potentially vulnerable species, warning the Cites system is too slow moving to keep up with new trends in threats to wildlife. Most countries lack any systematic data outside Cites, the study says. “Sometimes, it is years before things get listed and that means that they can be virtually extinct in the wild by that point,” said Hughes.

Species that are newly described are often rare and have a small range, meaning they are especially valuable to trade, and can be quickly wiped out.

Chris Shepherd, a conservation advocate at the Centre for Biological Diversity, who was not involved in the study, added that he had observed the wildlife trade for decades and that new species were continually appearing.

“The demand for wildlife, especially live wildlife traded for pets, is growing fast, as is the number of species involved,” he said. “This trade is pushing an ever-growing list of species towards extinction, and as such, putting in place mechanisms to better monitor this trade are essential.”
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.summary: Study finds number of plant and animal species in use or sold in wildlife trade is more than twice as high as previously thought. Study warns that there are huge gaps in global assessments of how wildlife is traded. Past estimates have failed to keep up with changes such as the boom in the online pet trade.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: ‘No one cares about the little guy’: plastic nurdles still washing ashore in Sri Lanka five years after toxic spill
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Vandy Widyalankara in Pamunugama, Sri Lanka
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
A stricken container ship shed tonnes of the tiny pellets on the west coast in May 2021. Today, locals are counting the cost to marine life and livelihoods

O
n the beach in Pamunugama, on Sri Lanka’s west coast, women in uniform work under the scorching sun. They sift through rubbish washed ashore, searching among the usual litter for something much smaller: tiny plastic pellets.

Five years ago, in May 2021, this same beach was swamped with pellets as smoke rose over the Indian Ocean.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

In May 2021, after the MV X-Press Pearl caught fire 10 miles off this stretch of coast. The Singapore-flagged container ship was carrying 1,486 containers, including tonnes of hazardous materials such as nitric acid. As the blaze intensified, containers fell overboard and billions of pellets known as nurdles, which are used to make most plastic items, spilled into the sea before the vessel sank.

In the weeks that followed, hundreds of dead marine animals washed ashore, including more than 100 turtles and dozens of dolphins.

“The coconut trees turned black and died. Baby coconuts started falling. We know by experience that this is not normal and was a result of the disaster,” says Roger Peiris, who was working for the YMCA at the time and went on to advocate for fishers and other affected communities to have a greater role in the recovery efforts.

Five years later, nurdles are still washing ashore.

Jude Sulanta, a local fisher, says the problem gets worse during the monsoon season: “The nurdles come to the shore with the strong wind, when the sea is rough. When the sea is calm, they are stuck on the ocean floor.”

Damaged fishing grounds have made livelihoods increasingly difficult to sustain, say many of the fishers. And they are still waiting for compensation.

Those losses sit at the centre of a sprawling legal battle over responsibility. In July 2025, Sri Lanka’s supreme court issued a ruling ordering the companies behind the X-Press Pearl to pay an initial $1bn, with further compensation to be determined. The court also found serious failures by several Sri Lankan state authorities and ordered a fresh investigation into allegations of corruption surrounding efforts to assess and recover compensation.

More than a year later, almost all of the court-ordered sum remains unpaid. The vessel’s owner, X-Press Feeders, and insurer, London P&I, have disputed the ruling and its approach to maritime liability, while talks with the Sri Lankan government continue. A separate compensation case brought by Sri Lanka in Singapore remains active but is on hold pending related proceedings in London.

Although interim compensation was paid for income lost during the post-disaster temporary fishing ban, fishers say the way claimants were classified excluded many of the people affected.

“A lot of genuine fishers missed getting compensation,” says Sulanta.

Several fishers argued that larger operators and well-resourced parts of the industry were better placed to lobby officials, while small-scale fishers lacked the documentation, time or connections to make claims.

“The bigger boats and dry fish industry have better and more influential representation with the authorities,” says Anthony Nishantha, a local fisher who helped lawyers pursuing damages for the disaster. “Us smaller fishers don’t have the same lobbying power.”

An initial assessment by the government-appointed expert panel put the disaster’s environmental damage at $6.4bn (£4.8bn).

“The initial impacts included the direct effects on fishing caused by debris and parts of the damaged ship,” says Prof Prasanthi Gunawardena, an environmental economist and co-chair of the panel. “But based on research from elsewhere, we predicted that there would also be longer-term fishing losses.”

Fishers describe continued damage to fishing nets.

“When the fishing net is cast on the rocks, it pulls something like cotton wool,” Nishantha says. “This started happening with the disaster.”

They suspect contaminants from the spill are responsible, although the cause has not been independently established.

They also describe changes in rocky reefs where fish have traditionally gathered and bred. Knowledge of these grounds has been passed down through generations, allowing fishers to identify fishing areas without GPS technology.

“We are generational fishers,” says Ranga Fernando. “My father showed me where different types of fish gather.”

But, he explains, inherited knowledge has become less reliable since the disaster, as familiar patterns have changed. Nishantha points to Thambugala, a well-known fishing area close to where the vessel went down, where he says fish still gather but no longer appear to breed in the same numbers.

“Even just a few weeks ago, two or three turtles washed up on the shore,” he says. “That is usually very rare, but we are seeing these things more.”

Fishers say the impact on the lagoon in Negombo, which opens into the sea, has received less attention. Jude Anthony, who farms fish there, says nurdles and other pollution inundated his pens after the disaster, killing stock he had spent months raising.

“Everyone is talking about the fish that were destroyed on that day,” he says. “But even now we cannot fish properly.”

The fishers acknowledge that wider pollution from urban development was already affecting the industry. But they believe the X-Press Pearl disaster compounded existing problems. Combined with rising living costs, these pressures have made fishing increasingly difficult to sustain, pushing locals to sell their boats or seek work abroad.

“There are fewer people in the village. They went overseas to support their families,” Sulanta says.

The Centre for Environmental Justice (CEJ), which helped bring the supreme court case, says it is continuing to pursue enforcement of the $1bn ruling. So far, only about $1m has been paid.

“We are in the process of challenging the non-enforcement of the court order, nationally and internationally,” says Hemantha Withanage, co-founder and chair of the CEJ. “This is how corporations discriminate against less powerful developing countries.”

Five years of meetings, claims and uncertainty have left many fishers increasingly disillusioned, while the daily need to earn a living makes the pursuit of justice a luxury they cannot afford.

“No one cares about the little guy,” says Anthony. “We are not educated. We don’t know where to go to speak about these issues, so we are not taken care of. We can’t speak directly with the people at the top, so what more can we do?”

In the end, he says, fishers are left with little choice but to carry on: “We mind our own business, and we work and we live.”

A spokesperson for X-Press Feeders says: “We know and acknowledge that the sinking of the X-Press Pearl had an impact on the environment of Sri Lanka but cannot assume that all nurdles collected today must be originating from the X-Press Pearl incident, not least given there have been other substantial nurdle spills in Sri Lankan waters.”

They add: “We respectfully disagree with the ruling of Sri Lanka’s supreme court and could not make payment because the ruling relied wholly on assessments by Sri Lanka’s Marine Environment Protection Authority that international experts have since discredited. The supreme court also did not consider the ongoing compensation proceedings in Singapore initiated by the Sri Lankan government itself.”

The Sri Lankan government and London P&I did not respond to requests for comment.
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.summary: The Centre for Environmental Justice is continuing to pursue enforcement of the $1bn ruling. So far, only about $1m has been paid.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Warming UK seas could ‘fundamentally reshape marine ecosystems’ – report
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Karen McVeigh
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Four-year study warns destabilised marine food webs could jeopardise food security by 2050

Warming seas around the UK and the wider north-east Atlantic could destabilise marine food webs, weaken ocean health and jeopardise food security by 2050, according to a four-year study.

Scientists who projected the impact of climate breakdown on four key groups of marine life crucial to maintaining ocean ecosystems in the region said their results challenged assumptions that in middle latitudes, such as the UK, marine biodiversity was likely to increase across the board.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Instead, their projections highlight a predator-prey imbalance that could “fundamentally reshape marine ecosystems” in unforeseen ways, they said.

The seas around the British and Irish Isles, particularly the southern North Sea, have been identified as “marine climate hotspots”, one of 20 globally to have warmed the fastest over 50 years.

The new predictions, under a scenario of 3C (5.4F) of warming by 2100, found that while fish and seabed invertebrates may become more diverse by mid-century, key plankton groups lower in the food chain were likely to decline. This imbalance, the authors of the report said, could disrupt marine food webs and weaken the health and resilience of ocean ecosystems.

“What surprised us is that warming doesn’t increase or decrease biodiversity across the board,” said Elena Couce, a marine ecologist at the Centre for Environment, Fisheries and Aquaculture Science (Cefas), a British government agency, and co-lead author of the study.

“While some groups higher up the food chain, like fish, may gain species in parts of the north-east Atlantic, key plankton groups that underpin marine ecosystems are projected to lose species,” she said.

The research, led by Cefas and published in Science Advances, involved an international team of researchers from the University of East Anglia, the Marine Biological Association, UiT the Arctic University of Norway, the Royal Netherlands Institute for Sea Research and the Technical University of Denmark.

“When things get hotter, all the species from the equator are going to move north and south,” Cource said. “The UK is in the middle latitudes. So we expected diversity to go up, because you get species from the south that are more diverse than the species you lose to the north.”

Previous Cefas research looking at key fish species suggested warming in north-western European waters would result in climate “winners”, such as anchovies, seabass and sardines. Such conditions, however, are less suitable for climate “losers”, including Atlantic cod, haddock and coley.

The current study, focusing on ecosystems in UK waters and the wider north-east Atlantic including Ireland and France, found that by mid-century, fish and seabed invertebrate diversity could increase by about 12%, whereas phytoplankton and zooplankton diversity could decline by about 3% and 7%, respectively by 2050.

“If predator diversity rises while prey diversity falls, that has the potential to disrupt the food chain,” said Lily Greig, a marine ecologist at Cefas who also co-led the study. “Our results show that climate change could reshuffle marine biodiversity unevenly across the food web, and that gains in some groups do not necessarily mean the ecosystem as a whole is becoming more resilient.”

By identifying where biodiversity was changing fastest and which parts of the ecosystem were most at risk, the study could provide an “early warning system” of potential ecosystem change, the researchers said. The work has already been submitted to the government’s review of marine protected areas, which is looking at fishery management measures.

“Policymakers have a mandate to try to preserve or even increase biodiversity,” said Couce. “What we are trying to tell them is climate change is already changing biodiversity, and you need to take that into account before you can make other management plans.”

The scientists used multiple long-term datasets and advanced machine-learning techniques to determine the relationship between biodiversity and environmental change, which enabled them to predict climate-driven biodiversity change until 2100.
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.summary: Four-year study warns destabilised marine food webs could jeopardise food security by 2050. Warming seas around the UK and the wider north-east Atlantic could destabilise marine food web. Scientists projected impact of climate breakdown on four key groups of marine life crucial to maintaining ocean ecosystems in the region.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: ‘They have schedules to follow’: how fast ferries can threaten endangered whales in the Mediterranean
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Clea Skopeliti, Federica Rossi and Wouter Massink
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
A Guardian investigation has found that despite a recommendation to slow down, leading shipping companies continue to travel above advised speeds in a key habitat for cetaceans

M
arine biologist Alice Barbarioli waits with her camera trained on the horizon. A few minutes earlier, the hydrophone beneath the Pelagos research vessel detected codas – the sequence of clicks sperm whales use to communicate.

The sperm whale reveals its head and dorsal fin as those onboard the vessel in the Pelagos sanctuary, a conservation area established to protect marine mammals in the north-western Mediterranean, rush to take photos and note the rhythm of its breathing. After a few minutes, the animal arches its back, and begins to head back into the depths of the sea. They wait to catch a glimpse of its tail.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Barbarioli, the lead researcher of the citizen-science expedition, organised by the Tethys Research Institute, immediately notices an injury on its left fluke: “Given how precise the mark is, it’s probably the result of a [vessel] collision,” she says.

Collisions have long been recognised as a leading human-induced cause of death for the Mediterranean’s endangered sperm and fin whales. Now, a Guardian investigation using data from the maritime intelligence firm Veson Nautical, has found that large passenger and cargo vessels operated by four companies – the Grimaldi Group, Corsica Ferries, Baleària and Moby Lines – have frequently travelled through a protected habitat that includes the Pelagos sanctuary at 15 knots (17mph) or above – speeds that almost always kill cetaceans in cases of a collision. Strikes are unlikely to kill when a vessel is travelling below 10 knots.

Slowing vessels is the most effective mitigation strategy when rerouteing isn’t possible, according to conservation NGO Oceancare.

The sea between Valencia and Genoa, which includes the Pelagos sanctuary, is a key cetacean habitat, home to about two-thirds of the Mediterranean’s fin whales and more than a fifth of its sperm whales. In July 2023, the International Maritime Organization (IMO) created the north-western Mediterranean Sea particularly sensitive sea area (PSSA). In a voluntary speed recommendation (VSR), it advised vessels weighing 300 gross tonnes and above to sail at 10 to 13 knots in the area to reduce the risk of fatal collisions.

Despite the IMO’s recommendation, the Guardian, using additional data from Global Fishing Watch, found that ships with IMO identification numbers spent more than 280,000 hours travelling at 15 knots and above through the PSSA in 2025. The data also showed that ships spent more than 6,000 hours travelling above 25 knots. It builds on previous analysis that found the voluntary recommendations were largely ineffective.

In 2022 and 2025, ferries owned by the Grimaldi Group, including Cruise Roma – at more than 250 metres, the world’s longest cruise ferry – dominated the top-20 list of vessels spending the most time at 15 knots or above in the habitat.

Speeding remained concentrated among a few operators in the PSSA in 2025, with just seven vessels – four Baleària fast ferries and three Grimaldi cruise ferries – responsible for 70% of the hours spent above 25 knot. Seven Grimaldi cruise ferries amounted to about 8% of all hours recorded for all vessels at 15 knots or above in 2025.

The Guardian spoke to six captains – five current and one former – who have sailed in the PSSA since its designation. The seafarers, still or previously at the helm of ships owned by Grimaldi Group and Moby Lines, say their companies have not introduced measures to encourage slow steaming after the IMO’s VSR.

“As long as it’s only a recommendation, nobody will reduce speed,” says one Grimaldi captain. “It would mean overhauling the whole commercial system. The ferries in the area travel at 25 [knots], especially the ones carrying tourists. They have schedules to follow.”

Grimaldi and Moby Lines were contacted for comment but did not respond.

Thomas Folegot, the CEO of maritime tech company Quiet-Oceans, says that while slow-moving container vessels could stand to slightly cut speeds in the PSSA, it was far more challenging for ferries: “For their business, it’s a killer. [Passengers] will fly to Corsica.”

Quiet-Oceans and Oceancare’s analysis found that 80% of the journeys by merchant ships in the PSSA in 2023 were at speeds above 10 knots.

Simone Panigada, president of the Tethys Research Institute and chair of a scientific committee dedicated to the conservation of cetaceans, says it is time to “move, progressively, from voluntary to mandatory” rules on reducing collision risk.

“A binding framework would create more level conditions for all operators, encouraging compliance among shipping companies and ensuring the adoption of these measures doesn’t rest solely on individual corporate decisions,” he says.

The International Whaling Commission (IWC) told the Guardian it has recorded six incidents since July 2023 in the PSSA: five near-miss events and one collision. It believes most strikes go unrecorded.

While the annual time spent travelling through the PSSA above the key threshold of 15 knots remained high in 2025, it represented an 11% reduction compared with 2022. The time above 25 knots also fell by about a third between 2022 and 2025.

These overall declines are probably caused by factors including altered shipping routes, says Olivia Watkins, associate director at Veson Nautical, who adds: “The PSSA recommendation is unlikely to be a significant cause of the year-on-year decline in the data results.”

Wei-Jun Mun, director of public policy at the World Shipping Council, says the industry is committed to PSSA’s protective measures, while noting slower navigation involved “commercial trade-offs and operational concerns”, including having to add ships to a service for schedule reliability.

A spokesperson for Corsica Ferries says the company supports Mediterranean marine megafauna research and ship-strike mitigation through measures including continuous monitoring, crew training and the development of whale alert tools. Researchers from programmes including conservation project Life Conceptu Maris monitor wildlife using its ships, it says.

The company says it instructs captains to navigate with particular caution through the PSSA, and to lower speeds to 10 to 13 knots, “while seeking to avoid possible negative impacts of reduced speeds”, including on manoeuvrability. It says its captains have reported a reduced capacity to avoid cetaceans that appear suddenly when navigating at reduced speeds.

A spokesperson for Baleària says it is “committed to the conservation of marine biodiversity” and actively working to mitigate the risk of collisions, including through crew training and the use of real-time monitoring systems to allow captains to adjust speed and course where necessary. Baleària says none of its fast ferries had recorded a collision with cetaceans.

Baleària adds that it participates in marine conservation programmes, including the Life Conceptu Maris and Life Intemares initiatives.

In July 2023, the International Maritime Organisation (IMo) advised vessels weighing 300 gross tonnes and above to sail at 10 to 13 knots. In the area 25 knots also fell by about a third between 2022 and 2025.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Iran war is deepening the US energy crisis. A bad winter is ahead | Mark Wolfe
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Mark Wolfe
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Congress must act to ensure that families are able to heat their homes before the start of the season

H
eating oil may be the clearest warning yet of how the war in Iran is deepening the US’s energy affordability crisis. Families who heat their homes with oil are facing bills that could be 50% higher this winter, adding nearly $900 to the cost of keeping their homes warm. These families were already struggling before the war began.

As the Guardian recently reported, research by my organization found that electricity shutoffs in 10 states had increased 28% over the past two years. Millions of Americans were already falling behind on their utility bills, forced to choose between paying for energy, food, medicine and rent. Now they face another round of increases in gasoline, electricity and home heating costs.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The war didn’t create America’s energy affordability crisis. But it is making a bad situation much worse.

For families living on social security, minimum-wage workers and others with little room in their budgets, higher energy prices are taking an especially heavy toll. Even middle-class families are struggling to absorb another $100 or $150 a month for gasoline, groceries and home heating.

Heating oil is the canary in the coalmine for the broader affordability crisis.

Heating oil and diesel are essentially the same petroleum product, and both have been hit hard by the disruption to global energy markets. Higher diesel prices increase the cost of moving food, delivering goods and operating farms and construction equipment. Those costs eventually find their way into the prices families pay.

But for the millions of households that rely on heating oil, the impact is much more immediate. Unlike gasoline, which families can sometimes conserve by driving less, heating oil is essential for keeping homes warm. Families cannot simply stop filling their tanks when prices rise.

Trump described higher oil prices resulting from the war as “a very small price to pay for USA, and world, safety and peace”. But there is nothing small about an additional $878 in heating costs for a family living on social security or working for minimum wage. The president has also said that fuel prices will fall “like a rock” when the war ends. I hope he is right.

Even if the war ended tomorrow, energy prices would not necessarily return to their previous levels. Damaged refineries need repairs, shipping routes must reopen, and depleted petroleum inventories need to be replenished. That could take months. Families cannot postpone paying their heating bills while the oil market recovers.

Congress needs to act when it returns after the midterm elections and before winter arrives. We are calling on lawmakers to add $3bn to the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (Liheap), which helps low-income families pay their heating bills.

This would allow states to provide families with supplemental assistance to cover rising heating oil and electricity prices before the start of the winter heating season.

The problem extends beyond the poorest families. Many working families earn too much to qualify for assistance but still struggle to pay their energy bills. Congress should consider temporarily expanding eligibility for Liheap to struggling middle-class families, with additional funding to ensure that assistance to the lowest-income households is not reduced.

A recent survey conducted by Consumer Reports found that more than a quarter of all families reported reduced the heating and cooling in their homes to uncomfortable levels to save money and 19% cutback on groceries or switched to less expensive food options.

Without additional energy assistance, families will fall further behind, and some will face the possibility of losing heat during the coldest months of the year.

But Congress also needs to address the larger problem. For too long, we’ve measured America’s energy security by how much oil and natural gas we produce. Yet producing more energy at home hasn’t protected the US families from price shocks caused by wars overseas.

We need to think about energy security differently. That means expanding energy sources, including wind and solar, whose fuel costs cannot be driven up by a war. There is no strait of Hormuz for solar power.

That is the longer-term challenge. Right now, millions of families are heading into winter facing energy bills they cannot afford.

At some point, the war in Iran will end, but the affordability crisis will not end with it. Washington needs to help families get through this winter and make sure the next war thousands of miles away doesn’t once again determine whether they can afford to heat their homes.

Mark Wolfe is an energy economist and serves as the executive director of the National Energy Assistance Directors Association (Neada) representing the state directors of the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program and the co-director of the Center on Energy Poverty and Climate (CEPC). He also serves as an adjunct professor at the George Washington University public policy school

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production as Elon Musk focuses on robotics and AI
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Jasper Jolly
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Decision made in order for factory in Texas to be used for Cybercab, the carmaker’s self-driving taxi

Elon Musk has announced that Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck, marking the end of a failed effort to take a chunk of the lucrative market for pickups in the US.

The billionaire chief executive said production of the car would stop in about the middle of next year at the company’s factory in Texas in order to use the plant for the Cybercab, its self-driving taxi.

Musk did not say whether Tesla had plans to produce the vehicle in another factory, although that would probably require significant investment for the specialised tooling needed to make it.

Musk has pinned hopes for Tesla on robotics, artificial intelligence and an autonomous driving fleet rather than following the traditional carmakers’ approach of developing a steady stream of new models to entice private buyers.

It caps a tricky week for the world’s richest person, after Republican candidates he had backed with $446m (£332m) in donations lost in the US midterm elections. The paper value of Musk’s fortune fell by $113bn after the extent of the rout became clear, as stock market investors questioned whether a Democrat-led Congress could slow the pace of the AI boom.

Tesla shares fell by 11% on Thursday, while his AI and rocket launch company, SpaceX, dropped by 9%.

Tesla started deliveries of the Cybertruck in late 2023, after several long delays as the company tried to cope with the technical challenges of producing such an unusual vehicle – and particularly its steel shell.

The Cybertruck never made it on sale in Europe because it did not reach the required safety standards.

Even before sales began, Musk acknowledged how difficult it would be to make it a success. In a 2023 earnings call, he said: “We dug our own grave with Cybertruck,” and noted “enormous challenges” in increasing production and earning money from it.

Musk had said the company aimed to sell 200,000 Cybertrucks each year but it never approached that target. Tesla does not report sales of the trucks separately but in the third quarter of 2026 it delivered only 8,300 “other models”, which include the Cybertruck. The vast majority of its sales were the Model 3 saloon and the Model Y SUV, with 478,000 combined deliveries during the quarter.

Tesla also this year stopped production of its Model S and Model X, its premium saloon and SUV, amid declining sales for ageing products.

Tesla’s automotive focus has shifted to the Cybercab. Tesla has started offering paid trips in the car, which has space for two passengers and no steering wheel, in limited parts of Austin, Texas. However, it is unclear how quickly the company will be able to roll out the taxi service around the US or further afield amid close regulatory scrutiny of driverless car technology.

As well as the Cybercab, Tesla is still ramping up production of its long-delayed Semi electric lorry. Musk is also aiming to produce one other new model: the Roadster sportscar, which Musk revealed with a demonstration of a “flying car” version that used thrusters developed by SpaceX to drive up a curved ramp before flipping and landing. Tesla is aiming to start production of a road-bound version in 2028. Analysts do not expect the Roadster to make a large difference to Tesla’s future profits.

Beyond vehicles, the Texas factory will also be used to build Tesla’s Optimus humanoid robot.

Musk posted on X, the social network he owns: “Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production.”

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: Rural voters were feeling left behind before the midterms, poll shows
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Lauren Aratani
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Polling done for the Guardian shows plummeting support from a former key constituency of Donald Trump’s base

Q&A: Ask your questions about Democrats’ win in the midterms

Polling conducted by the Harris Poll for the Guardian before the election shows just how angry voters were and points to one key reason Republicans lost so badly: plummeting support from rural voters, once a key constituency of Donald Trump’s base.

Over the summer, 95% of Americans indicated they believed there was an affordability crisis, particularly because of steep gas and grocery prices. By October, 61% of voters believed the country was experiencing a recession, even though technically it wasn’t.

It’s hard to ignore the impact inflation has had on this election. Key voters had expressed for months deep discontent with what had become the status quo. Loggers in Maine said that tariffs against Canada were hurting their already-battered industry. Drivers in Texas facing three-hour commutes to work were spending $400 a month on gas. Farmers across the midwest said diesel prices were exacerbating a growing season beleaguered by drought.

Recent data showed the flip wasn’t just seen among Democrats and independents, who have held pessimistic views on the economy since Trump returned to office, but among some Republicans, too.

In February, right before the war in Iran began, 49% of Republicans said the economy was getting better. By October, that number would drop to just 28%.

The pain seemed especially acute for rural voters, long considered a core base for Trump.

The president had gained many of his supporters by angling himself as a successful businessman who would be an outsider in Washington. But soaring gas and diesel prices have been a major pain point in parts of the country where driving long distances is an everyday part of life.

Rural voters were much more likely to say that gas prices were hurting their finances and that they were in economic “survival mode”, or that one surprise bill could sink them, compared with their urban and suburban counterparts. They were also slightly more likely to say that Republicans had a bigger problem with corruption, or elected officials using their position for personal financial gain, than Democrats.

In the month before the midterms, the number of rural Americans who said the economy was getting worse climbed 17% since Trump took office, compared with a 5% increase for those in the suburbs and a 3% jump among urban voters.

Yet on the eve of the midterm elections, Trump was trying to speak a different reality into existence, one where gas prices were going down, wages were rising and the US’s trade with other countries had never been stronger.

“I’ve traveled all across the country, spoken at all of these rallies I’ve done over the last two and a half weeks, and America is ready to go. They’re ready to vote,” Trump said in front of the Lincoln Memorial’s Reflecting Pool on Monday. “I hope they’re ready to do the right thing.”

But the reality that Americans have been facing is vastly different, and Americans responded accordingly. Republicans in key races from Maine to Texas lost their toss-up races on Tuesday, and Democrats will have control of Congress for the next two years.

Democrats have promised they will be busy trying to address the issues that were at the forefront of the election: the Trump administration’s brutal immigration crackdown, corruption in the White House, rising healthcare costs and the economy, specifically higher prices.

Republicans are just starting to take stock of the role prices had on the election outcome. JD Vance on Wednesday said the loss was the “cost to pay” for the Iran war. “Any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there,” Vance said.

As much as the midterms were a “blue-nami” for Democrats, pre-midterm polls showed voters were still unsure about the party’s ability to deal with affordability. When asked which party had the solution to the affordability crisis a month before the election, 34% said that neither party had a solution. Democrats (27%) slightly edged out Republicans (24%), but many voters seemed unsure whether any party could deal with these pocketbook issues.

Similar polling conducted before the 2024 presidential election showed that key independent voters were feeling just as pessimistic about the economy. Inflation had reached a generational high in 2022, and many Americans felt that Biden and Democrats weren’t doing enough.

Price increases under Trump, particularly after the Iran war, have only gotten worse. But many voters are dealing with years of economic burnout and will expect results in the coming years.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: US stocks rise, dollar slides as investors digest Democrats’ midterm victories
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Joanna Partridge
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Government bond yields fall while initial fears ease over impact of election results on world’s biggest economy

US midterm elections – live updates

After US midterms, what will lame-duck Trump mean for global economy?

US stocks have surged as investors digest the Democrats’ victories in the midterm elections, lifted by hopes that Donald Trump’s turbulent policymaking would be restrained and shaking off initial fears about the impact on growth in the world’s largest economy.

The Dow Jones rose close to 3%, its best day in over a year, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq and the benchmark S&P 500 gained about 1.5% each when markets closed on Wednesday afternoon, turning around overnight falls in US stock futures after the news that the Democratic party won control of the Senate and the House of Representatives.

The price of oil dropped sharply as traders assessed the impact of the Democrats’ win on the war in Iran. Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, fell below $100 a barrel for the first time since early October.

In a social media post on Wednesday afternoon, Trump took credit for the jump. “Stock Market just hit another Record High,” he wrote. “Your 401(k)s are through the roof. Record Setting All!”

However, the US dollar fell against the currencies of America’s major trading partners, hitting a one-month low on Wednesday while coming under pressure from falling bond yields. Investors moved into US treasuries, viewed as a haven from the political gridlock anticipated during the rest of Trump’s final term in office.

The dollar index, which measures it against a basket of six currencies, slid to its lowest level in a month, with the pound hitting its highest level since mid-September on the back of a fragile dollar, while the euro also made gains.

The dollar also slid against the yen and the Swiss franc, currencies that traders tend to turn to during times of uncertainty.

Meanwhile, the yield, or interest rate, on the benchmark 10-year US treasury bond has fallen 4.7 basis points to 4.918%. On two-year bonds it has dropped 3.7bps to 4.597%. Yields fall when bond prices rise.

Across the US, voters rejected Trump and the Republican agenda, with the Democrats securing Senate seats in traditional Republican strongholds such as Texas, Iowa, North Carolina and South Carolina.

Axel Rudolph, the chief technical analyst at the trading platform IG, said: “The scale of the losses will inevitably raise questions about Trump’s ability to push through his agenda over the next two years, and markets are already reacting. The dollar is under pressure as investors reassess the political outlook, while gold and silver are benefiting as safe haven plays.”

Futures trading initially indicated US stock markets would open sharply lower, with the Nasdaq expected to slide on fears over the prospects for AI companies. However, indicators later suggested Wall Street could open higher as Trump’s conciliatory tone and rises on European markets cheered investors.

European markets rose yesterday. London’s FTSE 100 was up 1.8%, Germany’s Dax rose by 2.2%, France’s Cac 40 was 2% higher and Italy’s FTSE MiB index rose by 2.2%.

Bank and clean energy stocks, which have borne the brunt of Trump’s policies, were among the top risers in Europe. Bank stocks rose by 2.8%, while Denmark’s Vestas Wind Systems jumped nearly 5% and Ørsted soared 7.4%.

“Some individual names are nursing significant losses today,” said Kathleen Brooks, the UK research director at XTB. “SpaceX is down 5% in the premarket, and Tesla is lower by more than 4%. Elon Musk is considered an anathema to most Democrats.”

Musk, the world’s richest person, pumped $446m (£331m) into the midterms, funding Republican-aligned political action committees and groups.

Brooks said investors were reacting to expectations that a Democrat-controlled Congress could mean greater scrutiny for AI companies, which could also cast doubt on a potential merger of Musk’s two companies.

The price of gold, a traditional haven asset, rose by 2.2%, soaring past $4,000 an ounce.

AI-related shares tumbled during Asian trading hours, on expectations that Democrats will want to bring in greater regulation of the sector.

Chris Turner, the global head of markets at ING, said: “Investors will be parsing what this all means. For example, Gina Hinojosa won the Texas governor’s race on a ticket of wanting an immediate moratorium on datacentre buildouts.”

He added: “Given AI’s role in powering the US economy, speculation over whether a new Democrat Congress would slow AI capital expenditure plans briefly hit markets.”

Jesper Koll, an expert director at the financial services company Monex Group, said: “The AI momentum has turned negative, with or without the Republicans having a majority. The starting point for financial markets into this election, particularly for the equity market, has been adverse on AI.”

Trump’s style of governing through executive orders has prompted some analysts to question whether the Democrats regaining control of Congress will have much change on US policymaking.

“There’s still a number of areas where Donald Trump can influence the markets – trade and tariffs, foreign policy and existing regulations,” said Tai Hui, a market strategist at JP Morgan Asset Management.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Trump blamed Fox News for Republican losses even as network’s hosts went easy on him
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Jeremy Barr in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Fox News pundits hardly criticized the US president in midterms coverage but Trump was still quick to cast blame

US midterms 2026 live – latest updates

Track live results from all 50 states

Q&A: Ask your questions about Democrats’ win in the midterms

In the weeks leading up to Tuesday’s midterm elections, Donald Trump made clear that he would place some blame on his favorite cable channel, Fox News, if his party did poorly.

On election day, he didn’t disappoint.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Even before races really started to be called, Trump hit the network in multiple Truth Social posts, criticizing Fox for featuring Democratic pundit Jessica Tarlov; attacking Fox’s polls as “always the worst”; mocking some recent softness in the network’s year-over-year ratings trends and accusing Fox of being “AGAINST” him. Just before midnight, Trump directly placed blame on Fox News for the Republican party’s failure to hold on to the US House and Senate, writing that “FoxNews bears responsibility for these losses by constantly and consistently putting on the Dumocrat opposition, and worse.”

In a surreal moment, Trump then called into Fox’s election coverage around midnight and directly criticized the network’s polls as “terrible,” telling the network’s employees: “You ought to get yourself a good pollster, because your pollsters are the worst.” Fox News anchor Bret Baier pushed back gently, pointing out that “tonight, actually, the results are pretty close to what the Fox polls showed.” (Trump also made a dig about Baier – or Fox at large –not supporting him “when it wasn’t fashionable”.)

But while Trump was extremely critical of Fox News throughout the day and night, during more than six and a half hours of election night coverage viewed by the Guardian, commentators on the network seemed to take pains to not directly tie the party’s losses to Trump, and there were no suggestions that the party should back away from him.

Instead, several commentators on the channel turned the focus on voters for being “impatient” and wanting “instant gratification”, as host Jesse Watters put it just after 8pm. Many commentators said the president’s party historically performs poorly in the midterm elections. There were many attacks on Democrats, with conservative commentators in agreement that the party would overstay their welcome from voters and misinterpret their victory as a mandate, paving the way for Republican wins in 2028.

The only significant criticisms of the president focused on the White House’s messaging strategy and his decision to go to war in Iran.

“In some sense, Mr Trump was too successful in the first year and didn’t sell it enough in the second year,” said Larry Kudlow, a Fox Business Network host who served as Trump’s Director of the National Economic Council during his first administration.

Dana Perino, who served as press secretary to George W Bush, said: “From a messaging standpoint, a lot of times the administration has got too many balls in the air and it’s hard to figure out what is the headline we want to drive.”

And several commentators noted that voters seemed to be unhappy with the president’s decision to launch a war against Iran, particularly considering the rise in gas prices that resulted from it. Sean Hannity, the president’s biggest booster on the channel, agreed with Baier that the night’s outcome would have been different if he had not bombed the country.

“I think it’s prices. People are mad,” Watters offered later in the night.

Still, the overwhelming consensus from Fox’s election night panel – which included several former Trump administration employees, including his former press secretary Karoline Leavitt – was that the blame should not be squarely placed at the president’s feet. Instead, Leavitt singled out the media. “Unfortunately, I think the American people forgot about the good policy, [and] maybe listened to the lying media on the other side that is definitely in the back seat of the Democratic party,” she said.

Just before 10pm, Fox News host Will Cain said: “I look at the pros and the cons of the last two years under Donald Trump, and the pros significantly outweigh the cons.”

While primetime host Laura Ingraham acknowledged that the election was a “referendum on Trump”, she said that “overwhelmingly his policies have been phenomenal for the country. Overwhelmingly, the stuff he’s promised, he’s done, and it’s worked out fabulously.”

Despite his earlier comments, Hannity said that Trump’s policies “are rock solid”, that Iran “had to be done” and that his intervention will eventually be proven right.

One person who shared in the belief that the president was not responsible for the losses was the president himself. “I don’t view it as a hit on me,” Trump told the Fox News panel, adding that “historically, I think I’ll be judged for having done the right thing,” and largely placing the blame on the Republican candidates who were defeated. He repeated his contention that the outcome would have been different if he had been on the ballot.

This article was amended on 4 November 2026; a previous version incorrectly stated that Karoline Leavitt is Donald Trump’s most recent press secretary, when it is in fact Katie Zacharia.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: CVS Health to split pharmacy chain from health insurance
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Edward Helmore
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
CVS Pharmacy will be separate from CVS Health, housing major insurer Aetna and benefits manager Caremark

CVS Health, the largest US healthcare conglomerate valued at $117bn, has announced its plans split off its pharmacy chain from its health insurance and benefits businesses, ending an era in which healthcare companies grew into vast conglomerates.

In their announcement on Wednesday, CVS Health said they will split off its 9,000 pharmacies, in-store clinics and mail order prescription business into a business named CVS Pharmacy.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

A second company will keep the name CVS Health and house the major insurer Aetna and the giant pharmacy benefits manager Caremark, along with other businesses that provide home visits and primary care to older people.

The company has come under pressure from lawmakers and regulators over concerns that the healthcare giants, including CVS Health, UnitedHealth Group and Cigna, have become too dominant, leading to higher medical costs. The three companies control roughly 80% of the market. CVS Health in particular generated over $400bn in revenue last year.

A political pushback against healthcare gigantism has led Arkansas and Tennessee to pass laws aimed at preventing the companies from managing prescription benefits and running retail and mail-order pharmacies.

The Arkansas state representative Jeremiah Moore, a Republican who sponsored the state’s bill, told Politico last week: “The average American citizen is really tired of being pushed around and bullied, whether it be from the government or a monopolistic company.”

He added: “For far too long, they’ve taken advantage of these sick people, and it’s what I consider to be crony capitalism. They’re bending the rules to benefit their own bottom line.” Other states have proposed similar restrictions.

At the federal level, a bill introduced by the Missouri Republican senator Josh Hawley and Massachusetts senator Elizabeth Warren proposes an antitrust crackdown.

Hawley has described the legislation as “a major step toward restoring transparency and making healthcare more affordable for every American.”

David Joyner, CVS’s chief executive and chair, will run the healthcare solutions business.
 
 
 “Our history is defined by proactively evolving to stay ahead of what’s next in healthcare, and in today’s environment, that means delivering more affordability, greater access and a simpler experience,” said Joyner in a statement.

That marks a stark turnaround from CVS Health’s earlier opposition to legislative efforts to break up the healthcare giant, which a company spokesman said would “open the door to private equity stripping the entire U.S. healthcare system for parts”.

The announcement comes after a series of acquisitions that saw CVS Health expand into nearly every corner of the healthcare system. It began in 2018, when CVS and Aetna merged in a $70bn deal. Healthcare rivals, UnitedHealth and Cigna, also brought into the trend of harnessing an insurer, pharmacy benefits, and a mail-order business under one operation.

CVS Health, however, did not meet investors’ expectations for growth. In late 2024, its share price fell to $44, though it has since rebounded. The CVS Health breakup is planned for early 2028.

Midterms didn’t appear to have huge impact, though predicted wins for Democrats could mean more regulation

US tech stocks made a recovery on Tuesday afternoon after a selloff spooked investors over AI spending.

Tuesday’s midterm elections didn’t appear to have a huge impact on Wall Street, though investors are predicting Democrats get at least a majority in the House and potentially gain seats in the Senate, which could lead to more AI regulation.

The S&P 500 was up 0.37% at market closing on Tuesday, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq increased 0.83% for the day. The Dow dropped 0.38% following a 1.9% dip in Apple’s share price after the company released a worse-than-expected margin forecast due to the higher cost of memory chips.

Nvidia picked up a 2.3% gain after dropping over four sessions, while fellow chipmakers Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom and Micron Technology also jumped on Tuesday.

While many Americans say frustration with the higher cost of living will be a major factor in their vote on Tuesday, Wall Street has continued to soar off investments in AI, particularly the chips and infrastructure used to power the technology. The S&P 500 is up 10% for the year so far, while the Nasdaq and the Dow are up 9% and 7%, respectively.
