The UK embassy will be advising how best to handle this badly wounded president; how to influence his moves and steer him away from decisions that impact on the wellbeing of the UK. My advice would be to carry on pretty much as before, with one important qualification. We are seeing the beginning of the end of the Trump era. Power is already draining away from him: the vultures are circling. But this is not a man who will settle for just raging at the dying of the light; he will light bonfires to ward it off.

So we have to be careful not to appear to be distancing ourselves or moving on from Trump. His antennae are finely tuned to pick up signals of disrespect. This doesn’t mean turning up the dial on sucking up. But it does mean talking to him intensively, arguably even more so than at present, about the issues that matter to us – Iran, Ukraine, the future of Nato, the global economy. And we should resist the temptation to be seen to be cultivating possible successors from either side of the US political spectrum. Trump needs to believe that we recognise what is actually the case: that he is the president and will call the shots until 20 January 2029.

Kim Darroch was British ambassador to the US from 2016 to 2019, and is author of Collateral Damage: Britain, America and Europe in the Age of Trump

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Guardian view on cocaine and domestic abuse: new links between drugs and crime need investigating | Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Patterns of drug supply and use are changing and the government’s five-year-old drug strategy must evolve too

A
slight drop in the number of drug deaths over a year in England and Wales is the first such news since 2012. Over the past decade, the grim trajectory has been upward; the annual figure of 5,519 has more than doubled since the 1990s. Given this trend, any fall is a relief. But the spike in deaths linked to cocaine, which has overtaken heroin for the first time, as well as evidence uncovered by the Guardian of a link with domestic violence, points to the need for a drugs policy that takes account of changing usage.

Nearly six in 10 drug tests on people arrested on suspicion of domestic abuse were positive for cocaine in the year to June, while a previous study found that 59% of suspects tested positive for cocaine or opiates. Links between domestic violence and alcohol have been highlighted by campaigners since the 19th century. In 2022, a UK government report found that alcohol and drug use featured in around a third of 127 domestic homicides it examined.

But while some of the issues thrown up by substance misuse are similar – increased paranoia and aggression placing partners and other relatives of abusers at risk – there are specific challenges around illegal drug use that ministers need to address. One woman told the Guardian that she had covered up her former partner’s cocaine use because she feared police would find out that she had also taken it. Charities are frustrated by the way that the criminal penalties for drug possession make it difficult to offer and access support.

In Scotland, which has the highest rate of drug deaths in Europe, a pilot treatment room is operating in Glasgow, though a sharp rise in deaths suggests that while such rooms may be a pragmatic harm reduction measure, they are not a panacea. In England and Wales, a drugs strategy was launched in 2021 following a review by Prof Dame Carol Black. But while the then Conservative government accepted her recommendation to invest in addiction treatment and research, funding has since been frozen – while wastewater samples and crime figures show that cocaine use has boomed. In the year to March 2025, the police and Border Force made 269,321 drug seizures – the highest on record.

The spending review next year offers a chance for a reset that ministers should take. While cocaine use has traditionally been associated with higher disposable incomes, there are five times more drug deaths in the most deprived areas compared with the least deprived ones (London has the lowest rate). Liverpool’s Alder Hey children’s hospital recently opened a clinic to treat under-16s who have injured their bladders by taking ketamine.

Police have an important role in tackling traffickers. But ministers must recommit to the “whole-system approach” proposed by Prof Black. Reducing drug deaths should be part of wider efforts at reducing socioeconomic health disparities. Research should focus on effective treatment, and seek to understand the link between cocaine and domestic abuse. The impacts of the illegal drugs market have altered in the past five years. It is time for the authorities to catch up.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: Failing Grayling double reports for duty as Reform’s armed forces spokesperson | John Crace
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: John Crace
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
New recruit Angus MacIntyre bears an unfortunate resemblance to little-missed ex-Tory minister Chris Grayling

Y
ou can make a good case for Nigel Farage having been one of the most consequential British politicians of the 21st century. Without him there would have been no Brexit. And yet it is now beginning to look as if his time has come and gone.

The narcissistic qualities that have served him so well now threaten to finish him off. His skin is becoming thinner by the day. All that’s left is reflexive lashing out. A raging against the dying of the light. You’d need to have a heart of stone not to laugh.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

On Thursday, Nige was at the old Billingsgate fish market in central London for a press conference – not another one – at which he was to unveil his new armed forces spokesperson. Only this would turn out to be a press conference with a difference. Nige would not be taking any questions for the cameras.

You couldn’t help but think he was struggling to shake off the humiliation of insisting the pollsters were wrong about the Republicans in the US midterms. Trump would not be smashed, he said. The American voters saw it differently. And now The Donald was proving to be a liability.

It’s not just Nige who is suffering. He’s taking his whole team down with him. Not least those former Tory MPs who had thought the Conservatives were dead in the water. Danny Kruger was supposed to be the sensible one. The one who could provide a veneer of intelligence to the Reform project. Yet Nice Danny is rapidly morphing into Desperate Dan: a man now thinking he may have been a bit hasty and made the wrong call.

Desperate Dan had been roped in as the warm-up act. Usually the sort of meaningless gig that is delegated to Dicky Tice. It probably wasn’t in the script for Dan to use his five-minute gig to unload his full existential meltdown, but that was what he got. Angry Dan is a sucker for any conspiracy theory. The polls had been rigged to make it look as if Reform was in third place. And John Healey had only resigned as defence secretary so that he could get the job as chancellor in order to dismantle all the armed forces.

The madness apogee was reached when Desperate Dan declared that no politician in the whole country knew more about defence than Nige. In a war, Nige would be the first person trying to escape the draft with ingrown toenails. Reform have never even got round to naming a defence spokesperson or showing the slightest interest in the subject. Reform’s attendance in parliament for defence-related matters is pitiful.

Nige took centre stage to a standing ovation. There are still a few hardcore believers left. He craves the attention despite the ever-diminishing returns. “The world is more dangerous now than it has been for 80 years,” he said, with his trademark grin. He could be right, though he hadn’t stopped to consider whether Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump – two leaders whom he has openly admired – might have contributed to that. Nige has blamed the Ukraine war on Nato and was all up for joining the US in bombing Iran.

The 3.5% of GDP by 2035 was paltry, he continued. Though he didn’t commit to spending any more or saying how the increase would be funded. But help was at hand. Nige had tracked down the one man in the entire armed services who could save the country from its darkest hour. No matter that the RAF had rather overlooked the talents of the wing commander with 40 years’ service. Meet Angus MacIntyre, who last week resigned from the RAF to become Nige’s official wingman.

Cue a spectacular double take. Because the man who walked on stage was a dead ringer for Chris Grayling, the former Tory minister who had never yet found a job he couldn’t do worse than anyone else. Failing Grayling made a career out of his own incompetence. Mediocrity was a level of achievement to which he could only aspire.

Being Failing Grayling’s double is a cross no man should have to bear but Angus was determined to do his best. He was happy to report for duty as Reform’s shadow minister for the armed forces. This was Angus’s first lie in his new role. Start as you mean to go on. He is not and is never going to be a shadow minister. That role can only ever be done by a Tory as the official opposition. But maybe no one had yet got round to explaining such things to him. Angus was a grunt who operated on a need to know basis.

MacIntyre quickly moved on to his CV, which includes spells in the US and at Nato HQ. More lanyard class than man of action. Nor did he quite explain why he had finished his career only as wing commander despite four decades of service. You couldn’t help thinking Angus might have been passed over for promotion several times and that the RAF hadn’t quite appreciated his talents as much as he would have liked.

Still, Angus looks as if he has landed in the right place, sounding suitably swivel-eyed about net zero and condemning current attitudes towards the armed forces as “Marxist ideology”. However, it was a little weird that Reform’s new man from the military had nothing to say about either Ukraine or Iran. It would have been good to know if he shared Nige’s admiration for Putin and Trump and whether he, too, looks on not joining the Iran war as a missed opportunity. Nor did he say whether he intended to stand as an MP or who was paying him. Questions, questions.

“Have I got the right guy?” Nige asked the audience, as he joined Angus on stage for a last group hug. We will find out soon enough. But my bet would be that Angus may soon be feeling buyer’s remorse. Nige looks as if he is running on empty.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: No amount of sliding in the polls can shake Kemi Badenoch’s self-belief – or alter her party’s direction | Andy Beckett
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Andy Beckett
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Two years in to her leadership, Badenoch continues to take the Tories ever-rightwards, into comfort-zone Conservatism

W
hat happens to a political leader who is too sure of themself? Sometimes, huge confidence is a very useful, self-fulfilling quality: persuading party colleagues, activists, donors and voters that more can be achieved than is usually thought possible. Such utter conviction can keep everyone believing while the actual practicalities of a political project are worked out.

Yet when an air of absolute certainty turns out to be overconfidence, the bubble bursts. The politician may be revealed as disastrously complacent and lacking in judgment, having delusions of grandeur, or being fundamentally in denial. Especially in our era of online mockery and instinctive contempt for politicians, an overconfident leader can end up as a laughing stock.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

This week is the second anniversary of the start of Kemi Badenoch’s Conservative leadership. So far, self-assuredness has been her tenure’s central feature, the one aspect that many voters and journalists have noticed. “There’s a new captain, there’s a new coach, there’s a new owner … which is all me,” she told GB News last month, after a party conference where activists chanted “Kemi” and her assertive persona pervaded everything, as if the party had found another Margaret Thatcher.

Badenoch’s speeches, interviews and Commons interventions come riskily spiced with contempt, self-congratulation and advice to supposedly lesser political mortals: “I was right”, “let me explain”, “let me tell them [the government] some home truths”. She and her party now present themselves in a similarly self-aggrandising way. Unlike Labour and the other parties, she says: “We live in the real world.” The Conservatives are the party of “common sense”, “the no-nonsense party” that “get stuff done”. A long pamphlet the party recently published, with Badenoch’s name on the cover, about how it would approach governing is a little smugly titled: “The Right Way”.

When she became leader, the Tories were at 26% in Politico’s rolling average of polls: barely above their 24% vote share in the 2024 general election, the worst in their history. After two years of Badenoch’s aggressive leadership, covered ever more approvingly by the rightwing media, accompanied by regular crises inside Labour and Reform UK, the Conservatives have fallen to 21%. The forecaster Electoral Calculus currently predicts they will win 128 seats at the next election, almost three times fewer than Labour – and even this paltry tally depends on the electoral system hugely favouring the Tories over the similarly disliked Reform UK.

During previous periods of defeat and great unpopularity, the Conservatives pored over their mistakes in government, reconsidered policies, reassessed how their party related to society, and changed direction fundamentally. After losing power in 1945 – after 14 years, as in 2024 – they accepted that in office they had not done enough to reduce unemployment, stimulate the economy, or develop the welfare state. After losing power in 1974, they ditched their kinder Conservatism for the ambitious counter-revolution of Thatcherism.

Despite their electoral position now being far worse than in either 1945 or 1974, no such reinventions have taken place under Badenoch. Instead, the Tories have continued to travel rightwards, not in new directions as under Thatcher, but deeper and deeper into a Conservative comfort zone, where they have been loitering most of the time since David Cameron abandoned his government’s brief experiments with liberal Toryism in the early 2010s.

In this comfort zone, traditional Conservative remedies such as deregulating business, building more prisons, cutting taxes for the prosperous and reducing the poor’s welfare benefits are always right – regardless of how society is changing, or whether recent Tory governments have actually applied them, or done so successfully. Brexit’s failure is not to be acknowledged. Net zero’s necessity is to be avoided. Yet according to the Tories, it is Labour, the Greens and Liberal Democrats – who are all trying to develop fresh approaches to the climate crisis, and the outflanking of Brexit by shifts in geopolitics – who are “not serious”, as Badenoch patronisingly puts it.

It’s tempting to ascribe this narrow-mindedness to her character, which seems to lack much capacity for self-criticism. But parts of her life story may also have helped create and maintain her predictable rightwing perspectives. “I was born into a relatively wealthy family,” she told the Nigerian newspaper Peoples Gazette in 2024. Her father “was a doctor who had lots of oil company patients … and got paid very well”. She was educated privately in Nigeria, later worked in London as a director of the elite bank Coutts, and married a Tory activist who was also privately educated and worked in the upper echelons of finance. She represents an affluent rural constituency, North West Essex, with an above-average proportion of wealthy homeowners and retirees, groups that dominate her party’s remaining national support. With the huge exception of racism, it’s not clear she has encountered many social forces during her life which might have made her rethink her outlook.

But the Tories’ complacency extends far beyond Badenoch. Conservatism can be a comfort zone ideology: wanting to conserve the status quo implies that you think things are essentially fine as they are. Only when that status quo, and specifically Tory-aligned interests within it, are seriously threatened does the party switch to its less common iconoclastic mode, as it did under Thatcher in the turbulent, increasingly egalitarian 1970s. One reason the Tories aren’t doing that now is that, for all the rightwing talk about millionaires fleeing the country, the rich, big business and the City of London are still doing well here.

For non-Tories, the party’s long, ongoing holiday from reality may seem something to relish. The Conservatives’ stark decline since the late 1980s – with only one big general election win since, in 2019 – is certainly a great change after centuries of Tory hegemony, and still insufficiently noticed or discussed.

But their stubborn attachment to the same old assumptions also helps keep British politics, and how much of the media cover it, and many voters think about it, skewed to the right, by making traditional Conservative ideas about the economy and society still seem fairly respectable, and therefore realistic. Badenoch’s cocky leadership may be abruptly terminated after the next election. But unless a more open-minded Tory replaces her – which is currently hard to imagine – the “common sense” politics she says she stands for will destructively linger on.

Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnist

But their stubborn attachment to the same old assumptions also helps keep British politics, and how much of the media cover it.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: How irrational are Labour’s plans for migrant workers? To find out, read the small print | Frances Ryan
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Frances Ryan
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Despite the partial U-turn on care worker visas, the staff who keep the system afloat still face a hostile environment

If you want to see the senselessness of Britain’s immigration debate play out in real time, look no further than the crackdown on care workers’ visas that came to a head this week.

As part of its plans to force low-paid migrant workers to wait 15 years before settlement in the UK, the Home Office has been in a battle behind the scenes for the past six months to controversially include care workers in the policy. This is despite the social care system already facing critical staff shortages and the number of British citizens and immigrants taking the jobs dwindling.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

After a fierce backlash from health unions and Labour cabinet members, this week the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, announced a partial U-turn: an estimated 280,000 care workers and their dependents will be exempt and allowed to apply for indefinite leave to remain (ILR) after five years.

It’s a welcome reprieve from a policy that should never have been on the table. But check the fine print and this “watering down” will not protect every care worker. Only carers who earn £25,000 a year and entered or switched on to the care staff visa route before the white paper’s publication in 2025 will be eligible.

Those who don’t meet the strict requirements will have to get another five-year “health and social care” visa before applying for ILR – a move campaigners are warning will leave vulnerable workers open to exploitation from unscrupulous employers.

Ministers have not established what benefit any of this is meant to bestow on the British people, millions of whom rely on migrant carers to help them or their elderly parents wash and dress. Nor has anyone explained how Labour’s upcoming care reforms will work while alienating – rather than actively recruiting – more international staff, as recent tightened immigration rules already have.

Or, to put it another way: the government has simultaneously pledged to fix social care while creating a hostile environment for the migrant staff who keep the system afloat. It sums up not only the nastiness of it all, but the deep-seated irrationality that now plagues almost any mainstream conversation about immigration, with politicians across the spectrum seemingly contractually obliged to ignore basic common sense as well as decency.

Few things demonstrate this more than the obsession with the “contribution v cost” framing that dominates these debates, and which Labour has now threaded through its visa policy. On paper, it appears to many a fair and logical way to allocate visa rights. In practice, it rewards the wealthy and dismisses the value of working-class and predominantly female labour: while care workers will have to wait five or 15 years for ILR, a solicitor on £125,000 can get fast-tracked in only three. It is blatant classism, sure, but also fundamentally misses the very obvious tenet of capitalism that a worker’s “contribution” to a society and economy is not necessarily reflected in their wage packet.

That Mahmood has been doing the rounds in recent months using disputed figures to claim that granting ILR to care staff and their families for the next few years would cost the public purse £10bn over a lifetime suggests how unreliable – and outright ludicrous – the cost v contribution binary is. These are the people keeping our loved ones alive for the minimum wage and we’re still debating whether they’re a burden on the taxpayer.

Of course, evidence shows care workers are, to use that favoured phrase, “net contributors”. The Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) found this week that skilled migrants – including care workers – and their families due to settle in the UK under current rules are expected to boost the public purse by a staggering £115bn through taxes.

Such a figure doesn’t even include the many other ways care workers save the country money: by enabling family members to keep paying income tax rather than quitting their jobs to be an unpaid carer; supporting younger disabled people to get to the office and stay in work; or keeping older people out of expensive hospital beds by reducing their risk of falls.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

And yet we are losing something if we accept the idea that a migrant’s “contribution” is only in economic terms, as if the Home Office can scan a human being at the border and put a price tag round their neck. Anyone who has ever relied on a good carer knows there is value that can’t be measured on a spreadsheet: the security of knowing there is someone to help you get out of bed in the morning; the dignity of having a regular shower; the laughter that comes with a shared joke as you write the shopping list together.

You won’t see many of these people on front pages or hear their voices on radio call-ins. But the people providing care and those who rely on it will “contribute” considerably more to the debate than the non-disabled white contrarians who so persistently dominate it.

If it is a “legitimate concern” for the public to worry about immigration, it is legitimate for a disabled person to be afraid there will be no one to help them cook dinner, or for a migrant to worry about where they’ll live next year.

Because here’s the thing about fears: some are irrational, and others are not. Labour would do well to remember which ones it should listen to and which it should challenge.

Frances Ryan is a Guardian columnist
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.summary: Home Office has not established what benefit any of this is meant to bestow on British people. Frances Ryan: It is legitimate for a disabled person to be afraid there will be no one to help them cook dinner.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: Great British Railways: new dawn for a new network but with plenty of old problems to fix
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Gwyn Topham Transport correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Experts predict a baptism of fire for GBR in 2027, with likely issues ranging from clapped-out trains and track to extreme weather-related stress

T
he glad tidings brought by the minister were that the wait was almost over: the establishment of Great British Railways could be wrapped up by Christmas, at least in law. But with a renationalised industry facing fresh storms in 2027, some in the railway world are wondering if they should be careful what they wish for.

The legislation that will rip up how rail has been run, anticipated for the best part of a decade, is being chewed over in its final stages in the House of Lords. It now has, the rail minister, Peter Hendy, told an industry conference in London this week, “a fair chance of getting royal assent” before parliament’s winter break, allowing a new arm’s-length body with overall control of Britain’s railway, spanning the track and train services.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Great Western Railway will come into the government stable in December, with the remaining private train operations, East Midland Railway, Avanti and CrossCountry, due to be nationalised next year.

There will be plenty to fix, as politicians and rail bosses acknowledged. Lord Hendy opened the Railway Industry Association’s conference by describing every train in the north of England as “clapped out”; Jeremy Westlake, the chief executive of infrastructure manager Network Rail, concluded the event by bringing up the two derailments in 24 hours at the peak of a summer of delays.

Some of the solutions may appear easier within an integrated, nationalised industry. The site of the future Great British Railways (GBR) HQ in Derby has now been picked, even if it remains unclear how many of rail’s leaders fancy decamping there, and exactly where the power will lie.

It won’t be, said Hendy, an all-powerful “Kremlin in Derby”, with control instead largely given to regional managing directors, something so far instigated at South Western and Southeastern. For Hendy, the rewards of the new structure will be a single point of accountability, and the end of a “culture of blame” under privatisation where contracts pitted operators against Network Rail, especially in times of disruption or delay.

Personifying for now the GBR ideal of track and train in harmony are Westlake and Alex Hynes, the chief executive of DFTO, the state operator managing the renationalised train services, who discussed their bromance in another joint appearance on stage at the London conference. Hynes said he had told train staff to “go find your new best friend on the trackside … We try to role-model it.”

It remains to be seen if either will be for the chop next year, when the newly appointed chair of GBR, John Kingman, picks one overall integrated boss. The flip side of the road to reform and integration for some, especially non-frontline managerial staff, has been prolonged uncertainty, as roles merge or disappear.

But GBR should mean being able to move resources more easily around the railway, be it people or trains. Hendy cited Great Western’s problems with former Transport for Wales trains, which had deteriorated after being replaced in service: “There’s nothing more stupid than watching some trains halfway through their lives that have been parked in a field … miserably failing on a daily basis because the industry wasn’t coherent enough. You can’t believe how stupid that is.”

Likewise, he said, most train companies “have been desperately short of drivers … That’s crackers. We can fix that – and I think it’s really important to fix those basic things. They will take time.”

Some, though, wonder where the GBR legislation will land rail under future governments. One of the missions was to end the micromanagement of rail by central government: when the 73-year-old Hendy, a railwayman and politician, eventually steps away, the separation – or lack of it – may become clearer.

Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning

after newsletter promotion

Hendy said GBR would at last give the railway a long-term strategy; opponents argue it does not bind it clearly enough. Others are worried that the Treasury could step in more than ever, threatening rail’s limited financial independence. Darren Caplan, the chief executive of the Railway Industry Association, said his organisation remained “very concerned that a future secretary of state could reopen five-year funding settlements, making funding even less certain”.

Richard Holden, the Conservative shadow transport secretary, warned that rail could “lose out to the competing demands of that day [and] have to get in the queue. Will a new train win out over a new hospital? I doubt it.”

Olly Glover, the transport spokesperson for the Lib Dems, who are more positive about the bill but also voted against it in its current form, said: “They’ve raised a lot of expectation as a result of so-called nationalisation. But the truth of it is the benefits will take time and are only going to materialise if the Treasury is willing to sanction more spending.”

Money has been tight, even though the railway hopes fare revenues are finally on track to match pre-pandemic income in the coming years. For now, the state of the railway has reflected spending on renewing it: cut from nearly £5bn a year to less than £4bn in the last five years, according to the regulator, the Office of Rail and Road. It was, said the ORR’s interim CEO, Feras Alshaker, “expected that its reliability would decline in the period”.

As record levels of compensation for delayed journeys this summer show, it certainly has. That level was compounded by the extreme temperatures and changing climate; but as several speakers at this week’s conference pointed out, the outlook is for much worse as GBR takes shape, with a “super El Niño” event likely to test the infrastructure as never before.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘Finally there’s hope’: UK weighs up opportunities and risks after Trump’s midterms disaster
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Pippa Crerar Political editor
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Senior British politicians and officials highlight potential to end Iran war but warn US president is not yet ‘a spent force’

Andy Burnham was having dinner at the Commonwealth summit in Antigua when the results of the US midterm elections started rolling in.

UK government officials in the Caribbean with the prime minister scrolled through their phones with growing incredulity as the scale of the Republicans’ defeat became clear.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

“We knew it was going to be bad for Trump but it was historic result after historic result: Kansas, South Carolina, Texas,” one said. “We’ve been dealing with this constant anxiety over Trump’s erraticism and what he might do next for years. Finally, there’s a bit of hope.”

As he faced the cameras the following morning, Burnham struggled to disguise his relief that the US president could be restrained.

“I feel the world has an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all and that’s the cost of living,” he said. “But I can’t get people’s cost of living pressures down until the conflict in the Middle East is resolved … I’ll be working for de-escalation, to make it very clear.”

Burnham will not be alone in urging restraint. The energy price shock and subsequent interest rate hikes caused by the US war on Iran have severely affected economies around the world.

It is the main reason why this set of midterm elections – in which the Democrats took control of Congress – are the most consequential for the UK in decades, with the potential to have a greater impact at home than almost any domestic announcement.

Earlier this month, the prime minister admitted his first budget had been “less radical than he had hoped”, with the global economic volatility forcing the government’s hand.

But while the trajectory of the Iran conflict is the inevitable focus, it is not the only direct impact of the Republican rout on the UK. Trump’s potential approach to Russia and Ukraine, the threat of more tariffs and the wider political ripples of the “blue tsunami” are all being pored over at Westminster.

While the US president’s domestic powers will be constrained, he still wields significant influence over foreign policy – and is likely to use it.

“We’ve all learned over recent years that all of this lands on the desk of just one decision-maker in Washington. How he interprets these elections matters more than how they’re seen in any other global capital,” one UK government insider said.

Yet there are expectations that Trump could still be curtailed by a Democratic-run Congress trying to push the party’s domestic agenda while also holding the Trump court to account and using up all his spare bandwidth.

“Congress probably will become a thorn in the president’s side, so he may become distracted by those issues rather than international ones,” said Sarah Elliott, the director of the special relationship unit at the Prosperity Institute.

David Miliband, a former UK foreign secretary now based in New York, said: “There is a chance that the cross-party congressional majority to support Ukraine finds its voice and leverage. I hope so.

“Maybe the impact of tariffs on prices will prompt a second look. But the presidency remains ‘imperial’ in foreign policy, so there are no guarantees.”

Kim Darroch, the UK’s man in Washington the last time Trump was in office, said the president still had the ability to wreak chaos on the world stage.

“You can’t formally declare war without congressional approval but you can engage in conflict. He can impose tariffs and insult allies and cosy up to dictators. All of that is still open to Trump,” he said.

“My instinct is that he’s held his views about the uselessness of allies, the value of tariffs, the world being about bigger powers for decades. He’s not going to change his mind now.”

However, over the past few days, the mood music in Washington toward Iran already appears to have shifted. There is hope in diplomatic circles that the midterms have strengthened the resolve in Washington for a negotiated conclusion to the war.

Miliband said: “I would guess that the odds on renewed assault on Iran have lengthened, and the pressure for resolution will be strengthened.”

Others, however, are more cautious, warning that Trump, who appeared to agree with JD Vance’s post-result assessment that the war was to blame, had a record of unpredictability.

Emily Thornberry, the chair of the Commons foreign affairs committee, said: “Equally likely – and that’s the problem – is that he might use his three aircraft carriers and his buildup of troops in the Gulf and just decide he’s going to invade. Honestly, we don’t know.”

Lord Darroch said: “Trump could go for one last massive attack, particularly focusing on blowing up nuclear sites. Then he could walk away and be able to say it’s been obliterated – again.”

Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox

after newsletter promotion

UK ministers are, however, cautiously optimistic. The markets appear to be as well – with oil prices dropping sharply after the results.

“We know all the risks. We know he could change his mind on Iran again, that he could strike a deal with Putin that locks out Ukraine, that he could announce more indiscriminate tariffs,” one minister said. “But we also see this as a moment of opportunity.”

Thornberry highlighted the Democrats’ very different foreign policy agenda. “Let’s see what happens. I think they come in from January and believe that they’ve got a mandate to finish the Iranian war,” she said.

“On top of that, they are much more sympathetic, as is the general public, to the plight of the Ukrainians and believe that the American president is not playing fair.”

Labour figures are already building links in the new-look Congress, with some Democrats proposing a bill modelled on Labour’s approach to Israeli settlers in the West Bank.

UK ministers say they have had no indications that Trump is planning more tariffs – though acknowledge they could be taken by surprise. “If the UK does something big on legislation or regulation surrounding big tech or AI, then you can imagine it happening,” one said.

But some in UK policy circles argue that a Democrat-run Congress could help advance some of the UK’s international priorities, such as AI regulation or clean energy, both of which have been resisted by the Trump White House.

Government sources said that while they would revive traditional links between Labour and the Democrats before the next presidential election, they were proceeding carefully.

More than one cited the fact that Trump accused Labour of “interference” during the last presidential election after party staff volunteered for Kamala Harris’s campaign. “We need to be cautious – but also it’s entirely reasonable for us to engage with them,” a senior aide said.

Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, met Gavin Newsom, the California governor and a presidential hopeful, last year. But he also attended a college football game in Atlanta with his counterpart, Marco Rubio.

Others inside Labour – including at cabinet level – already have close ties with Democratic allies. Party strategists will reflect on the midterm election tactics, with a view to adopting parts that could work against their opponents on the populist right.

Labour MPs may be relieved that American voters have cast their verdict on Trump and his combative style of politics, with the US just the latest in a list of countries that have rejected rightwing populism at the ballot box.

But party strategists warn against assuming Reform UK would necessarily suffer the same fate. “It’s all about the cost of living: unless we show that we have the answers voters could still look elsewhere,” one said.

Republicans also deny the era is over. Elliott said: “As long as immigration is on the rise and there is poor assimilation of immigrants in western countries, rightwing populism will be a force in politics.”

Senior Labour figures have cautioned against looking too celebratory over the results. “It wasn’t a ringing endorsement of the Dems, just like the last election here wasn’t about an outpouring of affection for Keir,” they said.

“In both cases it was about giving the incumbent a kicking, and all of us progressives need to be careful not to take the wrong message from it.”

UK officials insist it is business as usual as far as Trump is concerned. “It’s important we show respect for the fact that his administration has two years to go,” one said.

Darroch cautioned British politicians against prematurely – or too overtly – focusing on Trump’s potential successors.

“Burnham has to be careful he doesn’t appear to be moving on from Trump and dismissing him as a spent force,” he added. “He will be there until the end. Trump will not gallop gently into a golden sunset. He will rage against the weakening of his grip on power.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: UK ministers say they have had no indications Trump is planning more tariffs. But they say they are cautious about the prospect of more tariffs. Some in UK policy circles argue that a Democrat-run Congress could help advance some of the UK's international priorities.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: ‘I feel free now’: Shabana Mahmood’s immigration shake-up provokes mixed emotions
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Chris Osuh, Aamna Mohdin and Diane Taylor
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Some relatives of British citizens say they feel left behind, but announcement has brought relief to many care workers

“The only time we’re regarded as human beings is when they need a lot of hands onboard, like during Covid. But after that, we’re tossed away like we’re some rubbish,” Aneisha Williams says.

Williams, 39, was months from qualifying for indefinite leave to remain after 10 years in the UK. But claiming housing benefit could delay her settlement for years under Shabana Mahmood’s “earned settlement” plans.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Under pressure from Labour MPs and unions, the home secretary this week offered qualifying care workers a five-year settlement route. But others, among them partners and former partners of British citizens, face continued uncertainty.

Williams, a supermarket worker from London, married a British man in her native Jamaica and joined him in the UK in 2016. Her daughter, now 18, is British. During the Covid crisis, her marriage broke down, leaving them homeless while Williams was on a family life visa.

Migrants with no recourse to public funds can have that restriction lifted in cases of hardship, as Williams did. Housing benefit transformed her life without affecting her settlement prospects at the time.

Last year, Mahmood proposed adding up to 10 years to the settlement qualifying period for benefit claimants. This week she said applicants must have spent five continuous years without relying on benefits.

While Mahmood says family members of British citizens will retain existing settlement pathways, how that protection applies to people whose marriages have broken down or who claimed benefits remains unclear.

“We were never told this would happen, and never would have taken the help if we did, even though my past situation was very grim,” Williams said. “I was due to qualify in a couple of months – now it could be another 10 years.”

Research has found most people on the existing “10-year route”, which Williams is on, are Asian or Black. Williams added: “It’s a racist policy – and it’s like every other year they come up with something that makes you feel further hopeless.”

Ashley, a civil servant from Sheffield who asked to use a pseudonym, arrived from the US in 2017 and moved from student and graduate visas to a spouse visa after marrying a British man in 2025. She expected to qualify in 2027 under the 10-year long-residence route, which the government plans to end. With transitional arrangements unclear, she fears waiting until 2030, by which time she estimates she will have spent £25,000 on visa and healthcare charges.

“I’m one of the privileged immigrants – from a white English-speaking country, I have a PhD. I’m married to a British citizen. And it is still so unbelievably hard,” she said.

Mahmood’s announcement brought relief to many care workers. Under the revised plans, those who entered the route before May 2025 and earn at least £25,000 a year can qualify after five years, rather than the 15 originally proposed. Others face another five-year visa before settlement.

Rasika Samarasinghe, who arrived from Sri Lanka in October 2022 and earns just over £25,000 caring for elderly people, is planning a double celebration. As well as the settlement change, the Home Office has reversed its refusal to let his wife, a teaching assistant, and their three children, aged 12, nine and eight, remain in the UK as his dependants.

Sign up to Breaking News UK

Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox

after newsletter promotion

After sending the family “go home” letters, the Home Office told them the refusal should be disregarded. The Guardian understands similar decisions affecting other care workers’ families have also been reversed.

“I felt so shocked and hopeless when the Home Office said my wife and children could no longer stay here,” Samarasinghe said. “The children are delighted they can stay at school with their friends. Now we can plan our future. I feel free now.” His wife is organising a party for their church friends and everyone who supported them.

The government began restricting care workers’ family visas after the Home Office estimated in 2023 that about 120,000 dependants had joined 100,000 care worker applicants.

Care workers have been barred from bringing family since March 2024, and overseas recruitment was banned from July 2025; Samarasinghe’s family arrived before both. A spokesperson for the Home Office said it did not routinely comment on individual cases, but that applications initially rejected could be approved after a review.

Naga Kandiah of MTC Solicitors welcomed the Home Office’s U-turn, saying: “This is a hugely significant and positive outcome. This family came to the United Kingdom lawfully … We are delighted that this family can now move forward together with renewed hope, security and peace of mind.”

Amenzei Ogiemwonyia, a care worker who campaigned with the Unison union, said: “We organised and refused to be silent, and that’s what the Fairer Visa Campaign was all about: standing up to the rightwing press, lies, propaganda and politics. Some of us are elated – but we still need to read the fine print.”

Campaigners remain concerned. Dr Dora-Olivia Vicol, the chief executive of the Work Rights Centre, called the response, apart from the care-worker concessions, “bitterly disappointing”, and said it was “deeply unfair” that some workers who came expecting a five-year route would now wait 10 years. The Home Office estimates that about 500,000 people will have to wait longer than five years for settlement, which officials say will save billions from the welfare bill.

But claiming housing benefit could delay her settlement for years under Shabana Mahmood's 'earned settlement' plans. Workers who came expecting a five-year route would now wait 10 years.

https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.title: ‘They’re just live experiments’: the dark and deadly world of looksmaxxing
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.author: Adrian Horton
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.text:
A disturbing new docuseries delves deep into a world where men are pushing their bodies to the extreme – and some of them are dying for it

I
f you’ve heard the term looksmaxxing – the manospheric pursuit of male aesthetic beauty via steroids, peptides, cosmetic surgery and total commitment – you probably know the name Clavicular. With more than 2 million followers and a cluster of mainstream media profiles, the 20-year-old streamer born Braden Peters has become the chiseled face of a once fringe movement to achieve algorithmically defined good looks by any means necessary, from daily methamphetamines to breaking your jaw with a hammer. Clavicular has courted attention for a nihilistic worldview expressed in blunt, idiosyncratic argot: “hardmaxxing”, “bone smashing”, anything to increase your “SMV” (sexual market value).

Baffling, horrifying or grimly compelling, depending on your view, Clavicular would be a fascinating documentary subject. Indeed, news of a possible Clavicular documentary has percolated all year, after the influencer filed a cease and desist letter against Disney/Hulu for allegedly filming him backstage at a New York fashion show in February. (It’s far from his most serious legal matter this year – last month, he pleaded not guilty to charges that he raped a 17-year-old girl at his family’s Massachusetts home in May 2025.) But the docuseries in question, Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death, was never actually about Clavicular, who appears only in publicly available snippets. It instead trains its focus upstream of the bone-smashing, on the infamous influencer’s influences: the so-called “biohacking” scene that inspired the youths’ fixation on extreme body modification. And in particular, supplement guru Dr Tony Huge and his acolytes, in the aftermath of the suspicious death of his close associate, the “penis enlargement” expert known as “Leo Longevity”.

“This was a very fringe movement when we began this documentary,” said Stacey Lee, the director of the three-part series. But its influence seemed to expand as rapidly as the subjects’ roided muscles once filming commenced in 2024. “Clavicular grew up on Leo Longevity,” Lee said. “These kids are growing up on that. They are feeding on these projections of masculinity, and we are watching it in real time. What Tony was putting online 10 years ago is being recreated in shorter, faster, far more extreme forms.”

To be clear, the man born Anthony Hughes never advocated for moderation. A former bankruptcy attorney turned bodybuilder with muscles that appear perpetually at risk of bursting through his skin, Tony initially made his “biohacking” name for trying, on camera, the “fat-burning” “supplement” DNP that could, in even mildly excess doses, melt internal organs. A prolific user of steroids and experimenter with substances from the dubious to illicit, Hughes projected brawny confidence at a time when, as he puts it in the first episode, “Society doesn’t have a place for masculine men any more.” (Get Huge is, among other things, a very difficult watch for those with an aversion to “manosphere” bluster, or needles, which jab with stunning frequency.)

To his 250,000 online followers, Hughes hammered the mantra: “a day natty [natural] is a day wasted”. To not be biohacking was to be “beta and controllable”, missing the opportunity to be bigger and better. “They’re just live experiments,” said Lee of the mindset. “Every day is another science experiment to see what I can do with my body in order to augment it.” Ubiquitous daily injections in the face, neck, arm, rear is “the world. To them, it’s like drinking water.” To skirt US regulatory scrutiny – and, as later episodes explore, civil lawsuits and criminal investigations – Hughes relocated to Pattaya, Thailand, in 2017, where he gathered a clique of “passport bros” for content and a self-proclaimed “harem” of paid women. (“A man should only have as many girlfriends as he can leg press,” he says while holding up a pyramid of Thai women.)

Lee, a mother of a nine-year-old son concerned by the far-rightward lurch of male influencers, caught up with Hughes there in 2024, “and immediately it was just doors wide open”, she recalled. “Tony’s whole philosophy is radical transparency – ‘come on in, nothing to hide here’.” The camera crew trailed Tony and two close associates, Elon Muscular and Connor Murphy, as they gym, roid, rip through Pattaya’s sex-work scene and, above all, film. But it was transparency in name only. “We realized quickly that these guys are performers,” Lee said. “They create characters for the internet. And the character for the internet projects radical transparency. What does the human, when the internet is turned off, what are they like?” For young men, “these guys are projecting this blueprint for how to live their lives. We wanted to puncture that and get beneath it.”

Part of that was simply asking questions about what happened to Leo, born Laith Abdullah Algaz, who was found dead in the house he shared with Hughes in January 2023; authorities ruled the cause as blunt force trauma, source unknown. A self-proclaimed penis enlargement expert who fled to Thailand after his estranged wife filed a restraining order, Leo quickly developed an intense bromance with Hughes. (As Elon recalls: “They were more than friends. There was fire between them.”) But the relationship was souring by the end – and Leo, as Lee uncovered, was not the first Tony Huge “ride or die” to actually die. As Get Huge gets deeper, Lee learns that four other close Hughes associates have either died or disappeared under questionable circumstances since 2018, ranging from overdoses to house fire to hanging. And the camera pans out to the making of the documentary itself, as Hughes, Elon Muscular and Murphy, each surely surpassing the daily injectables limit – Murphy claims to be taking anywhere from a dozen to 100 “compounds” per day – snipe at each other and scrap for narrative control.

Lee declined to offer a theory on what happened to Leo or the other men in Hughes’s orbit. “It was more important for us that the theories become a conduit to expose the different systems of this masculine philosophy,” she said. “When people die, I think most people would just be like, ‘Hold up, let’s pump the brakes.’ But that doesn’t happen because they’re part of a community, there is a sense of belonging and they’re almost reinforced in this mindset of like, ‘Oops, we got the experiment wrong, let’s not do that next time.’

“It is really disconcerting when these really complex emotional problems that everyone faces are simplified down to like, get a bigger jaw. Fix your brow line. And make your penis bigger.”

Get Huge certainly contains many disconcerting observations, from the ridiculous (Elon Muscular’s attempt to brand Hughes “the Hugh Hefner of biohacking”) to the sinister (Hughes requesting his “girlfriends” always be naked or wearing “sexy clothes” in his bedroom). But it is a surprisingly empathetic look at an emotionally stunted scene. At one point, Lee point-blank tells Elon that he is enough. “Someone should tell me how I’m supposed to be enough,” he responds.

Get our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every Friday

after newsletter promotion

“I don’t think anyone sets out to do extreme dangerous, violent things,” Lee said of her approach. “I think this really begins in a very human place that we can all relate to, which is how do we become the best version of ourselves. But in this looksmaxxing, biohacking, bodybuilding world where there’s this notion of perfection – and I think we can relate to this as women, too – when those goalposts keep shifting, it’s very hard to know when enough is enough.”

It may never be; in July of this year, two months after filming wrapped, Murphy drowned in the lake behind his house at the age of 32. Eyewitness and police accounts suggest he was experiencing a psychotic break; he had recently documented his attempts to inject himself with pure gold. His death was an emotional blow to Lee and her crew. “Just tragic,” she said. “We were completely floored. We were really upset.” Murphy had, she said, “seemingly become more unstable”, over 18 months of filming. “And I said to Tony and Elon and the friends around, like, ‘Are you guys worried about Connor?’ And this is the hard thing with someone like Connor – he’s like, ‘I’m just performing. This is an act.’ We were trying to penetrate that. Like, what is a performance? What is real?”

“We were definitely witnessing and trying to document what we were experiencing in real time,” she added. “But I think what was the more surprising thing was how everybody else didn’t have any concerns.” The series, she hopes, will present “a more complicated, multidimensional person behind this online performance”.

Get Huge offers few answers, either to the question of what happened to Leo Longevity and Connor Murphy, or how to get someone out of nihilistic spiral in an interminably aesthetics obsessed world. “Where the solutions lie in all of this is what we’re consuming online – looking for more authentic, real role models for young men to look up to,” Lee said. Short of that, Get Huge proposes two supplements in short supply: compassion and skepticism. “We weren’t coming in here pointing a finger,” said Lee. “We want audiences to have these conversations. We want audiences to think, decipher, discern what is real and what is not.”

Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death is available on Hulu in the US on 10 November and Disney+ elsewhere

Four other close friends of Leo Longevity and Connor Murphy have either died or disappeared under questionable circumstances since 2018.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: Yes, saunas are great – but have you heard of this amazing thing called a bath?
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Lucy Knight
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
Ever since the ancient Greeks, we’ve suspected that soaking in hot water is good for your health. Now science has proved it

A
t a time when many of us feel overwhelmed, overstretched and over-reliant on screens, it’s unsurprising that the wellness industry is booming, with spa facilities – saunas in particular – becoming increasingly popular places to rest the body and mind.

But if a trip to the spa seems like too much effort or money, then good news! An alternative could be waiting for you right behind your bathroom door: hot baths. Though washing habits have shifted towards showers in recent years, the majority of UK homes are still fitted with bathtubs. Not only is bathing less expensive than a sauna session; it may be more effective at lowering blood pressure and boosting the immune system, according to research from the University of Oregon.

Other studies have suggested that a bath’s benefits could be comparable to aerobic exercise, and that it may reduce blood sugar levels. Now, scientists at Manchester Metropolitan University, with funding from the British Heart Foundation, are exploring whether immersion in hot water can relieve the symptoms of peripheral artery disease (PAD), a common circulatory disease that usually affects arteries in the lower legs, making walking painful.

Stockport-based Ken Heywood, 75, took part in an eight-week heat-therapy trial after the symptoms of PAD, first diagnosed when he was 38, worsened. He was monitored as he attended hot-tub sessions three times a week, with the water heated to 40C (a few degrees warmer than hot tubs are generally set).

By the end of the trial, “my blood pressure had got better, certainly my walking had got better”, says the retired engineering manager. He surpassed his aim of completing his daily dog walks without having to stop at every bench, and managed to climb to the top of the hill in his local park, an incline that previously would have “terrified” him, he says. Since the trial ended, Heywood has kept to three baths a week at home, alongside physiotherapy and exercise – and he’s still noticing positive results.

Bathing in hot water improves blood circulation “because our core temperature rises, and that will drive the blood to the skin, away from organs”, says William Carey, one of the academics running the trial. This process is particularly helpful for someone like Heywood, whose body is not sending blood to his legs as efficiently as it should be, but it is likely to be good for most people’s cardiovascular health, says Carey. (He caveats this with a recommendation to consult your GP, particularly if you have low blood pressure.) Since his involvement in the research project, “I tend to take a hot bath every so often,” he adds.

The idea of baths being good for your health is generally associated with the ancient Greeks and Romans, who popularised bathing and spa treatments. “Humorism” was a system of medicine practised between the fifth century BC and 17th century AD that referred to what physicians considered the vital body fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile. These “humours”, when imbalanced, caused illness. The humours were thought to be either hot or cold, or dry or moist, and if you were believed to have a dry humour in excess, bathing in hot water was considered “a good way of rebalancing things”, says medical historian and retired GP Roger Rolls. According to the theory, bathing could treat medical conditions ranging from cataracts to arthritis.

When microbes were discovered in the 17th century, humorism was debunked, but doctors continued to find bathing effective for certain aches, pains and skin diseases. Some of that may have been a placebo effect, Rolls concedes, but there was some truth to the belief in bathing’s healing effects. Even now, he says, “quite a lot of hospitals have their own hydrotherapy department”, using immersion in water to help rehabilitate people with neuromuscular disorders.

Baths also offer us a mental break. Influencer Grace Booth, who bathes four or five times a week, says: “As a busy working mum, I rarely have time to myself, and I really struggle with feeling I should always be doing something productive. My mind can run away with me, so baths are my enforced relaxation time.” Booth, who posts on Instagram and TikTok as gracebooth97, has attracted hundreds of thousands of followers with pictures of the “themed baths” her husband creates for her (for example, at Easter he adorned the bathroom with egg-shaped candles). After a bath, “I feel so rested and re-centred,” she says. “We put so much thought into a calming bath and bedtime routine for children, but somehow forget to give ourselves the same wind-down time.”

Heywood, who took baths infrequently before his involvement in the trial, has found mental as well as physical benefit in “lying there and just relaxing”. He plans to continue including hot baths in his routine, alongside an increased exercise regimen, both of which appear to be reducing his pain. But bathing is “the easy bit”, he says, so the fact it has so many benefits feels like a huge win. “It’s a lot easier than exercising on a treadmill.”

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: Autism, masking, and building a more inclusive world | Letters
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Guardian Staff
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Readers respond to an article by John Harris on the rise in the number of people labelled autistic over the last 20 years

John Harris’s article addresses all the main issues that are being debated around autism (‘The term is becoming unrecognisable’: have the experts who believed in a single autism spectrum changed their minds?, 1 November). However, I feel it did not go far enough to broaden our understanding of the challenges experienced by autistic people who do not have a learning disability.

From a young age I sensed that I was experiencing the world differently to other people. I was bullied, and worked hard to fit in. I was fortunate as structurally I had a stable life that mitigated some of the more challenging aspects of my life. Things started to get less manageable when I entered adulthood and left home.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Since the age of 25 I have experienced bouts of depression and ongoing anxiety, often resulting in breakdowns, or what I now understand to be autistic burnouts. Throughout adulthood I have seen numerous medical professionals and repeatedly been directed towards therapies, designed to deal with anxiety and depression, which have had limited success in addressing my life challenges.

Despite having a postgraduate education, I have struggled to hold down many jobs and have had to leave most due to stress. I have ongoing relationship problems. I don’t have children, partly due to reluctance and health issues. I suffer from fatigue and sleep issues.

I was finally diagnosed with autistic spectrum disorder at the age of 53. My diagnosis has allowed me to understand my life; what has been harder is getting other people (including health professionals) to understand how challenging it is for me. If there were more stories published that went beyond accounts of obsessional collecting behaviours or discussing whether people make eye contact, perhaps there could be a greater understanding of what autism can look like, informing experts on how to support people appropriately and how to categorise it.
 
 Louise King
 
 London

Having spent years working adjacent to mental health services, I have come across many people with “classic” autism. I remember when Asperger’s was dropped and “autism spectrum disorders” came into use, I initially mistook the “spectrum” as a continuum we are all on. I know I was wrong, but I wonder if this framework holds a broader social truth – a spectrum with classic autistic people at the far end, Asperger’s a little way along and most people between the middle and the opposite end.

I’m not autistic, but I’m socially uncomfortable. I can confidently present to an audience of hundreds and my grasp of language is good – but I hate using the phone, don’t like meeting people, avoid parties and need my own space a lot. I think that makes me an introvert, but that’s another term that has been adopted as an “identity” rather than a defined classification. As psychiatrists and psychologists taught me, most diagnoses are essentially descriptions; if a description sounds like you, is long-lasting and is a significant problem for your functioning, then you get that label. What this idea misses is that almost everyone finds some aspects of life functionally difficult.

Rather than continuously expanding clinical classifications to grant people validity, perhaps we should focus on creating a society where anyone (or their advocates) can declare what they struggle with, and have our communities and services respond with appropriate flexibility and understanding.
 
 Salli Ward
 
 Market Harborough, Leicestershire

John Harris quotes Uta Frith calling masking “completely unfalsifiable”, then moves on as if no one had tried to falsify it.

People have. Will Mandy’s group at University College London built the standard masking questionnaire and has spent years publishing its weaknesses, which is what good science looks like. Meng-Chuan Lai and colleagues measured masking by comparing how autistic adults present in a clinical interview with how they perform on social-cognition tests, a gap no one can produce simply by saying they mask.

At Birkbeck, University of London, Jagdeep Wadhwa-Brown is now recording neural activity in autistic adults during social tasks, alongside their own accounts of masking. The study is at an early stage, but it is exactly the kind of test Frith says cannot be done. The neuroscientist Francesca Happé has described watching the mask slip in a tired house guest. That is an observation, not a feeling.

Between us, every week we assess people who present with what is sometimes called “internalised” autism: people who make eye contact, hold down demanding jobs and have spent decades being told, like Abigail Stow (who featured in Harris’s article), that they “can’t possibly be autistic”. The measures need work, and the researchers say so. But “the measure needs work” and “the phenomenon does not exist” are different claims, and only one was put to readers.
 
 Dr Louise Legg
 
 Counselling psychologist, London
 
 Dr Emma Bede
 
 Clinical psychologist, London

Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: EU charges TikTok with failing to protect users’ mental health
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Jennifer Rankin in Brussels
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Regulator’s initial ruling says algorithm ‘can be harmful’ and led young and vulnerable viewers ‘down rabbit holes they can’t easily escape’

TikTok has been charged by the European Commission with failing to protect users’ mental health by exposing them to a relentless stream of content that risks worsening eating disorders and anxiety in a case that strikes at its business model.

Issuing a preliminary ruling on Friday, the EU regulator said TikTok’s algorithm “can be harmful” and was leading young and vulnerable users “down rabbit holes they cannot easily escape from”.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The Chinese-owned short-video platform, which has 189 million users in the EU, was found to have failed to prevent users from being served up repetitive content on themes such as body image or isolation, which can lead to anxiety, sadness, worsen existing eating disorders or mental health problems.

Officials said their investigation focused on legal content, where a single video might not be problematic, but the cumulative effect of watching scores of them on one theme could damage users’ mental health.

TikTok’s safeguards to mitigate the risks of “rabbit-hole effects” – where users are served narrow and repetitive content to keep them engaged – were found to be ineffective. For example, officials said, if a user checked a “not interested” button on a video about eating patterns, the algorithm would still offer them similar content on diet and body image. Similarly, refreshing a feed only provided a brief respite from a stream of content on one topic, it found.

“Every time a user scrolls or likes a video on TikTok, the algorithm serves more of the same leading users down rabbit holes they cannot easily escape from,” said the European Commission’s lead official on tech policy, Henna Virkkunen. “TikTok needs to step up its efforts to protect users’ wellbeing, including those of minors.”

In response, a TikTok spokesperson said: “The commission has made a series of statements that are fundamentally inaccurate and distort our platform’s architecture and our commitment to user safety.

“We have a strong record of protecting our community while giving users direct and intuitive control over their content experience.”

The company argues that its policies prohibit content that promotes disordered eating and risky weight-management behaviours. It also says that more than 79 million users in the EU used its “not interested” or keyword filters to screen out unwanted content in the first six months of 2026.

The Molly Rose Foundation, which was set up in memory of 14-year-old Molly Russell, who took her own life in 2017 after being exposed to a torrent of harmful online content, welcomed what it called the landmark findings “to seek to hold TikTok to account for the way their algorithm drives young people down rabbit holes of despair”.

A survey for the charity earlier this year found that nearly half of girls and a third of all UK teenagers saw suicide, self-harm and eating-disorder content on social media in a week.

The foundation called on the UK regulator, Ofcom, to open an investigation into TikTok’s “extremely damaging” algorithm.

The EU investigation strikes at TikTok’s business model, which is built on keeping users scrolling as long as possible.

EU officials want TikTok to change the design of its ForYou feed, to give users greater control over the content they see.

“We are addressing a business model,” a commission official told reporters, saying that a business model focused mainly on engagement “can potentially create a risk” especially for minors and vulnerable adults.

The findings are part of a broader investigation launched in February 2024 under the Digital Services Act, which obliges large internet companies to take action to prevent a wide range of harms, from disinformation to damage to mental health.

The commission has already found the company violated EU rules over its “addictive design” for features such as infinite scroll. The company said at the time “the commission’s preliminary findings present a categorically false and entirely meritless depiction of our platform” and that it would challenge the findings.

A complaint about lack of transparency over who paid for TikTok’s advertising was resolved when the company made binding commitments to change its policies last December.

TikTok, which now has a chance to examine the investigation file and mount a defence, could agree to change its recommender system to avoid a fine.

If EU officials uphold the finding, the company could be fined up to 6% of its global worldwide turnover.

In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org
