https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: This is an age of anti-vaccine unreason – and even NHS staff are not immune | Polly Toynbee
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Polly Toynbee
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
When fewer than half of health service workers have taken up the flu vaccine, there is little hope for the rest of us

G
ood news. Edward Jenner’s rustic thatched hut in his Gloucestershire garden where he conducted his first smallpox vaccination in 1796 has just been saved by English Heritage. Here Jenner gave free vaccinations every week to local people. Here he became the single human being to save more lives than any other person who has ever lived.

This triumph of the age of enlightenment, at a time when a third of children died before adulthood, is too easily forgotten. But enlightenment itself has been in retreat, with Robert F Kennedy Jr, Donald Trump’s health secretary, leading the vanguard of unreason, dismantling vaccination programmes and stirring vaccine conspiracy and paranoia around the world. His infectious messaging has contributed to falling vaccination rates in rich as well as poor countries. Here’s hoping this week is the end of that Trumpian rolling back of reason.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

What would Jenner think now as the winter flu season approaches? Last year fewer than half of frontline NHS staff in England were vaccinated, with only one in 10 trusts reaching the (very low) NHS target of 60% protected against flu. Healthcare workers have a high risk of catching flu, spreading it to vulnerable people and to their own families, and taking sick days when they are most needed. These people are trained in science, steeped in evidence of the extraordinary value of vaccines, and yet many are reluctant. Doctors were the staff group that scored the highest, but still only half of them got vaccinated – half! – instead of influencing the public towards protection.

Overall, healthcare workers in GP practices were the most likely to take up the vaccine, with 53.5% covered: they have most access, and are likely to be prodded by colleagues. But even so, that’s disgracefully low for people with signs on their noticeboards urging patients to get the jab (free for NHS and care staff, under-16s, over-65s and vulnerable people). Official figures show an astonishing difference between the best and worst NHS trusts, from the highest at 77.2% to the lowest at 0.6%.

Why so few? The reasons, finds the National Institute for Health and Care Research, are complex. The easiest to solve are practical obstacles – for example, badly timed clinics not matching work on the wards, instead of anytime drop-in sessions. But deeper reasons suggest staff lack the motivation or are suspicious of employers, with some “feeling like the organisation does not care”, finds the NIHC.

Some don’t think flu is serious, others that vaccines don’t work, or that protective equipment and hand gels will do. Some don’t trust vaccine safety information, while others fear secret side-effects and distrust pharmaceutical companies.

Ethnic minority staff are more likely to be vaccine hesitant out of general mistrust of institutions they feel are not on their side. But, as compilers of the latest NHS guidance stress to me, the variation in rates of vaccination is miles wider than the smaller disparities in ethnic makeup or social differences in staff: that can’t account for that yawning 77.2% to 0.6% gap.

Something happened during the pandemic that stopped NHS staff getting vaccinated. Despite the heroic risks they took then, Covid has left a strong residue of mistrust, alongside a poisonous stream of anti-vaccine misinformation on social media. Meanwhile, the anti-science right keeps stirring suspicion of anything the state recommends. Before Covid, 74% of NHS staff took the flu vaccine, but now the official target has fallen to just 60%, though the NHS constitution commits to a 100% offer of the jab to eligible groups.

The mystery is why NHS staff, most of whom are dedicated to their patients, don’t do the right thing of their own accord. As a matter of patient safety, vaccination should be a compulsory condition of NHS service (excluding those who cannot be vaccinated for medical reasons). Anyone working with children needs a DBS check, drivers need licences, doctors and nurses need qualifications. Compulsion was ordered in late 2021 as some staff refused the Covid vaccine mid-pandemic, but it was rescinded almost immediately when surveys suggested 80,000 people might lose their roles. No one dared test if that would really happen, when losing so many staff would do more damage to patients than the risk of infection.

What would work? The NHS coordinator I spoke to said that trusts with high staff vaccinations encourage close colleagues to act as persuaders and explainers, convincing all but a few adamants. You wonder about the working culture of hospitals with very low rates and disaffected staff.

The NHS has 1.55 million staff, reaching deep into every community. They should be vaccine advocates at a time when fewer children under five are getting their full routine jabs – down again this year, failing the World Health Organization’s 95% threshold for herd immunity.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The next flu pandemic is a matter of “when, not if”, says the WHO. For national herd immunity, we need compulsory vaccination as a civic duty, along with compulsory voting and paying your taxes. Flu vaccines last winter prevented about 100,000 hospitalisations, but in a bad flu wave an average of 2,660 patients a week will occupy a hospital bed. But fearful politicians think that this is a price worth paying rather than face down libertarian anti-vaxxers.

What would Jenner think of today’s NHS staff? This smallpox saviour faced fierce opposition but his work was later championed by the pro-science Prince Albert, who erected a statue in his memory in Trafalgar Square, amid demonstrations by anti-vaxxers and the military who regarded those plinths as theirs. Within a year of Albert’s death in 1861, they shunted Jenner off to a remote spot in Kensington Gardens and erected on his plinth Maj Gen Sir Henry Havelock, who died of dysentery at the siege of Lucknow while putting down an Indian rebellion.

Time, I think, for a national vaccination day, in keeping with our current life-sciences success. Jenner should be brought back from exile in a triumphal carriage to his plinth and Sir Henry – well, anyone who wants him can have him.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Nadeem Badshah
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Doctor who was helping response to outbreak in Africa taken to specialist isolation unit at Royal Free hospital

A British doctor who tested positive for Ebola while working in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has returned to the UK for specialist treatment.

The patient, whose identity is unknown, was transported home on a medical evacuation flight, the Department of Health and Social Care said on Thursday. They are now being cared for in a specialised high-level isolation unit at the Royal Free hospital in Hampstead, north London.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Dr Renu Bindra, the deputy director for all-hazards public health response at the UK Health Security Agency, said: “UKHSA and the NHS have well-established and robust infection prevention and control protocols to limit the risk of onward transmission, and the risk to the wider public remains low.”

A humanitarian organisation sent the doctor to DR Congo to help in the response to the outbreak, which is the second largest on record. It is the first case involving a British national contracting Ebola in the current outbreak.

The Royal Free's isolation unit has strict protocols in place to prevent the patient coming into contact with any members of the public, and all staff treating the patient are equipped with the necessary personal protective equipment alongside other measures to prevent transmission.

Ebola is a highly contagious, severe and often fatal illness spread through direct contact with body fluids such as the blood or vomit of infected people, or dead bodies.

The current outbreak, declared in May by DR Congo’s health ministry, has surpassed 10,000 cases and 5,000 deaths. It has spread to Kenya and Uganda in east Africa, and last month Nigeria confirmed a case in its capital, Abuja.

People with the disease tend to fall ill two to 21 days after contact with an orthoebolavirus. Initial symptoms include fever, aches, pains, and fatigue, but can then progress to diarrhoea, vomiting and unexplained bleeding.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: Cancer diagnoses in England hit record high of more than 1,000 people a day
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Anna Bawden Health and social affairs correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
While NHS is identifying more cases, it is failing to meet timescale targets on diagnosis and treatment, experts say

Cancer diagnoses in England have hit record highs, with more than 1,000 people a day diagnosed, NHS figures show.

But experts warned that although the health service was identifying more cases, it was still failing to meet timescale targets on diagnosis and treatment.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

According to the latest cancer registration statistics, more than 373,000 people were diagnosed with cancer in England in 2024, the highest figure on record. On average, NHS England diagnosed 1,021 people a day with cancer in 2024, up from 972 a day in 2023.

Prostate, breast, lung and bowel cancers accounted for half of all new diagnoses.

The figures showed improvements in stage at diagnosis: 56.7% of first new cancers were diagnosed at stage 1 and 2 in 2024 compared with 55.8% in 2023.

Prof Peter Johnson, the NHS national clinical director for cancer, said the figures showed the health service was “moving in the right direction” and were testimony to NHS staff’s hard work.

He said: “NHS teams across the country are taking tests and checks closer to the people who need them, and with new treatments being developed all the time, we will continue to do all we can to get people seen and treated for cancer as early as possible.”

Experts urged caution, however, given the NHS is failing to meet its timescale targets. The latest monthly NHS figures show that 78.6% of patients in England urgently referred for suspected cancer were diagnosed or had cancer ruled out within 28 days in August – below the target of 80%.

The health service is lagging even further behind on treatment. The proportion of patients who began treatment for cancer within 62 days of an urgent referral or consultant upgrade was 71.9%, well below the target of 85%.

Dr Ian Walker, the executive director of policy at Cancer Research UK, said: “While NHS staff are diagnosing more people with cancer every day, too many are still being caught at a late stage.”

The health service needed additional support to reduce the number of cancers diagnosed at a late stage and treat patients on time, he added.

Walker said: “The UK government pledged to improve early diagnosis, cancer waiting times and access to treatment in its national cancer plan for England. It now needs to keep its foot on the pedal to ensure cancer patients aren’t let down. The situation won’t change without focused effort from the government, clear accountability, and a guarantee that the NHS will get the specialist staff and equipment it needs.”

Dr Hilary Williams, the clinical vice-president at the Royal College of Physicians and a consultant in medical oncology, said: “More than 1,000 cancer diagnoses every day is a stark reminder of the growing demand on NHS cancer services.

“An ageing population is an important factor in the increase in diagnoses, but we must also recognise the role of obesity, which is a major and often overlooked risk factor for cancer.” She added that alongside preventing cancer, the NHS needed to continue improving early detection, including through the expansion of targeted lung cancer screening.

Williams said: “As more people are diagnosed and live longer with cancer, we must ensure they can access the specialist care and support they need.”

Steven McIntosh, the chief partnerships officer at Macmillan Cancer Support, said the figures also masked persistent health inequalities. “We know that who you are and where you live can still have a significant impact on how likely you are to get cancer, as well as how quickly you are diagnosed and your chances of survival,” he said.

Rachael Franklin, the deputy chief executive of Breast Cancer Now, said with diagnoses at an all-time high and overall incidence increasing, “breast cancer remains the biggest killer of working-age women in the UK, with one in seven women diagnosed in their lifetime”.

“That’s why it’s so important that people of all ages are breast aware and get anything new or unusual checked by a GP as soon as possible. We also urge all eligible women to attend their screening appointment when invited,” she said.
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.summary: More than 373,000 people were diagnosed with cancer in England in 2024, the highest figure on record. On average, NHS England diagnosed 1,021 people a day with cancer. Prostate, breast, lung and bowel cancers accounted for half of all new diagnoses.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: Beware ‘sun, sea and surgery’ cosmetic tourism packages, experts advise
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Nicola Davis Science correspondent

British College of Aesthetic Medicine launches checklist as part of ‘vet it before you get it’ campaign

Cosmetic tourism is often sold as a package of sun, sea and surgery, but experts have said travelling overseas for procedures can end in infections, disfigurement and death.

Nora Nugent, a consultant plastic surgeon and former president of the British Association of Aesthetic Plastic Surgeons, said travelling to countries such as Turkey for surgery came with myriad risks – and not just on the operating table.

“Actually, the risks start from the moment you step on the plane to after you return home, and until you’re fully healed and you’re out of the clotting risk time,” she said, noting that travel itself could increase the risks of clots. A lack of in-person aftercare is also a concern.

The British College of Aesthetic Medicine has launched a checklist as part of its “vet it before you get it” campaign, intended to help potential patients make better and safer choices about overseas cosmetic surgery.

As well as setting out red flags to look out for, the campaign suggests those seeking cosmetic surgery independently verify a surgeon’s qualifications, determine what emergency facilities are available near the chosen clinic and find out what insurance the practitioner has in place.

Nugent said a major driver for patients seeking procedures in countries such as Turkey was their relative cheapness, but that prices were high in the UK as a result of factors including the higher cost of living and higher fees for medical indemnity and insurance.

Chrissie Wolfe, the founder and chief executive of Lupa Law, a specialist medical negligence practice, said there could be a host of difficulties in making a claim should a procedure go wrong overseas, and that even if compensation were awarded, it could be far lower than in the UK.

“Turkey is the most popular destination by far for cosmetic surgery, but it is absolutely the most difficult from a legal perspective,” she said. “When something goes wrong, it’s incredibly difficult to put right.”

She said those looking to undergo cosmetic surgery abroad should be wary of clinics selling bundles of procedures or time-limited deals, noting that one patient had gone to Turkey for a tummy tuck but was upsold a “mummy makeover” that included a breast uplift.

“She came back and had a very severe infection,” she said. “She ultimately ended up losing most of her left breast and the entire right breast on a procedure that she didn’t even want in the first place.”

Wolfe said the marketing of travelling abroad for cosmetic surgery as a glossy holiday was problematic. “It shifts the patient’s mind away from the seriousness of what they’re actually embarking on,” she said.

It is not the first time overseas cosmetic surgery has sparked warnings. The then health secretary, Wes Streeting, urged caution over such procedures in 2024.

Data, however, suggests growing numbers of residents in Great Britain are travelling overseas for medical treatment. According to data from the Office for National Statistics, about 524,000 did so in 2024, including cosmetic procedures, up from 431,000 in 2023.

Brazillian butt lifts (BBLs) have the highest risk of death, but other overseas procedures have also left patients with problems.

Nugent cited the case of a woman who had developed abscesses and infections in her neck after a facelift. She needed long-term antibiotics and drainage procedures and was left with significant scarring.

Another woman in her late 20s had a breast lift and labiaplasty abroad after pregnancy. She ended up with a loss of tissue on one breast, her implant exposed and over-reduced labia. As a result she needed corrective surgeries, including to redo the lifts and improve the labiaplasty.

“But you can’t get things back to how they were,” said Nugent.

A third woman underwent a tummy tuck overseas, she said, but the wound came apart and required surgical cleaning. She has been left with scarring and a dip in her tummy.

“These are three examples of patients who suffered fairly horrific complications from procedures that were meant to improve how they looked and how they felt about themselves and have ended up doing exactly the opposite,” Nugent said.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/liv.title: Burnham says long-awaited 10-year plan may be delayed until January – as it happened
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/liv.author: Andrew Sparrow
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/liv.text:
Andy Burnham has confirmed that his long-awaited 10-year plan may be delayed.

In his speech outside No 10 on the day he became PM, Burham declared that “later this year” he would “bring forward a new plan for Britain, a 10-year plan, laying out a path from where we are now to where I believe we all want Britain to be”. The document has been described as the core policy statement coming from No 10 this year, with some insiders briefing that the budget was relatively low-key because key announcements were being held back for the 10-year plan.

But we may have to wait a little longer then expected until we see it. In an interview with Hugo Gye from the Economist, when asked when it would appear, Burnham said:

We may go into the new year, to be honest ... December or January, I think we will need to leave that open.

Burnham was speaking after Ailbhe Rea in the New Statesman published an article yesterday suggesting that, even when the initial 10-year plan announcement comes at the end of this year (or in January), that won’t be the final word. Rea said:

Yet, with expectations high, some familiar with the process are already worried that the Ten-Year Plan may be another kicking of the can. I can reveal that it may not be the long, comprehensive document that we might have expected, and will be the beginning – not the end – of a long consultation process.

It will be a speech, delivered by the prime minister before Christmas, to tick the box of a plan delivered “later this year”, accompanied by a document that may be “slimmer than expected”. It will mark the beginning of a six-to-nine-month process of consulting with the public, think tanks and everybody else about government priorities – as well as kickstarting work across government to define what some of its plans will look like in more detail. That process, in turn, will set the priorities for the spending review, itself a procedure that will take months. Suddenly, critics fear, we are looking at a government spending well over a year discussing its plans without taking the major action to address them.

Andy Burnham has said he wants to “recast” the UK’s deal to cede control of the Chagos Islands after resistance from Washington, which said the agreement could instead be modelled on America’s Greenland deal with Denmark.

Andy Burnham has confirmed that his long-awaited 10-year plan may be delayed. (See 12.42pm.)

Shabana Mahmood’s changes to the migration system could harm women and children, a Labour MP has warned, as members of her own party continue to raise concerns with the home secretary’s proposals.

The EU is seeking a firmer pledge from the British government to guarantee European students discounted rates on university tuition fees before a much-anticipated summit this month.

For a full list of all the stories covered on the blog today, do scroll through the list of key event headlines near the top of the blog.

Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, has said her officials are “extremely excited” about one of the more obscure, but potentially most significant, changes in last week’s budget – the creation of a new category of “preventative” spending.

Internal government spending negotiations are all about DEL (departmental expenditure limits), and standard government accounting differentiates between resource DEL (day-to-day spending) and capital DEL.

Last week John Healey, the chancellor, announced that he would create a new category of ringfenced spending in the spending review next year – preventative DEL, or PDEL. This will ensure that budgets are protected for measures involving early intervention to create savings in the long term.

Giving evidence to the Commons health committee yesterday, Cooper said that her public health officials were “extremely excited” about this announcement. She said:

We think a lot of our investment across not just public health but across the NHS has benefits in terms of keeping people healthy and in work. A lot of those treatment budgets have a consequence in helping people work as well as in the direct prevention.

Cooper said that, as a former Treasury minister, she knew that preventative programmes designed to deliver benefits in the long term were “the areas that always come under shortest-term pressure”.

Asked how rigorous her definition of preventative spending would be, she replied:

Mine would be quite broad; we do not yet know what the Treasury’s will be …

A lot of our treatment services have an impact, in saving money elsewhere. Mental health is a really good example, as we know that a lot of young people who are not in work could benefit from mental health support.

Cooper is already in a better position than most other cabinet ministers because the health budget is one of the few that it nominally protected from real-terms cuts.

Heather Stewart, the Guardian’s economics editor, wrote a good column on the potential benefits of PDEL at the weekend.

Peter Walker has also posted these on Bluesky about what Angus MacIntyre said when Peter asked him why he did not mention Ukraine in his first speech as Reform UK’s armed forces spokesperson.

In a 16-minute speech on defence, Reform’s new armed forces spokesperson did not mention Ukraine or Iran once.

Worth noting that I asked MacIntyre about this after and he said this was simply as his speech was to introduce him and his role, and that Ukraine/Iran are very much a focus

Peter Walker is a senior Guardian political correspondent.

Polling numbers which have seen the Conservatives climb above Reform UK are not credible, Nigel Farage has said, claiming that there had been “jiggery-pokery” intended to restore the two-party system.

Farage made the claim unprompted while speaking to reporters after a speech when he was asked if Reform UK had failed in vetting, given the number of councillors and candidates found to have said offensive things or, in some cases, charged with serious offences.

The Reform UK leader said that while politicians from other parties had been arrested for alleged offences, it was only those connected to his party – notably this week’s charging of George Madgwick, its leader on Hampshire county council, with 12 counts of rape and other offences – that led to “a BBC push notification – the others don’t”.

Digressing into polling, he said:

What I will tell you is this: the jiggery-pokery that is going on with polling is utterly astonishing. And if you believe the polls you’ve seen this week, you’re not understanding what’s going on out there. On the raw data, we’re four points higher, and the Conservatives are nearly four points lower than the reality.

And I know there’s a desperate push from the establishment – let’s get back to two-party politics, let’s get back to Tweedledum and Tweedledee. Let’s get back to total failure. Let’s make sure there’s no change.

It simply isn’t true. What you’ve seen from the polling industry is nonsense, and I mean that.

He did not offer any evidence for the claim.

Farage adopted a different line in a recent GB News appearance when he said he did not mind being behind in the opinion polls because he thought that would make campaigning easier. (See 1.51pm.)

Peter Walker is a senior Guardian political correspondent.

The main lesson for Reform UK from the Republicans’ huge defeat in the US midterm elections is “keep your promises”, Nigel Farage has told reporters in his first comments since the results.

Speaking after a media event at which the party unveiled their new armed forces spokesperson, Angus MacIntyre, a former RAF officer, Farage said Trump was also being punished for the “bizarre” decision to wage a long-term conflict with Iran.

Asked if he had learned something from the US results, Farage said:

Yes, keep your promises. Trump was very good in the first term and the second term in keeping his promises, but he broke a promise. That was no more foreign wars, and we’re eight months in, and the resultant rise in gas and diesel prices, more than anything else, is what did them in.

The key focus must be keeping your promises, and the cost of living, of course.

Asked if the Iran war – which Farage did not initially oppose – was a mistake, Farage said:

No question about it. I mean, to have quick tactical strikes from Diego Garcia, to try and maybe not halt, but at least slow the nuclear weapons programme, I totally agree with that …

But would I have said to them, ‘Yes, come on, let’s go to war for the next eight months or three years’? No, of course not. And that is so bizarre.

The government has announced it is spending £13m on another wave of Valour-recognised support centres for military veterans and their families. In the first round, 14 organisations got funding earlier this year, and another 21 organisations are now getting money. “An estimated one million veterans and their families in the UK will benefit from easier access to local services, thanks to the Valour network expanding,” the government says.

Shabana Mahmood has been accused of causing “distress and uncertainty” to hundreds of thousands of refugees by quietly introducing plans to force them to wait up to 30 years before being granted the right to settle in the UK, Rajeev Syal reports.

The latest episode of the Guardian’s Politics Weekly UK podcast is out. It features Pippa Crerar and Kiran Stacey talking about the US midterm elections results, and what lessons they may offer to Labour.

After MacIntyre finished his speech, Farage did not take questions on camera in the main hall where the rally was taking place. But he is speaking to journalists in a “huddle” shortly.

MacIntyre says, if Reform UK wins the election, it will end ongoing prosections of veterans.

And future prosecutions would only be allowed with the consent of the defence secretary, he says.

(This is not that different from the situation that will apply under the Northern Ireland Troubles bill, currently going through parliament. It says any Troubles-related prosecutions will only be allowed with the explicit consent of the attorney general.)

MacIntyre complains about the prosecution of veterans over alleged war crimes. Veterans should be treated as heroes, but they are treated as criminals, he says.

Human rights lawyers dissect the decisions taken by servicemen in the heat of battle, life and death situations that no civilian can imagine.

Government lawyers use the luxury of hindsight, often decades on, to drag our veterans through the courts, treating them as criminals at every stage.

This is unjust and immoral.

We are witnessing the Marxist rewriting of history’s narratives, calling evil good and good evil.

A functioning society celebrates, not criminalises, its armed forces personnel.

My colleague Peter Walker is at the Reform UK event. He has posted these about Angus MacIntyre.

I am at a Reform UK event at which they are about to unveil their new armed forces [spokesperson], a just-retired RAF officer called Angus MacIntyre. As someone who ended a 40-year military career just last week he has no apparent social media presence, which must be useful for Reform.

Note he is armed forces spokesperson, not the main defence brief. Two years-plus from the election, that brief for Reform is still unfilled, as are a few other fairly key ones eg health.

MacIntyre seems like a real believer. This is him on asylum: “Uncontrolled illegal migration has brought hundreds of thsouands of undocumented fighting-age males, many with combat eperience and operatives from hostile states into the heart of our communities.”

He also says that zet zero has “collapsed our industrial base, and they put our energy sovereignty at risk”. He is a confident speaker, so my guess is we’ll see a fair bit more of him. But he is also a complete political novice, so there is always a risk of something going wrong.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: Regulation of counsellors and psychotherapists would protect patients | Letters
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Guardian Staff
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Readers respond to the recommendation by an independent commission that the profession be regulated

The independent commission established by the professional bodies that represent counsellors and psychotherapists in the UK makes a case for statutory regulation that is long overdue (Report, 2 November). Ella Janneh, who won damages in a civil case against her therapist, is right that most people assume the safeguards already exist, and the commission is right to say that they do not. What happened to her shows what that mistaken assumption can cost.

I write as the chairperson of the Irish Association of Humanistic and Integrative Psychotherapy and as a psychotherapist for more than 20 years. I trained in the UK and have practised in Ireland ever since. In both countries, personal therapy and supervised practice have long been the foundation of training.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Coru, Ireland’s health regulator, has overruled its own counsellors and psychotherapists registration board and published training standards requiring no personal therapy, no clinical supervision and no minimum training duration if it can be believed, despite strong opposition from the main training and accreditation bodies.

Requiring personal therapy and supervision is essential. It helps to screen out those unfit to hold power. Without these standards, abuse survivors risk being failed again. Clients deserve a therapist who has worked through their own pain, rather than bringing it into the room with a vulnerable person. Statutory regulation must safeguard the integrity of the profession and protect the public by placing personal therapy and clinical supervision at its core. A regulated title offers no real protection if the training behind it has been hollowed out.
 
 Jacky Grainger
 
 Irish Association of Humanistic and Integrative Psychotherapy

At last there is interest in statutory regulation for counsellors and psychotherapists. This is not the first time this idea has been broached. Indeed, the profession previously made great efforts to interest the government in controlling the title. As early as 1991, the UK Council for Psychotherapy was discussing the route to this. The Liberal Democrat peer John Alderdice tried to interest David Cameron’s government, but it was dismissed as not important.

It took me seven years to become a psychotherapist, with personal therapy throughout. We need counsellors and psychotherapists who understand, through their own experience, the emotional difficulty of undertaking therapy, but who also have the intellectual background and ethical integrity to help others to change and move forward with their lives.
 
 Lesley Murdin
 
 Former director, WPF Therapy

Not all counsellors and psychotherapists want statutory regulation. While many of us share concerns about harmful therapists at work, we also know that legally protecting titles does not eradicate abuse or malpractice – it may even hide abuse behind enhanced professional status. We also need to be cautious of unintended consequences of statutory regulation, which could further restrict access for marginalised groups due to increased costs for training and accreditation.

The current system of therapists accredited by the Professional Standards Authority may be imperfect, but offers potential ways forward that deserve close attention before we rush into the statutory protection of titles.
 
 Andy Rogers
 
 BACP-registered counsellor and psychotherapist, Basingstoke, Hampshire

Your report on the call for statutory regulation of counsellors and psychotherapists highlights a gap in public protection that should have been addressed years ago.

It’s extraordinary that someone seeking mental healthcare, often at a particularly vulnerable point in their life, cannot necessarily take for granted that the person treating them is appropriately qualified or subject to enforceable professional standards.

As the founder and CEO of an independent mental healthcare organisation, I welcome the call for change from the commission established by the professional bodies, but would argue that regulating individual practitioners is only part of the answer. We also need to examine the ethical conduct of organisations providing mental healthcare, including the transparency of their relationships, whether referrals are always made in patients’ best interests and how conflicts of interest are managed.

Last month, in response to these concerns, we partnered with colleagues across the sector to launch the Independent Mental Healthcare Ethical Practice Charter, establishing shared principles for greater transparency, accountability and ethical practice.

Statutory regulation of practitioners is long overdue, but it should be accompanied by greater scrutiny of the organisations operating within the sector.
 
 Maryam Meddin
 
 Founder and CEO, the Soke

The case made for statutory regulation of psychotherapists applies equally to sports therapists. People seek sports therapy for injury treatment, pain management and rehabilitation. Yet “sports therapist” is not a legally protected title. Voluntary registers provide some reassurance, but cannot prevent an unregistered, inadequately qualified individual from using the title.

In worst-case scenarios, we have seen individuals struck off from other statutory registers for abusing patients, only to reinvent themselves as “sports therapists” and continue to pose a threat to the public. The Society of Sports Therapists has been seeking statutory regulation for years to ensure that the public can identify who is properly qualified, and for action to be taken against those who present a risk. The Health and Care Professions Council has approved our application on three separate occasions, but the necessary legislative action has still not followed. Significantly, 94% of our members support this change.

It is high time that the government applied the same public protection principle across therapeutic professions and completed the process. Regulation is not a badge of professional status; it is a safeguard for patients and a means of protecting the many responsible practitioners who deserve public confidence.
 
 Simon Bowen
 
 CEO, the Society of Sports Therapists

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘Revenge of the nerds’: US midterms deliver a win for science – and a rebuke of Maha
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Jessica Glenza
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
The wins for Democrats come after years of cuts and upheaval to US health and science infrastructure

Q&A: Ask your questions about Democrats’ win in the midterms

A political organization behind a wave of Democratic doctors and scientists winning elections up and down the ballot is calling the stunning rebuke of Trumpism the “Stem swing” and “revenge of the nerds”.

The wins come after years of cuts and upheaval to US health and science infrastructure, as Democrats spent big on health-related ads and as voters rejected the Make America Healthy Again (Maha) movement.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

“It’s clear from the results: 2026 was a healthcare election,” said Erik Polyak, executive director of 3.14 Action, a group that worked to elect Democratic health professionals and scientists across the country. “We’ve heard a lot about affordability. Healthcare affordability is the No 1 piece of that. Our doctors and scientists are certainly well-equipped to lead on those issues.”

Among the history-making lawmakers are Democrats Dr Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Dr Annie Andrews of South Carolina. The last time a Democratic doctor held a seat in the US Senate was in 1969 – the era when Medicare and Medicaid were passed into law. They are far from alone: 3.14 Action is still tallying wins and waiting for results among “hundreds” of obscure state races, some of which are not even reporting results yet.

“The voters’ message is simple and clear: enough,” Dr Richard Besser, president and CEO of the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, a philanthropic organization dedicated to improving Americans’ health, said in a statement.

“People across America are frustrated by the high cost of living, exhausted trying to make ends meet, and fed up with a ridiculously expensive and complicated healthcare system,” said Besser. “They want leaders who understand how hard it is and will do something to make their lives better.”

Doctors and scientists have long held leadership roles in Congress, but until this election, the overwhelming majority were Republican. Perhaps unsurprisingly, scientists studied this: from 2011 to 2020, 86% of the physician-members of Congress were Republican and three-quarters were from southern states.

The 2026 election turned that on its head. Republicans like Dr Mariannette Miller-Meeks of Iowa and Senate candidate Dr Roger Marshall – both allies of the US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr – lost. Races for three more Republican doctors were too close to call. Meanwhile, all incumbent Democratic doctors won their races.

Galvanizing Americans behind science did not come without a cost. Trump and Kennedy brought upheaval to nearly every American scientific institution and corner of American healthcare, from the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to Medicaid, the public health program that insures 72 million Americans.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has lost up to one-third of its staff in the midst of a record-breaking measles outbreak. The National Institutes of Health (NIH), the world’s largest public funder of biomedical research, lost leadership and saw path-breaking research stymied amid disruptions, cancellations and censorship. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) struggled to keep up with a historic outbreak of diarrhea-inducing cyclosporiasis. On election day, New York health authorities announced that a child in the state had died of measles for the first time in 30 years.

Kennedy disrupted and defunded federal work on vaccines to placate a base of zealots, as four in 10 “Maha voters” worried about healthcare prices. He also became a key figure for doctors and scientists to rally against. Before the election, 3.14 Action said that Kennedy was “our No 1 recruitment and fundraising tool – hands down”.

Democrats capitalized on this upheaval. Healthcare was the second-biggest issue in campaign ads, according to the Cook Political Report, with Democrats running more than 158,000 healthcare-related ads versus 61,000 for Republicans. 3.14 Action alone spent $23m on independent ads, most targeting health issues including – as corruption became a defining issue of the race – standing up to pharmaceutical companies and insurers.

High-profile Democratic candidates often spoke about local healthcare challenges. In South Carolina, as a measles outbreak took hold in February, pediatrician Andrews was able to give specific health advice even as federal authorities downplayed the dangers.

“I never in a million years, when I was in medical school, thought that I would be running for the US Senate and also talking about measles nearly every single day,” Andrews told the 19th at the time.

El-Sayed pitched a vision of Medicare for All that would save rural hospitals threatened by the Republican-led One Big Beautiful Bill Act. His call and response with the crowd was direct: “Money in your … ” “Pocket!” “Money out of … ” “Politics!” “Medicare for … ” “All!”

In Ohio, where Dr Amy Acton prevailed, her experience as a health director during Covid-19 turned out to be an asset, rather than a liability. In Iowa, Democrat Christina Bohannan, who is not a doctor but a law professor, pledged to spend more on research as rising cancer rates became a bipartisan political issue in the state.

“Americans who believe in science are fired up,” said Polyak. “We’ve flipped at least 10 Republican seats and the final number is the low 30s,. Flipping control of the House in 2026 ran through Democratic doctors and scientists – and we led the charge.”

New Democratic lawmakers face far-reaching challenges when they are sworn in. The most draconian cuts of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act go into effect on New Year’s Day 2027. Among the most emblematic are work requirements for Medicaid. All told, cuts are expected to result in 17 million people losing insurance in the next decade.

They will also be faced with enormous insurers and drug companies, which will seek to push back and influence lawmakers as Democrats hammer out consensus on wide-ranging health proposals pitched during the campaign, from a public option to government-backed single-payer healthcare. And public health political organizations are already calling for Kennedy to be removed from office.

“In a lot of ways, this election represented the beginning of the end of RFK Jr’s disastrous leadership,” said Polyak. “It’s clear Americans want something different – they didn’t elect all these Democratic scientists just to oppose Trump. People want to see an alternative agenda, they want to see what Democratic scientists can deliver for them.”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Some now suggest a monthly dose of art can boost wellbeing. But the last thing we need is another item on our to-do lists

A
s the long autumn subsides and we finally head into winter, so we hit that point in the calendar when two rival theories of seasonal survival play out: one, the permission-giving invitation to give up and power down, encapsulated by Scandinavian hygge and Katherine May’s 2020 blockbuster Wintering; and two, the exhortation to push through the discomfort and get out there. If the midterm results in the US give us a huge boost this week, still we have to keep going until spring.

The latest contribution to the get-up-and-out-there branch of motivational badgering comes in the form of a report by an arts charity suggesting that, as with exercise and being in nature, our baseline mood may be improved by exposing ourselves to art on a regular basis. According to Art Fund, a national body that promotes access to the arts, a person’s mental and physical wellbeing may be meaningfully affected by abiding by a handy acronym – RDA for recommended dose of art – and attaching it to what appears to be an entirely arbitrary prescription, namely 60 minutes of art ingestion a month. According to Daisy Fancourt, a professor of psychobiology and epidemiology at University College London who wrote the report’s foreword, do this and, “alongside having a balanced diet, regular exercise and spending time outdoors”, your health will thank you.

Not signed in before? Create an account

I don’t mean to sound sceptical. There are excellent reasons for promoting this theory: the ability of art in any form to take us out of ourselves and put us back in a slightly different place. What is fascinating to me is how Art Fund has found it necessary to sell the idea by appealing to a standard that, if not antithetical to art, exactly, seems at the very least to be highly irrelevant. In other words, the key sell for engaging with art in this case is that there is science – a real expertise! – backing it up, to reassure those on the fence that it’s not all a clanging, nebulous waste of time.

There’s probably a way to blame Malcolm Gladwell for this, or take your pick from any number of other narrow-track, extremely literal thinkers who don’t trust any experience of life that can’t be tabulated. And while Art Fund is just conforming to publishing trends, which require measurable takeaways from every single thing we do, I can’t help finding something dispiriting and babyish about the way they’ve gone about it. Not to get too Walter Pater about it all, but the minute you start trying to measure future benefits in relation to standing in front of a painting or reading a book, not only do you wander into upsetting territory where phrases such as “value proposition” and “what’s the unlock on this?” reside, but it risks interfering with the experience itself.

I know, I’m being a snob. The enthusiasm for boiling life down to a series of self-optimising items on an endless, dreary to-do list, however, does get a bit much at times. In this particular case, it is technically true, I suppose, that art belongs in a very broad category with nutrition. And you can hold two apparently contradictory thoughts in your head at the same time, so that the fleeting experience of being immersed in an artwork can live alongside the understanding that there is some future, unspecified benefit to the exercise.

But when so much weight is put on health and welfare as the ultimate goal, it does risk shifting the experience from pleasure to chore. A more accurate presentation of the value of art might be that going to the National Gallery for the afternoon is less like eating a bowl of grains and doing a quick workout than spooning frosting into your mouth, fixing you greedily and indulgently in the thrill of the moment. Only guess what?! Without the cholesterol!

Is the science of art-as-health-benefit a real science? I’ll never find out because, apparently, I have no desire to improve myself by reading the data – although if curiosity or a whimsical need to do something I’m not interested in ever gets the better of me, I’ll certainly look into it.

All of which misses the point, of course, which is about selling a laudable and true idea about how art enriches your life to a possibly sceptical public. I tip my hat to Art Fund for framing this conviction in a publicity-friendly way, which is surely more sensible than wanging on about hard, gemlike flames and watching it dive to the bottom of the news list. Just allow me a quick eyeroll first.

Palantir’s controversial £330m health contract is to be extended before ministers draw up plans to replace it with a British alternative, the FT has reported.

Health secretary Yvette Cooper has faced calls from MPs and campaigners to axe the US tech firm’s contract to deliver the flagship government AI system.

The system aims to connect scattered medical files, speed up hospital discharges and improve surgery scheduling among other potentially life-saving improvements. But a review has concluded that removing Palantir from NHS data systems by triggering a break clause in its contract would be too disruptive, the FT reported.

Ministers instead plan to launch a procurement process for a UK tech alternative, with Palantir to potentially be replaced in two years.

Palantir’s UK and Europe chief executive, Louis Mosley, said ending its contract would be “putting politics above patients” and accused critics of “Palantir Derangement Syndrome”.

The company has contracts to supply AI to the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s homeland security crackdown, while its billionaire founder, Peter Thiel, has questioned democracy, said tech companies can “unilaterally change the world” and called technology an “incredible alternative to politics”.

The plan is expected to be signed off soon but Green party leader Zack Polanski accused Labour of “betrayal” and said it was “allowing the corporate capture of our most beloved institution by a genocide and Donald Trump supporting tech corporation.”

The reports today that Labour is to keep Palantir in the NHS shows that the huge sums of money paid to the likes of former Labour ministers, Peter Mandelson and Tom Watson, looks to have paid off.

Any evidence of patient benefit is highly contested by NHS staff and many NHS trusts have rejected the use of Palantir’s platform.

That’s all from me, Tom Ambrose, and indeed the UK politics live blog for today.

A Scottish government official warned there were “clearly significant impacts and risks” from plans to site a number of hyperscale data centres in Scotland, documents released under freedom of information (FoI) laws have revealed. The deputy director for domestic climate change said there were “various concerns about the way forward”, citing concerns about possible impacts on energy bills and on water usage, PA reported.

Staff at the Scottish government and four of its agencies are being balloted on potential strike action in a row over a mandatory level of office working.

The government has mandated that staff should work from one of their offices 40% of the time, which the PCS union – which represents civil servants – said is “unacceptable”.

The government is considering placing restrictions on smart glasses amid concerns the technology is being used to surreptitiously film women, a minister has said.

Speaking in the House of Commons, the safeguarding minister, Satvir Kaur, hinted at a ban on selling the technology “to certain users”.

The benefits of smart glasses must be weighed against the harms they can cause. The government is already looking into options to restrict smart glasses in certain settings and restricting the sale to certain users.

The minister said people who used smart glasses for filming already risked breaking the law in certain settings, such as in a court where cameras are prohibited.

An energy minister has told the bosses of Great Britain’s biggest energy suppliers to do more to help households get on top of their unpaid energy bills this winter, before the government spends almost £2.5bn to help write off the country’s record high debts.

Energy bosses were summoned to a roundtable meeting on Thursday to discuss the government’s plan to pay down the energy debts of about 2.4m of the hardest-hit households.

The debt relief scheme is part of a wider “circuit-breaker” strategy put forward by the chancellor in the annual budget statement last month. This includes measures to tackle household energy debt, which could reach £7bn by the end of the year.

The minister for energy consumers, Polly Billington, is understood to have told bosses from energy companies including Octopus Energy, British Gas and EDF Energy that suppliers would still need to play a “crucial role” in tackling the longstanding issue of problem debt alongside the government’s multibillion-pound support package.

Suppliers are expected to proactively identify customers who may be under financial strain and offer help such as debt payment plans or pointing them in the direction of debt advice services.

The government is also planning to work with the industry to make it easier to spot households that may need extra help, and to modernise payment systems to make it easier to pay. “And therefore, anything else should be made illegal.”

Asked about Mark Nowak’s suggestion, Mahmood told the same broadcaster:

I haven’t taken any options off the table. I’m also not going in with a fixed mind about what the right clarifications of the law might be.

It’s important to get the right balance between religious expression in this country, which is something that many of us of a faith, including myself, hold very dearly, but do so in a way that is within what we expect of our citizens for the purposes of the criminal law.

Burnham said the move would help deal with the frustration of applying for a job without knowing the salary, while officials say that publicising pay will help those in work know if they are being paid fairly in comparison with others.

The prime minister said:

Whether you’re a young person starting out or a parent trying to support your family, you should know what a job pays before spending your time and effort applying for it.

That’s why we will make it a legal requirement for all employers to say what you pay.

But breaking down barriers is only one part of the job. We also need businesses to open more doors and give young people the experience and confidence to take that first step into the world of work.

Paul Nowak, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, said: “Anyone who’s searched for a job knows how frustrating it is to read ‘competitive salary’.”

Recent research by the Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development found less than half of employers always published salaries ranges on job adverts, while less than a fifth always published specific salaries.

Experts say omitting pay details from job adverts makes it harder for young people to know which jobs to apply for, and makes it easier for employers to give lower pay offers to some candidates, including women.

Andy Burnham will meet the EU leaders Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa on 20 November in Brussels, with the aim of signing three agreements – on food and drink, carbon markets and youth exchange – as well as pledging a “trusted partnership” on steel and defence industries.

But a longstanding dispute over whether EU students should pay costly international tuition fees at British universities remains unresolved and could delay the implementation of the food and energy deals, which are worth billions to the British economy.

The EU wants a return to the pre-Brexit status quo where European students paid the UK domestic rate of university tuition, rather than international fees, which can be about four to six times higher for an undergraduate degree.

European Commission negotiators have proposed postponing an agreement on tuition fees by six months to ensure the success of the November event, where Burnham is expected to show his commitment to much closer ties with the EU.

But at least six member states, including in central and eastern Europe, want the university fees issue settled by the summit, while many are seeking a firmer commitment on the issue from the British government, according to four EU sources.

One EU diplomat told the Guardian: “Having a youth experience scheme without an agreement on tuition fees has very little added value,” noting the much lower cost of university education in many EU countries and therefore potential greater advantage to British students.

A second EU diplomat said there was cautious optimism about the November summit, but “a large majority” wanted “a more convincing British commitment” on tuition fees.

A government spokesperson said: “We do not comment on leaks or provide a running commentary on live negotiations. We are building an ambitious, close relationship with the EU that will strengthen our economy, protect British industry, and create more opportunities for young people across the UK.”

For the EU, the creation of a youth experience scheme, known as Yes, which will enable those aged 18 to 30 to live, work and study on both sides of the Channel is a high priority. The erosion of people-to-people links is seen as one of the big losses of Brexit, and many European officials studied in the UK, making the issue especially resonant.

EU officials argue the bloc has leverage, saying the food and drink deal – a Labour manifesto pledge estimated to be worth £5.1bn a year to the British economy – would come into force only if there was a satisfactory agreement on tuition fees.

Similarly, the agreement to relink emissions trading systems sundered by Brexit, which would protect British exporters from European carbon taxes, could also be delayed pending agreement on tuition fees.

A leaked version of the summit statement hints at the link between the trio of agreements, looking forward to “their joint and timely entry into force”.

Separately, EU sources have suggested without a deal on tuition fees, the EU could delay talks on British reintegration into the European electricity market that are expected to intensify next year. To secure its return to the market, the UK would have to pledge an “appropriate” contribution to European cohesion funds aimed at boosting economic development in poorer regions.

This week the Guardian reported that the UK was prepared to spend up to £450m a year to give EU students discounted university tuition fees if Brussels allowed Britain access to the Made in Europe industrial programme.

The EU said there would be no deal on Made in Europe at the November summit because the bloc was still finalising its position on the key draft law, the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA).

Targeted at strategic industrial sectors, such as electric cars and renewables, the law would mean public subsidies and contracts would only go towards products made in Europe.

France, supported by many lawmakers in the European parliament, is pushing for a narrow definition of Made in Europe, while Germany leads a larger group of countries that don’t want to exclude trade partners including the UK.

While Britain is keen to resolve the issue, EU lawmakers are not expected to finalise the IAA text until next spring. In a significant milestone, France and Germany struck a compromise on Made in Europe favourable to the UK, but it only applies to cars, not the other industrial sectors in the IAA such as renewables and nuclear technology, or other draft proposals aimed at promoting European preference.

In a win for the UK, the draft summit statement proposes a “trusted partnership” on strategic industries, starting with steel and defence. The aim is to stop either side becoming collateral damage of the other’s trade defence measures targeted at China’s heavily subsidised imports.
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.summary: France and Germany struck a compromise on Made in Europe favourable to the UK. But it only applies to cars, not the other industrial sectors in the IAA.

Google announced that schools restricting AI entirely will lose access to Google Search. What do you think of this?

Google announced this week that schools restricting AI entirely will lose access to Google Search. Chris Phillips, vice-president for education at Google, told the New York Times that “search and AI are deeply integrated” so if a school has banned AI, students “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available”.

Since Google owns roughly 91% of the global search engine market share across all devices, this is a seismic announcement for US students.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: Cambridge asks Post Office inquiry barrister to lead review into death of Jason Arday
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Richard Adams Education editor
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Jason Beer KC will examine university’s handling of claims against Arday and protection offered to academics in spotlight

The lead barrister for the Post Office Horizon inquiry has been appointed to head an independent review into the death of the Cambridge academic Jason Arday.

Jason Beer KC will examine the handling of allegations of research and other misconduct made against Arday before his resignation as well as the university’s recruitment and support for him as its youngest ever black professor at the age of 37.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Beer said he would consider whether wider institutional changes were needed at Cambridge after looking into the protection it offered to academics facing significant public and media scrutiny and the procedures around the appointment of Arday.

The professor of the sociology of education died at his home in south London while facing widely publicised allegations of plagiarism and inconsistencies in statements about his career.

Arday denied the accusations of plagiarism but Cambridge said on 5 August it would open an investigation into his academic qualifications. He resigned hours after this was announced and was found dead nine days later.

Beer said Cambridge had asked him to conduct an independent, thorough and searching examination of its institutional arrangements and the decisions it made over Arday.

He said: “I will look not simply at what the university’s policies and procedures required but also at whether they were themselves reasonable; how they operated in practice; who was responsible for making decisions; what information was reasonably available to them; whether relevant concerns were recognised and properly addressed; and whether the university’s various structures and functions worked together effectively – all in the case of Prof Arday, and more broadly.

“I hope that those who have relevant knowledge or experience will feel able to contribute to the review. Their perspectives may be important in understanding not only what happened in Prof Arday’s case but whether there are wider institutional changes to be made.

“I will take seriously my responsibility to treat participants with sensitivity, to respect confidentiality and to ensure fairness to anyone whose actions may be examined.”

Sign up to Headlines UK

Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning

after newsletter promotion

Beer’s review is the second of two independent reviews of Cambridge’s involvement with Arday. The first, announced by the university in September, asked Nazir Afzal, a former chief crown prosecutor for north-west England, to focus on the support given to Arday in the immediate period before his death.

A veteran of public inquiries, including working for NHS England in the Covid-19 inquiry, Beer is best known for his role as lead counsel to the Post Office Horizon IT statutory inquiry that investigated the wrongful criminal prosecution of nearly 1,000 post office operators.

Prof Deborah Prentice, Cambridge’s vice-chancellor, said: “Jason Beer is an eminent legal expert who will bring vast experience of leading complex reviews and inquiries. We are equally thankful to the distinguished panel of independent experts he has convened to assist him in this important task and look forward to receiving their findings and recommendations in due course.”

He will consider whether wider institutional changes were needed at Cambridge. Beer said Cambridge had asked him to conduct an independent, thorough and searching examination of its institutional arrangements and the decisions it made over Arday.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: More than 900 academics urge UK to reverse decision to bar Andreas Malm
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Matthew Taylor
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Blocking Swedish writer’s entry for event with Palestine Action co-founder is attack on free expression, letter says

More than 900 academics have voiced their opposition to the government’s decision to block the climate academic Andreas Malm from entering the UK, warning that the move represents “a grave violation of academic freedom and freedom of expression”.

Malm, the author of How to Blow Up a Pipeline and a leading climate scholar, was prevented from entering the UK last week by the Home Office after being told that his presence in the UK “may not be considered to be conducive to the public good”.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

He had been due to attend an academic conference on Wednesday, appear on the BBC, and participate in a public discussion organised by the publication Tribune alongside Huda Ammori, a co-founder of the proscribed organisation Palestine Action.

Hundreds of academics have signed an open letter voicing their concern at the move and calling on the government to overturn the decision.

“The ability of scholars to travel, exchange ideas and participate in public debate – including on politically contentious issues – is fundamental to a free and democratic society,” the letter says. “Excluding academics because of their political views or the topics they discuss sets a dangerous precedent and risks creating a chilling effect on academic and public discourse.”

Malm, an associate professor at Lund University in Sweden and an internationally recognised climate academic, said he had been “kept in the dark” by the UK’s immigration authorities over the reasons for his electronic travel authorisation (ETA) being revoked, but said he suspected it was because of his plans to appear on a panel alongside Ammori from Palestine Action.

Speaking to the BBC earlier this week, he said: “I cannot see any other explanation than the scheduled appearance of me on stage for a panel on Wednesday evening in London, together with Huda Ammori. That … makes me somehow a terrorist or associated with terrorism, and therefore barred from travelling to the UK. That’s pretty scandalous.”

He said the move was “just a very small part of a major trend: this drift into authoritarianism that is targeting the Palestine movement, the climate movement, and others who oppose the destructive forces that are in control of this world.”

A Home Office spokesperson said: “Cancelling or refusing an ETA can take place for a range of reasons, including where there are concerns that an individual poses a threat to public safety or seeks to spread extremism.

“It is not a ban on coming to the UK. Those in this position can still apply for a visa, enabling further consideration of circumstances and suitability for entry to the UK.”

The letter has so far been signed by more than 1,400 individuals from over 250 academic institutions, including some of the world’s leading universities.

Fabian Dablander, an assistant professor at the London School of Economics, who initiated the letter, said the numbers showed the strength of feeling in the academic community.

“The letter quickly attracted hundreds of signatures, reflecting the academic community’s deep concern about the threat this decision poses to academic freedom and the UK’s reputation as a place for open intellectual debate,” he said.

Malm was prevented from entering the UK last week by the Home Office. He was due to attend an academic conference on Wednesday, appear on the BBC and participate in a public discussion with Palestine Action co-founder Huda Am

https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.title: UK apologises to Ukrainian child refugees who were told to study Russian
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.author: Matthew Weaver
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.text:
Exclusive: Schools minister launches new Ukrainian GCSE and says she is sorry students were pushed to study Russian in its absence

The UK has apologised to Ukrainian child refugees who were told to study Russian in English schools, as it launched funding for a new GCSE in Ukrainian.

Ukrainian children who were forced to seek refuge in the UK after Vladimir Putin’s invasion in 2022 say it was “insulting” that their teachers suggested they study Russian in the absence of a GCSE in Ukrainian.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Announcing the new qualification, the schools minister, Georgia Gould, said: “So many students were pushed into having to do Russian. I’m really sorry that they were put in that position. It’s really important that they will have access to a Ukrainian GCSE.”

The new qualification, which will be ready in England in 2028, is being developed by the AQA exam board, with the help of a £340,000 grant from the Department for Education.

It comes after years of lobbying from the Ukrainian government and Ukrainian community groups on behalf of more than 30,000 Ukrainian children who have fled to the UK. In a letter to the DfE in 2024, the education ministry in Kyiv said: “We are deeply concerned that due to the lack of Ukrainian GCSE, many Ukrainian children are being pressured by their school staff to pass the Russian GCSE.”

Gould said: “It was one of the Ukrainian government’s asks of us that we deliver a Ukrainian GCSE, and one of the asks from the community and young people. We’re really proud to be able to do it, and proud of that partnership with the Ukrainian government.”

The Ukrainian language has been at the cultural frontline of the conflict with Russia. Putin has banned Ukrainian books and the teaching of Ukrainian in land Russia has occupied.

Gould said: “Whether it’s military support or this the kind of cultural support, our message as a British government is we stand absolutely steadfast behind the Ukrainian people.”

Ukraine’s education minister, Andrii Butenko, said he was grateful to the UK government. He said: “This will give Ukrainian children forced to leave their homes by Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine an equal opportunity to choose their native language as a GCSE subject. We will continue working with AQA and the DfE to develop a high-quality and accessible qualification.”

Gould made the announcement on a visit to St Mary’s school in west London, the centre of a network of 13 Ukrainian-language schools in the UK. She was introduced to Vitalii Andronik, 20, who told the Guardian in 2024 how he had been urged to study Russian GCSE as a 15-year-old refugee. Gould told him: “I’m really sorry that you were put in that position.”

Andronik welcomed the new qualification and the apology. He said: “It’s too late to me, but I want future generations of refugees to study Ukrainian. It’s a recognition of the trauma that we went through. It’s brilliant news to hear that in future kids here won’t have to study Russian.”

Sofiia Chonka, 16, who fled to London from Zakarpattia in south-west Ukraine in June 2024 with her family, said: “I was told to study Russia in year 9, I just said ‘no’. I didn’t want anything to do with Russia – they killed my people and injured my family.”

Chonka, who has just started A-levels, said she would take the new exam when it was available. “It’s such a beautiful thing to be speaking Ukrainian when the Russians are trying to mute you.”

She added: “I’m really sad that it has taken so long, but at least they are starting the process, and some of my younger friends will have the opportunity to do it.

“It’s a stereotype that they are similar languages – they are completely different. Because Ukrainian is so beautiful, the Russians don’t like it. They can’t ban it, they can’t ban people.”

Inna Hryhorovych, the head of St Mary’s Trust, who has been calling for the GCSE since Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014, said: “It’s still hard to comprehend that we don’t need to fight for this any more.” She said her next campaign would be a new A-level in Ukrainian.

Gould said: “We’re just doing GCSEs for now. Let’s see how it goes. But we really want this to be a success.”

The minister said exams board had been nervous about developing a new qualification for a relatively small cohort of students. She said: “Despite the challenges of a smaller qualification, we really wanted to put financial resources to making it possible, and I’m grateful that AQA has come forward.

“I want this to happen as quickly as possible for people, but I’m really glad that it is happening now. Some of the students sitting here today will be able to study this GCSE.”

She encouraged British children to study for the new qualification as an act of solidarity. “I think it would be wonderful if more people were taking up Ukrainian GCSE,” she said, and she joked that Ukrainian children could tutor their friends as a “side hustle”.

When Gould announced the plan to a dozen Ukrainian pupils, they applauded and in unison said “diakuyemo”, or “thank you very much”.
