https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/attack.title: Attackers Exploit Critical Siemens IoT2050 Flaw to Plant Remote Command Backdoors
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/attack.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/attack.text:
A maximum-severity security flaw impacting Siemens SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced devices has come under active exploitation, VulnCheck has revealed.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-58115 (CVSS score: 10.0), is a case of missing authentication for a critical function that could be exploited by an unauthenticated remote attacker to run arbitrary code.

"SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced devices running Industrial OS with Node-RED installed contain a missing authentication vulnerability in the Node-RED HTTP interface that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to create malicious flows and execute arbitrary code on the underlying server with maximum privileges," Siemens said in an advisory released back in August 2026.

The issue has been remediated in versions 4.3.4.1 or later. As mitigations, Siemens recommends that users uninstall Node-RED or harden the installation by following the steps below -

As of October 30, 2026, VulnCheck said it observed attackers attempting to weaponize CVE-2026-58115 against its honeypot network in an attempt to download and run a Linux bot.

"The attacker's request was a complete exploit," VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity said. "It deployed a Node-RED flow, triggered it automatically, and pulled a binary from an attacker-controlled server, all behind three layers of encoding."

Specifically, the malicious flow is designed to run a shell script wrapper, which uses wget to retrieve the botnet binary for AMD64 architecture from 85.215.73[.]250. Curl is used as a fallback if the wget attempt fails. In the final stage, the binary is saved as "/dev/shm/.b" and executed.

Since then, the attackers behind the campaign have switched to a two-stage process where the wget command is used to retrieve another shell script ("wget.sh") from the same server.

Another request has been found to run wget/curl against "45.194.90[.]57:38472" to fetch a payload called ".sys_update," save it on disk as "/tmp/.kworker" in an attempt to disguise it as a harmless kernel worker thread," and then execute it. The exact functionality of "wget.sh" or ".kworker" remains unknown, as they could not be retrieved.

"Several requests deployed no downloader at all. Instead, the flow exposes an HTTP in endpoint (for example /cmd, or a randomly named path) wired through a function node to an exec node with addpay enabled, so the attacker could run arbitrary commands later by passing them in a query parameter," Garrity said. "This backdoor survives even if a memory-backed implant is lost on reboot."

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/attack.title: Attackers Target Unpatched CryptoPayment Gateway Flaw That Can Expose Wallet Credentials
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/attack.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/attack.text:
Threat actors are attempting to exploit an unpatched maximum-severity security vulnerability in the CryptoPayment Gateway WordPress plugin, according to findings from Defused Cyber.

The vulnerability in question is CVE-2026-81648, which carries a CVSS score of 10.0. Successful exploitation of the flaw could permit unauthenticated users to delete arbitrary files on the server and extract sensitive data, including stored wallet credentials.

"The CryptoPayment Gateway WordPress plugin from 1.2.1 to 1.2.2 does not apply an authorization check on one of its AJAX endpoints, allowing unauthenticated users to invoke administrative operations, including deleting arbitrary files on the server, overwriting the payment gateway configuration and recovering stored wallet credentials in cleartext," according to a description of the flaw on the NIST National Vulnerability Database (NVD).

The vulnerability affects versions 1.2.1 through 1.2.2, which is the latest version. There are no known fixes for the flaw, according to WP Scan. As of August 28, 2026, the plugin has been closed on the WordPress Plugin Directory and is no longer available for download due to an unspecified "security issue."

Statistics show that the plugin has been collectively downloaded 1,845 times, including 20 downloads over the last seven days. It's unclear if it's actively installed on any WordPress sites.

"We are observing in-the-wild exploitation attempts against CVE-2026-81648, a critical (CVSS 10.0) flaw in the CryptoPayment Gateway for WordPress," Defused Cyber said in an X post. "The attacks we recorded came from infrastructure that markets themselves as 'Anonymous KYC-Free VPS Hosting.'"

In the absence of a fix, site owners are advised to remove the plugin, rotate wallet keys, and audit for any suspicious changes.

Some attacks this week didn't need much of a trick. A fake support call, a trusted extension, a shared link, or a device with no password. Small things that people barely think about. Yet each was enough to cause serious trouble.

Then there were the bigger messes. Billions stolen, hidden networks of hacked devices, poisoned software, and attackers finding new ways to turn normal tools against their users. Even the places meant to keep money and systems safe ended up with problems of their own. The strange part is how often the damage started somewhere nobody was looking.

And that's before getting to the long list of fresh bugs, shady services, and scams making the rounds. Quite a bit to sort through. Here's what made the list.

N. Korea Sets New Record with Binance $6.43B Crypto Theft — The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has officially attributed the theft of more than $6 billion in virtual assets from Binance to a North Korean hacking group called TraderTraitor. The haul eclipses the $1.46 billion plundered from Bybit in February 2025, making it the largest cryptocurrency theft in history. The funds were stolen across 11 blockchains, 82% of which were on Ethereum and Bitcoin. Of the $6.43 billion stolen by TraderTraitor, $2.85 billion of the assets have been frozen on-chain by Tether, Circle, Ripple, Arbitrum, and Optimism.

Access the Gartner® CTEM report to see how the Mythos platform continuously maps cross-domain attack paths and isolates key choke points to break active lateral movement to critical assets.

Bugs drop weekly, and the gap between a patch and an exploit is shrinking fast. These are the heavy hitters for the week: high-severity, widely used, or already being poked at in the wild.

Check the list, patch what you have, and hit the ones marked urgent first — CVE-2026-115889, CVE-2026-115893 (Wasmtime), CVE-2026-90975 (Fireblocks mpc-lib), CVE-2026-91141 (COVESA vsomeip), CVE-2026-88781, CVE-2026-75775, CVE-2026-75779, CVE-2026-93489, CVE-2026-17518, CVE-2026-75753, CVE-2026-102438, CVE-2026-14911, CVE-2026-16528, CVE-2026-19386, CVE-2026-19396, CVE-2026-93495, CVE-2026-14157, CVE-2026-13313 (ASUS), CVE-2026-114573, CVE-2026-9082, CVE-2026-118539 (Drupal), CVE-2026-114595, CVE-2026-114596, CVE-2026-114597, CVE-2026-114598 (EPICS Base), CVE-2026-97631 (TianoCore EDK II), CVE-2026-115881, CVE-2026-115884 (GoAhead), CVE-2026-110720 (HashiCorp consul-k8s), CVE-2026-90885, CVE-2026-85250, CVE-2026-88901, CVE-2026-88900, CVE-2026-78165, CVE-2026-85251 (Apache Camel), CVE-2026-115547 (Okta), CVE-2026-114349, CVE-2026-111551 (Apache Kafka), CVE-2026-118306, CVE-2026-118331, CVE-2026-118348, CVE-2026-118344, CVE-2026-106378 (Google Chrome), from CVE-2026-117860 through CVE-2026-117954, from CVE-2026-118005 through CVE-2026-118017 (Mozilla Firefox), CVE-2026-98432 (Linux kernel), CVE-2026-18672, CVE-2026-19219 (Telerik UI for ASP.NET AJAX), TRA-2020-14 (Kodi), CVE-2026-107239, CVE-2026-107238, CVE-2023-22793 (Veeam), CVE-2026-103401, CVE-2026-103402, CVE-2026-103403, CVE-2026-103404, CVE-2026-103405, CVE-2026-103406, CVE-2026-103407, CVE-2026-103408, CVE-2026-103409 (Juniper Networks Session Smart Router), CVE-2026-111585 (TeamViewer), CAN-2026-2035970 (Intelbras IP cameras), CVE-2026-103594, CVE-2026-112709, CVE-2026-112710, CVE-2026-93857, CVE-2026-103593, CVE-2026-93865, CVE-2026-93866 (WatchGuard Fireware OS), CVE-2026-101296, CVE-2026-101356, CVE-2026-103119 (Apache Tomcat), CVE-2026-112816 (Canonical LXD), CVE-2026-93680, CVE-2026-110186 (Langflow OSS), and a preauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability in TightVNC.

That's about it for this week. Some attacks were carefully planned. Others worked because someone clicked the wrong thing, trusted the wrong tool, or left something exposed. Different methods, same result. And with so many systems connected to other systems, even a small mistake can travel further than expected.

The bigger concern is how normal some of these attacks have become. Nothing particularly clever is needed when the easy routes still work. Keep an eye on what has access, check what needs fixing, and don't assume familiar means safe. See you next week.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/google.title: Google Disrupts 1.3 Million-Device Android Botnet, Says TV Box Maker Sold Criminal Access
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/google.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/google.text:
A botnet of more than 1.3 million Android devices, mostly TV set-top boxes, lost control of its servers in late October in a takedown led by Google.

Google says it is highly confident that device maker Videostrong intentionally put a backdoor in the boxes and sold access to criminals.

They used the boxes for ad fraud and to pass other people's internet traffic through owners' home connections. The backdoor is still on the boxes, and owners cannot remove it themselves.

Videostrong, based in Shenzhen, China, makes Android TV boxes and other devices under its own name and for other brands. The backdoor, called x.cpe, was built into many device models and brands over several years. Google does not believe a rogue insider or a mistake was to blame.

Google used legal action to take down the domains and servers that controlled the botnet. It also took down the control domains of more than a dozen malware families loaded through the backdoor. Japan's National Police Agency, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Plume, Synthient and TrendAI worked with Google on the operation.

Because the criminals behind that malware also spread it in other ways, Google expects the action to cut off their access to at least 10 million more infected devices. It warns that backdoor operators and the criminals who buy from them quickly switch to new tools when one part of their setup is disrupted.

Google has cut ties with Videostrong. It banned the company, and any future subsidiaries or affiliates, from building or selling certified Android devices and from supplying software to other certified device makers.

The x.cpe backdoor runs as a system app inside the firmware, with system-level access, according to Google's analysis. It reports to the botnet's command-and-control (C2) servers and waits for orders. To install software silently, it first turns off the app checks in Google Play Protect, Android's built-in security feature.

Through the backdoor, the botnet's operators could install apps without the owner knowing, run commands, capture the screen and map the network the box sits on.

Google says it saw Videostrong's operators use some of these powers. They took live screenshots, sent keystrokes, copied out account details, device information, app lists and system logs, and opened reverse shells, which give a remote command line into the box.

Most of the criminals' modules, the add-on programs loaded through the backdoor, turned the boxes into residential proxies or sold their spare bandwidth. A residential proxy service sells access to a home internet connection, so a customer's traffic appears to come from an ordinary household. Other modules faked views of online ads.

Most infected devices are Android TV set-top boxes, but the backdoor also turned up on telehealth devices, karaoke machines and digital signage.

TrendAI, Trend Micro's enterprise business unit, counted 1,472,554 infected devices across 206 models between June 3 and October 1, and says the real number is at least that high. Malaysia, Brazil, Iraq, Mexico and Taiwan had the most. The U.S., Germany, the U.K., Australia and Canada each had about 26,000 to 42,000.

Synthient, which tracks proxy networks and botnets, has published a list of 182 device model names seen in the campaign. The list warns that a model name alone does not confirm that a box is infected.

Synthient's report focuses on MECOOL-branded boxes, which it links to Videostrong. It bought a MECOOL KM9PRO Max and found the backdoor preinstalled. Plume, which makes Wi-Fi software for internet providers, found more than a dozen different devices using the botnet's control server, most of them from MECOOL.

Because x.cpe is part of the firmware, removing it does not stick. It reinstalls itself when the box restarts. TrendAI says the backdoor runs as a system app signed with the maker's key, so cleanup needs "vendor action, platform protection or replacement of the device."

Plume recommends a full factory reset, because the modules may have installed more backdoors, but it does not say whether a reset removes x.cpe itself. Synthient goes further, telling consumers to throw the boxes away for good because they pose a high risk of malware.

For organizations, Synthient recommends these steps:

TrendAI advises companies with remote staff to treat unmanaged consumer devices on home networks as part of their attack surface, and to keep corporate access behind managed devices.

In Google's account, x.cpe passes settings from the C2 server to other Videostrong apps, including its YokaTV Player streaming app. One of the GitHub accounts that hosted the botnet's packages is named yf-videostrong.

Synthient, which worked with Google, also concluded with high confidence that Videostrong runs the operation. It points to a document signed by Videostrong's research and development director in an open folder on one of the botnet's servers, and to a Videostrong web domain that shares an IP address with the operators' control panel.

Plume found that Videostrong supplies both the firmware for these devices and tools to manage them remotely.

Google requires device makers to go through a set of compatibility and security tests. It says Videostrong hid its code to bypass a gap in those tests and loaded the malicious code after a device's first boot.

Google has changed its review process and is improving its checks of the firmware on certified Android TV devices.

As of November 2, Videostrong's own website listed products it calls "Google Certified Android TV Box" and "Google Certified Android TV Stick."

Plume says the botnet included both Google-certified devices and devices running the Android Open Source Project (AOSP) version. Google's report does not say how many certified devices were affected.

When Google sued over the BadBox 2.0 botnet in July 2025, the more than 10 million devices involved were uncertified.

The backdoor, called x.cpe, was built  Google sued over the BadBox 2.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/darkbl.title: DarkBlinders Compromises Israeli Target and Iraqi Kurdish Government Cloud Environment
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/darkbl.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/darkbl.text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a cyber espionage campaign targeting Israel and the Kurdistan Region of Iraq by an Iran state-aligned threat actor between August and October 2026.

According to a report published by Dream Research Labs, the campaign has led to the compromise of a high-profile individual in Israel, along with additional compromises affecting a government cloud environment in the Kurdistan Region.

The activity has been attributed to a threat actor known as DarkBlinders, an Iran-nexus group assessed to be active since at least September 2024 and linked to attacks aimed at aviation infrastructure and telecommunications in the U.A.E. and Iraq. It exhibits no technical overlap with other known hacking groups.

Attacks mounted by the group are known to rely on spear-phishing as an initial access pathway to lure recipients into opening trojanized utilities or clicking on attacker-controlled websites that host similar tools as direct downloads.

Previous attack chains documented by Elastic Security Labs and Group-IB have led to the deployment of SHELBYLOADER (aka HOTAIR), which is launched via DLL sideloading to ultimately execute a backdoor called SHELBYC2 (aka AEROSTAT) that uses GitHub for command-and-control (C2), data exfiltration, and remote control. Elastic is tracking the threat cluster under the moniker REF8685.

Then early last month, Palo Alto Networks shed light on a campaign dubbed Blinder Tunnel in which the threat actor, which it calls CL-STA-1178, was observed masquerading as the Dubai Airports IT department to distribute malware-laced coding challenges to high-value targets.

The bogus recruitment scheme was first detected in late March 2026, although evidence indicates that the attackers were staging and testing attack infrastructure as far back as November 2025.

The social engineering campaign is assessed to have approached specific targets with lucrative job offers to trick them into executing a self-contained application that mimicked a career portal and instructed them to complete a questionnaire.

Submitting the questionnaire does not cause any data to be exfiltrated or initiate any response from an external domain. Instead, it's meant to serve as a harmless decoy and build credibility before delivering the next stage payload containing the malware in the form of a Microsoft Visual Studio project archive that's dressed up as a coding assessment.

The attack chain makes use of three techniques to establish persistent access: A malicious C# project ".csproj" file is used to trigger AppDomainManager injection, followed by DLL sideloading to deliver an updated version of SHELBYLOADER (aka ShelbyLoader V2), which then launches SHELBYC2. Also deployed via SHELBYC2 is a tunneling utility called Blackwood.

"The attackers behind the activity used tailored social engineering techniques to masquerade as Dubai Airports recruiters, using a trojanized Visual Studio coding challenge to target a high-value job seeker based in Iraq," Unit 42 said.

"The campaign is characterized by misuse of built-in developer tools and DLL sideloading. Attackers also used AppDomainManager hijacking to bypass security monitors like ETW [Event Tracing for Windows]."

The latest findings from Dream show that the threat actor continues to rely on social engineering, while combining both credential phishing and malware delivery. This involves the use of government, webmail, and cloud-service lookalike domains to collect credentials or present attacker-controlled file downloads. Some of the highlighted domains include -

The threat actor has also been observed setting decoy brand domains for a fake videoconferencing application called StarkMeet (stark-meet[.]com, stark-meet[.]online, and stark-meet[.]website). Installing and launching the app leads to the execution of ShelbyLoader V2 and SHELBYC2.

The development is also a sign that the threat actor is trying out different methods for malware delivery, ranging from coding assessments to counterfeit software.

Dream said the DarkBlinders activity belongs to the same operational cluster as UNC5795 and Dust Specter, citing infrastructure and malware overlaps. Dust Specter, documented by Zscaler in March 2026, refers to a suspected Iran-nexus operation targeting government officials in Iraq by impersonating the country's Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

"Historical server fingerprints, overlapping victimology, and supporting attribution research lead us to assess with medium confidence that UNC5795 and UNC5187 may represent related sub-clusters within the broader APT34 group," it added.

"Their overlapping focus on Iraqi government entities adds context to this technical connection and suggests a shared intelligence collection interest. Combined with their respective APT34 associations, these findings support a medium-confidence assessment that the two clusters are operationally related and may belong to the same broader group."

The disclosure comes as Prince of Persia (aka Infy), a lesser-known threat group sponsored by the Iranian government, has been observed running one of its C2 servers ("68.65.122[.]203") from the U.S. this year. The server was likely built in July 2026.

The infrastructure is a second-stage C2 server associated with Tornado, a Tonnerre variant that's dropped via one-day software vulnerabilities and uses both HTTPS and the Telegram API for C2. The emergence of new C2 servers in late May 2026 follows three months of inactivity, which has been described as the "longest downtime in nearly two decades of activity by the threat actor."

"We have been monitoring Prince of Persia's exfiltration activity for the past six months," Tomer Bar, associate vice president of security research at Semperis, said. "The number of victims remains low, which could indicate either targeted attacks or difficulties infecting new victims."

"The Iranian threat actor decided to host its new C2 server on U.S. soil — at the same time as the beginning of the recent hostilities between Iran and the United States. This is the last place we expected to find the threat actor hiding."
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/darkbl.summary: Report says Iran state-aligned threat actor has been active since at least September 2024. The group has been linked to attacks aimed at aviation infrastructure and telecommunications in the U.A.E. and Iraq.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/critic.title: Critical Langflow Flaws Could Let Unauthenticated Attackers Run Code on Servers
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/critic.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/critic.text:
Two critical flaws in Langflow could let a remote attacker with no account bypass authentication or run arbitrary code, IBM said last week.

Langflow is an open-source tool for building AI agents and workflows, and its vulnerability reports go to IBM. Every release from 1.0.0 through 1.12.8 has the flaws, and the only fix is version 1.13.0.

Neither flaw is in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, as of the catalog's October 30 update. Six other Langflow flaws are listed there, most recently CVE-2026-9198, which was added in August.

The four Langflow flaws in IBM's bulletin, first published on October 28 and updated the next day, are:

One of the flaws is "unauthenticated remote code execution exploitable through model context protocol tool enumeration," according to IBM. Through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), Langflow can offer its flows as tools to AI apps that support MCP.

A module in the public Metasploit Framework already cites CVE-2026-93680, the authentication bypass. It connects to a Langflow server's MCP endpoint without credentials, starts a session, and lists the tools the server offers. It does not run code or commands on the server.

Its author lists Langflow 1.5.0 through 1.11.4 as affected, a narrower range than IBM's.

When automatic login is enabled, Langflow logs users in as superusers without prompting them to sign in. The setting LANGFLOW_AUTO_LOGIN is enabled by default in Langflow 1.12.8. Its code description warns that it "bypasses authentication and should only be used in development environments."

The module was tested on Langflow 1.8.4 with automatic login turned on. Another of the four flaws is "an incomplete remediation of an auto-login security control," according to IBM. The bulletin does not say whether servers with automatic login turned off are vulnerable.

Langflow 1.13.0 came out on October 22. Version 1.12.8, released the same day, still has the flaws, and PyPI lists no later 1.12 release as of November 2. IBM offers no workaround for servers that cannot upgrade yet.

Langflow 1.13 turns automatic login off by default. To upgrade:

On October 29, IBM also published CVE records for 29 other Langflow flaws and named versions 1.12.4 and 1.12.5 as their fixes. One of them, CVE-2026-104339, could also let an attacker with no account run arbitrary code, and IBM rates it 9.8. None of the 33 records, these four included, lists 1.13.0 as affected.
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/critic.summary: IBM releases four Langflow flaws, and the only fix is 1.13.0. The flaws are in the CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. The latest version of Langflow is 1,12.8, released on October 22.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/is-you.title: Is Your SOC Ready for AI Agents? A Maturity Check Before You Deploy
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/is-you.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/is-you.text:
Forty percent of security teams now use AI every day, and another 56% are testing it. Only 4% have no plans to adopt it, according to Prophet Security's State of AI in Security Operations 2026 survey of more than 250 CISOs, SOC leaders and practitioners. For the teams still testing, the next decision is whether their own SOC is ready.

AI SOC readiness has two parts: whether a SOC has the problems AI SOC agents are built for, and whether it has the data access, context, written standards and oversight rules that AI agents need to investigate alerts accurately in its environment. A SOC does not need to be far along a maturity model to be ready. AI agents do their first work on the bottom layer, alert handling, and the analyst hours they return give a team room to work on the layers above it.

The next section describes those problems. Technical readiness covers four areas: access and context, an investigation standard with baseline metrics, rules for what the agent may do, and a plan for the time it gives back.

The SOCs that gain the most from AI SOC agents usually recognize several of the problems below, whether an outside provider works their alerts or their own analysts do.

If an MDR or MSSP works your alerts:

If your own analysts work the queue, including whatever the provider sends back:

AI SOC agents are built for this work. They are designed to start on each alert as it arrives, whichever tool raised it and at whatever hour. They can pull the context an outside provider lacks from your own systems and record the evidence behind each conclusion, so your team can check it. Some can also run a hunt the day a new threat is disclosed, which turns "are we impacted?" into a set of queries with answers. The analyst hours they return can go to the detection and hunting work that waits today.

If several of these problems sound familiar, the need is there. The next question is whether your SOC can support a deployment.

Prophet Security's SOC maturity model, the SOC Hierarchy of Needs, has five levels: alert management, detection coverage, threat awareness, proactive hunting and posture improvements. Each level depends on the one below it. A team buried in alerts rarely gets to hunting, and a team that hunts without threat awareness has no clear idea what to look for.

Many SOCs have not yet stabilized the first level. In the State of AI in Security Operations 2026 survey, respondents said 28% of their alerts are never investigated.

AI SOC agents usually start at that first level, investigating alerts as they arrive. Newer platforms also run hunts and propose detections, work that reaches into levels two and four. Either way, the analyst hours they return go to work above the first level, so readiness depends on what the first level needs.

An AI agent investigates by running queries against your tools, so it cannot see anything it has no access to. If it can query the EDR but not the identity provider, it can describe what happened on the endpoint but not which account was behind it.

Readiness here has three parts:

A quick test: take five recent incidents and list every query a senior analyst ran to close them. Any query the agent could not run marks a gap to close before a pilot.

Data access also raises the most common objection. In our survey, 44% of teams cited data privacy and how AI models are trained, the most frequent roadblock respondents named. Ask each vendor whether your data trains their models and where your data is processed.

A pilot needs a written standard to grade the agent against. In many SOCs, only senior analysts know that standard, and it is rarely written down.

The standard covers which evidence closes a phishing case, when an impossible-travel alert needs a call to the user's manager, and what counts as enough to call an alert benign. Writing it down for your highest-volume alert types also gives new analysts an onboarding document.

Also keep a list of the detections that were switched off. In our survey, up to 40% of organizations had turned off some detections because they lacked the people to check them. When an agent investigates every alert, some of those rules can come back, and the list tells you where to start.

Then record the numbers you will compare against: the share of alerts investigated, mean time to investigate, time from alert to first look, and how often closed alerts are reopened. The survey gives a reference point. A thorough investigation takes an average of 75 minutes, and alerts often wait close to an hour before anyone opens them.

You can download our guide on detection engineering to learn more about how an agentic SOC benefits detection engineering.

Investigation and action carry different risks, and most teams treat them differently. In the survey, 57% of teams require a human to review every AI decision before an alert is closed. On response, 44% have AI recommend actions that people carry out, 30% let it handle low-risk remediation on its own, and no respondent gives it full, unsupervised autonomy.

A ready SOC has these rules written down before a pilot starts:

Starting with read-only access for investigations, then widening permissions as confidence grows, applies the same rules a SOC uses for a new human analyst. Prophet Security's framework for building trust in an AI SOC follows the same stepwise approach.

Answer each question yes or no. Part 1 checks the need, and Part 2 checks technical readiness. The level in parentheses shows which layer of the SOC Hierarchy of Needs each item belongs to.

Each yes is a problem an AI SOC agent can take on, and the more yes answers, the stronger the case for a deployment.

A "no" on any of the first four is worth fixing before a production pilot. The other four can be worked on during it.

Most items on the Part 2 list are configuration and documentation work: issuing API credentials, exporting asset and user context, and writing down the investigation standard. A workable order:

Some teams that are not ready consider building their own agents instead. The survey suggests caution: 72% of AI users had tried building internal AI tools, and 46% of those projects were abandoned, never reached production, or were replaced by a commercial product.

Building a functioning prototype is only a small chunk of the work. Most of the work is engineering and maintenance of integrations that take weeks to build but break when a vendor changes an API; rate limits to work around; model deprecations every six to nine months that force a full round of evals, guardrails, and prompt injection testing; and audit trails explaining why each alert was closed.

Prophet Security is the leading AI SOC platforms for enterprise SOCs, recognized in Rising in Cyber 2026, an honor voted on by more than 150 CISOs and security leaders. Its platform, Prophet AI, works from the stack a team already runs. First-generation AI SOC tools stopped at alert triage. Prophet AI enables an agentic SOC, with specialist agents for investigation, threat hunting and detection engineering.

Prophet AI SOC Analyst investigates every alert at every severity, around the clock, with the depth of a senior analyst. It queries SIEM, EDR, identity, cloud and email tools directly and records every question, query and piece of evidence behind a determination, so an analyst can rerun any query and check the work. It takes response actions only within permissions the customer sets, with human approval as the default.

Prophet AI Threat Hunter is built to answer "are we impacted?" It keeps a profile of each organization's industry, technology stack and the threat actors that target it. When a severe new threat emerges, hunts for it run automatically in the background. Scheduled hunts, including hunts against coverage gaps and questions the team writes in plain language, run on the cadence the team sets. Suspicious leads go to the SOC Analyst for a full investigation.

Prophet AI Detection Engineer takes on the detection engineering work that waits for spare time. It keeps a live MITRE ATT&CK coverage map built from the organization's own investigations, showing which techniques are covered, which have gone quiet and which are dark. It builds and tunes detections from what investigations, hunts and coverage gaps reveal, writes them in the rule language of the SIEM or tool they run in, and backtests each one against the organization's own history. Each change arrives as a reviewable proposal with its rationale and backtest results, and by default nothing reaches production until the team approves it.

Each product's findings feed the others. Investigations show which detections are noisy and where coverage is thin, hunts look in those gaps, and what the hunts find becomes new detections. The team teaches Prophet AI in plain language, and that guidance shapes how investigations run, how hunts are scoped and how detections are written. Customer data never trains its models, and the data plane can run inside the customer's own VPC.

https://www.darkreading.com/cybersecurit.title: UK Wades Into Tech Sovereignty Amid AI Policy Changes
https://www.darkreading.com/cybersecurit.author: Rob Wright
https://www.darkreading.com/cybersecurit.text:
Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

The UK is betting on domestic AI and cyber investment to reduce reliance on US tech — but security leaders question whether the funding is too fragmented and too late.

The UK has announced major investments in strengthening its cyber defenses, designed to stave off the rise of faster, more complex attacks enhanced by AI tools. In late October, the government unveiled a funding package of approximately $800 million to strengthen cyber defenses and AI security investments.

The move comes as Kanishka Narayan, the UK's minister of artificial intelligence, said in a speech last month that "it seems likely, if not inevitable, that our own cyber-defenses will be breached." He cited the recent trend of misaligned models escaping containment, citing the OpenAI incident in June during which an agent hacked an Australian government health agency.

But the UK government is also pushing toward another, related goal: digital sovereignty. In his speech, Narayan emphasized the need to "build in Britain to keep the public safe in Britain" and become less dependent on foreign providers, which has become a common goal for some countries following the US government's export control order for Anthropic earlier this year.

Related:UK Warns Its Critical Infrastructure Faces Grave Risk

"We want the world's leading companies investing here, but we will not accept dependence as the price of that investment," Narayan said.

But industry-watchers argue that government investment to strengthen cyber-defenses while also achieving greater sovereignty by encouraging homegrown tech might be difficult to do all at once.

Two turning points appear to have shifted government policy in the UK and Europe this year, both involving the same US company: Anthropic. The first came with the AI company's unveiling of Project Glasswing in April for its Mythos frontier model, which sparked concerns about a coming "vulnpocalypse" for enterprise security teams.

"It created an almighty whirlpool of conversations," says Tim Williams, CEO of London-based Quod Orbis, which specializes in continuous controls monitoring. "And then there were lots of concerns about what that meant, and everybody seemed to panic. I think that panic has settled down now."

But another event — the Trump administration's ban on foreign nationals using Anthropic's Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models has had a far more lasting effect. The ban didn't just impact overseas companies and government agencies; the export controls effectively forced Anthropic to pull all access for the two models for several weeks.

The implications of abruptly losing access to valuable — and perhaps critical — AI technology through a sudden change in US policy accelerated an already growing conversation about reducing dependency on American tech companies. A crucial part of the UK government's funding package is designed to fuel British AI startups and invest in home-grown companies.

Related:Third Serengeti Sweep Tops 1,400 Arrests as Investigations Mature

It's a solid idea, but infosec professionals see two issues with that approach. First, the funding package is split up between a number of initiatives, with approximately £154 million of the £600 million total devoted to strengthening current cyber-defenses, for example.

"If you look at the amount that they're putting into it, is that enough? Is that significant?" Williams asks.

Secondly, the UK is already well behind the curve with fueling homegrown AI and cloud companies. Amir Khan, managing director at Wire, tells Dark Reading that there's been chronic under-investment in emerging technologies in the country, which has led to missed opportunities in the past.

"In the UK, we had DeepMind before it was sold to Google [in 2014]," Khan says. "Had they known the impact that DeepMind would have now, would they still have sold it, or doubled down on it? Who knows? But it's another example of a large organization that grew in the UK, leaving to go to the US."

In fact, due to that kind of ongoing tech emigration, Khan says you could argue that the last good thing to come out of UK's technology industry was Cambridge Analytica — a company that become embroiled in a scandal involving Facebook.

Related:UAE Transitions 50% of Government Services to Agentic AI

Time and again, experts have argued that organizations can't counter AI-driven threats effectively without AI-enabled defenses. But that complicates matters for the UK, which is looking to achieve tech sovereignty in the aftermath of the Anthropic ban.

For one, in some part because of the issues outlined above, many of the major AI companies — OpenAI, Meta, SpaceXAI (now SpaceX Super Intelligence), and Palantir Technologies — are also based in the US. And while there are plenty of AI startups these days, those companies may not have the scale needed for national defense systems.

Additionally, there's also the cost component. Williams says many of Quod Orbis' customers are looking to reduce their dependency on a single vendor or provider, whether it's for cloud, software, AI, or other technologies. "There's no question that, in speaking to our clients, that concentrated risk is a concern for them," he says.

But moving from, for example, one cloud provider to four or five can be challenging, especially for mid-market organizations, he says. They may not have the budgets of large enterprises, and they probably rely more heavily on the commercial discounts that the cloud giants like AWS, Microsoft, and Google Cloud Platform provide. "If they're spreading that investment out across multiple cloud providers, that can become more expensive for them," Williams says.

Khan agrees and points to the recent example of France migrating off Windows for government workstations and moving to Linux. But leaving the Microsoft ecosystem will require France to add several more technologies from different vendors. "That, for me, defeats the purpose because you've essentially taken away one provider and pulled in six," he says. "That doesn't really give you the flexibility you want."

Khan argues the UK sometimes sets the wrong target for tech sovereignty. "We talk as though we have to build every chip, every cloud, and every application ourselves," he says. "As you can imagine, that's an enormous undertaking, and it doesn't really get to the heart of the issue. For me, the questions are, can we make our own decisions about the technology that we depend on? Can we operate it on our terms?"

The UK can retain such operational authority, he says, by choosing providers and vendors that build that kind of customer controls directly into their products and services; for example, Khan notes that Wire offers customer a private cloud option for the messaging platform that organizations can control and operate based within whatever country they're located.

Whichever providers or vendors the UK government chooses, officials should be asking several key questions before investing: who holds the encryption keys, who can interrupt the service, and how realistic is it to move off that technology?

In the meantime, the UK government will continue to focus on strengthening the country's cyber defenses through these investments and efforts like the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill currently. But Williams is unsure if they will be enough.

"It's a step in the right direction, absolutely," he says. "But is it the investment I would expect to see in terms of being really concerned about the threat to the UK?"

Senior News Director, Dark Reading

Rob Wright is a longtime reporter with more than 25 years of experience as a technology journalist. Prior to joining Dark Reading as senior news director, he spent more than a decade at TechTarget's SearchSecurity in various roles, including senior news director, executive editor and editorial director. Before that, he worked for several years at CRN, Tom's Hardware Guide, and VARBusiness Magazine covering a variety of technology beats and trends.

Prior to becoming a technology journalist in 2000, he worked as a weekly and daily newspaper reporter in Virginia, where he won three Virginia Press Association awards in 1998 and 1999. At TechTarget and Dark Reading, he has won several Azbee awards, including the 2026 National Silver Award for a series on vibe coding.

At Dark Reading, Rob currently covers security operations, cloud security, and Internet infrastructure. He has a keen interest in malvertising activity and the certificate authority industry, and has written extensively on both topics. He graduated from the University of Richmond in 1997 with a degree in journalism and English. A native of Massachusetts, he lives in the Boston area.

https://www.darkreading.com/cyber-risk/a.title: AI Gave Your Incident Archive a Second Job
https://www.darkreading.com/cyber-risk/a.author: Gerald Mako, Lemuel Valdez
https://www.darkreading.com/cyber-risk/a.text:
Security records are increasingly being used by vendors to train their models, creating new risks for enterprises.

Traditionally, security incident records have served a singular, very important purpose: to document what the organization observed, decided, and did. Closure notes, rule text, false-positive dispositions, and the reason why an alert was dropped are treated by security teams as records contained in the ticket queue. For organizations to reconstruct their decisions and, crucially, be accountable for them later, all of this evidence must be retained.

To be sure, security automation is anything but new. For years, SOAR platforms have executed playbooks, closed alerts, and recorded dispositions. They run a rule that customers wrote. The change is what happens to the record afterward, as a portion of the evidence has an alternate destination for a different purpose. Once incident records are ingested into a security AI system with permission to capture data for model building or validation, this evidence can become data the vendor uses for model development and validation.

Related:What We Missed: Knicks Phishing Test Goes Out of Bounds

A sufficiently large collection of prompts and related records can offer more than a glimpse into which signals are treated by the organization as meaningful, which detections are suppressed, what analysts mark as benign, and where it misses something.

A single closure is a comparatively harmless note. A series, however, presents a map; suppressing the same class of alerts delineates boundaries of concern. The rationales for closures indicate acceptable levels of PowerShell noise or failed logins that warrant a ticket. Tuning decisions encode which signals the team stops trusting and when. The contents of the ticket do not need to be accessed by an external party for it to understand the pattern, which is the sensitive portion.

This isn't about reconstructing an AI incident; that's a logging decision. Nor is it about prompt injection, or the familiar case of a vendor training on customer chat logs. The problem is what happens when ordinary security records acquire a second use.

Microsoft Security Copilot provides an option for the owner to allow Microsoft to capture and human-review Security Copilot data to enhance and validate Microsoft's security-specific model, which is built on the Azure OpenAI foundation model. The data captured for model improvement can include whatever Microsoft plug-ins and Security Copilot agents have used while interacting with the product. The documentation states that this data is not used to train the foundation model and is not shared with OpenAI. A second setting controls the capture of data for the purpose of product-performance reviews.

Related:9 Cyber Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today's Maze of Threats

The default for each setting depends on the method of provisioning the workspace. With the exception of Microsoft 365 E5 and E7 auto-provisioning, data sharing is enabled by default. The customer that enabled the setting has made an intentional decision, but the customer that has not viewed the settings page may not know which default applies. Using the service and allowing a vendor to capture data for model development or validation are different decisions, and Microsoft has already made them separable.

The archive had one job: namely, to help the organization reconstruct and defend its own decisions. Now the same records may be held by a vendor for model development or validation, which in turn creates new risks. A vendor breach puts the records outside the customer's network, while a legal demand can expose them without the customer's control. The retention rules and access controls were built for an archive the organization controlled, but they were not built for a second copy elsewhere.

An auditable record has to preserve more than the final decision. It has to distinguish what the organization knew, what the analyst decided, what the system was given, and what the system recommended. Otherwise, the model's observation effectively becomes the decision. Counsel asking what the organization knew at the time of the incident will not be satisfied by this. An auditor asking why the detections were tuned down should not be met with the closure rationale that also appears in the evidence stream.

Related:Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

This belongs in the procurement contract. A vendor's use of customer security records to provide a service does not by itself authorize their use for model improvement, and evidence retention and model development are different things that should require separate permission. Rule content, closure notes, and ticket text should not be covered by a generic AI clause. If the vendor wants the data for model improvement, then this should be an explicit, revocable choice.

Until these uses are formally separated, the archive has two functions. One of them continues, as expected, to be operated by the organization. The other turns all the evidence into the vendor's resource.

Research Affiliate, Cambridge University

Gerald Mako has more than a decade of experience advising European and Asian governments on artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, and technology strategy. His work focuses on AI governance, cyber resilience, and the security challenges created by increasingly autonomous systems.

Chief Information Security Officer, Cobham Satcom

Lemuel Valdez has led cybersecurity and security transformation across private equity portfolios, government, and critical infrastructure environments. He has advised and supported more than 20 PE-backed companies on cyber risk, due diligence, incident response, security architecture, and regulatory compliance.
