https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/mississi.title: Mississippi Senate: Longshot Ty Pinkins says he aimed to spoil Hyde-Smith, boost Colom vote
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/mississi.author: Dan Mangan
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/mississi.text:
Longshot Mississippi Senate candidate Ty Pinkins could be a spoiler in the race, where Democratic nominee Scott Colom is narrowly leading Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, a Republican.

Pinkins, who ran as an independent, said he stayed in the race after realizing from an April poll that he had no chance of winning.

He told a local TV station he hoped to boost Colom’s odds of beating Hyde-Smith.

Longshot Mississippi Senate candidate Ty Pinkins said that at first wanted to win — but that he stayed in to spoil.

Pinkins told a local TV station that after an April poll showed he had no chance of winning he remained in the race in order to boost Democratic nominee Scott Colom’s chances of beating Republican incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.

Pinkins’ purported strategy might pay off.

Colom is narrowly leading Hyde-Smith in ongoing counting by just 1,936 votes, a margin of just 0.2 percentage points, with 96.2% of the vote counted, according to the Associated Press. That margin is about one-tenth the size of Pinkins’ share of the vote, 2.1 percentage points.

Pinkins has won just 20,010 votes so far out of the nearly 952,000 votes already counted.

“The only thing I did was stay in the race and let people shoot arrows at me,” Pinkins said in an interview with WTVA in Mississippi on Thursday. “That is it. And that’s a ... low price to pay to get someone in this race that I think can help people in the Delta and all across this state.”

“The portion of the vote that I drew — and people were concerned about splitting the Black vote — what I actually did was split the Republican vote,” he said.

Pinkins told the station in Tupelo that he intentionally avoided campaigning in areas with large Black populations to avoid cutting into the vote share of Colom, who, like Pinkins, is Black.

That tactic worked, he said, as the election results show he got most of his support from areas with relatively low Black populations.

“I’ll be the boogeyman,” he said. “But I’ll tell you this: The independent in this race pulled most of his votes from a Republican, and for the first time since Reconstruction, a Democrat who is a Black man is leading.”

Pinkins, a lawyer who previously ran for Mississippi secretary of state, was the Democratic nominee for Senate in 2024. He was crushed by Republican Sen. Roger Wicker, who won nearly 63% of the vote, compared with about 37% for Pinkins.

Despite that showing, the U.S. Army veteran decided to take another crack at the Senate in 2026.

But in the spring, he saw the writing on the wall for his candidacy.

“I got in this race to win,” Pinkins told WTVA. “In April, I knew I was going to lose, but I also knew that I was pulling 70% of the Republican vote based on the [SPLC Action Fund and Impact Research] poll.”

SPLC Action Fund, when it released the poll, said, “Sagging favorability numbers for Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith could open up a path to victory for Democrats.”

“Independent Ty Pinkins has the potential to play spoiler for either candidate,” SPLC Action Fund said in April.

In the WTVA interview, Pinkins said, “I probably attended maybe, maybe six events over the summer” as part of his campaign.

“Six events. I don’t have to,” Pinkins said. “Why? I’m not going to win. So why go to these Black communities that he’s going to?”

Pinkins said all he had to do was visit counties that have relatively low Black populations and “talk to some Republicans that said they’re going to vote for me.”

“They were literally calling me and sending me emails: ‘We’re going to vote for you because we don’t want to waste our vote on Cindy Hyde-Smith, we don’t want to hold our nose and vote for her, so we’re going to vote for you. Please stay in the race,’” he said.

The campaigns of Colom and Hyde-Smith did not immediately respond to CNBC’s requests for comment.
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/mississi.summary: Longshot Mississippi Senate candidate Ty Pinkins said he stayed in the race after realizing from an April poll that he had no chance of winning. Pinkins has won just 20,010 votes so far out of the nearly 952,000 votes already counted.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/automake.title: Where's the growth? Legacy automakers face a tougher 2027 as costs rise, market tightens
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/automake.author: Michael Wayland
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/automake.text:
Automakers are warning that they’re facing higher commodity, logistics and memory costs while pricing power is becoming harder to extend to consumers.

Several Wall Street analysts have said companies will need continued pricing strength and additional cost savings to offset inflation, higher investment spending and a potentially weaker economy.

Meanwhile, global light-vehicle production is forecast to be essentially flat in 2027 at about 91.65 million units, according to GlobalData.

DETROIT — There’s a growing concern that the global automotive industry may be stuck in neutral, if not reverse, heading into 2027.

The auto industry — from the companies to their customers — has been surprisingly resilient this decade, but there are fears that rising costs, weaker vehicle pricing and a more challenging market could threaten profits and growth going forward.

Automakers also face pressure outside the U.S. from an onslaught of Chinese carmakers, a thinner new-product pipeline after retreating from some all-electric plans, and company- and region-specific challenges.

“With investor focus increasingly shifting to 2027, the setup appears challenging,” Barclays
 analyst Dan Levy said in an investor note last month. “Rising inflation, continued China pressure, affordability concerns in the U.S., and a flat global production outlook suggest another year of limited earnings growth.”

Several Wall Street analysts have said automakers will need continued pricing strength and additional cost savings to offset inflation, higher investment spending and a potentially weaker economy just to maintain their current levels.

“It’s a little bit more optimistic in the U.S. and then very pessimistic in Europe,” RBC Capital Markets analyst Tom Narayan told CNBC. “As a whole, there’s some negativity on ’27.”

Automakers from the U.S. to Europe to Asia have been facing a growing list of headwinds.

For U.S.-based legacy automakers, Ford Motor
 said it expects next year’s results to be in line with 2026, while General Motors
 grew more cautious about its ability to continue growing earnings as much as it had previously expected.

“We continue to believe that 2027 will be another strong year and better than 2026, assuming customer demand remains strong, and commodity, logistics and other recent cost pressures moderate,” GM CEO Mary Barra told investors Oct. 20.

GM CFO Paul Jacobson said that while it’s too early to officially forecast, the company is facing additional inflationary costs that could lead to another $2 billion headwind in 2027, like it expects this year. He specifically cited costs of commodity inflation, logistics and DRAM, or dynamic random-access memory chips as challenges.

Those chips are critical components in modern vehicles and are used for everything from temporary data storage and real-time processing from infotainment systems to safety-critical systems.

GM and others have been able to offset outside pressures through cost cuts, operational efficiencies and resilient consumer demand for higher-margin vehicles. However, there’s a limit to what companies can do.

“There’s only so much pricing you can push to consumers,” Narayan said. “They’re already at pretty high pricing.”

European automakers including Volkswagen
, Mercedes-Benz and BMW
 in recent weeks reduced their 2026 earnings forecasts in response to U.S. tariffs, the growth of Chinese automakers and rising costs.

Most recently, BMW this week said accelerated restructuring measures would reduce its automotive pretax earnings margin this year by 2.5 percentage points. The company said the restructuring should support “positive effects” into 2027 and a 3% to 5% pretax profit margin for 2028. That compares with a 5.3% automotive margin last year and 3.4% during the third quarter.

Chrysler parent Stellantis
, which has large operations in Europe and the U.S., is facing its own challenges, as it’s in the midst of a restructuring that aims for a low-single-digit adjusted operating margin this year. It has maintained a 2026 guidance that includes a mid-single-digit percentage increase in net revenue and a low-single-digit adjusted operating margin.

In Asia, South Korean automaker Hyundai Motor, which has experienced notable growth in recent years, also cut key metrics when it reported earnings late last month. The company lowered its 2026 wholesales target to 4 million vehicles, down from 4.16 million, and cut its operating-margin target to between 5.5% and 6.5%, down from a previous goal of 6.3% to 7.3%.

Toyota Motor
 is an outlier for its most recent quarter and outlook, as the world’s largest automaker increased its full-year operating income forecast by 500 billion Japanese yen (about $3.2 billion) on Thursday.

Toyota’s results were boosted by weakness in the Japanese yen as well as strong hybrid vehicle demand in the U.S. However, the increase in operating income was its first in six quarters.

Broadly, the changes to earnings and outlooks come as production for the global industry slows.

Consulting and insights firm GlobalData expects global light-vehicle production of about 90.96 million units in 2026, down 2.1% compared with last year. It forecast a production increase of less than 1% next year. That comes on the heels of strong annual growth earlier this decade, led by China.

Cox Automotive reported the average transaction price of a new U.S. vehicle in September was more than $50,500. That was just shy of the record of $50,614 in December 2025.

Lofty vehicle prices have led to record-high and record-long financing deals, as well as concerns that customers are getting priced out of the new-vehicle market.

The typical U.S. new-vehicle payment reached $776 a month in September, the highest since December 2023, according to Cox Automotive.

Cox Automotive chief economist Jeremy Robb, discussing the third quarter for the automotive industry, rated the overall economy, buyer ability and borrowing costs as cautionary “yellow lights.”

But he did have some “green lights,” such as good credit availability and employment conditions, which could give some relief for automakers and consumers, many of whom need vehicles for their everyday lives.

Robb said there’s a “tug-of-war” between headwinds such as rising costs, interest rates and fuel prices and tailwinds such as growth in liquid assets and savings that has helped offset some of the additional costs.

“Consumers remain under financial pressure, but the vehicle demand continues to hold, showing more resiliency in the auto industry than we’ve seen in other parts of the economy,” Robb said during a Sept. 24 call, noting consumer sentiment remains low.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/small-bu.title: Small retailers brace for 'huge hit' this holiday season as shipping costs spike
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/small-bu.author: Laya Neelakandan,Leslie Josephs
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/small-bu.text:
As shipping costs surge due to high fuel prices, small- and medium-sized retailers struggle to keep up, and they face a difficult holiday season.

Some small business owners told CNBC they’re considering raising their shipping fees or getting rid of free shipping to keep up with the pressure.

Experts say it’s nearly a record year for shipping costs, and while larger players may be able to emerge unscathed, smaller companies are bearing the brunt.

When Jenni Shields began her small business eight years ago selling handmade hair accessories, she paid $2.93 to ship an order, or close to $4 in today’s dollars when adjusted for inflation.

Last year, Shields said, an average shipping label for her products cost around $4.50. But when she took a typical batch of orders to her local U.S. Postal Service office last month in Kansas City, Kansas, she was shocked to see that it was an average of nearly $6 per package.

Shields is just one of the small- and medium-sized retailers who are struggling to keep up with rising shipping costs as the price of fuel continues to trend upward.

Small business owners such as Shields are facing a difficult holiday season. Customer demand is strong, but some retailers said their profits will be dented — if not eaten up entirely — by higher shipping and other costs.

Shields said she charges her customers $6 in shipping fees, which includes roughly $1.50 to cover her packaging supplies. The dramatic upswing this year means she’s no longer breaking even on her orders and instead eating the added costs, she said.

“I am losing money at this point, and I’ve really taken a huge hit this year,” said Shields, the owner of Evie Pearl Handmade, which sells bows, quilted headbands and other accessories. “I feel like it’s just been this slow increase up [in shipping costs], and I feel horrible.”

The surge in fuel prices since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in February has driven up the cost of shipping by sea, air, rail and road.

That means higher costs across the board, including for shipping giant Amazon
, which reported an 11% increase in shipping expenses in the third quarter compared with last year, to individual retailers.

Globally, air cargo is going for about $3.37 per kilogram, up 43% from a similar period a year ago, according to transportation marketplace Freightos. Judah Levine, Freightos’ head of research, said in addition to higher fuel, demand for fast shipping of hardware used to build data centers is helping to boost air freight rates, even weeks before peak last-minute holiday packages take to the skies.

For businesses, that runup is going to “squeeze their margins in the near-term,” said Jason Seidl, managing director and transportation analyst at TD Cowen. “Larger companies tend not to be exposed to the spot market, and they’ll have what we call dedicated deals in place.”

But that doesn’t help smaller companies, which are walking a delicate line of not wanting to alienate customers who have enjoyed free shipping for nearly a generation.

Todd Shelton, founder of the eponymous 23-year-old New Jersey clothing company that makes high-end men’s jeans, T-shirts and button-up shirts locally, said he started charging customers for return shipping this week for the first time after absorbing the higher expenses this year. The shipping is deducted from customers’ refunds.

Shelton said his costs have been rising for materials, too, such as his imported Japanese denim and shirt fabric from Portugal. The company is still profitable, but the higher costs have eaten into profit margins as they stay elevated, he’s considering raising prices or charging for shipping to customers, he said.

Shields said she’s considering raising her shipping fees for the first time in six years to keep up with the increases.

The holiday season is one of Shields’ busiest. But she said she’s seen a slowdown in sales because of shipping fees.

“I can’t compete with Amazon on the free shipping. I can’t do that. I can’t afford that,” she said. “I’m seeing so much of my percentage that’s supposed to come back to me and my family being put towards the shipping costs.”

With no sign of fuel prices declining significantly, Shields, who runs her business out of her spare bedroom at home, said she’s not sure that small businesses will be able to emerge on the other side of the holidays.

Shippers including UPS
, FedEx
 and USPS have all instituted holiday surcharges, with prices varying by package type and lasting through the end of the season. Though that’s typical during the peak holiday period each year, those charges have continued to rise over the past few years.

But even as costs everywhere climb, consumers are still spending.

According to the National Retail Federation, retail sales through the end of the year are expected to grow 4.2%, translating to total spending of $1.01 trillion. That’s compared with last year’s holiday sales totaling $972 billion, which was 3.1% growth.

Some of that growth is from inflation, meaning consumers are simply paying more for the same goods.

“Customers all expect to spend more this holiday, but part of why they expect to spend more is they expect things to cost more, not because they’d like to spend more or they were hoping to get more quantity of stuff,” said Aaron Cheris, the global retail practice head at Bain & Company. “So what I suspect happens is that non-discretionary categories do fine, because you buy the food you were going to need to buy anyway, but then the amount of cash that’s left over for [discretionary] goods is less.”

Still, Cheris said it’s shaping up to be a record year for shipping costs, which is putting immense pressure on smaller retailers. That means many retailers may find themselves in financial distress in the first quarter of next year as they struggle to make it through the holiday season.

He added that larger retail companies will also have to reckon with rising costs, though they may not feel those effects until later quarters because they have shipping contracts that have already been locked in and have control over their own delivery fleets.

“If anything, it benefits the scale players over the little players, but it’s kind of a little bit bad for everybody,” Cheris said. “I think that is the challenge.”
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/small-bu.summary: Experts say it's shaping up to be a record year for shipping costs. Small retailers may find themselves in financial distress in the first quarter of next year.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/tesla-cy.title: Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production in Texas next year to ramp Cybercab, Musk says
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/tesla-cy.author: Michael Wayland,Lora Kolodny
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/tesla-cy.text:
Elon Musk said Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at Gigafactory Texas around mid-2027.

Musk said the change will make room for increased production of Tesla’s Cybercab robotaxi.

The Cybertruck and its polarizing design gained a niche following, but it did not achieve mass-market sales and has faced several recalls.

Tesla
 CEO Elon Musk on Friday said the electric vehicle maker will “be winding down” production of the Cybertruck at its Texas gigafactory around the middle of next year.

Musk, who hailed the Cybertruck as the future of the pickup truck segment, said in a post on X early Friday morning that the end of production at the massive facility would make room for manufacturing of its Cybercab robotaxi.

The Cybertruck is exclusively produced at the company’s plant in Texas alongside the Tesla Model Y and two-seat Cybercab, which Musk has touted as a crucial product for the automaker moving forward.

Musk did not say whether the company would produce the Cybertruck at a different facility, but he later responded to a user on X who called the update an “end of an era” and said the Cybertruck was the “best vehicle Tesla has ever made.”

“True, but the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time,” Musk said.

Tesla began Cybertruck deliveries in late 2023. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment from CNBC.

The Cybertruck and its polarizing design gained a niche following, but it did not achieve mass-market sales, despite Musk’s pre-launch prediction that annual sales would eventually total 250,000.

“Trucks have been the same for a very long time,” Musk said when the truck was unveiled in 2019. “Like 100 years. Trucks have been basically the same. We want to try something different.”

While Tesla does not break out its sales by model or region, Cox Automotive estimated sales of the Cybertruck last year at 20,237 units in the U.S., down 48% from 38,965 in 2024.

One big buyer of the Cybertruck last year was Musk’s aerospace and tech conglomerate, SpaceX
, which spent $131 million buying up the angular steel trucks at Tesla’s suggested retail price, according to a SpaceX financial filing.

The distinct look of the vehicle made some owners a target of rude gestures and more serious road rage, one owner told CNBC last May, after Musk became the biggest funder of Donald Trump’s presidential campaign and led the so-called Department of Government Efficiency, an effort to slash the federal workforce and regulations.

Wired wrote in an October 2025 feature story, “There is likely no object that feels more emblematic of US president Donald Trump’s return to the White House than the Tesla Cybertruck.” The magazine interviewed owners who described being spit on and sworn at due to their choice of vehicle.

The Cybertruck’s specifications also fell short of those Tesla advertised early on, and in some cases fell short of those offered by leading fuel-burning pickups. There have also been many quality and production problems associated with the vehicles.

The 2024 Tesla Cybertruck was the subject of 11 voluntary recalls, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration website. Issues ranged from a “trapped” acceleration pedal risk that could cause unintended acceleration, to software defects and an inverter fault that could result in sudden loss of drive power.
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/tesla-cy.summary: Elon Musk said the change will make room for increased production of Tesla’s Cybercab robotaxi. The Cybertruck is exclusively produced at the company’'s plant in Texas alongside the Tesla Model Y and two-seat Cybercabs.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/moderna-.title: Moderna raises 2026 outlook as CEO says newer vaccines are gaining traction
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/moderna-.author: Annika Kim Constantino
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/moderna-.text:
Moderna smashed third-quarter revenue and earnings estimates and hiked its outlook for full-year sales growth.

The biotech company now expects 2026 revenue growth of 15% to 25%, up from its previous guidance of up to 10%.

In an interview, Moderna CEO Stéphane Bancel pointed to new product launches and the “diversification” of geographies.

Moderna on Friday smashed third-quarter revenue and earnings estimates and hiked its outlook for full-year sales growth, as some of its newer products gain momentum and Covid vaccine revenue outperforms.

Shares of Moderna rose roughly 3% in premarket trading on Friday.

The biotech company now expects 2026 revenue growth of 15% to 25%, up from its previous guidance of up to 10%.

“The new product and the diversification of geography is what has led to such a strong Q3,” Moderna CEO Stéphane Bancel said in an interview ahead of the results.

For example, he said the company is seeing the “full-year impact” of its next-generation mRNA Covid vaccine, which won U.S. approval in May 2025. Bancel noted that Covid is a seasonal business and vaccine contracts are typically established in the first quarter, so Moderna’s shot only had a “small launch” to start with last year.

Moderna’s new stand-alone flu shot, which was approved in the U.S. in August, will similarly have a “limited launch” in the country in 2026 given the timing, he said.

In a separate interview on CNBC’s “Squawk Box,” Bancel said Moderna’s geographic expansion in Canada, the U.K. and Asia helped boost results. The company’s work to lower costs also resulted in a profit in the quarter, he added.

“It’s the sales that are stronger and the costs that are also lower,” Bancel said.

Here’s what Moderna reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

Moderna’s third-quarter revenue jumped 29% to $1.31 billion, boosted by higher Covid vaccine sales in international markets and helped by deliveries under long-term government partnerships. Revenue was $780 million in the U.S. and $533 million in international markets.

The company posted a net income of $162 million, or 38 cents per share, for the third quarter. That compares with a net loss of $200 million, or a loss of 51 cents per share, reported for the year-ago period.

The results come weeks after Moderna and Merck unveiled promising late-stage data on their experimental personalized cancer vaccine in combination with immunotherapy Keytruda in certain melanoma patients. Despite the positive results, investors battered Moderna’s stock after part of the data was leaked on social media just days before trial investigators were set to present it at a European medical conference.

Bancel called it a “surprising reaction,” but said that the companies also saw a positive response from others on Wall Street, including long-term investors and analysts who examined the full data in depth. He added that the doctors in the field “were so impressed with the data,” and many expressed that they hope to use it in their day-to-day practice.

Moderna’s stock has skyrocketed more than 700% this year, largely on optimism about the potential for the shot.
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/moderna-.summary: Moderna CEO Stéphane Bancel said new product launches and the “diversification’ of geographies’s geographies are helping boost results. The biotech company now expects 2026 revenue growth of 15% to 25% to 15%

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/wonder-c.title: Marc Lore's Wonder confidentially files for IPO
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/wonder-c.author: Amelia Lucas
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/wonder-c.text:
Wonder has confidentially filed for an initial public offering, the company said.

Founder Marc Lore previously started Diapers.com and Jet.com, which he sold to Amazon and Walmart, respectively.

Wonder advertises itself as “the best restaurants from across the country, all in one place,” available for delivery and takeout on its vertically integrated app.

Food startup Wonder has confidentially filed for an initial public offering, the company said Thursday.

Created by serial entrepreneur Marc Lore in 2018, Wonder advertises itself as “the best restaurants from across the country, all in one place,” available for delivery and takeout on its vertically integrated app.

Originally envisioned as a new take on food delivery through sprinter vans outfitted with mobile kitchens, Wonder has grown to roughly 170 brick-and-mortar locations throughout the U.S. Its locations serve menu items from more than two dozen “restaurants” across a variety of cuisines, some with branding from celebrity chefs.

Starting Nov. 17, the company plans to introduce more dining options through Wonder Create. Influencers, entrepreneurs and brands can pay $10 a month to start their own restaurant business based out of a Wonder location and earn a portion of the revenue from orders.

Wonder has spent at least $1 billion on acquisitions, such as delivery service Grubhub, meal kit brand Blue Apron and delivery and logistics provider Relay, along with some buzzy restaurant concepts. Wonder has been able to afford such expensive dealmaking thanks to more than $3 billion in venture funding.

Wonder’s Series D fundraising round earlier this year raised its pre-money valuation to $9 billion.

With the proceeds from an IPO, Wonder will be able to make more acquisitions and work toward its goal of making food more accessible, Lore told CNBC in September.

But as a public company, Wonder will also likely face investor scrutiny. Weak consumer sentiment has weighed on restaurant stocks recently, plus market volatility has resulted in a shaky IPO market for companies across a range of industries.

Lore previously founded Diapers.com and Jet.com, which he sold to Amazon and Walmart, respectively.
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/wonder-c.summary: Wonder has confidentially filed for an initial public offering, the company said. Founder Marc Lore previously started Diapers.com and Jet.com, which he sold to Amazon and Walmart. The company plans to introduce more dining options through Wonder Create starting Nov. 17.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/wendys-r.title: Wendy's rejects $1.4 billion takeover proposal from Nelson Peltz’s Trian
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/wendys-r.author: Amelia Lucas
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/wendys-r.text:
Wendy’s on Thursday said that it is rejecting a $1.4 billion takeover offer from a group of investors led by Nelson Peltz’s Trian Fund Management.

Wendy’s said the proposal does not reflect potential gains from the burger chain’s turnaround strategy.

The company also said its same-store sales declined again in the third quarter, though it beat Wall Street’s earnings and revenue expectations.

Wendy’s
 on Thursday said it is rejecting a $1.4 billion takeover offer from a group of investors led by Nelson Peltz’s Trian Fund Management.

The group offered $7.35 per share in cash on Oct. 28 to take the struggling burger chain private. In addition to Trian, it included investment firms BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street Partners, plus Flynn Group, one of Wendy’s largest franchisees.

In February, Wendy’s board formed a committee of independent directors to assess any potential bid from Trian in response to a regulatory filing from the firm. The committee found that the proposal “substantially undervalues” Wendy’s and does not reflect potential gains from the chain’s ongoing turnaround strategy, the company said in a press release Thursday.

“Our confidence rests firmly in [CEO] Bob Wright’s proven track record of seasoned industry leadership, including restaurant business turnarounds,” Art Winkleblack, Wendy’s board chair and a member of the independent committee, said in a statement.

Trian declined to comment on Wendy’s decision.

To stave off a hostile takeover, Wendy’s has adopted a shareholder rights plan — or poison pill — with a one-year duration, as of Wednesday, the company said. Wendy’s added that the investor group led by Trian rejected an offer from Wendy’s for a standstill agreement that would have paused additional share purchases, adding to Wendy’s decision to use a poison pill.

The rejection is the latest in the long-running saga between Peltz and the burger chain, which dates back to an activist campaign he led more than two decades ago. A Peltz firm has even owned Wendy’s before. In 2008, his company Triarc, which also owned Arby’s, bought Wendy’s in a $2.3 billion deal. It later sold Arby’s, turning Wendy’s into a stand-alone company again.

In 2024, Wendy’s named Peltz as chairman emeritus after he spent 17 years on the company’s board. Trian executive Peter May and Peltz’s son, Bradley, still sit on Wendy’s board.

Wendy’s also reported its third-quarter results on Thursday. Its same-store sales declined for the seventh straight quarter. However, its quarterly earnings and revenue topped Wall Street’s expectations.

Shares of Wendy’s fell less than 1% in morning trading. The takeover offer had lifted the stock, which has lost about 60% of its value over the last three years.

Wendy’s is not the only restaurant chain that has found itself in the crosshairs of activist investors. Applebee’s owner Dine Brands
 recently adopted a poison pill to block a takeover bid from investment firms Arkhouse Management and Cobblers Cove Capital.
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/wendys-r.summary: Wendy’s said the proposal does not reflect potential gains from the burger chain’'s turnaround strategy. The company also said its same-store sales declined again in the third quarter, though it beat Wall Street’S earnings and revenue expectations.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/expedia-.title: Expedia CEO says AI agents aren't changing booking habits — yet
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/expedia-.author: Maggie Roth
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/expedia-.text:
Expedia CEO Ariane Gorin told CNBC that the company has not yet seen AI agents affecting customers’ booking habits.

She said complexities in the travel industry would make it difficult for AI to fully replace travel services.

The company reported fourth-quarter guidance below analysts’ expectations.

Expedia
 CEO Ariane Gorin said Thursday the company hasn’t yet seen artificial intelligence agents affecting the way customers book, but the early signs show potential for an industry shift.

“It’s a great way for people to do inspiration, to do trip planning,” Gorin said in an interview with CNBC. “We haven’t seen it change the way they’re actually doing booking.”

The comments come as personal AI agents like Meta’s
 Muse and OpenAI’s Dots enter the mainstream, promising to tackle everything from scheduling to shopping for everyday Americans. Opportunities in travel planning and booking could pose a competitive threat to traditional sites like Expedia.

Gorin said Expedia is “working with all of the agents” to make sure it surfaces in AI results, to understand how the agents get information and to make sure that the company has the necessary integrations.

She acknowledged it’s possible that AI agents could develop their own travel programs and eventually claim market share, but she said complexities within the industry — customer service, for example — would be difficult to fully replace with artificial intelligence.

“People were already shopping across a number of places, so the agent can do that in a much easier way,” Gorin said. “But when it comes to actually booking — being confident that the content that you’re getting is right, the amenities are right, the price is right, if something goes wrong, someone’s going to actually either solve it for you, answer the phone, be there for you — I don’t think those agents are going to do it for you, and that’s why people trust Expedia and come to us.”

Shares of Expedia were down about 12% Thursday after the company delivered weaker-than-expected guidance for the fourth quarter on Wednesday. The company forecast revenue of between $3.69 billion and $3.75 billion for the final three months of the year, making the midpoint lower than analyst estimates of $3.74 billion, according to FactSet.

Gorin attributed the “moderation” in Expedia’s fourth-quarter guidance to “geopolitical events in the Middle East and Europe,” the midterm elections and the company moving its fall sale from the fourth quarter to the third quarter. But she noted the company reported a strong third quarter, as total gross bookings rose 11% and revenue climbed 12%.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/visa-hol.title: Consumers are spending on physical gifts even as travel tops wish lists, Visa survey finds
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/visa-hol.author: Laya Neelakandan
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/visa-hol.text:
Even as travel and experiences top wish lists, consumers are prioritizing spending on physical gifts this holiday season, according to Visa.

The gap comes as higher airfares and general inflation force consumers to be more intentional about their spending.

Still, much of the holiday sales growth expected this season is tied to inflation.

Consumers are hoping for more travel and experiences this holiday season, but physical gifts continue to win the lion’s share of their wallets, according to a new report from Visa
 on Thursday.

The report found that more than half of survey respondents are putting travel and live events at the top of their wish lists. Still, only 15% of those respondents are prioritizing spending on experiences for others, while 27% of them plan to favor physical gifts.

That gap between what shoppers want and what they plan to buy is largely due to higher travel costs, lower consumer sentiment and an emphasis on value, according to Michael Brown, Visa’s principal U.S. economist.

“There is some interesting trade-offs there that we’re seeing on the part of consumers,” Brown told CNBC. “If I’m traveling more, I’m probably going to be gifting those physical goods less, so this is really the broader context.”

The survey was conducted among roughly 4,660 U.S. adults ages 18 and older, designed to be representative of the broader population of consumers.

Brown said budget pressure also factors into traveling for the holidays, as Visa expects more people to celebrate the holidays “a little bit closer to home” than in the past given rising airfares and general inflation. In September, consumer prices rose 3.7% annually, driven higher by surging energy costs.

Airlines have hiked the price of plane tickets this year as their fuel costs have risen by billions of dollars due to the war in the Middle East. And even if fuel prices drop, executives have said fares are likely to stay high, with fares up more than 22% in September compared with a year earlier, according to the consumer price index.

Those trends mean consumers will likely be more intentional about where they’re spending, especially as inflation drives up prices across the board.

“Consumers are aspirational. They want those experiences, they want to travel, they want to be out in the world,” Brown said. “However, the economic reality is with prices rising, with economic uncertainty, they need to balance the reality of today’s economic environment with those aspirations.”

The report also found that only households with an income above $200,000 spent more on trips departing between Nov. 1 and early next year compared with 2025 into 2026. On the other hand, many other income groups pulled back on their travel spending.

“If you think about that segment, a lot of them own equities, and the equity market runup over the last several months has created a lot of positivity among that specific affluent demographic, and I think that’s one of the factors that continues to motivate even aggregate macro spend today,” Brown said.

Meanwhile, less affluent shoppers are placing an emphasis on value. Visa’s consumer survey from October showed that roughly one-third of consumers with an income below $100,000 are going to switch to lower-cost brands or stores when shopping for holiday gifts this season.

Though Visa is projecting a 4.5% year-over-year increase in holiday sales growth, much of that figure is due to inflation. Without those price increases, sales are expected to rise just 1.1% this year, down from the 1.3% increase during the 2025 holiday season.

Ultimately, Brown said the survey findings may be encouraging for the broader retail scene this holiday season. With less emphasis on travel and more projected spending on physical gifts, it could boost the sector at a time when spending is under pressure.

At the same time, he said that consumers may just be expecting to spend more this holiday season because they’ve become accustomed to the higher prices.

“But, of course, consumers are internalizing higher prices of things, and I think that’s why they’re reporting higher anticipated spend this year,” Brown said. “I think these numbers just need to be looked at through the lens of the inflation and particularly consumers’ perception of where inflation is going to go. I think that weighed heavily on consumer psychology this season.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/04/elf-beau.title: E.l.f. Beauty posts 51% sales increase, raises full-year guidance
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/04/elf-beau.author: Laya Neelakandan
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/04/elf-beau.text:
E.l.f. Beauty posted stronger-than-expected quarterly results on Wednesday as CEO Tarang Amin told CNBC the company continues to see broad-based growth across its portfolio.

The company said its net sales grew 51% for the quarter, reaching $520.8 million.

It also raised its full-year guidance across net sales, adjusted EBITDA, adjusted net income and adjusted earnings per share.

E.l.f. Beauty
 on Wednesday blew past Wall Street expectations as it posted a 51% increase in net sales in its second fiscal quarter.

The beauty company said it saw its 31st consecutive quarter of net sales growth, attributing the streak to strong performance across its portfolio. The revenue spike was driven by both retail and e-commerce channels across the U.S. and internationally, the company added.

“The thing I’m most pleased about is we saw strength across our entire portfolio,” CEO Tarang Amin told CNBC in an interview. “Every one of our brands contributed strong growth this quarter.”

Amin added that E.l.f. is the most-searched brand on TikTok Shop and the No. 2 brand in cosmetics on the platform. The company also said it saw strong results for Rhode, the skincare brand it acquired last year.

The company raised its full fiscal-year guidance following the better-than-anticipated quarter. It now expects net sales in the range of $2 billion to $2.03 billion, compared with a previous range of between $1.94 billion and $1.97 billion. It also upped its adjusted EBITDA projection to a range of $421 million to $427 million from between $401 million and $407 million.

E.l.f. said it now expects adjusted earnings per share for the year to come in between $3.82 and $3.86, exceeding prior guidance of between $3.50 and $3.55 per share. It’s also expecting a net income range of $231 million to $233 million, up from a previous range of $212 million to $215 million.

It had already raised its guidance last quarter after outperforming its expectations.

Amin said the company is “very bullish” on the holiday season, expecting high sales through the end of the year.

Here’s how the company performed in its second fiscal quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

For the period ended Sept. 30, E.l.f. reported net income of $30.03 million, or 50 cents per share, up significantly from roughly $3 million, or 5 cents per share, the year prior.

Net sales grew 51% to $520.8 million.

E.l.f. also saw significant growth in its international channels, with business up 165%. Amin told CNBC that only 25% of the company’s business is outside of the U.S. and that it has a “tremendous opportunity” to build on that momentum.

The company also said its gross margin increased 1.6% during the quarter, including a 0.3% benefit from tariff refunds. Amin previously said the retailer planned to fully reinvest that money into pricing and marketing to continue driving growth.

Though E.l.f. received most of its refunds in its first fiscal quarter, some of those funds flowed through the second quarter, and the company expects to receive a yearly total of around $55 million. Amin told CNBC on Wednesday that the company lowered the price of about 10% of its units by $1 because of the tariff benefits.

“We’re seeing great unit momentum based on that,” he said.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/04/cvs-heal.title: CVS Health plans to split itself up. Here's why a breakup could make sense now
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/04/cvs-heal.author: Annika Kim Constantino
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/04/cvs-heal.text:
CVS Health announced plans to split into two publicly traded companies by the first half of 2028, separating its pharmacy business from its insurer, Aetna, and pharmacy benefit manager, Caremark.

Analysts say that after a roughly two-year turnaround the company’s retail pharmacy business and other units may be strong enough to stand on their own.

CVS in 2024 considered a breakup but ultimately walked away from the idea.

CVS Health
 plans to break itself up — and this time, the bet looks a lot more viable.

The healthcare conglomerate on Wednesday announced plans to split into two publicly traded companies by the first half of 2028. CVS would separate its pharmacy business – including roughly 9,000 retail locations – from its major insurance business and pharmacy benefit manager, Caremark.

The move comes more than two years after CVS considered a breakup but ultimately walked away from the idea. At the time, analysts questioned whether the retail pharmacy business could survive on its own.

“Back then, the idea of retail standing alone was unthinkable,” Brian Tanquilut, senior equity research analyst at Jefferies, told CNBC.

But the economics of the businesses have changed: CVS’s retail pharmacy business has become more consistently profitable, while its insurer, Aetna, has improved its performance despite persistently high medical costs in Medicare Advantage plans. That could make it easier for the company to separate the units — and for investors to recognize the value of each on its own, rather than valuing them together as one sprawling healthcare conglomerate.

“For us, it’s showing the stability of the pharmacy,” Michael Cherny, senior research analyst at Leerink Partners, said in an interview. “This business is a much different business from the one that’s been considered three years ago, five years ago, 10 years ago, where there had been a litany of headwinds that the pharmacy just couldn’t overcome.”

CVS CEO David Joyner told CNBC’s “Squawk on the Street” on Wednesday that back in 2024, the company was “in a turnaround” without the flexibility, cash or business performance to execute a split. Now, CVS has posted eight consecutive quarters of beating Wall Street earnings estimates and has raised its guidance several times over the last two years, thanks to improvement across its PBM, pharmacy and insurer.

Since taking the helm in 2024, Joyner has pursued an aggressive turnaround plan that involves $2 billion in cost cuts, store closures, leadership shakeups and efforts to rein in Medicare Advantage costs.

The company also now expects to generate at least $15.5 billion in operating cash flow in 2026, a roughly 70% increase from $9.1 billion in 2024, and says it has reached its leverage target ahead of schedule.

“What’s changed in two years is the fact that we now can look at this business and the assets that are assembled and really determine, without any distress or without anything that we have to do, what is the right strategic decision to make,” Joyner told analysts on a call Wednesday, adding that the decision comes “out of strength.”

While investors have largely cheered CVS’s progress in recent years, Wall Street appeared more pessimistic about Wednesday’s announcement, as the company’s shares dropped about 12%.

CVS’s retail business has benefited from changes in the competitive landscape, including the widespread retrenchment and store closures of Walgreens, Rite Aid and other pharmacy operators over the last few years. That’s created opportunities for CVS to gain market share, some analysts told CNBC.

CVS has also introduced changes to its pharmacy reimbursement model. Its CostVantage program is designed to replace the traditional process with a more transparent, cost-based model. Some analysts say that has helped the company better align reimbursement with the cost of dispensing prescriptions and contributed to steadier profits.

Those developments represent a meaningful shift for a business that has faced years of pressure from declining prescription reimbursement, store closures and competition from online pharmacies and other retailers.

That doesn’t mean the retail pharmacy has become a high-growth business. CVS’s retail pharmacy segment remains a relatively low-margin operation, with adjusted operating margins of roughly 4% to 5%. But analysts say it may now be stable and profitable enough to operate independently – even if investors value it at a discount to CVS’s other businesses.

In a note Wednesday, RBC Capital Markets analyst Ben Hendrix said the lower valuation investors assign to the retail pharmacy unit has weighed on CVS’s overall value and obscured the earnings strength of businesses like Aetna and Caremark.

The underlying growth of the insurance and PBM businesses is also stronger than that of retail pharmacy, Tanquilut said, after accounting for changes to Caremark’s rebate arrangements.

Aetna in particular has gotten a better handle on medical costs by exiting unprofitable markets, expanding value-based care models, and tightening utilization management.

The breakup also comes as Caremark faces mounting scrutiny over PBM practices, including state-level legal and regulatory challenges involving the businesses and their relationships with pharmacies.

Republicans in Tennessee and Arkansas have passed laws that would ban any one company from owning both a pharmacy and a PBM — thought the Arkansas measure has been held up in court. Cherny noted that legal hurdles involving PBMs in other states have continued to pile up.

“Through what seems to be a never-ending litany of state lawsuits, it feels like it’s been under more pressure,” Cherny said. “It’s unclear if it just became, for lack of a better term, too tenuous to move forward with those two entities combined as one. I’m not sure.”

Even so, Joyner told the Wall Street Journal that the company wasn’t splitting up because of regulatory issues. CVS has said the separation follows a strategic review and is intended to give each business greater focus and flexibility.

The move also marks a significant departure from the integrated healthcare strategy CVS spent years building.

CVS spent roughly $70 billion to acquire Aetna in 2018 and argued that combining health insurance, pharmacy benefit management, retail pharmacies and health providers under one roof would help coordinate care and create a competitive advantage. CVS was still promoting that model as recently as its investor day last year.

The proposed split suggests the company now sees more value in separating at least some of those businesses – though it is not abandoning vertical integration altogether.

Aetna and Caremark will remain together in the healthcare company, alongside CVS’s specialty pharmacy, its primary care clinic Oak Street Health and its home-visit provider Signify Health. The separate pharmacy company will include roughly 9,000 retail stores, mail pharmacy operations and MinuteClinic, a retail medical clinic located inside certain CVS locations.

Both sides are large enough that they can stand on their own, Cherny said. Caremark is one of the country’s three largest PBMs, while CVS has one of the largest retail pharmacy footprints in the U.S.

But separating the company raises questions about how much of the commercial relationship between the businesses can survive.

The relationship has historically benefited both sides. As it stands, Caremark can use CVS’s extensive retail footprint to offer members convenient access to prescriptions and steer them toward CVS locations through preferred pharmacy arrangements. Programs such as Maintenance Choice, for example, give eligible members the option to fill certain maintenance medications at CVS retail pharmacies or through mail order.

Those arrangements also helped direct prescription volume to CVS’s stores, giving the retail pharmacy unit an important source of customers. Because the businesses shared a parent company, the financial benefits of that relationship ultimately went to CVS as a whole.

In a note, RBC’s Hendrix also raised questions about how the split could impact Aetna’s Medicare Advantage quality ratings, which determine whether health plans qualify for bonus payments from the government. Retail pharmacists have played a role in engaging Aetna members, and a separation could complicate that relationship.

But Joyner told analysts Wednesday that the synergy between the two businesses would be “preserved in commercial agreements between the two organizations,” adding that “we don’t need the integration of an operating structure.”

Joyner said CVS will be working on those potential agreements over the next 15 to 18 months.

Preferred pharmacy networks are common across the industry, and separate ownership does not prevent Caremark from continuing to favor CVS pharmacies through negotiated arrangements, Cherny said. The difference is that under separate ownership, the profits from those arrangements would no longer accrue to a single company, he noted.

“The issue is not whether the companies can continue working together in some capacity, but whether any future contractual arrangements preserve the SAME competitive advantages and flexibility as today under common ownership,” Cherny said in an afternoon note on Wednesday.

Still, both businesses face challenges on their own.

Tanquilut cautioned that some of CVS’s recent retail pharmacy gains have come as Walgreens and other competitors have closed stores, raising questions about whether the growth can be sustained. The business also remains exposed to consumer pressure and competition from online pharmacies.

Caremark, meanwhile, faces continued regulatory scrutiny and potential headwinds from changes to the federal 340B drug discount program, which requires drugmakers to offer discounted medications to eligible hospitals and other healthcare providers serving low-income and vulnerable patients.

CVS participates in the program by providing pharmacy services to those organizations, but tweaks to manufacturer data-sharing policies and potential reimbursement changes could weigh on that business in 2027, Tanquilut said.

Aetna, meanwhile, is still working through a multiyear plan to rebuild its margins, as it looks to improve the profitability of its Medicare Advantage business.

Ultimately, CVS is betting that the value of letting investors assess its businesses separately will outweigh the benefits of keeping them under one roof. The split will test whether each can thrive independently.
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/04/cvs-heal.summary: CVS Health announced plans to split into two publicly traded companies by the first half of 2028. The healthcare conglomerate on Wednesday announced plans for the split. The move comes more than two years after CVS considered a breakup but ultimately walked away from the idea.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/04/flutter-.title: New Flutter CEO bets on FanDuel promotions to win customers as profits suffer
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/04/flutter-.author: Contessa Brewer
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/04/flutter-.text:
Flutter’s new CEO Dan Taylor issued his first earnings report as CEO on Wednesday.

Third-quarter revenue and adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization missed Wall Street’s expectations.

Taylor said there’s been fierce competition for customers but FanDuel is improving the product and seeing good momentum.

Flutter’s
 new CEO Dan Taylor is counting on better products and more generous customer rewards to help convert FanDuel’s improving engagement into stronger profits.

Taylor’s been at the helm for just five weeks and issued his first earnings report as CEO on Wednesday, with third-quarter revenue and adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization missing Wall Street’s expectations.

The company’s stock is down more than 60% year to date.

Yet Taylor says the company is now on the right track.

“We made some changes to the product,” Taylor told CNBC in an interview. “Fundamentally, the way you win this business is by delighting customers, delivering the very best experiences and delivering to them in the way that they want, with the right overall proposition.”

FanDuel also launched a nationwide rewards program in September that Taylor said has “resonated really, really well.”

The early customer numbers are improving. Average monthly players on FanDuel’s U.S. sportsbook rose 9% in the third quarter, while bet counts increased 15%, Taylor said.

Flutter’s earnings release showed total U.S. average monthly players up 12%, including 24% growth in iGaming. Sportsbook handle, or the total amount wagered, rose 13%, but sportsbook revenue grew just 4% as promotional spending increased.

Taylor said the company plans to keep investing in customer experience. He said Flutter sees room to improve its structural margins over time by changing the mix of products customers use.

Flutter has increased its media spend to build FanDuel Predicts, its predictions platform to rival Kalshi and Polymarket, but the cost of sales as a percent of revenue is forecast to be 58% for the full-year 2026 and into 2027.

Taylor said there’s fierce industry competition for customers but even still, FanDuel trading volume has skyrocketed 271% since July.

The FanDuel Predicts app added 140,000 new customers in October, Taylor said.

Taylor also defended the long-term opportunity in the U.S., pointing out about half the country still does not have access to regulated sports betting and 90% lacks regulated online gaming.

He argued that expanding legal markets is not a partisan issue because regulated betting offers consumer protections and gives tax revenue to states.

For the third quarter, Flutter reported an adjusted loss of 18 cents per share, compared with analysts’ expectations for a loss of 28 cents, according to LSEG. Revenue rose 2% to $3.87 billion, below the roughly $4 billion LSEG consensus, while adjusted EBITDA fell roughly 25% year over year to $360 million, also below expectations.

The company posted a net loss of $1.15 billion, including an $873 million non-cash impairment tied primarily to Brazil, which banned sports betting and online gaming in September.

Taylor said the company was disappointed by Brazil’s provisional measure, but took the impairment to “set ourselves up to win long-term.”

The complications in Brazil and unfavorable sports results in the U.S. and internationally led Flutter to cut its full-year revenue midpoint by $300 million to $17.61 billion and lower its 2026 adjusted EBITDA outlook by $160 million to nearly $2.5 billion.

In the meantime, capital returns are on hold: Taylor said Flutter needs to bring leverage back into its target range of 2 to 2.5 times over roughly the next 24 months before it can consider buybacks again. For now, he said, the priority is organic growth and paying down debt.

— CNBC’s Mallory Leonard contributed to this report.
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/04/flutter-.summary: FanDuel CEO Dan Taylor says the company is on the right track. Taylor says there’s been fierce competition for customers but FanDuel is improving the product and seeing good momentum. The company’'s stock is down more than 60% year to date.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/04/cvs-to-s.title: CVS to split off drugstore business in major breakup of healthcare giant; shares fall 10%
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/04/cvs-to-s.author: Annika Kim Constantino
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/04/cvs-to-s.text:
CVS Health plans to split into two separate public companies by the first half of 2028 in what would be one of the largest corporate splits in history.

The move would reverse the company’s massive $78 billion acquisition of its insurer, Aetna, and dismantle the vertically integrated healthcare conglomerate it created in 2018.

The plan would separate CVS’ roughly 9,000 retail pharmacies from its major insurance business and pharmacy benefit manager, Caremark, one of the nation’s three largest PBMs.

CVS Health
 plans to split into two separate public companies by the first half 2028 in what would be one of the largest corporate breakups in history, the company announced Wednesday.

The move would reverse the company’s massive $78 billion acquisition of its insurer, Aetna, and dismantle the vertically integrated healthcare conglomerate it created in 2018. The plan would specifically separate CVS’ roughly 9,000 retail pharmacies from its major insurance business and pharmacy benefit manager, Caremark, one of the nation’s three largest PBMs.

The decision follows a “comprehensive strategic review” by the company’s board of directors, according to a news release. Shares of CVS closed more than 12% lower on Wednesday.

It’s a stunning reversal for the healthcare powerhouse, which has spent the last two decades working to turn itself into a one-stop health destination. The move also comes as CVS’ aggressive turnaround plan under CEO David Joyner shows substantial progress, with the company pursuing $2 billion in cost cuts, store closures, leadership shake-ups and efforts to rein in Medicare Advantage costs.

But Joyner told CNBC’s “Squawk on the Street” on Wednesday that the decision to split is “out of a position of strength,” pointing to recovery in Aetna’s Medicare business and solid performance in the retail pharmacy.

“So it’s all about the strength of the business that affords us the opportunity to make what we think are the right strategic decisions for the future of this company,” he later added.

CVS shares have jumped roughly 70% since Joyner took the helm in October 2024, bringing the company’s market value to $117 billion.

The two new companies would both be publicly traded.

The insurance and PBM company will retain the CVS Health name and be run by Joyner, while the other company will be called CVS Pharmacy and be led by Prem Shah, who is currently group president of CVS Health. Additional leadership positions and board members will be announced at a later date, CVS said.

Existing CVS shareholders will own stock in both companies after the split. The Financial Times on Tuesday first reported the breakup plans.

The company’s pharmacy business raked in $37.66 billion in 2025 sales, while its insurance unit booked $36.29 billion in revenue and the healthcare services segment generated $51.24 billion.

CVS on Wednesday also posted third-quarter earnings and revenue that topped Wall Street expectations. Total sales climbed to $108.40 billion, from $102.87 billion in the prior-year period.

Sales were boosted by year-over-year growth in the company’s healthcare benefits and health services segments. Meanwhile, revenue in its pharmacy services business slid from the previous year.

On Wednesday, CVS said it will lump its insurer and PBM with its primary care business Oak Street Health, home visit provider Signify Health and the company’s specialty drug business.

CVS also said the split will allow the two companies to experience a “focused strategic agenda” and greater ability to “innovate, adopt technology, increase efficiency,” among other benefits.

It’s not the first time CVS has weighed splitting the company. In October 2024, CVS engaged advisors in a strategic review of its business and considered breaking up its retail pharmacy and insurance units.

But Joyner told CNBC that the company was “in a turnaround” at that time without the flexibility, cash position or business performance to execute a split.

In an interview, Leerink Partners analyst Michael Cherny said the split shows “the stability of the pharmacy,” which has won market share from competitors and is seeing gross margins stabilize thanks to CostVantage, a new pharmacy reimbursement model introduced by CVS last year that the company bills as more transparent.

“This business is a much different business from the one that’s been considered three years ago, five years ago, 10 years ago, where there had been a litany of headwinds that the pharmacy just couldn’t overcome,” he told CNBC on Wednesday.

One potential concern for investors is whether the retail pharmacy will lose its competitive advantage of being directly linked with a PBM, which negotiates drug prices and manages prescription drug benefits on behalf of insurers and employers.

But Joyner told analysts Wednesday that the synergy between the two businesses “are going to be preserved in commercial agreements between the two organizations,” adding that “we don’t need the integration of an operating structure.”

Cherny said the rationale for the split could also extend to the state legislative scrutiny over the company’s level of vertical integration.

The potential breakup also comes as pharmacy benefit managers face mounting bipartisan scrutiny in Washington, D.C., and across states. Republicans in Tennessee and Arkansas have passed laws that would ban co-ownership of PBMs and pharmacies. Those have been challenged in court by CVS and other companies.

PBMs have been criticized for opaque pricing practices, their growing market power and potential conflicts of interest when they are owned by companies that also operate insurers and pharmacies.
