https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.title: France investigating if bogus bomb threats against airlines linked to 'foreign powers'
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.text:
French prosecutors have opened a probe into bogus bomb threats targeting dozens of commercial flights in Europe over the past week, notably including whether foreign powers could be involved.

The investigation aims to find "the authors of the emails who disseminated this false information ... and to determine any potential links they may have to foreign powers", the office of the Paris prosecutor told AFP.

Several such instances concerned flights passing over French territory. The French government, for its part, has also said that the origin of the threats was being investigated.

Ireland's government said Friday that the hoax bomb claims sent to Irish media outlets were "likely" part of a "co-ordinated campaign of disruption" linked to the threats to airlines.

No explosives were found in any of the incidents so far, and those responsible have not been identified.

READ MORE
French blood banks foil new cyberattack targeting refrigerators

Some of the messages came in emails signed "fighters of the Male State", which matches the name of a radical misogynist group in Russia, though AFP has not confirmed any link of it to the messages.

The group's founder, Vladislav Pozdniakov, denied any involvement, saying on social media Friday that the "movement does not exist since 2021".

European countries are closely watching for any Russian interference against economic sectors in Europe and even in daily life as Moscow's war against Ukraine grinds towards its fifth anniversary.
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.summary: French prosecutors open probe into bogus bomb threats targeting commercial flights in Europe. Several such instances concerned flights passing over French territory. Ireland's government says hoax bomb claims were "likely" part of a "co-ordinated campaign of disruption" linked to the threats.

https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.title: Paraguay’s impeached president charged over bank collapse
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.text:
Paraguayan prosecutors charged ex-president Santiago Pena and took him into custody Saturday over a banking crisis that saw millions of people cut off from their money, sparking major protests.

Pena, Paraguay's youngest-ever president at 47, was removed from office by the Senate on Friday, just three days after the collapse of a leading bank with which he had business links.

READ MORE
Impeachment trial of Paraguay's President Pena begins after bank scandal resignation

He had offered to resign but lawmakers impeached him instead, stripping him of the immunity he would have enjoyed had he stepped down.

In a fast-moving sequence of events, Pena was brought before prosecutors on Saturday and charged with "breach of trust and mismanagement for personal gain."

Ueno Bank was a popular online bank that held accounts for nearly half of Paraguay's 6.5 million people, plus more than $800 million in government funds.

Its collapse rocked this small, normally stable country, leading to street protests.

Pena, who came to power in 2023, owned shares in the bank's holding company, Ueno Holding, until he sold them last year.

He is accused of using his influence as president to steer millions in government deposits to Ueno Bank and of hiding or downplaying its financial woes, even though he was warned about questionable loans and solvency issues.

Pena is also accused of a conflict of interest for naming former Ueno Bank director Carlos Carvallo to run Paraguay's Central Bank.

Pena's lawyer Ricardo Preda denied the charges against his client and said that in Paraguay, it is not the president but rather a minister who decides where government money is deposited.

After a hearing with Pena on Saturday, Judge Hernan Otazu told reporters he had ordered the former president taken into pre-trial custody and held at the same Asuncion facility where he was taken after his removal from office on Friday.

The judge froze the assets of Pena and Carvallo, who faces the same charges as the former president, plus one of falsifying government documents.

Pena declined to make a statement during the hearing, Otazu said.

The Central Bank said it has started paying out money to Ueno Bank customers caught up in the collapse and that more than 50 percent have recovered their funds.

Giovanni Catolinom, 40, was not one of them. He trembled as he told AFP that funds from his new travel agency -- around $16,000 -- were still trapped in the bank.

"I lost 16 years of work," he said, crying.

Pena was replaced by Vice President Pedro Alliana, who promised not to abandon the depositors, including pensioners, affected by Ueno's demise.

On the streets of Asuncion there was rejoicing over Pena's ouster.

But news that Alliana, who is from the same right-wing Colorado Party as Pena, would take over angered some demonstrators.

"He's from the same team, he knew about it (the trouble at Ueno)," Edson Vazquez told AFP.

The collapse of Ueno rocked usually stable Paraguay.

Thousands of people took to the streets furiously demanding their money back after the Central Bank took control of Ueno, citing fears for its solvency.

Pena's removal was a further blow for US President Donald Trump's network of allies in South America.

Trump's favorite for Brazilian president, Flavio Bolsonaro, was defeated by left-wing incumbent Lula Inacio Lula da Silva last month.

Alliana will serve out the remainder of Pena's term, which ends in 2028.
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.summary: Santiago Pena is charged with "breach of trust and mismanagement for personal gain" Pena was removed from office by the Senate on Friday, three days after the collapse of a leading bank with which he had business links. The bank's collapse rocked Paraguay's normally stable, normally stable country, leading to street protests.

https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.title: Gunman who killed at least six in Krakow ‘fascinated’ by far-right ideologies, government says
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.text:
Six people were killed and at least 15 wounded on Saturday when a gunman opened fire in the landmark historic centre of Poland's second city of Krakow, in the country's deadliest shooting in decades.

Three bodies – of two women and a man – were later found at the suspect's home, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said, adding there was "much to suggest that they are members of the (suspect's) immediate family".

Tusk also announced Poland would hold two days of mourning over the shooting that he called an act of "terrorism".

Polish Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said the gunman appeared to be "fascinated by far-right ideologies".

A British national was among the killed, according to Polish police chief, Marek Boron, and five foreigners were among the wounded in hospital, the authorities said.

"Two people who have not yet been identified," Boron said referring to the victims killed.

READ MORE
Bomb threats against European airlines force Warsaw airport closure, affect several flights

The suspect – a Polish citizen born in 2002 – drove a car onto Krakow's Main Market Square and began shooting at random people, said police.

Two officers were wounded as they tried to stop the man, the police said, before shooting the suspect who was later detained and taken to a hospital.

"Everything suggests that the perpetrator held very, very radical views. A number of weapons were found in the car he was driving," Kierwinski said.

"Everything suggests that he was fascinated by far-right ideologies" and held "ultra-nationalist views," he added.

The man was wearing military-style clothing at the time of the attack, said Kierwinski.

Andrzej Fijolek, spokesman for the chief of police, said the attacker had used a semi-automatic rifle similar to the American AR-15.

The authorities have not yet disclosed the nationalities of all the victims of the attack, Poland's deadliest shooting since the fall of communism in 1989.

"Our highest praise goes to the heroic police officers who risked their lives in the line of duty," Tusk said.

Witnesses told AFP they saw people take refuge in shops and restaurants in the surrounding streets.

"I saw a man shooting at people and walking around the square," Annette, a woman in her sixties, said.

"It's a tragedy for Krakow, we've never seen anything like this before," she added.

"I saw one person who was dead... and several others lying a bit farther away, whom people were still trying to resuscitate. They were taking off their clothes, trying to stem the blood with those clothes," said musician Daniel Wolny, 32.

"It's very frightening to think that there are still risks in Europe – risks of a terrorist nature," Stella, a 22-year-old tourist from Rennes, northwest France, said.

"Krakow has always been an extremely safe city... this is probably the first situation of this kind we can remember in our lifetime," said 33-year-old Gabriel Bogdan, an employee at a bar near the square.

Deadly shootings are extremely rare in Poland, a European Union and NATO member of 38 million people.

But the country has been on high alert following a series of stabbings in October, which Tusk denounced as a "cult of violence".

Warsaw, a staunch ally of Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, has repeatedly warned of Russian sabotage and hybrid warfare on Polish soil, accusations rejected by Moscow.

Poland is also seeing a sharp rise in the number of firearms licences. In 2025, more than 50,000 new licences were issued, bringing the total to 411,000, according to police figures.

The historic city of Krakow in southern Poland was once the country's capital and attracts millions of tourists every year.

Poland's conservative-nationalist president Karol Nawrocki said on X he was awaiting "a full explanation of the circumstances surrounding these dramatic events".

"The safety of Poles is an absolute priority," he added.
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.summary: Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk says three bodies found at suspect's home. Police say gunman appeared to be "fascinated by far-right ideologies" Police say suspect was wearing military-style clothing at the time of the attack.

https://www.france24.com/en/pope-leo-cal.title: Pope Leo calls on Uruguay's Catholics to be 'bridge builders'
https://www.france24.com/en/pope-leo-cal.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/pope-leo-cal.text:
Pope Leo XIV urged Catholics in Uruguay, Latin America's most secular country, to be "bridge builders" for the faith on Saturday and praised the favourite local brew, mate, on the second day of his South American tour.

Just three weeks after undergoing surgery for lung cancer, the 71-year-old pontiff has embarked on a 12-day tour of the continent where he served nearly two decades as a missionary.

Latin America is the world's most Catholic continent but the number of people who define themselves as Catholic has plummeted in the past 30 years, from 80 percent to 55 percent, a Latinobarometro poll showed.

In the northwestern city of Paysandu, Leo urged Uruguayans to be "bridge builders" and "share the joy" of their faith.

WATCH MORE
A Green pope? Vatican describes environmental destruction as an 'ecological sin'

He drew applause as he paid homage to the local tradition of sharing a herbal infusion called mate (pronounced ma-tay), sipped from a gourd with a metal straw.

Mate "teaches us to share and be together", the pope told thousands of faithful who braved early morning drizzle for the mass in a park, many clutching one of the hot drinks.

"Mate has even made its way to Rome," Leo joked.

Gladys Soria, 81, travelled to the mass with her daughter Adela from a small town around 50 kilometres away.

Soria told AFP she had recently undergone surgery and could barely walk but "found the strength to come".

On Sunday afternoon the pope heads to his predecessor Francis's homeland of Argentina, where he will ⁠meet and give a speech to President Javier Milei, a self-proclaimed "anarcho-capitalist" seen as a close ally of US ⁠President Donald Trump. Trump publicly ​lambasted Leo earlier this year after the pope criticised the US-Israeli war on Iran.

Leo will then travel on to Peru, where he served as bishop and which claims the pope as one of its own.

Leo took Peruvian citizenship during his many years in the Andean country.

On Friday, in the first speech of his tour, delivered in a half-empty square in Montevideo, he advocated for universal healthcare.

His own lung cancer diagnosis made him think of the "many men and women" who do not receive a timely diagnosis or treatment, he said.

Leo's speech also stressed the importance of supporting those whose physical or mental suffering cannot be eased.

Without referring specifically to euthanasia, which was legalised in Uruguay last year, he said each person should be supported to "live with dignity, receive the care they need, and be accompanied until the natural end of his or her life".

Liberal Uruguay's decision to make assisted suicide legal has been fiercely contested by the Catholic Church.

The pope said the Church wanted to "alleviate suffering whenever possible" and impress upon the sick that "their lives always retain meaning".

Leo's visit to Uruguay is the first to the country by a pope in the nearly four decades.

He will return to Montevideo on Saturday afternoon to visit Casavalle, the neighborhood with the highest homicide rate in the capital, as well as the Catholic University and the Centenario Stadium, where he will preside over a prayer vigil for 60,000 people.

(FRANCE 24 with AFP and Reuters)

He praised the favourite local brew, mate, on the second day of his South American tour. The 71-year-old pontiff has embarked on a 12-day tour of the continent where he served nearly two decades as a missionary.

https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.title: 'We must change everything,' French far-left presidential candidate Mélenchon says
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.text:
Hard-left French presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon pledged to raise the minimum wage and restore the country's retirement ​age to ‌60 in a speech launching his 2027 election programme on Saturday.

Mélenchon, 75, ⁠is viewed as the strongest contender on the left and recent opinion polls have shown him reaching the presidential runoff ‌next April against far-right candidate Marine Le Pen – but also indicate ⁠he would lose in the second round.

Addressing some 20,000 supporters at a mass rally in the Paris suburb of Le Bourget, Mélenchon nevertheless made it clear he was targeting the Élysée Palace to succeed President Emmanuel Macron.

"I have only one reasonable thing to propose to you. It is, in fact, quite moderate. Just one thing: we must change everything," he said.

"We are paving the way for a major political shift in France," added Mélenchon.

Taking aim at the centre-right Macron, he referred to recent demonstrations and rioting in France over the past months.

"We are living through a strange moment. It is the death throes of the Macron era marked by savagery, police brutality, and the unpredictable, violent outbursts at the end of demonstrations," he said.

He accused Macron of presiding over a "dark end to his reign" and said that the far right under Le Pen had "no idea other than racism".

His manifesto, titled "L'Avenir en commun" ("A Shared Future"), is the fifth edition of the platform of his party, France Unbowed (LFI), and ​largely reaffirms policies that have formed the backbone of Mélenchon's previous ‌presidential bids.

READ MORE
French presidential election: How far-left Mélenchon became a Gen Z favourite

Among its flagship pledges is the repeal of President Emmanuel Macron's pension reform, which gradually raised France's minimum retirement age from 62 to 64 in an effort to shore up ‌public finances.

LFI says it would restore retirement at 60 for people who have contributed to the system for 40 years.

The ​programme also calls for increasing the net monthly minimum wage to €1,700 from around €1,480 and includes plans to abolish the flat tax on capital income, raise taxes on the wealthiest ​households and cap prices for essential foods.

READ MORE
French candidates race to claim the cost-of-living issue ahead of 2027 vote

LFI also reiterates its support for a ​gradual phase-out of nuclear power in favour of a fully ​renewable electricity system, including scrapping the planned EPR2 reactor programme and not extending the lifespan of nuclear plants beyond 60 years.

On ​foreign policy, Mélenchon's programme reiterates his long-standing criticism of NATO and calls for France's gradual withdrawal from the military alliance, starting with an exit from its integrated military command.

France previously withdrew from NATO's integrated military command in 1966 under president Charles de Gaulle, a decision later reversed under right-wing president Nicolas Sarkozy in 2009.

LFI's programme also criticises German influence on European Union economic policy, describing Berlin as Europe's chief defender of "ordoliberalism", an ⁠economic philosophy centred on strict budget rules, price stability and independent monetary policy.

The programme calls for greater protection ⁠of domestic industry, including ​measures to encourage the relocation of production to France, and advocates a more interventionist role for the state in the economy.

(FRANCE 24 with Reuters and AFP)
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.summary: Jean-Luc Mélenchon launched his 2027 election programme on Saturday. He is viewed as the strongest contender on the left and is seen as the frontrunner in the presidential runoff. He has been seen as a strong contender against far-right candidate Marine Le Pen.

https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.title: Retired tennis star Gaël Monfils named captain of France's Davis Cup team
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.text:
Gaël Monfils, who recently retired from tennis after a 22-year playing career, has been appointed captain of the France Davis Cup team, the French Tennis Federation (FFT) announced Saturday.

"Drawing on his 22 years on the professional circuit, Gaël Monfils will bring all his top-level experience to the France team," the FFT said in a statement.

The 40-year-old succeeds Paul-Henri Mathieu, who had held the role for three years.

"It's an immense source of pride to become captain of the French national team," said Monfils.

"This blue shirt means so much to me. I want to build a real collective project and create the momentum that will allow us to go and win titles together."

WATCH MORE
Gaël Monfils out in first round of final French Open appearance

The popular Frenchman had been on a lengthy farewell tour this season but quietly ended his career by removing himself from the list of active players with anti-doping authorities last month.

He had been expected to make appearances in Lyon and at the Paris Masters but confirmed his retirement on October 26 after his wife, Ukrainian player Elina Svitolina, announced their separation.

"It was a very big decision because of my separation from Elina, which hurt me deeply as a human being," said the two-time Grand Slam semi-finalist, who reached the last four at Roland Garros in 2008 and the US Open in 2016.

Monfils, who won 13 ATP titles, was honoured during a ceremony at the Paris Masters this week, where he described it as a "very difficult moment to say goodbye".

He will have time to settle into his new role. France are not due back in Davis Cup action until February 2027 after failing to qualify for this year's finals in Bologna.

Monfils will be supported by former Davis Cup team-mates Richard Gasquet and Gilles Simon.

As a player, Monfils reached two Davis Cup finals, in 2010 and 2014, but never lifted the trophy.

https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.title: French presidential election: How far-left Mélenchon became a Gen Z favourite
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.author: Gabrielle Nadler
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.text:
Crowds filled the streets of Paris as part of a nationwide general strike and new protests on November 5, just five months before France’s presidential election. Far-left presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s silver hair and round-framed glasses were instantly recognisable in the crowd.

He has been pictured at several youth-driven demonstrations in recent months, sporting a wide smile, his fist raised. Mélenchon’s affinity for the young protesters appears to be mutual. The founder of the France Unbowed (La France Insoumise or LFI) party decidedly won the support of 18- to 34-year-olds in the 2022 presidential election. And recent polls suggest that in 2027 – with the youth predicted to be on his side – Mélenchon could make it to the election’s second and final round, to face off against far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who is leading the polls.

WATCH MORE
France's fed-up youth: Can presidential candidates connect with student movement?

Much of Mélenchon’s left-wing platform proves popular among young French voters, notably its promises to fight climate change, redistribute wealth and stage a “citizen’s revolution” to encourage public participation in government.

“Mélenchon is the last revolutionary on the left, and this is what young people are aspiring to. They are frustrated, they have been frustrated for a long time,” said political scientist Thibault Muzergues.

Livia Jampy, a 25-year-old co-chair of the LFI youth group and a city council member in Montpellier, said the party takes the French youth's political concerns seriously. “People will use any excuse to claim that young people who support Mélenchon are illegitimate or that we don’t understand anything [the party is] doing,” said Jampy. “We understand very well what’s going on.”

Mélenchon and his party have made a conscious effort to empower their young base. The LFI’s youth group, Jeunes Insoumis.es, tries to reach voters online and in the streets. LFI also hosts an annual "summer university" for people under the age of 26 that this year included a meeting with Mélenchon himself.

But Mélenchon remains controversial among France’s broader electorate. He has taken flack for encouraging the ongoing student protest movement, which at times has been marked by violence. His political adversaries have blamed his confrontational rhetoric for the civil unrest, with French President Emmanuel Macron saying the youth are being "exploited" by political forces. Since the October 7, 2023 attacks in Israel, he has also been regularly accused of anti-Semitism.

In his previous presidential run, Mélenchon was criticised for his perceived leniency towards Russia and pledging to leave NATO if elected.

Muzergues said young voters feel less concerned by these international issues, but are determined to see systemic reform in France. People “underestimate the radicality of this vote”, he added. “It is not a protest vote. It is a vote to say the system has not worked for us and needs to be changed. Not cosmetically, but profoundly.”

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/t.title: SA government plans to ban ticketless parking fines
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Local Government

The Adelaide City Council's Park Safe car can scan for illegally parked vehicles using cameras mounted on top. (ABC News)

The government will introduce legislation to parliament to make it mandatory for council inspectors to physically issue parking fines.

The changes will prevent councils from posting fines to drivers after a camera car has driven past.

The Local Government Association of SA says it was not consulted on the planned changes and that a ticketless system allows for better efficiency.

The South Australian government plans to ban councils from issuing ticketless parking fines.

Under the planned reforms, councils would be banned from posting fines to drivers after a camera car has driven past, and it would be mandatory for inspectors to leave a physical ticket on the car or hand it to the driver.

The South Australian premier highlighted the City of Adelaide's Park Safe program — which uses a car with cameras on top to scan for illegally parked cars and take high-quality photos — as an example.

The council has previously said the images are reviewed by trained officers to verify whether an offence has occurred.

A recent council report showed that on average, 25 per cent of contested fines were withdrawn following requests for reviews by parking information officers so far this year.

Dallas Coull says he never received fines before the City of Adelaide's Park Safe car came into effect. (ABC News: James Wakelin)

Tour bus operator Dallas Coull, who spoke at the government's press conference about the reforms, said he had never received fines before the Park Safe program but had received "dozens and dozens" since its implementation.

"There's actually a hotel in the CBD that don't pick up [at] anymore because we get kept getting fines," he said.

Fiona Garwood says she welcomes the proposed ban on ticketless parking fines. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

In nearby Rundle Mall, shopper Fiona Garwood welcomed the planned changes, saying she would "rather have things done by a person".

Fellow shopper Levi Adams said he had seen the council's Park Safe car in the CBD before and agreed with the government's proposed reforms.

"I'm concerned about AI in every aspect of life, so I really don't need it to be in parking fines as well. The less, the better, in my opinion," the 23-year-old said.

Peter Malinauskas says the regulation was modelled on similar reforms in New South Wales. (ABC News: James Wakelin)

Mr Malinauskas said AI technology could still be used, but any ticket would need to be physically issued by a council inspector at the time of the alleged offence.

"If they've got someone in the car and someone gets out of the car, looks at the circumstances … that's OK," he said.

"It's the practice of the car and the AI machine only forming the judgement that we are regulating out."

Heather Holmes-Ross says people can contest ticketless parking fines as they can with other fines such as red light speed cameras. (Supplied: Local Government Association of South Australia)

Local Government Association of SA president Heather Holmes-Ross said it was "unusual" that the state government had not consulted them on the planned reforms, and questioned whether it would extend to other ticketless fine systems.

"The technology we're talking about is the same technology that's used by red light cameras, phone detection — it's all the same software — so we're a little confused about why it would be that just parking data is being attacked here and not all data that's collected by AI," she said.

But the state government said there was an "important distinction" between enforcing parking restrictions and road safety laws.

"Parking fines are mostly issued to stationary cars whereas that is clearly not the case for a speeding car," a spokesperson said.

The spokesperson said the state government would consult stakeholders, including the LGA.

Ms Holmes-Ross, who is also the mayor of Mitcham in Adelaide's inner-south, said there were several councils trialling the technology around the state in a bid to improve efficiency, with human oversight.

"If you drive past 10 or 20 cars, then that video can be viewed, and those fines can be mailed out," she said.

"If you're stopping and you're giving out those 20 individually, it just takes more time.

"So if there's a way of doing it accurately and more efficiently, it's better for everyone."

The Jillaroos try to take down Fiji in the Women's Rugby League World Cup semifinals before the Kangaroos endeavour to join them in reaching the men's decider as they meet Samoa.

Follow all the action in our live blog below.

Choose what information you see below by using filters

Jess Skinner has gone to her bench, introducing Kezie Apps, Keeley Nizza and Keilee Joseph.

They have their first really impactful set of the game as a result, with Abbi Church breaking down the right, but brought down by Taina Naividi and going within centimetres of being put into touch.

Australia is trying to make the sort of defensive statement that Fiji has made early, but the over-commitment is allowing offloads and some quick metres through the middle.

Yet again the Jillaroos start their set on their own tryline and can't get over halfway.

I can't remember the last time I saw this happen to the Jillaroos.

This has been a fantastic start from Fiji!

The Jillaroos have steamrolled all comers so far in this tournament, and while there's still a long way to go in this game, the Fijians have stepped up and are bringing incredibly defensive intensity, plus a sharp long kicking game to start this semi final.

They've been rewarded with forcing plenty of uncharacteristic errors from the Australians, and we shouldn't be too surprised that they've scored first since they've made a habit of making fast starts throughout this tournament.

The small crowd here is loving seeing a bit of a challenge to the women's international rugby league establishment.

A bomb forces Tamika Upton to come from inside the in-goal. She somehow escapes, but the follow-up run from Jaime Chapman ends prematurely as Sereana Naitokatoka strips her.

Was it a knock-on? Perhaps, but play is allowed to continue.

A play the ball close to the line scatters defenders and Luisa Yaranamua throws a big dummy before diving over from the base of the ruck.

And she converts for a stunning 8-0 lead!

The defence from Fiji is unbelievable right now.

Jocelyn Kelleher finds the sideline with her kick-off, giving the Jillaroos a perfect attacking platform.

But the defence forces Isabelle Kelly about 15 metres back.

Then Simaima Taufa is Loren Ieli, and then Tiana Penitani-Gray loses the ball on a short pass from Tarryn Aiken.

The Fijians are right on top here.

Simaima Taufa is penalised for crowding the play the ball and Luisa Yaranamua pots the goal to make it 2-0 to Fiji after 12 minutes.

It's the first time since the 2013 World Cup final that the Jillaroos haven't scored the opening points in any international.

The kicking game of Fiji once again forces Australia to truck it off the tryline and the Jillaroos are struggling.

They won't be helped by a dropped ball from five-eighth Jocelyn Kelleher, who then cops a spray from the Fijians, prompting a bit of push and shove.

The up-and-in defence from Isabella Waterman rushes Tarryn Aiken and forces another fumble.

Australia is under the pump early and Fiji's defence is aiming up to stop the Jillaroos from getting any sort of momentum too.

Talei Holmes and Sereana Naitokatoka go within centimetres of scoring the opener for Fiji.

Credit the Jillaroos defence for denying them, but Fiji matches with driving defence to make life difficult for Australia getting out of their own territory.

The Bulikula's first kick of the game is high out to Abbi Church, who decides to take it right next to the sideline before being dumped into touch.

She flicks a pass back in-field and it's dived on by Fiji.

A little bit of panic maybe from the Jillaroos as the rushing Fijian defence creates a dead end, forcing a u-turn and drawing the error from Millie Elliott.

The second women's semifinal gets underway with Millie Elliott flying into the defence, followed by Simaima Taufa.

And then a big charge from Shaylee Bent earns the Jillaroos a penalty as Fiji is penalised for a strip. Can't be starting behind the eight ball against the Aussies.

It's time for the Noqu Masu of Fiji.

One of the great pre-game traditions in world sport.

The Bulikula and Jillaroos are on the pitch at the Sydney Football Stadium.

How must the Fijians feel ahead of their first World Cup semifinal against the almighty Jillaroos?

No edition of the Women's Rugby League World Cup has been played without New Zealand reaching the final, and the Kiwi Ferns have done it again this time out.

The world number two reached their seventh straight decider, awaiting the Jillaroos or the Bulikula.

Tiana Penitani-Gray is returning for the Jillaroos in the back row after missing last week's win over Wales with a foot injury.

But neither team is making any late changes this afternoon.

Hello and welcome to Semifinal Day II: Reckoning.

Today we learn who will join the New Zealanders in the men's and women's Rugby League World Cup finals, with Australia's Jillaroos up against first-time semifinalists Fiji and the Kangaroos meeting Samoa in a rematch of the last men's decider.

We'll have live coverage of both matches included some expert insights from Amanda Shalala and Nick Campton at the Sydney Football Stadium.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/s.title: Snow blankets parts of NSW just weeks away from summer
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Snowy Mountains local shares video of spring snow. (Madeleine McVie via Instagram)

Snow has fallen in parts of NSW after a cold front dropped temperatures and produced rain and storms.

A Thredbo local says the snow was "beautiful", but "unexpected" after a warm winter.

Suburbs that hit 30 degrees Celsius on Saturday dropped by more than 10C by the evening.

Parts of New South Wales have been blanketed in snow just a few weeks out from summer after a strong cold front swept along the state's coast.

David Crock from the Bureau of Meteorology said November was a "very volatile time of year", with the cold snap not that unusual, but was always "striking when it happens".

"We saw snow maybe down as low as 400 to 500 metres through parts of Tasmania yesterday, also snow on the Alps through Victoria and NSW down to about 800m," he said.

Thredbo dropped to -5.0 degrees Celsius overnight. (Supplied)

The heat in the north of the country, the senior meteorologist explained, coupled with a really cold ocean in the south was behind the change.

"So we've got that really strong temperature gradient between northern Australia and the Southern Ocean," he said.

"And that's what creates these strong cold fronts with a big push of cold air up through NSW and even into southern parts of Queensland."

On Saturday, Sydney hit 29.7C just after lunch time, dropping to 14C by the evening.

The massive drop was also experienced in Penrith, which went from 31.5C at 3pm, to 14C by late evening. Night time in Parramatta hit 13.C after sweating through 30.4 earlier in the day.

The change also brought heavy rain and storms.

Thredbo, in the state's alpine region, received a dumping of snow overnight when temperatures fell to -5.0 degrees Celsius.

It was 0C on Sunday morning and snow was still falling.

An unseasonably warm and wet June brought a challenging start to the 2026 snow season and while a snow base came by July over the higher slopes, the lower alpine regions missed out on full coverage.

Madeleine McVie said while it was unexpected after a warm winter, it was "beautiful" and enough to build a snowman.

"It certainly was hard to get out of bed. It is very cold down here," she said.

"We got a little bit [of snow] a couple of days ago, and yesterday it started snowing about four in the afternoon.

People who had gone hiking at Mount Kosciuszko were ecstatic, she added.

"They certainly wasn't expecting it to snow down here in November.

"And we're prepping for our mountain biking season, so we weren't expecting it either."

On Sunday, cooler temperatures hovering between 10C and 12C degrees dominated across the state.

Strong southerly winds and hazardous conditions are forecasted along the NSW coast on Monday, with the chill expected to continue.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/a.title: Swans, Hawks prevail in AFLW elimination finals
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Fri, 30 Oct, 8:15 am, Final score, Cats 88, Bulldogs 20

Sat, 31 Oct, 2:05 am, Final score, Saints 45, Power 51

Sat, 31 Oct, 4:05 am, Final score, Tigers 33, Kangaroos 101

Sat, 31 Oct, 6:05 am, Final score, Lions 35, Blues 40

Sat, 31 Oct, 8:15 am, Final score, Eagles 39, Hawks 94

Sun, 1 Nov, 1:35 am, Final score, Giants 53, Suns 62

Sun, 1 Nov, 2:05 am, Final score, Bombers 38, Magpies 31

Sun, 1 Nov, 4:05 am, Final score, Crows 29, Demons 47

Sun, 1 Nov, 6:05 am, Final score, Dockers 36, Swans 37

The Swans prevailed in an elimination final scrap against the Bulldogs. (Getty Images: Matt King)

AFLW superstar Chloe Molloy has once again lifted Sydney to victory, with the Swans defeating the Western Bulldogs by 29 points in an elimination final.

League-leading goalkicker Molloy pulled off a surprise cameo down back to help the Swans claim a 7.4 (46) to 2.5 (17) win at a wet and windy Henson Park on Sunday.

Sydney will next play Geelong in an away semi-final. The Bulldogs' season is over.

Molloy's leadership in a wet-weather scrap proved the difference for the Swans, with the former Swans co-skipper finishing with one goal, 12 intercepts, and 14 contested possessions.

Tanya Kennedy was just as crucial for the Swans, locking down Bulldogs co-captain and gun midfielder Isabelle Pritchard.

Pritchard, on return from a knee injury, was kept to just 14 disposals and three clearances as Kennedy laid 17 tackles.

Fellow Bulldogs midfielder Ellie Blackburn, also returning after being rested in last week's loss to the Cats, led the visitors with 29 touches and a goal.

Swans captain Lucy McEvoy needed just 20 seconds to score the opener with a long bomb from outside the 50-metre arc thanks to the strong breeze.

A rushed behind gave the Bulldogs their sole score of the first quarter, as the hosts made the most of conditions to fire off their four unanswered goals and build a 24-point lead.

The Bulldogs could only manage one point with the breeze in the second, with Molloy helping limit the damage with five contested possessions and four intercepts as a defender.

Molloy's stint in defence forced Bulldogs coach Tam Hyett to bring defender Vaomua Laloifi into the forward line, and the pair's battle continued well into the second half.

Sunday's final turned into a slog after torrential rain came in the third quarter, with the Swans doing just enough to maintain a 25-point lead en route to victory in front of 4,325 dedicated fans.

Hawthorn has broken through for their its AFLW finals victory in an 18-point defeat of Gold Coast.

A commanding third quarter paved the path for the Hawks to prevail 8.9 (57) to 6.3 (39) at People First Stadium on Sunday.

Hawthorn, who bombed out of the finals in straight sets in 2024 and 2025, will face Carlton in the first semi-final next Saturday night at Princes Park.

Eliza West (29 disposals, one goal) and Laura Stone (21, two) were outstanding for the Hawks, while Casey Sherriff, Hayley McLaughlin and Jasmine Fleming all picked up 20 touches.

Jenna Richardson was a wall in defence, with a game-high 11 marks while completely blanketing Suns forward Dekota Brown.

The Davies sisters — Darcie and Georja — impressed for Gold Coast, who were also chasing their maiden AFLW final success.

Charlie Rowbottom battled hard for her 20 disposals (18 of them handballs), a figure matched by Niamh McLoughlin and Daisy D'Arcy.

Adding injury to insult for the Suns, young gun Ava Usher suffered a serious-looking injury to her right knee in a heavy collision with teammate Maddy Brancatisano in the dying stages.

Hawthorn kicked two goals in the last 77 seconds of a high-octane opening term — through Poppy Stockwell and Jacqueline Dupuy — to lead by six points.

The Suns responded to take a three-point half-time lead, but Hawthorn raised its pressure in the third quarter and Gold Coast couldn't go with it.

The Hawks' backline repelled 11 consecutive entries from the Suns, while their midfield trampled Gold Coast at clearance and on the outside.

Hawthorn had 33 more disposals for the term, 13 more tackles and pulled ahead by 15 points at three-quarter time.

Mikayla Nurse goaled early in the fourth quarter to give Gold Coast a sniff, but the Hawks continued to pile on the pressure and exorcise their own demons.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/a.title: NZ election figures tell story of disenchantment and fracturing
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/a.author: Stephen Dziedzic
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The executive wing of New Zealand's parliament is colloquially known as the Beehive. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

If you're a fan of elections and numbers, then the New Zealand election offers a fascinating smorgasbord.

After all, it's an improbably tight result on the raw figures.

More than 2.4 million party votes have been counted so far, with just 3,650 votes separating the two major parties. Labour has 710,330 party votes compared with National's 706,680, though hundreds of thousands of special votes are yet to be counted.

That margin was somehow even tighter (about 1,500 votes) just before 10pm last night, prompting Henry Cooke, the political editor of New Zealand newspaper The Post, to marvel at the mirror columns of red and blue.

"Millions of people will vote in this election but the party vote margin between the two 'major parties' could fit in Auckland's St James Theatre," he posted on X.

Most New Zealand political observers are now (very understandably) fixated on the minutiae of the vote, the party machinations, the overhang, the special votes, and whether National will need to bring in political newcomers Opportunity in order to keep their hold on government.

Christopher Luxon told supporters on election night his party had a path to government.  (Reuters: David Rowland)

National has a clear edge over Labour on seat numbers, with 42 seats projected compared with Labour's 36 seats. There's an increasingly settled view that Prime Minister Christopher Luxon has an easier avenue to power than Labour leader Chris Hipkins, who would have to navigate a much more torturous pathway to the top job.

The preliminary results do not include 400,000 or so special votes, which are yet to be counted by the New Zealand Electoral Commission. Special votes have historically boosted Labour's vote share, although election analysts say it is unclear whether they will be sufficient to push National and its coalition partners below its perilously thin majority.

The results in the New Zealand election are anything but clear with the two major parties — Labour and National — in the tightest of races.

After a muted speech at National HQ on election night, Mr Luxon sounded decidedly more confident when talking to journalists in Auckland this afternoon, saying his party could claim a mandate to govern.

"Ultimately, New Zealanders have given us the biggest seats in parliament, 42 seats as it stands today, and a pathway to form a government," he said.

Still, if you're taking a broader view and asking what this election might tell us about New Zealand's political trajectory then there's a subterranean story that deserves as much attention as the blow-by-blow race for the Beehive.

When you pick through the latest data two figures really jump out, because they tell us a story of disenchantment and fracture in the New Zealand electorate.

New Zealand's coalition government faces a fragmented and increasingly disenchanted electorate.

The first: New Zealand's two major parties, Labour and National, secured only 59 per cent of the party vote between them.

This is the first time since 1996, when New Zealand embraced its MMP* voting system, that the two major parties have fallen beneath 60 per cent of the vote.

The last time this almost happened (back in 2002) it was off the back of a smashing victory by then prime minister Helen Clark, who secured more than 41 per cent of the vote while National crashed to only 21 per cent.

One commentator put it neatly last night when he mused that it was probably time to stop talking about the "major" and "minor" parties, and just talk about the "seven parties" in New Zealand.

Of course coalition politics have always been a major feature of New Zealand politics since 1996, because MMP strengthens the hand of minor players.

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong addressed the party faithful at an event in in Auckland. (Jonathan Killick/Stuff via AP)

But the surge in the minor party vote, as well as the dramatic re-emergence of Qiulae Wong and Opportunity (from outside parliament too) might hint at a deeper realignment.

The contrast with 2020 is stark. Jacinda Ardern's Labour party won an outright majority of the party vote at that election, allowing it to govern alone. The current results raise questions about whether New Zealand's era of majority style politics is over.

It feels more likely that political polarisation and a fragmenting information space will continue to fuel the rise of other players, with future leaders navigating constantly coalescing, shifting coalitions between several parties.

Of course, this isn't a shift merely contained to New Zealand, look at the way One Nation has up-ended federal politics in Australia, where the major parties are also seeing a steady long-term decline in support.

The second figure worth dwelling on from this election is turnout, which dipped down to 74.6 per cent, the second lowest in New Zealand's history.

Attention is beginning to turn to the voter turnout numbers and what is behind the drop. (AP: Alex Robertson)

It's a number that might worry those tracking democracy's vital signs in New Zealand, which has a long and proud record of civic participation.

There are plenty of things that could explain this drop.

The weather wasn't exactly pleasant in New Zealand on Saturday with heavy rain and showers (particularly in the north) which may have kept people at home.

Some analysts have pointed to new enrolment rules as a possible factor after New Zealand introduced a requirement for voters to enrol 13 days before voting began.

Again, disenchantment and political disconnection are hardly unique to New Zealand.

But for leaders trying to navigate tumultuous and uncertain times, they make the hard task of building — and maintaining — a political mandate for difficult decisions all the harder.

* New Zealand uses a mixed-member proportional (MMP) voting system, under which voters cast one vote for a local MP and another for a political party. The party vote largely determines how many seats each party receives in parliament.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/c.title: Residents bought into communities but may end up living in 'wastelands'
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/c.author: Tony Ibrahim
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Housing Construction Industry

Rinnah Roque (left) and her mother's home is across the road from an unfinished Bathla housing development. (ABC News: Tony Ibrahim)

Rinnah Roque worries the view beyond her landscaped front garden will remain a construction site.

The 60-year-old committed to a growing community in Sydney's north-west when she bought a three-storey townhouse off the plan in Box Hill.

Across the road, a hive of builders were working on 47 homes as part of a project from the developer Bathla.

"I worked so hard to be able to buy a property for my mum and myself," she said.

Construction work on Hynds Road stopped after Bathla entered administration. (ABC News: Tony Ibrahim)

But for the past two months, the symphony of construction noise has been replaced by silence.

"All of a sudden everything stopped, and what's so frustrating is everything was just left behind," she said.

The residential development dividing Hynds Road is one of hundreds caught up in the $3.4 billion collapse of Bathla Group.

And it is among dozens of sites that were part way through construction when the money stopped flowing.

In some cases, the private equity companies that are owed money by Bathla have taken control of the projects they invested in, and are racing to find builders that will finish them.

The Box Hill development is among hundreds caught up in the collapse of Bathla Group. (ABC News: Tony Ibrahim)

But interviews with experts and industry stakeholders reveal that builders may be reluctant to guarantee the work of cash-strapped Bathla, posing the risk some sites could "languish".

Bathla declined the ABC's requests for interview and comment.

The quality of the work already undertaken at Bathla's construction sites would be difficult to assess by the builders that are considering finishing the projects, said Lyndall Bryant, a leading property economics professor at Queensland University of Technology.

"If you're a builder coming into a job that's half-finished, you don't want to be warranting the work that someone else has done," she said.

"If the concrete's been poured, you don't want to be saying, 'Oh yeah, I guarantee that that concrete's been done properly.'"

Lyndall Bryant says some builders may be hesitant to take on half-finished jobs. (ABC News: Aisling Brennan)

She said reviewing plumbing or electrical work would be challenging if walls were already erected.

A private equity company that spoke to the ABC but declined to be named said the builders it was talking to were being cautious however, it remained confident one would be appointed.

A former major lender says Bathla was expanding too quickly, leaving it vulnerable when the property market turned.

Urban Taskforce Australia, a group lobbying for developers and equity financiers, said it believed most of the projects would be completed.

"Where I would be concerned is if we were to find developments with substantial defects, where basically the cost to rectify those defects is greater than the value of the land with an approval on it," chief executive Tom Forrest said.

"I can't see that being the case in lots of occasions."

Bathla was forced to stop construction at 45 sites after it was placed into administration in August, according to documents filed by the administrator Teneo to the NSW Supreme Court.

About a dozen of these sites are situated in Sydney's west, in areas such as Marsden Park, Box Hill, Rouse Hill and Pemulwuy.

Many are in new areas, clustered together.

Developments at Marsden Park in Sydney's west are among those where construction has stopped. (ABC News: Tony Ibrahim)

Professor Bryant said the delay or failure of a project in these locations could leave communities "fractured".

"Those areas really could become almost wastelands for a number of years," she said.

"These sites attract vandalism, they're not maintained, and it just brings down the whole area.

"Unfortunately it's a negative impact on property values — and that's for the people who already live in those communities."

Ms Roque said if this scenario were to eventuate in Box Hill, it would be "a horror story".

"That will impact probably us mentally and even the whole family," she said.

Rinnah Roque (left) says it would be a "horror story" if the area become a "wasteland". (ABC News: Tony Ibrahim)

Urban Taskforce Australia said any drop in property values would be a "short-term blip".

"My hope is that the fracturing of the community doesn't happen because ultimately the market will come in and complete those homes," Mr Forrest said.

Two Sydney councils are among the most exposed.

Construction had stopped on eight Bathla projects in Blacktown Council, and at four sites in The Hills Shire Council.

Both councils are owed money by Bathla, and have registered as creditors with the administrator.

The councils could be left spending more money while bringing in less.

The Hills Shire Council and Blacktown Council are the most exposed from the Bathla collapse. (ABC News: Tony Ibrahim)

They might have to spend money building infrastructure such as roads and sewage that Bathla has yet to contribute to the developments, Professor Bryant said.

"Blacktown Council is at risk of having to spend significant money on infrastructure for projects that are on the fringe that might only service a few people," she said.

And they would be missing out on money they anticipated from rates, unless these developments are finished.

"I think that they should be concerned at Blacktown City Council because any major hiccup like this means delay in their cash flows," Mr Forrest said.

Blacktown Council declined a request for interview and comment.

The Hills Shire Council Mayor, Michelle Byrnes, said the collapse of Bathla was "another hit to public confidence in the construction industry".

Michelle Byrne says the public's confidence in the construction industry has been dealt another blow. (ABC News: Declan Bowring)

"I'm devastated for the buyers across Sydney who have been left stranded by Bathla's collapse," she said.

Some investors have seized control of the Bathla sites they invested in and are racing to finish the projects.

One of them said the goal was to break even, with any profit considered a bonus.

Asian private equity company PAG has already appointed the builder ParkView to its 300-unit development in Pemulwuy.

Other private equity companies told the ABC they were in discussions with builders.

Private credit firms are striking deals to recover their money following the $3.4 billion collapse of property giant Bathla Group.

Ray White Capital, which owns the site in Box Hill, said it expected the site to be finished before April 2027.

Leda Group has taken control of a 240-unit development in Marsden Park, and said it was in advanced discussions with a builder.

But not all of Bathla's sites have been taken over by a creditor.

Among them is a 49-home housing estate in Lochinvar in the NSW Hunter Region.

The restructuring and insolvency firm Mackay Goodwin has been appointed to "assess available options".

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/s.title: Cancelled AI data centre 'victory for people power' after backlash
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/s.author: Shannon Corvo, Else Kennedy, and Alexander Lewis
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Members from the Stop the Cooks River AI Project (SCRAP) are calling the backtrack a "win for people power". (Supplied: SCRAP)

Plans for another controversial AI data centre in Sydney have been scrapped, with a community group hailing the decision as a "victory for people power".

The facility, which was set to become part of a proposed logistics hub on the Cooks River at Arncliffe in the city's south, faced backlash from the local community after it was revealed in July last year.

Developers Stockland and John Boyd Properties proposed to redevelop the rezoned 18.3-hectare Kogarah Golf Club site into an estimated $3.5 billion logistics precinct including an AI data centre.

Stockland and John Boyd Properties withdrew their plans for the AI data centre. (Supplied)

Stop the Cooks River AI Project (SCRAP), which consists of hundreds of members, had been protesting against the development since forming in August.

Group organiser Paddy Gibson said surrounding residents were celebrating the "very good win for people power".

Mr Gibson said it would have posed a risk to the fragile local ecology around the river, which is called Goolay'yari in local Indigenous languages, which was already recovering from "industrialisation over the years".

"There's endangered plants and other animal species in the green space," he said.

"There's plenty of people trying to work on remediating what is a very polluted river, and we were worried that this would set back those efforts."

Paddy Gibson says there are endangered plants and other animal species at the proposed data centre site. (Supplied)

He also mentioned concerns about power usage and possible water contamination.

A Stockland spokesperson said the partners were now focused on building a "world class logistics precinct which does not include a data centre as part of the amended Concept Masterplan".

"The project will also deliver a one-kilometre public foreshore link along the Cooks River and the future delivery of the 14-hectare Pemulwuy Park, as well as local road upgrades and improved active transport connections."

The spokesperson said the group would continue to engage openly with stakeholders as planning for the logistics precinct progressed.

Bayside Greens councillor Peter Strong who had led council's opposition to the project said the decision was "very heartening".

Mr Strong said forums and outdoor events about the project had attracted large numbers of residents.

His main concerns were about excess energy and water use, noise, and the way AI was being "used and weaponised against the best wishes of humanity".

"That space has become a bit of a wildlife sanctuary since nothing much has happened with the old Kogarah Golf Club since they sold it," Mr Strong said.

Locals were concerned with the impact on water use and energy. (Supplied)

He said the withdrawal sent a message to the state government that "the council should have more of a veto on these data centres".

In August, the Minns government released its data centre policy framework which they said balanced the interests of households and investment in NSW.

A recent report following a parliamentary inquiry into data centres noted that the guidelines should have been in place "before developing any planning fast-track processes for these projects".

The government has until February next year to respond to the report.

Canterbury Labor MP Sophie Cotsis said she looked forward to seeing the revised logistics hub masterplan including a public foreshore link, road upgrades and improved active transport connections.

"The Minns Labor Government has established the Cooks River Consolidation Project to resolve longstanding tenure issues along the river," she said.

"As the local MP I am focused on working together with my colleagues and government agencies to see investment in the naturalisation of the river banks."

Protesters at Merrylands rallying against a proposed AI data centre. (ABC News: Alex Lewis)

It is the latest in a series of proposed data centres to be scrapped following community opposition.

An AirTrunk data centre proposed in Lane Cove was also dropped, and another in Guildford in September.

Residents at Merrylands in Western Sydney have also rallied against the $1.1 billion Project Pluto Data Centre proposed by the Goodman Group, to be located next to the Guildford West Sportsground.

Labelled a state-significant development, locals said it was approved in July behind their backs.

The project did not receive a single submission from the public, with some locals saying they never received a letter.

Goodman Group said it had sent correspondence to more than 1,200 homes and businesses, three times.

SCRAP said it would continue campaigning against the logistics hub on the riverfront and for a ban on all new AI data centres.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/l.title: Final Garage Sale Trail after 16 years of re-homing second-hand goods
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/l.author: Sarah Forster
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/l.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Recycling and Waste Management

Kalie Chaney hosted a vintage themed garage sale at Kanwal, on the NSW Central Coast. (ABC Central Coast: Sarah Forster)

Around 12,000 households across Australia are taking part in the final Garage Sale Trail.

The event has re-homed more than seven million items since 2010.

Individuals are encouraged to continue re-selling or re-purposing unwanted items after the official event concludes.

From casual beginnings in Bondi in 2010  to a nationwide annual event, the Garage Sale Trail has found a new home for more than seven million pre-loved items and, in doing so, generated $52 million for sellers.

It is a long way from what co-founder Darryl Nichols said started as a "smell of an oily rag production".

He and friend Andrew Valder called for community members in Sydney's Eastern Suburbs to host a second-hand sale.

To their surprise, 130 people signed up, and it grew from there.

The success and the impact are beyond anything they could have imagined.

Darryl Nichols co-founded the Garage Sale Trail in 2010. (ABC Central Coast: Sarah Forster)

"They go along with Vegemite, going to the beach, watching the cricket in summer and all that good stuff.

"When the internet sort of started to kick in, in the late 90s and early 2000s, and we saw … marketplaces like eBay enter the game, maybe the humble old garage sale did take a bit of a hit.

"But we've certainly found over the years that the Garage Sale Trail provides a wonderful opportunity for people who have been thinking about having a garage sale but never sort of got around to doing it ."

More than 7.2 million second-hand items have been sold through the Garage Sale Trail since 2010. (ABC Central Coast: Sarah Forster)

This year, the final event occurs across two weekends, with Sunday, November 15, to be the final day.

Mr Nichols said it was the right time to walk away.

"Perhaps there's someone out there … that might be interested in taking on the custodianship of Garage Sale Trail … but we feel like we've made a strong contribution and we're ready for the next chapter."

According to the NSW Environment Protection Authority, Greater Sydney is on track to run out of landfill space by 2030 unless more is done to reduce waste.

In a statement, the EPA described the Garage Sale Trail as "a fantastic initiative that helps to divert waste from landfill and reduce illegal dumping by encouraging reuse as part of a circular economy."

From her garage sale at Kanwal on the NSW Central Coast, Kalie Chaney agreed.

"I honestly don't think I could work at a tip because it would break my heart seeing all the things people throw away," she said.

The NSW Environment Protection  Authority says the Garage Sale Trail helped divert waste from landfill and reduce illegal dumping. (ABC Central Coast: Shauna Foley)

Ms Chaney collects items from the 1960s and 70s.

"Things were made to last back then … whether it's furniture or Tupperware or dinner plates, they are still usable," she said

"It's good to save them, because a lot of these items [would otherwise] go to landfill."

Recycling and reuse aside,  there is something about a garage sale that gets people talking.

Bill Mallie popped into Ms Chaney's garage sale for the social aspect.

Bill Mallie says garage sales bring the community together. (ABC Central Coast: Sarah Forster)

"At my age I need to get rid of stuff, I don't need to bring stuff in."

"[But] it's neighbours … helping each other clearing out stuff, recycling things [so] they don't wind up in the dump … what a great idea."

Mr Nichols said the social side of the movement has been almost as profound as its environmental side.

"The average person that gets involved makes about 30 new neighbourly connections through the day," he said.

Around 12,000 hosts are taking part in the final Garage Sale Trail. (ABC Central Coast: Shauna Foley)

"When you have a garage sale … people drop their guard a little bit because you're putting all this stuff out the front of your house, it kind of says a little bit about who you are and provides this lovely opportunity for people to connect."

"At the end of the day, it's the contribution it's made to keeping perfectly great stuff out of landfill and bringing local people together that probably is the real win for our nation."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/p.title: Palestinians return to destroyed West Bank homes after IDF siege
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/p.author: Matthew Doran and Sami Sockol
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/p.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Unrest, Conflict and War

Palestinians return home to destruction after 11-day siege in Hebron.

The father of one of the Palestinian gunmen who killed two Israeli soldiers in the West Bank says he does not support his son's actions.

He said he would have tried to stop his son, had he known what he was planning.

Thousands of Palestinians returned to their homes in Hebron this week after a controversial 11-day siege ended.

Standing on the rubble of what was once his family's home, Wael al-Jabaa was stony-faced as he described the events of the past fortnight — and in particular the actions of his son, which prompted the destruction of the property.

Israeli authorities ordered the demolition in Hebron's west, after 27-year-old Hamouda al-Jabaa and another gunman opened fire on Israeli soldiers at a military checkpoint on October 23.

The men killed two Israeli soldiers and injured others during the 20-minute shootout before they were shot dead.

The house of Hebron gunman Hamouda al-Jabaa, where Wael al-Jabaa also lived, was destroyed. (Reuters: Mussa Qawasma)

Mr al-Jabaa said he would have tried to stop his son, had he known what he was planning.

"It was not easy. It was very difficult for us," he told the ABC.

"I love my son and I don't hate our son — but sometimes I support him and sometimes I don't support him.

"An act like this has caused us a lot of losses. We lived a normal life. Now we have losses."

The demolished house of Palestinian gunman Hamouda al-Jabaa. (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

The shooting triggered an 11-day siege of Hebron, with the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) launching a major military operation in the West Bank's largest city.

"We will act to destroy this place, to change it completely," Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in the hours after the shooting.

The gunmen's homes were demolished and dozens more buildings destroyed in a show of force from Israeli authorities.

The IDF launched an operation after two soldiers were killed by Palestinian gunmen. (Reuters: Mussa Qawasma)

Hundreds of families were also forced from their homes, mostly in the Al-Jalda and Ein Deir Bahha neighbourhoods, as soldiers went from building to building claiming to search for weapons and terrorists.

Wael al-Jabaa was among dozens to be arrested. He was held for 10 days, and had cuts on his wrist from where he said handcuffs were secured too tightly.

He told the ABC he was not allowed access to a toilet for the first three days of his detention.

"I peed on myself when in detention. Why?" he said.

"My son was 27 years old, he was married and had two children — how could I be responsible for his actions?"

Wael al-Jabaa says his wrists were injured from handcuffs. (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

He said he did not support acts of violence against Israeli forces, saying they were not worthwhile given the significant power imbalance.

"You cannot resist them, you can't use any other means, you have to be silent and co-exist with them," he said.

The ABC asked the IDF for a response to Mr al-Jabaa's claims of mistreatment, but its response did not address the allegations.

Thousands of Palestinians were permitted to return to their homes this week after Israeli forces withdrew, but many returned to properties that had been damaged, vandalised or robbed.

Among them was the Mujahid family, who returned to their flat to find soldiers had ransacked bedrooms and broke furniture.

Abed al-Shakour and his family couldn't access their home for 10 days. (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

"I was the first house in the whole neighbourhood … that the army entered," one member of the household, Abed al-Shakur, told the ABC as the family slowly cleaned their home.

"They knocked on the door and entered here without saying much. They said, 'You have five minutes to leave your house. There is a military operation in the area and you have to leave the house.'

"So we left the house for 10 days. When I came back to my house, as you can see, it was all destroyed."

Abed al-Shakur said he had to buy new mattresses for his two young sons because the old beds had been drenched in urine.

The bedrooms in Abed al-Shakour's apartment were trashed. (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

He also said his eight-year-old son, Yamen, had chest pain from the stress of the eviction.

"We took him to the hospital, they did a heart test and did a full examination," Abed said.

"They examined him and said he was in a psychological shock."

Neighbours told the ABC many of the flats had been left with rubbish strewn throughout, including used condoms.

Down the street, tenants were returning to a commercial building that had been taken over by Israeli soldiers.

The complex usually houses doctors' clinics, lawyers and other companies. But during the siege, said one business owner, it became a base for the IDF.

Obaida Mujahid alleged that several cameras had been stolen during the siege. (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

Obaida Mujahid, who owns a camera and production company on the third floor of the building, told the ABC a sniper was stationed on the balcony overlooking the roundabout below.

"[The IDF] destroyed them [homes and businesses]. They had a whole building for them as headquarters to sleep in," he said.

"They were smoking hookah, it was a mess here."

Mr Mujahida also said at least 10 of his cameras and 17 camera lenses had been taken by soldiers, along with computer hard drives.

IDF soldiers had been sleeping in this apartment, where the door was knocked off its hinges. (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

In response to allegations of vandalism and theft of property in the Al-Jalda neighbourhood, the IDF said: "Troops were given clear guidelines and procedures to preserve residents' property, prevent damage to homes during the operational activity, and leave the area as orderly and clean as possible upon departure.

"The homes were searched to rule out the presence of weapons at the sites; therefore, some doors were breached during operational activity because the apartment owners had left them locked.

"The IDF is not aware of claims regarding property damage; should concrete allegations of damage to property be presented, they will be thoroughly examined."

It also said it was not aware of allegations relating to the theft of cameras from Obaida Mujahid's company.

Hebron, which is home to more than 200,000 people, is often the site of confrontations between Palestinians and Israeli security forces, given the presence of Israeli settlers living in pockets inside the city limits and other large settlements on the outskirts.

Demolitions were carried out around the site of the shooting in the Farsh al-Hawa neighbourhood. (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

The siege was met with condemnation from Palestinian officials and the United Nations, with High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk saying he had "grave concerns of unnecessary and disproportionate use of force".

"Collective punishment is a grave violation of international law," he said in the days after the operation began.

"Threats to empty and erase entire neighbourhoods also raise serious concerns of ethnic cleansing."

Hebron's Governor Khaled Dudin told the ABC the siege had "paralysed" the local economy, which has broader impacts on the rest of the West Bank.

"Two [Palestinians] launched an attack and they punished 600 families," said Governor Dudin.

"This is collective punishment for citizens who have nothing to do with this."

Khaled Dudin says a change in government will be positive for Palestinians. (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

He argued there was a political motive behind it too, given the shooting and subsequent siege occurred just days before last month's Israeli election.

"It was a big competition to get the votes of the settlers, and the only way to get votes of settlers is the mistreatment of the Palestinian people," Mr Dudin said.

"Palestinians always pay the bill of the Israeli election."

The governor believed that the forceful response was the Israeli military carrying out the wishes of the right-wing Netanyahu government, which is propped up by pro-settlement politicians.

National security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir is a resident of Kiryat Arba, the large Israeli settlement on the eastern edge of Hebron, while finance minister Bezalel Smotrich is also a settler.

Itamar Ben-Gvir went to the funeral of one of the IDF soldiers killed in the attack. (Reuters: Shir Torem)

Bezalel Smotrich went to the scene on the day of the shooting. (Reuters: Ammar Awad)

Mr Dudin said he hoped a new Israeli government, perhaps led by former IDF chief Gadi Eisenkot, might not take such punitive measures in future — even though Mr Eisenkot and other challengers to Mr Netanyahu are not promising wholesale change to Israel's policies in the occupied West Bank.

Even with the IDF withdrawing its troops, most of the roads in and out of Hebron remained closed to traffic or choked due to searches by Israeli forces.

The checkpoint where the shooting took place was among those still shut, although the ABC witnessed the gate being opened by soldiers to allow demolition machinery to move through.

Demolition equipment leaving Hebron through the Farsh al-Hawa checkpoint. (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

Debris and rubbish after IDF demolition in Farsh al-Hawa, Hebron. (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

Several buildings around the checkpoint had been destroyed, with locals reluctant to speak to the media about what they had seen due to fear of further reprisals.

But the damage done to the city extends beyond destroyed buildings, said Palestinian human rights activist Issa Amro.

Issa Amro said the siege had a big impact on businesses in Hebron. (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

No-one was able to leave or get into the city during the siege, which impacted businesses. Children could not attend school for 12 days and now many Palestinians do not feel safe in their homes, he said.

"The current Israeli government believe in making the Palestinian civilians pay the price, and they want to show that they can do whatever they want to Palestinians as a kind of revenge," he told the ABC.

The ABC asked the IDF how it was lawful to destroy buildings with no connection to the gunmen, but it did not respond specifically to that question.
