https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/n.author: Courtney Barrett Peters
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Courtney Barrett Peters

Topic:
Religious Schools

Catholic Education NT has written to parents informing them that they may notice police around schools.  (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Parents at Northern Territory Catholic schools have been told to expect an increased police presence after two teenagers were charged with terrorism-related offences within in a week.

It comes after a teenage girl faced court on Wednesday charged with collecting or making documents likely to facilitate terrorist attacks, a week after a teenage boy faced court on the same charge.

Church leaders are calling for calm and unity, saying the police presence is "precautionary" and that "at no point we were aware there was any real threat to safety".

Thousands of parents with children at Northern Territory Catholic schools are being warned to expect "an increased uniformed police presence around your school" after two teenagers were charged with terrorism-related offences in less than a week.

A teenage girl, who cannot be named for legal reasons, faced the NT Youth Justice Court on Wednesday charged with collecting or making documents likely to facilitate terrorist attacks, a week after a teenage boy faced court on the same charge.

Just hours before pick-up on Friday afternoon, Catholic Education NT (CENT) emailed families and carers from 18 schools across the territory, informing them it had "assisted police and relevant authorities since the commencement of the investigation" into the terrorism allegations.

The letter to parents at all 18 Catholic schools in the NT says the additional police presence isn't a response to "a specific or imminent threat". (ABC News)

In the letter, seen by the ABC, CENT director Paul Greaves urged the school community not to "speculate about the allegations, identities, motivations and potential outcomes", saying "appropriate safeguarding measures" were in place.

"In some circumstances you may notice an increased uniformed police presence around your school," he wrote.

"Police will continue to work closely with CENT and provide further advice where appropriate."

Adam Rice says authorities have identified "a number of schools" during the investigation. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

On Wednesday, Australian Federal Police Acting Assistant Commissioner Adam Rice revealed authorities had identified "a number of schools" as part of the Joint Counter Terrorism Team (JCTT) investigation.

The same day, a JCTT spokesperson confirmed detectives had seized material from a Top End home which allegedly revealed a "mixed ideological motivation, including glorification of mass casualty attacks at schools".

Speaking to the ABC yesterday, Bishop of the NT Charles Gauci called for calm, urging the community to come together to help reduce the risk of radicalisation.

With technology evolving at a rapid pace, Bishop Gauci said children needed support in their formative years now more than ever.

"This is part of a larger question," he said.

Charles Gauci says social media literacy is key to addressing youth radicalisation. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"How do we help our young people really, really grow in their understanding of values?

During the same interview, Mr Greaves said CENT chose to send the email to all of its schools so as not to "indulge in speculation".

The NT Police Commissioner has raised the alarm about the growing issue of extremism and radicalisation.

"We haven't held back anything, transparency I think's really important to build trust," he said.

"That trust I hope we're maintaining in assuring families, assuring students, assuring staff that at no point we were aware there was any real threat to safety."

Mr Greaves clarified officers would not be actively patrolling schools but would be "driving around" or "coming in" to gather evidence as part of the investigation.

"There have been cases where police have been attending schools and people have noticed that," he said.

"It's because this is the ongoing nature of the investigations, police need to talk to people not just at our schools, [but] in other parts of the community as well."

Jumbunna Institute for Indigenous Education and Research director Lindon Coombes said while police had a job to do, their presence could be particularly triggering for some First Nations students.

"A police officer in uniform does not make every child feel safe," he said.

"For some Aboriginal children, it can have precisely the opposite effect.

"We need to be very careful that in trying to protect children from a potential threat, we don't turn their schools into places of fear and intimidation."

George Newhouse says the increased police presence should be "subject to ongoing review". (ABC News: Simon Amery)

National Justice Project chief executive George Newhouse said while he recognised the importance of early intervention, community trust in authorities was central to helping support young people who were exposed to extremist material online.

"Police have acknowledged that preventing youth radicalisation requires families, schools and communities to work together," he said.

"That requires trust, engagement and support, not simply more police.

"Any additional police presence must have a clear justification, be limited to what is necessary and be subject to ongoing review."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/health/2026-.title: Chronic pain affects one in two women in midlife, report finds
https://www.abc.net.au/news/health/2026-.author: Lauren Roberts
https://www.abc.net.au/news/health/2026-.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

ABC Health & Wellbeing

Topic:
Women's Health

Chronic pain disproportionately affects women. (Getty Images: NickyLloyd)

Women are up to 70 per cent more likely to experience chronic pain than men, according to a recent report from the international Menopause Society (IMS).

Chronic pain is pain that lasts more than three months, or keeps recurring.

In women, these pain symptoms often appear in midlife, likely due to factors such as fluctuating hormones, menopause-related biological shifts, lack of sleep and lifestyle changes.

Listen to the Health Report to hear more about women with chronic pain in menopause.

The IMS report estimates about half of all middle-aged women experience chronic pain, describing the condition as "often under-recognised, underdiagnosed and inadequately treated".

Rossella Nappi, IMS president and obstetrician and gynaecologist at the University of Pavia in Italy, says the report aims to empower women and health workers to talk about the condition.

"Chronic pain in midlife is a very important subject and highly neglected," she says.

"Sometimes the pain becomes widespread and it's present in every day of their life."

So what do we know about chronic pain in women and what can people do to minimise the severity of their symptoms?

We don't know for sure.

Adelaide University senior lecturer in pain science Jane Chalmers says this is one of the "hardest questions to answer" in her field.

"Trying to understand why certain people or certain groups are more vulnerable to others is often multi-factorial and very layered," she says.

"And that's because we can't separate a human's psychology and sociology from their biology."

Women often experience multiple, overlapping chronic pain syndromes, such as fibromyalgia and chronic pelvic pain.

While not everyone feels pain in the same way, some research suggests women may be more likely than men to experience central sensitisation, making the brain more likely to produce pain signals.

Nicolette Ellis wants women's chronic pain to be taken seriously, with many patients currently feeling dismissed. (Supplied)

And then there are social factors.

Chronic Pain Australia chair Nicollette Ellis, who is also a pharmacist specialising in chronic pain, says women often manage the majority of caregiving responsibilities, which may add to stress levels.

The relationship between stress and chronic pain is complex, but stress may worsen pain intensity for some people.

Hormones play a role.

During menopause, which marks the end of a woman's reproductive years, the body produces much lower amounts of oestrogen and progesterone.

Lower levels of oestrogen can lead to joint pain, stiffness and weakening of muscles.

Nearly three in four women experience joint or muscle pain during perimenopause. (Pexels: Kampus Production)

But these hormone levels can fluctuate day-to-day, explains Royal Australian College of General Practitioners menopause health subgroup chair Sharon Vasey.

This fluctuation can lead to migraines, she says.

But it's not all about hormones. Professor Nappi says lifestyle factors also play a key role in how we age.

"If we do not exercise properly, if we don't eat adequately and if we are not active very much in our life, pain will be an issue," she says.

"If we have menopausal symptoms, such as sleep disturbances, for example, or mood changes, this will affect the experience of the pain."

The IMS report focuses on three common symptoms: musculoskeletal pain, migraine and pelvic pain.

According to the report, nearly three in four women experience joint or muscle pain during perimenopause.

But figures from Chronic Pain Australia's 2026 National Pain Report paint a more complex picture.

The group surveyed more than 6,000 Australians, finding women experience an average of 4.6 different types of chronic pain, such as migraines, back, pelvic, joint or nerve pain.

With so many women reporting multiple symptoms, Ms Ellis says it's important not to treat types of pain in a "silo", but to consider the whole body and how different systems interact.

For women approaching midlife, Dr Vasey says it's important to get enough sleep, stay active and eat a healthy diet.

She says the first step for people experiencing pain symptoms is to speak to their GP.

"There's lots of things that can be done, women don't have to put up with chronic pain," she says.

Australia has a new set of guidelines for managing the symptoms of menopause, that include hot flushes, night sweats, and a frequent need to urinate. Here's what it means for you.

Dr Vasey, who is also a practising GP, says menopausal hormone therapy can help ease the severity of some symptoms for some women, but medication isn't the only option.

It can also be helpful to see an allied health worker, such as a physiotherapist.

As many people with chronic pain experienced a delayed diagnosis, Ms Ellis says it is important health workers take pain symptoms seriously.

"The earlier we can treat [chronic pain] the better the outcomes," she says.

And a broader level, Monash University professor of occupational rheumatology Karen Walker-Bone says more needs to be done to support women approaching midlife.

This means making sure women have the financial stability to retire when they want, and to ensure emotional household labour is shared in an equitable way.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/u.title: The father and son farmers who sent a message to Donald Trump
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/u.author: Elias Clure and Daniel Pannett
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/u.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Kansas farmer Fred Levendofsky chose not to support the Republican Party this time. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

Fred Levendofsky has worked the land in rural Kansas for over half a century and, like many farmers here, was a fervent backer of Donald Trump.

Across the US Midwest, agricultural communities have been among the president's most fierce defenders and reliable supporters.

Mr Levendofsky, 68, voted for Trump twice. But not a third time.

Fred and Nick Levendofsky have seen their business hurt by the Trump administration's policies. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

Two years into Mr Trump's second term, Mr Levendofsky's overheads have skyrocketed.

The cost of diesel fuel he uses to run machinery and vehicles has increased by about 40 per cent from last year, and his total expenses have jumped by about 50 per cent.

"How long are we going to wear the cost? Things need to change," he told the ABC from his 360-hectare farm in the state's north.

This week they did. Kansas has sent senators from Mr Trump's Republican Party to Washington DC for almost a century but at Tuesday's midterm elections, Democrat Adam Hamilton claimed a comfortable win.

The GOP incumbent, a physician worth an estimated several million dollars, faced criticism after the New York Times reported that his former obstetrics practice sued more than 700 patients over unpaid bills and charged an 18 per cent annual interest rate. Mr Marshall called the report a "hit job".

Riding a wave of anti-Trump sentiment around the country, the Democrats surged in both the House and Senate races to take control of both chambers. It means the president's political life over the final two years of his term will be more difficult, although he still wields immense power.

While Kansas had been safe Republican ground for generations, the GOP top brass had grown increasingly worried that Marshall would lose, and pulled out all the stops to save the seat.

The party was so concerned that the president made a last-minute stop in the state last weekend to hold a rally in a bid to energise his base.

Adam Hamilton celebrates at his official election night party on Tuesday. (Reuters: Nathan Howard )

It did not work. Marshall still lost convincingly to megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton, who pitched himself as a religious centrist who would bring decency back to American politics.

"I'm glad a message was sent to Washington," Fred Levendofsky told the ABC.

"I'd hope that now we've got a Democrat-controlled House and Senate, that they'll work with Mr Trump and hopefully they can sort this oil issue."

While soaring fuel costs are something being felt around America — and it is particularly pronounced in Kansas — people's gripes with the federal government run much deeper.

Adam Hamilton is the first Democratic senator from Kansas in almost a century. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

The war in Iran, and the billions of dollars being spent on it, is deeply unpopular. The president's multiple trade wars have also hurt the farmers' bottom lines.

"Things just aren't working; it's all going backwards," said Nick Levendofsky, Fred's 41-year-old son and a senior member of the state's farmers' union.

International demand for Kansas cereal, grain and beef has withered due to China's retaliation to the Trump administration's sweeping tariffs.

The White House announced an assistance package for farmers late last year, in which they could claim one-off lump sums of cash linked to the size of your land.

"It doesn't matter how big a farm you are, you're dealing with these same issues and I think more than anything, they want a market. We want trade, not aid," Nick said.

"Frankly, the government cheques aren't even covering our losses and, you know, farmers have lost over $US40 billion ($58.3 billion) since the trade war started. It's probably way more than that now."

Nick Levendofsky is sceptical about the state of the US under Donald Trump. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

Both the Levendofskys were once registered Republicans but are hoping their state's new blue senator can help stand up to the president.

"As far as what he did when we did the war with Iran, I do think they needed to stop the business with nuclear weapons, I understand that and I understand we all as Americans probably need to shoulder some of that expense," Fred told the ABC.

"It's been very difficult. A year ago, we were able to harvest the grain, and at the end of the year I was able to sell the grain and pay my expenses on the crops and had a little bit left over.

"This year, that's not going to happen. We probably won't even have enough to pay for the fertiliser and seed because of the increase in fuel."

Nick Levendofsky shows off some of the farm's produce. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

While Kansas commands just six Electoral College votes in presidential contests, the erosion of Donald Trump's rural base — collapsing by more than 30 percentage points in some precincts — suggests the party can be competitive in territories once deemed hostile.

The Democrats flipped Republican Senate seats in Texas, Maine, North Carolina, South Carolina, Ohio and Iowa this week, and remain a chance to take two more in Mississippi and Alaska, too. Many of those states had backed the Republicans for decades.

"We're looking at a political opportunity for the Democrats not seen since Watergate," said Matt Harris, a political scientist at Park University in neighbouring Missouri, told the ABC.

"Kansas now has to be on the table in the presidential elections.

"And I think this shift speaks to the dissatisfaction about the economy, the dissatisfaction about some of the choices that the Trump administration has made, but I think for Democrats, the message is: what are you going to do to deliver on those things?"

Topic:
World Politics

During his victory speech on Tuesday evening, Mr Hamilton wore a pin that said "love one another" and stressed the need for people on both sides of politics to work together.

Buoyed by the party's historic victory this week, Democrats are hoping they can continue to build momentum in the state when the next presidential election is held in two years' time.

"Kansas doesn't have a lot of Democrats, but people wanted change," Nick Levendofsky said.

"We want moderate politics back in Kansas, and I think the senator-elect is hopefully going to deliver on that."

Donald Trump still enjoys support in the Midwest, but many voters have turned on him. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/d.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Food delivery driver Feng Jianming was fatally stabbed during an alleged altercation.  (Supplied)

Victorian Premier Ben Carroll says community safety is his top priority, after a deadly attack involving two delivery riders in Melbourne's CBD.

Feng Jianming, 47, was fatally stabbed on Friday night while making a delivery for HungryPanda.

A 51-year-old man has been arrested over the incident.

Victorian Premier Ben Carroll has vowed to make "whatever changes are necessary" following the fatal stabbing attack of a delivery driver in Melbourne's CBD.

Chinese national and father of two Feng Jianming was fatally stabbed on Friday night while making a delivery run for HungryPanda near the Queen Victoria Market.

Another food deliver rider, aged 34, was injured in the alleged altercation.

A 51-year-old man was arrested over the incident.  (ABC News)

On Sunday, Mr Carroll said he would continue to work with the Transport Workers Union and other representatives to ensure the safety of gig economy workers.

"As premier I will ensure I do everything I can with the Chief Commissioner of Victoria Police that, no matter where you work, no matter where you shop, no matter where you live, that you are safe," he said.

"We do know that often people in the gig economy, people who are doing transit deliveries, are some of the most vulnerable Victorians and they do need proper protections in place and workplace safety."

Homicide Squad detectives have arrested a 51-year-old Footscray man over the incident.

Floral tributes were placed outside the State Library where people gathered for the vigil.  (ABC News: Keira Proust)

In a statement published on the social media app WeChat, the Chinese consulate said a representative held an urgent telephone conversation with Mr Carroll on Saturday in which the premier conveyed his condolences to Mr Feng's family.

"Consul-General Fang [Xinwen] undertook to convey Premier Carroll's message to the family as soon as possible, and requested Premier Carroll, the Victorian government and police to handle the case fairly and in accordance with the law … and effectively safeguard the lives and legitimate rights and interests of Chinese citizens," the statement said.

"The Chinese Consulate-General in Melbourne attaches great importance to the case and immediately activated its emergency consular protection measures."

The consulate said it would continue to maintain communication with local authorities.

HungryPanda said it was deeply saddened by Mr Feng's death and extended its condolences to his family, friends and the wider rider community.

"Our thoughts are also with the rider injured in the incident," the company said in a statement.

The company said it was in contact with Mr Feng's family and was helping to arrange their visas to travel to Australia.

"The company will cover the family's travel expenses, funeral costs and necessary related arrangements, alongside an additional financial support payment.

"We are seeking to contact the injured rider to understand his circumstances and offer appropriate assistance."

HungryPanda says it will meet with Melbourne riders during the week to discuss safety concerns. (ABC News)

The company said it was planning to meet with members of its Melbourne delivery riders next week to discuss their concerns and to help find ways to improve safety.

"HungryPanda has reached out to the City of Melbourne, the Victorian government and Victoria Police to discuss rider and community safety, seek their support and explore practical measures to address risks in public spaces.

Last night hundreds of people attended a vigil for Mr Feng, with many raising concerns about safety in the city.

"This is not how we're picturing Melbourne would be like," international student Xi Ip said, who was among those at the vigil.

"We were expecting a safer community. We don't want anything like this to ever happen again. That's a 47-year-old man who has a family to support.

"This is a pure tragedy … We want police to protect not just citizens but all of the community in the city."

Hundreds gathered at a vigil for Feng Jianming in Melbourne's CBD on Saturday. (ABC News: Keira Proust)

Another student Xenith Yen said she was considering moving back home to Shanghai.

"I feel so unsafe in this city and I am paying a very high rate of tax but I don't get anything back from this city. I want to go back home."

Student Casper Ge called on the state's leaders to do more.

"It's everyone's right to have a safe city when they're doing their job. I feel very bad for this poor man."

Casper Ge attended the vigil. (ABC News)

Ria Li, who lives next to the scene, said she had lived in Melbourne for two years and was concerned about her safety because of drug use in the CBD.

She said she wanted to see steps taken by the government and Hungry Panda, which she said was a well-used delivery service among the Chinese student community, to improve driver safety.

"In Melbourne's CBD, international students are not a small group," she said.

"It's very depressing, it's very unfair that … someone's husband, someone's son and someone's dad got killed. It's really depressing as a Chinese to see such tragedy happen right next to my apartment."

NRL Women’s Premiership

Elexis Riley from Moranbah has dreams of playing for the NRLW one day.  (Supplied: Wanderers Australia)

Growing up with a house full of brothers, Elexis Riley was never going to be far from a game of footy.

While some teenagers are still figuring out what they want to be, the 16-year-old from coal country in central Queensland is already dreaming of one day competing in the National Rugby League Women's (NRLW) premiership.

Five years ago, Riley's family moved from Rockhampton to Moranbah.

Despite living in the small regional coal-mining town with a population of just under 9,000, she's still had a lot of opportunities, from playing in the local league to being selected to play in representative competitions.

Elexis Riley (right) with the winning trophy from the 2026 season, playing for her local team, the under-17s Moranbah Miners rugby league team.  (Supplied: Elexis Riley)

Elexis plays for the Moranbah Miners in the under-16 girls competition and just finished the 2026 season as the leading try scorer, crossing the line 17 times.

That followed a breakout season in 2025, which saw her picked for the Mackay Cutters under-15 girls academy.

Her footy has even taken her overseas. She's just returned home from a tour program with independent sports organisation Wanderers Australia, where she represented her country against teams in the United Kingdom.

"It was really good, we thought the teams were going to be a lot harder, but they were really easy to play," Elexis said.

Elexis Riley playing against Culcheth Eagles in England.  (Supplied: Wanderers Australia)

But the biggest win of her sporting career so far has been her selection for the under-17s North Queensland Cowboys Academy in Townsville.

"It's actually wonderful … I was not expecting to take my footy this far … everything opened up to me and I had so many opportunities," she said.

Cowboys headquarters is 550 kilometres from home but she's been able to take part in the program remotely.

"They give us training and we have to do all of our gym work and stuff to keep up," Elexis said.

"And they can track us on how we go and then we go back there at the end of December."

While it's a bit to juggle on top of her year 11 schoolwork, she manages to get most of it done.

The remote training is a way the Cowboys team can spread the program to Queensland's many vast regions.

Ty Williams moved into the role of NRLW senior assistant and development coach of women's elite pathways at the North Queensland Cowboys two years ago.

"We thought, as staff here, instead of bringing all the athletes to us, which we do once or twice a year …. to get out there and see them in their own environment as well," Mr Williams said.

"Our main focus is how do we provide an opportunity for those young female athletes within our region to progress through to the highest level."

He said partnerships with local feeder clubs the Northern Pride, Townsville Blackhawks, Mackay Cutters and the Central Queensland Capras were integral.

"It's important to know that the progression or the pipeline for them to achieve the NRLW dream is through [those] clubs," Mr Williams said.

With attention already turning towards the 2027 competition, the young players will head into pre-season training over the next couple of weeks.

"The ultimate goal is to have our pathways programs playing against the likes of the Broncos and the Titans moving forward and potentially Redcliffe," Mr Williams said.

Elexis Riley travelled with Wanderers Australia at the end of September, to play in rugby league matches across England.  (Supplied: Wanderers Australia)

Elexis hopes to follow in the footsteps of arguably the world's best player, Tamika Upton, who also hails from Rockhampton.

Upton, 27, has risen through the ranks in recent years, first debuting with the Brisbane Broncos in the NRLW in 2019, going on to win five premierships, and now holding the title of captain.

She was awarded the league's top gong in September, making her a three-time Dally M Medal winner.

"I used to go for the Broncos and I still do, but now that I'm in the Cowboys, it's hard," Elexis said with a nervous laugh.

Topic:
Federal Parliament

Matt Canavan has repeatedly said the EU free trade agreement is a bad deal for farmers. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Matt Canavan has said the EU free trade deal goes too far on climate change commitments, but supports Australia staying in the Paris Agreement.

The Queensland senator also said he would prefer to live next door to a nuclear power station than a wind turbine.

Senator Canavan said he texted Trade Minister Don Farrell to have a "constructive" discussion about the deal.

Nationals leader Matt Canavan says Australia should stay in the Paris Agreement, but has rejected backing a free trade deal with Europe he says will bind the country to net zero.

The Queensland senator, who recently announced his bid for pre-selection for the lower-house seat of Capricornia in central Queensland, said it was important to take measures to reduce emissions where the country could afford it.

"I think we should take measures to reduce emissions over time. It's perfectly reasonable, in a way that doesn't hurt our economy," he said on ABC's Insiders.

"What we can't afford is a mad pursuit of net zero."

The government has set a legislated target to bring down greenhouse gas emissions to net zero by 2050.

Senator Canavan said the EU free trade deal would legally bind Australia to the Paris Agreement, an international climate change treaty, which goes beyond our current commitments.

The provisional text of the deal "includes the obligation to refrain from any act or omission which materially defeats the object and purpose of the Paris Agreement" and that each party shall promote "measures that contribute to the transition to a net zero and low greenhouse gas emission, sustainable circular economy and climate-resilient development".

While Senator Canavan was supportive of Australia staying in the Paris Agreement, he said this was "not what we have signed up to".

"The binding commitments in Paris amount to, having a policy to reduce emissions, taking measures to meet those targets and then reporting against that," he said.

"The purpose and objects [of the Paris Agreement] go further. They include a broad object of carbon neutrality in the second half of the century.

"So what the government is trying to do here is use the EU free trade deal as a backdoor way to bind Australia to net zero."

Senator Canavan added that he wanted to be "constructive" about the free trade deal and has texted Trade Minister Don Farrell to discuss the details.

"He's been talking to me through the media … I texted Don the other day and we'll try and catch up. I'm happy to be constructive," he said.

Senator Farrell has previously said the free trade agreement would yield $10 billion worth of trade and that "there is no renegotiation here".

It is understood the trade deal reaffirms existing climate obligations.

Senator Canavan has repeatedly said his party would not support the agreement in its current form, arguing it is a raw deal for farmers, particularly those in the dairy industry.

"I can't sign off on a deal that wipes out Australian dairy farmers, exposes them to unfair competition, because this deal does not deal with the massive European subsidies that go to dairy — the cheese mountains that result from that — and our dairy industry would be sacrificed," he said.

The Minerals Council has said the deal would benefit companies dealing in critical minerals, which are facing heavy competition from China, by removing tariffs on exports to Europe.

Senator Canavan acknowledged the deal would benefit some industries, but said a local critical minerals company in his region had never mentioned European tariffs, instead saying the carbon tax was a bigger issue.

When asked if he would back a nuclear-powered data centre in the electorate he hopes to one day represent, the Queensland senator said he would welcome it, but the location was always dependent on the will of the local community.

"I'd welcome nuclear power here every day of the week," he said.

"I'd much prefer a nuclear power station next door to me and a 300-metre wind turbine."

The prime minister is due to fly to Türkiye for the UN climate summit COP31 this week.

Shane Bond was fearsome across all formats, though injury limited him to just 18 Tests, 82 ODI's and 20 T20I's (AAP Images/NZPA, Ross Setford)

Fast, fearsome, and fragile were words often associated with former New Zealand fast bowler Shane Bond, whose promising cricket career was drastically curtailed by injury.

He debuted as a 26-year-old against Australia in Hobart in 2001, but it was in his next series, against Bangladesh, where he truly announced himself.

He took 11 wickets in two Tests at an average of 13, and it looked like the beginning of a long and lucrative career.

But Bond's back had other ideas. A stress fracture kept him out the game for almost two years from 2003.

Shane Bond is considered "patient zero" after his successful back surgery allowed him to continue his international career. (Phil Walter: Getty Images)

A meeting with back surgeon Grahame Inglis offered him hope he could overcome his injury by undergoing a little-known surgery that is now commonplace in the fast bowling fraternity.

"If I can't fix this, then the career is potentially over," Bond said of his decision to undergo pars stabilisation surgery in 2004.

"He [Inglis] talked about a procedure that he had done, one on a New Zealand high jumper and one other athlete.

While other injuries limited Bond to just 14 more Tests before he retired in 2009, his back didn't trouble him again.

Renowned New Zealand spinal surgeon Rowan Schouten was working with Dr Inglis at the time and said Bond was "patient zero in this whole story."

Bond took 147 ODI wickets, including a stunning hat-trick against Australia at Bellerive Oval in 2007. (AAP Image/Andrew Cornaga)

The success of that surgery laid the groundwork for a procedure that Schouten and his team have now performed on around 30 professional cricketers.

When surgeons in the UK stopped performing the procedure and Dr Inglis retired, Dr Schouten became the world's leading authority on repairing spinal stress fractures in fast bowlers.

Rowan Schouten says pars stabilisation surgery isn't a new procedure, but has recently become popular with cricketers. (Supplied: rowanschouten.co.nz)

"We were kind of left as the last man standing with experience on international fast bowlers and since then it's taken off essentially," he said.

"We're dealing with calls and connections from all around the world, from the UK, India, South Africa, Europe, Bangladesh, everywhere."

Bond still helps fast bowlers who have struggled with back issues and is often approached for advice.

He's coached Jofra Archer, Jason Behrendorff and James Pattinson, who all had the surgery and returned to play at the top level.

When a fast bowler is considering spinal surgery, like Australia's Lance 'Wild Thing' Morris did in 2025, it sounds like a drastic step.

But Dr Schouten said the surgery was straightforward and "not that extreme".

It involves grafting the spine to stimulate repair, before putting screws and wires around the injured portion to provide stability.

After years of back issues, Lance Morris is finally fit and firing, and the West Australian is keen to put his name in the frame for a Test call up once again.

"We've got a few little added components to it that we believe are important ... but it's a pretty standard technique," he said.

The injury, often referred to as a stress fracture, is common across sport and very prevalent in cricket.

Dr Schouten stressed the surgery is not a fusion, and most stress fractures do not need it.

"You need to preserve all that spinal motion that these guys need to be able to bowl full pace," he said.

Cameron Green opted for surgery in 2024, following several stress fractures during his career. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

If a player did opt to go under the knife, the recovery involves a six-to-nine month rehab program.

"Some stress fractures in some players become a recurring theme," Dr Schouten said.

"And then if you do that, if you have that two or three times in a row over multiple seasons, it can really disrupt a career."

Topic:
Unrest, Conflict and War

Donald Trump discussed mediation efforts with Qatar on Friday. (Reuters: Eric Lee)

Explosions have been heard on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz and tankers in the strategic waterway have caught fire after hitting mines.

Meanwhile, Iran's Revolutionary Guard says it has lifted a self-imposed limit of 2,000 kilometres on the range of its ballistic missiles.

Here's what to know about the situation in Iran.

For weeks, US President Donald Trump has said he is considering launching a new wave of strikes on Iran after the US midterm elections, which were held on November 3.

The Middle East and beyond have been on edge about the prospects of the US resuming full-scale operations against Iran for the first time in almost two months.

The president said on Friday that the US military had carried out new limited strikes against Iran, targeting an Iranian air defence system, describing the action to reporters as "minor".

Experts fear a global economic fallout from further Iran strikes. (Sarah Ferguson)

That same day, he discussed efforts to de-escalate tensions in the Middle East in a call with Qatar's emir, the Gulf state leader's office said.

The two discussed Qatar's mediation efforts, which are aimed at reaching "a comprehensive agreement that ends the crisis and achieves security and stability in the region".

The Associated Press has reported that Iran is reviewing proposals presented by Qatar that address differences with the US about Tehran's nuclear program.

The development is raising hopes that the two sides could be inching toward indirect talks on one of the thorniest issues that Mr Trump says must be resolved as part of any deal meant to end the more than eight-month-old war.

But one of the officials stressed that the Iranians remained unwilling to engage in negotiations with the Trump administration over its atomic activities until the US agreed to several conditions.

Both officials were not authorised to comment publicly on the delicate negotiations and spoke on the condition of anonymity.

Usman Khawaja has defended the timing of his bombshell revelations about how many people knew about the plot to rough up the ball with sandpaper during the Cape Town Test in 2018.

In a lengthy Instagram post, Khawaja said Steve Smith convinced him not to come forward with the revelations earlier.

Khawaja said the fact he had held back the book until after Australia's Test return to South Africa last month was proof this was not a money-making venture.

Usman Khawaja insists he has not thrown anyone under the bus with his bombshell ball-tampering revelations that have rocked Australian cricket.

One day on from admitting sandpaper had been used in the Test prior to Cape Town 2018 and the entire team was responsible, Khawaja defended the timing of his claims.

In a five-minute long Instagram explanation, Khawaja revealed he had planned to go public with the details days after the incident before the suspended Steve Smith talked him out of it.

He also detailed how he made another attempt to ensure the entire team took the blame for it in 2021, before a public statement from the bowlers denied any knowledge.

But Khawaja said he had made a promise with his childhood friend David Warner to spill the details of the saga post-retirement in his book, believing Warner, Smith and Cameron Bancroft had taken the fall for the entire team.

"I haven't thrown anyone under the bus," Khawaja said.

"The guys that are currently in the team right now and the other people that were there on the South African tour, including me, we're not the victims.

"These three guys took the blame for all of us. They're the victims … people telling them that they're cheats, getting nailed by the crowd. Public humiliation."

Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith were both put through the ringer. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Ashley Vlotman)

Extracts from Khawaja's memoir Sabr, which will be released on Tuesday, detail how an Australian player applied sandpaper to a ball in the change room in the second Test against South Africa at St George's Park in 2018.

When teammates saw how scuffed up one side became, they realised how much it would swing and Khawaja claims Bancroft volunteered to use the substance.

While Khawaja says that was initially only done at the start of sessions when entering the field, the tactic then expanded to on field in the next Test in Cape Town.

Khawaja also alleges in the book that a member of Australia's coaching staff had encouraged Bancroft to ramp up whatever he was doing with the ball, before the West Australian was caught by cameras and eventually umpires.

In the post on Sunday, Khawaja said he would "not deny" that everyone knew, and revealed how he wanted to go public in 2018 once Smith, Warner and Bancroft were suspended.

"I told Smudge [Smith] that I was going to come clean to the media," Khawaja said.

Usman Khawaja says Steve Smith talked him down from going public earlier. (Getty Images: Eurasia Sport Images/Ayush Kumar)

"I couldn't believe the penalties he got. But Smudge being the man and leader he was, he talked me out of it.

"He wanted to take the blame. I argued with him, but he was having none of it. That's the first time I try to come out."

Khawaja claimed he spoke extensively with then-coach Justin Langer and Todd Greenberg in 2021 about the team taking collective responsibility, with Greenberg then CEO of the players' union before becoming boss of Cricket Australia.

Darren Lehmann rejects Usman Khawaja's claims the entire Australian camp knew about the 2018 sandpaper plot, but says "everyone around the world" was ball tampering up until that day.

The 39-year-old then said he never felt comfortable talking about it while back in the Australian team from 2022.

But he argued the fact he had held back the book until after Australia's Test return to South Africa last month was proof this was not a money-making venture.

"Call me a chicken or whatever you want. I didn't know how to do it because I was still in the team," Khawaja said.

"I was always conscious of putting my team first, but I'm not in that team anymore. What I say now isn't a reflection of them anymore.

"I stuck up for all cricketers in the past with the ACA [players' union] fighting for what I thought was right. This is no different.

"These three guys deserve justice and I haven't pointed fingers at anyone."

Khawaja has also been critical of Cricket Australia (CA) over its handling of the investigation into Cape Town, and that he was not interviewed.

CA has maintained it is "comfortable" with its findings from 2018 that only Warner, Smith and Bancroft knew of the idea.

Other players including bowlers Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon distanced themselves from the incident, insisting they had no knowledge "of a foreign substance" being taken on the field.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/w.author: Samantha Goerling
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/w.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Watch recordings by WA cyclists of close calls on the road.

Cyclists want police to issue fines rather than cautions to drivers who disregard the one-metre passing law.

Cyclist Peter Hatton has made four reports to police but no-one has been fined.

Police say they assess each report individually and that cautions are recorded in the system.

Since installing front and rear cameras on his bicycle last year, Peter Hatton has made four reports of dangerously close calls with drivers who were flouting the safe passing law.

Since 2017, drivers have been required to leave a one-metre gap when passing a cyclist at 60 kilometres an hour or less and 1.5m when overtaking at a higher speed.

Drivers who fail to do so incur four demerit points and a $400 fine.

Peter Hatton has documented his close calls with motorists.  (Supplied)

Mr Hatton said police were unable to identify the driver in the first incident he reported and that the other three resulted in cautions with driver education.

"[In one instance] in the debrief I had with the investigating officer, they mentioned that this gentleman had thought we were riding three abreast and he should perhaps teach us a lesson," he said.

Peter Hatton has purchased cameras for his bike.  (ABC News: Samantha Goerling)

Six cyclists have died on Western Australia's roads so far this year and Mr Hatton says he has become increasingly concerned about his safety.

"I have a high-vis helmet, high-vis shirts, reflectors on my ankles, I have three flashing red lights on the back of my bike, one flashing white light on the front," he said.

Police say the safety of all road users is taken seriously and that every report is assessed on individual circumstances and the evidence available.

"Depending on those circumstances, the appropriate response may include education, a caution, an infringement or other enforcement action," WA Police said in a statement.

"A caution is a formal warning which is recorded and is visible to officers who may encounter the recipient in the future."

Cyclists say it's time to move past cautions and fine drivers who get too close when overtaking.  (ABC News: James Carmody)

Amy's Foundation, formed in honour of Amy Gillet, a top cyclist killed in a bicycle accident in Germany, campaigned for the safe passing laws now in place nationwide.

Managing director Katherine Bates said the foundation's surveys of riders indicated the issue was under-reported.

Katherine Bates says only one in five cyclists report close passes in WA. (ABC News: Dean Caton)

"We know that, from Western Australia, only about 20 per cent of people who experience close passes on their bikes even bother to report it," she said.

"Of that 20 per cent, only 30 per cent then proceed to even hear back from the police.

"It keeps people off bikes and the power imbalance firmly in the hands of drivers.

"It's only consistent enforcement that will make a difference."

WA Police say each incident is assessed on an individual basis.  (ABC News: James Carmody)

The WA Road Safety Commission said it was working with peak body WestCycle to make roads safer.

"Real change is possible when we have a shift in culture that recognises that every person sharing the road deserves to get home safely," the commission said in a statement.

"The key focus of the partnership includes an engaging Ride Safely Together social media campaign promoting mutual respect between cyclists and drivers, with a particular focus on compliance with the safe minimum passing distance."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/s.title: Serial child rapist's court-enforced exile a potential legal first for WA
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/s.author: Will Corbett
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Child Sexual Abuse

Dennis McKenna is due to walk free from prison after serving more than 15 years.  (ABC News: File)

One of Western Australia's worst serial paedophiles will be barred from the town where he committed his crimes, in what is believed to be a legal first for the state.

Dennis McKenna abused dozens of boys in Katanning while a warden at St Andrew's Hostel throughout the 1970s and 80s.

St Andrew's Hostel was demolished in 2024. (ABC Great Southern: Mark Bennett)

McKenna's apprehension and conviction took years, but he eventually served more than 15 years in prison for abusing 29 victims.

And in less than two weeks, he will walk free from prison.

The Supreme Court ruled this week that despite McKenna's high risk of reoffending, his release into the community could be safely managed by 41 stringent conditions.

One of them permanently bans him from Katanning — the small town 240 kilometres south of Perth that still bears the scars of his years of predatory abuse.

Katanning shares the landmarks of larger farming hubs across Australia: a main street lined with federation buildings, with the major rail line cutting through the centre of town.

But McKenna's abuses have left a long-running stain on the close-knit community.

Supporters in the community helped shield him from scrutiny, until victims and whistleblowers won critical breakthroughs.

Katanning sits about 240km south of Perth. (ABC News: Andrew Chounding)

Shire president Kristy D'Aprile said the news of McKenna's exile was welcome.

"I think it's a really important condition for our community," she said.

"I thought if the state government believes he is fit for release, they would surely provide some protection for our community."

Kristy D'Aprile welcomes Dennis McKenna's ban from visiting the town. (ABC News: Anthony Pancia)

Lawyer John Hammond represented 25 of McKenna's victims during a compensation battle more than a decade ago.

He said it was the first time he'd heard of such a ban in WA.

"I haven't seen a situation where a high-risk offender has been banned from the whole town," he said.

"Particularly the size of Katanning."

He said the ruling sets a healthy precedent.

Perth lawyer John Hammond represented some of McKenna's victims. (ABC News: Dominic Briggs)

"The court should use its power to ban people such as McKenna from towns where they've caused so much damage," he said.

"McKenna's actions left a black stain on the town, and it has taken a long time for the town to recover."

Attorney General Tony Buti said his sympathy lay with McKenna's victims and their families.

"Dennis McKenna's record of child abuse is abhorrent, and the impact of his crimes is truly horrific," he said.

McKenna is prohibited from seeking out his victims. If he is to accidentally run into one of them, he is to avert his gaze and move at least 100 metres away.

His movements will be electronically and physically monitored, any relationship must be disclosed to authorities, and he is banned from any contact with children.

Some people, however, believe the measures imposed by the Supreme Court don't go far enough.

Todd Jefferis was one of the first victims to come forward and has campaigned for fellow survivors for decades.

Todd Jefferis was one of the first to speak out against McKenna. (ABC Great Southern: Will Corbett)

He said the measures do not come close to what is needed.

"We've asked for restrictions on where he can actually go, and we asked if Albany was one of those places," he said.

"It is bothering me because the state's solicitors' office and all those involved have failed the victims and the victims' families.

"They know how bad this guy has been and what lengths he went to to do what he did, and then hide it. Why they would let this guy back on the street is beyond belief."

Mr Jefferis said the state needed to make an example out of McKenna.

"They had an opportunity here to actually show some courage and go 'we are going to draw a line in the sand'," he said.

"Send a message to every paedophile, if you get caught, you're staying [in prison].

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/n.title: Extraordinary scenes as fog descends on 'farcical' FA Cup tie
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/n.author: Simon Smale
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
England Soccer

Spot the ball? You'd be hard pushed to see anything at Moss Lane in these conditions. (Supplied: TNT Sports)

Does a defeat count if nobody saw it?

Altrincham fans may well be wondering that this weekend, after fog descended upon its FA Cup first round tie against Notts County at Moss Lane in Manchester.

League One side Notts County, featuring Australian former Sydney FC striker Luka Smyth, had taken a first half lead before Manchester-based Altrincham, of the fifth-tier National League, hit the front.

A late equaliser for Nottingham-based County, who won the FA Cup back in the 1893/94 season, forced extra time.

However, by that stage a heavy fog had enveloped the entire stadium, meaning extra time and penalties were played in scarcely believable conditions.

It made one slightly pity the commentators.

"I don't want to worry anyone — we can't see those dugouts at the moment because of the mist," Steve Bower said on the BBC in the closing stages of normal time, before fatefully adding that "it's getting heavier".

"We will try our best to let you know who has got the ball."

Former Notts County striker Mark Stallard said on the BBC Radio Nottingham call that "We're looking around … no-one knows where the ball is."

"We genuinely cannot see the linesman or the players on the far side. It's slightly farcical having to commentate for radio listeners."

At least he was only supposed to be summarising.

"I can just about see the bright white numbers on their shirts, but I am struggling to see what is happening on the far side of the pitch," his play-by-play caller Adam Hassell said.

The scenes were reminiscent of another famous foggy incident involving legendary Charlton goalkeeper Sam Bartram.

On Christmas Day, 1937, a London pea souper rolled into Stamford Bridge and completely covered the field.

In his autobiography, Bartram recalled seeing "fewer and fewer figures as we attacked steadily" over the course of the match, right up until a policeman appeared on the edge of his penalty area.

"'What on earth are you doing here?' he gasped. 'The game was stopped a quarter of an hour ago. The field's completely empty,'" Bartram wrote.

"When I groped my way to the dressing-room, the rest of the Charlton team, already out of the bath and in their civvies, were convulsed with laughter."

Fortunately, nothing like that happened in Altrincham, with the game eventually going to penalties, which took place in front of the Altrincham fans.

The Notts County fans, 100 or so metres up the other end of the ground, were left to guess what was happening based on the reactions they could hear through the gloom.

The Notts County fans didn't have the greatest view of the shootout …  (Supplied)

They weren't the only ones.

"He's put it wide, I think," commentator Adam Summerton said on TNT Sports as Max Sanders stepped up for Notts County.

"It's hard to tell, I'm sorry, but it's so hard to see up here.

"No, it's in. I'm really sorry, it's so hard for us to see up here," he added as the replay was shown on his monitor.

At least Altrincham fans could see if the ball had gone in or not. (Supplied: TNT Sports)

Meanwhile, Notts County's fans started celebrating after a pause of a couple of seconds, presumably because the Altrincham fans were not.

That pattern continued all the way through the shootout, right up until the final spot kick was taken, by "I think it's [Rosaire] Longelo," Summerton said.

He scored, and Notts County was through to the second round.

At least, I suppose, nobody could see the Altrincham players' disappointment.

Don't worry Eddy Jones, I think most people couldn't see your penalty miss. (Getty Images: Jess Hornby)

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/p.title: Spectacular cave site 'neglected' after five years closed to tourists
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/p.author: Aiden McNamara
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/p.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Travel and Tourism

The Princess Margaret Rose Cave in Victoria's Lower Glenelg National Park. (Supplied)

The Princess Margaret Rose Cave, near Mount Gambier, has been closed to the public since 2021.

Some locals feel the site has been neglected but are cautiously optimistic after visible signs of construction.

Parks Victoria is hoping to reopen the cave in late 2027 after another delay to its timeline.

The reopening of the Princess Margaret Rose Cave has been pushed back yet again.

Public tours of the popular site, 2 kilometres east of the South Australian border, started in the 1940s but stopped in 2021 when the operators retired amid COVID-era travel restrictions.

Today, the spectacular site named after the sister of Queen Elizabeth II is not exactly fit for a royal visit.

"They've had to put gates on to stop the vandalism,” local tourism operator David Graham said.

David Graham said the site was not past the point of no return.   (ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara)

The cave entrance is within the “dilapidated” visitor centre which Mr Graham recently entered with little difficulty, after he stuck his finger through a hole left by a missing doorhandle next to a cracked window.

The door has since been locked, but Mr Graham said the absence of a permanent occupant at the nearby residence made the location a target.

Elsewhere on the site, there were shards of broken mirror, ripped floors and a large hole inside a shower near the campground and cabins.

A tour of the Princess Margaret Rose site in 2017 (Supplied: Ghurunchi)

Local Liberal MP Roma Britnell said it was disappointing for the community.

"It's just been left to fall into disrepair and neglect,” Ms Britnell said.

The Victorian taxpayer is earmarked to pay $2,135,000 for work at the Princess Margaret Rose Cave site, including new toilets, and upgrades to the wastewater infrastructure and visitor area.

Parks Victoria said work was complete on new cave lighting, handrails, improvements to the steps, and upgrades to electrical systems.

“We know how important the caves are to local tourism, and we’re getting on with the work to reopen them,” a Victorian government spokesperson said in a statement.

Mr Graham said the latest works were a "promising sign" the cave is going to reopen one day.

The foundation for a new toilet block, a short walk from the cave.  (ABC News)

In October, a large sign went up near the car park with information about the upgrades.

“Completion: December 2026,” the text on the sign reads.

Parks Victoria’s website was also updated last month with new details about the project timeline.

“Unforeseen contractor availability constraints affected project scheduling, resulting in a revised time frame for construction works,” the website reads.

The government agency now expected the site to re-open in late 2027.

David Graham runs a cabin and boat hire business in the nearby riverside town of Nelson.  (ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara)

Mr Graham said the re-opening date had been repeatedly delayed.

Mr Graham, a member of the Nelson Tourism Association, said the continued closure was hurting the local economy.

"It [the cave] contributes to everyone in the area being profitable," he said.

Local fisherman Kym Muller has visited the cave site off the Glenelg River many times since childhood.

Fisherman Kym Muller hopes the cave will reopen soon.  (ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara)

He said there were "magnificent" lights inside to highlight stalagmites and stalactites.

"It was a very, very pretty cave when it was open, so a lot of tourists came through here," he said.

While the cave has been closed for more than five years, frustrated holiday-makers have been relatively common in the car park.

Gerry Anthony and Vicki McRae said road signage should make the closure clearer to prevent disappointment.  (ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara)

"To get right to the front entrance and find that it's just not open is disappointing," traveller Gerry Anthony, who towed a caravan to the closed site, said.

Mr Graham said it was "hard to say" whether there was enough signage.

"[Locals] drive and we see the signs often enough …that's not to say that people do know it's closed," he said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/j.title: Calls for more funding as Victorian JP numbers dwindle
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/j.author: Sarah Buchecker
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/j.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

ABC Mildura-Swan Hill

A justice of the peace centre opened in Altona Bunnings earlier this year.  (Supplied: Loretta Cormack)

Justice of the peace volunteer numbers have dropped to concerning levels in Victoria, despite demand for their services continuing to grow.

JPs are operating out of a Bunnings store and shopping centres to better connect with communities.

The Royal Victorian Association of Honorary Justices is calling for government funding to recruit and train more volunteers to keep pace with other states.

Loretta Cormack has volunteered as a justice of the peace (JP) in Victoria for the past 51 years but often felt hidden from view.

Now, she has found a place to base herself, offering JP services at hardware store Bunnings.

"Our poor police stations were so undermanned that they were having to close their doors," Ms Cormack said.

"We knew we had to find somewhere safe, we had to find somewhere that had plenty of parking [and] we had to find somewhere that was accessible to the community."

Loretta Cormack last year celebrated 50 years as a justice of the peace. (Supplied: Loretta Cormack)

JPs can witness a range of legal documents, including statutory declarations and affidavits, and can certify true copies of documents.

Most JPs in Victoria operate out of police stations, libraries or council offices, with a handful of shopping centres also offering the service in Corio, Geelong, Airport West, South Morang, Waurn Ponds and Wendouree.

The Altona Bunnings in Melbourne's west, where Ms Cormack volunteers, is the first to offer Victorians access to a JP while they shop.

Ms Cormack said being in the retail space meant volunteers were able to interact with more people, particularly those who did not want to enter a police station.

Justices of the peace are available six days a week at a Bunnings store in Altona. (Flickr: Scott Lewis)

"Our presence is open to the public, far more than it is in the police station," she said.

A Bunnings spokesperson said the move was part of their community service program.

"Justice of the peace volunteers are welcome to use our space, like cafe areas, to offer a convenient service to community members," they said.

Doctors, pharmacists and police are also able to sign important documents, although some might refuse due to time constraints in their busy roles.

Ms Cormack said the demand for JPs had been "booming" since she moved into the hardware store and that the Hobson Bay area needed more volunteers to keep up with demand.

"We're an older generation, we need new people coming through," she said.

In Victoria, there are 3,699 registered justice of the peace volunteers but Royal Victorian Association of Honorary Justices (RVAHJ) president Rodney Lavin said the state's active numbers were likely much lower at about 2,000.

Rodney Lavin says Victoria deserves as much access to JPs as other states. (Supplied: Rodney Lavin)

"About 1,500 [volunteers] are in nursing homes or many of them actually died or they're very sick or they're very old," he said.

Victorian JP numbers are drastically lower than interstate. There are 80,000 JPs in Queensland, 65,000 in NSW and about 7,000 in South Australia.

More than 70 members gathered in August to campaign for more justice of the peace funding. (Supplied: Rodney Lavin)

Mr Lavin said Victoria had not received government funding to train JPs since the 2021–2022 budget.

RVAHJ members have called for whichever party forms government after the November 28 state election to fund training for 5,000 new recruits, and commit to 500 more each year.

Staff from the office of Liberal leader Jess Wilson said the party had not committed to funding JP training. The ABC also contacted the Labor Party for comment but did not receive a response.

Mr Lavin said volunteers were ready and available, they just needed training.

The Department of Justice and Community Safety said a multi-year recruitment campaign between 2022 and 2025 successfully appointed 800 new JPs.

Mildura in north-west Victoria was one of the locations to benefit from thee new recruits.

Sue Mason works twice a month in Mildura as a justice of the peace. (ABC News: Sarah Buchecker)

Volunteer Sue Mason said there were 20 volunteers attending the local signing station, and they were meeting demand.

"We're not too bad here in Sunraysia because we had a late intake about three years ago, which we got an extra 15 [JPs]," she said.

Ms Mason said the extra recruits relieved some of Mildura's older long-standing volunteers, but she was worried about the future.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/m.author: Jarrod Whittaker and Ashlee Aldridge
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/m.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Missing Person

William was reported missing when he failed to return from a walk while camping with another teenager. (Supplied: Victoria Police)

William, 17, went for a walk while on a camping trip with another teenager and failed to return.

A major search operation is underway for the teenager who was last seen on Friday afternoon in Walhalla East.

Anyone with information is urged to contact Crime Stoppers.

A mother has described the disappearance of her 17-year-old son in Victoria's east as one of her worst nightmares, as an extensive police search continues through dense bushland.

William was camping with another teenager in Walhalla East, near Cowwarr, when he walked a short distance to another part of their camp near Stoney Creek Road and T2 Track, but failed to return.

His mother, Elizabeth Barkley, said Will, as he is known as, had little camping experience, was unfamiliar with the area and had a poor sense of direction.

She said her son, who has level two autism and anxiety, would likely be distressed.

William was last seen on Friday about 4pm.  (Supplied: Victoria Police)

Will was last seen wearing only a pair of shorts and work boots. His mobile phone was left at the campsite.

Ms Barkley said he had also left behind an esky containing food and water when he walked back up the track to collect other camping equipment.

Police later found the esky further up the track, but there has been no sign of Will.

Will is about 1.9 metres tall and is fit, prompting his mother to fear he may have travelled a considerable distance since disappearing.

"I'm just really worried. He has been out there for two days. He is probably cold and hungry," she said.

"I just hope he is curled up somewhere and has gone to sleep. He is a deep sleeper."

Ms Barkley described the disappearance as "one of her worst nightmares".

"You don't know where he is, whether he is still alive, if he is OK. I just want him back home," she said.

Will's mother Elizabeth Barkley says she is living one of her worst nightmares as she waits for news about her son. (ABC News)

Acting Superintendent Melanie Hamshere said between 65 and 70 people were involved in the search, with specialist police deployed to the area.

She said Will and his friend had walked down to a camping area after being dropped off by his mother.

He later returned toward the drop-off point to collect the remaining equipment, a walk of about 20 minutes.

Police believe he became disoriented during that trip.

His friend searched for Will before reporting him missing.

During the search an older-style white ute with a canopy stopped to help the friend.

The couple helped collect the camping gear and transport the friend back up the track to meet Ms Barkley.

Police are now urging the pair to come forward as they may have information that could assist the investigation.

Acting Superintendent Melanie Hamshere says there are growing concerns for Will on Sunday afternoon. (ABC News: Jarrod Whittaker)

Acting Superintendent Hamshere said the esky had been found, but other items were still missing.

She said the surrounding bushland was thick, dense and treacherous.

The search, which began shortly after Will was reported missing, has involved the Police Air Wing, drones, water police, officers on motorbikes, mounted police and the dog squad.

"It's been quite cold overnight for both nights."

She said police were concerned about the length of time Will has been missing and the limited clothing he was wearing.

"The longer he is out there the more difficult it is for him."

Police have described the search area as thick, dense and treacherous terrain. (ABC News)

Ms Barkley said Will was not afraid of approaching people and would likely speak to anyone he encounters.

She described her son as a "good kid" who loved football and soccer.

She said the past few days had been "absolutely horrible", with little sleep and constant worry about her son.

She said Will was a "mum's boy" and would be missing his family.

Ms Barkley also urged anyone who had come across camping equipment in the area, including blue or black pillow, a table or and old tackle box to contact police.

"You see these things on the news that happen to other people and you just don't think it is going to happen to you until it does," she said.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Dutchman and Spaniard in two-horse race for ECB presidency
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: Mark Schroers
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
The choice for European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde’s successor probably comes down to Dutchman Klaas Knot and Spaniard Pablo Hernandez de Cos.

The Netherlands and Spain each nominated their former central-bank chiefs to replace Lagarde when she departs in February, Kyriakos Pierrakakis, who heads the group of euro-area finance ministers, said Friday in a statement. De Cos currently leads the Bank for International Settlements.

“At its next meeting on 9 November, the Eurogroup will take stock of these candidacies,” the group said.

While no other candidate was proposed before Friday’s deadline of 5 p.m. in Brussels, a surprise late-stage contender could yet appear once political bargaining starts in earnest, just like Lagarde did in 2019.

Her position is part of what Greece’s prime minister has called a “grand bargain,” including the jobs of Executive Board member Isabel Schnabel and Chief Economist Philip Lane, with the former leaving the ECB early in January 2027 and the latter in May, when his eight-year term ends.

That will be one of the biggest reshuffles of the six-strong board since the institution’s inception more than 25 years ago. If Knot were to become president, it would even involve a fourth job as his fellow countryman Frank Elderson would have to leave.

The changes come at a delicate time, with inflation running at double the ECB’s 2% target and fiscal stress worrying investors in France.

While the euro zone’s 21 finance ministers will assess candidates on Monday, the final decision rests with European leaders. That puts the spotlight on an informal summit scheduled for Nov. 13 and a special one on Nov. 26-27.

Crucial to the selection will be an agreement between the leaders of the region’s two biggest economies, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron.

Both countries are looking to maintain their presence on the ECB board, with Spain also pushing for a seat after Vice President Luis de Guindos retired earlier this year.

France appears keen to get Lane’s position and is well prepared. It can pick from candidates including Bank of France Deputy Governor Agnès Bénassy-Quéré and former OECD official Laurence Boone.

Germany’s coalition has yet to agree on a candidate to replace Schnabel, with former International Monetary Fund official Tobias Adrian and Bundesbank Vice President Sabine Mauderer among those in the running.

In an interview with Swiss newspaper Tagesanzeiger published Saturday, de Cos said policy makers need to be “vigilant” about inflation risks, though so-called second-round effects stemming from an Iran-war induced energy price surge haven’t materialized so far.

He also indicated concern over high debt levels in some economies, a risk factor in a period when the cost of borrowing is likely to rise further.

De Cos declined to comment directly on his candidacy in the interview.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: JCG-discovered “Godzilla” seafloor formation wins heritage status
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
The Japan Coast Guard said that the “Godzilla Megamullion,” a massive seafloor formation discovered during its 2001 continental shelf survey, has been selected for the International Union of Geological Sciences’ list of 100 Geological Heritage Sites.

The JCG announced the designation of the megamullion, located southeast of the remote Tokyo-administered Pacific island of Okinotorishima, on Friday.

A megamullion is a dome-shaped seafloor structure formed when mantle rocks are exposed on the ocean floor through fault activity associated with seafloor spreading.

Located on the Philippine Sea plate, the Godzilla Megamullion measures about 125 kilometers in length and 55 kilometers in width, making it roughly 10 times larger than a typical megamullion. It is believed to be the largest such formation ever discovered.

The megamullion was named after the giant monster Godzilla because of its enormous size and was registered internationally under that name in 2021.

Studies of the Godzilla Megamullion conducted by an international team led by Japanese scientists have produced important findings on mantle structure and the processes involved in plate formation. The site was recognized as a globally significant geological reference point for scientific research, according to the JCG.

This marks the third round of selections for the IUGS geological heritage list. Other Japanese sites previously chosen include the Nojima Fault in Hyogo Prefecture, which triggered the 1995 Great Hanshin Earthquake.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.text:
BAKU – Some fans of popular Japanese television drama “Vivant” have been flocking to Azerbaijan, hoping to see with their own eyes where the second season of the hit series was filmed.

Hugging the western shore of the Caspian Sea, Azerbaijan will likely continue welcoming more Japanese visitors, including growing numbers of “set-jetters,” or people who travel to locations where famous movies and TV shows are filmed. One travel agency has said that package tour sales to the country have been strong.

Among the set-jetters who visited Azerbaijan in late October was Mayumi Kishi, 47, from Tokyo. Standing before the ruins of a bathhouse at the Palace of the Shirvanshahs in the country’s capital of Baku, which appeared in the drama as Jerusalem, Kishi said: “This is it. The character came out from this spot.”

Squealing with delight, she took photos on her smartphone.

Kishi had already planned to visit Azerbaijan even before learning about where the drama series was filmed. After a suggestion by her travel companion, she decided to stop by and pay a visit to one of the places that served as the drama’s filming locations. She said that she watched the drama before the trip to familiarize herself with the filming locations.

“I hope that people who have watched Vivant will visit” the country, she said.

Bukinist, a bookstore in Baku, appeared in the drama as a base for “Beppan,” a purported secret intelligence unit within Japan’s Self-Defense Forces that is at the center of the drama series.

Japanese visitors have become a daily sight at the store crammed full of books. Saying that such visitors walk around the store taking photos and videos, the store manager in his 50s added that the drama has helped create a warm bond between the two nations.

Japanese travel agencies have begun offering set-jetting tours.

In cooperation with Tokyo Broadcasting System Television Inc., which produced the TV drama, Hankyu Travel International launched a travel package to coincide with the airing of the latest season. Some departures between late November this year and October next year already have waiting lists.

“Sales have been strong, thanks to the impact of the TV drama,” an official of Hankyu Travel said, adding that the company is thinking of opening up more booking slots.

The Azerbaijani side has welcomed the rising interest generated by the drama.

Speaking in a recent interview, Rashad Azizov, director-general of Azerbaijan’s Cinema Agency, said that the Japanese drama is making “history” by providing an “opening moment” to create a “bridge” between the two nations.

He expressed hopes for more Japanese tourists to visit his country to enjoy its historic sites, architecture and cuisine.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Magnitude 5.7 quake injures dozens in central Japan
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
A strong 5.7-magnitude earthquake shook central Japan early Sunday, injuring dozens of people, shattering windows and disrupting train services, officials and local media said.

The quake struck at 1:04 am in Shizuoka Prefecture, the Japan Meteorological Agency said. No tsunami warning was issued.

Authorities reported no deaths, but the quake shattered storefront windows and knocked items off shelves and caused transport disruption in parts of the country.

An emergency official in Aichi said authorities had received 16 reports of mostly minor injuries.

Authorities in neighboring Shizuoka said at least three women sought emergency medical care, including a woman in her nineties who injured her shoulder after falling from her bed during the shaking.

The local Chunichi Shimbun newspaper and Tokai Television separately reported at least 24 were hurt across the two regions.

In Toyohashi city in the Aichi region, windows of a car dealership were found shattered after the quake.

A large book store in Toyota city, also in Aichi, reported that its merchandise dropping from shelves.

The quake also forced temporary delays and suspensions of regional train services Sunday morning, including the Shinkansen bullet trains.

The quake was felt as far west as Osaka, where a foreign resident was taken to hospital after falling from a second-floor apartment when the shaking startled them, local media reported.

Officials in Osaka couldn’t be reached for immediate comment.

Separately, a 4.3-magnitude quake struck the Kumamoto region at 10:53 am (0153 GMT) Sunday, the Meteorogolical Agency said.

There were no immediate reports of serious damage or injuries from the second quake.

The southwestern region is still trying to recover from a 7.1-magnitude tremor that killed 38 people, flattened homes and left tens of thousands without power in July.

Japan sits on the Pacific “Ring of Fire” and experiences hundreds of earthquakes every year.

The country is haunted by the massive 9.0-magnitude undersea quake in 2011, which triggered a tsunami that killed or left missing around 18,500 people and wrecked the Fukushima nuclear plant.

The drill is based on a scenario in which an earthquake off the western coast of Hokkaido causes equipment failure at the plant’s No. 3 reactor, rendering its cooling system inoperable.
