What do you get the man who doesn’t seem to want anything? From fiery condiments to chef’s knives, slippers to portable speakers, these ideas are sure to hit the spot

The best Christmas gifts for mums in 2026

Gifts for dads, grandads and other father figures can often feel like a shot in the dark. What do you get for someone who doesn’t seem to want anything, or who already has it all?

Shared experiences or promises of peace and quiet are popular options, but they are tricky to wrap. Which is where my recommendations come in.

Each gift I’ve featured has been put through its paces by me for the past few months and has made it into this list because it has become something I reach for on a near-daily basis (or, in the case of the AeroPress coffee maker, multiple times a day).

Testing has involved cooking copious amounts of rice, making my home smell like a greenhouse and rolling my sleeves up in the garden (and I don’t think I’ll need to sharpen my knives for a while). So rest assured, my suggestions have the approval of at least one 34-year-old dad with a toddler (me).

Despite the rise in Apple Pay and its Android equivalent, wallets still have their place in a pocket. This neat design from Roka London has three interior compartments for cards, coins and receipts. Made from a durable recycled canvas, it has retained its good looks after months of cut-and-thrust testing, and kept its contents dry in a downpour when my trousers weren’t as lucky.

Chilly’s Series 3 water bottle

A water bottle should last longer if it’s easy to clean, and Chilly’s latest even comes with a telescopic brush to make keeping on top of seals and its stainless steel straw a cinch. It’s leak-free and promises to keep its contents cold for a whole working day (and beyond – Chilly’s says up to 45 hours), while the flip lid allows for one-handed drinking on the go. It ticks all the water bottle boxes.

For more, read the Filter’s guide to the best water bottles

Personalised gifts can be hit and miss, but this high-quality print from Good Team On Paper falls firmly in the former camp. The company will design a poster based on the memorable kits of any team (from non-league to national sides), and the result is a tasteful piece of art that is a cut above most sporting merch. My Arsenal-mad brother confirmed the early 90s yellow and black JVC away shirt was a particularly accurate representation.

Don’t be fooled by its colour. This spade might scream bling, but it’s an invaluable addition to any garden shed. It can break up rock-solid borders in no time, and its sharp tip has been great for dividing perennials.

Tomato vine refillable candle starter pack

Brighten up any WFH setting with a candle from Pott. Its collaboration with Isle of Wight Tomatoes is a welcome change from traditional scents and has brought a deep, summery tomato vine smell to my office as the nights have drawn in. Its jazzy pot can be used again with a candle refill, making it a longstanding staple of any desk.

UE Wonderboom 4 portable speaker

Electronics and outdoorsy dads don’t always mix well, but this portable speaker from Ultimate Ears is up to the challenge, including being submerged in water (it has an IP67 rating) and getting dropped in the sand by my toddler during a day trip to the beach. Its sound quality is surprisingly strong and bassy for such a small package (10.4cm high), and the audio doesn’t break up when cranked to the max.

Reusable earplug discovery pack

An earplug is an essential part of my sleep routine, though they rarely stay in until the morning. Happy Ears solved this issue with this discovery pack, helping me find a size that fits. Rather than completely blocking noise, they take an ambient edge off, and their use isn’t limited to the bedroom: they’ve been great for swimming and help at gigs, too.

The North Face wash bag

Although on the small side, this wash bag seems Tardis-like and has managed to fit all the essentials for weekends away and longer stays without taking up loads of room in luggage. Its zipped compartment means you don’t have to rummage for small items like contact lens cases and tweezers, and its integrated hanging loop was helpful when sink space was at a minimum.

Swap out the plastic pump bottle for this face cleansing bar from Lifejacket. The bar itself lasted about three months of daily use and left my face feeling clear, refreshed and ready for bed after a day of sweat from exercising.

Horace mattifying face moisturiser, 75ml

For time-poor dads who aren’t au fait with a solid skincare routine, a moisturiser keeps things simple while soothing dry skin. This pick from French brand Horace packs SPF30 coverage, a matte finish with no glossy sheen, and instant absorption so it takes seconds to apply.

For more, read our guide to the best face moisturisers

Bob body wash bar starter kit

This refillable applicator and bar set from Bob lets you ditch the plastic bottle of shower gel. The applicator’s bristles help get a real lather going, and the bars themselves leave skin feeling clean and smelling subtly of peppermint and lime for the rest of the day.

An AeroPress is the gateway method to making great coffee at home. Relatively mess-free, simple to clean and a fraction of the size of an espresso machine, I have used one daily for more than 10 years.

For more, read our guide to the best coffee machines for every home and budget

Folding knife sharpener

Sharp knives are safe knives – a blunt blade is more likely to slip – and this neat tool from Joseph Joseph has become a great, compact addition to my cutlery drawer. Dull, old knives have been given new life with some swipes on the coarse and fine ceramic sharpening wheels; its non-slip feet mean it feels secure to use.

For more, read our guide on how to look after your kitchen knives

Substitute his scratched non-stick and its microplastic particles for stainless steel. I’ve found this tri-ply frying pan brilliant for steaks, stir-fries, scrambled eggs; its high sides mean it can even work for stews. Plus, it will survive contact with metal implements and over-enthusiastic scrubbing.

For more, read our guide to the best frying pans

Yep Kitchen Sichuan chilli crisp, 160g

Sichuan peppercorns are something of an acquired taste, but if you’re buying for a fan of the mouth-numbing spice, this chilli crisp lingers on the tongue and lips. Great in stir-fries, dolloped on dumplings or slathered on scrambled eggs, it adds a tingly sensation to any dish.

Hario cold brew bottle, 550ml

Cold brew isn’t just for summer: this Hario glass brewer is a feature of my fridge long into the depths of winter. The simplicity of brewing is the big draw – stick ground coffee and cold water in before bed and wake to a beautifully balanced cup. Having a batch to hand means it can also be used for cocktails such as carajillo and espresso martini without a coffee machine.

Spending more than £100 on a knife may seem excessive, but this 8in Wüsthof chef’s knife has left the rest of my block firmly in the shade. Its handle has a satisfying weight that keeps you in control, while the blade is remarkably sharp and adept at everything from deboning chicken thighs to finely chopping garlic.

For more, read our guide to the best (and worst) chef’s knives

The Rambler is a rock-solid reusable cup from outdoor specialist Yeti, and its cup-holder compatibility makes it ideal for dad’s taxi. For an extra £8, it’s possible to add a personalised message to create a unique gift for your one-of-a-kind.

For more, read our guide to the best travel mugs

Bruichladdich the classic laddie whisky, 70cl

A contemporary take on a classic, this 10-year-aged single malt scotch is an approachable drop with a sweet nose and warming, biscuity taste that should get the seal of approval from aficionados and newcomers alike.

For more, read our guide to the best whisky

Bird & Blend tea infuser

This infuser makes brewing a mug of loose leaf tea straightforward. Fill with tea, plonk in a mug, pour over water and hey presto, you’ve got the taste of a teapot without the big clean-up operation and the convenience of a teabag minus the microplastics.

A hot drink instantly tastes better when it’s served in posh crockery, and Villa Bologna’s handmade and handpainted striped number has an artisan feel without the associated price. Dishwasher safe and able to hold 400ml of tea or coffee, it’s a serious upgrade on his faded Sports Direct mug.

after newsletter promotion

Bombom Korean barbecue sauce, 420g

Whether drenched on tofu, stir-fries and rice, or used as a marinade for chicken or salmon, this Korean soy and garlic barbecue sauce was an instant hit in my household. It’s moreish … so won’t last long.

Black Lines negroni, 500ml

Negroni’s three ingredients – gin, Campari and vermouth – make it one of the most straightforward cocktails to create, but not all serves are made equal. Black Lines’ premixed concoction is better than most, and means aperitivo hour is only the uncorking of a bottle away.

Gluten-free, vegan and carbon-negative, Jiddler’s Tipple craft beer creations are as guilt-free as they come. Its hoppy core range – which is included in this gift set with a vintage shirt pattern-inspired pint glass – all sit under 3.8% ABV too, so are less likely to leave a headache the next morning.

Rothaus Alkoholfrei pils 0.4%, 8 pack

Low-alcohol doesn’t have to be boring, as this Rothaus brew proves. After sampling a pint of the crisp, smooth 0.4% wheat beer in the summer, I was thrilled to find it came in a bottle for sober sipping at home. The flavour profile is perfect for the festive period, but also a welcome treat in warmer weather.

Forest Feast dark chocolate cashews, 120g

Swerve the chocolate orange stocking filler this year for a packet of these Belgian chocolate-covered salted cashews instead. A luxurious taste that perfectly balances the bitterness of dark chocolate with a hit of salt; buy a pack for yourself too, as they won’t be offered around.

Vina Real Rioja Gran Reserva Especial 2018, 75cl

If your old man knows his way around the wine aisle, then this special rioja is a sure-fire hit. A 2018 vintage that won’t break the bank, it has fruity notes that go well with red meat or manchego. Its ageing potential means it will also be a welcome addition to any burgeoning cellar (if it makes it through the festive period).

Yum Asia Kumo rice cooker

This rice cooker has become an invaluable addition to my kitchen, and a gadget that earns its place on a limited work surface. It’s simple to use – add water and rinsed rice, select the type (white, brown or short grain) – and about 40 minutes later you’re left with fluffy individual grains with no effort. For big families, Yum Asia’s Sakura has a larger capacity and can make up to 16 portions of rice in one go.

For more, read our guide to the best rice cookers

Running socks, per pair

A great stocking filler for the parkrun-obsessed pops, these socks from Hoka have a plush, cushioned feel underfoot when pounding the streets. They stay firmly in place even if you pick up the pace courtesy of an anti-slip silicone strip on the ball of the foot.

A base layer with fashion credentials, this moisture-wicking short-sleeve from Nike subbrand ACG keeps things cool during a run but won’t look out of place when they’re not working out. A slightly thicker front panel keeps the chill off on colder starts while mesh panels at the rear and armpits handle hotspots with ease.

A fleece for all occasions, this versatile pullover from Arc’teryx has been a brilliant addition to my wardrobe. The organic cotton has a soft touch against bare skin and is great for lazy days around the house. But it’s equally adept when heading out in the cold for a walk or layering as part of a smarter get-up.

Weeknight Vegetarian by Joe Woodhouse

This has become a firm fixture on my cookbook stand, filled with quick fresh recipes that make veg, beans and vegan protein such as tofu sing – from fast-assembly jobs like the WFH-friendly store-cupboard bean salad to the hearty lentil cottage pie that will have him converted from the beef version.

The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout

Elizabeth Strout’s Booker prize-shortlisted novel has a father as its focus and deals with themes inside and outside the home through protagonist Artie Dam’s lens. Funny, sad and at times a real thinker, it’s a refreshing break for anyone caught in the thriller loop.

London Falling by Patrick Radden Keefe

An engrossing nonfiction read with the mysterious death of a young man as its focal point, Patrick Radden Keefe’s bestseller is a page-turner that sheds light on London’s dark underbelly, complete with lies, deceit and dirty money.

Warm and luxurious, the recycled polyester fleece hooded dressing gown from Chelsea Peers belies its price. It’s the first thing I reach for in the morning and has even stayed on deep into the afternoon on those video-call-free work-from-home days.

Darn Tough is known for its hiking socks, but I feel its lifestyle lineup is a step above any high-street hosiery. Despite their lightweight construction, the cushioning is the sort of support you expect from thicker walking socks, while the merino wool adds warmth in winter without getting sweaty on hotter days.

Flannel pyjama bottoms

Comfortable in a wide range of temperatures and showing no signs of wear after several washes, these posh pyjama bottoms are worth the expense, and you won’t need to replace them in 12 months.

Slippers are a Christmas gift staple, but these suede M&S mules are an upgrade on any run-of-the-mill moccasins. The shearling lining gives your feet a cosy cuddle, and an antibacterial treatment keeps them smelling fresh, despite hours of wear.

This soft, stylish beanie from Cornwall-based B Corp Finisterre is minimalist in design and made from merino wool. It keeps the warmth in and the cold at bay without blocking my ears, making it great for ear pod use or staying alert for any impending toddler tantrums.

Brewery merch can often be naff, but this collaboration between Guinness and Manchester-based UN:IK is a legitimate addition to any T-shirt drawer. It pairs the Irish stout’s classic posters with a washed-out design and is a great gift for any G-splitting pros.

Extra virgin olive oil subscription

This small-batch extra virgin olive oil subscription is ideal for foodies who want to add punch to a dish – whether it’s salads, pasta or drizzled on Greek yoghurt. Handpicked and cold pressed in Crete, two bottles come directly from the farmers every two or three months, and for £30 a pop it beats supermarket fodder hands down on taste, price and sustainability.

Workshop Coffee subscription, three months

For adventurous types who are happy to have their taste buds tested, the Workshop single-origin coffee subscription offers a rotating selection of roasts. Available for filter or espresso brewing and as whole beans or ground for various brewing methods, a new brew arrives through the letterbox each month, and can be as varied as a lightly roasted zesty Ethiopian and a dark and deep Colombian cup.

National Trust individual membership, one year

Although you might have to get creative with your presentation of this gift (time to fire up Canva and dust down the printer), for less than two pints of beer a month (£8.40), you can provide free entry (and parking at most properties) to more than 500 National Trust sites around England, Wales and Northern Ireland (with some access to Scottish sites). Whether it’s interesting family days out, short solo walks around some grounds, or interesting ways to break up a long car journey, this pass will have you covered.

Christmas shopping can be tough, but the Filter is here to help. We’ve been testing Christmas presents all year to help you find thoughtful, creative and genuinely brilliant gifts for everyone on your list. Browse our other gift guides for hundreds more tried-and-tested ideas, from gifts you can make yourself to toys for every age group.

Charlie Allenby is a health and fitness journalist who also became a parent in 2024, meaning he juggles testing gear around nap times (or combines the two with his trusty running buggy). https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: ‘What is this emotion telling me?’ How anger, fear and jealousy can point the way to a better life
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Anita Chaudhuri
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
It’s tempting to ignore uncomfortable feelings – but maybe they’re the key to a happier, more successful future. Time to increase your psychological flexibility …

S
omething infuriating happened to me recently. My local gym closed down, and overnight what I laughingly call my fitness regime was toast. Quite literally, because now instead of plodding, spinning and lifting tiny dumbbells, I was spending my early mornings guzzling lavishly buttered sourdough.

Obviously, I could have brainstormed alternatives, from going for a run outside or taking an online class to – simple plan – joining one of the five other gyms in my neighbourhood. But instead I chose to see the inconvenience of it all. I grew creakier and crankier by the day.

Eventually, I forced myself to find a new venue. It’s cleaner, friendlier and a third of the price. It’s also further away, but I reframed my grumpiness about that by incorporating the extra walk into my warmup.

I didn’t realise it at the time but what I was grappling with is a concept known as psychological flexibility. And it is being cited as a powerful strategy that can help us to persevere with our goals. So what does it actually involve?

“Psychological flexibility is a skill. We all have it to different degrees. Some of us have it more naturally than others but it’s something that we can develop,” says Rachael Skews, a behavioural scientist and coach. She specialises in acceptance and commitment therapy, a process designed to expand psychological flexibility. “It’s really a combination of three core elements,” she says. “First, being engaged with what matters most to you as an individual. Second, being present in the moment and having a flexible sense of who you are in the world. The third thing is being open to whatever comes along. You respond to life by embracing the fact that every experience could contain something interesting and valuable.”

Unlike positive thinking, then, psychological flexibility is about acknowledging rather than drowning out or denying uncomfortable feelings such as anger, anxiety or fear, and using them as feedback for action. It’s also about letting yourself off the hook when you face insurmountable obstacles, unlike another pop psychology model, grit, which is characterised by powering through, no matter what.

Janette, an executive assistant, discovered how helpful this approach can be when she started a new job working for the boss of a large company. “Unlike previous roles, the work was home-based and remote, with the CEO in another country. From the outset I hated it. I wasted a lot of time crying, and trying to find another position. It was only when I confided in a friend that we realised the source of my misery was neither my superior nor the workload, but the fact that I don’t thrive as a Lone Ranger.

“It wasn’t a particularly social organisation, and all of the other assistants seemed happy to work at arm’s length. I couldn’t change the culture, so instead I signed up for a local co-working space, which gave me a ready-made community of people to vent to and have lunch with every day. I love the job now.”

There is a body of research illustrating the benefits of this mindset. In one large analysis of multiple studies, higher psychological flexibility scores were linked to better overall mental health. The research revealed that accepting difficult feelings encouraged people to take action – as opposed to drowning out reality with positive thoughts, which leads to avoidance.

A big part of it comes down to what psychologist Susan David calls emotional agility. She defines this as being able to fully experience all of life’s emotions – the difficult ones like fear, anger and jealousy, as well as states of joy, gratitude and optimism. The goal is not to let any one feeling drive behaviour or actions.

“It’s about living in the world as it actually is rather than how we wish it to be,” says David. “There’s this societal messaging that says we’ve got to be positive all the time, and full of gratitude for everything. We’ve been encouraged to view certain emotions as ‘good’ or ‘bad’ and that the only worthwhile ones are related to happiness.”

David suggests that rather than labelling feelings as positive or negative, we should view them as data. “Emotions offer us clues. So, say you are feeling lonely. If you tell yourself that you shouldn’t feel that way, or that you must count your blessings no matter what, you are blocking an important signal. Instead, ask yourself, ‘What is this emotion signposting?’”

For example, if you realise you need intimacy and a sense of belonging, that is more likely to prompt you to leave the house and meet new people – unlike pretending everything is perfect the way it is or that things will magically improve without taking action.

Is there not a danger that you might get overwhelmed by negative emotions? “No, because emotions are not directives. Just because I feel something doesn’t mean it is true,” says David. “In evolutionary terms, our emotions exist to help us to understand our needs and values.” Rather than viewing them as fixed, it can be helpful to remember that emotions are volatile and fleeting.

She counsels against over-identifying with any one emotional state. “These days, we live in a society where people behave as if emotions are calling the shots, eg ‘I feel sad’ or ‘I feel triggered.’ We need to recognise that we own the emotion – it doesn’t own us. We own our values, our choices, our next steps, and our ability to tell ourselves, ‘Even though I feel sad now, I can choose what I want to do in this world and who I want to be.’ It’s all about having agency over your life and not being victimised by how we feel.”

Gabriele Oettingen is professor of psychology at New York University and the University of Hamburg. The author of Rethinking Positive Thinking, she has been immersed in the science of goal-setting for more than 25 years. The most surprising and consistent finding across her research is that positive thinking on its own does not reap rewards. Anticipating obstacles, learning to course correct and planning for possible failure are the determining factors for success.

“If you dream and fantasise in isolation, it will certainly improve your mood in the short term,” she says. “I could sit here and imagine that I’ve marked this pile of exams on my desk, and that I’ve finished writing my next academic paper, also on my desk. I would feel fantastic and then I could focus on all the amazing options for my Friday night.”

The downside is that when we daydream about having achieved a goal, we relax and the energy needed to actually do it fades. Her research has covered various scenarios, from losing weight to finding a job to getting together with someone on whom you have a crush. “The more positively people fantasised about those fulfilled wishes, the less success they had, be it three weeks, three months or two years later.”

Over time, chronic daydreamers lose momentum because they don’t take the action necessary to achieve their goals. Far better to rehearse the various scenarios that might derail your big plans.

“Obstacles give you energy,” she says. “They allow you to understand what you can do in order to overcome them.” An obstacle might be a habit or a belief, but she counsels against making it about another person. “It’s best to choose an inner obstacle. Don’t fall into the trap of saying: ‘Everything is my boss’s fault.’ Reframe it as: ‘The resentment I feel towards my boss is what’s stopping me.’ If you focus on an external obstacle, you have no control over changing it.”

Someone who discovered the truth of this is Nick Jaye, AKA Bald Chef Nick. He struggled all through school and was told that he was “too stupid” to be a chef. So, he left at 15 without qualifications. Diagnosed with dyslexia, he credits a flexible mindset with his eventual success. He spent 40 years doing well as an estate agent before finally retraining as a chef in his late 50s. But there were many obstacles in his path.

“I knew I would have to adjust my approach, so I rewrote every piece of printed material from the course so that I could read and learn in my dyslexic way.” Not only did his adaptability help him to realise his goal; those pieces of paper became the spark for his book Deliciously Dyslexic. The first cookbook created for people with the condition, it features large fonts, tinted backgrounds and single-sentence paragraphs designed for adults and children.

“I know I am no longer that small, nervous and shy child who was told he was stupid. Instead, I see opportunities everywhere to learn, take on challenges and meet new people. This is what I wanted when I made the decision to retrain. I don’t get nervous any more, just excited. All my life I’ve learned to adapt to having a neurodiverse mind. My charity work, teaching, cooking and helping as many people as I can delivers a daily dose of acceptance and patience with myself and those around me.”

It’s a great reminder that psychological flexibility isn’t about changing who we are but changing how we approach the challenges we face. I fully intend to transform my own mindset, just as soon as I’ve buttered this lovely slice of seeded loaf …

Check in with your five-year-old self, and your 85-year-old self. “When we’re feeling stuck – a sure sign of psychological inflexibility – what we need is perspective,” says Susan David. “It’s easy to focus on choices that are only about you in this moment. Should I spend the money now? Should I quit the job now? It can be helpful to bring other perspectives. What would a young version of you say about this? How about the you that’s at the end of your life? This helps us to think more expansively.”

Ask yourself, WTF. “When you’re having a big reaction to something, a good way of remembering that emotions are not facts is to ask yourself: what the func? As in: what is the function of this emotion? Ask yourself, what is this telling me about my needs, my values and how I should move forward in the world?” David suggests.

View goals as experiments. “It’s great to have a goal but it’s best pursued with an experimental mindset. That will allow you to recognise when a great idea could also be course corrected into something slightly different,” says Skews. “Goals don’t need to be set in stone. Sometimes, the goal is just to give you direction.”

Think variation, selection, retention. “In behavioural science we use these terms to sum up the mechanics of flexible goal-setting,” says Skews. “Success is about varying what you’re doing, selecting what you think is working well and keeping on doing that.”

Make an ‘if … then’ plan: If you are trying to achieve a challenging goal, make a contingency plan for how you are going to tackle obstacles. An example might be knowing you always reach for crisps when you’re watching a favourite TV show. Planning ahead, and ensuring you have a supply of fruit and nuts on hand, or other healthy snacks, will make it easier to stick to your goal. “Some obstacles are really hard to overcome – for example, when there are very strong impulses or emotions. Making a plan links the future outcome with the obstacle, and engaging your subconscious, so you can more easily respond in the moment,” says Oettingen.
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.summary: Psychological flexibility is a concept known as psychological flexibility. Psychologist Susan David says we should be able to fully experience all of life’s emotions.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Tennis world number one Rybakina withdraws from WTA Finals due to virus
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Defending champion Elena Rybakina has pulled out of the Women’s Tennis Association (WTA) Finals, saying she was not physically ready to compete, allowing Ukraine’s Marta Kostyuk to take her place in the eight-player field at Indian Wells.

Organisers on Saturday cited a viral illness as the official reason for the world number one’s “disappointing” withdrawal, but said the world number one needs time to recover from the physical toll of a demanding year.

Tournament director Garbine Muguruza, a former world number one and two-time Grand Slam champion, said she had spoken with Rybakina and that the Kazakh had been unable to recover in time after struggling with physical problems late in the season.

“We love Elena, and we know that she was feeling so-so in Tokyo as well,” Muguruza told the Reuters news agency. “I spoke to her today, and she really couldn’t recover on time.

“What we want is for her to feel good, to go rest, to recover. We don’t want her to feel like she has to play — only if she’s ready to.”

Rybakina, who won two Grand Slam titles this year, also withdrew from ⁠the quarterfinals of the Pan Pacific Open in Tokyo last month because of a neck injury.

Rybakina’s absence deprives the event of some star power, but Muguruza said the round-robin format and depth of the field would ensure a high-quality tournament.

“We have the best players,” said Muguruza, who triumphed at the WTA Finals in Guadalajara in 2021.

“I know our world number one is not going to be able to play, but we have an amazing field, the very best,” she added.

“Every match could be a Grand Slam final. You really need to be ready. You cannot give one inch.”

Kostyuk, who is making her WTA Finals debut after a breakthrough season that included the Madrid title and a rise into the top 10, was already in Indian Wells as an alternate and practising when Rybakina withdrew.

Muguruza said the Ukrainian, known for her signature post-match backflip celebrations, had earned her opportunity.

“Marta is great. She’s had a breakthrough year,” Muguruza said. “With this year, we have many first-time players in the Finals, and that’s very exciting. It’s very hard to qualify.”

Kostyuk has been outspoken about Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and does not shake hands with Russian or Belarusian opponents. Muguruza said the tournament would support players in making their own decisions.

“They’re free to do whatever they feel,” she said. “We are open and supporting them.”

Rybakina’s withdrawal could create an opening for world number two Aryna Sabalenka to make inroads in the rankings.

Sabalenka, who won the Indian Wells title earlier this year, has the chance to reduce the gap at the top of the rankings, according to Muguruza, who highlighted Russian teenager Mirra Andreeva as a player comfortable in the California desert.

“Of course, Aryna might be thinking that this can be a good opportunity,” she said.

The WTA moved the finals to Indian Wells from Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, with Muguruza saying player safety had been the decisive consideration amid conflict in the Middle East region.

“It clearly felt no longer safe to be in a region where there is conflict,” she said. “Taking care of the players and looking ahead to what could be safe, comfortable and secure, relocating felt the best decision.”

Muguruza said players had responded positively to the switch to Indian Wells, where she competed regularly during her career.

“When we knew that Indian Wells could be the next venue, it was just a joy,” she said, adding that ticket sales have been strong. “The whole thing is just perfect.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.title: Democrats’ congressional win could strengthen Ukraine’s hand against Russia
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.author: Mansur Mirovalev
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.text:
Kyiv, Ukraine – Kyrylo, a wounded drone technician from eastern Ukraine, does not care much about the results of midterm elections in the United States.

Tuesday’s vote brought on a “blue wave” of victories for the Democratic Party, which will control both houses in the new Congress and provide a check on President Donald Trump.

But it means little to the Ukrainian servicemen.

“We already learned how not to depend on America,” said the 37-year-old, who is recovering from a heavy contusion in a Kyiv hospital after a Russian glide bomb hit his bunker.

He asked Al Jazeera to withhold his last name in accordance with wartime protocol.

“Trump has let us down so many times, sold us to Russia and we’re still standing and kicking Russian [butt],” he said. “We no longer depend on American money and weaponry. The whole world wants to buy our drones now.”

Under Trump, Washington gradually stopped footing much of Ukraine’s wartime bills. While the amount of financial and military aid nearly reached $200bn from Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion to late 2024, since 2025, the US assistance has slowed to a trickle.

From October 2025 to March, Kyiv received a mere $8.2bn in military aid as part of “legacy pipelines” dating back to US President Joe Biden’s administration. The deals will have cost another $13bn when the supplies are over.

Even though Europe took over most of the financial weight, coughing up $83bn in 2025 alone, almost a third of all weaponry comes from US companies, according to the Kiel Institute, a German think tank.

Some aid may be restored, and the Democrats have pledged to scrutinise Trump’s ties to Russia and conduct sweeping investigations focused on alleged corruption within the Trump family.

The investigations will include their ties to Russian politicians, intelligence and oligarchs, such as Umar Kremlev, who reportedly paid hundreds of thousands of dollars for Donald Trump Jr’s wedding celebrations in the Bahamas in May.

The Democrats have already signalled their readiness to issue subpoenas and force the disclosure of executive branch records, including the ones related to Ukraine, once they take control of Congress on January 3.

“Ukraine’s positions may become stronger,” Volodymyr Fesenko, head of the Kyiv-based Penta think tank, told Al Jazeera. “But we need to keep bipartisan support.”

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said of the midterm results, “We have bipartisan support.” He said he was “thankful to the Republicans, but Democrats very clearly state their support of Ukraine and providing aid to it.”

But getting more backing from the US Congress is not going to be easy as several Republicans who supported Ukraine have lost their seats.

The “blue wave” unseated Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, who cochaired the Congressional Ukraine Caucus and was one of Kyiv’s staunchest supporters.

Other notable pro-Ukrainian Republicans are Don Bacon of Nebraska, a self-described “Reaganite” staunchly opposed to Russia, and Mike Lawler of New York, who voted for the Ukraine Support Act.

At the same time, Kyiv needs to appoint a new ambassador to Washington. Olha Stefanishyna, a former deputy prime minister, was fired in August during a probe into her “illegal enrichment”.

The ambassador works with Congress and organises contacts with Kyiv and trips by lawmakers to Ukraine.

“That’s why first of all a new ambassador has to be appointed,” Fesenko said.

And while some supporters of the Democrats urge their party to impeach Trump, Kyiv would be on the losing side, analysts said.

“God forbid if Ukraine becomes the focus of a [third] impeachment because of the negative experience during Trump’s first presidency,” Fesenko said. “It made Trump form a stable negative attitude towards Ukraine.”

Trump’s first impeachment in 2019 concerned accusations that he pressured Kyiv to investigate Biden and Biden’s son Hunter, who had been on the board of Burisma, a Ukrainian natural gas company implicated in corruption schemes.

The Democrats said Trump froze $390m in military aid to Ukraine as leverage at a time when Kyiv badly needed US arms to continue fighting Russia-backed separatists.

Now, before the new Congress takes office, Trump is likely to pressure Ukraine to accept a fast-tracked peace deal with Russia.

“Because when Russia isn’t willing to concede, the fastest way to solve the matter – either through a truce or through freezing the war – is only possible if [Trump] twists Kyiv’s arms,” Kyiv-based analyst Igar Tyshkevych told Al Jazeera.

“That’s why the next two months will be rather complicated for Ukraine,” he said.

Because Trump at the moment has Republican majorities in both houses, he will “try to show the effectiveness of his policies to decrease the possible level of confrontation with the new Congress”, Tyshkevych said.

The new Congress will have to deal with a dilemma rooted in allegations of corruption involving top Ukrainian officials and their purported embezzlement of US aid.

“On the one hand, there’s a political conviction to keep supporting Ukraine and on the other hand the political necessity to put an end to questions, suspicions and accusations of Ukrainian leaders in corruption,” he said.

Pro-Kremlin voices are already counting Moscow’s possible losses.

“The Democrats will double down on their efforts to prevent Trump from establishing a dialogue with Moscow, demand the resumption of direct US military aid to Kyiv, insist on the restoration of transatlantic unity on the Ukrainian issue and propose new sanctions against Russia and its main trading partners,” Moscow-based political analyst Andrey Kortunov wrote in an opinion piece for the Kommersant daily.

The Democrats “will initiate investigations into how he negotiates with us”, Moscow-based analyst Malek Dudakov told the Gazeta.ru daily.

The Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs dismissed the concerns, saying Moscow’s foreign policies “don’t depend on the fluctuations of the political barometer in other nations”.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, meanwhile, spoke in flattering terms, saying, “President Trump continues to exercise his powers. We sincerely hope that he will continue his peacemaking efforts.”
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.summary: US aid to Ukraine has been reduced to a mere $8.2bn from October 2025 to March. The Democrats have pledged to scrutinise Trump’s ties to Russia and conduct sweeping investigations. The Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs dismissed the concerns.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.title: Floods in Gaza leave tens of thousands without shelter
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.text:
Flooding caused by heavy rains has damaged shelters and tents belonging to tens of thousands of displaced Palestinians across the Gaza Strip, authorities said.

Reporting from Gaza City in northern Gaza on Sunday, Al Jazeera’s Ibrahim al-Khalili said the makeshift tents many Palestinians have been forced to live in do not provide adequate shelter from harsh weather.

“The latest storm exposed just how fragile the protection is. In just a few hours, heavy rains and strong winds tore through shelters families had spent days trying to reinforce,” al-Khalili said.

He reported seeing soaked mattresses, pillows and clothes, saying nearly 400,000 displaced Palestinians are sheltering in locations considered “highly vulnerable” to more flooding.

Heavy rain and strong winds have hit Gaza since late Friday, flooding 70,000 tents and bringing down dozens of walls, according to the Government Media Office.

The flooding comes amid a humanitarian crisis in Gaza, as Israel continues to impose severe restrictions on aid supplies to the war-ravaged territory.

Reporting from Deir el-Balah in central Gaza, Al Jazeera’s Ashraf Abu Amra said displaced families whose shelters were flooded had not received food aid since early Saturday.

Jonathan Veitch, UNICEF special representative in Palestine, said the majority of people are living in “terrible conditions” and called for more funding to provide much-needed aid.

Gaza’s Government Media Office reports the storm caused damage estimated at $3m. But relief organisations have been struggling for years to bring in relief and support.

The Gaza Civil Defence said it received at least 1,500 emergency calls. The agency said more than 2,000 buildings are at risk of collapse and that at least 300,000 tents are needed to provide adequate shelter for displaced people affected by the weather conditions.

Israel’s genocidal war, which began on October 7, 2023, has devastated homes and infrastructure in Gaza, and continuing restrictions on aid, shelter supplies and reconstruction materials have hampered relief efforts.

More than 74,640 people have been killed since the genocidal war began on October 7, 2023, in response to a Hamas-led attack on southern Israel. Since a “ceasefire” took effect in October 2025, Israel has killed at least 1,610 Palestinians.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.summary: Heavy rain and strong winds have hit Gaza since late Friday, flooding 70,000 tents and bringing down dozens of walls. The flooding comes amid a humanitarian crisis in Gaza, as Israel continues to impose severe restrictions on aid supplies to the war-ravaged territory.

https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.title: Former Palestinian detainees at mercy of Israel amid perpetual detention
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.author: Fayha Shalash
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.text:
Ahmed Abed (a pseudonym due to ongoing threats of arrest) still feels like a prisoner despite being released from an Israeli jail to the occupied West Bank nearly two years ago.

Despite being technically “free”, Abed, 43, is still often rearrested by Israeli forces or summoned by intelligence for interrogation.

Hundreds of other Palestinians in the occupied West Bank face similar ordeals after being released from Israeli prisons. Their homes are sometimes raided twice a week; they can be detained, assaulted and interrogated on the spot before being released.

Every day, organisations dedicated to prisoners’ affairs document the arrests of dozens of Palestinians across the West Bank as part of large-scale operations that frequently target former detainees. Most of those detained are released after hours of interrogation, in what appears to be a campaign of intimidation by Israel against former Palestinian prisoners.

Abed was released as part of a prisoner exchange deal between Hamas and Israel in January 2025, having served 22 years of a life sentence. Since his release, he has faced persistent harassment by the Israeli military.

Just days after Abed’s release, he was summoned by Israeli intelligence for questioning. They informed him that they were unhappy with the political decision to carry out the exchange deal and warned they would rearrest him if he made the “slightest mistake”.

Since his release, he has been arrested six times and summoned for interrogation five times. Each time, his home has been raided and his family terrorised by Israeli soldiers. His father was once arrested simply because Abed happened to be outside his house at night.

“Whenever there are reports of Israeli military activity in the city, my family goes into a state of high alert; no one sleeps all night,” he told Al Jazeera. “Some neighbours even leave their homes, fearing they might be raided as part of the collective intimidation campaign imposed because of me.”

When Abed is arrested, he is often forced to walk for several kilometres handcuffed and blindfolded, accompanied by soldiers. He is then placed in a detention centre under dire conditions, deprived of food and water, subjected to beatings and verbal abuse, and then the threats begin.

“Every time, they threaten to send me back to prison to the point where I feel as though two-thirds of my body are still in captivity, with only one-third outside,” he said. “The threats vary, but the underlying message is always the same: I am not permitted to do anything ordinary or live a normal life like everyone else.”

Abed avoids family gatherings, fearing his presence may bring them harm, and so limits his interactions to his immediate family. An Israeli officer warned him that if he were to go to the mosque to pray, he would be arrested.

“The Israeli officer told me, ‘We have zero patience for you. Any behaviour we deem inappropriate, or any movement we find suspicious, we will rearrest you immediately,’” Abed added.

Although he managed to earn both a bachelor’s degree and a doctorate during his time in prison, he has been unable to secure a job. When employers learn about his repeated arrests, they refuse to hire him. Instead, he has to rely on day-labour work to cover his basic costs.

A former prisoner from Qalqilya says he is arrested on average twice a week during the frequent Israeli military sweeps of the city, where former detainees are targeted. He was recently warned during one interrogation that if he ever set foot on a football pitch, he would be arrested. This puts his job as a referee in jeopardy.

Abdullah, another former prisoner from the city who also requested not to use his real name, told Al Jazeera that he has been arrested so many times since his release in 2000 that he has lost count. But he says he has spent a total of 17 years in custody since his “release”.

He was recently held under “administrative detention”, lasting from November 2023 to February 2025, during which he was subject to physical and psychological torture. By the time he was released, he had lost 60kg (132 pounds).

Abdullah, who supports a family of seven, is repeatedly arrested and released after a few hours, but only after his children have been terrorised and his home ransacked.

His employer grew frustrated with his repeated detentions and found a replacement for him.

“After losing my job, I began working on a piece of land I inherited from my father. However, due to arrests and threats, I can never find the right time to tend to it,” he said. “I often fall behind in irrigating, applying pesticides, or tilling the soil, all of which have taken a toll on my seasonal yields, leaving me with more losses than profits.”

Since the outbreak of the war on the Gaza Strip in October 2023, the occupied West Bank has witnessed a wave of Israeli arrest campaigns and pogroms. Israeli troops now make regular incursions into towns, refugee camps, and homes, as well as arrests at military checkpoints to detain former prisoners.

Palestinian prisoner advocacy organisations have documented approximately 26,000 arrests in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, between October 2023, when the genocidal war on Gaza began, and early October 2026. This figure includes more than 800 women and nearly 2,000 minors. The total encompasses individuals who were subsequently released, not just those who remain in custody.

Amani Sarahneh, a spokesperson for the Palestinian Prisoner’s Society, told Al Jazeera that Israeli operations in the West Bank have evolved into a continuous, round-the-clock wave of detentions. On average, between 10 and 15 Palestinians are arrested and remain in Israeli custody every day.

These arrests not only take place at night, as they did before, but also during daylight hours, at military checkpoints, and through field interrogations.

“The persistence of these campaigns has led to a ‘normalisation of fear’ among the citizens, which has significantly impacted social relations, particularly in villages where residents live in a state of constant anxiety, fearing that occupation forces might storm their towns or public spaces and arrest groups of people at any moment,” she told Al Jazeera.

These arrests are frequently accompanied by physical assaults and abuse, with detainees held for long hours while handcuffed and blindfolded. The victims’ family homes are frequently ransacked and possessions taken away during the Israeli raids.

“These policies also include using family members of those targeted, such as wives and sisters, as hostages to exert pressure,” Sarahneh said.

“The impact of these campaigns has extended beyond the detainees and their families, deepening a sense of fear and apprehension among the general public, who now worry that the arrests could reach a much wider segment of the population,” Sarahneh said.
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.summary: Ahmed Abed was released from an Israeli jail to the occupied West Bank nearly two years ago. He has been arrested six times and summoned for interrogation five times since his release. Abed, 43, has been detained, assaulted and interrogated on the spot before being released.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.title: Rent-a-grandchild: Businesses offering companions to elderly grow in India
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.text:
New Delhi, India – Both daughters of S Budhiraja live in the United States. Yet, when he and his wife head out to the market in Gurugram, a bustling business district on the outskirts of India’s capital, a young man walks beside them.

It is 26-year-old Roney Raju, their “hired grandson”.

Across Indian cities, a small but growing number of companies are now selling what families once took for granted: someone to take care of ageing people. Chores include taking them to the temple, sitting with them during a hospital visit, playing cards, or simply listening to them.

Some firms call such workers “children for hire”; others call them a “grandchild for rent”.

India, the world’s most populous country, is growing older quickly.

People over 60 made up 10.5 percent of its population in 2022, a demographic projected to nearly double to 21 percent by 2050, according to the India Ageing Report 2023 by the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) and the International Institute for Population Sciences.

That means about 347 million elderly Indians – a number almost equal to the entire population of the US, the world’s third most populous nation – will need specialised care by 2050.

Several Indian startups see the opportunity, with the Indian government estimating the senior care industry at about $7bn.

Raju, holding a master’s degree in social work, works for one such company in Gurugram. He has been looking after the Budhirajas for the last few months.

“I was comfortable with him from the get-go,” Budhiraja, who is in his 80s, told Al Jazeera. “I feel he understands me 200 percent.”

Raju describes the bond in the same vein. “Right now, he is family to me,” he said. The couple, he said, see him as “their proxy child, and much more than a service companion”.

The bond has deepened over the past months. When Budhiraja was admitted for surgery, Raju kept track of the doctors and the medicines. He would even call to check on them after his shift had ended.

Raju’s boss Gaurav Mittal says many clients actually come to treat their companions “like their own grandchildren”.

He charges 450 rupees ($5) an hour for 10 hours of service in a month, or 400 rupees ($4.5) per hour if it is 25 hours. Like a mobile phone recharge, unused hours are rolled over to the next month.

In a country with an average per capita income of about 220,000 rupees ($2,750) a year, Mittal’s service caters to a small minority of urban, financially secure families.

Mittal said the idea for his company came from home. After his father died four years ago, his mother had to leave their hometown and move in with him. She was sociable and had money to spend, but depended on family members to go anywhere.

“The world is not designed keeping the senior citizens as the central pillar,” Mittal said.

The idea for such startups, however, is not entirely new.

A 2017 report counted at least five startups offering young companions to seniors. In 2022, the late Ratan Tata of the Tata Group promoted a Mumbai-based startup whose tagline says: “Everything Grandkids Do!”

The companions who work for these companies undergo police verification before they start working for a senior person. Before working alone, they often shadow a senior staff member on home visits.

Most companions are trained in psychology, social work or hospitality.

Vinay Kumar works as a companion for a firm based in the southern city of Hyderabad.

“We are not just taskmasters, but we develop a relationship with our clients. We support them and spend quality time with them so that they don’t miss their close ones,” he told Al Jazeera. “They may still do, but we try.”

The 2023 United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) report projects that older Indians will outnumber the country’s children by 2046. And many of these seniors are lonely.

In 2022, India conducted the Longitudinal Ageing Study, a national survey of more than 72,000 people. It found that 20.5 percent of middle-aged and older adults reported moderate loneliness, while 13.3 percent categorised their loneliness as severe.

Among people over 60 who lived alone, more than a third (37 percent) reported feeling lonely, the study found.

Globally, a study commissioned by the World Health Organization in 2025 found that loneliness affects one in six people and is linked to about 871,000 deaths a year.

Santosh Abraham, CEO of a Bengaluru-based startup founded in 2015, says while the children of elderly people are worried about medical emergencies or market errands, their parents mostly had a different concern.

“I am lonely, I don’t have anyone to talk to,” Abraham recalled one of his clients as saying. “I have done so much for my family and society; there is no recognition for it.”

Abraham said the most common request he gets is one that “nobody says out loud”.

“A senior calls us claiming to feel unwell. A care manager arrives, finds nothing wrong, and is then asked to sit and talk for an hour,” he said. “They just want company.”

Kumar said companions like him have to “understand their pain”.

“Most of the seniors who are living alone are very lonely. They want someone to play cards or indoor games with. Someone wants to go to a movie, or a temple, or parks, or attend local programmes,” he said.

Abraham said some seniors find a stranger easier to confide in. “With a companion, there is no baggage,” he told Al Jazeera.

For the young people doing the work, the line between their job and a relationship blurs quickly.

Raju says the visits to the Budhirajas are harder than office work. “Forming an emotional connection is never easy and is different each and every time,” he said.

Kumar, in Hyderabad, agrees. He said his clients often tell him about health problems that they hide from their children living in another city or abroad so as not to worry them.

He recalled a client who went from shutting the door on his face because he did not know English or Hindi to paying for his driving lessons and introducing him to people as his “god-gifted son”. When the man died in 2023, his son asked Kumar to perform the final rites alongside him.

Kumar once even cut short his 12-day marriage leave because one of his clients kept calling, asking him to come. “I genuinely feel these seniors are my own parents and grandparents,” he said.

Others are more cautious about what the job demands.

Prashanth Reddy, founder of the Hyderabad-based company that Kumar works for, said companions must understand boundaries.

“Companions are there to provide support, not to replace doctors or mental health professionals,” he said.

Abraham agreed. He said he underlines one golden rule during his training sessions with aspiring companions: “Talk less and listen more.”

The children of such elderly people who buy the services of these companies say paying takes out the awkwardness of asking neighbours or relatives for help.

“When you pay for a service, you don’t have to feel like you’re asking someone for a favour,” says Vinnay K, a US-based software professional, who has been hiring a companion for his ageing mother for five years.

Shilpa Bandyopadhyay, assistant professor at Jindal Institute of Behavioural Sciences near New Delhi, told Al Jazeera that hiring a companion “should not automatically be interpreted as evidence that their families have failed”.

She said a growing demand for professional elderly care raises harder questions about a family-centric society like India’s.

“Do we recognise ‘companionship’ as a legitimate and continuing need of our older family members or see eldercare mainly as food, shelter, healthcare and physical help?” she asked.

She argued for “a more balanced ecosystem of ageing” that brings together families, community networks, accessible public spaces and affordable professional services, without romanticising traditional family structures or dismissing new ones.

“At the end of the day, the question isn’t who lives with an older person,” she said, but “rather whether the older person feels seen, heard, safe, valued, and meaningfully connected”.

Back in Gurugram, Budhiraja is asked how he would feel if Raju did not show up for work tomorrow.

“I will make sure he comes after finding out why he couldn’t come,” he said. “I need him. As you grow older, the needs are more.”
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.summary: People over 60 made up 10.5 percent of India's population in 2022, a demographic projected to nearly double to 21 percent by 2050. For the young people doing work, the line between their job and a relationship blurs quickly.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Khawaja denies throwing ‘anyone under the bus’ over Sandpapergate scandal
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Usman Khawaja has denied he has “thrown anyone under the bus” a day after the former Australian cricketer released an excerpt from his autobiography claiming the entire team had been aware of ball-tampering during a 2018 tour of South Africa.

The scandal – called Sandpapergate over Australia’s scuffing of the ball with sandpaper during the March 2018 Test in Cape Town – sparked a major integrity crisis for Cricket Australia.

Captain Steve Smith and batsmen David Warner and Cameron Bancroft, who was caught with the sandpaper in his pocket, were banned for their part in the scandal.

In a video posted on Instagram on Sunday, Khawaja said he had wanted to “come clean” about the incident since 2018.

“I haven’t thrown anyone under the bus,” added the 39-year-old, who retired from international cricket in January.

“The guys currently in the team and the other people who were there on the South African tour, including me, we’re not the victims.

“These three guys [Bancroft, Warner and Smith] took the blame for all of us, and they’re the victims.”

Khawaja said he had spoken with the three players and promised Warner he would share his side of the story.

“These three guys deserve justice, and I haven’t pointed fingers at anyone,” he added.

“I’m still searching for what I was searching all those years ago: For us – me included – to take the blame together as a team so we can all move on from this once and for all.”

Khawaja, who retired after 88 Tests, defended waiting so long to make the claims, denying it was a marketing ploy to sell his book.

He said he wanted to go public in 2018 once Smith, Warner and Bancroft were suspended.

“But Smudge [Smith] being the man and leader he was, he talked me out of it.

“He wanted to take the blame. I argued with him, but he was having none of it. That’s the first time I tried to come out.”

Khawaja said he again almost spoke up in 2021 when bowlers Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon all denied publicly that they knew about the ball-tampering.

But after extensive talks with then-coach Justin Langer, he decided not to, he said.

Khawaja said he never felt comfortable talking after that while back in the Australian team from 2022.

“Call me a chicken or whatever you want. I didn’t know how to do it because I was still in the team,” Khawaja said. “I was always conscious of putting my team first, but I’m not in that team any more.”

Australia’s Test side returned to South Africa for the first time since 2018 last month and were beaten 2-1 by the hosts in the three-match series, which was overshadowed in part by discussions of the scandal and the upcoming release of Khawaja’s book.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.title: ‘Don’t bring your camera’: Filmmakers face extortion in Lagos
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.author: Pelumi Salako
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.text:
Lagos, Nigeria – Half an hour after Nurudeen Sanni and his crew began shooting a documentary in Ajah, several men surrounded them and demanded 100,000 naira (about $75) before they could continue filming.

As the crew negotiated, one of the men slapped a crew member who tried to protect the cameras. A scuffle broke out, and the men produced knives and cutlasses. The crew fled, but one member was stabbed in the neck and seriously injured, Sanni said.

“The painful part was that we saw a member of our crew being beaten and we could not do anything,” said Sanni, a 40-year-old sound recordist.

His experience illustrates the risks that filmmakers, content creators, photographers and journalists say they face while working on the streets of Lagos, Nigeria’s largest city and commercial hub.

Men locally known as agberos, a term commonly used for street touts, including some who collect levies from commercial transport operators, have been accused of demanding money from people filming in public and threatening those who refuse to pay.

In August, music video director ThankGod Omori, known professionally as TG Omori, described a night shoot in Ikoyi that was disrupted at about 3am by a crowd demanding money. He said he left the set in the hands of his assistant directors and security personnel, with one scene still unfinished. The following morning, he learned that the men had broken through a gate and injured a security guard who had refused them entry, according to Nigerian newspaper PUNCH.

Actress and content creator KieKie has also described being confronted by men after filming a short video in Obalende. She said they initially demanded one million naira (about $750), but she paid approximately 700,000 naira (about $525) after negotiations. For a separate shoot around Kara, near Berger, she said she spent close to 500,000 naira (about $375) on security.

Stanley Ikechukwu, an analyst at Lagos-based risk advisory firm SBM Intelligence, said creators regularly reported harassment and extortion. He described the situation as a “war on camera”.

Nabila Okino, an analyst at global risk advisory firm Africa Practice, said filmmakers were particularly vulnerable because abandoning a location could mean losing time and money.

“Because filmmakers often need to shoot in specific locations, those demanding money know that there is a cost to abandoning a location and starting again, which gives them leverage to extract cash,” she told Al Jazeera.

For journalists, the consequences extend beyond the cost of filming. Threats and harassment can prevent reporters from covering events and leave some communities and incidents underreported.

When Karina Adobaba-Harry covered the demolition of Makoko in January for News Central, the Nigerian television channel where she works as a camera operator, men in the area approached her crew and demanded money before they could film.

“That was funny to me because we are here to tell your story, you want the government to hear your voice … and you want us to still pay you. That sounded ridiculous to me,” she told Al Jazeera.

Adobaba-Harry said she regularly encountered men demanding payments while reporting. Some left when she explained that she had no money; others threatened to seize or damage her camera. She said reporters had sometimes paid out of their own pockets or used miscellaneous funds provided by their employer.

Ikechukwu said such incidents could affect what the public learns about events in the city.

“A reporter who is harassed or whose camera is seized while covering a flood, a fire, or a protest is not just being robbed, the public is being denied information. It creates self-censorship. Reporters will start avoiding certain areas, and the news will only come from ‘safe’ places,” he told Al Jazeera.

For small production teams, unexpected payments add to the cost of camera rental, location fees, crew wages and transport. Some also budget for security or money they may be pressured to hand over after arriving at a location.

Adobaba-Harry said she had learned to change her demeanour when confronted by men demanding money.

“Sometimes, you have to take up the persona of the agbero so that when they see that you are not as calm, they will leave you,” she said.

She said many victims did not report incidents because they doubted that complaints would lead to action.

“Even if you report, chances that you will find the guys there [are] low. It is seen as a normal thing in Lagos, except if your life is in danger. But if it is just a case of wanting to take money from you, nobody will care,” she said.

Ikechukwu said the risk of being targeted had become another consideration for filmmakers planning a shoot.

“A filmmaker has to budget for ‘settlement’ on top of camera rental, location, crew, and food. It increases cost. It kills spontaneity; you cannot just see a beautiful Lagos moment and capture it. You have to think, ‘Will I be harassed?’” he said.

Okino said authorities should work with community leaders, market and park associations and other local groups to establish clear rules for filming in public spaces and ensure harassment and extortion are not tolerated.

Foreign content creators documenting Lagos have also reported harassment. In September, Chinese travel content creator Xiao Jony shared a video of men confronting him while he was filming at a market in the city.

He said they demanded money and that, over a stretch of about 10 kilometres (6.2 miles), he encountered more than 20 checkpoints where people asked him for payment. It remains unclear who operated the checkpoints or whether they were linked to any government agency.

Okino said such experiences could discourage tourists and production companies from filming in Nigeria.

“They may decide that the cost and risk of producing content in Nigeria outweigh the benefits. At the margin, that could mean choosing neighbouring countries with more predictable and straightforward filming environments instead,” she said.

Ikechukwu said videos showing tourists being harassed could undermine efforts to promote Nigeria abroad.

“We tell the world, ‘Come to Lagos,’ but our own behaviour says, ‘Don’t bring your camera,’” he said.

Gbenga Omotosho, Lagos state’s commissioner for information and strategy, said nobody had the authority to demand money from people taking photographs or filming in public.

“If there are ruffians who are saying that before you can take a picture, before you can walk the street, you have to pay them money, that is not acceptable; that kind of case will be handled by the police, the government will not stand for that nonsense,” he told Al Jazeera.

For photojournalist Jean-Fidele E Ananou, the threats have changed how he documents Lagos. He used to go out daily to photograph what he describes as the beauty of the city. He has since stopped because of concerns for his safety and equipment.

“When you think about the whole thing, it just doesn’t make sense. When you see other people from other countries taking pictures of their country, it just makes you wonder why can’t it be the same here. It’s just a really crazy menace,” Ananou, 31, told Al Jazeera.

“For photojournalists and street photographers, it is getting increasingly difficult to tell stories,” he said.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.summary: One crew member was stabbed in the neck and seriously injured, according to a Lagos state official. The threat of harassment could discourage tourists and production companies from filming in Nigeria.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.title: The anti-Netanyahu: Can Gadi Eisenkot give the world a different Israel?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.author: Simon Speakman Cordall
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.text:
Israeli President Isaac Herzog has tasked the leader of the Yashar (“Straight”) party, Gadi Eisenkot, with assembling a government after elections left no political alliance with a majority in the Knesset.

Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff, will now have 28 days, with the possibility of a 14-day extension, to put together a government before Herzog allows an alternative leader, most likely Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, to try to do the same. If this fails, then new elections would be called.

But as things stand, Eisenkot is unlikely to be able to form a majority government of the kind Netanyahu has relied upon to force through his right-wing policy agenda.

He may have to rely upon the support of at least one of the two parties representing the ultra-Orthodox community, which have often been allies of Netanyahu. It will also be critical for him to persuade some of the more right-wing elements of his opposition bloc to get the support of Arab parties outside the government.

How far he will be able to go in this is uncertain for a man whom observers described as less comfortable with the subterfuge and political guile often attributed to Netanyahu.

Eisenkot emerged as the leader of his volatile opposition bloc just days before the October 27 elections, and even then, messaging from within the coalition appeared confused, contradictory and seemingly absent of any central coordinating figure.

So far, any support from the ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism Party, which has broken with its traditional ally Shas in declining to endorse Netanyahu, is likely to come in return for the continuation of the de facto shield afforded to young ultra-Orthodox men who refuse military service.

Support from parties representing Palestinians with Israeli citizenship, even if offered from outside the government, is likely to come in return for at least some meaningful effort to tackle the violent crime wave that has been allowed to engulf Palestinian communities inside Israel.

They will also want the epidemic of violent settler pogroms, which have swept through the occupied West Bank with the seemingly active encouragement of Netanyahu’s government partners – particularly far-right Ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich – to stop.

But Aida Touma-Sliman, a Knesset member from the left-wing Hadash party and a member of the Palestinian-led Joint List, said developments in recent days showed that Eisenkot doesn’t want to rely on Palestinian voters.

“He appears much more willing to compromise with the ultra-Orthodox religious parties, particularly over the law governing military conscription, than risk being seen to depend on Arab support.”

One of the primary issues that whoever leads the country next will have to deal with is Israel’s standing in the United States. Israel’s reputation has fallen to an all-time low among the American public due to the genocidal war on Gaza and the US-Israel war on Iran, which Netanyahu is accused of convincing US President Donald Trump to start.

On the eve of what turned out to be disastrous midterm elections for Trump, he announced an end to the $3.8bn military aid package extended to Israel annually.

Irrespective of the last-minute announcement, Trump’s Republican Party suffered historic losses, and senior officials, including Vice President JD Vance, blamed the war on Iran.

Carnegie Endowment senior fellow Aaron David Miller acknowledged Israel’s reputation in the US was at a low ebb, one that Eisenkot – with his discomfort over the public stage and reluctance to speak in English – would need to address.

“Perceptions of Israel are fairly entrenched. Essentially, the public’s been watching the region in split screen since 2023. On one screen, there’s the carnage inflicted by Hamas on October 7 [2023], and on the other, there’s the death and destruction unleashed by Israel in response.”

“In the eyes of many, Israel is no longer David but Goliath,” he told Al Jazeera. “Ahead of Eisenkot may be the toughest US landscape any Israeli prime minister has to navigate.”

For now, at least, Eisenkot has the backing of the majority of Israelis as much for what he isn’t as for what he is.

Unlike Netanyahu, the well-polished son of a privileged Ashkenazi Jewish family who has nevertheless sought to leverage the grievances of Mizrahi Jews, Eisenkot represents a more genuine package.

Born in Tiberias to parents from Marrakesh and Casablanca, he grew up in the equally remote southern port city of Eilat before joining the army at 18, later rising to the rank of chief of staff. He then followed the well-worn path of senior Israeli military officers into politics, eventually serving in the national unity government assembled by Netanyahu after the Hamas- led attacks on southern Israel on October 7, 2023.

Described by both allies and opponents as both “menschy” (decent) and “schlumpy” (unkempt), Eisenkot’s careworn appearance reflects, at least in the eyes of some voters, his personal connections with the October 7 attacks and subsequent genocidal war on Gaza.

His son Gal was killed in Jabalia in northern Gaza in December 2023 while taking part in the war, followed a day later by his nephew Maor.

In November 2024, another nephew, Yogev Pazy, was killed in Gaza. This has created a persona around Eisenkot at odds with Netanyahu’s family, whose relatively glamorous lifestyle appears far removed from the Israeli public’s current situation.

“He seems very military in his bearing, very steady and a man you don’t always know what he’s thinking,” Yossi Mekelberg, a senior fellow at Chatham House, said. “I think he’s offering what Israel needs above all else right now: a sense of normalcy and the understanding that there are rules that apply equally and to everyone, including the government.”

But this will make little difference for Palestinians. Eisenkot is the architect of the Dahiyeh Doctrine, which advocates the use of disproportionate force and widespread destruction against civilian communities resisting Israeli force. It is far from clear if Eisenkot’s appointment as premier will make any difference to the yawning gulf in rights between Jewish and Palestinian citizens of Israel.

Eisenkot was reported to have expressed resentment at having to sit alongside such far-right figures as Ben-Gvir and Smotrich during his eight-month tenure in the national unity government. But he has nevertheless overseen punishing policies upon both Palestinians and Arabs in neighbouring states.

As chief of staff, Eisenkot oversaw brutal operations against Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank as well as overseeing extensive air strikes against Iranian targets and arming rebels in Syria.

From 2015 to 2018, years overlapping with his tenure, United Nations figures record about 650 Palestinians killed by Israeli forces or in conflict-related incidents. The toll included 295 deaths in 2018 alone. Among them were 189 Palestinians killed and thousands wounded during the Great March of Return protests in Gaza, including 35 children.

A UN commission later found reasonable grounds to believe that Israeli forces under his command had committed serious violations of international law, some potentially amounting to war crimes or crimes against humanity.

During the 2006 war in Lebanon when Eisenkot is credited with having devised the Dahiyeh Doctrine, Israel killed 1,109 people, about 860 of whom were civilians. There are no numbers for the tens of thousands of people killed under Eisenkot’s tactic in the years since.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.summary: Gadi Eisenkot has been tasked with assembling a government after elections left no political alliance with a majority in the Knesset. He will now have 28 days to put together a government before Herzog allows an alternative leader to try to do the same. If this fails, he will be the architect of the Dahiyeh Doctrine,

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Hossam Hassan sacked as Egypt head coach over ex-wife scandal
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
The Egyptian Football Association (EFA) has dismissed national team coach Hossam Hassan, citing concerns over the image and stability of the national side after a series of controversies surrounding his marital life.

The EFA said on Saturday that it had reviewed recent events and their “negative impact on the positive image and stability” of the national team before deciding to part company with Hassan and his coaching staff, adding that “maintaining stability of the team is top priority”.

Ali Maher, currently in charge of club side Ceramica Cleopatra, was appointed his successor.

The move came three days after Egypt’s Supreme Council for Media Regulation banned Hassan from appearing on media platforms over a case linked to his private life and former wife.

Local media reported lawyers representing Hassan had filed a complaint against his ex-wife, Dina Mostafa, known publicly as “Dan Adam”, alleging forgery of official documents and bigamy.

Those allegations were denied by her representatives.

On the pitch, a 0-0 home draw with Angola in a Nations Cup qualifier in September came under scrutiny after Hassan substituted talisman Mohamed Salah in the 60th minute.

The Trabzonspor forward left the national team camp, and the EFA said he avoids playing on artificial pitches and, therefore, would miss the qualifier against South Sudan that same month, which Egypt won 5-0.

Hassan’s future had already been under scrutiny following a string of disputes after Egypt’s run to the last 16 of the 2026 World Cup, the country’s best-ever performance at the tournament.

The former striker, who took charge in March 2024, also led Egypt to the semifinals of the Africa Cup of Nations before a fourth-place finish.

Hassan, who received a three-match ban from FIFA after criticising the referee following Egypt’s knockout World Cup defeat by Argentina, left the national team after 38 matches in charge, winning 21, drawing 10 and losing seven.

Former Egypt attacker Mido said in September the situation had “gone out of control” and called for officials to intervene.

Maher, 52, will take charge before Egypt’s Africa Cup of Nations qualifying matches against Malawi on November 13 and 17.
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.summary: Hossam Hassan has been sacked as Egypt's national team coach. The EFA said it had reviewed recent events and their “negative impact on the positive image and stability’ of the national team. Hassan's future had already been under scrutiny following a string of disputes.
