https://www.dw.com/en/never-again-holoca.title: 'Never Again!': Holocaust remembrance under pressure
https://www.dw.com/en/never-again-holoca.text:
Only a few Holocaust survivors remain who can share their stories firsthand. Meanwhile, voices calling for an end to what they describe as a "cult of guilt" are growing louder. How can Holocaust remembrance survive?

Young people pose inside a crematorium oven at the Buchenwald concentration camp memorial, laughing while they give the Nazi salute and take pictures of each other. "In a sense, they're trophies to post on social media for them to boast about — breaking the ultimate taboo," Jens-Christian Wagner, director of the Buchenwald and Mittelbau-Dora Memorials Foundation, told DW.

"Incidents like this have become more frequent in recent years. We have seen memorial trees planted in honor of concentration camp victims cut down. When something like this happens — and it happens regularly — I find it particularly despicable because, because it ultimately kills these people a second time," added Wagner.

Wagner is part of the curatorial team behind the exhibition "Never Again! Against Forgetting the Crimes of the Nazi Regime" in Bonn's Bundeskunsthalle, or the Art and Exhibition Hall of the Federal Republic of Germany. Wagner says that Holocaust remembrance is under pressure, and the subject of intensifying attacks.

Critics have dismissed remembrance as a "cult of guilt" or "national masochism." With right-wing populism on the rise and historical revisionism becoming more common, Wagner worries about how Germany will remember the victims murdered by the Nazi regime. He is also concerned about the future of democracy. And soon, there will be no Holocaust survivors left to tell the true story of what happened.

The new exhibition tackles this concern head-on with numerous works of art and historical artifacts.

"I hope that perhaps even some people who don't already believe it's important to confront Nazi crimes will find their way to the exhibition," Wagner says. Memorial sites also attract visitors who aren't necessarily convinced of the need to confront these parts of history. Many of them are students. "Let's not kid ourselves: When a teacher says 'We're going there,' it's always a mandatory visit."

For today's young people, the Nazi era seems like the distant past, Wagner explains. "When you tell them to remember something that their grandparents didn't even experience, it naturally feels like an emotional burden. They can practically see the finger being wagged at them, and that doesn't exactly encourage learning."

A two-hour lecture won't have much of an impact if pupils aren't even paying attention. Instead, Buchenwald organizes full-day programs that allow students to explore historical sources together and make sense of history for themselves.

The next step, Wagner says, is to show young people that this chapter of history isn't closed. Visitors are encouraged to make connections between the past and current events like migration, for example. "For the longest time, people have been discussing migration almost exclusively in terms of threats to public safety and crime. This broadly marginalizes certain groups — a mechanism that also worked for National Socialism."

Eva Umlauf knows firsthand what it means to experience exclusion in its most extreme form. She is a patron of the Bonn exhibition. Now, she's 83.

But in November 1944, she was just two years old when the Nazis deported her, her pregnant mother and her father from the Novaky labor camp in Slovakia to Auschwitz-Birkenau, the notorious Nazi concentration and extermination camp. She was saved from the gas chambers by mere days; the Nazis stopped using them as the Red Army advanced, hoping to hide evidence of their crimes.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The camp was liberated on January 27, 1945. Three months later, Eva's sister Nora was born. But her father, her mother's siblings and her grandparents were all murdered. Eva barely survived herself. She suffered from tuberculosis, rickets and whooping cough, as well as edema caused by starvation. "Forget about the child. She won't survive," a doctor told her mother. But he was wrong.

Her mother returned to what was then Czechoslovakia with her two daughters, settling in Trencin. Eva Umlauf has no conscious memories of Auschwitz, but she carries her family's trauma deep within her. Her mother never talked about what happened. Even so, Eva knew from an early age that she was a survivor. Her family rarely mentioned the camp by name, but one sentence came up again and again: "They stayed there." Eva knew that meant "they" were dead. And then, there was the number tattooed onto her arm: A26959.

Her mother taught her daughters not to draw attention to their Jewish identity — antisemitism was widespread throughout Czechoslovakia at the time. The small family managed to avoid harassment.

Eva wanted to become a pediatrician, so she studied medicine. In the 1960s, she met her future husband, Jakob, who had also survived the Holocaust. He was an architect, active in Munich's Jewish community. They married in 1966, and Eva moved to Germany. She could hardly have imagined that she would one day live in the country of the perpetrators. "I don't hate Germans," she says. "But I cannot forgive. How can you forgive the deaths of 6 million people?"

It was not until much later that she first spoke publicly about the horrors of her early childhood. In 2011, she delivered a commemorative speech in Auschwitz on the anniversary of the camp's liberation. Since 2025, she has served as chair of the International Auschwitz Committee. A heart attack in 2014 motivated her to write her first book. "I was in intensive care. I thought to myself: If I get out of here healthy, I'll write a book."

Her memoir, "The Number on Your Forearm is Blue Like Your Eyes," was first released in 2016. The English translation followed in 2024. Since its publication, hardly a day has passed without someone asking Eva Umlauf to share her story.

She is appalled by the disrespectful behavior of young people at former concentration camps and by growing ignorance about the Holocaust. Sometimes, people even ask if she's too old to have a tattoo. But she also recalls a young man on the Munich subway who noticed the number on her arm and told her: "I want to apologize to you for what my ancestors did to you."

Eva Umlauf never imagined that antisemitism would once again become so widespread in Europe and the United States. Nor did she expect the rise of Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party. "I go into schools. I'm so overwhelmed by the number of requests asking for my availability. And yet, the AfD is growing faster than I can reach students. It makes me think all this work is for nothing," she told DW.

Germany must never again fall under a right-wing dictatorship, she stresses. "'Never again' sounds nice, but all I can say is: It's happening again! Wouldn't 'Here We Go Again: Never Again' make a good title for the exhibition?"

She also shared her message to young people in the exhibition catalog, "Never Again": "You are not responsible for the crimes of your grandparents and great-grandparents. But you are responsible for the future. (…) You are the generation that will shape our world. Make it a place where everyone can grow up safely, regardless of their background, faith or skin color." She continues: "You don't have to be perfect. You just have to stay alert. Take care of your country."

The exhibition "Never Again! Against Forgetting the Crimes of the Nazi Regime" in the Bundeskunsthalle in Bonn runs through May 2, 2027.

This article was originally written in German.

Eva Umlauf's memoir, "The Number on Your Forearm is Blue Like Your Eyes," was first released in 2016

https://www.dw.com/en/poland-begins-two-.title: Poland begins two days of mourning over Krakow shooting
https://www.dw.com/en/poland-begins-two-.text:
Mourners left candles in Krakow's main market square to honor the victims of the attack. Police confirmed that the bodies found at the suspect's home were those of his parents and sister.

Poland began two days of mourning on Sunday, a day after killed six people and wounded 15 others were shot in Krakow's main market square.

The attack occurred in Main Square (Rynek Glowny) in the Old Town of Poland's second-largest city on Saturday. The area is a popular tourist attraction.

In addition to the six people killed in the square, three bodies found at the suspect's home were the bodies of his sister, mother and father, police said Sunday.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has labeled the attack an act of far-right "terrorism," but authorities have not given a possible motive.

Poland's national prosecutor's office said it had launched an investigation into the Saturday shooting, saying that it constituted a suspected "terrorist offense."

Mourners left candles in the square to pay tribute to the victims of the shooting. Black flags and Polish flags with black ribbons were also seen in the city.

The square remained partially sealed off on Sunday morning as authorities continued investigations.

The 24-year-old suspect, who was wearing military fatigues at the time of the attack, allegedly shot at people at random as he drove around the square.

He was wounded by police and is in critical condition in hospital.

Polish authorities say the man held right-wing extremist and ultranationalist views.

"Everything indicates that he was fascinated by far-right ideologies," Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said at a news conference.

A British national was among the dead, and among the wounded were citizens of Austria, the United Kingdom, Germany, Portugal and Russia, according to authorities.

Two police officers were wounded while confronting the suspect and are in hospital. Officials have launched an appeal for blood donations for one of the officers, who is in critical condition.

The Krakow Carriage Driver's Association told Polish news agency PAP that several horse-drawn carriage drivers were seriously injured in the shooting.

Police said on Sunday that three bodies found at the suspect's home were those of his sister, mother and father.

The family home is in the town of Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski, around 150 kilometers (93 miles) northeast of Krakow.

Police said that several firearms were seized from the apartment.

The suspect had no previous criminal record, according to Polish media reports.

He and his father were members of a shooting club.
https://www.dw.com/en/poland-begins-two-.summary: Police say bodies found at suspect's home were those of his parents and sister. Six people were killed and 15 others were wounded in the attack on Saturday. The attack occurred in the Old Town of Krakow's main market square. Mourners left candles in the square to honor the victims of the attack.

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-news-fried.title: Germany news: Friedrich Merz set to confirm presidential nominee
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-news-fried.text:
The executive committee of the German chancellor's CDU party is expected to finalize its nomination for the country's president. DW has more.

This is a roundup of the top stories from and about Germany on the weekend of Saturday, November 7, and Sunday, November 8, 2026:

Police in Berlin are still looking for a 13-year-old girl who disappeared on the way to school on Tuesday.

In a statement, Berlin police said they could not rule out that the girl, who has been identified as Lisa T., "has been the victim of a crime."

"Based on the current state of the investigation, it is assumed that the child did not leave her home environment voluntarily," police said.

Around 220 police officers were deployed in the Marzahn district of the German capital on Saturday, with a police spokesman saying that the search was time-consuming because of the large number of houses and parks in the area.

The search began on Friday, supported by sniffer dogs and a police helicopter.

Women on the executive boards of Germany's leading listed companies were earning almost as much on average as their male colleagues in 2025, a study by consultancy EY says.

According to the study, female board members at companies listed on the DAX, MDAX and SDAX indices, not including chief executives, earned an average of €2.20 million ($2.45 million) last year.

That is a rise of 2.4% from 2024.

Their male counterparts, on the other hand, saw a nearly 2% reduction in their pay down to €2.23 million, which reduced the pay gap from €121,000 to €26,000.

The study also found that there were more women serving on executive boards in 2025 than a year previously, with 101 female board members compared with 88 in 2024 and just 33 in 2013.

"Women on executive boards are no longer the exception. That is also reflected in salaries," said EY partner Jens Massmann.

The executive committee of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU) is scheduled to meet in the evening to finalize the party's nomination for the post of German president.

So far, Merz has declined to confirm widespread reports that his party will join with Bavarian allies, the Christian Social Union (CSU), in putting forward Bavarian parliamentary speaker Ilse Aignerfor the job, but he is expected to officially do so at the meeting.

The actual announcement of the choice of the conservative CDU/CSU bloc for a successor to President Frank-Walter Steinmeier will be made on Monday.

The new German head of state is to be chosen on January 30 by a special assembly, the Federal Convention, which comprises all 630 members of the Bundestag and an equal number of electors who represent the state parliaments.

Aigner, 61, who enjoys support from within all the major parties, is seen as have good chances of taking the largely ceremonial job as German head of state.

If she were to become president, she would become the first woman and the first CSU member to hold the position.

We are resuming our coverage of all things Germany after an overnight break.

On the agenda for today: a meeting of leaders from Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats, where the chancellor is expected to confirm that his party will join coalition partners in nominating Bavarian parliamentary speaker Ilse Aigner for the post of German president.

Ahead of the anniversary of the 1938 November pogroms on Monday, the head of the Anne Frank Zentrum in Berlin has warned that Holocaust denial is becoming more prevalent among young people.

And a survey has shown that most people in Germany are in favor of both a fuel price cap and a windfall tax on oil corporations.

Iranian opposition leader Reza Pahlavi on Saturday received a "Freedom Prize" in Frankfurt in the central German state of Hesse.

Some 18,000 people rallied to show support for Reza Pahlavi, according to a police statement.

The event was held at St Paul's Church. The building hosted the Germany's first-ever elected parliament in 1848-1849, known as the Frankfurt Assembly.

Pahlavi is the son of the last shah of Iran, Mohammed Reza Pahlavi, an autocrat who fled into exile after being deposed in a 1979 revolution.

The 1979 revolution was followed by the transformation of Iran into an Islamic republic and the consolidation of power around the Shiite Muslim clergy.

Pahlavi was handed the prize by the Friedrich Naumann Foundation, which is tied to the pro-business Free Democratic Party (FDP).

Read the full story here.

A man allegedly doused an 18-year-old with a flammable liquid and set him on fire in southwest Berlin.

According to a statement issued on Saturday by police in the German capital, the victim was hospitalized with burns.

The 18-year-old had been out with a 17-year-old female companion on Friday evening. An argument broke out with a 24-year-old man who allegedly sexually harassed the woman.

The suspect who was arrested by police reportedly poured flammable liquid over the younger man and set him on fire.

Police were initially unable to say how the fire was extinguished. "He was wearing a jacket," said a police spokesman.

Emergency services took the 18-year-old to hospital to be treated for burns on his hand and torso.

Chancellor Merz has declined to confirm media reports that his Christian Democrats (CDU) has agreed with its conservative ally, the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), on the CSU's Ilse Aigner as nomination for the next German president.

Merz said on Friday only that his party had agreed with the CSU to present its nomination on Monday.

According to media reports, Aigner, the current speaker of the Bavarian state parliament, would be put forward as a joint candidate of the three coalition parties — CDU, CSU and center-left Social Democrats (SPD) — as a successor to President Frank-Walter Steinmeier.

Merz said earlier this week he wanted to see a woman ​elected as president.

Aigner has also received strong verbal backing from some SPD and Green lawmakers.

If elected by the Federal Convention, which is made up of the lower house of parliament or Bundestag, along with representatives from the 16 federal states, Aigner  would ‌become Germany's ⁠first ⁠female head of state, and also the first CSU member to hold the position.

In his interview with papers of the Funke media group published on Saturday, Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said he soon expected a replacement for the French-German FCAS fighter jet project that fell flat this year.

Pistorius said he believed that an alternative would be decided on by the end of March 2027, adding that he was very interested in Germany's aviation industry playing a role in an such project.

He said there were "two options on the table."

One was "participation in the Global Combat Air Program (GCAP) of the British, Italians and Japanese," with discussions underway as to whether Germany's involvement could "lead to a long delay, which would barely be acceptable to all participants."

The second option, he said, was that the European aerospace company Airbus developed its own project with other European partners for the start of the 2040s.

In October, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham offered Chancellor Friedrich Merz the chance to become involved in the joint development of a new fighter jet within the GCAP program.

Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig has defended the right of young people to call for their rights in demonstrations, despite the violence that marred last weekend's Gen Z protests.

"The overwhelming majority of demonstrators were peaceful," she told the daily Neue Osnabrücker Zeitung.

"And it is young people's good right to demonstrate on the issues that concern them," she said, adding that she did not feel that the situation was equivalent to that in neighboring France, where recent protests have been accompanied by considerable rioting.

At the same time, she stressed that looting and violence toward security forces were "serious offenses," saying that she was already working on a law that would allow harsher penalties for attacks on police and other emergency personnel.

But Hubig spoke out against imposing a general ban on protests that have been planned in two weeks' time, saying that would send "a completely wrong signal."

"We are always expecting young people to become actively involved in politics," she said.

"It is the right of young people to take to the streets and call for better education and social justice."

Hubig is a member of the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), the junior partner in Germany's conservative-led coalition government.

Defense Minister Boris Pistorius has said he believes that the German armed forces, or Bundeswehr, will not need conscripts to achieve the necessary level of recruitment.

Pistorius told newspapers from the Funke media group that the Bundeswehr currently had some 190,000 members, the highest level in 13 years, meaning that voluntary recruitment measures were working.

"If this trajectory continues, we will have no problems with growth," he said, and there would not have be be "a discussion about conscription of whatever kind."

He said he understood the concerns of teenagers and young adults who recently protested against the idea of military conscription.

"But when people say at demonstrations, 'we don't want to die at the front or in war,' I can only say: We don't want that either," he said.

He said that was precisely the reason why strong armed forces were necessary "that can act as a deterrent so we don't get into a situation in the first place where we have to fight somewhere."

Pistorius also said the Bundeswehr, currently male-dominated, was seeking to employ more women, saying the armed forces would be "particularly strong if it represents the breadth of our society."

The city of Frankfurt am Main is bracing for another day of protests and traffic disruption on Saturday, with large numbers of Iranians expected to hold protests and counterprotests.

The demonstrations are being prompted by the appearance of exiled Iranian opposition politician Reza Pahlavi, who is to receive a peace prize in the name of Iran's people from the Friedrich Naumann Foundation, which is affiliated with the neoliberal Free Democrats (FDP).

Pahlavi, the son of Iran's last shah, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, under whose autocratic rule Iran was governed from 1941 to 1979, was expected to attend a large demonstration in the city's Ostpark and possibly speak there.

Barriers, loudspeaker towers and a stage have already been set up at the park, which is to be the final destination of a march by demonstration participants.

Counterprotests are also expected amid criticism of Pahlavi's presence by Iranian organizations, people held in prison under his father's rule and a number of leftist German parties.

The former German ambassador to the UN, Joachim Rücker, and the erstwhile justice minister, Brigitte Zypries, have also signed an open letter protesting the honor given to Pahlavi.

The last time Pahlavi visited Germany was in April, when he accused Germany and other European countries of standing by while the clerical regime in Iran violently clamped down on protesters.

Frankfurt also saw protests a week ago, with mostly peaceful Gen Z demonstrations calling for better living conditions and education hijacked in the evening by people wanting to loot and vandalize.

https://www.dw.com/en/india-delhi-chokes.title: India: Delhi chokes on most polluted Diwali eve in 10 years
https://www.dw.com/en/india-delhi-chokes.text:
Delhi was ranked as the world's most polluted major city on the eve of Diwali. Delhi's air pollution is expected to get worse in the coming days. DW has more.

Here's a roundup of headlines from across India on Saturday, November 7, and Sunday, November 8:

Activist Sonam Wangchuk has said he is the subject of a witch-hunt by the Ladakh Lieutenant Governor's office, which he accused of targeting him in a smear campaign for standing with the youth of the country and participating in protests.

"I am being continuously witch-hunted and defamed and our schools are being harassed in every possible way by the LG administration in Ladakh," said Wangchuk, who is a member of Leh Apex Body (LAB), a representative body of the people of Ladakh.

In a video message on Saturday to Indian President Droupadi Murmu, Wangchuk asked her to intervene, saying, "Madam President, for the last six years. We don't have rights like in the rest of the country or democracy."

In 2019, Ladakh lost the special status it shared with the former state of Jammu and Kashmir under Article 370 and became a separate Union Territory. The change meant that the Indian central government in New Delhi now directly governs the Himalayan region.

Since 2019, several political and civil society groups in Ladakh have been demanding greater autonomy and, in many cases, statehood.

Wangchuk said two social media pages, Ladakh Lens 1 and Ladakh Vision 1, surfaced on October 14 and that the former was allegedly created to defame him through "unfounded allegations," while the latter was aimed at "praising the Lieutenant Governor's work" in Ladakh.

The Ladakh administration has not responded to the allegations so far.

Wangchuk also accused the Ladakh administration of targeting institutes like his that have "earned national and international repute."

Earlier this month, the Ladakh administration directed the Himalayan Institute of Alternative Learning (HIAL), led by Wangchuk and his wife Gitanjali J. Angmo, to halt activities at its Phyang-based school until the Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh High Court issues further notice.

Wangchuk has questioned the approvals being demanded by the administration.

Delhi awoke Sunday morning enveloped in smog with poor visibility after the previous night saw the worst air quality for Diwali eve in 10 years.

India's Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) said the Indian capital had a "very poor" air quality index (AQI) of 362 on Saturday. The worst polluted pre-Diwali day was in 2016, when the AQI hit 404 on October 29, according to the CPCB.

The air quality is forecast to turn "severe" on Sunday, with Diwali celebrations adding to the pollution.

Swiss monitor IQAir, meanwhile, ranked Delhi as the world's worst polluted major city on Saturday.

While vehicular emissions and stubble burning in neighboring states of Punjab and Haryana are major contributors to air pollution, Diwali celebrations, which involve large-scale burning of firecrackers, add to the pollution in the city.

The government had already ordered schools in and ​around Delhi to offer online classes, and ​encouraged people to work from home ahead of ⁠the Hindu festival of light.

Hello, we are back again with all the news from India.

Diwali celebrations are in full swing, with cities lit up by colourful lights and social media feeds awash with pictures of people dressed up for glamorous Diwali parties.

In the capital, however, like every year, the toxic air continues to dampen the mood. This year, Delhi saw the worst air on Diwali eve in 10 years.

Up in the north, activist Sonam Wangchuk has alleged that he was being continuously witch-hunted by the Ladakh administration.

Stay tuned as we bring you more updates from India through the day.

Indian Prime Minister Nardendra Modi extended Diwali greeting to the nation in a video on X.

He said he would celebrate the festival with soldiers, as he does every year.

Sanitation workers in state capital Bhopal ended their indefinite strike after three days following late-night talks with Chief Minister Mohan Yadav, according to Indian news agency Press Trust of India.

According to the sanitation workers' union, the breakthrough came after the state government agreed to initiate the regularization process for workers employed for 25 days a month, a move which will allow a pay hike.

According to local media, the sanitation workers had four major demands: a pay rise, compassionate appointments, regularization of jobs and an end to the short-term gig worker contract system. Their primary demand is an increase in the monthly wage from Rs 10,500 (about $111) to Rs 25,000.

The protest had left Bhopal, which was named the cleanest state capital in India in 2023, littered with heaps of uncollected garbage.

The workers claimed that more than 100,000 workers participated in the agitation across Madhya Pradesh.

One of India’s most successful fast bowlers, Mohammed Shami, has announced his retirement from Test cricket.

The move brings his 13-year career to an end, but he will continue to play white ball formats.

The 36-year-old cricketer announced in an Instagram video that he was ending his career in whites.

"I am bidding farewell to the white jersey, but never to the memories associated with it. When I wore India's Test jersey for the first time, I had only one dream — to do something for my country. Since then, every wicket, every struggle, every injury, and every comeback has taught me something," Shami said.

Shami made his Test debut against the West Indies at the Eden Gardens on November 6, 2013. He finished with 229 wickets at an average of 27.71, including six five-wicket hauls.

His international red ball journey spans 229 wickets from 64 matches, making him the sixth most successful pacer in Tests for the country behind Kapil Dev (434), Zaheer Khan, Ishant Sharma (both 311), Javagal Srinath (236), Jasprit Bumrah (234).

Shami last played for India in Tests in the World Test Championship final against Australia at The Oval in 2023.

Since then, injuries have disrupted his career, but he remained an important part of India's white-ball setup.

Shami clarified that his retirement would not mark the end of his playing career. He said he would continue to play white-ball cricket and could also turn out in four-day matches occasionally.

Social media platform X said that police orders it received to remove online accounts of two of India's most ​prominent free speech groups were fake.

Lawyers representing X told the court that someone impersonating Delhi police had sent the emails.

X received orders through its online reporting form in the name of a ​senior Delhi police officer seeking removal of the online accounts of free speech groups, the Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) and the Software Freedom Law Centre, ⁠India (SFLC.in).

The orders claimed the groups had defamed the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, parent organization of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

After an internal investigation, the social media company's lawyers on Friday told the Delhi High Court that, "It ​turns out this was somebody playing an impostor, somebody impersonating Delhi police who has sent this."

The orders had sparked an uproar on social media this week and were challenged for their legality by Amnesty and India's main opposition party.

The Supreme Court of India on Friday said that vehicular pollution is a major contributor to the deteriorating air quality in Delhi and questioned the effectiveness of the government's measures to curb it.

The bench, comprising Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, opened the proceedings with a jibe saying, "I hope you all are enjoying the weather in Delhi."

This week, Delhi's Air Quality Index (AQI) has remained above the "hazardous" 300 mark.

Air quality in the capital regularly plummets at the outset of winter, as weather conditions help trap pollutants.

"A major cause of the pollution is vehicular pollution. Look at the roads in Delhi, look at the roads connecting Delhi to the NCR (the National Capital Region)… the kind of bumper-to-bumper traffic… that's the major cause," the CJI said.

The court examined the steps taken by the government to control the rising levels of air pollution.

Expressing concerns over the failure of measures to curb air pollution in Delhi over the years, the court said, "To think we can achieve air quality of less than 100 AQI in Delhi during winters is utopian when 'very poor' and 'severe' have become the new normal."

On stubble burning, the court said farmers should be given economic incentives and practical alternatives.

The court also encouraged responsible celebrations during festivals, particularly Diwali, where firecrackers being set off adds to the air pollution.

"Why don't we revert to our original customs?" the CJI said, adding celebrations should be accompanied by a sense of responsibility towards the environment.

https://www.dw.com/en/poland-gunman-kill.title: Poland: Gunman kills 6 in Krakow main square, police say
https://www.dw.com/en/poland-gunman-kill.text:
A suspect who fired from a car killed at least six people, including a British tourist, in Krakow's main market square. Officials said the man was fascinated with "radical" and "far-right" ideologies.

At least six people were killed and 16 injured in a shooting on the main market square in the southern Polish city of Krakow on Saturday, officials said.

The suspect, a 25-year-old Polish man who allegedly acted alone, was wounded during an exchange of fire with police, authorities said.

"Until now in Poland we haven't had such drastic cases of terrorism," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told reporters in Krakow.

"That's what we have to call this cruel attack on people's lives here in Krakow," he added.

The gunman aimed at random people as he drove through the city's main square, which is a popular tourist attraction.

"At around 3 p.m. (1400 GMT), a man who had driven into the market square in a car began shooting at random people from inside the vehicle," police said on X, adding officers were among the wounded.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"The perpetrator was shot by police ‌officers and is currently being ‌transported ​to a hospital," police said. Authorities later clarified that the man drove to multiple spots in the square and opened fire at each with an automatic weapon.

Later Saturday evening, Polish police chief Marek Boron said a British citizen was among those killed.

"There are six fatalities: four women and two men; three Polish women, one British national, and two people who have not yet been identified," Boron told reporters.

Krakow police had earlier said that five of the 16 people injured in the shooting were non-Polish nationals. An Interior Ministry spokesperson confirmed that they came from Austria, Germany, Portugal, Russia and Britain.

On Saturday night, Tusk said that the bodies of two women and a man were found in the suspected shooter's home by police.

There was "much to suggest that they are members of the [suspect's] immediate family."

The residence is located in Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski, a city about 150 kilometers (93 miles) northeast of Krakow.

"We have the next acts of this tragedy," Tusk told reporters.

Polish Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said that the suspect, whom he declined to identify, was "fascinated by far-right ideologies" and held "ultranationalistic" and "very radical" views.

The man wore military-style fatigues and a bulletproof vest and used a long gun in the attack, said Katarzyna Cislo, a spokesperson for the Krakow police,

Numerous other weapons and ammunition were found in the suspected gunman's car.

Prime Minister Tusk posted on X that police were investigating the attack and called it a "tragic" incident.

Tusk later said Poland would observe two days of mourning for the victims of the shooting.

Polish President Karol Nawrocki wrote on X that his thoughts were with the victims and wounded, as well as their families.

The European Union's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said the shooting was a tragedy that will be felt far beyond Poland, adding that "Poland does not stand alone."

"I am deeply saddened by the events in Krakow. My thoughts are with the victims and their families," German Chancellor Friedrich Merz wrote on X, adding that "Germany stands alongside Poland as a friend and partner during these difficult times."

Krakow is located about 250 kilometers (155 miles) from Warsaw, the capital of Poland.

With a population of over 800,000, Krakow is Poland's second-largest city, as well as a popular tourist destination.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmzx.title: Government 'looking seriously' at banning under-16s from Vinted and eBay
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmzx.text:
Vinted and eBay could be included in the list of platforms set to be banned for under-16s, the culture secretary has said.

Lisa Nandy said the government was "looking seriously" at including the retailing websites in the social media ban "in order to keep children safe".

The UK's social media ban for those under the age of 16 is set to come into force in March next year, with children barred from accessing platforms such as Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat.

In response, eBay said it was looking forward to "understanding more and continuing to work constructively with the government". Vinted has not responded to requests for comment.

Asked on the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg if the government was looking to ban under-16s from Vinted and eBay, Nandy said: "We are looking seriously at doing so in order to keep children safe."

It came after the Sunday Times reported that the UK's social media ban was being expanded to include the platforms, which are popular for selling second-hand goods.

The newspaper said the move was over fears that messaging functions allowed strangers to groom children. It suggested similar reselling platforms, Depop and Facebook Marketplace, would also be included in the list of banned sites.

Businesses and individuals sell a host of goods on eBay, which has been a major global player in the online reselling market for years. The platform states on its website that it currently requires all of its members to be over 18 years old because listings involve "entering into a contract".

Vinted also says its users need to be at least 18 years old. The site, which mostly sees users buy and sell unwanted clothes and other fashion items, has grown rapidly in recent times to reach 17 million UK users.

An eBay spokesperson said the company was "focused on providing a trusted and safe marketplace experience for our millions of customers".

"While the details of the proposed legislation are not yet clear, we look forward to understanding more and continuing to work constructively with the government," they added in a statement.

The government announced it would ban under-16s accessing social media in June this year, with children prevented from accessing 10 of the biggest platforms.

YouTube will also be banned for under-16s, but YouTube Kids - a version of the video-sharing app designed to be safe for children - will not be included.

A complete list of affected platforms has not yet been released, but the government said it would cover those "whose purpose is to enable social interaction and which allow users to post material".

That means platforms which have livestreaming or features that enable the potential for strangers to contact children will also be restricted, which includes gaming sites.

It does not mean that Roblox, the biggest gaming site in the UK for eight to 12-year-olds for example, will be banned for under-16s. However, certain features such as its chat function will be restricted.

The UK's ban comes after a similar one was introduced in Australia last year.

Many children there have found ways to get round it, but the UK has said it intends to take a tougher approach.

In recent weeks, attention has turned to how such a ban would be enforced.

Last month, the communications regulator Ofcom set out its recommendations for the most effective ways to identify which of the UK's millions of social media users are aged over 16.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c209.title: How cleaning up the air is speeding up global warming - and revealing a bigger problem
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c209.text:
This July, during Britain's record-breaking hot summer, a curious row broke out on X over climate science.

Reform's deputy leader Richard Tice shared a Telegraph article headlined: "Heatwaves caused by fall in pollution." He said cleaner air, rather than carbon dioxide, was behind higher temperatures and claimed the public had been "gaslit".

He was wrong to suggest that carbon dioxide is not the primary driver of global warming. But the science he was distorting is real - and much more interesting than his original claim.

The fossil fuels that we've been burning for more than a century produce two very different kinds of pollution. As is well known, carbon dioxide warms the Earth. But less well-known is sulphur pollution, which forms vast numbers of tiny particles in the air and reflects sunlight back into space, partly counteracting the warming effect of carbon.

Thanks to clean-air policies around the world - like the US's Acid Rain Program in the early 1990s, that reduced gas pollution from power plants - sulphur emissions are falling sharply while carbon dioxide emissions remain near record highs.

Scientists increasingly believe the loss of that cooling effect is slightly speeding up global warming.

The past three years were the three warmest ever recorded, and the Met Office says 2027 is "very likely" to replace 2024 as the warmest year on record.

And away from social media, the argument over Tice's tweet raised an even more interesting - and worrying - question. Is it possible that our planet is actually more sensitive to greenhouse gases than we imagined?

And if so, might the climate be changing more rapidly than we feared?

Global temperatures jump around naturally from year to year. El Niño, for example, a natural warming of the Pacific Ocean, can temporarily push them higher. So a run of record hot years does not necessarily mean the underlying rate of global warming has increased.

Reto Knutti and his team at ETH Zurich have tried to strip out the effects of El Niño and other natural fluctuations to reveal the underlying trend.

"It's pretty clear that the rate of warming has accelerated," says Knutti, a professor of climate physics at the Swiss university and a former co-ordinating lead author for the IPCC - the UN-backed body that produces the world's most authoritative assessments of climate science.

A separate study published this year reached a similar conclusion after accounting for several major natural influences.

And it seems aerosols are playing a role.

Burning coal and oil releases sulphur dioxide, which forms tiny particles known as sulphate aerosols. These particles are bright and reflect some sunlight before it can reach and warm the planet's surface.

You've probably heard the greenhouse analogy used to explain global warming. Gases like carbon dioxide make it harder for heat to escape from the Earth, rather like the glass windows of a greenhouse.

Well, sulphur pollution acts a bit like dust on the greenhouse windows. The more dust that gathers on those windows, the less sunlight gets inside, and the slower the greenhouse heats up in the first place.

Dr Øivind Hodnebrog, a principal researcher at Cicero, the Norwegian climate research institute, has studied how falling aerosol pollution affects the climate. "Sulphate aerosols, they are really small particles, but they are bright particles," he says.

As well as reflecting sunlight, aerosols also cool the planet by changing the formation of clouds. Aerosols act like tiny seeds around which water vapour can condense, making some clouds brighter or longer-lived. Pollution from ships can even create bright trails through marine clouds visible from space. So more aerosols mean brighter clouds and more reflection, and so less warming.

But sulphur pollution also damages human health (it can get into our lungs and make it harder to breathe), and causes acid rain, which can destroy forests and kill fish - and so countries have spent decades cutting it. Emissions have fallen sharply in Europe, North America and China, while new rules have also reduced sulphur pollution from shipping.

In our greenhouse analogy, it's as if we've wiped some of the dust away from the windows of the greenhouse, allowing in more sunlight.

And while carbon dioxide remains in the climate system for centuries, sulphate aerosols survive in the atmosphere for just days or weeks. So when sulphur emissions fall, their cooling effect disappears almost immediately.

The effect is strongest where sulphur pollution has fallen fastest. One study estimates it has added around half a degree to summer warming in western-central Europe since 1980.

Prof Piers Forster, a climate scientist at the University of Leeds and another senior author of the IPCC's most recent assessment, estimates that declining aerosol pollution may now be adding around 0.05C to 0.1C of warming per decade.

But aerosols can only explain part of the recent acceleration in warming. Greenhouse gases remain much more important.

Forster estimates they are currently adding around 0.2C of warming globally per decade. "It is a very significant contribution," he says of the aerosol effect, "but it is not as important as the greenhouse gas contribution by quite a long way."

"The aerosols have masked some of the greenhouse gas warming from earlier," is how Hodnebrog explains it.

"Masked" - that's an interesting word he uses. What he means is cleaner air is not causing the underlying warming; it is removing some of the cooling that had been holding that warming back.

So if cleaner air is only responsible for part of the recent acceleration in global warming, what else is at work?

To see what else might be going on, scientists zoom out and look at the Earth as a whole: how much energy it absorbs from the Sun, and how much heat it loses back into space.

Scientists call the difference Earth's energy imbalance.

Cleaner air is part of that picture. Fewer sulphate particles mean less sunlight is reflected away - in our greenhouse analogy, the windows are cleaner.

For a long time, the Earth has been absorbing more energy than it loses. That surplus is what warms the planet. And Knutti says that imbalance has roughly tripled over the past two decades - although the precise increase depends on which years are compared.

Greenhouse gases principally work by making it harder for heat to escape out into space. That's what we're all familiar with. But when you look at Earth's energy imbalance, you find that there's also more sunlight getting in (and therefore more heat that can be absorbed).

So what else might be letting more sunlight in?

Much of that change appears to involve something we have already encountered in this story: clouds. We saw how sulphur pollution can make some clouds brighter and longer-lived, reflecting more sunlight away. But global warming itself can also change clouds. As some parts of the ocean warm, low cloud cover can diminish. That matters because clouds are bright, while the ocean beneath them is dark. Remove some cloud and more sunlight reaches the sea, where much of it is absorbed as heat.

That can create a feedback: warming reduces some cloud cover, which allows more sunlight in, which produces still more warming.

And the oceans are certainly heating up. The World Meteorological Organization says the oceans have warmed more than twice as fast over the past two decades than they did between 1960 and 2005.

Dr Paulo Ceppi, a climate physicist at Imperial College London, says his research suggests this feedback loop between climate change and clouds is more important than sulphur pollution in explaining the recent decline in low clouds.

But there's still lots of uncertainty. Scientists say the impacts of cleaner air, natural variations and the effects of warming itself are all tangled together. And, when I asked Knutti how much of the cloud change came from each, his answer was simple: "We don't know."

And this is where the story takes an even more worrying turn.

That uncertainty matters because clouds are one of the hardest things to represent in the computer simulations scientists use to project future warming. Some models show more warming than others for the same amount of greenhouse gas emissions.

Scientists call this variability "climate sensitivity": how much the climate responds to gases like carbon dioxide.

And the recent observations give Knutti and his colleagues a new way to test those models. They found that models which best predicted the recent warming, as well as the rise in the Earth's energy imbalance, are also the ones with a more sensitive climate.

In other words, the models that predict more warming are looking like the most accurate.

His team's analysis suggests that the same emissions could produce about 25% more warming than we previously thought.

And a study published in the journal Science last year points in a similar direction. Models which projected relatively little warming struggled most to reproduce the observed rise in Earth's energy imbalance.

Under policies governments currently have in place, the world is estimated to be heading for around 2.8C of warming by the end of the century. Forster says that if this new evidence proves correct, the same broad emissions path could instead produce warming closer to 3.5C.

It sounds serious - but there are important reasons for caution.

Warming appears to have accelerated, but Forster says that does not mean it will keep doing so. He points out that the recent observations that underpin these estimates cover a relatively short period.

"We have to be very cautious of how we go about interpreting observations that last for one or two decades," he says.

The satellite record is short, natural variations are large, and these new studies do not overturn previous estimates.

But still, some scientists are alarmed.

So - is cleaning up the air making global warming worse?

In one narrow sense, yes. Removing sulphate pollution takes away some of the cooling that had been counteracting greenhouse warming. That really has contributed to the recent acceleration. But cleaner air has not caused climate change.

The aerosol story may help explain part of that acceleration. But the wider evidence raises a more worrying possibility: that the climate responds more strongly to greenhouse gases than central estimates have assumed.

If that's correct, the same emissions could produce more warming than we expected. Climate risks increase with every fraction of a degree of warming, with the potential for more severe heatwaves, floods, droughts, and wildfires as temperatures rise.

Some of the science we have explored here is complex and important questions remain unresolved. But on the central point, the science is clear: the more greenhouse gases we emit, the warmer the planet will become.

And, if the climate really is more sensitive than previously thought, cutting emissions quickly becomes even more important.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/08/nx-s1-602.title: A desert stirs to life: Chile's Atacama erupts in its biggest floral display in decades
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/08/nx-s1-602.author: John Bartlett
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/08/nx-s1-602.text:
A field of colorful wildflowers blankets the Atacama Desert in northern Chile, transforming the world's driest non-polar desert into a vibrant landscape during the rare flowering desert phenomenon, known locally as the Desierto Florido, or Desert Bloom.

COPIAPÓ, Chile — A vast swathe of Chile's Atacama Desert is now a patchwork of pinks, yellows, lilacs and purples stretching across the craggy desert floor as far as the eye can see.

This winter, heavy rains brought by the El Niño super cycle caused flash floods in the Atacama Desert, with some areas receiving the heaviest rainfall since records began in the 1950s.

Floodwaters in July and August destroyed or damaged dozens of homes, forcing hundreds of people to evacuate.

A field of wildflowers blooms across Chile's Atacama Desert during the rare flowering phenomenon known as Desierto Florido, or Desert Bloom, triggered by unusually heavy rainfall that awakens dormant seeds. The brief blooms transform the world's driest nonpolar desert into a landscape of pink, purple, yellow and white. Huasco, Chile, Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026.

But the floral bloom that followed has been the largest and most colorful in 30 years — and perhaps ever.

The rainwater penetrated deeper into the parched ground than it has in decades, allowing millions of seeds, bulbs and tubers to sprout above the surface. Many had lain dormant for decades under the sand.

More than 200 species are in flower. A month ago, the first plants to emerge created a pale-yellow haze. This was followed by a soft purple hue as other bulbs germinated. Now, almost every indentation and crevice in the desert is streaked with color.

Scientists studying the phenomenon say there are patches of desert in bloom where flowers have never previously been recorded, suggesting that bulbs have remained dormant there since before the phenomenon was first studied in detail in 1997.

Moisés Grimberg has served as the administrator of Llanos de Challe National Park for the past three years and has worked in protected area management for 18 years. His work focuses on protecting the flora, fauna, and fragile ecosystems of the coastal desert near Huasco, Chile, while also managing the influx of tourists during the rare flowering desert phenomenon, known locally as the Desierto Florido. Huasco, Chile, on Monday October 19, 2026. Tamara Merino for NPR.

"This is a natural seed bank, a dormant archive that becomes a living one with the rains," says Moisés Grimberg, the administrator of Llanos de Challe National Park.

"But it's a race against time — this brief biological window allows these species to complete their life cycle, which lasts roughly two to three months."

Llanos de Challe is a 113,000-acre national park along the arid coastline, where waves lap at pristine white sand beaches.

Grimberg says the park normally receives about 10,000 visitors a year. But with the desert in bloom, 15,000 tourists have visited over the last few weeks alone.

Across the desert, the roads are lined with tourists' cars. According to Chile's national tourism board, the region is expected to see around 300,000 overnight trips during the two months the desert is in bloom.

Among the star attractions are the nectar-filled, crimson flowers of the garra de león, with their long tails of flame-like green leaves. This endemic flower is coaxed out of dormancy by the rains and grows along just a few miles of this stretch of coastline in the Atacama Desert — nowhere else in the world.

A Garra de León flower blooms in the Atacama Desert of northern Chile during the rare flowering desert phenomenon, known locally as the Desierto Florido. This striking native flower is known for its vibrant red petals and is one of the region's rare and emblematic desert species. Canto del Agua, Chile, on Tuesday October 20, 2026. Tamara Merino for NPR.

This bloom occurs every few years in what is the driest nonpolar desert on Earth. But scientists say the phenomenon is becoming more frequent as changes in the climate bring unseasonal rains.

The phenomenon gives rise to a thriving, transient ecosystem, with insects hatching and attracting lizards and bats, as well as larger mammals such as the guanaco.

A guanaco stands amid a carpet of Malvilla and Pata de Guanaco wildflowers during the rare flowering desert phenomenon, known locally as the Desierto Florido, in the Atacama Desert of northern Chile. Canto del Agua, Chile, on Tuesday October 20, 2026.

Biologists from INIA, Chile's national seed bank, are collecting specimens to analyze in their laboratory before the brief flowering season ends.

"It's very exciting," said Ana Sandoval as she delicately shook seeds free from their casings to take back to INIA's taxonomist at its base in northern Chile.

"It's as if the desert is awakening. Sometimes people think it's an empty, arid place, devoid of life, but actually our desert is just waiting for the right conditions, and any precipitation, to awaken it."

The seed bank wants to preserve the genetic material and unique adaptations each plant has developed to survive the extreme, arid conditions.

Sandoval points out different ways plants harvest water as she walks. Some leaves are covered in fine hairs; others have a thick waxy cuticle.

A national park dedicated to the desert bloom was created in June 2023 to protect a 141,000-acre area where flowers spring up every few years. Now local authorities want to go further.

A cactus, which survives year-round despite the desert's extreme temperatures, stands amid a carpet of Malvilla and Pata de Guanaco wildflowers during the rare flowering desert phenomenon, known locally as the Desierto Florido, in the Atacama Desert of northern Chile. Canto del Agua, Chile.

Miguel Vargas, the governor of the Atacama region, is beginning the process of seeking UNESCO World Heritage recognition for the desert bloom phenomenon.

"This represents a tremendous opportunity to strengthen special interest tourism and diversify our regional economy, which is currently heavily reliant on mining," he said. "Receiving UNESCO recognition would put the Atacama region on the world stage."

A couple of tourists visits the Atacama Desert during the rare flowering desert phenomenon, known locally as the Desierto Florido, in northern Chile. Huasco, Chile, on Monday October 19, 2026.

Vargas hopes this will become Chile's eighth World Heritage site within a couple of years.

This year, the bloom is projected to last until mid-November.

As the flowers begin to fade, scientists will be left with two tantalising questions: was this the Atacama Desert's largest flowering event on record, and might closer examination reveal any previously unknown species among the millions of plants?

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/08/nx-s1-601.title: In Maine, a new approach to practicing medicine in the sky
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/08/nx-s1-601.author: Elaine Appleton-Grant
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/08/nx-s1-601.text:
Elaine Appleton-Grant

Flight nurse Denise Saucier begins loading a stretcher and equipment into a helicopter on the tarmac at LifeFlight of Maine's Bangor headquarters. It takes only a few minutes for the crew to prepare for takeoff.

Clipboard in hand, pilot Will Bradbury stands near a helicopter at LifeFlight of Maine's Bangor headquarters. He's running down emergency landing tips with his crew.

"If we need to get out quickly because of smoke or fire, just watch the terrain so that you're not walking uphill into the rotors," he reminds flight nurse Denise Saucier and paramedic Brian Merklin.

The team is getting ready to take off on a medical transport flight. Saucier folds herself into the compact helicopter. She's worked for the air ambulance service for seven years and still calls it a dream job.

Dream job or not, the life of a flight clinician is hard and, given the headwinds slamming rural healthcare, getting harder.

Pilot Will Bradbury runs down emergency landing tips with his crew ahead of a flight from LifeFlight of Maine's Bangor headquarters.

Since 2015, demand for medical flights in Maine has doubled. In 2025, LifeFlight crews flew 3,031 flights, more than one every three hours. This year, demand is up another 10%.

Nationwide, air medical services are filling the gaps left behind as rural hospitals close, convert to outpatient-only rural emergency hospitals, or stop offering unprofitable services like labor and delivery.

And, as Medicaid cuts estimated by the Congressional Budget Office at $911 billion over ten years take effect, it's going to get worse. Hundreds more rural hospitals or maternity departments are at immediate risk of closing. With every closure, medical care gets further away.

And, increasingly, ground ambulance stations, many of which are also struggling to keep their doors open, can't meet the need. That leaves flight clinicians like Saucier and Merklin seeing more patients every day.

"We're seeing this across the board. The need for air medical services is increasing year over year," says Nicholas George. He runs the ETHOS Database, a national tracking system for air medical programs.

When the rural health care system breaks, EMS — on the ground and, increasingly, in the air — is the backstop.

For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.

Every week or two, Saucier finds herself on a flight to one of Maine's thousands of islands. Occasionally, crews even land in the state's vast forests and mountains, then take snowmobiles to reach patients.

But "scene calls" to roadside — or trailside — accidents are less than 10% of LifeFlight's transports. (They're a higher percentage in urban areas.)

Most are interfacility transports, like today's. They'll stabilize a patient at a small, local hospital and fly them to a larger, better resourced one.

Saucier glances out the window for hazards. The view still reminds her of the role the organization plays in Maine, one of the country's most rural states.

"You go so long of a distance without seeing any houses, any roads," Saucier says. "It really hits home how rural Maine is and how necessary EMS is in the state."

And the pressure is on air ambulances as ground services in Maine are increasingly strained. The system is so fragmented that patients can fall through the cracks. Last year, a woman in a small northern Maine town died while the county dispatch center called 10 ambulance services. None responded.

Pilot Will Bradbury guides the helicopter during a flight over rural Maine (right). The view out the window includes some of the many lakes near Bangor (left).

Air ambulance services, though, come with unique challenges, particularly since the COVID-19 pandemic. It's been difficult to retain staff with the medical expertise to treat everything from heart attacks to injuries to fragile newborns, and who can stick with the demanding job without burning out.

Almost a quarter of ground-based EMS workers leaves the field every year. While there's no comprehensive staffing data for air medical services, flight clinicians face a slew of unique stresses, including dangerous conditions; long shifts and unpredictable hours; ever-increasing training and certification requirements; and significant mental health burdens. And then there's the pay, which is low throughout emergency medical services.

For years, LifeFlight retained only 60% to 70% of its workers, says CEO Joe Kellner.

"This is a really hard job," Kellner says. "By their job description, they are seeing people on their worst day, over and over again."

A specialty ambulance designed to transport newborns who need critical care. Northern Light is one of Maine's large hospital systems; it works in partnership with LifeFlight of Maine. By the end of the year, Maine will have lost 12 of its labor and delivery departments, causing a statewide shortage of birthing centers.

This year, for the first time in nine years, LifeFlight is nearly fully staffed. One of the nation's handful of independent nonprofit air medical companies, LifeFlight has taken an innovative approach to the problems that plague the industry, including a combination of better training, higher pay and in-house mental health support.

Mike Abernethy, an EMS expert and retired emergency medicine professor at the University of Wisconsin, considers the company one of a handful of model programs for the industry. LifeFlight of Maine is a nonprofit, unlike much of the industry, which is dominated by for-profit businesses with reputations for charging exorbitant prices.

"There's just absolutely no comparison in the aviation and medical quality of these programs" versus an average for-profit air medical business, Abernethy argues.

When Kellner, a paramedic himself, became CEO in 2023, he began addressing the recruitment and retention problems. What LifeFlight calls the "Critical Care Academy," a six- to eight-month orientation program, is intended to address both issues.

Emergency critical care advances quickly. So most clinicians need regular education, both to remain successful on the job and to get hired in the first place.

Seen through the window of a control room, Chuck Hogan, LifeFlight of Maine's chief clinical officer, (left) stands next to a "breathing, bleeding" dummy in a fake hospital room. He's preparing for a simulation of an emergency, designed to test clinicians' skills.

On another day at headquarters, four instructors sit in a claustrophobic control room. Through a window looking into what appears to be a hospital room, paramedics Daniel Horne and Brad Alleger are undergoing an annual skills assessment, a simulation of a real-life medical crisis.

Dr. Dave Saquet turns on a mic and coughs. "It's hard to breathe," he whispers urgently. "It hurts everywhere."

His voice seems to be coming from the patient — a breathing, bleeding mannequin lying on a hospital bed.

"What happened to you?" Horne asks.

"My house was on fire," Saquet chokes out.

A wall monitor displays the patient's vital signs — which Saquet is manipulating on his laptop.

Medics and nurses here do simulations often, both to pass the Critical Care Academy, and also to stay up to date on occasional but critical events, like emergency births, newborn resuscitation, and burns. Before the assessment ends, the paramedics will have tried and failed to intubate the patient. After that "failure," they performed an emergency procedure to enable breathing, switching from the mannequin to a pig trachea.

Because it's hard to find recruits qualified enough for the rigorous training, the company also started a mentorship program for people considering applying. Some even attend the academy, gaining skills even if they'll never work for LifeFlight.

Success comes slowly: Recently, LifeFlight hired one of last year's mentees.

Kellner instituted an unusual change that he says even nurses endorse: LifeFlight raised paramedics' pay to match flight nurses' compensation. Industrywide, paramedics make less. That keeps costs down, which is why pay equity is rare. Kellner believes the change has helped with recruitment.

Another experiment: LifeFlight hired a full-time mental-health counselor.

EMS workers' rates of post-traumatic stress injury, anxiety and depression are more thanfive times higher than the average American's.

"That has led people to leave this profession," Kellner says.

That was true for paramedic Brian Merklin, who was working for a different service in Nevada during the pandemic.

"We got hit really hard," he says. "The crews were just flying nonstop. We did four-day shifts, so for 96 hours we were just going, going, going."

About a third of the staff quit, he says. "They were getting air medical service plus COVID, right in the teeth."

Eventually, Merklin too needed a break. He left the profession for a few years. Then, when he felt the urge to fly again, he found LifeFlight.

A LifeFlight of Maine helicopter and crew at the company's base at Bangor International Airport in Maine.

The helicopter, which took off from Bangor, lands on a community hospital's rooftop helipad. Merklin and Saucier hurry to the patient's side. Most LifeFlight patients are unconscious or too ill to consent to share their stories, so the details are private. The injuries are shocking. If this patient doesn't get to a trauma center quickly, they might die.

Merklin and Saucier are unfazed.

But it's this kind of incessant trauma exposure that makes mental health support for first responders so invaluable.

Merklin serves on a peer support team.

"There's a lot of lip service paid … to the cost to your mental health in this profession. But this is the only place I have ever worked that actually provided support," he says. "I would love to see it take hold in other areas."

If counseling keeps two or three people from leaving, it's a wise investment, Kellner argues: "The cost of training somebody new into our organization is about $100,000."

As both air and ground EMS become even more essential, the task is to recruit and keep more people like Merklin and Saucier.

Because, if hundreds more hospitals do close, highly trained EMS workers may be the only people standing between patients dying and getting the care they need.

Elaine Appleton Grant's reporting was supported by the National Institute for Health Care Management.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/08/nx-s1-539.title: Climate change is altering the colors we see in the world: an illustrated journey
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/08/nx-s1-539.author: Connie Hanzhang Jin
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/08/nx-s1-539.text:
Imagine the bright tones of coral under the sea. What do you see? What colors come to mind?

One of the ways that climate change will alter — or has already altered — our world is by shifting the familiar colors of nature. When warming ocean waters bleach the vibrant colors of coral to white, that’s one example.

“Many young scientists who are working on coral reefs don’t realize that what they’re seeing is vastly degraded,” says Anya Salih, a scientist who has studied coral reefs and their fluorescent colors for decades. “It’s often hard to perceive how it was to what it is now.”

This change of color isn’t just aesthetic. For coral, bleaching leaves them vulnerable to disease and other stressors that can lead to death. In other situations, these color changes have more complex impacts, ones that scientists are still trying to understand.

An illustrated journey

A shifting landscape in the Arctic

Every summer, massive climate-driven wildfires spread soot across huge swaths of the Arctic, covering the ice in a blanket of black particles. Soot pollution from oil and gas operations, as well as commercial shipping and increased tourism, contributes to the problem at both poles.

The dark particles coat white snow and soak up heat from the sun, exacerbating melting that was already happening more quickly because of climate change. Increased melting in the Arctic leads to sea level rise, which threatens communities across the world. And the soot itself pollutes the air and water it seeps into.

“We know that the high northern latitudes are warming faster than the rest of the planet,” says Douglas Morton, an Earth scientist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center. These changes are shifting the colors of the Arctic landscape.

Source: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration

Beyond the Arctic ice at the pole, farther south, lie vast regions of permafrost: soil that has remained frozen for years.

But the warming climate is causing permafrost to thaw.

And in some places, crack and collapse.

As permafrost thaws deeper into the soil, nutrients become more available and plants can grow deeper roots. These conditions can stimulate plant growth and enable larger vegetation like trees to gain a foothold, turning the landscape greener.

These established plants also trap snow in the winter, insulating the plants from the cold and promoting further plant growth.

And in some places, crack and collapse.

As permafrost thaws deeper into the soil, nutrients become more available and plants can grow deeper roots.

These conditions can stimulate plant growth and enable larger vegetation like trees to gain a foothold, turning the landscape greener.

These established plants also trap snow in the winter, insulating the plants from the cold and promoting further plant growth.

A 2020 study in Nature Communications used satellite data to estimate Arctic vegetation over time, sampling thousands of sites across Alaska, Canada and western Eurasia. The researchers found that between 1985 and 2016, about 38% of the sites showed greening.

“Not everywhere in the Arctic is green,” says Logan Berner, a terrestrial ecologist with the University of Alaska Southeast, who led the study. “But there’s enough greening that if you look at the average greenness of the Arctic over time, it’s going up.”

According to Berner, who grew up in southern Alaska, this consistent increase in average greenness tracks strongly with an increase in summer temperatures.

Annual rate of greening, 2000-2025

Annual rate of greening, 2000-2025

Annual rate of greening, 2000-2025

Source: NOAA’s Arctic Report Card 2025

Though the Arctic might seem far away from us, Berner notes that it’s a “bellwether for the kinds of impacts that climate change can have.” And increased greening can negatively impact the people who live in the Arctic and rely on its natural resources. For example, as shrubs expand across northern lands, they can shade out berry patches that people rely on for food; changing weather patterns can also affect the timing of fruit and its quality.

“People have coined the term that lakes are sentinels in the landscape,” says David Butman, a professor at the University of Washington who focuses on biogeochemistry and satellite remote sensing. Lakes react quickly to changes in the environment, so measuring lake color through satellite monitoring can help quantify those changes.

Butman worked on a 2021 study in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America (PNAS) that measured green wavelengths in more than 400,000 lakes in the boreal Arctic zone in North America. Researchers found that green values declined by 15% between 1984 and 2019, meaning that, to the naked eye, these lakes got significantly darker.

Thawing permafrost is a possible reason. As it thaws, soil can mix with lake water, making it darker. The researchers found that the greatest declines happened in warmer and wetter regions.

The darker a lake gets, the more heat it can store, according to Butman. “You can imagine, you know, a black car and a hot day,” he says. The darker a lake is, the longer it stays warm after the summer, disrupting the natural timings of processes like fish life cycles and algae production. When soil or other outside material sinks to the bottom of a lake, microbes consume oxygen to break it down, leading to the production of methane, a potent planet-heating gas.

On a global scale, many lakes fall within the green-blue color spectrum. Bright blue lakes, often depicted in illustrations, are rarer than green lakes.

In 2022, scientists Xiao Yang and Catherine O’Reilly led a study in Geophysical Research Letters that analyzed the color of more than 85,000 lakes. They found that blue lakes are generally found in northern places with cooler summers and are covered in ice in the winter, such as Moraine Lake in Canada or Lake Baikal in Russia.

Globally, approximately 31% of the Earth’s lakes are blue.

Yang and O’Reilly predict that fewer blue lakes will exist as summers get warmer and winter ice cover decreases due to climate change.

The birds and the bees

Many animals have appearances that blend in with their surroundings for survival. When those surroundings start to shift, animals such as the snowshoe hare begin to stand out. The snowshoe hare’s white winter fur sticks out with less snow on the ground, leaving it more vulnerable to predators.

Researchers haven’t found evidence that hares are adapting the timing of their molts to align with their changing winter. But some insects have already changed coloring. North American male dragonflies, for instance, have adapted to warmer climates by losing color on their wings, according to a study in PNAS.

Losing some of the heat-absorbing color can help the dragonflies stay cooler, but the males also lose color that helps attract females. And researchers predict this will continue to be the case in the future as the climate continues to warm. An even tinier example is a specific kind of bee.

Sevan Suni is an associate professor at the University of San Francisco who studies interactions between plants and pollinators. She has been going to Costa Rica for the last 15 years to study a group of bees commonly known as orchid bees.

These bees are the sole pollinators for about 200 species of orchids in Central and South America. Their bodies look almost jewel-like, with shiny iridescent shells.

Year after year, Suni noticed that one species of bee, the champion’s orchid bee, seemed to shift color from blue-green to orange-red. She and others discovered that, in hotter areas, the number of orange-red bees has increased over time while the number of blue-green bees has decreased.

The areas that increased in temperature faster over time also had more of the red-orange bees. It’s unclear what’s driving this change. The darker blue-green color could be hotter, absorbing more heat. Or the blue-green bees may be more vulnerable since the color of their environment is changing. Due to deforestation in Costa Rica, they may be less camouflaged in a less green environment. Either way, Suni has concerns about potential impacts.

“As a biologist, I’m always interested in biological variation,” she says. “It worries me a little bit if the blue-green morph has an important ecological function and they’re getting less prevalent over time.”

A last gasp of hidden color

Warming ocean waters bleach colorful corals, turning them white. The corals expel symbiotic algae, losing a food source and becoming more vulnerable to disease. Corals can recover after bleaching, but the longer and more frequent the bleaching, the more difficult recovery is. In some cases, corals turn stunningly fluorescent and colorful at the start of bleaching and after — a last bright gasp of life.

These neon colors, usually visible only under ultraviolet light, are always present to some degree, says Anya Salih. Salih, a fellow at the University of Technology Sydney, has studied coral reefs and their fluorescent colors for decades. She dives at night to scan reefs with blue lights.

“Sometimes when I dive with people who are not used to seeing this, I would have to hold their tank so that they don’t turn upside down,” she says, “because in that very colorful, psychedelic world, you lose the perspective of up and down in the water.”

Algae in healthy coral absorb sunlight for energy. When the algae leave due to stress, turning the coral white, more light travels through the remaining skeleton.

The coral becomes white and bleaches, making it more vulnerable to disease and death. Sometimes the coral turns colorfully fluorescent before bleaching.

A healthy coral and algae depend on each other. The coral provides the algae a place to live, and the algae provide the coral with its main sources of nutrients and color.

If stressed, often because of higher ocean temperatures, algae leave the coral.
