https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: Second world war veterans outnumber former PMs for possible last time on Remembrance Sunday
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Matthew Weaver
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Andy Burnham takes part for first time alongside eight ex-premiers as 12 veterans participate in ceremony

Second world war veterans outnumbered former prime ministers for what could be the last time at the national service of remembrance at the Cenotaph in central London.

The number of veterans from that conflict has dwindled to about a dozen, the oldest of whom was Jeffrey Brereton who served in the RAF. He volunteered for the RAF in 1940, at the age of 19, and served as a mechanic on Hurricane aircraft during the Battle of Britain.

The number of former prime minister has swelled to nine, all of whom attended as Andy Burnham took part in the ceremony for the first time. They included John Major, 83, the oldest living former prime minister; Keir Starmer the most recent ex-premier; and Liz Truss the shortest-serving.

Some of the spouses of former prime ministers joined Burnham’s wife Marie-France van Heel on a balcony overlooking Whitehall. She was flanked by Victoria Starmer and Hugh O’Leary, Truss’s husband; Theresa’s May’s husband Philip; Gordon Brown’s wife Sarah, and Rishi Sunak’s wife Akshata Murty.

Reform UK’s leader, Nigel Farage, laid a wreath for the first time. Only leaders whose parties hold six seats or more are entitled to take part, and over the last year defections from the Conservatives have taken Reform beyond that threshold to eight MPs.

Other politicians who laid wreaths included Kemi Badenoch, Sir Ed Davey, Shabana Mahmood and Sir Lindsay Hoyle.

The first wreath was laid by King Charles, who was dressed in a field marshal’s uniform. He was joined by his son, William, wearing the black uniform of a lieutenant colonel of the household cavalry.

Minutes before the ceremony, one of the soldiers in the parade on Whitehall was taken away on a stretcher after fainting. Charles led the two-minute silence which was broken only by a crying baby in Whitehall.

A gun was fired to mark the end of the silence before the last post was sounded by the buglers of the Royal Marines. After the service about 10,000 veterans took part in a march-past with more than 300 different armed forces and civilian organisations represented.

Some veterans waved and saluted as they began the march after the wreath-laying ceremony. Some of the older members were in wheelchairs and one group, many of whom were adorned with medals, rode mobility scooters.

They were applauded by the crowd as they marched swiftly through Whitehall. The youngest taking part was eight-year-old Ronan Doncaster, who walked in honour of his father: a guardsman with the first battalion Coldstream Guards who died in April 2024.

In Enniskillen in Northern Ireland, the Irish taoiseach, Micheál Martin, and the Northern Ireland secretary, Chris Bryant, attended a memorial service. In 1987, the event was targeted by an IRA bomb that killed 11 people on the day and a 12th victim, who never woke up from a coma, years later.

In Scotland, the first minister, John Swinney, led tributes at a service outside Edinburgh City Chambers. A military parade marched down the Royal Mile from Edinburgh Castle, led by the RAF Central Scotland Pipes and Drums.

A service attended by veterans, faith leaders and representatives of the Armed Service was also held in George Square, Glasgow, with a silence at 11am followed by a wreath laying ceremony.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘We feel the love’: Epstein survivors overwhelmed by messages of support at pop-up art exhibition
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Victoria Bekiempis
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Visitors to a touring show drawing attention to Epstein’s crimes have left thousands of ‘powerful’ notes – and survivors say it means a great deal

When Danielle Bensky first went to The Donald J Trump and Jeffrey Epstein Memorial Reading Room, she didn’t know what to expect.

“What happens if I walk in and survivors’ names are just plastered everywhere?” Bensky wondered about the reading room, a traveling exhibition of Epstein investigative files, first held in a New York City gallery this May. “I was a little worried in the beginning that this would be a form of exploitation for survivors.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

“Instead, it was just so beautifully done.”

The reading room is meant to bring attention to Epstein’s crimes and law enforcement’s decades-long failure to act. The former financier, who counted numerous high-profile men among his associates, was arrested in 2019 for sexual abuse of teen girls but killed himself in jail.

While Ghislaine Maxwell was arrested and found guilty of luring teen girls into Epstein’s orbit, documents reveal that law enforcement officials were well aware of their crimes decades prior. Survivors have called for greater transparency and legal actions against any other participants in their sexual abuse.

Bensky also didn’t know what would happen when David Garrett, founder of event organizer the Institute for Primary Facts, floated an idea to make the exhibit more interactive. There was a cork board in the final room and Garrett told Bensky he was going to keep it there when this exhibition opened to the public, so visitors could leave notes.

“I was like, ‘Oh, that’s such a great idea,” said Bensky, who is among the Epstein survivors pushing for accountability and justice. “That’ll be so cool to see.”

About a week after the reading room officially opened, Bensky returned and saw “at least six or seven corkboards that were full and overflowing with notes”. There were notes with drawings and notes with abject sadness and “sometimes, it was pure rage”.

“Sometimes, it would be a note directly to a survivor. Sometimes it was a note directly to themselves, and it got everybody involved,” she said. “Even members of survivors’ families were leaving notes. It was just a really beautiful display of our democracy.”

Bensky said the notes have given her hope amid years of institutional failures.

“Being seen in this process has been pretty remarkable.” Visitors have written, “We’re here with you, we stand with you, and we believe you” – demonstrating the “really beautiful empathy that comes with every single note”, Bensky said.

“There have been days where I felt like I couldn’t really do much. I felt really debilitated,” Bensky said. “The reading room can be a lot when you’re walking through your trauma all day, and you’re meeting all kinds of people.

“But so many of us will just go and sit in the room with all the notes and read the notes, and it’s like, ‘Wow, what an extraordinary thing to actually be seen and be believed by so many people at this point.’”

Liz Stein, an Epstein survivor, expressed similar sentiments about the power of these notes.

“It started out with one bulletin board, and I will never forget seeing that one initial bulletin board and just really feeling like, ‘Oh my goodness, people are really reacting to that,’” Stein said. When the first reading room installation ended, these notes “took up the better part of the downstairs of the exhibit”.

“The love that people show us is overwhelming, and every time we do these events with the reading room, every single time, people hug us, they tell us what we mean to them, and a lot of times they’ll say, ‘But it doesn’t matter. I’m just someone you don’t know from somewhere you don’t live,’” Stein said.

“And it’s like, no, we might not know your individual names, but we feel the love.”

“This wall with the note cards is a really tangible visual representation of how much support we have, and that fuels us in a way that I don’t think people quite understand.”

Garrett said that the idea for a notes space came at the last minute. He thought that people might experience deep emotions from the exhibit and might feel the need for support.

So, organizers put up a cork board with information about the national suicide prevention hotline as well as resources for those experiencing gender-based violence. Without thinking about it too much, Garrett decided to leave some extra notecards and pens.

“We just put them out and said, “if you want to write a note to the survivors, you can do that,” he told the Guardian. “We didn’t think that we would need more than that two foot by three foot corkboard.”

“By the end of the first day, not only was the corkboard full, but [notes] were taped up all around the cork board.” After just one day, visitors had left about 300 cards.

For the next 10 days, the producer would buy more cork boards everyday. There were 30 by the time the reading room ended its initial exhibition. “Every surface on that basement downstairs was full of cork boards and full of cards.”

The reading room would come to have seven stops – New York City; Washington DC; Des Moines, Iowa; Columbus, Ohio; Detroit, Michigan; Dallas, Texas; and Fort Lauderdale, Florida – and a traveling bookmobile that made about two dozen stops. In total, visitors left approximately 12,500 or 13,000 notes, Garrett said.

The reading room kicked off several months before highly contentious midterm elections dealt Republicans numerous blows which, some commentators said, was due to voters rejecting Trump. The president and Maga Republicans have been saddled by his administration’s handling of the files since he took office.

The White House rejected criticism of Trump’s handling of the files.

“Just as President Trump has said, he’s been totally exonerated on anything relating to Epstein,” White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said.

“And by releasing thousands of pages of documents, cooperating with the House oversight committee’s subpoena request, signing the Epstein Files Transparency Act, and calling for more investigations into Epstein’s Democrat friends, President Trump has done more for Epstein’s victims than anyone before him.”

Trump’s DoJ rebuffed criticism of their handling of these files and condemned the reading room.

“This sham tour is traveling to politically competitive areas and shamefully using victims as political pawns,” a DoJ spokesperson said in a statement.

“The non-profit’s fundraising ploy, which often hosts candidates for office, is a disgrace. It’s thanks to this Department of Justice that they even have those files, released in compliance with the Epstein Files Transparency Act under the most transparent administration to date.”

The words from supporters, both in person and notes, have provided encouragement to keep pushing for justice in spite of institutional roadblocks, Stein said.

“Your courage is louder than the people who tried to silence you,” was among Stein’s favorite notes. Another, Stein recalled, said: “One of these girls could have been me or my friends.”

“Money and power should not dictate justice,” Stein said of another memorable note.

Bensky also recalled one particularly powerful message.

“There was one that was just so simple,” Bensky recalled. “I think it literally just said: ‘It wasn’t your fault.’”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: The Donald J Trump and Jeffrey Epstein Memorial Reading Room is a traveling exhibition of Epstein investigative files. The White House rejected criticism of Trump's handling of the files.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: US datacenter demand spurs increased fossil fuel pipeline projects as rules are discarded
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Tom Perkins
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Trump administration has gutted regulations that protect lives and natural resources as pipeline build-out continues

Datacenters are spurring a boom in fossil fuel pipeline projects at a time when the Trump administration is gutting rules that protect from disasters along the lines, a new review of federal records shows.

The report, compiled by the Environmental Integrity Project, also found pipelines are being built to meet demand for natural gas exports fueled by wars in Ukraine and Iran. Federal records identified almost 200 pipeline projects that are proposed or in the works, and would collectively span 17,000 miles (27,000km).

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Not only has the Trump administration targeted laws that protect the environment and human health from pipelines’ risks, it has also pledged not to enforce regulations around them, the report adds.

The findings bring into focus a little-considered environmental threat in artificial intelligence and datacenter proliferation – the US already records about 1.7 pipeline accidents, spills, fires or explosions per day, and these projects would almost certainly lead to more.

The pipelines could help supply the at least 98 gas-fired power plants proposed to serve datacenters, and, if all the lines are completed, they would transport about 40% more natural gas daily than what the system carries today.

“This is the largest boom in a couple decades … and it coincides with all this deregulation,” Alexandra Shaykevich, research manager with the Environmental Integrity Project, said. “That’s concerning because the pipelines do usually operate safely, but they can leak and explode, and so there are big risks for communities across the United States.”

Most of the pipelines would carry natural gas across 42 states, though many of them are concentrated in several fossil fuel-producing regions. About 42 are in or cross Texas, 27 are in Louisiana, and nine each are in Pennsylvania and Illinois.

Advocates say they’re especially worried because of the wide-ranging attacks on foundational environmental protections, from the Clean Water Act to the Endangered Species Act, that until recently have been wielded to stop the riskiest projects, protect from accidents or hold polluters accountable.

The report states that over 25% of the projects have requested an expedited environmental review, and the administration is largely using legally dubious mechanisms to push them through, like invoking the “energy emergency”. That has accelerated permit approvals, reduced the scope of environmental studies, and limited public and community input, the report alleges.

Meanwhile, the administration has used the Defense Production Act to push through projects over the objections of states. In March, it jump-started the Santa Ynez oil pipeline in Santa Barbara, California, despite the state shutting it down in 2015 following a major spill that harmed about 150 miles (240km) of coastline. The act is also being used to attempt to ram through controversial plans for the 125-mile (200km) Constitution pipeline that would run from Pennsylvania to upstate New York, which the latter has opposed.

The Trump administration in January issued a memo stating that it would “refrain from taking any enforcement action” against companies that violated Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration regulations. By 2025, it had already cut the average number of enforcement actions initiated in half, recording only 117.

The administration is also raising the risk of accidents and explosions by allowing companies to increase the pressure of pipelines in densely populated areas and letting them conduct fewer pressure tests, the report alleges.

It has made changes like this despite the regularity of accidents, including some that are deadly. The report points to a March 2023 disaster in which a crack in a gas pipeline in West Reading, Pennsylvania, caused an explosion in a chocolate factory that killed seven workers and injured 10 others. Last month, two workers were killed when a New Mexico pipeline exploded.

The pipelines could also destroy thousands of acres of federally protected wetlands. At least 81 of the projects are expected to damage more than 19,000 acres (7,700 hectares) of federally protected wetlands, the report found. This also comes as the Trump administration attempts to strip 94% of federal wetland protections.

The dangers of this are felt in south-west Louisiana, which holds a large concentration of pipelines because of the high number of export terminals along the Mississippi River. These already cut through and harmed sensitive wetlands and fishing grounds, said James Hiatt, executive director of For a Better Bayou.

“The people who live here carry the risks and bear the burden while the profits go elsewhere,” Hiatt said.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: How CrossFit helped shape the macho fitness culture of Trump’s America
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Edward Helmore
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
The movement founded by Greg Glassman grew into an empire, helping popularize the masculinity aesthetic embraced by Pete Hegseth and RFK Jr

Comparative machismo is hardly new, but when Donald Trump publicly admired Senator Jon Husted’s backside earlier this month, later telling advisers it made the since-defeated Ohio incumbent more “interesting” to voters, the senator leaned into the compliment, saying it gave him extra motivation to “get down to the gym”.

Would that odd exchange have taken place without CrossFit, the fitness empire founded by college dropout and gymnast Greg Glassman in the 1990s that grew to 15,000 gyms across 160 countries before he was drawn into public controversy at the height of #MeToo and the social justice movement in 2020?

The question is not directly addressed in The Glass Box, an astonishing new account of Glassman’s spectacular rise and fall and of a fitness movement that encouraged adherents to participate in high-intensity workouts. “Hard Work Pays Off” was the mantra; “Mechanics, Consistency, and then Intensity” was the programming; and “Forging Elite Fitness” was the goal. It was an aesthetic and attitude that even bled into right-wing politics and militarism.

But it did not begin that way. At seminars, CrossFitters were first encouraged toward the Zone Diet (“eat meat and vegetables, nuts and seeds, some fruit, little starch, and no sugar”), and later the paleo diet, also known as the caveman or stone age diet, that imagined what humans would have eaten in the Paleolithic era, all the better for the grunting that accompanied “constantly varied, high-intensity functional movements”, as Glassman put it.

Glassman had polio as a child and had used gymnastics to rebuild his strength. It was until his 30s that he began working as a personal trainer in Santa Cruz, California, and developed a system of weightlifting, gymnastics, and sprint conditioning. He opened his first gym in 1995 and was hired by the police department to train their officers.

Overbooked by demand from private clients, he started group classes and the CrossFit community and empire was born, with Glassman himself attaining guru-like status. He was, by turns, charming and irascible, and prone to bluntness and profanity. He told his wife, Jenai: “This next year I’m going to have a lot more sex, either with or without you.”

He was also accused by former employees and CrossFit athletes in a New York Times exposé of creating a culture of “routine and rampant sexual harassment”.

Glassman denied such conduct. A spokesperson said the negative accounts were “a collective effort to devalue the company and buy it for scraps”. He linked racism and the Black Lives Matter movement to the pandemic, tweeting “It’s FLOYD-19.” He once said on a Zoom call: “I do not mourn George Floyd.”

Stories about profligate spending on private jets, restaurants, alcohol, Mariachi bands and stays at the Four Seasons emerged; Glassman explained he was not the CEO of a publicly traded company caught with his hand in the till.

“The till was mine,” he said. “I owned 100 per cent of the company.”

Calum Marsh, author of The Glass Box and former CrossFit devotee, says the program had been developed as an accessible, “easy, safe way of training, mainly for people who were overweight, senior citizens and the infirm – something that could be done by anyone”.

As it evolved, Marsh says, it became popular with people in the military, the police and first responders. “People in those fields gravitated to it because, at its extreme, it can be very intense. So it became popular as a more rugged, macho version of a typical workout and moved away from its original ethos.”

Alongside that, CrossFit gained a political reputation. The company had been founded shortly before 9/11, and the new workout ethos complemented the era of what Marsh calls a “more self-determined and hardened, battle-ready stance. It was a perfect time for CrossFit to take off.”

Of course, every era finds its complementary physical aesthetic. CrossFit launched a website that could be accessed by military personnel serving in Afghanistan and the Middle East. “CrossFit pursued and cultivated an affinity by naming workouts over fallen service members and plastering its website with images of people in the military, guys jumping out of helicopters and doing pull-ups on the end of a tank.”

The association, though never formalized, stuck, and can still be seen today in Trump administration figures, including defense secretary Pete Hegseth, who made physical fitness a military priority and his own physical training, a centerpiece of his command.

Robert F Kennedy Jr also has prioritized viral fitness challenges and high-intensity workouts that mirror CrossFit, along with displays of his own physique. Hegseth and Kennedy launched the online “Pete and Bobby Challenge” as part of Kennedy’s “Make America Healthy Again” (Maha) platform.

“There’s a big premium paid to being perceived as being manly and rugged, and that totally ties into the early Bush-era, CrossFit style,” Marsh says. The aesthetic of CrossFit gyms cultivated in that era – “no mirrors, no vanity, rough garage-style” – is what they tried to re-assert in the Trump era.

The CrossFit aesthetic arrived in contrast to an early period of fitness culture. TV personality Tony Robbins developed a time-efficient routine that promoted cold water immersion, mental “priming” exercises, rhythmic breathing exercises and a fast 15-minute high-intensity workout.

The message then, according to Marsh, was to be able to get fit without really trying. That, too, had developed out of the 1980’s era of “Jane Fonda’s Workout” and the dawn of the health club – upscale boutique places with soft jazz meant to appeal to suburban moms or businesspeople. Then came the 90s era of the ThighMaster and Buns of Steel.

“Everything about the way they were marketed and positioned was to de-emphasize how difficult they were,” he says. The message of CrossFit was the opposite. “It was unheard of at the time,” Marsh says. “You’re gonna have to try. It’s going to be brutal. You’re going to bleed and vomit.”

Looking back further, Marsh points to 1930s Germany and the body aesthetics of the Nazis captured by Leni Riefenstahl’s Triumph of the Will. That, he concedes, is an extreme example. Physical prowess and the body mirror the culture, and vice versa.

“It’s both responding to changes that are political and helping to shape them,” he points out. “It’s in the air and in the culture and part of what makes these things manifest.”

The book arrives at a time when figures from bodybuilding’s golden age, Arnold Schwarzenegger and Sylvester Stallone, who translated their physiques into movie stardom and have re-emerged as avuncular cultural heroes. Stallone’s recent autobiography The Steps made No 1 on nonfiction book sales charts when it was released last month. Schwarzenegger, too, has been recast as a pro-immigration voice of Republican reason.

In the end, Glassman was forced to resign and sell CrossFit after his history of highly questionable remarks became public. But he kept the company jets and collected a $200m payout.

“He made a few political blunders and stupid errors of judgment that brought him an immense amount of backlash. He tried walking them back, he stepped down, and when that wasn’t enough, he ended up selling,” Marsh says. “It was probably a long time coming.”

But Glassman’s legacy on fitness is undeniable “in ways that are so broad that they’re hard to believe”, Marsh says. CrossFit’s revolution, he says, was not just the manner and equipment of working out, but the social culture of it.

“CrossFit’s unique quality was its community-oriented classes,” Marsh, who met his wife at a class, says. “They were very social, close-knit, and people built relationships in ways that would not happen if you just went to the gym with your headphones on.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: The Glass Box was founded by college dropout and gymnast Greg Glassman in the 1990s. The company had been founded before 9/11 and was founded before the era of the CrossFit was the opposite of the message of the 1980s.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.title: Could Iraq’s Kurdish region return to two separate administrations?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.text:
Disagreements between the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) over the formation of a new government have led to the threat of two rival administrations emerging in the Kurdish region of northern Iraq, analysts say.

The dispute between the two dominant political forces in the semiautonomous Kurdistan Regional Government, which traditionally has operated under a power-sharing agreement, escalated after a parliamentary session was held last week in Erbil without the PUK’s participation.

PUK leader Bafel Talabani responded by withdrawing his party from the government, and a threat is growing that a rival administration could be formed in the party’s Sulaimaniyah base.

Independent Kurdish politician Yasin Aziz said the latest developments have deepened the historical divisions between the KDP and PUK.

“I believe the spectre of two administrations in Kurdistan is now very close, and the outlines of such a scenario are becoming clear. … The events have been painful and rapid. The differences between the two parties were significant and have now led to a breakdown in relations,” Aziz told Al Jazeera.

“There had been hopes that the two sides would reach an agreement, but activating parliament without the PUK deepened the divisions between the KDP and PUK.”

The KDP, which is led by Massoud Barzani, is the biggest party in the region, and its strongholds are in Erbil and Dohuk.

Since the first Gulf War in 1990 and 1991 and the establishment of a US-led “no-fly zone” in northern Iraq, Iraq’s Kurds have largely governed themselves, separate from the national government in Baghdad.

The Iraqi Constitution enacted after the 2003 US-led invasion of Iraq recognised the northern Kurdish region as a federal entity with its own legislative, executive and judicial powers.

There is a historical precedent for the possible separation of powers in this region between two rival authorities. When a conflict erupted between elements of the KDP and PUK in the 1990s, the two parties formed separate local governments in Erbil and Sulaimaniyah, respectively.

While there have been no recent violent flare-ups between the two parties, political distrust remains deep.

During the sixth parliamentary elections in the region on October 20, 2024, the KDP won 39 seats and the PUK 23. This left a 16-seat gap between the two parties.

But the KDP’s ability to form a new government was still dependent on reaching an agreement with the PUK and other parties, such as the New Generation Movement, which secured 15 seats in the last election.

The PUK has so far refused to collaborate, so after a two-year wait, the KDP reactivated the regional parliament on Wednesday without its rivals.

Although the rivalry between the two parties is longstanding, Aziz argued that the current crisis is more serious and deeply rooted than previous political disputes.

“Given the political stubbornness of both parties, I do not expect an agreement or understanding to be reached soon,” he said. “Both sides must make concessions to each other. The party willing to make greater concessions will demonstrate greater concern for the Kurdistan region.”

Aziz was clear in laying blame for the deepening divide.

“The responsibility for deepening this conflict lies with the leaderships of Kurdistan’s two main parties,” he said. “Their failure to recognise the risks posed by continuing these disputes is one of the reasons we have reached this point.”

Subhi Mandalawi, a member of the KDP, blamed the current impasse on the refusal of the PUK to form a new government with the KDP.

“Following the Kurdistan parliamentary elections, the PUK delayed the formation of the new government. They were counting on the KDP being unable to secure the legal quorum needed to convene a parliamentary session,” Mandalawi told Al Jazeera. “But we held a parliamentary session without the PUK in 2018 as well, and they subsequently joined the government and parliament.”

Mandalawi insisted that the door remains open for the PUK and other political parties but warned that prolonged divisions would lead to deeper problems for the Kurdish region.

“Continuing to obstruct legislative institutions two years after the elections is unacceptable and harms the Kurdistan region domestically, regionally and internationally,” he said.

“Threatening to divide the Kurdistan region is a hasty, ill-considered and unrealistic decision. No party leader can take such a step, and the PUK would be the biggest loser if it went ahead with it.”

Despite the differences, there is little risk of a return to conflict between the two parties. “We are brothers, and there can be no fighting among us,” Mandalawi said.

Mahmood Khoshnaw, a senior PUK official, said the KDP’s decision to convene parliament without his party has worsened political tensions in the region.

“Activating parliament without the PUK represents a departure from the principle of partnership and from political realities, and there will be consequences. If a prime minister is appointed in Erbil, we will take the same step in Sulaimaniyah. Whatever the KDP does, we will do the same in Sulaimaniyah,” Khoshnaw warned.

“The situation in the Kurdistan region is heading towards chaos unless the crisis is addressed rationally and realistically. Activating parliament without reaching an understanding with the PUK has had a negative impact on relations between the two parties.”

Despite this, there are questions about whether Sulaimaniyah could legally separate from the Kurdish regional government.

Ramadan Albadran, an independent political analyst and constitutional affairs expert, said the dispute is not a constitutional issue about the KDP’s convening of parliament but a deep political crisis with the potential to create security repercussions for the region.

The Iraqi constitution also provides no mechanism for dividing the region into zones of influence between the KDP and PUK.

“If the PUK moves to separate Sulaimaniyah from the Kurdistan region, that would not be a legal or constitutional act,” Albadran said.

“If it takes place without a mandate from the elected Kurdistan Regional Government, it would be closer to an act of rebellion since there is no legal provision permitting withdrawal from or the dismantling of a region in this manner.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.title: Poland mourns six killed in attack as authorities launch ‘terrorism’ probe
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.text:
Poland has begun two days of national mourning after an armed man killed six people in central Krakow, as the national prosecutor’s office opened a “terrorism” investigation.

The 24-year-old Polish suspect opened fire on Saturday in the heart of Krakow’s historic city centre. A British national was among those killed, according to police, and nationals from Austria, Britain, Germany, Portugal and Russia were among the 15 wounded, authorities told the PAP news agency.

Three more bodies were later found at the suspect’s home in Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski, about 150km (93 miles) northeast of Krakow. Police said they were his parents and a sister.

The suspect was also wounded during police action and is in critical condition in hospital.

Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office said on social media on Sunday it had “launched an investigation today into yesterday’s attack in Krakow”, adding it was probing “the killing of six people … using a firearm, and the attempted murder of many others, including police officers, this act constituting a terrorist offence”.

Daniel Prokopowicz, a spokesperson for the office, said it was “highly likely” that the killings in Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski and Krakow were carried out by the same person, but that investigations were ongoing.

According to media reports, the suspect, Michal O, had a valid gun licence and no prior criminal record.

Polish Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski stated the attacker was influenced by far-right and ultranationalist ideologies and views.

Meanwhile, Krakow’s main market square and ⁠the surrounding streets remained closed on Sunday, with police allowing only essential service workers.

Many nearby cafes were closed and flags ⁠at the city hall were at half-mast. Mourners placed candles in several locations in the area.

The traditional hourly trumpet call from St Mary’s church on the square was suspended for 12 hours to commemorate the dead, the first time this has happened since 1939, the Polish Press Agency reported.

The 24-year-old suspect opened fire on Saturday in the heart of Krakows' historic city centre. A British national was among those killed, and nationals from Austria, Britain, Germany, Portugal and Russia were among the 15 wounded.

https://arstechnica.com/science/2026/11/.title: Physicists listened to electrical noise to crack a superconductor mystery
https://arstechnica.com/science/2026/11/.author: Jacek Krywko
https://arstechnica.com/science/2026/11/.text:
Tuning in to electronic noise can tell us whether electrons have paired up or not.

Superconductors carry electricity without resistance, but most only work a few degrees above absolute zero. In the late 1980s, copper-based materials called cuprates were found to superconduct at higher temperatures—reachable with affordable liquid nitrogen. Yet nearly 40 years later, physicists still don’t agree on why.

In a recent Science study, a team of physicists led by Milan Allan of Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich and Ingmar Swart of Utrecht University in the Netherlands has found some answers by listening to the faint electrical crackle of current flowing into a cuprate.

Central to the mystery of cuprates’ high-temperature superconductivity is a strange state called the pseudogap. “The pseudogap is a phenomenon of missing electrons,” Allan said. Above the temperature at which cuprates become superconducting, some of their electrons seem to vanish—measurements find far fewer of them at the energies where they should be. “Everybody knows that from different probes, you see that there’s these vanishing electrons, but nobody knows why,” Allan said.

Over the decades, physicists have put forward two main competing explanations. The first hypothesizes that the electrons get stuck in some sort of structure. In this view, electrons freeze into patterns, such as charge density waves, and superconductivity develops separately. The alternative explanation tightly links this phenomenon to superconductivity. “Other people think they’re missing because they form pairs,” Allan said. Pairs of electrons, called Cooper pairs, are what carry current in a superconductor. If, as the material cools, these pairs appear before the material becomes superconducting, they would be a precondition of superconductivity, a waiting room of sorts, where pairs exist but can’t yet move together in lockstep.

Settling this proved extremely hard. “Lots of different experimental signatures are kind of lumped inside this,” Allan said. Different instruments all see something, but their readings, Allan said, are never conclusive. “It’s always something kind of incoherent, hard to grasp,” he said.  What the researchers needed was a way to see pairs directly, and Allan and his colleagues figured it out.

The team decided to listen to shot noise—tiny fluctuations caused by the arrival of individual charges that form the stream of an electric current. Allan says it resembles rain drumming on the roof.  “If you imagine that you have raindrops and then all of a sudden you make the drops twice as heavy, there’ll be more noise,” Allan said. “With the electrons it’s similar. If you have two electrons coming always together, because they’re associated with pairing, then it will be more noise.”

The researchers did this measurement with a scanning tunneling microscope, which passed current between a needle-sharp tip and a cuprate sample, letting them listen to the noise at specific energy levels and different locations on the surface. In conventional superconductors, pairing produces a clean doubling of the noise. In cuprates, the signal is much weaker, because single electrons keep flowing alongside the pairs.

Making the instrument sensitive enough to discern the pairs took years. “What it took is very talented and persistent students who worked for, I don’t know, four years on this to get it working,” Allan said. “There was not a single trick. It was electronics craftsmanship.”

The team examined crystals of a cuprate known as BSCCO, cooled to a few degrees above absolute zero, and compared the noise to the energies at which electrons go missing. By adjusting the voltage between the tip of the needle and the sample, the team could choose the energy of the electrons they were listening to, a bit like turning a radio dial. If the pseudogap came purely from frozen patterns, the team reasoned, the extra noise of pairing should only kick in at energy levels associated with superconductivity. Instead, pairing showed up right at the pseudogap energy.

“The fact that there is more noise indicates that pairing is associated with this large gap,” Allan said. The pseudogap’s energy varies from spot to spot on the surface, but wherever the team listened, the extra noise always started rising at the local pseudogap energy. The same pattern held in samples with different chemical compositions.

Ruling out other sources of noise, such as atoms shifting on the surface, took a lot of effort. “Noise is super hard to interpret, and that was basically the thing that we had the most sleepless nights about,” Allan said. The decisive check involved placing the samples in magnetic fields of up to six tesla, which suppresses pairing while leaving the overall pattern of missing electrons largely intact. As the magnetic field grew, the noise dropped back toward the single-electron level, exactly as expected if pairs were behind it.

The strength of electron pairing can be expressed as the energy required to pull a pair apart. Lowering the temperature helps boost pairing because the warmer a material becomes, the more violently its particles jostle and the more pairs get broken. In conventional superconductors, two ingredients needed for superconductivity—pair formation and phase coherence—occur simultaneously at the critical temperature. (Phase coherence is where the electrons start moving together as a fluid.) In cuprates, Allan and Swart’s study points to a different sequence.

The pairing energy the team measured is well above the temperature at which the material superconducts. “So the picture that emerges is that you first have pre-formed pairs, and then only at lower temperatures, phase coherence sets in,” Swart said. That suggests the superconductivity bottleneck is not getting electrons to pair, but getting the pairs to move together.

“If you have pairing at such high energies, that means that you might be able to push Tc [superconducting temperature] higher,” Allan said. “This is something people hoped for in the very early days of cuprates, and now everybody’s afraid to even mention that. But to me it gives hope.”

An optimistic reading of the results is that cuprate electrons could theoretically pair at room temperature, and we only need to make them coherent to achieve a room-temperature superconductor. The team, though, thinks that’s a bit naive. “I think Ingmar and I both believe that it’s not going to be that simple, because you have all kinds of other effects that are coupled there,” Allan said.

The researchers also stress that their experiment does not fully answer the central question. It rules out the idea that the pseudogap comes from frozen patterns alone, but not that such patterns are intertwined with pairing. “Whatever the detailed explanation of the pseudogap is, pairing should be part of it,” Swart said.

Because the technique used in the study loses sensitivity as temperature rises, the team couldn’t yet listen above the superconducting temperature, where the pseudogap is usually defined. “Hopefully other groups will do that,” Allan said. “What limits Tc, especially if the energy of pairing is high? What happens at Tc? That’s for me the most interesting question.”

Swart wants to make noise maps of the surface with higher resolution and, eventually, an instrument that can detect coherence directly, which he hopes should give us separate markers for the onset of phase coherence and electron pairing. Allan, meanwhile, increasingly thinks the route to better superconductors runs through chemistry, aided by AI, rather than pure physics. “When it comes to trying to make the superconducting material better and increase Tc, I have more hope in direct trial and error,” he said.

Science, 2026: 10.1126/science.adt3444
https://arstechnica.com/science/2026/11/.summary: The pseudogap is a phenomenon of missing electrons, scientists say. The team listened to the faint electrical crackle of current flowing into a cuprate. The researchers stress that their experiment does not fully answer the central question.

https://www.space.com/entertainment/spac.title: Who is King Ghidorah? The cosmic connections of Godzilla Minus Zero's foe
https://www.space.com/entertainment/spac.author: Robert Lea
https://www.space.com/entertainment/spac.text:
The three-headed Kaiju's origins aren't just space-based; one of the largest structures in the universe shares its name.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Godzilla goes toe-to-toe with long-time foe King Ghidorah in Godzilla Minus Zero, which opened in theaters on Friday (Nov. 6). Though the three-headed golden Kaiju might seem like a natural native of Monster Island, King Ghidorah actually emerged from the depths of space.

However, it isn't just the origins of King Ghidorah — also known as Monster Zero in the Godzilla movie Invasion of Astro-Monster (1965) — that are this beast's only cosmic connection. One of the largest structures in the universe, the King Ghidorah Supercluster, was named in honor of Godzilla's primary antagonist.

King Ghidorah is a three-headed, twin-tailed golden dragon from the stars, first introduced in the fifth Godzilla movie, Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster (1964).

In this first appearance, part of the Shōwa era (1964–1975) of Godzilla history, Ghidorah ravaged Venus, wiping out its population 5,000 years before arriving on Earth encased within a highly magnetic meteorite. Ghidorah was bested this first time by Godzilla, Rodan, and Mothra.

Undeterred, Ghidorah returned for a rematch just a year later in Invasion of Astro Monster (1965), after being discovered supposedly terrorizing the inhabitants of Planet X, a world found beyond Jupiter. In this movie, it is revealed that Ghidorah is less a king and more a pawn, under the control of calculating Xiliens as part of a plan to subjugate Earth. This will become a theme.

Freed from that control, Ghidorah returns to deep space, once again falling under the thrall of an alien race in 1968's Destroy All Monsters.

This movie sees Ghidorah hold its own against a who's who of kaiju, eventually succumbing to the combined might of Godzilla, Minilla, Mothra, Rodan, Manda, Gorosaurus, Anguirus, Kumonga, Baragon, and Varan.

Even with three gravity-beam-blasting heads, that is hardly fair!

Ghidorah returned with some backup for a final time in the Shōwa era in 1975's Godzilla vs. Gigan. This time, Ghidorah and his tag-team partner Gigan (who resembled a giant one-eyed space chicken) were under the control of cockroach-like Nebulans. Getting mind-controlled three times is just embarrassing!

Fortunately, the Shōwa era drew to a close in 1975 before Ghidorah was forced into servitude for a fourth time.

Ghidorah returned in the rebooted Godzilla timeline of the Heisei era (1991–1998) in 1991's Godzilla Vs. King Ghidorah, but its cosmic origins are gone. The Heisei Ghidorah begins life as three genetically engineered creatures called Dorats in the future before being morphed into a three-headed form via nuclear exposure.

Ghidorah was given a spiritual origin in the Millennium era's Godzilla, Mothra, and King Ghidorah: Giant Monsters All-Out Attack (2001), actually serving as a protagonist, helping Mothra in halting Godzilla's rampage.

Ghidorah is once again an extraterrestrial in Universal Pictures' MonsterVerse movie Godzilla: King of the Monsters (2019), being described as having "fallen from the stars" in ancient times before rising to challenge Godzilla.

Now King Ghidorah is back once again in Godzilla Minus Zero, maintaining his extraterrestrial origin story and once again challenging Godzilla to an epic kaiju battle.

Those are some of the fictional versions of this golden beast, but what does it look like in reality?

Arguably the most impressive feat of King Ghidorah has been to make itself such an important part of pop culture that astronomers took note.

The King Ghidorah supercluster is a collection of galaxies located around 6.7 billion light-years from Earth. Covering an area of the sky equivalent to 19 full moons, as seen from our vantage point, this cosmic Kaiju was discovered in late 2022 by Japanese astronomers using data from the Subaru Telescope.

The King Ghidorah supercluster is comprised of at least 19 individual associated galaxy clusters. It stretches out for an incredible 1.3 billion light-years, meaning the entire Milky Way could fit across it around 12,300 times. That makes it the largest supercluster ever discovered.

To put into context just how monstrous the King Ghidorah supercluster is, consider the fact that it has a mass equivalent to 10,000,000,000,000,000 suns, 10 times as massive as the Milky Way's home supercluster, Laniakea.

Even Godzilla may think twice before attempting to tussle with that particular King Ghidorah!

See King Ghidorah in action in Godzilla Minus Zero, which is showing in theaters in the US and UK from November 6. You can see the preceding movie, Godzilla Minus One, on Netflix.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/new-york-.title: D.C. is a New York town: The president, next speaker and Senate majority leader grew up within 11 miles of each other—what it means for the Big Apple
https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/new-york-.author: Catherina Gioino
https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/new-york-.text:
On the eve of the midterm election, Gov. Kathy Hochul told a Brooklyn crowd how she planned to use New York’s new clout.

“I cannot wait when I call up Hakeem Jeffries and say, ‘Mr. Speaker, I kind of need a few more billions of dollars for New York,’” she said at a rally in Williamsburg, according to THE CITY. “Then I call Chuck Schumer: ‘Mr. Majority Leader, I need a few more billions of dollars for New York State.’ Get used to it, America. Because we’re in charge.”

Less than 24 hours later, Democrats won both chambers of Congress, and if Jeffries and Schumer win their leadership votes come January, two Brooklynites will lead Congress opposite a Queens-born president. For the first time in U.S. history, sons of New York are poised to run both chambers of Congress and the White House.

Hochul, again, come Tuesday night: “Can you imagine New York state having both leaders of both bodies in Congress? Everybody’s going to want to move to New York because we’re the political club of the nation,” per Crain’s reporter Jack Grieve. “Imagine a world where I actually have a Congress, a House and a Senate, that are not fighting me, but working as partners to deliver even more for New York.”

The three men grew up within about 11 miles of one another: President Donald Trump in Jamaica Estates, Queens, and Schumer and Jeffries just a few miles apart in Brooklyn, in Midwood and Crown Heights.

The last time the House and Senate were led by people from the same state was when Texans Sam Rayburn and Lyndon Johnson held the top jobs, respectively, an overlap that ended in 1961. Jeffries would also be the first House speaker from New York state in nearly 160 years, in addition to being the first from New York City and the first Black speaker.

New York came close once. In 2018, after Schumer became the Senate minority leader, Queens Democrat Joe Crowley was the House’s fourth-ranking Democrat and a likely successor to Nancy Pelosi. He also chaired what City & State called arguably the most powerful county committee in the state. Then Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez beat him in a primary and Jeffries succeeded Crowley as chair of the House Democratic Caucus, the post that set him on the path to the speakership today.

New York’s reach in Washington extends beyond just Congress. Two of the nine Supreme Court justices were born in New York City: Sonia Sotomayor in the Bronx and Elena Kagan in Manhattan. Outside of Gotham, Chief Justice John Roberts was born in Buffalo and Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh, who took over the central bank in May, was born in Albany.

So the question now is what can the Big Apple and Empire State reap from the outer-borough love? Is it going to be like how Brooklyn’s own Biggie said in his 1994 instant bop “Juicy,” that the two chambers of Congress will get to “Spread love, it’s the Brooklyn way”?

Or as the Queens-bred 50 Cent said, will the president tell them that he (and potential but improbable White House spox Nicki Minaj) is “from Queens where we are taught to handle beef on our own”?

Politics aside, it’s all about infrastructure for Gotham City.

At the top of the list of wishes is Gateway, the $16 billion rail tunnel under the Hudson River. The idea dates to 2004 and survived New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie’s cancellation of an earlier version in 2010.

Just last fall, during the government shutdown, Trump froze its funding. “It’s billions and billions of dollars that Schumer has worked 20 years to get—it’s terminated,” he wrote on Truth Social—and then he later suggested he’d restore the money if Penn Station and Dulles International Airport were renamed for him. This past July, a federal judge permanently blocked the freeze.

There’s also Sunnyside Yard, a plan to build 12,000 homes over a Queens rail yard that the mayor’s office says would need more than $21 billion in federal grants. When Trump visited Gracie Mansion in September, the first visit by a sitting president in decades, he and fellow-Queens-rep Mayor Zohran Mamdani discussed the project.

Trump said he’d been watching the site for 35 years. In the 1980s, he floated an arena there for his New Jersey Generals football team. “You’re going to need a lot of federal approvals and probably some federal money to do it,” he told Mamdani in front of reporters, before insinuating that he would be open to giving the city the funds to do it.

New Yorkers also want money for the Second Avenue subway extension, plus relief for the more than 20,000 affected by changes to SNAP and the more than 400,000 facing Medicaid changes. Following Tuesday’s wave, Rep. Gregory Meeks of Queens predicted New York “will get its fair share,” per NY1. Even Mamdani, who seems to have gain favor with the president, said following the midterms that having leaders “from our city and of our city” is “of incredible importance.”

New York knows what it’s like to lose in Washington. During the city’s 1975 fiscal crisis, the New York Daily News summed up the federal response in a famous headline: “Ford to City: Drop Dead.”

After Hurricane Sandy, the state’s congressional delegation sought about $60 billion in federal aid, and after a very public debate between Ted Cruz and Schumer, was offered just a little more than $27 billion. (Schumer, for his part, following the devastation of Hurricane Harvey in Texas, gave Cruz the funds he requested years later.)

“It definitely would have been different if New Yorkers had been in charge,” Pete King, then a Republican congressman from Long Island, told the New York Times. “If you have to have Democrats in charge, as a New Yorker it’s better to have Schumer and Jeffries.”

Who knows what happens next. In addition Trump, Schumer, and Jeffries, New York has even more muscle to flex: Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin is a former Long Island congressman; Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand is in charge of the Democratic Party’s Senate campaign arm, and Bronx-and Queens Rep. AOC is weighing a 2028 presidential run or a Senate bid.

Maybe they all do what Ja Rule suggested in his 2004 song and tell the rest of the country: “We from New York.”

https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/trump-mid.title: Republicans saw Indian Americans as ‘natural conservative voters.’ But Trump’s second term undid the gains as their support for Democrats shot up
https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/trump-mid.author: Mia Osmonbekov
https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/trump-mid.text:
In 2024, Donald Trump appeared to make inroads with Indian Americans, a traditionally Democratic voting bloc. He won the support of 30% of Indian Americans that year, up from 22% in 2020, according to a report published on Nov. 2 by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. Its charts show that up until January of this year, GOP support was increasing among Indian women and men aged 40 and older.

But two years into Trump’s second term, and those gains vanished ahead of the midterms. Just 19% of the 1,000 Indian American adults surveyed from Oct. 7 to Oct. 27 by Carnegie intended to vote for the Republican in their House district, compared to 62% intending to vote for the Democrat. In Senate races, Democrats held a similar advantage over Republicans at 63% to 21%.

The reversal coincided with the Trump administration’s crackdown on legal immigration through H1-B visa restrictions, increasingly vocal anti-Indian rhetoric from some Republicans, and renewed concerns about the rising cost of living, contributing to the GOP’s declining appeal to even the Indian Americans it began winning over.

Devesh Kapur, a professor of South Asia studies at Johns Hopkins University who co-authored the Carnegie report, told Fortune that economic concerns drew Indian Americans toward Trump in 2024, when voters were frustrated by inflation and the rising cost of living under Joe Biden.

But those same anxieties, compounded by Trump’s immigration politics and a rise in anti-Indian racism, helped turn Indian American voters away again.

“It’s a combination of these three factors,” he said.

A blatant example of what Kapur refers to as the “racist rhetoric in the MAGA crowd” came in September, when Bo French, the GOP candidate for Texas’s railroad commissioner, posted a photo on X of a crowd of South Asian students celebrating a University of Texas at Austin football victory.

“I heard UT graduation this year looked like this,” French wrote. “I didn’t believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.”

While members of his party like Sen. John Cornyn condemned the post, its existence revived Indian Americans’ concern that Republicans don’t fully welcome the community.

Amrita Bhasin, the CEO of AI-powered supply chain platform Sotira, told Fortune that more vocal anti-South Asian rhetoric by political figures pushed away Indian American voters more than changes to immigration policy alone.

“I actually don’t think the racism is any worse than it was pre-Trump,” she said. “What’s different now is that politicians and people in power feel comfortable saying racist things out loud, specifically about South Asian people.”

In her view, Trump proposing a $103,265 surcharge on companies hiring workers with an H1-B visa in August also played a role. H1-B visa holders generally can’t vote, but Indian Americans may have relatives, friends, or colleagues whose ability to work in the country depends on the program.

Indians represent 71% of all H1-B visa approvals and have a strong presence in tech jobs and other highly skilled professions, so these restrictions send a message that they don’t belong, Bhasin said.

“I think the H-1B is part of it, but really the H-1B is a symptom of a bigger issue,” she said. “When you see that this work is not being respected in the same way, it feels like the Republicans maybe are not on the side of Indians.”

Republicans have long believed Indian Americans should be receptive to their platform. David Frum, a former speechwriter for George W. Bush, called Indian Americans “natural conservative voters” because of their high incomes, educational backgrounds, and entrepreneurship.

Indian journalist and now Council on Foreign Relations senior fellow Sadanand Dhume penned a 2012 essay for the conservative American Enterprise Institute saying that “interests, values, and history all suggest that the natural political home for Indian-Americans is the GOP.”

But Kapur said the “growing grip” of evangelical Christianity in the GOP has limited its appeal to Indian American voters. The Carnegie report found nearly one in three Indian American Christians (31%) identified as Republicans, compared with 21% of Hindus, 10% of Muslims, and just 8% of those with no religious affiliation.

“Since the majority are not Christian, that alone becomes a singular sort of impediment,” Kapur said. “There’s no way to get around it.”

The tension over religion surfaced notably in Texas politics. In 2023, Democratic state lawmaker James Talarico pointed to the potential alienation of Hindu students during a legislative hearing on a GOP bill requiring public schools to display the Ten Commandments.

“How do you think it makes a Hindu student feel to have a poster in every classroom that says ‘thou shall not worship any God before me’?’ he asked.

Three years later, Talarico beat GOP candidate Ken Paxton to become the first Democrat to win a U.S. Senate seat in Texas since 1988. In Fort Bend County, which includes the Houston suburb of Sugar Land and its sizable Indian American community, Talarico won 63% of the vote compared with Paxton’s nearly 35%, according to county election returns.

But Indian Americans voting against Republicans in the midterms doesn’t mean they did it out of stronger loyalty to Democrats. About 35% of Indian Americans who planned to vote Democrat in the midterms said they were motivated by opposition to Republicans, rather than support for Democrats, per the Carnegie report.

“Anger or feeling of antipathy towards the Republican Party was clearly an important factor over and above the support for the Democrat Party per se,” Kapur said.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/08/trump-ta.title: How Democrats will try to end Trump's tariffs
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/08/trump-ta.author: Kevin Breuninger
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/08/trump-ta.text:
Democrats are preparing to challenge President Donald Trump’s signature tariff policy as soon as they take power in the next Congress.

Democratic leaders plan to speed legislation to the House floor that reasserts Congress’ authority over trade.

Democrats such as Rep. Jamie Raskin are also laying the groundwork to launch tariff-related investigations.

Trump’s tariffs were already under pressure: They are being challenged in multiple lawsuits, and some Republicans have distanced themselves from the duties on Canada and others.

The battle for Congress is over. The war over President Donald Trump’s tariffs is about to heat up.

The knotted web of tariffs that Trump spent the last two years weaving could soon face its biggest threat, as Democrats prepare to unload their new legislative firepower against the Republican president’s signature policy.

Democrats have made no secret of their plans to bombard Trump and his associates with investigations as soon as the next Congress is sworn in. They are also preparing a first-100-hours legislative blitz, putting forward a series of bills that would unwind much of Trump’s agenda.

Both prongs of attack will take aim at Trump’s unprecedented use of tariffs, which Democrats have quickly identified as a main target following their landslide victory in Tuesday’s midterm elections.

Ending Trump’s tariff regime, and especially his trade war against Canada, is something Democrats “absolutely have to do immediately,” Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., told MS NOW’s “Morning Joe” Thursday.

Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the Democratic minority leader who could be elected House speaker in the next Congress, has made clear that ending Trump’s tariffs is a top priority.

“We should restore congressional authority as it relates to tariffs, because the Trump tariffs are making life more expensive for the American people,” he said at a press conference in late August.

If picked as speaker, Jeffries would speed legislation to the House floor that reasserts congressional authority over trade.

Democrats are also laying the groundwork for investigations into Trump’s tariffs, which the party folded into its winning campaign message linking high costs with alleged Trumpworld corruption.

Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, on Oct. 28 asked Trump to hand over records related to tariff exemptions. Trump, Raskin alleges, has wielded the exemption power to cut “sweetheart deals” for industries whose leaders have plied the president with gifts.

The plans are likely to ratchet up the pressure, both legally and politically, that Trump’s tariffs were already facing.

The administration is already embroiled in multiple lawsuits challenging different parts of the government’s tariff policy.

The most recent suit, filed Oct. 20, targets Trump’s use of a Great Depression-era law to impose 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods.

Another court case accuses Trump of trying to recreate the near-global “liberation day” tariffs that the Supreme Court struck down as illegal in late February. The administration has since been ordered to refund $166 billion in tariff revenue it had collected under the scrapped policy.

Congress, not the president, holds the power to levy taxes under the U.S. Constitution. Over decades, the legislative branch has ceded some of those powers to the executive. But Trump has asserted virtually unchecked tariff powers – which Democrats say they are intent on clawing back.

“Every day Trump insists on his indiscriminate taxes on so many of the products Americans need, he digs a deeper hole for Republicans enabling his tariff spree,” said Sen. Ron Wyden of Oregon, who is poised to lead the Senate Finance Committee when Democrats take it over.

“If Democrats somehow had a veto-proof majority, or if voters shame Republicans into doing the right thing, there would be no shortage of trade policies to address,” Wyden said in a statement to CNBC before Election Day.

“One of the most obvious priorities would be repealing Trump’s tariffs on Canada, which are raising prices and harming communities on both sides of the border,” he said. “I’ll also continue to work to ensure Congress has the final say on tariffs, so future presidents can’t reenact Trump’s economically disastrous trade taxes.”

The Wall Street Journal, citing Wyden, reported Thursday that Democrats are eyeing the Canada trade war as the “first target” in their efforts against his tariff agenda.

As Wyden’s statement suggested, the Senate’s rules will hamper Democrats’ anti-tariff efforts.

Despite their blowout victory Tuesday night, the party will still lack a 60-vote filibuster-proof majority in the Senate, giving Republicans a crucial tool to block legislation even in their diminished state.

Trump is also poised to lean heavily on his veto pen in the next Congress, presenting a major obstacle for Democrats’ legislative priorities.

Overriding a presidential veto requires two-thirds majorities in both the House and Senate, meaning that even with their historic electoral gains, Democrats would need significant Republican help to force a bill into law over Trump’s objection.

Democrats may consider it worthwhile to pass legislation even if Trump vetoes it, as doing so could help them build political narratives in the 2028 election cycle. But they may have other options available.

“Absent the brute force of a veto-proof coalition, Congress might consider other political solutions, such as adding riders on ‘must-pass’ bills or negotiation with the administration,” Kit Johnson, a senior tax manager for BDO’s customs and international trade group, told CNBC in an email.

Trump has said he plans to use the veto power to force Democrats to the negotiating table. But when it comes to tariffs, it’s hard to imagine what deal Trump might accept.

Trump has tried to reshape U.S. trade, foreign and economic policy around his asserted power to slap steep duties on imported goods. He describes tariffs as a win-win, praising them as both a powerful negotiating tool and a major revenue generator.

After Tuesday’s election, Trump seemed to suggest tariffs were non-negotiable.

“If I took tariffs off — we have 3,000 plants under construction right now. Every single plant would stop building,” Trump told CNBC’s Eamon Javers in a phone call Wednesday.

Since taking office in January 2025, Trump has hiked tariffs on nearly every country on the planet, leading to multiple protracted trade wars, most notably against Canada and China. He insists Americans do not share the burden of the duties, even though tariffs by definition are taxes on foreign goods paid by those importing them. The nonprofit Tax Foundation estimates Trump’s tariffs have raised the average U.S. household’s tax burden by $820 in 2026.

Trump has also consistently overstated the amount of revenue the government has amassed through his tariffs. He claimed before Election Day that tariffs enabled him to offer every U.S. adult $5,000 “dividend” checks if Republicans were to win both chambers of Congress – a plan that would cost roughly $1.2 trillion. But the duties – which are collected from U.S. importers – have only brought in around $300 billion in total between January 2025 and July 2026, according to the Penn Wharton Budget Model.

What’s more, about $138 billion of that total has been refunded since the Supreme Court ruling in February. Nearly $20 billion in tariff collections are still set to be refunded.

Most voters do not share Trump’s rosy view of tariffs. Sixty-five percent of respondents to the CNBC Voter Poll on Nov. 3 said the duties have hurt the U.S. economy, while just 22% say they helped.

What remains to be seen is how hard Republicans in Congress will push back on Democrats’ efforts.

A number of GOP lawmakers came out against the duties during the campaign, as their opponents gained ground blaming inflation on Trump’s tariffs and the Iran war.

As they try to regroup and look forward to the 2028 election cycle, some Republicans – who largely supported free trade prior to Trump’s political rise – may be less willing to continue aligning themselves with Trump’s aggressive protectionism.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/08/frequent.title: Using miles to fly for Thanksgiving? These are the most expensive and cheapest routes
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/08/frequent.author: Leslie Josephs
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/08/frequent.text:
Airplane tickets using frequent flyer mile redemptions will be expensive this Thanksgiving travel season.

Limited capacity, high demand and expensive fuel have made airline tickets pricier this year.

Airline ticket prices have surged this year, especially for travel over the holidays. Don’t expect many bargains if you’re booking flights with miles, either.

Tickets bought with frequent flyer miles for flights between large U.S. airports over the Thanksgiving travel period will cost 32% more than last year’s holiday, according to data from Seats.aero, a miles and points redemption search site. While fares have skyrocketed this year, airline executives last month said demand remains strong.

Airlines have largely gotten rid of static mileage redemption charts in favor of dynamic pricing, making budgeting for an award ticket more difficult. Dynamic pricing means redemption costs change depending on demand, routes and other factors.

Many of the most expensive routes this Thanksgiving are understandably longer, including from Hawaii, but the list also includes a nonstop from New York to Houston.

Here’s how mileage redemptions for the holiday are stacking up, based on one-way flights on average as of early November and compared with last year:

Jet fuel prices have surged since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28, which has eaten into airline profits. Carriers have sought to pass costs along to consumers as much as possible.

Even some of the cheapest routes for award tickets are more expensive than last year, including for short routes like Tulsa, Oklahoma, to Dallas Fort Worth International Airport.
