https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/08/amazon-h.title: Amazon's Astro home robot has fans but looks destined for the 'trash heap.' Why it's trying again
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/08/amazon-h.author: Annie Palmer
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/08/amazon-h.text:
Amazon has formed a new home robot team and is hiring for a “new-to-world robot product,” according to CNBC’s analysis of job posts.

The company has tried to break into the consumer robotics market before with the launch of its $1450 Astro device in 2021, but the product never made it out of beta.

Recent advances in artificial intelligence and robotics technology have kickstarted a new wave of humanoid development.

Jeff Bezos made a bold bet in 2017. A sci-fi and robotics enthusiast, Bezos was convinced that consumers would have a robot in their home in the not-too-distant future.

The Amazon
 founder and then-CEO told a group of the company’s top device executives to get to work on building one, and within a few years, the team came up with the $1,450 Astro.

The public got its first look at Astro, essentially an Alexa-equipped tablet on wheels that can autonomously navigate a home, recognize faces and act as a roving security monitor, when it rolled on stage at Amazon’s fall 2021 event.

But it never evolved beyond an invite-only product. Astro shipped to just a few thousand customers, some of whom now believe the robot’s days are numbered. The company also released an Astro for businesses in 2023, before sunsetting it less than a year later.

Amazon isn’t giving up on Bezos’ dream of a household robot just yet, despite its stumbles with Astro.

Over the past several months, the company has assembled a new team that’s working on a “new-to-world robot product,” according to a CNBC analysis of job posts.

“Robots are about to step out of the movies and into our homes,” a recent job listing for an engineer, which has since been removed, stated. The post details a product capable of navigating “dynamic home environments” and “autonomous operation alongside family members.”

Amazon is known for making long-term bets at the risk of “being misunderstood” in the short term if it gives the company an early advantage in new markets, like it did with the Alexa voice assistant or Kindle e-reader.

CEO Andy Jassy reminded investors of this approach in his latest annual letter, where he said artificial intelligence and robotics were among the “biggest inflections of our lifetime.”

“We try to anticipate what will make customers’ lives easier and better every day, and invent the next inflection,” Jassy wrote.

Analysts also expect the humanoid market to surge in the coming years. Barclays forecast in a January report that the global market, which it currently values at $2 billion to $3 billion, could reach roughly $40 billion by 2035, or as high as $200 billion “under the most optimistic scenarios.”

Earlier this year, Amazon redeployed much of the team behind Astro and brought in an MIT roboticist to work on the home robot project, LinkedIn profiles show.

It also made a splashy acquisition to supercharge the effort.

In March, Amazon scooped up New York-based Fauna Robotics, which has built a 3.5-foot-tall humanoid called Sprout. At the time, the company said Fauna would become part of a new division dubbed the Personal Robotics Group.

Some Personal Robotics Group staffers previously worked in Amazon’s Lab126 R&D unit, which has been behind many of Amazon’s most successful consumer hardware products, like the Kindle e-reader, Echo smart speakers, Fire TV and Fire Tablet. Lab126 was also behind one of Amazon’s biggest flops, the Fire Phone.

It’s unclear what kind of home robot the group is developing, or the types of tasks it could handle, but a June job posting hinted at an effort to “create robots that are not just functional, but delightful.”

Amazon could be looking to adapt Fauna’s robots for homes or businesses. The Sprout humanoid, which was designed to be “friendly and capable” with expressive yellow eyebrows, has primarily been used by developers, as well as commercial and academic researchers.

An Amazon job posting published online in October describes a “Field Support Engineer” who can assist with customer support and on-site repair, while another listing seeks a user experience designer to “define what it feels like to live with a Fauna robot.”

“Our goal is simple: make robots people actually want to live and interact with in everyday human spaces,” the listing states.

Amazon spokesperson Brad Glasser told CNBC in a statement that the company acquired Fauna because it’s “committed to tackling the challenges that can unlock the personal robotics category.”

“We’re optimistic about a future where personal robots are helping people in meaningful ways in everyday life, and we intend to play an important role in making that future a reality,” Glasser said.

Glasser noted that there remains a substantial gap between what’s possible in a controlled lab and what’s possible in settings like the living room or a lobby. Amazon is working with the robotics community to solve these challenges, he said.

Emily Lugo Velez has been living with the Astro in her North Carolina home since 2023. Lugo Velez, who worked in IT and now runs an AI advisory business, said she and her husband weren’t fazed by the robot’s $1,000-plus price tag and quickly joined the waitlist.

“We spent so much money on this thing,” Lugo Velez, 52, said in an interview. “I feel like we’re just stuck with it, and we’ll let it run around the house until it eventually dies, then send it to the trash heap.”

She said she still uses the device to check on her pets and appliances when she’s out of the house. But beyond that, Astro has primarily become a party trick and a “trip hazard.”

Most days, she tells Astro to go back to its charging dock.

Executives who worked on Astro had discussed making it more capable by attaching an arm to pick up and inspect items without breaking them, said Ken Washington, who served as Amazon’s VP of consumer robotics until 2023.

He told CNBC that he pushed for a bipedal robot, but leadership disagreed.

“We had Jeff [Bezos] in for show and tells and reviews, and I watched his body language pretty closely,” Washington said. “I think he was disappointed with the lack of functionality, but I think he was impressed with its ability to map and navigate an undefined space under all lighting conditions.”

For all the struggles with Astro, Amazon has a rich history in robotics.

The company acquired Kiva Systems for $775 million in 2012, which introduced mobile robots to its vast fulfillment network. Since then, Amazon’s warehouse automation efforts have ballooned to over one million robots across its facilities that can pick, sort and ferry items to workers.

But homes offer unique obstacles for robots to navigate.

“The home is a completely different space,” said Jeff Burnstein, president of the trade group Association for Advancing Automation, who has been in the robotics industry for 45 years. “Children, pets, grandparents, stairways. Nobody’s home is set up exactly the same, so it’s a much more challenging environment for a robot, certainly a robot that’s walking.”

Amazon may have more luck its second time around because the tools for building robots have advanced by “leaps and bounds” over the past few years, said Colin Angle, a co-founder and former CEO of Roomba maker iRobot.

Amazon attempted to acquire iRobot in 2022 before walking away from the deal two years later amid growing regulatory pushback.

“The toolkit that the Astro team had when they did it was clubs with nails in them, just incredibly primitive,” Angle said. “It’s difficult to understate just how much the robot industry has changed in the last two years.”

Advances in AI models, sensors, battery systems and key mechanical components like actuators have spurred a new wave of development around robots for industrial and consumer use.

Elon Musk’s Tesla
 has been developing its bipedal Optimus robots since 2021. Startups including Apptronik, Boston Dynamics, China’s Unitree, Figure and 1X are also building humanoids. Agility Robotics
, the company behind the bipedal Digit robot that counts Amazon as one of its backers, went public via a SPAC on Thursday.

Venture capital firms poured $33.4 billion into robotics and physical AI companies in the first half of the year, compared with $28.7 billion for all of 2025, according to PitchBook data.

Most humanoids are being developed with the manufacturing, logistics and healthcare industries in mind, but a growing group of companies are attempting to build robots for the home.

Apple
 is reportedly working on several home robot projects, including a tabletop device that resembles the Pixar lamp. Hugging Face, which Nvidia
 agreed to acquire for almost $13 billion in September, released the $399 Microduck in August. Angle, in May, launched a startup building fuzzy companion robots called Familiar Machines & Magic. Companies including Sunday, Tau and Nori claim their robots can help with household chores like folding laundry and clearing the table, but they remain mostly prototype or niche devices.

″[Astro] was so ahead of its time,” Washington said. “It was such a big, massive leap that I felt like we had the right to own the home.”

The robot’s limited functionality and its $1,000-plus price tag likely made it a tough sell for many consumers, said a former Amazon employee who worked on Astro, who asked not to be named in order to speak frankly about the project.

“Our poor little Astro was around $2,000 when it came out, and that’s a lot,” the ex-employee said. “That’s a lot for a consumer, and they want a robot that does a lot.”

Amazon takes a long term view on new markets like personal robotics, and values what can be gained by being an early entrant, Glasser said.

Astro was designed to help Amazon build competencies and focus its ambition, he added. The company has applied many of the learnings, talent and experience from Astro into its other robotics efforts, Glasser said.

In Facebook groups for Astro owners, users have complained of diminished customer service and griped that Amazon’s AIexa+ AI assistant isn’t supported on Astro.

Some users have interpreted this to mean Astro could be discontinued. Others have tried to dump their units at a discount on eBay and Facebook Marketplace.

Glasser said Amazon continues to support Astro customers.

Joe Martin, an Astro owner who lives near Tucson, Arizona, said he feels he’s gotten his money’s worth out of the device over the past four years. He’d welcome another robot into his home if it could do more, like helping out around the house.

“Astro was $1,000 and it was pretty limited, but if it could bring a drink to me or dust furniture, I’d be intrigued by that,” Martin, 65, said. “I think that’s right around the corner.”

https://www.cnbc.com/make-it/2026/11/08/.title: Brands are sponsoring IRL communities. Some experts say that could spell their end
https://www.cnbc.com/make-it/2026/11/08/.author: Gili Malinsky
https://www.cnbc.com/make-it/2026/11/08/.text:
On a brisk Saturday in October, more than 80 people try to shuffle into the small Corner Bookstore in New York City’s Upper East Side. They’re part of local literary community Lit Club NYC’s quarterly book crawl. Today’s event, where some attendees are “slightly over sci-fi” and others are in their “rom-com era,” is sponsored by Tinder.

The Lit Club-Tinder partnership was facilitated by Offline, a platform for connecting hosts of gatherings across the U.S. with advertisers keen to sponsor their events. The goal is to help advertisers “deliver outsized media performance and drive growth,” according to Offline’s website. Offline founder Andrew Roth, 28, is also keen to help hosts ensure their gatherings are sustainable long term.

Kelly Chervin is just such a host. Chervin, 35, founded Lit Club in March 2025 as a way to meet other Latina readers and connect over literature. But she has bills to pay. “If we want to have a literary community be around sustainably,” says Chervin, “then paid partnerships are part of that.”

For the Tinder collab, Chervin makes $20 per attendee, and must throw in deliverables like social media posts highlighting the partnership. On Lit Club’s Instagram, a recent post included the line “You can now discover events like these on the @tinder app!”

Whether community members will stay connected when a sponsor gets attached remains to be seen. Some experts are optimistic about the opportunity this kind of marriage presents, while others are certain it will eventually bring about communities’ demise.

Either way, many intimate gatherings around the country are quickly adding a sales pitch.

Roth began his career by founding Gen Z-focused research and consulting company DCDX while studying at Vanderbilt University in 2020. The company has worked with major brands including Chipotle, Hinge and Spotify and was recently acquired by Visible Ventures for an undisclosed sum. Roth will stay on as a Board Advisor.

In 2024, while still at DCDX, Roth had the opportunity to work on an advertising campaign for fragrance company Le Monde Gourmand at in-person events with communities like those on which Offline now focuses.

He says it made him wonder: “Can we bring those [advertising] dollars into the real world and help these communities be preserved?” In September 2025, he and fellow entrepreneur Chris Banks officially launched Offline.

The company’s platform enables hosts of gatherings across the country, from mom groups to run clubs to literary circles, to create a profile including details about how often events happen and how many people tend to show up. Brands can then use the site to match with profiles and events that fit their target audience and create a brief for a campaign that hosts can submit ideas to.

Offline now features more than 900 communities altogether, says Roth, with hosts making an average payout of $2,500 to $3,000 per event.

“The language we always use is ‘intimacy at scale,’” he says.

For hosts like Chervin, the opportunity to generate revenue is critical. Lit Club’s current income streams include ticketed events, a monetized newsletter and brand partnerships.

Chervin is choosy about the partnerships she takes on, she says. They have to feel organic. The Tinder tie-in, for instance, checks a couple of boxes: “Tinder really wants to move to in-person connection,” she says as an example, which is at the core of her mission as well.

Michael Lombardo, 43, discovered bird watching in 2019 and was immediately struck by how fun and present the activity was. It made him feel “like the eight-year-old version of myself,” he says, “where I was actually inhabiting the world.”

Lombardo founded the McGolrick Bird Club in April 2023. Named for Brooklyn, New York’s McGolrick Park, the free, weekly meetup convenes every Saturday morning, when he and others go bird watching. The event now has about 100 weekly attendees, and many of them are repeat guests.

Lombardo recently started dabbling with brand partnerships and connected with Offline earlier this year. For him, any partnership would have to benefit the community in some way, he says. But as a freelance graphic designer and writer, it’s something he’ll consider given the bigger picture of his life and priorities.

“I do need to support my family,” he says. “I have two children.”

Experts differ on what they think introducing the element of advertising to the groups could mean for the human connection they provide.

Amit Kumar, an assistant professor of marketing, psychological and brain sciences at the University of Delaware, is hopeful about the potential of these events, regardless of a brand’s involvement. For him, the point is to create as many opportunities as possible for people to meet.

“As long as they actually are allowing people to engage with one another and connect with one another,” he says, “there’s a potential benefit to that.”

Professor of sociology at Cornell University Benjamin Cornwell is not so sure. A community that got together organically through a genuine, shared interest is no longer organic once fueled and harnessed by a profit-motivated company, he says.

When that happens, community organizers risk introducing unwelcome messaging. Members may “lose faith in the original purpose,” he says, adding that some will even “drop out.” That won’t necessarily happen immediately, he says. But, “it’s inevitable.”

Back at the book crawl, attendees’ opinions differ about Tinder’s involvement.

Some think it’s cool Tinder is branching out into IRL events. Others don’t like the implication that the event is somehow a ruse to meet a significant other, rather than a way to just meet people in general. Some people don’t mind as long as the company doesn’t feel too pushy in its agenda.

In September, Chervin partnered with an AI company at one of her events and appeared in an ad for Meta’s AI tool Muse.

That sparked a conversation among members about which partnerships make sense for the community. Many understood the importance of corporate contributions to Lit Club if they want the events to be sustainable long-term, she says. Ultimately, Chervin lost no paid subscribers.

But among her larger community, she says, “a few people did tell me they don’t think they can come back.”

Roth stands by the financial ecosystem Offline is trying to build.

“If 10 years from now people look at us and say, ‘Oh, these are the evil guys that bastardized IRL,’ so be it,” he says. “But I’ll look at that and say, you know, we paid out a billion dollars to organizers, and we’ve created I don’t know how many more events.”

https://www.scmp.com/news/china/military.title: Is China getting faster at integrating new nuclear missiles into its forces?
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/military.author: Gabriel Dominguez
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/military.text:
Newest ICBM the DF-61 has progressed to routine drills but that does not necessarily point to more efficient development, analysts say

But analysts told the SCMP that the fast progress could be to do with similarities between the DF-61 and the older DF-41 ICBM, though little is publicly known about the new missile.

China has not disclosed technical specifications for the DF-61, including its range or how many nuclear warheads it can carry.

Estimates vary considerably, with the SCMP previously reporting a possible range of 12,000km (7,450 miles) to 15,000km (9,320 miles), while defence intelligence company Janes has estimated a maximum range of about 18,000km (11,180 miles) and capacity for up to 12 nuclear warheads.

The Pentagon has assessed that the older DF-31A – with a range exceeding 11,000km – can reach most of the continental United States. The DF-41 has an estimated range of up to 15,000km, according to the Centre for Strategic and International Studies.

In a CCTV report marking the 66th anniversary of China’s first successful ballistic missile launch, Shao said the DF-61 had completed development, design finalisation, trial fielding and reliability verification before it was unveiled, suggesting it was already technically mature.

He said its compatibility with the rocket force’s command, communications and support networks, together with the service’s experience training ICBM crews, had allowed units to familiarise themselves with the weapon quickly.

Shao added that routine training involved field manoeuvres, repositioning and launch procedures – all aimed at strengthening the ability of land-based nuclear missiles to survive an attack and get past enemy defences.

The missiles are intended to allow China – which has a no-first-use nuclear policy – to retaliate if attacked with atomic weapons.

Ankit Panda, a nuclear weapons specialist at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, said earlier Chinese ICBMs had generally taken far longer to enter service, judging from open-source evidence and US intelligence assessments. He said the DF-61 “does appear to be notably quicker”.

But that comparison has limits. “We don’t have good enough public or open-source information about the development and testing of this system yet,” Panda said.

Tong Zhao, another Carnegie nuclear specialist, compared the histories of two earlier missiles. The DF-31 was first publicly displayed in 1999 but, according to many international researchers, did not enter operational service until around 2006. In comparison, the DF-41 underwent a series of reported flight tests between 2012 and 2018, according to Janes, before it was unveiled at a 2019 military parade.

China has disclosed neither the DF-61’s development timeline nor a verifiable flight-test record. However, Beijing said last year that all weapons showcased in the 2025 parade – where the DF-61 made its debut – were in service already.

Zhao said the DF-61’s progress might be considered unusually fast if it was an entirely new design, but that might not be the case if it was an upgraded DF-41 with improvements made to its launch procedures, survivability or its ability to break through missile defences.

Mackenzie Knight-Boyle, of the Federation of American Scientists’ Nuclear Information Project, said the DF-61 and DF-41 had nearly identical launchers and missile canisters, though images of the DF-61 missile had not been publicly released.

“The speed at which the missile has progressed through training as well as its compatibility with existing command and support networks would make sense if it is, in fact, a modified version of the DF-41 ICBM rather than an entirely new missile,” Knight-Boyle said.

“We can’t assume from this … that the rocket force has become faster or more efficient at developing new ICBMs,” she added.

Beyond questions about its development, the DF-61’s operational readiness is also difficult to establish. Entering service does not necessarily mean full operational readiness, which also requires trained personnel, launch vehicles, infrastructure and the ability to carry out assigned missions.

A former US intelligence analyst, speaking on condition of anonymity, said he had not yet seen any satellite imagery confirming an operational DF-61 unit. Deployment would also depend on available infrastructure and sufficient production of missiles and launch vehicles to equip operational units, he said.

A faster integration of new missile systems could have broader strategic implications.

David Logan, an assistant professor of security studies at Tufts University, said China’s increasingly survivable nuclear forces could embolden Beijing to use military force by reducing its vulnerability to a US nuclear first strike.

But greater confidence in its arsenal’s survivability could also reduce the risk of unintended escalation, he added, by easing fears of losing its weapons before they could be used.

“The bottom line is that systems like DF-61 may lead to greater uncertainty on the US side about China’s ability to flexibly scale and shape its strategic force,” Panda from Carnegie said.

“This could drive insecurity in the United States and intensify competitive pressures.”

https://www.dw.com/en/iran-us-strikes-sh.title: Iran: US strikes ship after Hormuz blockade breach
https://www.dw.com/en/iran-us-strikes-sh.text:
The US military said a vessel trying to leave an Iranian port was hit due to the naval blockade on the country. On its part, Iran said three "non compliant" oil tankers caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz.

The United States struck a commercial ship attempting to breach its naval blockade on Iran, the US military said Sunday.

According to the US Central Command (CENTCOM), the cargo vessel "tried to depart regional waters after visiting an Iranian port," before its stern was struck by "precision munitions" shot from a US military aircraft.

In a video posted by CENTCOM, an explosion can be seen on the M/V Huda's stern as a result of the shooting, with the ship's civilian crew ignoring "repeated warnings."

The authorities in the UAE said 22 people had been rescued due to a fire on a vessel in the Gulf of Oman.

The US naval blockade on Iran, intended to pressure the country into lifting its own blockade on the Strait of Hormuz, has been in force for months.

Iran's own blockade of the waterway, through which a fifth of the world's oil and gas supplies flowed before the war started in late February, saw energy prices spike around the world.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards said three "non-compliant" oil tankers caught fire while going through the Strait. Tehran has regularly attacked vessels going through the Strait of Hormuz without its approval.

Elsewhere in the Middle East, the escalation between Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen and Saudi Arabia continued to rage.

Saudi Arabia said it had intercepted incoming missiles shot in the direction of the capital, Riyadh, on Sunday.

Debris from the interception damaged a building belonging to state-owned oil company Aramco. No casualties were reported, but some of the building's floors were heavily damaged, witnesses told AP.

Saudi Arabia accused Yemen-based militant group Houthisof launching two ballistic missiles and two cruise missiles.

While Houthis carried out such attacks in the past, the rebels have not claimed responsibility for the attack yet.

According to the Houthis, 33 people were killed in Saudi-led attacks on Yemen's rebel-held capital, Sanaa, on Saturday.

https://www.dw.com/en/should-ai-companie.title: Should AI companies pay for the journalism they use?
https://www.dw.com/en/should-ai-companie.text:
Publishers say AI chatbots are using their reporting to answer readers' questions while sending back less traffic and less money. Should the companies that build these tools pay for the journalism they rely on?

Millions of people now use AI chatbots as a source of news to find quick answers to questions about current events.

A 2026 survey by the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism, which questioned more than 90,000 people worldwide, found that 10% use AI chatbots for news on a weekly basis, a figure that is significantly higher among younger audiences.

Explaining what is happening in the world, why it matters, and what it means has traditionally been the work of journalism. Media organizations send reporters into the field, commission investigations and conduct research, producing stories that help audiences understand global events. But as more people turn to AI tools for information, the relationship between those producing journalism and those distributing it is changing.

"In the past, search engines like Google indexed our websites and directed users to their articles, generating traffic in return," Julia Becker, publisher of Funke Media Group, told a panel at the Global Media Forum (GMF) in Berlin. "But now that exchange has broken down."

"AI companies draw on our quality reporting to generate answers, yet the reporting itself often remains largely invisible by the end of this process," said DW Director General Barbara Massing in a keynote address at the forum.

Their remarks reflect a worry that is growing across the media industry. Publicly available news is copied and summarized by AI chatbots, while news organizations are becoming less and less able to rely on the money and visibility that used to come from distributing that work.

There has been growing concern about how copyrighted material is collected, used, and reproduced by artificial intelligence, and whether the companies that build those systems should pay the people and organizations that created the material.

Media houses are now pressing "Big Tech" companies to ask permission before using their work and to pay for it.

In October, German broadcasters ARD and RTL, along with the country's Federal Association of Digital Publishers and Newspaper Publishers (BDZV) and the Association of Private Media (VAUNET), called for stronger copyright protections for media companies.

In the US, lawsuits are adding pressure. The New York Times has sued internet company Brave Softwar for allegedly using its content without permission and getting around its paywall.

Meanwhile, legal institutions in the EU, including the European Court of Justice (ECJ) are examining whether AI-generated answers can themselves infringe copyright.

In February, a coalition of media organizations, including the Guardian, the BBC, and the Financial Times, called for rules that would give publishers more control over how AI systems copy and reproduce their content.

The problem goes beyond whether AI companies may use journalism. It also concerns how publishers and journalists can get paid when their work becomes part of the answers AI systems generate.

"AI systems shouldn't just use quality journalism. They should also pay for it," Massing said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Professor Martin Senftleben, who directs the Institute for Information Law at the University of Amsterdam, separates two ways AI companies use journalistic material: Training their models and generating responses to individual user questions.

Payment for training is a more complicated legal question, he said. The more urgent issue is what happens when an AI system uses journalism to answer a question in real time.

He argued that European copyright law may already offer a way to address part of the problem. Under existing EU law, publishers and journalists may be able to claim payment collectively, without waiting for a new legal framework.

"What are we waiting for? Germany is a large member state. This should be introduced in Germany," he told the forum.

One option, Senftleben suggested, is a legally required payment system in which every AI response that draws on journalism triggers a payment. A collecting organization would gather the money and distribute it among publishers and journalists, in the same way that music royalties are collected and distributed.

Once such a system exists, publishers and authors could use its rates as a starting point when negotiating individual licensing deals with AI companies.

Lutz Mache, senior manager of government affairs and public policy at Google, told the GMF panel that Google is willing to negotiate agreements with German media companies and to discuss new AI products with them.

Google has also started testing other ways to pay publishers for their contributions to AI-generated answers. Its "AI Contribution" pilot, which is being tested with selected publishers, aims to reward content that plays a significant role in answers produced by products such as Gemini and AI Overviews. But the program is still an early experiment, not a general payment system open to all publishers.

Microsoft, Anthropic, and OpenAI have recently said they support clearer, standardized signals that let website owners state whether their content may be used to train AI models.

However, not everyone thinks more regulation is the answer.

Jörg Heidrich, a lawyer who specializes in technology law and serves as AI commissioner at the German media company Heise, warned against adding new rules without considering their effects on the wider tech sector.

Europe has already fallen behind in the global AI race, he argued. More regulation, he warned, could make it harder for European companies to compete with major providers based elsewhere.

Heidrich also pointed to smaller players, including startups, independent developers, and research institutions. They depend on access to data to build and train AI systems. He argued that the debate over copyright and payment risks overlooking these groups, and that new restrictions could hurt their work.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmvg.title: Nandy rejects claims of politicising Remembrance Sunday after Erasmus row
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmvg.text:
Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has rejected accusations of politicising Remembrance Sunday after being criticised for linking the event to the UK rejoining the European Union's Erasmus scheme.

Her department announced on Saturday night that "as we mark Remembrance Sunday, Erasmus+ will give a new generation the chance to build connections across Europe".

That sparked a backlash from the Conservatives who said "veterans did not fight for a student exchange scheme" and accused her of making an "EU membership pitch".

Nandy said she was "horrified" by the Tory response and insisted the expanded EU scheme for study and work would help young Britons recognise wartime sacrifice.

The UK is rejoining the scheme in January, six years after leaving as part of the Brexit deal.

On Saturday, the Department for Culture, Media and Sport drew comparisons between that scheme and events on Sunday to commemorate veterans.

Referring to the scheme, Nandy said in her department's press release: "As we remember the immense courage of those who served our country, we honour them by building the best opportunities for the next generation through closeness and collaboration with our allies."

Conservative Party chairman Kevin Hollinrake described her comments as "tone deaf and frankly shameful" and called on Nandy to apologise.

He said the bonds that veterans forged "run far deeper" than Erasmus.

"It is not a day for a Labour minister to try to make an EU membership pitch," he added.

Reform leader Nigel Farage told the BBC: "For Lisa Nandy to use Remembrance Sunday to announce this and say it's all about peace, it's all about the war - I find that very, very poor taste."

Peter Sharples, chief executive of the Veterans Institute, told The Telegraph people should "just honour the fallen" on Remembrance Sunday rather than discussing "party political matters".

Asked about the row on the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme, Nandy stood by her initial remarks.

"It was Winston Churchill after the Second World War who talked about extending the hand of friendship across Europe and making sure that we honoured the legacy of that generation," she said.

She said that after Brexit "we closed off opportunities for young people from this country to understand not just the impact that generation made here in the UK, but the way in which they went off and fought for the freedom of people across Europe".

Asked to respond to accusations she had chosen Remembrance Sunday to "promote part of the new deal the government has done with the EU", Nandy said she was "not choosing today or any day actually to promote a deal with the EU".

Pressed about linking the day to what the government believes are the cultural benefits of the scheme, Nandy said: "There was a time where that wouldn't have even raised an eyebrow as somehow political, it was just common sense - and it is common sense."

The UK is paying £570m to join the expanded Erasmus+ scheme, which the government said was a 30% discount. It will include free year-abroad placements for UK university students and their European peers as well as cultural exchanges.

The government said free train passes would be available for 18-year-olds to visit EU countries by themselves or with up to five friends.

Youth groups will also get to do short exchanges in other countries, with a focus on areas of the country less engaged with Erasmus previously such as the north of England and Midlands, the government said.

Applications will open for Erasmus+ later this month.

Farage described Erasmus as a "terrible scheme" and "wildly expensive" compared to the Turing Scheme, which ministers introduced in 2021.

He also criticised ongoing negotiations between the UK and the EU for a new youth mobility scheme, ahead of a major summit on 20 November.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he wants an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and EU.

But the EU's former Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier has warned that the UK cannot "cherry pick" which elements of the single market to which it subscribes.

Nandy said on Sunday that most of the benefits of Brexit promised in 2016 "have not been realised" and "there are trade-offs and choices to be made" on Britain's future relationship with the EU.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Cop31 must deliver climate progress that people can see is real, host says
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Adam Morton in Melbourne, and Fiona Harvey, Oliver Milman and Graham Readfearn in Antalya
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
High-stakes talks involving 190 countries begin on Monday as world grapples with El Niño supercharged by fossil fuels

The Cop31 summit must produce progress, “a tangible outcome ... that people can see is real”, its host has said as scores of world leaders and representatives of close to 190 countries gather in Turkey for the UN climate talks.

The high-stakes meeting begins on Monday, as countries around the world grapple with the strongest El Niño weather system on record, supercharged by fossil fuels, which is set to take hundreds of thousands of lives and cause damage costing trillions of dollars.

Friction is expected between the rich and poor worlds over who pays for the impacts of the climate crisis, and the slow pace of cutting greenhouse gas emissions. Temperatures have broken records this year, surpassing the limit of 1.5C above preindustrial levels aimed for in the 2015 Paris climate agreement.

Adão Soares Barbosa, the chair of the Least Developed Countries, a negotiating group of 44 nations, said: “Keeping 1.5C within reach by minimising the duration and magnitude of the overshoot, delivering accessible and predictable climate finance, strengthening adaptation, and addressing loss and damage [caused to poor countries by extreme weather] are not political choices but matters of survival. The credibility of the Paris agreement will be measured not by promises made, but by commitments fulfilled, and lives protected in vulnerable countries.”

Unusually, the talks will have dual hosts: they will take place in the Turkish city of Antalya but the formal negotiations will be presided over by Australia, following a compromise reached last year over their competing bids.

Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate and energy minister and president of negotiations for Cop31, told the Guardian in an interview: “We need a tangible outcome focused on implementation [of emissions cuts and finance] that people can see is real. We need progress, it needs to be a step forward on previous Cops.”

Australia also wants a “strong, ambitious outcome” to raise the plight of low-lying countries in the Pacific region for whom the climate crisis poses an existential threat. “We need to finally elevate some of the issues so important to our Pacific family,” Bowen said. “[Only] 0.2% of the world’s available climate finance goes to small island developing states for adaptation, for countries whose very existence is at stake.”

But climate advocates and more than 500 scientists in Australia said Australia must stop approving coalmines and gas projects if it wanted to escape the charge of hypocrisy.

The summit will have a notable absentee, with the US refusing to send a delegation for the second year in a row. The Trump administration wants no part of “extremist climate policies” embraced by other countries, according to a White House spokesperson.

Donald Trump expressed glee shortly before the US midterm elections about the huge profits made by oil and gas companies due to the Iran war, which he started and has caused an increase in living costs around the world. “I don’t give a damn,” the president said at a recent rally in Georgia. “I’m going to say it: we’re making a frickin’ fortune.”

However, a group of 20 Democratic members of Congress have made the trip to Antalya, buoyed by their party’s stunning success in the US midterms last week that will enable them to stymie Trump’s attempts to dismantle pollution rules and withhold financial support for clean energy.

Developing countries and civil society will seek to put climate finance and justice at the heart of the Cop31 talks. Rukiya Khamis, the east Africa programme manager at the 350.org campaigning group, said: “Across east Africa, people are facing the devastating impacts of a climate crisis they did not cause. From prolonged droughts to destructive floods, we are losing homes, livelihoods and access to food and water. Yet the money needed to respond to these impacts remains out of reach for many of the countries and communities most affected. It is fundamentally unjust that those least responsible are being left to carry the greatest costs.”

Sign up to Down to Earth

The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential

after newsletter promotion

This summer more than 50,000 people died in Europe due to heatwaves, severe wildfire smoke shrouded swathes of North America and a glacier collapse in Nepal triggered a landslide that caused more than 1,500 deaths, while the El Niño weather event, described as “staggering” by scientists and still to reach its peak, is gathering strength.

However, while the pace of progress on cutting global emissions has been slow, the Iran war has spurred many countries to see fossil fuels as expensive and vulnerable to shocks, while renewables continue to plummet in price.

Simon Stiell, the UN’s climate chief, said before the talks: “Climate impacts hit every population and every economy harder each year. [But] almost every major economy, and many medium-sized and smaller economies, now see climate action as a central driver of economic growth, jobs, and affordable and secure energy.”

Cop host Turkey also wants more countries to switch to electric technologies, such as electric vehicles and heat pumps, as these are many times more efficient than their fossil fuel counterparts. A target for 35% of global final energy to come from electricity by 2035 will be on the table, but faces opposition from some.

Both presidency countries rely heavily on fossil fuels. Australia is one of the world’s leading exporters of coal and liquefied natural gas. The centre-left Labor government has targets to reach net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, and have more than 80% of its electricity generated by solar and wind by 2030, but is off track to meet them.

Labor also faces a political threat from the resurgent rightwing One Nation party, which dismisses climate science. One Nation and the Liberal and National party coalition want to scrap the net zero goal.

The UK energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, said: “This summer, we all felt it: climate change is here, in Britain, now. No country can tackle it alone, which is why Cop31 matters. The answer to high bills and climate change is the same – more clean, homegrown power, creating good jobs and warmer homes. Cop31 is about Britain’s national interest.”
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.summary: The Cop31 summit will take place in Turkey on Monday, with 190 countries in Turkey. Temperatures have broken records this year, surpassing the limit of 1.5C above preindustrial levels. Labor government has targets to reach net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: UK spent £100m on zombie Brexit border inspection posts
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Lisa O’Carroll and Joanna Partridge
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
Five of seven facilities in England and Wales never reached operational stage as Tories vacillated over plans to check goods

The UK wasted at least £100m in taxpayers’ money to set up zombie Brexit border inspection posts that were never used, it has been revealed.

The overall cost of Brexit was put at an estimated £4.7bn by the National Audit Office last year but this included years-long transformation of the software used for customs declarations and other systems built to cope with the UK leaving the single market.

Now fresh information from HMRC on the exact spend on the seven “inland border facilities” has come to light. The sites were built but quickly decommissioned as the Conservative government at the time vacillated over plans to check goods coming in from the continent.

Five of the seven “inland border facilities” in England and Wales never got to operational stage because the Tories decided not to implement all the border checks after concluding food coming from the EU would be the same high standard as it was before Brexit.

Portsmouth port, which is owned by the city council, spent £23m on building its border control post, which has never been used at full capacity because of the decision to scale back the checks.

The port received £17.1m in government funding for the project, leaving the council to make up the £6m shortfall, which could otherwise have been spent on essential services.

The EU launched all the checks in Calais, Dublin and other European ports from day one as the UK was treated as a “third country” overnight. The most controversial British zombie facility was known as “Dover white cliffs”. Furious residents at the village of Guston were told of the plans for the inland border facility on 31 December 2020, just hours before a “transition year” ended and Brexit was due to be implemented with supposed checks on all lorries coming across the Channel.

Information from HMRC, released under a freedom of information request, shows the facility has so far cost the taxpayer £28m, even though it remains a field. The Department for Transport paid £21m to procure the site and spent a further £7m on initial ground works, including an archaeological survey for any roman remains.

Another £17m was spent on a border facility in Birmingham planned at the airport car park. Newly released information shows it cost £11m to build with £6m in “closure costs”.

Another £20m was spent on sites in Warrington and in Ebbsfleet, a town just south of the Dartford Bridge on the Thames estuary. The Warrington site, on the former Shearings holidays coach stop at Appleton Thorn, was chosen because there were no suitable sites available for lorries coming from Ireland into Liverpool, Holyhead and Heysham ports.

Local people vehemently opposed the site at the time. It cost £7m to buy, £9m to build and £1m to decommission.

Another £10m was spent preparing customs and other checks at the former car park at Eurostar Ebbsfleet International train station, which cost £4m to convert into a lorry park and £6m to close, according to HMRC data.

A further £5m was spent on another site tucked away off the M11, just south of Stansted, at North Weald airfield. This airfield was commandeered for the same purpose, to avert congestion on the M25. It cost £3m to build and £2m to close down.

HMRC said Birmingham, Ebbsfleet and North Weald “did not require the acquisition of land”. The decision to build Brexit lorry parks so far from Dover underlined the lack of preparation for the UK’s departure from the EU.

Most of the UK’s lorry traffic is concentrated in Dover, but as a designated area of outstanding beauty it was impossible to conduct the post-Brexit customs and standard checks near the port.

The UK finally opted for a site 20 miles inland at Sevington in Kent, but even that was last minute. The government previously revealed in a parliamentary question that total capital costs ran to £154m.

This included £30m on the acquisition of farmland between Sevington and Mersham for Britain’s principal Brexit border facility and another £70m to build.

HMRC has revealed through freedom of information that the operational costs have run to £179m, money that would not have been spent had Brexit not happened.

The second site that remains operational is Holyhead – a small site close to the main road to the port which receives goods from Ireland. According to the FoI, the site cost £14m to acquire and another £23m to build.

The figures are separate to investments made by Eurotunnel, the Port of Dover and other ports including Portsmouth. Eurotunnel spent €50m (£41.7m) on building the infrastructure for Brexit checks for trucks and €90m on changes for passengers, including an entry and exit system that has never been activated by the French.

The £23m border control post at Portsmouth, the UK’s second-busiest cross-Channel port, now faces an uncertain future. The hi-tech facility was built to government specifications to handle post-Brexit checks. Two trailer checks take place on average each day, according to the port’s director, Mike Sellers, compared with the 80 checks originally envisioned.

He said: “Given the border post’s location within the operational port, ideally we would look to repurpose it rather than demolish it, but it will cost us almost as much to repurpose as to demolish. It was bespoke and built for food import checks and biosecurity, it is not suitable for general warehousing and will have to be changed.”

Sellers and Portsmouth city council’s leader are among the ports calling on the government to provide compensation for the border posts that will become redundant when the UK government’s deal with the EU comes into force.
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.summary: Portsmouth city council's leader is among the ports calling for compensation for border posts. The UK government's deal with the EU comes into force in the coming months.

https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/n.title: Women in media alleging abuse too often not protected, Lisa Nandy says
https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/n.author: Pippa Crerar Political editor
https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/n.text:
Culture secretary says there is still a problem in the industry and public life after Russell Brand conviction

The culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, has said there is still a problem with exploitation and abuse in the media industry and a failure to properly deal with allegations after Russell Brand’s conviction for rape and sexual assault.

She said women who came forward were too often not protected by institutions across public life, including in politics, and that huge power imbalances meant speaking up came at a very heavy cost.

Nandy told the media industry that “time is up” to bring in systems to protect vulnerable whistleblowers, and said that while the BBC had taken action in recent years, other organisations still had to take the issue seriously.

Brand’s conviction on Thursday renewed scrutiny of how the UK’s entertainment industry has treated celebrities accused of abusing their power, with some women saying they feared that speaking out could harm their careers.

Brand faces sentencing on Monday after being found guilty of raping a woman and sexually assaulting three others.

Nandy said last week that the case must be a wake-up call to the media world and beyond, after widespread concerns over failures to confront Brand’s behaviour. It emerged after the verdicts that he is under investigation for two further rape allegations.

In an interview with the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme, Nandy was asked whether she thought there was still a problem in the media and creative industries. “Yes, I do, and I think hand on heart I can’t say to you as the culture secretary that this is not happening today. In fact, if I had to wager, I would say it is,” she said.

“The biggest reason I say that, and I won’t say it lightly, is because I do not see that much has changed in terms of the way that institutions in the media industry and across public life, including politics, deal with women who very bravely come forward to allege abuse. I think they’re not protected.

“I think that they work in industries like politics and media where the power imbalances are huge, where they’re often on short-term flexible contracts, and where who you know and reputation is often the key to career advancement. Speaking up has a very heavy cost.”

She praised the BBC for signing up to the Creative Industries Independent Standards Authority, a whistleblowing body, and for taking other steps in recent years, but she said there was more the corporation could do.

“There are other institutions that haven’t done that, and time is up,” she said. “It really is time for the media industry to take this seriously and to put those practices into action.”

Nandy had said earlier on Sky News Sunday Morning that the government was considering what further steps it could take to help protect whistleblowers in such circumstances.
https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/n.summary: Lisa Nandy says there is still a problem in the media and public life after Russell Brand conviction. She says women who came forward were too often not protected by institutions across public life. Nandy said the case must be a wake-up call to the media world and beyond.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: ‘I just got AI emails rejecting my application – or no reply at all’: this is the soul-crushing reality of being a Neet | John Harris
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: John Harris
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Alan Milburn describes them as a ‘lost generation’. Those I spoke to just want to know what they have to do to finally get a job – and a chance in life

C
allum Atkinson is 23 years old, and lives in the Greater Manchester town of Rochdale. Until very recently, he was one of hundreds of thousands of young people in the UK reckoned not to be in education, employment or training: what officialspeak rather coldly terms a Neet, and therefore part of a huge national problem being investigated by the former New Labour high-up Alan Milburn, whose final report on young people and work is due any day now, and will be a big, hyped-up political event.

Milburn – quite rightly – thinks the UK’s estimated 981,000 Neets represent the profound risk of “a lost generation” and a “moral crisis” that is already upon us. If you are interested in matters of finance as well as ethics, you may also be aware that the annual cost of maintaining such young people was recently put at £125bn, which is more than the British state spends on either education or defence.

Until a month or so ago, Callum told me last week, he was one tiny element of those statistics. He has three A-levels graded at A, B and C, respectively in maths, further maths and computer science: although educational failure is a major factor in the current crisis, 21% of Neets have at least one A-level or its equivalent, and 15% have graduated from university. What his life so far does point up, however, is the labyrinthine lunacy and callousness of the modern labour market, and how its serial failures are often only finally mended by small, ground-level organisations.

Six months ago, his last spurt of employment – working in finance, “organising invoices, making sure suppliers got paid on time, doing Excel reports” – lasted three months, before he collided with problems in his personal life and fell into a spell of depression. When he was let go by his last employer, he was put on universal credit. Most days, Callum told me, he sat in bed applying for jobs using his phone. “Maybe 600 or 700 at least. And the most I usually got back was an AI email saying, ‘I’m sorry, we’ve decided not to go through with your application, please try again next time.’ Or there was no reply at all.”

And so to some good news. Not long ago, Callum was pointed in the direction of a new Manchester-based charity called Breakout. The people there arranged mentoring sessions and work experience placements. He is now an undergraduate at the University of Salford, studying computer science and artificial intelligence – but what his life experience so far seems to have left him with is only the vaguest sense of his own future. When I asked him for his thoughts on the subject, there was an uneasy silence. “My plan is just to get through university,” he eventually said.

Breakout was founded by Roman Dibden, a spirited 30-year-old who himself has experience of being a Neet. When we spoke last week about the Milburn review, he said he had one big concern: that the kind of outsourcing corporates who tend to land government contracts would be the main beneficiaries of its recommendations. The fact that Milburn wants local authorities to deliver his recommendations, Dibden said, may well force such companies into a cosmetic reinvention: “My fear is that will see the same big providers putting on a grassroots badge and carrying on like before,” he said. “But these are real human lives we’re talking about. We need people who actually get it.”

Humanity, however, is a waning factor in the UK’s increasingly bamboozling jobs machine. Dibden told me he was getting an increasing sense of recruitment systems in which applications written using AI are then robotically read by machines that respond with automated knock-backs, a process that renders trying to get a job about as meaningful as buying a scratchcard or lottery ticket. “People can give the jobcentre evidence of so many hours of job search because they’ve scattergunned it out,” he said. “But it leaves young people completely at their wits’ end.”

The day after that conversation, I spoke to another 23-year-old on Breakout’s books: Raihan Ali, who last did any paid work at Christmas in 2025, when he temped at a discount store for 16 hours a week. Like Callum, he is no academic slouch: though the pandemic meant he didn’t sit any formal GCSE exams, he got the second-to-top grade – an eight – in maths and combined science, and a B and two Cs at A-level in maths, physics and chemistry. Once he had decided to take a vocational rather than academic post-school route, it took him nearly a year to get an apprenticeship, doing admin for a chemical company. He was paid £12,000 a year: soon enough, he realised that he wanted to get into accountancy, but an apprenticeship in that line of work lasted only a matter of months.

“It was kind of the dream job for me,” he told me. “But it was fast-paced; very demanding. And going in with basically little-to-no experience, I just couldn’t keep up. Six months later, I’m sat down with a senior manager and HR and they tell me, ‘We can’t keep you.’”

That rupture happened in early 2024. In Hyde, on the eastern edge of Greater Manchester, Raihan lives with his mother – who, like him, currently depends on universal credit – and two siblings, who are still in education. He has long felt a deep responsibility to provide for all four of his family. “I just thought, ‘Oh my God, what am I going to do now?’ I had money coming in, and suddenly there was nothing.” He then began a purgatorial two years of constant job applications, broken only by his brief spell of part-time retail work.

after newsletter promotion

“I’ve just ended up thinking that the good things that have happened to me have been sheer luck,” he said. “And all the bad things have been more like, ‘Well, yeah, no one wants me. I’m not good enough for that.’” On countless occasions, he has been told that he was effectively the runner-up. “And that’s just a terrible feeling, because what can I do to make someone believe that I’m actually the one that they want, rather than always being behind someone else?”

I had two last questions. The first was about his Bangladeshi heritage, and a grim fact cited in the interim report Milburn published in May last year, which pointed out that although Neet rates for young people from Pakistani and Bangladeshi backgrounds run at just below the national average, total adult unemployment among those in the same category currently runs at three times the rate of those classified as white British. “I’ve worried about things like that,” Raihan said. “When they see the name ‘Raihan Ali’ on my CV, do they not actually want me from that alone? I try not to think about them, ’cos it’s out of my control.” He paused. “But yeah. Yeah.”

We were talking via Zoom, and I noticed another of my open tabs, a report about the Milburn review, which bluntly pointed out that our cash-strapped prime minister will “need to find billions of pounds more to fund employment schemes if he wants to get young people back to work”. On an invest-to-save basis, Burnham agreed with that suggestion last week; by Saturday, there were news stories about an extra £6bn.

After 45 minutes spent talking about a country that seemingly cannot offer a future to even some of its comparative achievers, Raihan hinted that from his perspective, one other thing was needed: deep change to some of the most basic ways in which our economy works. Did he, I asked him, have any faith that things might get better? “I think the solutions will just need to be, like, big enough to actually make a difference,” he said. “You can’t take small steps here and there, can you? There’s going to have to be a gigantic amount of change for anything to actually work.”

John Harris is a Guardian columnist

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: New drug could be cure for common cause of high blood pressure
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Ian Sample Science editor
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Benefits of baxdrostat are unexpectedly found to remain up to two years after patients stop taking it

Millions of people with high blood pressure stand to benefit from a new drug that has stunned doctors by reversing a common cause of the condition for years after patients stopped taking the medication.

Patients who took the drug, called baxdrostat, saw their blood pressure improve during a six- to 12-month course of the daily pills, but unexpectedly the benefits remained up to two years later, with some patients no longer on any hypertension drugs and potentially cured of the condition.

“It’s very exciting to see,” said Prof Morris Brown, a hypertension specialist at Queen Mary University of London, who led the study. “Just under a quarter of the patients came off all treatment and had completely normal blood pressure.”

More than a billion people worldwide have high blood pressure, or hypertension, including more than 12 million in the UK. In five to 10 per cent of cases, the condition is caused by small nodules or benign tumours on the adrenal glands that cause them to overproduce a hormone called aldosterone. The excess hormone raises blood pressure by signalling the kidneys to retain salt.

The standard treatment for what is called primary aldosteronism is to surgically remove the affected adrenal gland, but other factors can contribute to the patient’s hypertension, meaning surgery is not always a complete cure.

Baxdrostat is known as an aldosterone synthase inhibitor (ASI) which suppresses the blood pressure-raising hormone. The drug was approved in the US earlier this year for patients with hypertension that is not controlled by existing drugs. It is being assessed by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice), which could make the drug available through the NHS next year.

The potentially curative effect of baxdrostat came to light in a small study that followed 14 patients whose hypertension improved dramatically during a three-month trial of the drug. They continued taking the daily pills for six to 12 months and then stopped. When doctors checked the patients up to two years later, their blood pressure was still lower. Details are published in the New England Journal of Medicine.

Mason Freeman, a professor of medicine at Harvard University, who was involved in the work, said it was too early to say if some of the patients were cured and a larger trial was under way to find out. “If this effect is common and very persistent then the approach to diagnosing and treating these patients is likely to dramatically change,” he said. “Everyone could be treated with the ASI in initial suspicion of the condition and if they responded well they could avoid the invasive diagnostic procedures and the surgery.”

Brown suspected the drug might cure primary aldosteronism because of an experiment in mice 20 years ago. It showed that deleting the gene needed to make aldosterone led to the loss of cells that churned out the hormone.

He suspects baxdrostat has a similar effect. When the drug suppresses aldosterone it causes a surge in highly active molecules called reactive oxygen species. These may selectively destroy the cells that overproduce the hormone.

“Those oxygen radicals are killing the cells and they disappear,” Brown said. “That’s what I think the mechanism is and it’s testable, it’s something we’re doing now in the laboratory.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.title: Egypt’s reopening of its embassy in Tripoli signals regional shift on Libya
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.author: Mohammad Mansour
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.text:
The reopening of the Egyptian embassy in Tripoli marks a fundamental political shift, both domestically and regionally, for Libya, analysts say.

Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty inaugurated the historic embassy building on Saturday, which had been closed for 12 years due to security concerns.

Libya has been politically divided since the fall of Muammar Gaddafi in 2011, with rival administrations formed in Tripoli in the west and Tobruk and Benghazi in the east.

Egypt was widely considered to be backing the eastern authority, effectively led by strongman and renegade military commander Khalifa Haftar, and his self-styled Libyan National Army (LNA), until recent regional developments led Cairo to rethink its approach.

Libyan political analyst Hazem al-Rayes said the reopening of the embassy in Tripoli – which was the seat of the internationally recognised government that Haftar was fighting – is a sign of this.

“I can consider that what Egypt is doing in its recent moves towards the capital, Tripoli, is an attempt to readjust its behaviour in the Libyan file … [for] five years, no Egyptian foreign minister visited the capital,” he told Al Jazeera.

Elias al-Barouni, a political science professor at Libya’s Nalut University, also believes the move goes beyond the resumption of regular consular services in Tripoli.

“We are facing an indicator of a shift in Cairo’s method of managing its relations with the Libyan parties, and a rearrangement of its priorities in dealing with the Libyan crisis,” al-Barouni told Al Jazeera.

There have been several significant political and regional shifts that have somewhat stabilised the volatile situation in Libya, where thousands have been killed in fighting between militias attached to rival political authorities.

In July 2026, Ankara and the LNA reached unprecedented coordination, spearheading agreements to develop military facilities, advanced surveillance systems, and training programmes in Turkiye for eastern Libyan officers.

The deputy commander of eastern Libyan forces and Haftar’s son, Saddam Haftar, has also paid visits to regional capitals, including Turkiye and Qatar, which have supported the United Nations-recognised Government of National Accord (GNA) in Tripoli.

In Libya, rivals recently signed the so-called “4+4 agreement” that sets out a roadmap for possible presidential and legislative elections over the next two years.

Badr Hassan al-Shafei, a professor of African studies and conflict resolution at Cairo University, told Al Jazeera that Egypt came to revisit its policy towards Libya after realising that its reliance on eastern forces, led by Haftar, was not conducive to its overall strategic interests.

“It is clear that Cairo … found that relying on one party or leaning towards one party in Libya, which is Haftar’s party, may not be the right bet perhaps at the present time or even for a while, since the Turkish intervention several years ago,” al-Shafei told Al Jazeera.

“Consequently, perhaps Egypt wants to create a balance or also send a message to Haftar that he should not act unilaterally and that acting should be in coordination with Cairo, so it worked to extend bridges of cooperation with Libya also …”

Egypt has also become more concerned about developments to the south of its border, particularly the expansion of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in Sudan, which had allegedly received support from Haftar.

“Today, Egypt is no longer the Egypt of five years ago when its policies and relations were limited only to the [eastern] authorities in Benghazi,” al-Rayes told Al Jazeera.

It is “convinced today that its ally [LNA], which it supported throughout the past years at the expense of the legitimate government in Tripoli … has distanced itself from it today, and it needs to readjust its political behaviour with Tripoli and with the legitimate government”, he said.

During Abdelatty’s visit to Tripoli, he discussed critical economic files with Libyan officials, including the 2019 maritime border memorandum of understanding signed between Tripoli and Ankara.

According to the Facebook page of the Egyptian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Abdelatty reaffirmed the importance of addressing Egyptian concerns regarding maritime demarcation between Libya and Turkiye in light of international law. The eastern parliament recently ratified the maritime agreement, which it initially opposed.

“Consequently, perhaps Cairo is trying to prevent the ratification of this agreement from causing damage to its interests in gas and oil exploration in the Eastern Mediterranean, and from that it wanted to extend bridges to Tripoli as well,” al-Shafei said.

“Instead of limiting itself to political and diplomatic objection from outside Tripoli, Cairo has become negotiating directly with the Libyan government that signed the agreement.”

Egypt might also be attracted to opportunities that reconstruction and the revival of Libya’s oil industry might bring.

“Perhaps with the reconstruction process, the incoming Egyptian labour will have priority, or even the currently present one will have its living conditions improved, not to mention the idea of the possibility of Egyptian investments and companies entering the reconstruction process,” al-Shafei said.

After years of backing rival sides, a new regional consensus means there is a greater likelihood of rivals in Libya reaching a comprehensive agreement to end the war, al-Rayes told Al Jazeera.

But al-Barouni cautioned that there is still a plethora of issues facing Libya, and only a comprehensive solution can end the divisions within Libya.

“The Libyan problem is not merely a dispute over the name of the head of government, but rather it is a dispute over the nature of power, the distribution of influence, control over institutions and resources, the future of the military institution, and the conditions for reaching elections,” al-Barouni said.

“If Cairo, Ankara, Washington, and other capitals agree on the necessity of ending the division, that is a development that can be built upon, but the success of any settlement remains linked to the ability of the Libyans to formulate an independent national project. Libya needs a settlement that ends the division, not a deal that redistributes the division.”

This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on the pressures of creating content for the internet, follow Mia Sato. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

Almost exactly a decade ago, the media industry was in the middle of a video revolution — or so it thought. In the mid-2010s, publications poured money into burgeoning social media video efforts, chasing the promise of reaching larger audiences and opening new lines of revenue. Print publications and digital news outlets alike hired teams, pumped out content, and entrusted platforms like Facebook with their reach and distribution.

That pivot-to-video slowly revealed itself to be a lot of smoke and mirrors when it became clear that Facebook had inflated video views. Newsrooms cut writers and editors in a move to video — and then cut those video teams when they realized the pivot had not paid off. For many in the media industry, social video brings to mind layoffs and instability rather than the promised abundance.

A “pivot” feels inadequate to describe the current emphasis on social video, not just in newsrooms but in society writ large. Social media companies have reorganized their feeds to emphasize video, spurred by the massive growth of TikTok during the pandemic. But the media industry is still playing catch-up, and in some cases it seems to have been slow to jump in (perhaps cautious given past experience).

https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/third-chi.title: The latest status symbol of the 1% is a third kid. ‘It has become rarer for everyone else,’ says an economist
https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/third-chi.author: Amanda Smith
https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/third-chi.text:
For decades, the markers of extreme wealth were easy to spot: the second home, the fancy cars, the Ivy League education. New analysis of Federal Reserve data points to a subtler one: a third child.

Mike Konczal, vice president of policy and research at the Economic Security Project and a former White House economist, studied households headed by 45- to 64-year-olds in his analysis of the Fed’s Survey of Consumer Finances, pooling five surveys from 2013 through 2025. He found that 49% of top-1% earners have three or more children, compared with about 40% of the rest of the top 10%.

Families with four or more kids are about as common in both groups, so the gap comes down to the third child: 34% of the 1% stop at exactly three, versus 24% of the merely affluent.

What changed isn’t the rich. Since the 1990s, families with three or more kids have become less common overall and among the rest of the top 10%, while the 1%’s share barely moved. “What’s new is that it has become rarer for everyone else,” Konczal writes.

Big families thin out in the upper middle class. Rank families by wealth instead of income, and among those wealthier than about three-quarters of Americans their age, but well short of the top, only about a third have three or more kids.

That’s well below families further down the wealth ladder. In the top 1%, half do.

Many of these families earn too much for federal child care subsidies, which are capped at 85% of a state’s median income, but not enough to hire their way around the problem.

Elaine Shi and her husband once thought they might have four kids. They stopped at three. Asked how much cost factored in, Shi, the CEO and co-founder of body-composition scanning company BodySpec, said simply: “None.” What settled it was their third child’s “firecracker personality,” along with her health during each pregnancy.

Shi doesn’t see that divide among the people she knows. “Candidly, this has not been my experience,” she says. What stands out to her is timing: “Relatively few of my peers in our late 30s have chosen to have three children because they started having the first one relatively late in life.”

Big families used to be ordinary. In 1976, about two-thirds of mothers in their early 40s had three or more kids; by 2016, 38% did, according to Pew Research Center.

The U.S. fertility rate, close to two children per woman in 1995, hit a record low of 1.57 in 2025, by a Wall Street Journal calculation using federal data.

Americans still say they want more: 42% called three or more kids ideal in Gallup’s July 2025 poll. But more than 7 in 10 say that raising kids is unaffordable for most people, according to BYU’s 2025 American Family Survey.

Shi’s third child arrived at a hectic moment. Her older two, about two years apart, were starting school, and their needs were diverging.

“It didn’t seem fair to drag an infant along to every gymnastics and swim class, nor did it seem fair to forego those kinds of activities to stick to a baby’s nap schedule,” she says. She was also mid-fundraise and needed to get back to work fast. “So we ended up investing in multiple caregivers to better meet everyone’s needs.”

The biggest financial change from two kids to three, she says, was “definitely childcare.”

Most families can’t hire their way out. Full-day care for a child cost $6,552 to $15,600 a year in 2022, or 8.9% to 16% of median family income, according to the Labor Department. And that’s for one child.

By one LendingTree estimate, a two-child household needs to earn $400,000 a year for childcare to be affordable.

A third kid often means a bigger house, too. The typical existing single-family home sold for $412,500 in 2024, about five times the median household income, according to Harvard’s Joint Center for Housing Studies. In the 1990s, it was closer to three times.

The U.S. recorded just over half a million more births than deaths in 2025, and Census Bureau and Congressional Budget Office projections show that cushion ending in the next decade, the Wall Street Journal reported. After that, population growth would depend on immigration.

Economists warn that fewer births mean a smaller future workforce, slower growth and more strain on Social Security.

Konczal cautions that his numbers show a correlation, but it’s the one you’d expect if money solves the hard parts of raising kids. He argues that some of what money buys the rich, like stability and support, could be offered to families now, through policy aimed at the years when kids are young and budgets are tightest.

Shi’s own fix is more about time than money. She and her husband run BodySpec together, and their favorite workday, she says, is Saturday.

The office is empty, and one of the kids usually tags along, most often her son, the middle child. He gets to build a LEGO set without his sisters taking it apart, then has lunch alone with his mom.

“Nobody told us this counted as work-life balance, but it’s the closest thing we’ve found,” Shi says.
