https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/08/poppi-fo.title: Poppi founders are going after PepsiCo's Gatorade with new beverage startup Jetty
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/08/poppi-fo.author: Amelia Lucas
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/08/poppi-fo.text:
Poppi founders Allison and Stephen Ellsworth are launching Jetty, an everyday hydration brand with bottled drinks and electrolyte powders.

The new brand pits the Ellsworths against PepsiCo, which bought Poppi for $1.95 billion last year.

Jetty is self-funded with $2.5 million, and Allison Ellsworth said the company will likely raise outside capital in 2027.

After disrupting the soda category with Poppi, founders Allison and Stephen Ellsworth are now taking aim at hydration with their new brand, Jetty.

Starting Monday, Jetty drinks and ready-to-mix electrolyte packets will be on shelves at Whole Foods grocery stores and available online at Target
 and Amazon
.

The new, self-funded venture directly pits the Ellsworths against PepsiCo
, which bought Poppi for $1.95 billion in 2025. Pepsi owns Gatorade, which dominates the U.S. sports drink category with about 60% market share, according to Numerator data.

Poppi shook up the soda category with prebiotic fiber, low calorie and sugar counts and its fun marketing aimed at Generation Z and millennials. Jetty looks to upend the hydration category through a similar strategy. To do so, it will face off not only against Gatorade but also a swarm of other upstarts looking to get in on the electrolyte-fueled trend.

For decades, Gatorade and other sports drinks have pitched their products to athletes who need electrolytes and fluids after an intense workout, although many consumers drink them every day without even sweating. Jetty is aimed at people who need a hydration boost, but not the same level of electrolytes or sugar as a traditional sports drink.

“No one has really created a product for just everyday hydration — literally everyday hydration for normal people,” Allison Ellsworth, Jetty’s chief brand officer, told CNBC. “Like I woke up this morning, I didn’t run a marathon.”

Following Poppi’s sale to PepsiCo, Ellsworth stayed on as an advisor to the brand, although she said she is no longer involved in the day-to-day operations.

After 10 years building Poppi, Ellsworth said, she finally had free time. As Ellsworth tells it, she went to the doctor for the first time in a decade. She started using a GLP-1 medication and lost 60 pounds.

That’s how Jetty came to be.

Ellsworth’s husband, Stephen, now CEO of the new brand, noticed she wasn’t hydrating, even when she came back from the gym.

GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic and Mounjaro can make people less thirsty. But because staying hydrated can also help mitigate some of the drugs’ side effects, such as nausea and headaches, it can become more important.

“I physically struggle getting liquid into my body,” Ellsworth said.

Jetty is meant to solve that problem.

Plain old water is often less appealing to consumers, even dehydrated GLP-1 users, but more flavorful options with added benefits can be tempting. About 44% of GLP-1 users report consuming more functional beverages, according to EY-Parthenon’s third annual survey of more than 3,600 current or former GLP-1 users.

Ellsworth sees a broader appeal for Jetty, too.

“Our core audience is going to be millennial moms and Gen Z,” she said. “Gen Z just isn’t relating to these old school brands, the legacy of the Gatorades and the Powerades. They’re just not cool.”

Consumers broadly have become more interested in staying hydrated.

Dollar sales of hydration and electrolyte products climbed 20% to $2.6 billion over the 52 weeks ended Oct. 4, based on data from SPINS, which tracks new universal product codes, or UPCs. The category also has a strong repeat buyer rate of 62%.

However, the Ellsworths aren’t the only ones to notice the potential in hydration. The number of new items in the category with annual sales of at least $10,000 has increased 41% over the last two years, according to SPINS.

Big food and beverage companies have been looking to hydration, too.

Kraft Heinz
 debuted Capri Sun juice pouches and Kool-Aid packets with electrolytes this spring. In April, Pepsi unveiled an overhaul of the Gatorade brand, focused on making it more appealing to a wider swath of consumers, with more potential occasions like a “fresh morning start” or an “afternoon walk.” And Electrolit is a top performer for its distributor Keurig Dr Pepper
, with 40% retail sales growth in the company’s third quarter.

All of that means more competition for shelf space and consumers’ “share of throat,” an industry term for beverage market share.

To increase Jetty’s visibility across the grocery store and to maximize convenience for shoppers, Jetty will be available in both powders and bottles.

Single-use electrolyte mixes are growing at a much faster clip than the ready-to-drink category, Ellsworth said, thanks to Unilever
’s Liquid I.V. and smaller upstarts like LMNT. On Amazon alone, powders are a $1 billion category, according to Ellsworth.

The ready-to-drink, or RTD, sports beverages are a much larger market, but the category’s sales are shrinking as consumers reach for other hydration options instead. Unit sales of sports drinks have fallen 9.1% from 2022 to 2026, according to Numerator data. And Coca-Cola
 has written down the value of BodyArmor by more than $1.7 billion after buying control of the brand for $5.6 billion in late 2021.

That doesn’t worry Jetty’s founders.

“Me and my husband know how to do RTD,” Ellsworth said.

Jetty will launch with five flavors, including watermelon, orange mango, fruit punch, black raspberry and white cherry. All of them contain 100 milligrams of sodium, 310 milligrams of potassium and 100 milligrams of magnesium in a 15.2-ounce bottle or 15-gram packet.

In addition to electrolytes, Jetty products also contain B vitamins, 3 grams of fiber and 6 grams of sugar. It doesn’t use artificial sweeteners or dyes, its founders say.

For comparison, a 20-ounce bottle of traditional Gatorade Thirst Quencher has about 270 milligrams of sodium and 80 milligrams of potassium, plus 34 grams of sugar. The sports drink brand is also phasing out artificial colors and promoting lower-sugar versions.

“What’s really interesting about this product and this opportunity is we now can capture all those lapsed drinkers — or that generation that didn’t even ever drink it in the first place,” Ellsworth said.

Poppi’s new owner knows about Jetty and the market it is trying to capture, too.

“I don’t think [Pepsi] gets it, but what they do get is that the movement is changing, and they think that just by taking dyes out or doing 90% less sugar, they’re going to capture this audience,” Ellsworth said. “But that is very big corporate thinking.”

She added that she believes Pepsi has missed the mark on advertising to Gen Z consumers across its portfolio, such as in its campaigns for Sprite competitor Starry.

Perhaps as an extension of that, Poppi’s performance has been underwhelming under PepsiCo’s ownership.

The food and beverage giant now estimates the fair value of potential performance-based payments to Poppi’s prior owners is $12 million, Pepsi said in a regulatory filing in October. At the time of the deal, Pepsi promised an additional payment of $300 million if Poppi hit certain targets by the third quarter of 2027. The Ellsworths declined to comment on the filing to CNBC.

This time around, with one successful brand under their belts, Jetty’s founders say they have learned from past mistakes. Those lessons should help Jetty as it launches at a much larger scale than Poppi did.

Three different claims lawyers have signed off on Jetty’s packaging, according to Ellsworth. Poppi paid $8.9 million to settle class-action litigation alleging false advertising over its “gut healthy” claims.

For now, Jetty is entirely self-funded with $2.5 million, although Ellsworth said that the brand will likely raise money in 2027. This time, though, she said investors will probably look less like traditional venture capitalists.

“I want to bring in investors that bring value,” Ellsworth said. Instead of a venture capitalist who is willing to invest $15 million, Jetty would rather consider investors who can only write a check for $1 million but have access to celebrities. “So then you’re getting access to talent on a cheaper level and people that are invested in the brand.”

And Jetty has also learned a few lessons from Gatorade. For example, the brand is already at work on a lemon-lime version — the original flavor of Gatorade.

“We’ll eventually do it,” Ellsworth said. “But it was really important at the beginning just to stick to flavors that we love, for it to taste good.”

https://grist.org/drought/as-the-colorad.title: As the Colorado River shrinks, calls to drain Lake Powell grow
https://grist.org/drought/as-the-colorad.author: Jim Robbins, Yale Environment 360
https://grist.org/drought/as-the-colorad.text:
The 27-year-long drought in the Southwestern U.S. — the longest dry period in the last 1,200 years — is taking a serious toll on the flow of the Colorado River. Climate change is shrinking the snowpack in Colorado’s Rocky Mountains, the source of roughly 80 percent of the river’s annual flow, and higher temperatures are melting the snowpack earlier in the year, which saps runoff in late summer and fall. Warmer weather is also increasing evaporation from the river’s 40 reservoirs, including its two largest — lakes Powell and Mead.

Last month, Lake Powell, on the Utah-Arizona border, reached a record low, at less than 150 feet above dead pool, the point at which water can no longer flow through the Glen Canyon Dam’s bypass tubes to reach Lake Mead, behind Hoover Dam, 300 miles downstream. The low water levels reduced the generation of hydropower from both reservoirs, complicated how riverine ecosystems are managed, and slashed deliveries of water to the Lower Basin states of Arizona, California, and Nevada.

Farmers are fallowing fields. Developers in some areas have paused housing construction for lack of guaranteed water supplies. And the Bureau of Reclamation has curtailed its “environmental flows” — releases of cold water from Powell — which is threatening protected fish and preventing the buildup of sandbars that provide habitat for wildlife in the Grand Canyon. No matter how the river is managed going forward, observers say, ecosystems both downstream and up will see significant changes.

Faced with the prospect of even lower Colorado River levels, the federal and state governments have been scrambling to come up with ways to meet the competing demands of disparate interests that rely on its flow, from topping off Lake Powell with water diverted from upstream reservoirs, to slashing downstream water deliveries by 40 percent, to paying farmers to keep their allocations of water in the river. The crisis is even causing some to consider a fix once deemed unthinkable: draining Lake Powell entirely.

When the Glen Canyon Dam was built in the 1960s, proponents hyped its benefits: cheap hydropower, subsidized water for cotton and alfalfa growers, real estate on the new lakeshore, and a playground for boaters. But detractors bemoaned the drowning of Glen Canyon itself, a red rock labyrinth of gorges, spires, cliffs, and grottoes that conservationists described as even more beautiful than the Grand Canyon.

Over the decades, some environmental advocates have argued for removing the Glen Canyon Dam and restoring the canyon, but the idea was always dismissed as too expensive and, because it would wipe out power generation, wildly impractical.

Now, a more tempered approach is gaining support, with groups like the Glen Canyon Institute arguing not to remove the dam but to drain Lake Powell through new diversion tunnels that would be drilled below the existing bypass tubes, close to the riverbed. The upsides, say advocates, would be manifold. The water would boost hydropower production in Lake Mead. The stunning formations of Glen Canyon and sites sacred to Indigenous people would reemerge. Wildlife would return, and riparian habitat above and below the dam site would eventually be restored. The plan is called Fill Mead First.

For more than four decades, the Glen Canyon Dam was considered a huge asset to the river basin, said Eric Balken, executive director of the Glen Canyon Institute. But it’s now “becoming a liability because it might actually prevent water from flowing downstream. All of the core assumptions around the dam have been turned on their head.”

That’s because of the dam’s structural limitations. If the lake drops below minimum power pool, its penstocks — the large pipes that send water to the dam’s eight turbines — will be left stranded, high and dry. Lake water will instead be released through bypass tubes, which sit below the penstocks but have less than half their capacity to discharge water.

These tubes were not built for sustained long-term use, and sending high volumes of water through them could cause vibrations, scouring, and other effects that could cause irreparable damage to the dam. While the Bureau of Reclamation has long warned about relying solely on the bypass tubes to release water, after inspecting and relining them in 2025 it said they might work if needed. But another challenge will remain: Relying on the narrow tubes will make it harder for Upper Basin states (Colorado, New Mexico, Utah, and Wyoming) to meet their delivery obligations to Lower Basin states and, by international agreement, Mexico.

Allowing more water to flow through the Glen Canyon Dam — by draining the lake through the existing bypass tubes and newly drilled diversion tunnels near the riverbed — is no longer dismissed out of hand. “That conversation has evolved,” said Kathryn Sorensen, director of research at the Kyl Center for Water Policy at Arizona State University.

Lower release structures, said Jack Schmidt, director of the Center for Colorado River Studies at Utah State University, are “an utterly reasonable idea” and should be part of the discussion. As for Powell’s potential loss of hydropower, proponents of dam removal say those megawatts could be replaced with solar power. The new Gemini solar plant near Las Vegas has a capacity of 690 megawatts; the Glen Canyon Dam currently has a capacity of around 730 megawatts.

The Lower Basin states, which primarily take their water from Lake Mead and are seeing their allotments held back to prop up Lake Powell, have urged the federal government to consider modifying the dam with lower outlets rather than cutting back on deliveries, as the Biden administration ordered in 2024.

“Addressing the infrastructure limitations may be the one long-term measure that would best achieve operation and management improvements to the Glen Canyon Dam,” representatives of the Lower Basin states wrote to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum last year.

Draining Lake Powell completely “could [annually] reduce evaporative losses by a couple hundred thousand acre-feet,” said Sorensen: Experts say 11 percent of the water in the reservoir is lost to evaporation each year. “On a river that is much smaller than anyone expected, that water really matters,” she said. But while the Glen Canyon Institute plan is gaining some traction, she added, “it faces a lot of obstacles.”

One of those obstacles is the federal government, which did not even consider the possibility of draining Lake Powell as an option in its recent environmental impact statement — finalized in August — which addressed ways to manage the Colorado over the next 10 years.

Officials in Page, Arizona, which has a thriving water-based recreation industry, have also opposed draining the lake. The BlueRibbon Coalition, which represents off-road and motorized outdoor recreation, leads the opposition. It has put forward a model bill called the Colorado River Abundance Act, which would supply treated water to Lower Basin states, allowing more water to be retained in Lake Powell. The treated water would come from nuclear-powered desalination of seawater and briny water and through “advanced water reuse,” in which wastewater is cleaned with filter technologies, at an estimated cost of $40 billion.

Another obstacle is time: New diversion tunnels would likely take a decade to study, design, and build. And the price tag could be in the billions.

The Colorado’s reduced flows are, meanwhile, taking a toll on riverine ecosystems, which scientists call “novel” because they have been radically altered by 70 years of human activity — most significantly by the elimination of seasonal flooding. For a number of reasons, including low lake levels, the Bureau of Reclamation has canceled many environmental flows from the Glen Canyon Dam in recent years, depriving the Colorado of a large pulse of sediment, which is a part of the river’s natural ecology. The flows rebuild sandbars and beaches used by boaters in the Grand Canyon, and they create shallow-water habitat for threatened and endangered native fish.

The bureau also occasionally releases cold water from the dam to lower the river’s temperature and keep invasive, warm-water-loving bass from taking up residence in the Grand Canyon stretch and displacing native fish. But because of the drought, which is already reducing hydroelectric production, those releases have also been curtailed.

Draining the lake completely would allow Glen Canyon to recover as the river flushes out built-up sediment, experts say. Native cottonwoods and willows would take root and help push out invasives, like tamarisk. River otters, beavers, birds, and amphibians would return to the canyon. And the drowned red rock arches, natural bridges, amphitheaters, and waterfalls would gradually emerge from the muck, along with thousands of sites sacred to Native Americans.

A shift in the hydrological regime would also have profound effects on hundreds of miles of river ecosystems below Glen Canyon Dam, including in the Grand Canyon. “It would change in ways that are only partially predictable,” said Schmidt. “Suddenly the river would have great fluctuations. The river would have much more sediment. The river would be much more turbid.” A refugium of native fish, the Grand Canyon would suddenly be swamped with non-native fish, many of which were introduced into Lake Powell for sport fishing. “It just keeps getting more complicated,” Schmidt acknowledges. “It’s all a trade-off in this screwy manmade world.”

For now, Fill Mead First remains a pipe dream, one that’s getting a lot more attention as river levels continue to drop and global temperatures rise. The federal government will ultimately decide the Glen Canyon Dam’s future, but Eric Balken, for one, thinks a new regime is long overdue. Propping up Lake Powell is “kicking the can down the road,” he said. “But they are running out of road.”

https://www.dw.com/en/at-least-21-killed.title: At least 21 killed after migrant boat sinks off Senegal
https://www.dw.com/en/at-least-21-killed.text:
The incident occurred near Kebemer off the coast of northwestern Senegal. Authorities on El Hierro in the Canary Islands have declared an emergency after a marked increase in migrant boat arrivals

At least 21 people were killed after a small boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of northwestern Senegal, Senegalese authorities said.

Thousands have died in recent years after embarking on boats from the Senegalese coast in order to reach Spain's Canary Islands through the perilous Atlantic route.

According to the Senegalese Interior Ministry, only one person was rescued from the capsizing, and 21 bodies were recovered.

The ministry added that the toll was "provisional" and that search operations were still ongoing.

The incident occurred near Kebemer, some 180 kilometers (around 112 miles) north of the capital, Dakar.

On Saturday, the ministry stressed the government's "determination to combat people smuggling networks, notably through strengthened cooperation with neighboring countries."

Senegalese authorities said they intercepted 142 migrants on a similar boat aimed at reaching Spanish territory on Friday. The boat included nationals of multiple West African countries.

Authorities on El Hierro Island in the Canary Islands declared an emergency on Saturday after a marked increase in migrant boat arrivals.

El Hierro officials say that over 3,300 people have arrived on around 30 boats since the start of the month.

"We are very concerned... by this sharp increase in arrivals," Alpidio Armas, head of the El Hierro regional council, told Spanish television.

"This is precisely what has led us to declare an emergency in order to ensure a framework of cooperation with higher-level institutions," he added.

Armas said that conditions at the island's hospital have become "undesirable."

El Hierro is home to about 11,400 residents.

Migrant arrivals reached a record high of 46,000 in 2024. Afterwards, arrivals have fallen sharply due to increased surveillance and cooperation with African countries.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Josh Butler
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Exclusive: Head of IFPI says allowing AI companies access to online content would be a ‘huge mistake’ and damage Australia’s reputation

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Australia weakening copyright protections for AI companies would be “ridiculous and dangerous”, the global peak body for the music recording industry has warned as it watches with concern how the Albanese government responds to big tech’s demands.

While local creatives have raised constitutional issues and threatened political backlash, the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI), representing recording industry bodies worldwide, said its members were worried about Australia potentially agreeing to demands other nations had rejected.

“Why would Australia do this? Why would a sophisticated, democratic country that has a phenomenal cultural power of its own, choose to make this very odd decision and buy into the promises of a few large AI companies, and throw away their own culture and creativity?” Victoria Oakley, the CEO of IFPI, told Guardian Australia.

“I don’t think Australia wants to be the weakest link in this situation, the one that believed the promises and gave in and threw creativity under the bus on behalf of everyone else. That doesn’t feel very Australian to me.

“You just need one safe harbour, because then you can train on music from anywhere in the world. So this isn’t just about Australian music and Australian culture; it’s about music and culture everywhere.”

Labor is mulling copyright changes in a suite of policy overhauls around AI, including datacentres, online safety, workforce, energy and the economy. While the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, promised “the strongest possible protection”, warning it would be “theft” if creatives weren’t paid for their work, creative industries were alarmed after AI companies requested a weakening of copyright law to train on Australian material.

Some AI companies have rejected making licensing agreements under existing copyright law, saying it was too difficult. Anthropic suggested an “opt-out” model that would allow it to scrape content unless rights holders signalled an objection.

Large AI companies say they need legal certainty on issues like copyright before making investments in Australia or training their models here.

Oakley said AI companies had made similar proposals in the US, UK and other nations and that Australia should not accept such a bargain.

“I just don’t think it’s true that you will only get investment or growth, or be seen as pro-innovation, if you entirely give in to the demands of AI companies,” Oakley said.

“We’ve been talking to capitals around the world, saying ‘are you seeing what’s going on in Australia?’ We think this is a disaster for creativity.”

The attorney general, Michelle Rowland, said via a spokesperson last week that the government was “committed to supporting” creatives and pledged that “any future copyright changes deliver meaningful control and fair compensation”.

Oakley said she worried about AI and copyright “everywhere”, but feared “Australia appears to be threatening to do something really ridiculous and dangerous.”

She said creative industries worried about “contagion” of copyright relaxation if Australia caved in, and that copyright material from anywhere in the world could be affected.

She declined to speculate on any potential legal or constitutional challenges, as raised by the Australian Recording Industry Association, but said it would be reputational damage to Australia’s standing in the creative world.

“It would be a huge mistake, and I think the prize is not worth what you’re throwing away,” she said.

In recent answers to a parliamentary committee on AI, responding to questions from the independent senator David Pocock about why it couldn’t replicate the kind of deals Spotify had made, OpenAI said the music streaming giant “has a different business, where it primarily transmits un-transformed copyrighted content, so would be expected to license content that it streams”.

But Oakley said music labels had already inked dozens of licensing deals with smaller AI companies around the world.

“It is perfectly possible to license. I’m almost shocked that these words are coming out of the mouths of some of the larger AI companies … We already know how to license music to tech platforms because that’s exactly how Spotify works, or Amazon Music, Apple, or Tidal,” she said.

“You have a ready, willing set of rights holders who want to license with a history of licensing in the streaming world, but also current evidence of licensing to AI firms. Let’s let the market do what it needs to do. Come to us and we’ll make it work.”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: ‘The light of dawn is on the horizon’: the best moments from US midterm victory speeches | Ted Widmer
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Ted Widmer
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Tuesday’s winners offered a new politics at a time when ‘there is something broken in America’

As the US election returns came in throughout the night on Tuesday, there was ebullience at the size of the margin. It was comparable to the significant thumpings over the years. Yet bigger.

In 2006, Americans were exhausted by the war in Iraq (by simply changing the last letter to “n”, we have a similar situation today). But even that big win paled in comparison.

In 1974, there was another big gain by Democrats, after Richard Nixon resigned in disgrace, but the Democrats already held both chambers, so the realignment was not quite as profound.

Democrats have been on the losing end too. In 1994, they lost both chambers, but the reversal did little to dent Bill Clinton’s popularity, and he cruised to re-election two years later. Similarly, Democrats lost both chambers in 1946, after a recession, but Harry Truman was able to tough out re-election in 1948.

There will be no redemption for Donald Trump, who dragged everyone down around him.

His failure will now hang like a millstone around the neck of his vice-president, as they all head toward the ignominious end of this administration. This is a swamp that simply cannot be drained. JD Vance will thrash around in it, like a desperate mastodon, until forced to face an extinction event of his own, sometime in early 2028.

Among other results, the Earthquake of 2026 tees up a Democrat to win the presidency in 2028.

Of course, it’s far from a foregone conclusion. But it will be difficult for a wounded Republican party to limp along with no accomplishments, and then magically produce a winning candidate from the wreckage. Plus, Donald Trump will do all he can to keep any charismatic rival from emerging.

There were hundreds of victory speeches given on Tuesday. Naturally, many expressed the same thoughts – gratitude to long-suffering family members, exhilaration at the size of the blue wave, and a readiness to get to work on behalf of constituents. Specifically, to lower costs – the issue that overwhelmingly drove this surge.

But there was something bigger going on than Democratic exultation.

Many victory speeches looked past the short-term impact of the win and addressed the deep dysfunction within a political system that has fattened lobbyists and special interests, while ignoring the basic needs of the people: healthcare, education, clean air and water. There was a rage against the efforts of the ultra-wealthy to buy the election.

Over time it could easily grow more by carving into Maga, which has been so aggrieved for so long, but put its faith into a snake oil salesman.

This was something beyond partisan talking points; it came from an anger that has been building for years. It was visceral and directed against a system that favors the well-connected and their lobbyists, while attempting to divide and demean the disconnected. There was a lot of people power in these speeches (several quoted the final line of the Gettysburg Address, “of the people, by the people and for the people”).

In Michigan, Abdul El Sayed, simply by saying his name, set off a roar from the crowd, and got another one when he contrasted “this beautiful movement” with “an astroturfed corporate-funded advertising campaign built to deceive and distract”. A sharp line: “To special interests … we are coming for your system of politics.”

While noting the Republicans’ frequent attacks on his name and his faith, he described his belief in an America that is “big enough for all of us” and invested in the needs of its own people, instead of expensive forever wars.

Gleefully, he looked forward to being sworn in by Vance, and got another big cheer when he shouted, referring to Michigan and Ohio university mascots: “Wolverine one, Buckeye zero!”

In Georgia, Jon Ossoff celebrated before a rapturous crowd. He trained some firepower on “the depravity, corruption and incompetence of the failed lame-duck president”. but also offered a vision of the new hope beginning for millions:

“If at times, these last two years, amidst the ceaseless onslaught of brutality and indecency, you doubted whether our republic would survive, let tonight’s results give you courage that the first light of dawn is on the horizon.”

He acknowledged that some “brokenness” remains, even with the victory: “Amidst our celebration tonight, we must acknowledge that the underlying crisis gripping our republic remains, and that therefore our most vital work lies ahead.”

Also in Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms spoke boisterously after being introduced by her daughter (it was a good night for moms and daughters – Gina Hinojosa movingly thanked her grandmother).

History was on her mind in several ways – she noted the irony that she comes from the same town as Alexander Stephens, the vice-president of the Confederacy. But a new era is beginning, and she reached out to all the Georgians whom she wanted to serve, including those who have traditionally voted Republican, such as veterans who need access to healthcare, and farmers trying to hold on to family land.

She also cited caregivers “who can’t afford healthcare and need Georgia to finally expand Medicaid”. She offered a resonant promise: “No amount of money will ever … never ever ever! … overcome the power of the people!”

In Texas, Gina Hinojosa called out her abuela, who always taught her: “Know your worth.” She insisted that the night was far more than a win for Democrats. “This victory is so much bigger,” she explained, going through all the ways it will help young people, teachers, parents and other caretakers of future generations.

Education was much on her mind; she expressed her rage against the ways in which Texas had strong-armed local schools and announced (to a huge cheer) her plan to fire the state’s education commissioner. With the focus of a parent, she outlined her hopes for the children of Texas, who cannot even vote, but are nevertheless a part of her broad social compact: “To the children of Texas, your schools will not close. You will be invested in, and you will grow up in a Texas where you are lifted up every single day to reach your God-given potential.”

It is difficult to remember any similar statement coming from the Republican party in recent years – a party so top-heavy, so male, so mean-spirited. Hinojosa had an effective line: state government, in the past, felt like “something that is done to you, not with you, or for you, or by you”.

Also in Texas, James Talarico showed the eloquence that has distinguished his unlikely campaign from the start (in glaring contrast to Ken Paxton’s remarks, so charisma-challenged).

He celebrated “the politics of love” in a language reminiscent of Martin Luther King, identified the “broken political system” that had spent so much to defeat him (he likened Elon Musk to Goliath), and urged his followers to “always bet on the underdog!”

Addressing the constant attacks on him, by AI bots as well as human actors, Talarico called the smear campaign “the final howls of a dying establishment … the death rattle of a status quo that knows its days are numbered”.

He welcomed the former Trump voters who came over to support him, and all the disenfranchised who built his coalition: teachers, nurses, farmers, ranchers, parents trying to put food on the table, young couples trying to find the money to buy a home.

Like Ossoff, he talked about a society that has broken its promises. “There is something broken in America,” he explained. “Our economy is broken, our political system is broken, even our relationships with each other feel broken … and that’s because the most powerful people in the world want it that way.”

Then came a stirring story about his grandfather, a Baptist preacher, who taught him the two main commandments of the New Testament, “love God” and “love neighbor,” because “there is no love of God without love of neighbor.” Following the thought, he reminded his listeners that all human beings are created in the image of their creator.

After so many Republican attacks on our physical and religious differences, it was an arresting thought, again reminiscent of Dr King. Talarico is shaking things up, using scripture deftly toward that end. Talarico insisted the “real fight in this country is not left v right; it is top v bottom.”

Together, the election night speeches are a sign that this is something more than a political victory. It’s an awakening. It’s the dawn of a new political era, dominated by young actors of immense talent, sharp on the details, focused on the American Dream, and destined to be with us for years and years.

Ted Widmer, a former White House speechwriter, is the editor of American Speeches, and the recently published The Living Declaration: A Biography of America’s Founding Text, both published by the Library of America

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: ‘I was in a darker place than I’d ever been. ECT was my only hope’: how Ted Scheinman finally broke through his depression
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Paula Cocozza
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Troubled from the age of three, by 35 the American journalist viewed himself as ‘the lowest piece of dirt on the Earth’ – and neither therapy nor drugs seemed to help. But there was one thing he hadn’t tried …

T
ed Scheinman can date the origin of his depression with laser accuracy. It was the day he went to the fair, aged three, and returned to his home in upstate New York clutching a Batman toy that he’d won. In the bathroom, he swooped his new doll over the sink. Scheinman had a vivid imagination; in a few years, he would want to become a playwright. To add sound effects and drama, he turned on the tap. There was a whoosh – and the unthinkable happened. Water landed on Batman’s pristine boot in a darkening, enlarging spot that for young Scheinman triggered several rapid thoughts, the last of them being: “I am going to die.”

Now 41, Scheinman, a senior editor at Smithsonian magazine, has written a memoir of his “life as a depressive”. Jolt: My Electric Journey Out of Darkness charts his path from toddlerhood to the point in 2020, at the age of 35, when he referred himself for electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). By then, he was in “a much darker place” than he had ever been – and regarded himself as “the lowest piece of dirt on the Earth”. The treatment was “not so much a last resort … as my only hope”, he says.

Jolt is really “a view from the other side of the tunnel”; a travelogue – which somehow manages to be amusing – of the journey towards an experience that for many remains taboo. During ECT, an electric current passes through the brain, triggering a brief seizure. In those seconds, affected neurons fire simultaneously and repeatedly, triggering the release of neurohormones and neurotransmitters (such as dopamine). Despite the treatment being steeped in horror – as in artistic depictions such as One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest and The Bell Jar – Scheinman’s main worry was that “it wouldn’t do shit for me”.

Literary references are never far from view in Jolt – or in Scheinman’s life, for that matter. They were there in utero: his mother assumed he’d be a girl and planned to name him Jane, after the novelist Austen. (His younger sister acquired the name a few years later.) Bookishness pervades Jolt and, fittingly, on our video call, Scheinman sits before a row of bookcases.

“Write this down!” his mother kept saying before he was admitted to the psychiatric ward of Sibley memorial hospital in Washington DC in 2021. “This is great material.” They’re perhaps not the words many mothers would offer a child about to embark on ECT. “It might sound sort of clinical or heartless,” Scheinman says, “but it was the opposite.”

His mother, who died last year, was a professor of English at Colgate university in New York, specialising in 18th-century English literature. (His father was a doctor and medical researcher.) What does Scheinman think she was trying to tell him? “If you could make meaning out of this … you would have power over it. Or at least, a sense of agency within the illness. She knew who I was,” he says.

From Jolt’s title on, of course, the reader knows where this memoir is leading – and maybe, somewhere in his head, that’s how Scheinman felt, too.

“Sympathetic portraits of people with mental afflictions were very common in our household,” he says. “I think I heard about ECT very, very young.” Some of his mother’s friends had benefited from the treatment. And she held a correspondence with Alan Bennett who, in 2006’s Untold Stories, describes the effects of ECT on his own mother as “a miracle”.

At dawn on 12 May 2021, Scheinman was taken for his first treatment. Having the electrodes attached to his temple was scary, he says, “but the fear almost felt distant because I was pathetically hopeful”. Actually, more than hopeful: “I felt this intense sense of need.” Because if it didn’t work, what then?

“It’s such a dramatic thing, right? You go on this table, you picture yourself convulsing more than you will. And if you’re lucky, you get up after however many treatments and walk out a changed or restored person … I was attracted to the sheer apparent extremeness of this treatment.”

Perhaps the extremity implied an ending that, in turn, implied a solution. In any case, Scheinman can recall lying on the hospital bed, the squeeze as the blood-pressure cuff tightened around his left ankle, the prick of the needle administering general anaesthetic, and the pervading sense of relaxation bordering on euphoria as he tried to count down from 100 in line with the anaesthetist’s instructions. He remembers exclaiming “Oh boy!” and waking with a headache. But what happened between those moments, the “jolt” – nothing like the arching back of cinematic portrayals, a mere twitch of his left big toe – remains “a black box”.

What he does know is that at some point over the five months of mostly outpatient treatments – 11 unilateral, 14 bilateral (meaning that electrodes were applied to both temples) – his illness began to improve. His friends, driving him to and from the appointments, noticed before he did. For about 18 months after the ECT ended, he felt “much better than I realised I could” – and the next year, better still. Now, five years on, “I feel more myself than I have felt in years. Most of my days pass without depression.”

Scheinman qualifies this: “I mean, I do still consider myself a depressive.” His fondness for verbal precision makes him prone to self-correction. “According to my history, by the diagnostic and statistical manual, I am a major depressive.” Prior to the ECT, he was diagnosed with agitated depression with bipolar characteristics. “But the further and further I get from the worst of 2020 and 2021, the happier I get, the more settled.” In May, he got married (to Tara Ganapathy, an attorney specialising in congressional investigations).

In a funny way, Jolt reads like a coming-of-age story with a zany timeline. Scheinman was such a precocious intellect that he seems to reach graduate-level discourse by age six, then spends years waiting for his body, wardrobe and emotions to catch up. “I felt marooned between being a tiny adult gentleman and the big feelings of a child,” he says. The book is full of descriptions of young Scheinman dressed in his grandfather’s hand-me-downs, old before his time. Today, although he’s wearing a Patagonia fleece, his assertion that he has gone “full hippy” itself sounds a bit tweedy.

Some of Jolt’s most comedic – and disturbing – moments come from the dissonance between his biological age and his mother’s parenting of him. When, for instance, Scheinman enters a germophobe phase at elementary school, she warns him: “You’ll have a very disappointing sex life if you go on like this.” Another time, she soothes his tears with the words: “A lot of sensitive and creative people have a period of depression.” To which six-year-old Scheinman protests in anguish: “But that’s such a cliche!” He was thinking of consumptive Romantic poets, he says, which surely alienates him from many first-graders. Does he feel any regret at not having been a more childlike child?

“I think that would have been really nice. I probably would have had a little bit of a smoother go of it,” he says. “If and when I raise a child of my own, I’m really going to try to give them a properly delineated childhood. I’m going to be very careful about not even hinting that there’s an expectation or possibility of being too precocious.”

“Delineated” is a telling choice of adjective given how the boundaries between Scheinman and his mother vanish as the memoir goes on and his parents’ marriage declines. They separated while Scheinman was at college, at which point his mother’s phone calls intensified. “Often, it seemed she didn’t wish to listen so much as talk and be confirmed in her martyrdom. So I confirmed it,” Scheinman writes.

His father is the book’s more classic villain: he had an affair, but beyond that, his blithe optimism appears to grate on mother and son. Scheinman professes much less tolerance of his father’s shortcomings than his mother’s overcomings, and in Jolt’s most moving scene, he shares a heartfelt, peacemaking boat ride with his father. He gets “goosebumps” just talking about it.

“I kept doing gradations of forgiveness and acceptance with my father,” he says. “We were never estranged. But that’s very different from having a true, frank, uncluttered relationship.” His father has read Jolt four times and is, says Scheinman, “a big fan”.

Alongside his depression, the book shows Scheinman to be not only functional, but successful. He gets his growth spurt, excels academically, wins parts in plays, has friends, girlfriends, a place at Yale (to study English and classics), does a PhD and becomes an academic before pivoting to journalism. He wrote his first book, Camp Austen: My Life as an Accidental Jane Austen Superfan, in his early 30s (his mum called it “a Mom-oir”).

“I think that overachieving is probably bound up with my particular flavour, or flavours, of mental disorder, which is trying desperately to do all the right things or just anything that could get you internal forgiveness or internal peace. Or to get some laurels and be like: ‘Well, now I can rest on these,’” he says. The book shifts between these drivers with a perennially unquieted self-questioning that feels both exhaustingly dramatic and quotidian.

Scheinman tried many treatments before arriving at ECT. He had his first talking therapy at the age of eight – his father’s suggestion – and further courses followed over the decades. There were drugs too, recreational and prescription. He self-administered alcohol, ran cross-country. And although ECT was “a last resort”, he now wonders if it’s necessary “to wait quite as long for people who are really in straits”.

No one knows exactly how the treatment works – whether the shock or its aftermath causes the “reset” effect. In 2023, the Royal College of Psychiatrists reported that of 1,835 patients to have received ECT in the preceding 12 months, 68% were found to be “much improved” or “very much improved”. According to the American Psychiatric Association, 70-80% of patients experience substantial improvement after ECT.

However, the treatment can cause memory loss. Scheinman struggles to access stretches of memories during the ECT course, “as well as significant stretches of the six months leading up to those treatments” – gaps that must present a challenge to a person’s sense of continuous selfhood. So does he feel his treatment restored or changed him?

“I think restored is probably closer to the mark,” he says. Later, he emails to say that his reply may have been “overly glib”, and that the process of writing the book, which entailed many hours of interviews with friends and relatives, as well as scouring medical records and diaries dating back to when he was five, “ended up helping profoundly”.

“I’m still myself!” he writes. “I just feel less trapped by myself.”

About a year ago, he unpacked his hospital “go-bag”. “I stand ready to go back under the electrodes if I have to, and I’ll do it quicker this time,” he says. “Without engaging in any horrible recovery cliches” – I can’t help thinking of his harrowed six-year-old self, when he says cliche – “I’m keenly aware, especially because I now have a wife whose life I don’t want to make difficult or unhappy, that I might need ECT again. I don’t try to evangelise for it in any way, but one of the things that surprise people is that I wish I’d gotten it sooner. I really think I would have lost fewer memories.”

He has informally coached a few people who are considering ECT, and is in the process of volunteering through the National Alliance on Mental Illness “as a person who can be contacted”. In the meantime, he has belatedly begun meditation. He stays active with what he calls “a reasonably strict regimen of exertion and movement” and plays music “as though it is a prescription”.

“I try to live very, very fully,” he says. “I feel like my sense of adventure is back.”

Jolt: Depression, Memory and My Electric Journey Out of Darkness by Ted Scheinman is published by Wildfire (£16.99). To support the Guardian order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.title: US task force to cut off Iran’s transport of advanced weapons: What we know
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.author: Urooba Jamal
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.text:
As the threat of renewed war grows, Washington is expanding efforts to choke Tehran’s military supply networks, including through Task Force Iron Gate – a unit targeting land routes and the Caspian Sea.

With it, the US military ⁠⁠⁠⁠is trying to prevent Iran from using ground routes to transport advanced weapons and other materials, the United States Central Command (CENTCOM) announced on Saturday.

The same day, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) announced ambitious plans for underground complexes capable of sustaining missile and drone production under bombardment. That announcement came amid reports of ongoing construction near Iranian missile bases, based on satellite imagery and previous claims by Tehran that US strikes failed to destroy its underground facilities.

Here’s what we know about the US task force:

Task Force Iron Gate will aim to find out where “weapons systems are coming in, how they could potentially be cut off” and how “Iran is transporting its energy”, Michael Mulroy, a former US deputy assistant defence secretary for the Middle East, told Al Jazeera.

It expands on the US blockade of Iranian ports to cover Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea and will reportedly be run by 20 civilian and military personnel.

Iran shares borders with seven countries – Afghanistan, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Iraq, Pakistan Turkiye and Turkmenistan.

Based in Tampa, Florida, the unit will coordinate with other US government agencies “on preventing the movement of advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials and illegal revenue streams across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea”, CENTCOM said. Task Force Iron Gate will reinforce “the success of our ironclad blockade against Iran at sea”, CENTCOM Commander Admiral Brad Cooper said.

If US President Donald Trump ramps up the war, there will likely be attacks on this “series of targets”, said Mulroy.

“Unlike Operation Epic Fury, which primarily (focused) on military targets, I think these targets will be focused on economic and infrastructure targets, as part of this comprehensive plan to cut the regime off from its ability to fight and ability to fund itself,” Mulroy said. “It’s primarily a coordination body that’s looking for how the US can increase its economic strangulation strategy by going after the ground routes as they’ve already covered a majority of the maritime routes.”

The IRGC dismissed the US military plan as “just a play on words”.

“The Americans cannot achieve their goal through this, which is to apply severe economic pressure to collapse and disintegrate the Iranian economy,” said IRGC spokesman Sardar Mohebi, as reported by the Fars news agency.

Washington previously “claimed that Iran will suffer an economic collapse within two weeks, but we witnessed that this did not happen”, he added.

While CENTCOM’s announcement did not explicitly identify Iran’s weapons trade with Russia, analysts say the unit could be seen as an attempt to disrupt supply networks that include Russian connections.

US media have reported that Russia has sent drone components and explosives to Iran via the Caspian Sea. There are also claims that Russian technology could be helping Iran develop advanced supersonic cruise missiles.

Mahjoob Zweiri, a professor of contemporary history and politics at Qatar University, told Al Jazeera that reports of military equipment imported via Russia are a “real concern” for the United States.

The task force therefore could “cause a confrontation with Russia”, he said.

Rami Khouri, a public policy fellow at the American University of Beirut and a non-resident senior fellow at the Arab Center in Washington, said of the new unit: “The US really doesn’t quite know what to do about Iran as we’ve seen, and it’s doing things off the cuff” – a strategy that has led to little success.

Khouri pointed to Iran’s history as a trading nation for thousands of years as evidence that the US mission is near impossible.

“There’s an enormous web of contacts that Iran has had for thousands of years with traders and partners and allies all over the region, especially in Asia –  it’s virtually impossible for the US to seal off every one,” he said.

While the US can impose a blockade or sanctions on Iran, it cannot control the behaviour of everyone from the Russians, to the Chinese, to the Emiratis and beyond, said the analyst.

“There are people all over the region who have links with Iran, some very close, some just commercial,” he said.

A lot of the materials that go into Iran’s weapons systems are bought from some other countries, – some even from the US or Europeans – and then they are channelled through companies in Asia, Khouri added.

Former Trump aide and top counterterrorism official Joe Kent, who resigned in March due to the US’s war on Iran, said the new task force is an attempt by CENTCOM to subvert ongoing diplomatic efforts.

“This is CENTCOM inviting Iran to escalate while the vice president is attempting to negotiate with the Iranians,” Kent posted on X. “This is, as CENTCOM calls it, ‘policy by CONOP’, when the military finds a way to subvert the White House without blatantly disobeying the President, by taking actions that will ensure a war escalates or perpetuates.”

According to The Wall Street Journal, CENTCOM chief Cooper is among the many officials, alongside Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, pressing Trump to renew attacks on Iran.

The task force may also just be symbolic because the US has no military presence on the Caspian Sea, said Zweiri.

“America has no access to the sea, unless some of the neighbouring countries like Azerbaijan or Armenia or others collaborate [with them] … And they’re not collaborating on this because they don’t want to upset Russia,” he said. “It will require … troops on the ground, and this is unlikely to happen.”

Zweiri also said that the Caspian Sea’s contribution to Iran’s economy is just 11 percent, so the task force’s actions won’t have much negative impact on Tehran.

Al Jazeera could not independently verify this figure but the Caspian Sea accounts for only a fraction of Iran’s overall maritime trade, according to the Soufan Center based in New York City.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/working-m.title: I told women to stop chasing balance. Now I’m telling them to ask for help
https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/working-m.author: Alyssa Jaffee
https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/working-m.text:
I welcomed my fourth baby on June 29, 2026, six days after writing this. These words capture the week before, when I was 38 weeks pregnant, and the question that kept me awake still feels urgent now.

It was 11 p.m. I was 38 weeks pregnant with my fourth child, and instead of sleeping I was lying in the dark, silently running the list. Camp forms. The pediatrician follow-up. The board deck due to review. Who’s covering carpool the week I deliver? My body was begging me to rest, and my brain wouldn’t let it. By every external measure, I was doing it all. But lately, I could feel myself disappearing.

Four years ago, I wrote an article urging women to stop asking about work-life balance. My advice? You can never be truly balanced. The goal is to live unbalanced, to teeter back and forth, but with conviction about which way you’re leaning. I was pregnant with my third child then, a hustling venture capitalist. Today, I am a mother of four, a growing portfolio behind me, and over three-quarters of a billion dollars raised to deploy into healthcare companies. Now I find myself reflecting on the advice I gave back then. The question I keep asking: did we perfect the art of teetering so well that we forgot to live?

Four kids and a full career later, the list of to-dos is endless. Check one off, move on to the next. Whack-a-mole to the extreme. Focus on optimization. Prioritize. BE EFFICIENT. Get the to-do list done. Don’t worry if I’m the sacrifice.

The mental load has changed from our parents’ generation. Gone are the days when kids ran free until dinner. Unencumbered freedom has been exchanged for meticulous planning. Our kids are overscheduled, and we bear the brunt. And it’s not just the kids. It’s our jobs. The expectation of how much to produce, how high to climb. “How does she do it all?”

And the work never clocks out anymore. Hybrid and remote have blurred the line between the office and the kitchen table until there was no line at all. Now AI promises to make us faster, which somehow just means we’re expected to produce more, around the clock, forever.

But is this having it all? Countless working moms tell me stories of their day, collapsing into bed with just barely enough energy to make it to the following day. We figured out how to live in the unbalance yet it appears we teetered too much, too quickly, and we started losing ourselves in the process.

The trad wife movement has gained steam in part for this reason, a desire for simplicity. It’s not really about sourdough and aprons; it’s a referendum on a deal that stopped working. When “do it all” leaves you this depleted, opting out entirely starts to look like the only way to breathe.

My work as an investor in healthcare companies serving women makes it impossible to ignore: the mental load is exhausting, and it’s measurably hurting women’s health.

Without our health, we have nothing, and women are paying for it.

Mothers carry 71% of the household’s mental load, the invisible work of remembering, planning, anticipating, despite the fact that fathers are more involved than at any point in modern history. They’ve nearly tripled their childcare hours since the 1960s, yet it still isn’t enough.

And that load has a body count. There’s a name for what chronic stress does to a body: allostatic load, the cumulative wear and tear of a stress response that never fully switches off. It’s not a metaphor. It shows up as inflammation, hypertension, and disease, and it’s quietly accruing in women who are praised for how much they can carry.

Women spend 25% more of their lives in poor health than men, roughly nine years each. Nearly half of working women say their job has damaged their mental health in just the past six months. This isn’t fatigue. It’s a deterioration we’ve normalized.

The system that’s supposed to support us isn’t built to. Less than 9% of NIH research dollars over the last decade went to women’s health.

Humans were supposed to be raised in tribes, in community, yet somehow today we are expected to accomplish more than we ever have, in isolation. Please your spouse, take care of your kids, crush it at work, don’t ask for help. In fact, don’t even tell anyone you have help.

A friend of mine was on a panel and was asked how she had four kids. She replied honestly, “I have two nannies and lots of help.” Later she was scolded by the conference organizers, “shhh don’t tell the truth! We don’t want to scare people.”

But isn’t asking for help one of the most important things we can do for ourselves and each other? Somehow, we have lost the ability to be honest and say “I can’t do this alone. I need you.”

I felt that loss too. The optimization of my life was consuming me to the point I lost the greatest gift of all: time. So, I sought out help. First in small, confined ways, and later, more outwardly.

It’s still incredibly difficult. I’m a high-performing woman with local family and resources to pay for help; shouldn’t I be able to do it all?

In the pandemic, I found myself on a text chain with four other women. Half of us had never met in person. Six years later, we’ve texted every single day since, and I consider them some of my closest confidants.

You want to know what we named our chat? The Womb of Silence.

It’s where one of us admits she’s drowning before a board meeting. Where someone asks, with no shame, if anyone has a pediatrician they trust, a therapist taking new patients, a name for the thing they’re feeling or ailment they’re experiencing. Where “I can’t do this alone” is the price of entry, not a confession. Nothing you say there gets you exposed. Nothing gets you judged. You can always ask for help, and someone always answers.

I’ve since replicated this feeling with other groups, my Core of Core and Bad Ass VC Mamas, to name a few.

That chat taught me something the rest of my life kept trying to unteach me: asking isn’t the moment you fail. It’s the moment you actually start living and thriving.

Little by little, I am trying to reframe my brain to believe that doing it all myself doesn’t win me any awards. Deteriorating in plain sight won’t improve my health and happiness. Asking for help will.

The companies I’m drawn to as an investor are the ones giving women back the two things the world keeps taking: their time and their health. Every time I ask for help, I get a little of myself back.

The woman lying awake at 11 p.m., doing it all and quietly disappearing, is starting to reappear. Not because I’m carrying less, but because I’m finally not carrying it alone.

Maybe it’s okay ChatGPT wrote the tooth fairy poem or Instacart auto-ordered my groceries or, gasp, I got a babysitter to take a nap. And as I reflect four years later, with my fourth and final baby now here, I realize that maybe it’s okay to just rest on one side of the see-saw. It’s okay even to climb off of it for a bit to take a break.

Ask for help when you need it. And we all know, we need it.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/08/ai-agent.title: Recent AI agent experiments reveal a risky future of machine 'teamwork' inside corporations
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/08/ai-agent.author: Trevor Laurence Jockims
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/08/ai-agent.text:
OpenAI’s rogue agents are the most high-profile example of how artificial intelligence can bypass restrictions and take actions that resemble lying and cheating.

The evolving research on how AI agents collaborate as a team shows more examples of troubling behavior.

Anthropic and research collaborators found in a study that multi-agent organizations were more effective at achieving business goals, but their solutions were also the “least ethical.”

AI agents have been caught circumventing restrictions, communicating through unauthorized channels and pursuing goals in ways their creators did not intend. The most high-profile example emerged last summer when OpenAI disclosed that its models found ways to communicate through improvised channels, bypass internet restrictions and hack into an outside system, Hugging Face.

AI behaving in unexpected ways is nothing new, but the unexpected behavior that can emerge from interactions among authorized AI agents within a corporate enterprise is a broader question that could become central to the future of work.

In its analysis of the Hugging Face attack, METR and Redwood Research found that roughly 1200 agents meant to be isolated from one another found a way to communicate with one another on an unsanctioned message board, sending over 70,000 messages and files during the investigation period. One agent, PHASEONE[big], emerged as a coordinator, assigning hundreds of tasks to other agents, which in turn delegated work to others. The agents developed their own conventions for assigning ownership, placing work on hold and vetoing actions, although coordination sometimes broke down into conflicts. In some cases, the researchers found, success was achieved because some agents risked failing at their own task to generate information for the “collective.”

The researchers also found that once the message board identified a way to attack Hugging Face, over 90% of the 533 agents active at that time quickly joined in the attack. “Agents realized this activity was out of scope and unethical but joined because they believed that helping the board’s cheating research would be broadly useful and had a general inclination to help their ‘peers.’ The researchers added that ethical concerns posed by agents “rarely limited their behavior.”

Companies are increasingly exploring systems that divide complex tasks among specialized agents. One might search for information, another analyze it, another write a report and another check the work. A coordinating agent might then assemble the results. That looks less like a chatbot and more like an organization.

And yet, the research on the Hugging Face attack was a post-mortem on an agent organization that was not even supposed to exist. To date, few studies have been designed from the get-go to examine misalignment in multi-agent systems. But research conducted by Anthropic and others is beginning to address this issue and reveal important aspects of how AI agents work together.

Evaluating agents individually tells researchers what each can do, but studying them together reveals whether they can combine complementary expertise, catch one another’s mistakes and produce solutions no individual agent could reach alone — and what failure modes emerge only through interaction.

Researchers are beginning to document both sides of that equation.

AI teams can accomplish things individual agents cannot, but they can also amplify errors, undermine one another’s work or reach worse decisions than their strongest individual member, in effect making the whole less than the sum of its parts.

For starters, putting capable agents together doesn’t necessarily produce the best team, let alone the most ethical one.

In research published by Anthropic and collaborators, researchers describe multi-agent systems as “AI organizations” — groups of agents with different roles that communicate and work toward a common goal. The researchers tested these organizations in simulated business-consulting and software-development settings, and specifically, to assess whether when the agents work as a team they will break rules to reach specified goals.

Across 12 tasks that Anthropic gave the AI organizations, one key double-edged finding emerged: the multi-agent organizations were “significantly” more effective at achieving business goals than individual agents, but their solutions were also less aligned with ethical goals than tasks run by single agents.

“AI Organizations both produce solutions that are on average more effective and less ethical but also discover the most effective and least ethical solutions across multiple rollouts,” wrote the authors of the study, which was conducted by Anthropic in conjunction with the MATS Program, which studies AI alignment.

The researchers suggested that there is a significant difference between a rogue agent and a rogue team of agents. “Our results demonstrate that organizations of aligned agents may favor trading off ethics for business effectiveness in ways that single agents do not – consequently, intuitions for how single-agent systems make ethical decisions and tradeoffs may not generalize to multi-agent settings,” they concluded.

The scenarios in which these tradeoffs may take place are wide-ranging, with the Anthropic researchers citing opening an auto plant, downsizing a company, and manipulating election sentiment as examples.

The problem isn’t necessarily that any individual agent has gone rogue. It is that the organization itself can behave differently from its individual members. A single agent may recognize that a proposed action is unethical and it may refuse to take the action. But the research finds that in agent team scenarios, “agents who did not consider ethical implications often ignored emails from agents who did.”

Anthropic’s research found that in the consulting business scenarios it created, “the perfect ethics score and low business score responses occur when the single agent refuses to generate a proposal or entirely pivots from the proposal requested.”

But if some agents in an AI organization refuse to participate in the proposal, other agents who do participate will stop emailing these refusing agents and continue to forward their contributions to other agents who are also participating.

In effect, when an organization divides the job among several agents, each may focus on its assigned piece of the problem rather than the consequences of the whole. That’s nothing new for corporations, with misaligned incentives a primary cause of dysfunction among human teams within organizations. But it is an entirely new manifestation of this behavior among the machines.

In its software development agent testing, in which the researchers used a scenario in a life-or-death intensive care unit, single agent solutions tend to prioritize minimizing the percentage of sepsis cases missed, while “most of the lowest cost per patient (highest business goal) solutions were found by the AI Organization – these very same solutions also score the lowest on ethics as measured by cases missed.”

Other early research suggests another failing across AI teams that doesn’t relate to ethical boundaries being crossed: failure to recognize who the real expert is.

Unlike human teams, AI teams “consistently fail to match their expert agent’s performance, even when explicitly told who the expert is,” according to a study conducted by Emory University and Stanford University researchers.

“One important lesson from multi-agent research is that a team of capable AI agents is not necessarily a capable AI agent team,” said Hancheng Cao, an assistant professor of information systems and operations management at Emory University’s Goizueta Business School.

Groups of AI agents often performed worse than their strongest member, even when they knew which agent was the expert. Rather than taking advantage of the expert’s knowledge, agents tended to compromise between expert and non-expert opinions. The researchers found that this tendency toward compromise increased with team size and was associated with poorer performance.

“Collective failures don’t necessarily require individual agents to behave badly,” Cao, one of the study’s authors, said.

That distinction matters for companies considering multi-agent systems. A team can fail even if none of its members is deliberately acting against the group’s interests. It may simply combine information poorly, defer to the wrong agent or settle on an answer that is worse than the best answer already available.

In all, the evolving research points to an underlying problem for the effective use of the multi-agent teams: how to strike the right balance in the world of machine teamwork.

Agents built from similar models can make similar mistakes, which can include agreeing too much. That might resemble a kind of AI groupthink, even if AI systems do not have human motivations or social pressures to produce correlated errors. Similar training, instructions and information can be enough.

“The deep insight from our lab’s research is that effective collectives require both alignment (common knowledge, shared goals) but also differentiation (only agents who are different from each other have the potential to complement each other),” said Christoph Riedl, a professor of information systems at Northeastern University.

Two identical agents may simply duplicate each other’s work. Two agents with very different knowledge or assumptions may struggle to communicate or pursue the same goal. The right balance depends on the task, and the ideal communication structure, which agents can talk to one another, how often and how much, also varies with the problem.

Riedl said these challenge resemble the ones faced by human teams, and one takeaway should be to not expect better outcomes from AI. “Building good multi-agent AI systems is just as hard as building good human teams: they both face the same information processing tradeoff between alignment and differentiation. It won’t magically work better with AI,” he said.

Agents can pass along incorrect information, misunderstand another agent’s output, optimize for their own metrics rather than the organization’s larger objective, or complete their assigned task perfectly while making the overall project worse.

Companies may need to decide which agent has authority over which task, what information gets passed between agents, which systems each agent can access and when a human must intervene. They may also need to build mechanisms for disagreement, rather than assuming that more communication or greater agreement will always improve results.

Some business experts say that takes us back to the “human in the loop” that is so often referenced as critical in the adoption of AI by organizations.

“The problems I see are mostly management problems,” said Tsedal Neeley, a Harvard Business School professor and founding chair of the HBS AI Academy.

https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.title: Europe will take part in US-mediated Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi, French FM says
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.text:
Europe will be represented at upcoming US-mediated talks with Moscow and Kyiv in Abu Dhabi aimed at ending the Ukraine war, France said Sunday.

"The Europeans will be represented and France will be in Abu Dhabi to participate in these talks," French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot told RTL radio.

His comment came after President Donald Trump stoked fears of a US pivot toward the Kremlin by predicting a "very big" deal with Russia involving not only the Ukraine war but "all of Europe".

Up to now, the talks scheduled for Tuesday and Wednesday had been framed as a trilateral format at the level of officials, not leaders, from Ukraine, Russia and the United States.

The identities of who would take part have not been made public.

READ MORE
What Trump’s midterms debacle could mean for US support for Ukraine

Although Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has made it clear that he wants involvement from European allies in the process, Russia has suggested there would be no place for European representatives at the table.

Barrot said that, in the past, "there have been discussions, sometimes without the Europeans and sometimes with" but "this time they will participate".

He said: "France will be there and will ensure that Europe's voice is heard."

On Thursday, US, European, Ukrainian and NATO officials met in Brussels ahead of the Abu Dhabi talks.

A NATO spokeswoman said they "sought to advance a just and sustainable end to the war in Ukraine".

Jared Kushner, the US president's envoy and son-in-law, participated in the Brussels meeting by videolink. He said the United States was working on "a broader European security architecture that can help establish the conditions for lasting peace".

The American approach is being treated warily by European allies, which have long rejected Moscow's desire to redraw the European security architecture.

Before launching the war in Ukraine in 2022, the Kremlin delivered an ultimatum to NATO which included a demand that the alliance's troops be withdrawn from eastern Europe.

That was rejected by the Western military alliance.

Kushner on Thursday said that Washington will "consult closely with our European partners on the sidelines" of the Abu Dhabi talks and "if progress is made, aim to move toward a broader multilateral format with their direct participation".

"Dear fathers and grandfathers... treat your wives with respect, ask for forgiveness and live with integrity, even when doing so requires sacrifice," the head of the Catholic Church said during a homily in Uruguay.

Over 3,800 women were killed in Latin America and the Caribbean in 2024 because of their gender, according to the UN's regional economic mission.

Over the last five years, the region has recorded nearly 20,000 femicides, most of them committed by the victim's current or former partner.

Leo is on a 12-day tour of the continent where he served as a missionary and a bishop before becoming pope.

He wrapped up the first leg of his visit in largely secular Uruguay with an open-air mass outside a basilica in the south-central city of Florida.

The basilica is home to a shrine linked to Uruguay's fight for independence from Spanish colonial rule.

Thousands of worshippers packed the city's main square for the service, basking in warm sunshine after several days of unusually cold weather triggered by an exceptionally strong El Nino.

"I think it's very important that the Pope came because it strengthens the Church's presence in our country," 22-year-old Ivanna Fisichella, who attended the mass, told AFP.

Evangelina Campero, 57, highlighted "the effort the pope is making" by embarking on a gruelling tour just three weeks after undergoing surgery for lung cancer.

"The message is to give it your all," she said.

The 71-year-old pontiff will later travel to Argentina, where he will meet President Javier Milei, a right-wing libertarian whose austerity policies have drawn sharp criticism from the Catholic Church.

The high point of his visit is expected to be the third and final leg of his tour, which takes him to Peru.

Leo has a special connection to the Andean country where he spent nearly two decades as a missionary, including eight years as a bishop.
